Kīngi Tūheitia's hui-ā-motu at Tūrangawaewae on 20 Jan 2024 drew ~10,000 people and was convened explicitly to hold the new government to account over the Māori Health Authority, te reo policy and the Treaty principles review. The Rātana celebrations the following week carried that kaupapa forward (ACT's Seymour absent; kotahitanga the stated theme). Waitangi Day 2024 saw a week of protest culminating in 1,000+ marching onto the treaty grounds, with Peters booed and Seymour drowned out over the Treaty Principles Bill. Checked for the disconfirming case — a quiet summer with no organised protest — and the opposite is documented: RNZ called it a historic year of hui and protest for Māoridom, extending to the ~42,000-strong hīkoi in November 2024.

statement: From a leak of a Cabinet paper from someone on the other side, to protests on your very first day, I suspect and I think many other people in this House suspect that this marriage is going to end in divorce.
criterion: Whether the National–ACT–NZ First coalition formally dissolves (a governing party withdrawing from the coalition agreement, or confidence and supply being withdrawn) before the next general election. True if the coalition breaks up before the end of the 54th Parliament; false if it remains intact to the dissolution of that Parliament.
reasoning: The criterion resolves at the dissolution of the 54th Parliament, which Wikipedia records as expected on 1 October 2026, with the general election on 7 November 2026. Today is 25 September 2026, so neither event has occurred and the prediction cannot yet be settled either way. State of play as of now: the National–ACT–NZ First coalition is formally intact. No party has withdrawn from the coalition agreement or from confidence and supply. There has been substantial public friction — the Peters–Luxon clash over OIA documents on the Iran strikes (April 2026), Peters vowing to repeal ACT's Regulatory Standards Bill, and Peters declining to state confidence in Luxon before his office reaffirmed NZ First's support — but the two 2026 confidence votes Luxon survived (April and August) were National caucus leadership votes, not confidence votes in the House, so they do not bear on the criterion. Looked specifically for the disconfirming event (a withdrawal from the agreement or from confidence and supply) and found none reported.

statement: So I’m really pleased with the package around tax, and I’m very confident that our finance Minister will find the money in order to pay for that.
criterion: The Budget 2024 documents (Budget Economic and Fiscal Update and the tax package costings, released 30 May 2024); true if the promised personal income tax reductions were legislated and funded with identified offsetting savings/revenue, false if the package was abandoned, materially cut back, or deferred.
reasoning: Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) delivered the personal income tax threshold increases, and Wikipedia's budget article records the bracket adjustments as 'unchanged from what National set out in the election campaign' — so not abandoned or materially cut back. They were legislated in the Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2024, enacted 4 June 2024, lifting all thresholds except the top band with effect from 31 July 2024. On funding, the criterion's test is identified offsetting savings/revenue: Treasury's Budget 2024 documents put the tax relief package at $14.725b over five years to 2027/28, covered by savings and revenue initiatives over the same period, itemised as agency baseline savings, closure of the National Resilience Plan and Climate Emergency Response Fund, expiring tagged contingencies, commercial building depreciation changes and the expanded waste disposal levy. Checked the disconfirming side: National's promised 15% foreign buyer tax — a named funding leg — was vetoed by NZ First and scrapped, and commentators noted the government increased borrowing over the forecast period and the start date slipped from 1 July to 31 July. Those go to how the money was found, not whether it was; the reductions themselves were delivered at the promised size, so this falls short of 'materially cut back'.

statement: Those people who hold up our community—the Cancer Society people, the health workers, the principals of our schools—are opposed, and many of them have mobilised in a rally that will be held here in Parliament next week.
criterion: News reporting and Parliament grounds event records for 11–15 December 2023; true if a public rally opposing the smokefree repeal was held at Parliament in that week, false if no such rally took place.
reasoning: A public rally opposing the smokefree repeal was held on Parliament's steps in Wellington on 12-13 December 2023, inside the 11-15 December window named in the criterion. Roughly 1000 doctors, nurses, public health workers and members of the public attended, organised by the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists - Toi Mata Hauora and Health Coalition Aotearoa, with a parallel Auckland event and a petition of ~45,000-47,000 signatures presented at Parliament. Opposition MPs including Verrall herself attended. The criterion's false condition (no such rally) did not occur. Coverage does not specifically name the Cancer Society or school principals among participants, but the criterion turns only on whether a rally happened at Parliament that week.

statement: Let’s see us go back to the failed, dysfunctional, disjointed polytech model that we have. That’s what this Government will do.
criterion: Legislation and Cabinet decisions on the future of Te Pūkenga; true if Te Pūkenga is disestablished and standalone regional polytechnics are re-established, false if Te Pūkenga remains as a single national institution.
reasoning: The Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, passed in 2025, disestablishes Te Pukenga and re-establishes 10 regionally governed polytechnics as independent institutions from 1 January 2026, alongside eight Industry Skills Boards replacing the workforce development councils. The criterion's false condition - Te Pukenga remaining a single national institution - did not occur. One qualification that does not change the verdict: Te Pukenga is renamed the New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology and persists as a transitional entity for up to 1-2 years, with four polytechnics (NorthTec, WITT, WelTec, Tai Poutini) remaining inside it pending viability decisions in mid-2026.

statement: Long-term projections forecast this site to remove 65,000 long-haul truck journeys off the road—with an associated 66 percent reduction in carbon emissions for each container movement—for international companies like Maersk, and, of course, New Zealand’s distribution hub for Kmart—which moved out of Auckland, just to comment on that—and New Zealand’s own Waitomo Group.
criterion: Tainui Group Holdings / Ruakura Superhub freight reporting and NZTA or Ministry of Transport road-freight data for the Waikato corridor. True if annual long-haul truck journeys displaced by rail-served movements through the inland port reach approximately 65,000 and a per-container emissions reduction of around 66 percent is documented; false if the displaced-journey figure is materially below that once the site is substantially built out.
reasoning: The criterion explicitly conditions the test on the site being substantially built out, with a resolve date of 2035-12-31. Ruakura Inland Port is still at stage 1: 9 hectares and roughly 60,000 TEU annual capacity, against a fully built 30 hectares and 1 million TEU. TGH's own modelling runs its road-displacement and emissions benefits out to 2051-2053 (approximately 890 kt CO2 reduced by 2053, around 1 Mt avoided by 2051, and roughly 50 million fewer road-km per year by 2053). The 65,000 long-haul truck journeys figure is TGH's published projection for the port at planned operating capacity, so the quote reports the developer's number accurately as a long-term forecast, but there is no realised annual figure to test yet. I could not find the 66 percent per-container-movement emissions reduction figure on TGH or Ruakura Superhub material; their published claims are cumulative tonnages and road-km, not a per-container percentage, so that component is currently unsourced rather than contradicted.

statement: My fear is that we have a situation where we are going to see rents rise in this country but also insecurity of rent—insecurity.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and MBIE tenancy bond mean weekly rent) for the two years following December 2023; true if the national rent measure rises materially above its December 2023 level, false if rents are flat or fall over that period.
reasoning: Stats NZ's CPI rent series — the stock measure the criterion names — rose 4.2% in the 12 months to the Dec 2024 quarter (the largest single contributor to that quarter's 2.2% CPI) and a further 1.9% in the 12 months to the Dec 2025 quarter, roughly +6% cumulative on the Dec 2023 base. The year to June 2025 was +3.2%, described by Stats NZ as the smallest annual rent rise in four years, so the rise decelerated but never reversed. MBIE bond data put the national mean weekly rent at $568 for the year to Sept 2025, above 2023 levels. Disconfirming check: the separate new-tenancy (flow) index published by HUD while Stats NZ's RPI was paused did turn slightly negative by 2025 (−0.4% nationally, −6.4% in Wellington, −0.6% Auckland), so rents on newly signed tenancies were flat-to-falling at the end of the window. That is a different measure from the two the criterion nominates, both of which rose materially. The 'insecurity' half of the prediction is not tested by the criterion as written.

statement: As I said in answer to the primary question, which the member may not have listened to, yes, the tax reduction package promised by the Government in the Speech from the Throne will be self-funding. I’ll tell you what else it’ll do: it’ll put real cash into the bank accounts of working people—bank accounts that have been eroded by a cost of living crisis presided over by that member, who over-taxed them, spent their money badly, and left the economy in tatters.
criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 documents (Budget Economic and Fiscal Update and the tax package funding table): true if the package is fully funded from identified savings and new revenue measures with no attributable increase in forecast net core Crown debt; false if it is funded by additional borrowing or if the promised offsetting revenue measures do not eventuate.
reasoning: The substance holds but is materially overstated. Budget 2024 delivered the package ($3.68b/yr, $14.725b over five years to 2027/28) and the Budget documents fund it from 240 identified savings and revenue initiatives worth about $5.86b/yr: $1.215b baseline departmental savings, $775m closing previous programmes, $879m from restricting Fees Free, $1.195b from the waste disposal levy, $578m from removing commercial building depreciation, $597m from the Climate Emergency Response Fund, $147m from tax-compliance enforcement. On the criterion's 'identified savings and new revenue' test, that branch is met. Three things pull against 'self-funding' as spoken. First, the funding is overwhelmingly reprioritised spending, not revenue the package itself generates — it is offset, not self-funding. Second, a promised offsetting revenue measure did not eventuate: the foreign buyer tax National campaigned on was killed by NZ First in coalition negotiations and replaced with savings and IRD audit funding. Third, BEFU 2024 lifted the bond programme $12.0b over the forecast period versus HYEFU, put the net core Crown debt peak at 43.5% of GDP in 2024/25, and pushed surplus out a year to 2027/28 — though Treasury attributed that to a $13.9b tax revenue downgrade rather than to the package, so there is no clean attributable debt increase and the criterion's 'false' branch is not cleanly triggered either. The IMF and OECD both warned before the Budget that the relief needed to be fiscally neutral and not debt-funded.

statement: It’s wrong, and it’s an inequity that this Government could address, but they will choose not to because, ultimately, they represent the elite interests of the landed gentry—those who own property and want to continue to have the benefit of untaxed capital gains where that wealth becomes concentrated, and that means we can’t afford to invest in public services.
criterion: Tax legislation and Budget/tax-policy announcements from December 2023 to the end of the parliamentary term: false if the Government enacts or formally announces a capital gains tax or an equivalent broad tax on income from capital assets; true if no such measure is enacted or announced by the end of the term.
reasoning: The criterion's false branch requires the Government to enact or formally announce a capital gains tax or equivalent broad tax on income from capital assets by the end of the term. Neither happened. The Government moved in the opposite direction: the bright-line test (the existing partial tax on residential capital gains) was cut from 10 years / 5 years for new builds to 2 years effective 1 July 2024, and interest deductibility for residential landlords was restored in stages to 100% from 1 April 2025. Luxon has called a CGT an 'economic wrecking ball', Willis a 'handbrake on the economy', and National is campaigning on no new taxes. The only costed CGT on the table is Labour's 28% policy announced 28 Oct 2025, which is an opposition proposal contingent on winning government, not a government enactment or announcement. On timing: the criterion's formal date (7 Nov 2026) has not passed, but the window is closed in substance — the House rose on 24 September 2026 and Parliament dissolves 1 October, so no legislation can be enacted, and a formal government CGT announcement during a campaign fought on a no-new-taxes promise is not a live possibility. I report correct rather than not_yet_due for that reason.

statement: Now, as the Reserve Bank wrestles with trying to bring inflation back under control, our Government will clarify the bank’s objectives and support public confidence that inflation can and will be returned below 3 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly CPI annual inflation: true if any quarterly print by the resolve-by date records annual inflation below 3.0%, false if annual inflation remains at or above 3.0% throughout.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether any quarterly Stats NZ print before 2025-12-31 records annual CPI inflation below 3.0%. Annual inflation fell below the threshold in the September 2024 quarter (2.2%), and stayed there: 2.2% in December 2024, 2.5% in March 2025, 2.7% in June 2025 (Stats NZ notes June 2025 was the fourth consecutive quarter inside the 1-3% band). Checked the disconfirming case — whether inflation stayed at or above 3.0% throughout — and it did not; the June 2024 quarter (3.3%) was the last print at or above 3%. Willis's accompanying commitment to clarify the Bank's objectives (the single-mandate remit change of December 2023) is outside what the criterion tests.

statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister: right now at COP 28, they are wrestling with that very issue, and they’ll be probably working days longer than that because they haven’t come to an agreement.
criterion: The UNFCCC record of COP28's scheduled closing date (12 December 2023) against the date the final plenary actually concluded: true if the conference ran days beyond the scheduled close, false if it closed on or before schedule.
reasoning: COP28 in Dubai was scheduled to close on 12 December 2023; negotiations went into overtime after Saudi objections to the draft, consultations ran through the night, and the closing plenary concluded on 13 December 2023 (reported as about 23 hours past the scheduled close). So the conference did run beyond schedule — the criterion's 'false' branch (closed on or before schedule) does not apply, and Peters was right that agreement had not been reached at the time he spoke. But the overrun was roughly one day, not the 'days longer' he predicted, so the substance holds while the magnitude is overstated.

statement: So those pricings should go down.
criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price data for the region affected by the charge, compared before and after its removal; true if the pump price falls by approximately the amount of the removed charge, false if prices do not fall or rise once the charge is gone.
reasoning: The charge referred to is the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax imposed by the previous Government (10c/L + GST = 11.5c/L), removed from 1 July 2024. The Commerce Commission's focus report on the removal found Auckland pump prices fell by an average of 8-11c/L relative to stations near to but outside Auckland between Saturday 29 June and Monday 1 July 2024 — a difference-in-difference design that strips out national price movements — and concluded the saving was passed through to consumers. The AA said the full 11.5c came off, and Gaspy 28-day figures showed 91 down ~12.4c, 95 down ~11.5c, diesel down ~9.3c. So prices fell by approximately the amount of the removed charge (the low end of the Commission's range, 8c, is somewhat short of 11.5c, which is the only respect in which pass-through was incomplete). Disconfirming check: Auckland pump prices did rise later in 2024, but that was attributed to crude, shipping and FX, not to the tax's absence, and the Commission's before/after comparison against just-outside-Auckland prices controls for it. Caveat on the criterion's named source: MBIE's weekly retail price series is national, so the regional test was answered using the Commission's Gaspy-based regional analysis instead.

statement: Nothing about this change will affect the support services and programmes that Oranga Tamariki provides for Māori.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki service and programme reporting (annual reports, iwi partnership arrangements) for the year following the repeal of section 7AA: true if no Māori-facing services, programmes or partnerships are discontinued or reduced in consequence of the repeal, false if any are.
reasoning: Section 7AA was repealed with effect from 7 April 2025. The partnership limb of Chhour's prediction largely held: the Act inserted a new section 7 requiring the chief executive to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations, OT's strategic-partnership page still lists its named partnerships (Ngāpuhi, Ngāi Tahu, Waikato-Tainui, Tūhoe, Ngāti Kahungunu and others), and I found no report of any iwi partnership being terminated or any named Māori-facing programme closed as a consequence of the repeal. Searching for the disconfirming case, the large-scale defunding that hit iwi and kaupapa Māori providers (190 contracts discontinued, 142 reduced) was a 2024 procurement decision predating the repeal, so it does not attach to it. However, the claim is materially overstated: at the same time as the repeal and on the same 'need not race' rationale, OT removed its 58% target for placing children with wider whānau and its 23% minimum target for the proportion of investment going to Māori/iwi organisations, and 7AA's mandatory annual public reporting on what OT did for Māori was removed (the s7AA reporting page has been frozen since April 2025 with 'we will update this section in due course'). Dropping the investment floor for Māori/iwi providers is a reduction in a Māori-facing commitment, even if no single service is documented as discontinued. The criterion's primary source for the year following the repeal — OT's 2025/26 annual report — was not yet published as at 25 September 2026 (the latest is 2024/25, ending 30 June 2025), and the Independent Children's Monitor's 2024/25 Māori outcomes report (June 2026) records funding decisions worsening service availability and that 'resource allocation does not reflect' Māori being the biggest stakeholders, without attributing this to the repeal. So: partnerships survived as she predicted; 'nothing about this change will affect the support services and programmes' does not hold in full.

statement: I may have paid once to go to that really bad circus that one time and I won’t be going back, but I have no doubt that if the Government continues on the trajectory they are on—and they will—New Zealanders won’t just be pledging to forego tickets to the next show; they will be wanting to leave the show early and asking for a full refund.
criterion: Major published NZ political polls (1News-Verian, Newshub/Reid Research, Taxpayers' Union-Curia, Roy Morgan) across 2024-2026 and the 2026 general election result: true if the Labour/Greens/Te Pāti Māori bloc leads the National/ACT/NZ First bloc in a sustained majority of polls during the term, false if the governing bloc retains a polling lead through the term.
reasoning: The criterion makes the 2026 general election result part of the evidence, and that election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 — six weeks after today's date (25 September 2026), so it has not happened. The poll limb is also not resolved either way. Through 2024 and most of 2025 the governing bloc led: Taxpayers' Union–Curia (8–10 Sep 2024) projected National–ACT–NZ First 67 seats to Labour–Greens–Te Pāti Māori 54, and Curia (2–6 Jul 2025) 65 to 57. The lead then flipped: Talbot Mills (1–10 Nov 2025) had Labour–Greens–Māori 62 to 59. Through 2026 the picture is contradictory rather than sustained in either direction — Roy Morgan had the National-led government ahead 49% to 41% in both July and August 2026 and 51% in June, while the Taxpayers' Union–Curia poll of September 2026 still projected the government bloc 64 seats to 56, and The Post/Freshwater Strategy (4–11 Sep 2026) projected an opposition-led government or a tied 60–60 parliament with both major parties under 30%. So the opposition bloc has not led a sustained majority of polls across the term, but neither has the governing bloc held an unbroken lead through it, and the event the prediction ultimately turns on is still pending.

statement: I look forward to being able to continue to move in a way that we see better moves for us as a country, and I want to make sure that in the upcoming weeks, months, and years, we will continue to interrogate this Government—as it struggles to find money for the tax cuts that it has promised New Zealanders, as we see that when the tobacco money runs out, as we see that there is no foreign buyers tax, and as we see that New Zealanders realise that the change that they voted for will not be delivered by this Government.
criterion: Government tax policy announcements and legislation through to the end of 2024: false if a tax or levy on foreign buyers of residential property is enacted or announced as proceeding; true if the policy is abandoned or never legislated, leaving no foreign buyers tax in place.
reasoning: The criterion asks only about the foreign buyers tax through to the end of 2024, and on that the prediction holds. National's proposed 15% tax on residential property sales to non-residents above $2 million (costed at about $740m a year and earmarked to fund its tax cuts) was abandoned in the coalition negotiations: New Zealand First opposed it, and on 24 November 2023 Luxon confirmed as part of the National–NZ First agreement that the foreign buyers tax would not go ahead. Checking for the disconfirming case — a tax or levy on foreign buyers enacted or announced as proceeding during 2024 — I found none; Budget 2024's tax package (threshold changes, FamilyBoost, in-work tax credit, from 31 July 2024) was instead funded by reprioritisation, extra IRD audit/compliance revenue and the Fees Free change, with the government explicitly stating it was 'not progressing the foreign buyers' tax'. No foreign buyers tax was in place at the end of 2024.

statement: We are not going to meet the 2030 dreamy, fairy-tale, aspirational figures that we’ll be freeing ourselves of fossil fuels as a source of generating energy.
criterion: MBIE Energy in New Zealand / quarterly electricity statistics for calendar year 2030: the prediction is TRUE if fossil-fuelled (coal, gas, diesel) generation still contributes a non-trivial share of electricity generation in 2030; FALSE if generation is 100% (or effectively 100%) renewable by the end of 2030.
reasoning: The criterion names MBIE Energy in New Zealand / quarterly electricity statistics for calendar year 2030; that data will not exist until 2031, and today is 2026-09-25. Interim evidence leans toward the prediction rather than against it: renewables supplied 92% of generation in the June 2026 quarter (third straight quarter above 90%), 94.5% in the March 2026 quarter, and a record 96.4% in Oct-Dec 2025 - so coal, gas and diesel still contribute a non-trivial share, and gas/coal generation falling 67%/66% year-on-year is a decline, not elimination. The 100%-renewable-by-2030 target itself was dropped by the incoming government in 2024 with no replacement deadline, and KPMG's 2023 assessment was that no one believed it was reachable. None of that is the 2030 figure the criterion asks for, so the prediction is not yet settleable.

statement: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily-smoking prevalence for 15–24 year-olds in the years after the repeal takes effect, compared with the 2022/23 baseline, plus any published Ministry of Health or University of Otago costing of the repeal. True if youth smoking prevalence rises above the pre-repeal baseline and a published estimate of roughly $1.3 billion in additional healthcare cost is borne out; false if youth prevalence continues to fall and no such costing is supported.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-06-30 and neither limb of the criterion can be settled yet, though the evidence so far runs against the prediction. Youth smoking: the 2024/25 New Zealand Health Survey puts daily smoking at 3.2% for 15-24 year-olds (4.4% for 18-24; 15-17 suppressed), and PHCC's reading is that this cohort had the largest fall from 2011/12 to 2022/23 but that prevalence 'did not decrease further between 2022/23 and 2024/25' - a plateau at a very low level, not a rise above the pre-repeal baseline the criterion specifies. Costing: the $1.3 billion is a real published figure, but it is modelled health-system savings over 20 years from full implementation of the Smokefree measures (cited by the then-government alongside 1,170 fewer smoking deaths in 10 years and 8,150 in 20), so it is a 20-year projection that cannot be borne out or refuted by 2027. A further complication for the criterion's 'years after the repeal takes effect': the repeal (royal assent 5 March 2024) removed denicotinisation, the retailer reduction and the generation ban before any of them commenced - the retailer cut was due July 2024 - so there is no post-implementation period to measure against.

statement: We are going to meet our carbon zero 2050 goals.
criterion: New Zealand's greenhouse gas inventory measured against the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 target: net zero for long-lived gases and a 24–47 percent reduction in biogenic methane on 2017 levels by 2050. True if the reported 2050 position meets the statutory target; false if it does not.
reasoning: The criterion is the reported 2050 position against the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 target - net zero for long-lived gases and biogenic methane 24-47% below 2017 levels by 2050. That inventory is 24 years away and there is no way to substitute an earlier reading for it. Interim evidence is contested rather than conclusive: the government's updated projections have net emissions within the second and third emissions budgets and describe the country as on track for 2050 despite narrowly missing earlier goals, while the Climate Change Commission's 2026 monitoring report assesses whether current policies actually set up the budgets and the 2050 target, and Climate Action Tracker rates New Zealand's overall performance poorly. Neither settles the statutory 2050 test.

statement: Let the message be very simple and very clear, let there be no confusion: ours is a Government which is going to get inflation under control.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation: true if the annual rate returns to and holds within the Reserve Bank's 1–3% target band during this parliamentary term; false if it remains above 3% throughout.
reasoning: Stats NZ CPI did return to the RBNZ's 1-3% band and held there for about five quarters (2.2% Sep 2024, 2.2% Dec 2024, 2.5% Mar 2025, 2.7% Jun 2025, 3.0% Sep 2025), down from 4.7% in the Dec 2023 quarter when Willis spoke — so the claim is not simply wrong. But it did not HOLD: annual inflation broke back above the band at 3.1% in the Dec 2025 quarter, stayed at 3.1% in Mar 2026 and reached 4.1% in Jun 2026 (petrol +27.5%), the highest since the disinflation began, and it is outside the band at the end of the term. The criterion's 'true' arm requires returning to and holding within the band; its 'false' arm requires remaining above 3% throughout, which did not happen. Substance holds for part of the term but is materially overstated as a durable achievement.

statement: But this bill will not put a single cent more in people’s pockets by Christmas. It simply won’t happen.
criterion: The enacted text of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill and any associated fiscal measure: true if the bill contains no provision transferring money to households and no household payment or tax change attributable to it takes effect before 25 December 2023; false if any such provision took effect by that date.
reasoning: The bill under debate on 12 Dec 2023 was the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill, enacted as 2023 No 64 (Royal assent 19 Dec 2023, in force 20 Dec 2023). Its enacted text does nothing but narrow the MPC's economic objective: it replaces s 9(1)(a) of the RBNZ Act 2021 with 'achieving and maintaining stability in the general level of prices over the medium term' and makes consequential wording changes in ss 136(1) and 138(1). There is no provision transferring money to households, no payment and no tax change. Checking the disconfirming side: the coalition's household money came much later — income tax threshold changes took effect 31 July 2024 and FamilyBoost from 1 July 2024 with first claims in October 2024 — so no household payment or tax change attributable to this bill took effect before 25 December 2023.

statement: It won’t do a thing before Christmas, and actually, the main thing it is likely to do is cause damage over the long run in terms of how monetary policy operates.
criterion: RBNZ monetary policy decisions and Stats NZ CPI/cost-of-living measures between the bill's passage and 25 December 2023; true if no change in monetary policy settings or measured cost of living is attributable to the Act in that window, false if an identifiable cost-of-living effect followed before Christmas.
reasoning: On the criterion's window: the Act commenced 20 Dec 2023, and the RBNZ's last monetary policy decision of 2023 was on 29 Nov 2023 (OCR held at 5.50%), before the bill's first reading; the next was 28 Feb 2024, again 5.50%. So no monetary policy setting changed between passage and 25 Dec 2023, and no cost-of-living measure was attributable to the Act in that five-day window (the Dec 2023 quarter CPI was not published until January 2024). The new Remit retained the same 1-3% target with a 2% midpoint, so even the framework signal was unchanged in substance. No identifiable pre-Christmas effect exists to falsify the claim. Caveat: the criterion tests only the 'won't do a thing before Christmas' clause; Robertson's main assertion of long-run damage to how monetary policy operates is outside the criterion and is not resolved here.

statement: After the words “over the medium term”, I would propose to insert “and continue to take a flexible approach to monetary policy that improves welfare by ensuring that monetary policy does not exacerbate periods of economic decline”, and, given what the Minister has said on this topic, I think that will be well-received in this committee.
criterion: The committee-stage and third-reading record for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill: true if the Minister indicated acceptance or the amendment (or wording to that effect) was agreed to; false if it was opposed and defeated.
reasoning: The amendment was not adopted. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Act 2023 (No 64), assented 19 December 2023, replaces s 9(1)(a) of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 with the single objective 'achieving and maintaining stability in the general level of prices over the medium term' and otherwise only swaps 'objectives' for 'objective' in ss 4(3)(a), 4(4)(a), 10(1)(a)(i) and 116(a). No wording about a 'flexible approach to monetary policy' or not exacerbating 'periods of economic decline' appears anywhere in the enacted text, and the consolidated s 8/9 objective quoted by RBNZ and Treasury ends at 'over the medium term'. The bill went through all stages under urgency on 12-13 December 2023 with only the introduction print (2-1) — no committee-of-the-whole amendment print exists — and Labour opposed it at third reading. Contemporaneous reporting of the committee stage records that opposition amendments expanding the economic objective (including ones in Grant Robertson's name) were ruled out of order as contrary to the bill's principles. Caveat: parliament.nz returned 404/403 to every fetch of the committee-stage and third-reading Hansard, so I could not read Willis's words on the night; the verdict rests on the statute as enacted, which is decisive on the criterion's operative test (whether the amendment or wording to that effect was agreed to). It was not.

statement: The members opposite are selling New Zealanders an untruth here, because they are claiming in this House that they are passing legislation that will reduce the cost of living by Christmas, according to some of those members opposite, and that simply is not going to happen.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI, food price index and household living-costs price index for the December 2023 and March 2024 quarters: the prediction is true if no fall in cost-of-living measures occurs by early 2024, false if those measures show a decline over that period.
reasoning: No cost-of-living measure fell by Christmas 2023 or early 2024. Stats NZ CPI rose 0.5% in the December 2023 quarter (annual 4.7%, down from 5.6% in September 2023) and rose again in the March 2024 quarter (annual 4.0%) — a deceleration in the rate, not a fall in the level. The household living-costs price index rose 1.2% in the December 2023 quarter, 7.0% in the year to that quarter, and 6.2% in the year to the March 2024 quarter. Both remained well above the RBNZ's 1-3% band throughout. Checking for the opposite: the only declines in this window are components, not measures — food prices dipped 0.1% in the month of December 2023 and fruit and vegetables were down 13.3% annually to March 2024, while overall food prices were still rising annually (the first annual food price fall in nearly six years did not come until June 2024), and rents (+4.7%, a series high since 1999) and rates (+9.8%) pushed the other way. Robertson's prediction that cost of living would not be reduced by Christmas holds on every measure the criterion names.

statement: I just suspect that, actually, that is going to have an effect on the prices that people pay, and they will be lower than they would have otherwise been, and people can start to feel some relief from the long, hard, grinding road of inflation they’ve been subject to by the previous Government for nearly three years now where inflation has been outside the target band.
criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation against the RBNZ 1–3% target band; true if annual CPI inflation returns to within the band within a year of this statement, false if it remains above 3% throughout that period.
reasoning: Judged against the criterion as written — whether annual CPI inflation returned to the RBNZ's 1-3% target band within a year of 12 December 2023 — it did. Stats NZ annual CPI inflation fell 4.7% (Dec 2023) to 4.0% (Mar 2024) to 3.3% (Jun 2024) to 2.2% in the September 2024 quarter, released 16-17 October 2024, the first time inflation had been inside the 1-3% band since 2021 and about ten months after the statement. It stayed in band at 2.2% in the December 2024 quarter, so this was not a one-quarter dip. Checking the disconfirming branch: the criterion's 'false' test is inflation remaining above 3% throughout the year, which did not happen. Note the criterion deliberately tests the band, not Seymour's implied causal claim that the dual-mandate repeal itself lowered prices; that attribution is not established here and the verdict does not rest on it.

statement: Basically, it’s going to be the working people—those who are going to be unemployed—that are going to be paying for this policy change.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate in the two years following the Act's enactment, measured against the December 2023 quarter baseline. True if the unemployment rate rises materially (more than a percentage point) above that baseline over the period; false if it stays flat or falls.
reasoning: Criterion: HLFS unemployment rate over the two years after the December 2023 enactment, vs the Dec 2023 quarter baseline; true if it rises more than a percentage point. Baseline was 4.0% seasonally adjusted (Dec 2023 quarter). Two years later the Dec 2025 quarter was 5.4% — a 10-year high, 165,000 unemployed — with Sep 2025 at 5.3%. That is a +1.4pp rise, above the one-point threshold, so the criterion's true branch is met. Caveat worth recording: the criterion measures only the aggregate labour-market outcome and cannot attribute the rise to the specific December 2023 employment-law change; the monetary-tightening recession is the mainstream explanation. Judged as written, the outcome the criterion asked for occurred.

statement: Yes, and I have received advice that transport is expected to achieve the first emissions budget period, 2022-2025.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission final accounting for emissions budget one (2022–2025), published after the period closes; true if transport-sector emissions fall within the reduction pathway assumed for that budget, false if the sector overshoots it.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific source: final accounting for emissions budget one (2022–2025) published after the period closes. That does not exist yet. The Climate Change Commission's July 2026 emissions-reduction monitoring report says EB1 (290 MtCO2e) is likely to be met with a 7.7 MtCO2e buffer, but states explicitly that 'the Commission's end-of-budget report in 2027 will give a full assessment using final emissions data.' The 2026 report gives no transport-sector accounting against EB1 at all — it only assesses transport as a risk to the second budget (2026–2030), where transport risk has risen to 'significant' after the vehicle emissions standards changes. Checked for disconfirming evidence: the 1990–2024 GHG inventory and Stats NZ 2024 industry/household series show household transport emissions easing slightly, but neither reconciles the transport sector against the EB1 pathway. No verdict is available until the 2027 end-of-budget report; searching found no basis to call it either way now.

statement: The tough economic conditions that our Government has inherited mean that the number of people on the jobseeker benefit is expected to keep rising until January 2025.
criterion: Ministry of Social Development monthly jobseeker support recipient counts from December 2023 through to at least mid-2025; true if the series rises to a peak at or about January 2025 and then declines, false if it continues rising materially past January 2025 or peaks well before it.
reasoning: Criterion: MSD jobseeker recipient counts from Dec 2023 to at least mid-2025; true if the series peaks at or about January 2025 then declines, false if it keeps rising materially past January 2025. The forecast behind the quote (HYEFU 2023) put the peak at 214,000 in January 2025, and the level was roughly right at that moment — 213,321 at end-December 2024, followed by three consecutive monthly falls to about 209,800 by March 2025. But that turn was seasonal, not the peak: the series resumed climbing to 223,512 in the December 2025 quarter, the highest figure in five years and +10,191 on December 2024, and was still 218,481 at end-June 2026 (up roughly 2,500 on June 2025). MSD's own guidance is to compare the same quarter 12 months apart, and on that basis the series rose through Dec 2025 and June 2026. Against the coalition's formation (about 190,000 in December 2023) the total is up more than 33,000. So it continued rising materially past January 2025 — the criterion's false branch.

statement: What we know is that this Government is rushing through legislation before Christmas that will see people lose their jobs.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey employment and unemployment series through 2024, read alongside sector reporting on the December 2023 urgency legislation. True if employment falls or unemployment rises materially over 2024 in the areas the legislation touched; false if employment holds or grows.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether employment falls or unemployment rises materially over 2024 in the areas the December 2023 urgency legislation touched. Stats NZ HLFS: unemployment rate 4.0% (Dec 2023 qtr) -> 4.3% (Mar) -> 4.6% (Jun) -> 4.8% (Sep) -> 5.1% (Dec 2024 qtr), the highest since Sep 2020; unemployed up 33,000 to 156,000 over the year; employment rate down 1.7 points to 67.4%; employment itself fell (-0.1% in the Dec 2024 quarter alone). In the specific areas touched by the pre-Christmas urgency bills: the Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) Amendment Act 2023 (passed under urgency 12 Dec, assent 19 Dec, scheme ended 31 Dec 2023) was followed by a sharp fall in EV sales from a 10% BEV market share in 2023; the Employment Relations (Trial Periods) Amendment Act 2023 (assent 21 Dec, in force 23 Dec 2023) extended 90-day no-grievance dismissal to all employers; and public-sector employment contracted, with just over 2,000 public service jobs lost between December and June and 500+ redundancies around the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora. I checked for the disconfirming case (employment holding or growing, as proponents of the FPA repeal and trial-period extension argued) and found the opposite. IMPORTANT LIMIT: the criterion is an outcome test, not a causation test. The bulk of the 2024 labour-market deterioration is attributed by economists to the monetary-policy-induced recession, not to the December bills, so the causal mechanism Waititi implied is not established by this evidence — only the outcome he predicted.

statement: I’ll make a prediction. The other side of the House, despite all their lamenting”—this is now National—“will not change it back because they won’t have the opportunity in the foreseeable future.
criterion: The parliamentary record for legislation reversing the Reserve Bank's dual mandate; true if no bill restoring the single mandate had passed or been introduced by a National-led government within a few years of the original prediction, false if such a bill was introduced and passed in that window.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a National-led government introduced and passed a bill restoring the Reserve Bank's single (price-stability) mandate within a few years. It did, at the first opportunity. Searching the quoted phrase surfaces Willie Jackson's speech of 12 December 2018 (NZ Parliament Hansard document HansS_20181212_054225000), the debate on the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Bill that created the dual mandate — so the prediction dates from 2018 and was being read back into the 2023 repeal debate. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill was the incoming coalition's very first bill: first reading 12 December 2023, passed under urgency, Royal assent 19 December 2023, removing the requirement to support maximum sustainable employment. National did change it back, and did so within days of having the numbers. The only reading under which the prediction survives is the narrow one that National had no opportunity during the 2020-2023 term (true, Labour governed alone), but the prediction as worded — 'not in the foreseeable future' — failed five years out. I checked for disconfirming evidence (any sign the dual mandate survived or the repeal stalled) and found none; the Act is on the statute book, and as of 2026 restoring the employment mandate is still only an election-campaign proposal.

statement: I know it’s going to be a bit of a rarity over the next 100 days, but it clearly shows that you can put together a regulatory impact statement very quickly.
criterion: Treasury/agency regulatory impact statements published for Government bills passed during the coalition's first 100 days (from 27 November 2023 to approximately 19 March 2024). True if most such bills proceeded without a published RIS or under an exemption/waiver; false if a RIS accompanied the majority of them.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether most Government bills passed in the coalition's first 100 days proceeded without a published RIS or under an exemption/waiver. Cabinet decision CAB-23-MIN-0468 suspended the RIS requirement for 100-day-plan proposals taken within the 100 days that solely involve repealing legislation — revealed by a leaked Treasury paper in December 2023 and then recited verbatim in bill explanatory notes and departmental disclosure statements. Checking the official disclosure statements bill by bill for Government bills assented 27 Nov 2023 to mid-March 2024: NO RIS / exempted — Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) (2023/6), RMA (NBE and SP Repeal and Interim Fast-track Consenting) (2023/8), NZ Productivity Commission Act Repeal (2024/9), Water Services Acts Repeal (2024/13), Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) (2024/20), Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment (2024/22), Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Maori Health Authority) (2024/26), Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) (2024/14, 'not prepared or available at the time that policy decisions were taken'), and Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal (2023/3, 'partially exempt', covered by a coversheet updating the 2021 RIS). That is nine. RIS present — Reserve Bank (Economic Objective) (2023/2, Treasury RIS Dec 2023, but with no independent quality review 'due to the urgent nature of the change') and Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal (2023/4, relying on an existing April 2023 IRD assessment plus a revised coversheet). Even if every remaining bill in the window (EU FTA, Legal Services, Social Workers Registration, Secondary Legislation Confirmation) had a full RIS, the no-RIS group still holds the majority. Disconfirming check: some 100-day items did get a RIS (the 90-day trial period extension, mandated teaching times), and proposals going to Cabinet after the 100 days still required one — which is consistent with Edmonds saying 'a bit of a rarity' rather than 'never'.

statement: What we are doing here—the legislation we are passing—is not going to materially change that.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI outturns for 2024 compared against the RBNZ November 2023 projection: true if annual headline inflation re-enters the 1–3 percent band at or after the projected quarter (September 2024) with no material acceleration, and RBNZ commentary does not attribute a change in the path to the single-mandate amendment; false if inflation returns to band materially earlier than projected and the Bank attributes that to the mandate change.
reasoning: The criterion's true-limb is satisfied on both halves. (1) Timing: the RBNZ's November 2023 MPS projected annual CPI back inside the 1-3% band in Q3 2024 — the Committee 'noted inflation is still expected to decline to within the target band by the second half of 2024', and Westpac's same-week review of that MPS records 'CPI inflation still gets back inside the range in Q3 2024'. Stats NZ outturns landed on that quarter, not earlier: Dec 2023 4.7%, Mar 2024 4.0%, Jun 2024 3.3% (still above band), Sep 2024 2.2% (re-entry), Dec 2024 2.2%. So re-entry was at the projected quarter, with no material acceleration through 2024 — the path decelerated monotonically. (2) Attribution: no RBNZ commentary attributes any change in the inflation path to the single-mandate amendment. Orr characterised the change as largely symbolic ('We can never ignore the impacts on the real economy, the labour market and so on, but [we can give inflation] primacy'), and the Bank had itself recommended inflation primacy in its own remit review, i.e. the amendment codified existing practice. Disconfirming check: if the mandate change had materially tightened the path, inflation should have re-entered the band before Q3 2024 and RBNZ MPS/OCR commentary should have cited the amendment; neither occurred — June 2024 was still 3.3%, above band. (Inflation did rise again later — 3.0% Sep 2025, 3.1% Dec 2025, 4.1% Q2 2026 — but the criterion is scoped to 2024 outturns, and that later rise is also not attributed to the mandate change.)

statement: They are a disgrace to this nation, and we’re going to get them out in the next two years.
criterion: The official result of the next New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission: true if the National/NZ First/ACT coalition does not form the subsequent government, false if it returns to office.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on 'the official result of the next New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission'. The 2026 general election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 (Prime Minister's announcement; Electoral Commission timetable confirmed — advance voting from 26 October, enrolment deadline 25 October, regulated period 7 August to 6 November 2026). Today is 25 September 2026, so the election has not been held and no declared result exists; the resolve-by date is 31 December 2026, still in the future. Nothing can be checked against the named source yet. Note for the record: the quote's own horizon ('in the next two years', i.e. by December 2025) passed without a general election being held, but the criterion as written directs the check to the next general election result rather than to that two-year window, so the correct answer is that it is not yet settled, not that it failed. Disconfirming check: I looked for any earlier (snap) election in 2024-2025 that would already have settled this — none occurred; the 54th Parliament ran its full term.

statement: I know that I have some different views on productivity, but I also am concerned that we’re about to dismantle the Productivity Commission and these are the kinds of institutions that have, in the past, been relied upon to give us advice.
criterion: Official records of the Commission's status; true if the New Zealand Productivity Commission is formally disestablished or closed, false if it is still operating as a Crown entity at the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion: true if the New Zealand Productivity Commission is formally disestablished or closed; false if still operating as a Crown entity at 31 December 2024. Official records show it was formally disestablished on 29 February 2024 — Treasury publishes its final annual report covering '1 July 2023 - 29 February 2024' and archives the body as 'Productivity Commission (2011 - 2024)', and the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act 2010 is held on the legislation site 'as at 29 February 2024' (its repeal date). The repeal bill was introduced under urgency on 30 January 2024 by the Minister for Regulation and was the first legislation dealt with in the 2024 legislative year; functions relating to regulatory quality passed to the new Ministry for Regulation, staff were not redeployed, Commission records transferred to Treasury, and its website was decommissioned in May 2024. So White's stated concern that the institution was 'about to' be dismantled was borne out within eleven weeks of the speech. Disconfirming check: I looked for any sign the Commission continued to operate, was reconstituted, or survived as a Crown entity in some reduced form — the Treasury archive, the legislation repeal date and the Crown entity listings all show it ceased to exist, with no successor Crown entity holding its advisory role.

statement: I know that the time will come when fair pay agreements also are in force again under the next Labour Government.
criterion: New Zealand statute record and government formation: true if a Labour-led government enacts legislation establishing sector-wide fair pay agreements (or an equivalent industry-award bargaining system) and it is in force by the resolve-by date; false if no such legislation is in force by then.
reasoning: The criterion requires a Labour-led government to enact and bring into force sector-wide fair pay agreement legislation by 2029-12-31. The Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 was repealed effective 20 December 2023 by the National-led coalition, and Labour has not been in government since. The next opportunity is the 7 November 2026 election, which has not yet been held; the resolve-by date is over three years away. No score.

statement: This new Government should be ashamed of the hollowness of this move, because if Labour regain the Government benches—which is going to happen in three years—our first hundred days will be about restoring mana and rights back to workers.
criterion: The official declared result of the next New Zealand general election (Electoral Commission): true if Labour is in government following that election, false if the incumbent National-led parties are returned to government.
reasoning: The criterion is the official declared result of the next general election. That election is set for 7 November 2026 and has not been held as of 2026-09-25; the National–ACT–NZ First coalition remains the incumbent government and no Electoral Commission result or post-election government formation exists yet. Polling is not the named source, so it cannot substitute.

statement: The Greens will ensure that this is a one-term Government and that the workers take back the power in this Chamber.
criterion: The result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if the National–ACT–New Zealand First coalition does not return to government; false if it is returned.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the 2026 general election result and the government formed after it. The election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 and has not occurred; Luxon's National–ACT–NZ First coalition is still in office serving its first term, so whether it is 'one-term' cannot be settled until after the vote and subsequent government formation.

statement: These are questions based on the Regulatory Standards Bill that David Seymour had and that will no doubt be reincarnated in this Parliament.
criterion: The Parliamentary bills register for the 54th Parliament: true if a Regulatory Standards Bill is introduced to the House before the 2026 general election; false if no such bill is introduced by then.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a Regulatory Standards Bill was introduced to the House in the 54th Parliament before the 2026 general election. David Seymour, as Minister for Regulation, introduced the Regulatory Standards Bill on 19 May 2025; it passed first reading on 23 May 2025 with National, ACT and NZ First support, and was enacted as the Regulatory Standards Act on 18 November 2025 — well before the 2026 election. Webb's prediction that Seymour's earlier bill would be 'reincarnated in this Parliament' is borne out, and the bill was not merely introduced but passed.

statement: Axing fair pay agreements will shave up to $10,000 a year off a bus driver’s salary—that’s just according to the Council of Trade Unions, who are a very reliable source, as we all know.
criterion: Bus driver pay rates in collective agreements and Stats NZ earnings data after the repeal, compared with the rates in force in December 2023 and with the pay settings the pending bus driver fair pay agreement would have set; true if any substantial group of bus drivers ends up as much as $10,000 a year worse off, false if bus driver pay holds or rises over that period.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on actual bus driver pay after the repeal versus the rates in force in December 2023: false if pay holds or rises. It held and rose. No fair pay agreement was ever concluded before the FPA Act was repealed on 20 December 2023, so MBIE/Employment NZ record that the repeal changed no worker's existing terms — the bus/coach driver FPA was still at the bargaining-initiation stage and never set a rate. Bus driver pay meanwhile continued upward on the pre-existing public-transport wage programme: Metlink settled at an average ~$30/h urban and $28/h regional from 2023, Auckland worked toward $30/h, and 2025–26 market data (Indeed average $29.94/h in Dec 2025; SEEK/Jobted ~$27.5–$30/h) shows rates at or above the December 2023 level. Nothing found shows any substantial group of bus drivers $10,000 a year (roughly $5/h) worse off. The $10,000 figure was a counterfactual against what an FPA might have delivered, which is unquantifiable because no proposed FPA terms were ever published — but on the criterion as written, actual pay did not fall.

statement: But we should not forget that the ones that are most penalised in this are those people that clean our floors, that look after our children, that drive our buses, that will be earning less this Christmas, that will afford less on their table, fewer Christmas presents.
criterion: Stats NZ Quarterly Employment Survey average hourly earnings for the cleaning, childcare/education support and road passenger transport sectors: true if earnings in those sectors fall between the September 2023 and March 2024 quarters; false if they hold steady or rise.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on QES earnings in the cleaning, childcare/education-support and road-passenger-transport sectors falling between the September 2023 and March 2024 quarters. They did not fall. QES average weekly earnings rose in both relevant ANZSIC divisions I could retrieve: transport, postal and warehousing (female $1,191.52 → $1,215.58; male $1,594.24 → $1,619.81) and education and training (female $1,111.55 → $1,187.37; male $1,398.39 → $1,524.96). Nationally, average ordinary-time hourly earnings reached $40.96 in the March 2024 quarter, up 5.2 percent annually — above the ~4 percent CPI — so real earnings also did not fall. The mechanism Andersen invoked could not have bitten anyway: no fair pay agreement had been concluded, so the repeal removed no existing pay. Caveat on scope: QES does not publish at the occupational granularity the criterion names (cleaners, childcare workers, bus drivers), and I could not retrieve the administrative-and-support-services division that is the closest proxy for cleaning; the verdict rests on the two divisions obtained plus the national aggregate, all of which moved up.

statement: We will make sure that these fair pay agreements become a reality when we are back on the Treasury benches in 2026.
criterion: The result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if Labour is in government following that election, false if it is not.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the 2026 general election and the government formed after it. That election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 and has not been held (today is 25 September 2026); advance voting starts 26 October. National governs with ACT and NZ First until then, so the prediction cannot be graded yet. Resolve-by date 2026-12-31 has not passed.

statement: Vehicle manufacturers said, quite clearly, between 2025 and 2028 they’re going to completely retool manufacturing in Asia, South-east Asia, and Europe to produce almost nothing but EVs and hybrids.
criterion: Global light-vehicle production statistics for 2028 by powertrain (e.g. IEA Global EV Outlook, ACEA and OICA production data); true if EVs and hybrids account for the overwhelming majority of new light-vehicle production from those regions by 2028, false if internal-combustion-only models remain a substantial share of output.
reasoning: The criterion names 2028 light-vehicle production by powertrain (IEA/ACEA/OICA). 2028 is two years away and no such data exists; the resolve-by date is 2028-12-31. Current state of the world for context only: IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 reports ~22 million electric cars produced in 2025 (about 1 in 4 new cars sold) and projects ~23 million and ~28% of global sales in 2026, with China near 60% and Europe about 1 in 3. Electrified output is growing fast but ICE-only models remain a large share today, so the claim is neither confirmed nor refuted yet.

statement: So if you currently drive a Ford Ranger turbo-diesel, you’ll be able to get one—according to the manufacturers—in a hybrid in the next couple of years that will be very, very low with any emissions.
criterion: Ford New Zealand's model range and NZTA new-vehicle registration records; true if a hybrid or plug-in hybrid Ford Ranger is on sale in New Zealand by the end of 2025, false if no hybrid Ranger variant is available to New Zealand buyers by that date.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a hybrid or plug-in hybrid Ford Ranger was on sale in New Zealand by the end of 2025. It was. Ford New Zealand confirmed Ranger PHEV pricing and specs in early 2025 (XLT $82,990, Wildtrak $89,990, Stormtrak $94,990) ahead of a mid-2025 NZ launch; DriveLife covered the NZ launch in June 2025; Auto Trader NZ published a New Zealand road test of the Stormtrak PHEV on 27 October 2025; and an Auto Trader NZ review published 22 February 2026 states the Ranger hybrid 'started arriving mid-year and up to and including November, Ford has found homes for 155 of them' — i.e. 155 New Zealand sales through November 2025. Disconfirming checks: the Ford Ranger model with a confirmed NZ delay is the Super Duty (pushed to 2027 on compliance grounds), not the PHEV; and although March 2026 registration commentary describes the Ranger PHEV 'arriving' at 88 units, the October 2025 NZ road test and the 2025 sales figure rule out a first-arrival date in 2026. Two caveats outside the criterion as written: the variant is a petrol-based PHEV rather than the diesel hybrid the speaker's framing implies, and the 'very, very low with any emissions' characterisation is not what this criterion tests (real-world economy reported around 2.9 L/100km in NZ testing, which depends on plug-in charging behaviour).

statement: It will result in between 100,000 and 350,000 fewer electric cars on New Zealand roads by 2030.
criterion: NZTA motor vehicle register EV counts at 31 December 2030 compared against the pre-repeal projected trajectory (Ministry of Transport / Drive Electric baseline with the discount retained). True if the shortfall against that baseline falls within 100,000–350,000 vehicles; false if it is materially below 100,000 or above 350,000.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against NZTA motor vehicle register EV counts at 31 December 2030 versus the pre-repeal baseline, with a resolve-by date of 2031-06-30. Today is 2026-09-25, so the observation does not exist. Searching confirms the 100,000-350,000 range was an existing published estimate at the time (Concept Consulting report for Drive Electric, December 2023, reported by Newsroom: ~100,000 fewer EVs by 2030 in its central case, with the wider band covering the weakened Clean Car Standard), so Woods was relaying modelling rather than inventing a figure. Interim trajectory only: the plug-in fleet was 135,348 (92,540 BEV + 42,808 PHEV) at end-2025 against a Climate Change Commission figure of up to 550,000 light EVs by 2030, and new-registration volumes collapsed after the discount ended. That is directionally consistent with a shortfall but settles nothing against the criterion, which requires a 2030 count.

statement: We are now starting to see—be it Rivian, be it Ford—a Ranger that is a hybrid vehicle coming on to the market next year.
criterion: Ford New Zealand model releases and NZTA new-vehicle registration records for 2024; true if a hybrid or plug-in hybrid Ranger was on sale in New Zealand during 2024, false if its release fell in 2025 or later.
reasoning: Speaking on 2023-12-12, O'Connor said a hybrid Ranger was coming to market 'next year', i.e. 2024. Ford revealed the Ranger PHEV globally in September 2024, but the New Zealand release was 2025, not 2024. Ford NZ and AutoMuse both stated the first-ever Ranger Plug-in Hybrid would launch in 2025 with pricing announced closer to launch; NZ pricing was confirmed in 2025 (XLT $82,990, Wildtrak $89,990, Stormtrak $94,990) and the drive launch was June 2025, with production starting late 2024 and NZ arrivals from 2025. The 2024 NZ Ranger range offered only 2.0L four-cylinder and 3.0L V6 diesel/petrol options, no hybrid. Checked for the opposite reading (order books or a mild-hybrid Ranger opening in NZ during 2024) and found none; NZ dealer order pages for the Ranger PHEV date from 2025. The criterion states explicitly that a release in 2025 or later is false.

statement: But we’re also confident that there will continue to be an increased uptake of electric vehicles in New Zealand, and that is because car manufacturers around the world are switching from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric vehicles and hybrids and other low-emission technology.
criterion: NZTA / Ministry of Transport new light-vehicle registration statistics for 2024 compared with 2023; true if battery-electric and plug-in hybrid registrations rose year on year, false if they fell.
reasoning: The criterion is new light-vehicle BEV and PHEV registrations in 2024 versus 2023: true if they rose, false if they fell. They fell sharply. EV share of new registrations dropped from 14.2% in 2023 to 5.2% in 2024, with new EV registrations falling roughly 21,611 to 6,748 (about -74%). January 2024 recorded only 244 new BEVs against 4,455 in December 2023. Mid-2024 monthly shares were BEV 5.8% (548 units) and PHEV 2.4% (227 units) in June, and BEV 6% / PHEV 2.4% (230 units) in July. Statista's own note on the NZ series attributes the drop between 2023 and 2024 to the Clean Car Discount ending on 31 December 2023, compounded by EVs losing their RUC exemption from 1 April 2024. I deliberately checked the disconfirming case: total EV fleet stock did keep growing (103,665 to 113,715, +9.7%), and Wikipedia's year table is cumulative stock which can be misread as rising registrations. But the criterion names registrations, and those fell for both BEV and PHEV. Brown's premise about global manufacturer shift may hold; the NZ uptake outcome he predicted for the period did not.

statement: They also, in terms of a further document that they sent through, which relates to some work by Concept Consulting, indicate that if policies and initiatives such as this are actually removed, then there is absolutely an expectation that the EV percentage of the sales mix to fall to similar levels to actually prior to the incentive coming in, prior to this scheme coming into place.
criterion: NZTA/Ministry of Transport new light-vehicle registration statistics for EV (BEV) share of new vehicle sales. True if, after the Clean Car Discount is removed at the end of 2023, the EV share of new sales falls back to approximately its pre-July-2021 level (low single-digit percent); false if it remains materially above that pre-incentive level.
reasoning: The predicted collapse happened but did not return to pre-incentive levels on any annual basis. Plug-in EV share of new vehicle sales fell from 19.8% (2023) to 7.7% (2024), with new EV sales down from 31,400 to 10,632, and January 2024 alone hit ~3% — 'the lowest uptake since 2020' and level with the pre-July-2021 baseline of roughly 2-3% of light-vehicle registrations (NZTA put it at ~2% of monthly light-vehicle registrations over the three years to mid-2021). But the annual floor settled at BEV 5.2% (2024) and 5.6% (2025), about 2-3x the pre-incentive level, i.e. materially above it, which is the criterion's 'false' branch. Looking for disconfirming evidence of a sustained collapse found the opposite: by 2026, BEVs were ~17% of passenger registrations year-to-date and plug-ins 33.9% of new passenger registrations in March 2026 (fuel-price driven), above the 2023 peak. Direction and immediate magnitude vindicated; the stated endpoint was overstated.

statement: They’re going to slow down progress, and that means it’s going to be more expensive later, it’s going to be harder for New Zealanders to access second-hand electric vehicles, because without the price incentive, we’re going to import fewer electric vehicles, which means there’s less vehicles in the second-hand fleet for New Zealanders to access.
criterion: Waka Kotahi / Ministry of Transport vehicle registration statistics for new and used-import battery and plug-in electric light vehicles; true if annual EV registrations in 2024 and 2025 fall materially below the 2023 level, false if EV registrations hold steady or grow after the scheme ends.
reasoning: The criterion's test — annual EV registrations in both 2024 and 2025 materially below 2023 — is met. New EV registrations: 31,400 (2023) -> 10,632 (2024, a ~66% fall, reported as the second-steepest national decline globally that year) -> ~14,600 (2025: 7,706 BEV at 5.6% share plus 6,885 PHEV at 5.0%), still ~54% below 2023. Used-import EVs, the second-hand channel she specifically named, also ran at very low volumes through 2025 (129 used-import BEV registrations in March 2025). Checked for the 'holds steady or grows' branch: it only appears outside the criterion window — used-import BEV registrations rose 373% year-on-year to 615 in March 2026 with the Nissan Leaf the fourth most popular used import, driven by the fuel-price shock rather than any restored incentive. I could not pin an exact 2023 used-import BEV annual total, so the volume comparison rests on new registrations plus 2025 used-import monthly levels.

statement: And that is progress, and it’s about to be taken away.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register: true if the Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) Amendment Bill receives Royal assent and the rebate/fee scheme ceases, false if the bill fails or the scheme remains in force.
reasoning: The Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) Amendment Bill, introduced by Simeon Brown, passed all three readings under urgency on 12 December 2023 — the day of the speech — received Royal assent on 19 December 2023, and came into force on 1 January 2024. The rebate/fee scheme ceased for vehicles registered after 31 December 2023. Neither of the criterion's 'false' conditions occurred: the bill did not fail and the scheme did not remain in force.

statement: So about now we’ll start to see those vehicles turn up in the second-hand market and be available to people much cheaper because we’ve created a pipeline and that’s what Government does well, right?
criterion: Used-vehicle listing and registration data for New Zealand (Motor Trade Association / Trade Me Motors / NZTA used registrations) for 2024: true if the volume of low-emission and electric vehicles in the domestic second-hand market rose materially over 2024 and their asking prices fell materially; false if second-hand supply and prices were flat or rising.
reasoning: The price half of the criterion is confirmed and the timing roughly held: by April 2024 industry reporting described a "flooded" used-EV market on Trade Me with "hundreds of pre-owned Teslas" listed, NZ-new EVs losing ~40% of value in year one and a further 40% in year two, and a documented case of a $75,000 EV trading in at $40,000 after 12 months. The supply half is only partly met on the evidence the criterion names: I found listing-level/oversupply reporting rather than NZTA used-registration volume data, and the oversupply is attributed to the post-repeal demand collapse and new-car discounting rather than to the pipeline White credited. Disconfirming evidence: the channel that actually supplies affordable used EVs in NZ, Japanese used imports (~80% Nissan Leaf), moved the other way once the used-EV rebate ended (2,519 used BEVs imported in 2025, 3% of used passenger imports), and industry sources in the same reporting said the real subsidy-era used wave would not arrive until 2026-27. Substance holds, mechanism and breadth overstated.

statement: I understand that Drive Electric have put the Minister on notice that if the scheme is removed, it could dramatically disrupt electric vehicle sales in this country.
criterion: Waka Kotahi / Ministry of Transport new and used EV registration statistics for 2024 compared with 2023; true if monthly EV registrations fall substantially (on the order of tens of percent) after the discount ends on 31 December 2023, false if EV sales hold roughly steady or continue to grow.
reasoning: Registrations fell far more than the "tens of percent" the criterion requires, immediately after the discount ended on 31 December 2023. New BEV registrations went from 4,455 in December 2023 to 244 in January 2024, with EV share of new sales dropping from about one in four to roughly one in 20 in a single month (model-level: Tesla Model Y 356 to 25, MG4 622 to 12). Across the full year, new EV sales were about 10,632 in 2024 against roughly 31,400 in 2023 (~66% down), EV share of new-car sales halved from ~20% to 10.6%, and NZ recorded one of the steepest year-on-year EV declines globally against a world average increase of 15.6%. Checked for the disconfirming case (sales holding steady or growing) and it does not appear; the MIA does attribute part of the decline to the economy, road user charges from April 2024 and ACC levies, but the criterion asks only whether registrations fell substantially.

statement: Does the official advice that the Minister is refusing to release before we vote on the legislation concur with the report released by Concept Consulting for Drive Electric that the reduced uptake of electric vehicles, because of the repeal of the Clean Car Discount, will see New Zealand spending over a billion more on imported oil from overseas and mean that we will import 100,000 fewer electric vehicles in the period from now to 2030, thereby increasing carbon emissions relative to if the scheme stayed in place?
criterion: NZTA/Ministry of Transport light electric vehicle registration statistics 2024–2030 compared against the Ministry's pre-repeal uptake projections, plus MBIE oil import data; true if cumulative EV imports fall short of the pre-repeal projection by roughly 100,000 and oil import spend exceeds it by over $1 billion, false if uptake tracks or exceeds the pre-repeal projection.
reasoning: The criterion's horizon is 2030 (cumulative EV registrations vs the pre-repeal projection, plus MBIE oil import spend) and today is 25 September 2026, so it cannot be settled. The underlying report is real and Genter's summary is within its range: Concept Consulting for Drive Electric projected 100,000 to 300,000 fewer EVs on the road by 2030 and one in 10 rather than one in five cars electric. Interim data is genuinely mixed: uptake collapsed in 2024 (new EV sales ~10,632 vs ~31,400 in 2023) and share was still around 11-13% in 2025, but 2026 has rebounded sharply, with BEV+PHEV at 28.5% of registrations year to date (vs 12.8% in the same period of 2025) and 36.7% in July 2026. Whether cumulative uptake ends up roughly 100,000 short of the pre-repeal projection, and oil import spend more than $1bn above it, remains open.

statement: Exports hit a high of $57.7 billion this year but are forecast to drop to $54.3 billion in the year to June 2024.
criterion: MPI SOPI actual food and fibre export revenue for the year ended June 2024; true if the outturn is at or near $54.3b (within about 2%), false if it lands materially above or below.
reasoning: McClay was quoting MPI's December 2023 SOPI forecast of $54.3b for the year to 30 June 2024, and the outturn came in just below it. Three later SOPI baselines imply the FY2024 actual: December 2024 SOPI (+7% to $56.9b for FY2025 => ~$53.2b), June 2025 SOPI (+12% to $59.9b => ~$53.5b), December 2025 SOPI ($62b for FY2026, '16% higher than two years previously' => ~$53.4b). That is roughly 1.5-2% below $54.3b, i.e. at or near the forecast within the criterion's ~2% tolerance. Some secondary coverage reports $54.3b as the actual outturn, conflating forecast with actual; under either reading the criterion is met. Aside not covered by the criterion: the record year was $57.4b (Beehive, confirmed after final data), not the $57.7b stated in the quote.

statement: Does he acknowledge that removing the smoke-free laws will mean more people will die from smoking while the only people who will benefit from this are landlords getting tax cuts?
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence and Ministry of Health smoking-attributable mortality series after the December 2023 repeal; true if smoking prevalence or smoking-attributable deaths depart upward from the pre-repeal downward trend, false if the decline continues at or above the pre-repeal rate.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2028-12-31, well in the future. The repeal took effect 5 March 2024. The most recent data the criterion names (NZ Health Survey 2024/25) puts adult daily smoking at 6.8% (95% CI 6.2-7.4), statistically unchanged from 6.9% in 2023/24 and down from 11.9% in 2019/20 - a plateau that predates the repeal rather than an upward departure from trend. No post-repeal Ministry of Health smoking-attributable mortality series has been published; available mortality figures are modelled projections (Otago/ASPIRE), not outturns. A mortality effect from a repeal of an unimplemented denicotinisation/generation ban would not be expected to appear in the data this early either way, so the criterion cannot yet be applied.

statement: You know, all the evidence seems to suggest that that will narrow over time.
criterion: Average new and used EV versus ICE purchase prices in New Zealand (Motor Industry Association registrations data and NZTA/Trade Me price series) comparing 2023 with the resolve-by year; true if the average EV–ICE price gap in comparable segments is smaller, false if it is unchanged or wider.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2026-12-31 and today is 2026-09-25, so the comparison year the criterion names is incomplete; no full-year 2026 MIA registration or NZTA/Trade Me average-price series exists yet for a segment-matched EV-vs-ICE comparison.
