Directional evidence so far favours the claim: the cheapest new EV in NZ is now the BYD Atto 1 at $30,990 and the MG4 range starts at $30,990, against roughly $46,000-$50,000 entry-level new EV pricing in 2023, with 90 fully-electric models on sale as at September 2026; Stats NZ import values show the reduced-emission vs internal-combustion vehicle import gap closing from $4.5b (YE June 2019) to $202m (YE June 2026). Disconfirming check: new EVs still carry an upfront premium over comparable petrol models, and NZ removed the Clean Car Discount from 1 January 2024, which raised effective EV purchase prices; that makes a proper segment-matched comparison necessary rather than assumable. Hold until the 2026 data is complete.

statement: I think they’re going to be very unhappy when they realise how much costs have inflated compared to the prices that they put in their manifesto for those so-called “roads of national significance”, which are really roads of private greenfields-developer significance, particularly in the Auckland region.
criterion: Published NZTA/Treasury cost estimates for the roads of national significance programme, compared against the costings in National's 2023 transport manifesto. True if the official estimates materially exceed the manifesto figures; false if the programme is costed at or below the manifesto figures.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether official NZTA/Treasury estimates materially exceed National's 2023 transport manifesto costings. They do. National campaigned on 13 RoNS at ~$17.4b; 12 of those same 13 are now costed at $25.5-31.4b on 2025/post-election NZTA figures, and the 13th (Whangarei to Port Marsden) went from National's $1.3b to $1.9-2.5b. Eight roads alone account for at least $5.1b of increase in two years with no construction started; NZTA's estimates for all but one of the 13 exceeded National's own campaign figures even in 2023. The expanded 17-road programme is now $44-54b. Transport Minister Chris Bishop conceded the cause on record: National used the costings available at the election and there has since been construction cost inflation. Some manifesto figures rested on estimates as old as 2015, predating post-Covid construction inflation. Checked for the disconfirming case (any road costed at or below the manifesto figure) and found the opposite pattern. Genter's added framing about greenfields developers and Auckland is rhetoric the criterion does not test.

statement: We know that there will continue to be an increased uptake of electric vehicles as more and more car manufacturers produce more and more electric vehicles and bring them into New Zealand, and we will continue to invest in the electric vehicle charging infrastructure to support this uptake over time.
criterion: NZ Transport Agency motor vehicle registration statistics for new and used light electric vehicles; true if annual EV registrations in 2024 and 2025 exceed the 2023 total, false if annual registrations fall below the 2023 level.
reasoning: The criterion is explicit: true if annual light-EV registrations in 2024 and 2025 exceed the 2023 total, false if they fall below it. Both years fell below. 2023 was the peak (final year of the Clean Car Discount, which ended 31 Dec 2023); EV owners also lost their RUC exemption from 1 April 2024. New EV sales fell roughly 70% year-on-year in 2024, against a 15.6% global increase. Plug-in fleet growth, which captures both new and used-import registrations, was +41.7k in 2023 (107,368 year-end), +11.7k in 2024 (119,040) and +16.3k in 2025 (135,348) - 2024 and 2025 each far short of 2023. Plug-in share of new registrations was about 11% in 2025 versus a materially higher 2023 level, and BEV share sat around 4-8% through 2025 against about 10% in 2023. Looked for the disconfirming case and found only partial support: the fleet kept growing in absolute terms, 2025 recovered on 2024, and 2026 has surged (28.5% BEV+PHEV share YTD to August vs 12.8% a year earlier) - but 2026 is outside the criterion's window. The charging-infrastructure half of Brown's sentence is not covered by the criterion.

statement: But they have cited—and I used this earlier today—that the research that they’ve provided to all members of the House shows that the new Government’s policy that they are seeking to progress under urgency this evening, to remove the discount and also to weaken the Clean Car Standard, would mean between 100,000 and 350,000 fewer electric vehicles (EVs) on the roads in New Zealand by 2030.
criterion: Drive Electric's published modelling and its stated baseline, compared against NZ Transport Agency light-EV fleet statistics at 31 December 2030; true if the observed fleet falls short of that baseline by 100,000–350,000 vehicles, false if the shortfall falls outside that range.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against NZTA light-EV fleet statistics at 31 December 2030 compared to Drive Electric's stated baseline, with a resolve-by date of 2031-03-31. That data does not exist yet, so the prediction cannot be settled. What is verifiable now is that Utikere characterised the research accurately: Drive Electric's published modelling gives roughly 100,000 fewer EVs on NZ roads by 2030 if only the Clean Car Discount is removed, rising to as many as 350,000 fewer (BEVs and PHEVs) if the whole Clean Car Programme goes, with emissions 900-3,000kt higher and economic costs of $0.9b to $2.7-3.5b. The 100,000-350,000 range and its attribution to the removal of the discount plus weakening of the standard are both as he stated. Directional evidence so far is consistent with the modelling (2024-25 uptake fell sharply), but consistency at the four-year mark is not resolution, and the criterion's test is a specific shortfall band measured in 2030.

statement: As I’ve already made clear, and as members will soon see, if you don’t have the price incentive at the point of purchase, you will get less uptake of the low-emissions vehicles, and then, if you’re relying on the emissions trading scheme, you will see higher fuel prices and people will have no choice to avoid those higher fuel prices because they’ve already purchased a vehicle that isn’t as fuel-efficient as it could be.
criterion: NZTA light-vehicle registration statistics for 2024 compared with 2023: true if the share of new zero- and low-emissions vehicles in registrations falls materially after the Clean Car Discount ends; false if that share holds steady or rises.
reasoning: The Clean Car Discount ended 31 Dec 2023 and the zero-/low-emissions share of new registrations fell materially, as the criterion requires. BEV share of new registrations went from ~35.5% in Dec 2023 to 3% in Jan 2024, 4.1% in Feb 2024, ~6.8% BEV / ~4% PHEV by Oct 2024, and 8.6% in Dec 2024. MIA's year-end 2024 commentary states BEVs and PHEVs 'both experienced a significant drop compared to the previous year' year-to-date. Disconfirming check: the whole new-vehicle market also shrank 13.5% in 2024, so volume alone could mislead — but the share fell as well, so the fall is not an artifact of a smaller market. Partial counterweight: non-plug-in hybrids grew (28.1% in Dec 2024), so under a very broad reading of 'low-emissions' the electrified total held up better; the plug-in share the criterion targets still fell sharply. The criterion does not cover the quote's second limb (ETS-driven fuel prices), so that was not graded.

statement: We’re very pleased to see that the current legislation which we’re reverting to has actually driven daily smoking down by two points, back to 6.8, and we’re on track to deliver Smokefree 2025.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 target period: true if it is below 5 percent (the Smokefree 2025 threshold); false if it remains at or above 5 percent. Māori daily smoking prevalence should be reported alongside, since the goal is framed for all population groups.
reasoning: The criterion's threshold is New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking below 5% for the 2025 target period; false if at or above 5%. The 2024/25 NZHS (fieldwork Jul 2024-Jun 2025, i.e. the target period) reports adult daily smoking at 6.8%, about 294,000 people — flat within 0.1% for three consecutive years (6.8-6.9% across 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25), so the trend is a plateau, not a decline toward the target. Maori daily smoking was 15.0% (~99,000 people) and the most deprived quintile 12.9%; Pacific 10.3%, European/Other 5.7%, Asian 4.5% — no population group below 5% except Asian. The Public Health Communication Centre's briefing on the same survey states the findings 'strongly suggest that the government's goal to reach a daily smoking prevalence of less than 5% for all population groups will not be achieved'. Disconfirming check: I looked for a later survey that might show a drop — the 2025/26 NZHS is not yet published as of Sep 2026, and a three-year plateau at 6.8% leaves no path to under 5% within the target period. Luxon's backward-looking figure (down to 6.8) was accurate; the forward claim of being on track to deliver Smokefree 2025 was not.

statement: Next time these guys get on to that side of the House, they’re just going to do exactly the same thing in response, and all of those grand plans that you’ve got that you’re going to spend the next three or six or nine years developing, they’re just going to get in and reverse them in the first three months, because that’s, apparently, what new Governments do because that’s the standard that’s been set by this Government.
criterion: The legislative and policy record of the first three months of the next change of government following the 2023 National-led coalition. True if the incoming administration repeals or reverses the flagship programmes of this Government within its first three months in office; false if those programmes are substantially left in place over that period.
reasoning: The criterion requires observing the legislative and policy record of the first three months of the next change of government after the 2023 National-led coalition. Prime Minister Luxon announced on 21 January 2026 that the next general election will be held on 7 November 2026. As of today (25 September 2026) that election has not been held, so there has been no change of government and no incoming administration whose first three months could be examined. The item's own resolve-by date of 2027-03-31 is consistent with this: the evidence window opens only after the election and a government formation. This is a timing verdict, not a failure to find evidence.

statement: In the 2040s, 100 percent ownership of Spark Arena will be transferred to Auckland Council.
criterion: Auckland Council property register and the Spark Arena BOOT agreement transfer date; true if ownership vests in Auckland Council at some point between 2040 and 2049, false if the transfer date falls outside that decade or the arrangement is varied so no transfer occurs.
reasoning: Spark Arena is a 40-year BOOT between Tātaki Auckland Unlimited (Auckland Council CCO) and QPAM Ltd; the arena's FAQ states ownership transfers to Tātaki Auckland Unlimited at the end of the rights period. The arena opened 24 March 2007, so the scheduled transfer is ~2047 — inside the 2040s as Brewer said. No transfer has occurred yet and no variation cancelling it was found, so the criterion (ownership vesting between 2040 and 2049) cannot be settled until then.

statement: That was when the city was just over 1 million people, and by the end of this decade, Auckland will likely be home to 2 million.
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimate for the Auckland region at 30 June 2030; true if it is at or near 2.0 million, false if it is materially below (e.g. under 1.9 million).
reasoning: The criterion names the Stats NZ Auckland subnational estimate at 30 June 2030, which does not exist yet (today is 2026-09-25). Evidence leans against the claim: Auckland was 1,816,000 at 30 June 2025, growing about 1.0% in the year to June 2025, and the Stats NZ 2023(base)–2053 subnational projections have Auckland reaching 2 million around 2033. Extrapolation gives roughly 1.9m in 2030, which sits right on the criterion's 'materially below' line rather than clearly under it, so an early call is not warranted.

statement: Just like his Treaty principles bill, it’s going to be a dead letter. It will be of no effect.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Treaty Principles Bill: false if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; true if it is defeated, lapses, or is withdrawn without becoming law before the end of the 54th Parliament.
reasoning: The Treaty Principles Bill was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with only ACT in favour. It never reached a third reading and never received Royal assent; the parliamentary record lists it as not passed. That matches the criterion's 'true' branch (defeated without becoming law before the end of the 54th Parliament).

statement: Concerningly, forecasts predict that by January 2025, there will be 198,500 people on the jobseeker benefit.
criterion: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets, Jobseeker Support recipient count for January/the March 2025 quarter; true if the figure lands close to 198,500, false if it is materially above or below.
reasoning: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets show Jobseeker Support at 213,321 at end of the December 2024 quarter and 209,838 at end of the March 2025 quarter — the two published quarters bracketing January 2025. Both are materially above the 198,500 forecast (roughly 11,000–15,000 higher, 6–7%). March 2025 was also up 21,852 (11.6%) on March 2024, i.e. the trend was rising, not settling at the forecast level. Checked for a disconfirming reading (a narrower sub-category such as Work Ready only) but the criterion names the headline Jobseeker Support recipient count, which is the figure above.

statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link; it’s going to be completed by this National Government in this term.
criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport completion and opening announcements; true if the project is declared complete (handed over or opened for passenger service) before the dissolution of the 54th Parliament, false if completion slips past that date.
reasoning: Auckland Transport announced and confirmed that the City Rail Link opened to passenger services on Sunday 13 September 2026, with the first weekday timetable from Monday 14 September; Railway Gazette reported the opening as having occurred. The 54th Parliament has not yet dissolved — the 2026 general election is on 7 November 2026 and Parliament expires 9 November 2026 — so opening for passenger service fell before dissolution, satisfying the criterion. Disconfirming check: no evidence of a slip past dissolution or of the opening being deferred/partial; the whole city-centre through-running network opened.

statement: Well, when fully implemented, the FTA is set to provide an annual boost to our GDP of up to $1.4 billion and to our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion each year.
criterion: Stats NZ and MFAT trade statistics once the FTA's tariff phase-ins are complete: true if annual New Zealand goods and services exports to the EU are up to about $1.8 billion above the pre-FTA baseline with a GDP uplift of the order claimed; false if the realised uplift is materially below that.
reasoning: The criterion requires trade statistics once the FTA's tariff phase-ins are complete (resolve by 2031-12-31). The NZ-EU FTA entered into force on 1 May 2024, with 91% of NZ goods exports duty-free from day one rising to 97% after a seven-year phase-in, i.e. full implementation around 2031; MFAT's own modelling — the source of the $1.4b GDP / $1.8b exports figures McClay quoted — is benchmarked to 2035. As of September 2026 the phase-ins are incomplete and no realised full-implementation uplift exists to test. Separately verifiable: the figures he cited match MFAT's published estimates and he correctly hedged them as 'up to'.

statement: Well, bad luck, it’s not going to last long—another vanity project.
criterion: The Public Service Commission's list of public service departments: true if the Ministry for Regulation has been disestablished or merged into another department by the date below; false if it still exists as a standalone department.
reasoning: The criterion settles on 2026-11-07; today is 2026-09-25, so the date has not passed. Current state as at today: the Ministry for Regulation (formed 1 March 2024) is still a standalone public service department and is listed by the Public Service Commission as one of the five central agencies (DPMC, PSC, Treasury, MfR, Social Investment Agency), CE Grainne Moss. The 2026 machinery-of-government changes disestablished/merged Environment, Transport and Housing & Urban Development into the new MCERT (1 July 2026) but did not include MfR; coverage of the Budget 2026 public service reforms does not name it, and no disestablishment or merger has been announced. So the standing evidence points toward 'false' (the prediction wrong), but it is not yet settleable under the criterion as written.

statement: But on balance, now that we’ve seen the work that they’ve done over the years, we actually think that it would be a shame to disestablish the commission, because it does mean that there will be less research and informed debate on complex issues facing the country.
criterion: Count of broad public inquiry reports on long-term economic and social policy published by Crown agencies (principally the Ministry for Regulation, which inherits the funding) in the two years after the Commission's disestablishment, compared with the Productivity Commission's average annual inquiry output. True if that output is materially lower; false if a successor body publishes inquiry-style public research at a comparable or greater rate.
reasoning: In the two years after the Commission's 29 February 2024 disestablishment, no Crown agency published broad public inquiry reports on long-term economic and social policy. The Ministry for Regulation, which inherited the funding and the Commission's 'functions', publishes sector regulatory-burden reviews instead: early childhood education (final report to the Minister December 2024, published 18 Dec 2024) and agricultural/horticultural products (review ran Aug-Dec 2024); the hospitality, product labelling, solar, telecommunications, hairdressing and 'State of NZ's Regulatory Systems' outputs fall in/after 2026. That is roughly one report a year, and each is a narrow red-tape review of one sector - not comparable to the Commission's ~1.4-1.5 broad inquiries a year (housing affordability, local regulation, using land for housing, better urban planning, low-emissions economy, state sector productivity, local government funding and financing, frontier firms, immigration settings, persistent disadvantage, technological change and the future of work, economic resilience), each with an issues paper, public submissions, draft and final report, plus ~50 research/working papers. Disconfirming check: no successor inquiry body was established 2024-2026; Treasury only re-hosts the archived material; Long-term Insights Briefings (e.g. MBIE/MFAT productivity LTIB 2025) are a pre-existing Public Service Act duty of every department, not new inquiry capacity; and none of the Commission's economists were redeployed. Output of the kind the criterion measures is materially lower, so the criterion's 'true' condition is met.

statement: Second of all, the final report the member’s referred to, I’m advised, will be reported back around mid-February.
criterion: Publication record for the Productivity Commission's 'improving economic resilience' / supply chain resilience inquiry: true if the final report was reported back or released in the first half of February 2024 (roughly 8–20 February), false if it appeared materially later, only at the 29 February wind-up, or not at all.
reasoning: The Productivity Commission released its final 'Improving Economic Resilience' inquiry report on Tuesday 20 February 2024 (media release timestamped 11:46am, issued by the Commission itself); the report cover is dated February (Huitanguru) 2024 and it was covered in the media that week. That is inside the criterion's stated true window of roughly 8-20 February 2024, and nine days before the 29 February 2024 wind-up - so it was not held to the disestablishment date and did not appear materially later. Seymour's 'reported back around mid-February' holds.

statement: If Te Arawhiti is shut down, the Government would lose hundreds of millions of dollars through litigation that you could have prevented.
criterion: Crown Law / Te Arawhiti / Te Puni Kōkiri annual reports and Vote appropriations for Treaty-related litigation and settlement legal costs after any disestablishment; true if such costs rise by hundreds of millions of dollars above the pre-2024 baseline, false if they remain within the historical range.
reasoning: Criterion resolves 2027-06-30; the decisive reporting is not available. Te Arawhiti was not shut down — on 13 Aug 2024 monitoring/settlement-compliance functions moved to Te Puni Kokiri, ~49-51 roles were disestablished, and on 24 Feb 2025 the remnant was renamed Te Tari Whakatau (Office of Treaty Settlements and Takutai Moana), retaining settlements and Takutai Moana functions. So the antecedent occurred only partly. On magnitude, no cost increase of remotely the predicted order has appeared: Te Arawhiti's entire budget was ~$50m/yr, the Waitangi Tribunal costs ~$12-14m/yr to operate (total Tribunal expenses $35m in 2023/24, incl. $19.4m legal aid), the wider Treaty system ~$20-40m/yr, and Treaty Principles Bill defence ~$800k. But the function transfer only completed Feb 2025, FY2025/26 annual reports are not yet published (Crown Law publishes in October), and Treaty litigation costs crystallise over years. Interim evidence runs strongly against the stated magnitude but does not settle the criterion within its window.

statement: So we included that chapter, which, again, is leading the way for international trade agreements, and we will see more countries include that as we move forward.
criterion: Free-trade agreements concluded worldwide after 31 January 2024; true if at least two agreements not involving New Zealand contain a dedicated indigenous-peoples or equivalent trade and economic cooperation chapter, false if none do.
reasoning: The criterion required at least two FTAs concluded after 31 Jan 2024, not involving New Zealand, containing a dedicated indigenous-peoples trade chapter. Two qualify. (1) Australia-UAE CEPA: negotiations concluded 17 Sept 2024, signed 6 Nov 2024, containing Chapter 17 'Indigenous Peoples Trade and Investment Economic Cooperation' — DFAT describes it as Australia's first Indigenous chapter in an FTA, with a First Nations Action Plan launched 26 Nov 2025. (2) Canada-Ecuador FTA: negotiations concluded 4 Feb 2025, including a dedicated 'Trade and Indigenous Peoples' chapter. Checked for disconfirming evidence: the Canada-Indonesia CEPA (concluded Dec 2024, signed Sept 2025) has no such dedicated chapter — Indigenous Peoples appear only once, in the Investment chapter — so adoption is not universal. One caveat not covered by the criterion: the 'leading the way' framing is debatable, since Canada's indigenous-trade chapter practice and the plurilateral IPETCA predate the EU-NZ FTA. The criterion asked only about subsequent adoption, which is met.

statement: On the surface, this is a good deal for New Zealand, that Māori will see little to no benefit from in the long run.
criterion: Stats NZ / MFAT export data and Te Ōhanga Māori reporting on Māori-owned enterprise exports to the EU in the years after entry into force: false if Māori-owned exporters record materially increased EU export value or new EU market entry attributable to the FTA, true if their EU export share is flat or declining while overall NZ exports to the EU rise.
reasoning: The claim is explicitly about the long run and the criterion resolves 2029-05-01; the FTA entered force 1 May 2024, so only one partial post-FTA year is measurable. The evidence so far cuts against the claim. Stats NZ's Tatauranga umanga Maori (released 29 Aug 2025) reports EU goods exports by 'other Maori enterprises' nearly doubling from ~$8m to $15m between 2023 and 2024 — wine, honey, value-added agricultural products — and Stats NZ links the growth to the FTA's entry into force. The EU is among Maori authorities' top export destinations, and in 2024 70% of Maori authority goods export value went to markets other than China and the US. Overall NZ exports to the EU rose 28% to $7.88b in the year to June 2025, so the Maori EU share rose rather than stayed flat or declined: the criterion's 'true' branch is not met and its 'false' branch is provisionally triggered. But that rests on eight months of FTA operation on a $15m base, which is too thin to settle a long-run claim; the 2029 window remains open.

statement: Well, you know, the member has been in Cabinet, so she’ll be aware that the Prime Minister is responsible for all Ministers. In respect of Casey Costello, I have full confidence in her, and I’m sure that, in time, that member will too.
criterion: Public statements by Carmel Sepuloni (Hansard, press releases, media interviews) about Casey Costello's performance as a Minister. True if she publicly expresses confidence in, or withdraws her call for the dismissal of, Casey Costello before the end of the parliamentary term; false if she continues to criticise Costello's fitness for office or to call for her dismissal.
reasoning: Seymour predicted Sepuloni would in time share his confidence in Casey Costello. No public statement by Sepuloni expressing confidence in Costello, or withdrawing criticism of her, exists anywhere I could find. The opposite held: Labour escalated, calling for Costello's sacking in October 2024 over the heated-tobacco-products tax cut (Verrall), attacking her Seniors performance in May 2025 (Leary), and Sepuloni herself was still challenging Costello directly in the House as late as 23 July 2026 during the virginity-testing bill debate. Costello remained a Minister through Budget 2026, so the government never conceded either. I checked specifically for disconfirming evidence (any Sepuloni praise or acknowledgement of Costello) and found none. The term formally closes 2026-11-07, about six weeks out, but the observed 2.5-year pattern plus an election campaign makes a reversal implausible; the criterion's 'false' branch (continues to criticise) is already satisfied.

statement: Many provincial and rural communities are already experiencing large shortages of doctors, and with many GPs planning to retire over the next 10 years, this issue will only get worse. A medical school which further considers the needs of rural areas will help ease the pressure felt on rural healthcare.
criterion: Rural GP workforce measures (RNZCGP workforce survey rural vacancy rate and rural GP headcount per capita) in 2034 compared with 2024: true if rural shortage measures have worsened, false if the rural vacancy rate has fallen or rural GP supply per capita has improved.
reasoning: The criterion as written requires RNZCGP workforce-survey rural vacancy rate and rural GP headcount per capita in 2034 compared with 2024. Today is 2026-09-26; the 2034 comparison point does not exist. The most recent RNZCGP Workforce Survey published is the 2024 survey (fielded Oct-Dec 2024, 1,374 respondents), which does report 35% of GP respondents intending to retire within five years and a projected ~300 GP shortfall by 2031 worst in rural areas - consistent with Reti's direction but nowhere near the evidence the criterion demands. I did not substitute an earlier comparison year, since the criterion names 2034 explicitly.

statement: Does she accept that because a person on the jobseeker is likely to be up to $50 worse off by the end of the decade, demand for hardship grants and advances will increase under her Government?
criterion: MSD hardship assistance statistics (special needs grants and recoverable advances, number and value per quarter) for 2030 compared with 2024: true if the volume of hardship grants and advances has risen materially, false if flat or falling.
reasoning: The criterion requires MSD hardship assistance statistics (special needs grants and recoverable advances, number and value per quarter) for 2030 compared with 2024, and the claim itself is pegged to a jobseeker being worse off 'by the end of the decade'. Today is 2026-09-26. MSD's published Benefit Fact Sheets currently run only to the June 2026 quarter, so the 2030 comparison point does not exist. As with the previous item, I did not substitute a nearer year for the one the criterion names.

statement: I’m very encouraged by the progress that has been achieved there in the horticulture sector, especially for our honey sector and for our seafood sectors, who are all going to see significant benefits once this EU-NZ free-trade agreement comes into force.
criterion: Stats NZ export statistics for honey, seafood and horticulture to the EU for the two years after entry into force (1 May 2024), compared with the two years prior: true if those categories show a material increase in export value to the EU, false if EU export value for them is flat or falls.
reasoning: FTA entered into force 1 May 2024. Two of the three named categories show large, clearly documented increases in EU export value: horticulture +38% to $1.17b in the year to June 2025 (kiwifruit +42% to $1.04b, then +69%/+$316m in the year to Dec 2025), and seafood +28% to $363m (hoki +29% to $141m, mussels +69% to $72m). Total goods exports to the EU reached ~$8.8b in the year to Dec 2025, up 29% and ~$3.1b above the pre-FTA level, well ahead of the $1.8b/yr forecast. Honey cannot be verified separately: neither Stats NZ nor MFAT publishes an EU-specific honey export series I could reach, so that leg is unconfirmed rather than confirmed. But there is no disconfirming evidence — the 17.3% tariff on manuka honey went to zero at entry into force (non-manuka phasing out over three years), and total NZ honey export revenue rose 11% to $419m to June 2024 and again in 2025. On the criterion as written (material increase vs flat/falling), the verified categories are materially up and none are flat or falling.

statement: One is that the Minister has not risen to answer—and will not—the very relevant question put to him by two members now on this side of the Chamber.
criterion: The Hansard record for the remainder of this committee stage; true if the Minister made no response addressing provisions for the affected staff, false if he rose and addressed that question.
reasoning: The Hansard record for the remainder of that committee stage (NZ Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill, In Committee, clauses 1 and 2, 31 Jan 2024) refutes the prediction. Genter's words appear at p.1069 of the Final Daily. On p.1070, immediately after her contribution, Hon David Seymour (Minister for Regulation) rose and said 'I want to turn to the question from Grant Robertson in relation to those staff', then set out at length that his first instructions to officials were to deal with staff in a way that was respectful and accommodated their needs and the Crown's obligations to them as a priority, that he would not comment further while negotiations were under way, that those obligations would pass to the Treasury, and that if the Treasury needed support to honour that commitment it would be provided. Only after that did Laura Trask move closure and the clause 1 and 2 votes were taken. He rose, and he addressed the affected-staff question.

statement: They will need to be registered to work in these roles, and this is likely to drive an increase in demand for the experience pathway over the coming years.
criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual reports for 2024/25 and 2025/26: true if applications for registration via the experience pathway rise relative to the 2023/24 baseline; false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion names the SWRB annual reports for 2024/25 and 2025/26. Only the first exists. The SWRB Annual Report 2024-2025 (year to 30 June 2025) shows the section 13 experience pathway rising against the 2023/24 baseline: new registrants by pathway went from 6% of 744 new registrations in 2023/24 (~45) to 10% of 583 in 2024/25 (~58) — a rise in both share and absolute number, and the report notes the s13 timeliness target was missed (63% vs 80%), consistent with increased pressure on that pathway. The 2025/26 report is not published (SWRB's year ended 30 June 2026; the publications page lists 2024-2025 as the most recent), and the stated resolve-by date of 31 Dec 2026 has not passed, so the criterion cannot yet be fully applied. Relevant caveat for when it can: s13 was repealed on 28 Feb 2026 with applications closing 27 Feb 2026, so any 2025/26 spike may reflect a closing rush rather than the sustained 'demand over the coming years' Sepuloni predicted. Evidence so far points toward the prediction holding.

statement: The termination of this work is anticipated to save a further $343 million, aligning with our Government's objective to curb irresponsible spending.
criterion: DIA/Treasury reporting or Budget documents on savings realised from winding up the water services entity; true if the avoided cost is around $343 million, false if materially less.
reasoning: The criterion requires DIA/Treasury reporting or Budget documents on savings realised from winding up the water services entity. No such reporting exists. The Water Services Acts Repeal Bill was explicitly exempted from a Regulatory Impact Statement under Cabinet's suspension of RIS requirements for 100-day plan proposals, so no official costed fiscal analysis of the repeal's savings was ever published. DIA's Annual Report 2024-25 does not quantify any savings, underspend or returned funding from winding up the water services reform programme (its only baseline saving in this area is $1.5m on Chatham Islands wharves). The $343 million figure appears nowhere outside Brown's own Hansard statement of 2024-02-13 - not in Treasury's Budget 2024 documents, not in the December 2023 mini-budget savings list, and not in press reporting including the main journalistic accounting of the programme's $1.2bn spend. Disconfirming check: I searched for evidence the repeal cost rather than saved money. Wind-up costs are documented (roughly $710,000 in redundancy for two establishment chief executives) and the ~$1.2bn already spent was largely sunk, but neither speaks to whether ~$343m of forward spending was avoided, so 'wrong' is not supported. The resolve-by date of 2026-06-30 has passed, so this is not not_yet_due; the named evidence simply was never produced.

statement: Mayors and councillors will be forced to increase rates, they will cop it from ratepayers, and ratepayers will cop it in the back pocket.
criterion: Council long-term plans adopted for 2024-34 and DIA/Stats NZ local authority rates data; true if average council rates increases over 2024-2026 run materially above the preceding trend, false if they do not.
reasoning: Stats NZ measures local authority rates annually in the September quarter. The series: +8.8% in the year to September 2023 (the preceding year), +12.2% to September 2024 (the largest rise in the series), +8.8% to September 2025. For 2026/27 the Taxpayers' Union dashboard records an average proposed increase of 6.92% (7.23% including water delivery reform costs). Trend anchors: Stats NZ itself notes the 2018-2025 average was around 7.3%, and an LGNZ-commissioned report put the average over the 20 years to 2022 at 5.7% per year. The 2024-2026 window therefore averages roughly 9.3%, materially above both trend anchors, satisfying the criterion as written. Two qualifications: the excess concentrated almost entirely in the 2024/25 year, and by 2026/27 proposed increases had fallen back to around the recent trend, so the effect faded rather than persisted. Separately, the criterion tests only the rates trend, not McAnulty's implied causal attribution of the rises to the Three Waters repeal, which this data can neither confirm nor refute - councils also faced infrastructure backlogs, insurance and interest costs over the same period.

statement: Ultimately, councils will then be faced with putting in place higher rate rises, meaning higher costs for households who are already stretched to the limit.
criterion: Council long-term plans adopted mid-2024 and LGNZ/DIA rates data for the 2024/25 year; true if average territorial authority rates increases for 2024/25 are materially higher than those set for 2023/24, false if they are flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether average territorial authority rates increases for 2024/25 were materially higher than those set for 2023/24, and is false if they were flat or lower. Both available measures show a clear acceleration. Stats NZ CPI: local authority rates and payments rose 12.2% in the year to the September 2024 quarter, against 8.8% in the year to September 2023 - a 3.4 percentage point acceleration, and the largest rise in the series. The Taxpayers' Union's independent tally of adopted long-term plans put the average district council increase for 2024/25 at over 14%, with outliers such as Buller at 31.8%, Napier 23.7% and Hamilton 19.9%. For context, the LGNZ-commissioned figure for the 20 years to 2022 was 5.7% per year. Disconfirming check: I looked for evidence 2024/25 increases were flat or lower, and found none - every source points the same way. The falsification condition is clearly not met. Note the criterion tests only the rates outcome, not Pham's causal chain from the repeal to those rises.

statement: I feel sorry for the mayors who are sitting in the gallery today, because I don’t think they’ll be around very long once they have to implement the rates hikes that they will be implementing in their councils.
criterion: Results of the October 2025 New Zealand local body elections for the Otago/Southland mayors referenced (Clutha, Central Otago, Gore, Dunedin): true if a clear majority of the incumbent mayors named are voted out or do not return to office, false if most are returned.
reasoning: October 2025 results for the four named mayoralties: Dunedin — incumbent Jules Radich stood and lost, excluded on 8.05% of primary votes, Sophie Barker elected (Newsroom ties the national turnover explicitly to rates rises: 31 of 66 councils elected new mayors). Clutha — Bryan Cadogan did not seek re-election after 15 years, Jock Martin elected. Central Otago — Tim Cadogan had already resigned in October 2024 to work at Taumata Arowai; his replacement Tamah Alley was re-elected with 60.29%. Gore — Ben Bell re-elected with 3,392 to 1,508, more than 2:1, on the district's highest-ever turnout. So three of four are not in office, which satisfies the criterion's literal 'voted out or do not return' threshold, but only one (Dunedin) was actually rejected by voters; two departures were voluntary and unrelated to rates, and the incumbent who did face voters after implementing rises was returned comfortably. The prediction's substance ('they won't be around long once they implement the rates hikes') holds nationally and for Dunedin, but is materially overstated for the named group.

statement: We’ll either have councils going bankrupt or councils not meeting their regulatory requirements in terms of water standards.
criterion: Whether, by the resolve-by date, any New Zealand territorial authority becomes insolvent or is placed under Crown/statutory intervention for inability to fund water services, OR Taumata Arowai formally records councils failing drinking-water or wastewater standards on funding grounds. True if either occurs; false if all councils remain solvent and compliant.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-12-31, fifteen months after today's date, and neither limb of the criterion is yet cleanly satisfied. Limb 1 (insolvency or Crown/statutory intervention for inability to fund water services): no New Zealand territorial authority is insolvent. Water-related interventions exist but not on that ground — the October 2024 Crown Observer at Wellington City Council was appointed over the opposite complaint, that WCC was funding 94% of water capex from rates rather than debt and would overcharge ratepayers by $700m; the March 2026 Crown Review Team at Wellington Water followed the 4 February 2026 Moa Point treatment-plant collapse, and its report found systemic leadership and asset-management failure including that Wellington Water had no funding plan for the plant, but that is a review of a company, not a Crown intervention in a council for inability to fund. Wairoa's Crown Manager relates to a flood-protection project, not water-services funding. Limb 2 (Taumata Arowai formally recording councils failing standards on funding grounds): non-compliance is formally recorded — a compliance order against Queenstown Lakes over the untreated Two Mile plant, 10 of 29 advised councils unable to meet the end-2025 treatment-barrier deadline, and the Network Environmental Performance Report 2024/25 (27 July 2026) recording 'considerable non-compliance with wastewater consent conditions' and 11,535 annual overflows — but the regulator attributes these to capacity constraints, rainfall, poor asset condition and blockages, not to funding. The claim is trending toward its true side but the funding attribution the criterion requires is not on the record, and the window is still open.

statement: I predict that in three years’ time, when we come back to an election again, we won’t have updated legislation that’s working. We won’t have any new council-controlled organisations. We won’t have the investment that we needed, but we would have seen ratepayers having a significant increase in the cost of their rates.
criterion: As at the 2026 general election: (a) whether replacement water services legislation has been enacted and is in force; (b) whether any new water council-controlled organisations have been established under it; (c) whether territorial authority average rates increases since 2024 exceed the pre-reform trend on LGNZ/Stats NZ local authority financial statistics. True if all four hold, false if the legislation is in force and new water CCOs exist.
reasoning: The criterion's explicit falsifying condition is met. (a) Replacement legislation is enacted and in force: the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 (No 42) came into force 27 August 2025. (b) New water council-controlled organisations exist under it: five began operating on 1 July 2026 — Tiaki Wai (Wellington region, five councils, replacing Wellington Water), IAWAI Flowing Waters and Waikato Waters Ltd, the Kaikoura-Hurunui joint organisation and Selwyn Water — with a further 13 expected within twelve months, plus Water Hawke's Bay established. (c) Her rates limb did hold: average increases of roughly 12.2% (2024), 8.4% (2025) and 6.9-7.9% (2026/27), about 34.5% cumulative over three years against 13.7% inflation, with rates the largest single contributor to CPI in the June 2025 quarter. The 2026 general election has not yet been held, but nothing on 7 November can undo (a) or (b), so the prediction is already settled against her on two of its three specifics.

statement: It will mean the road where that culvert exists does not have to close when we have heavy rain in Nelson, and it will mean that the businesses in that area, like our meatworks, won’t suffer economic loss if we have a heavy rain event.
criterion: Nelson City Council and local road-closure records for the road crossing the Saxton Creek culvert after the upgrade is commissioned: true if no flood-related closures or reported business flood losses occur at that site during subsequent significant rain events, false if the road closes or those businesses report flood damage in a comparable rain event.
reasoning: The upgrade was delivered as described: the Main Road Stoke culvert went from 1.8m/1-in-5-year to 7.9m/1-in-100-year capacity and the $40m Saxton Creek project is complete and officially opened. Since commissioning, Nelson has had several significant rain events — flash flooding 26 May 2025 (central city: Rutherford, Vanguard, Van Diemen Sts, not Stoke), states of emergency 27 June and 11 July 2025, and a 200mm event on 2 June 2026 (surface flooding reported on SH6 Stoke between Quarantine and Salisbury Rds, north of the Saxton crossing, no closure at the culvert). I found no report of Main Road Stoke closing at the Saxton Creek crossing, and no report of Wakatu/Saxton businesses or the meatworks suffering flood losses, in any of those events — notable because the pre-upgrade 2022 closure of exactly that stretch (Salisbury Rd to Saxton Rd roundabouts, Saxton Creek flooding) was reported. Short of full confirmation because the evidence is absence-of-reports rather than a positive council statement, and the 2025 events were centred on Tasman rather than the Stoke catchment, so a truly comparable rain event at that site may not yet have occurred.

statement: I’d suggest you won’t be voted in next time.
criterion: Results of the October 2025 New Zealand local body elections for the mayors and councillors the speaker is addressing — those who campaigned against the Three Waters reform and are consulting on the large rates increases he names (Far North, Hamilton, Buller, Porirua). True if a majority of those incumbents lost their seats or did not return; false if a majority were re-elected.
reasoning: October 2025 results for the four councils named in the criterion: Far North — incumbent mayor Moko Tepania re-elected (51.9% of primary votes, defeating Ann Court) and 7 of the 10 incumbent councillors who stood were returned; Porirua — incumbent mayor Anita Baker re-elected to a third term; Buller — incumbent mayor Jamie Cleine defeated by Chris Russell by about 135 votes (1,432 to 1,331); Hamilton — incumbent mayor Paula Southgate did not stand, announcing in January 2025 that she was stepping down, so Tim Macindoe's win (18,275 to Sarah Thomson's 10,183) unseated no incumbent. Only one of the four mayors was actually voted out, one retired, and two were re-elected; adding the councillors, the clear majority of incumbents returned, which is the criterion's 'false' branch.

statement: So, with the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023, my question is: why is it that he’s getting rid of it when we know that it will need to be replaced and, essentially, there’ll be something very similar put in its place?
criterion: Legislation enacted by the current Government for water services economic regulation and consumer protection: true if a statute is passed conferring economic regulation of water suppliers (e.g. on the Commerce Commission) plus consumer protection/dispute resolution comparable to the repealed Act; false if no such replacement framework is enacted.
reasoning: The Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023 was repealed on 17 February 2024 by s10 of the Water Services Acts Repeal Act 2024, and the Government then enacted a replacement framework: the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 and the Local Government (Water Services) (Repeals and Amendments) Act 2025 (passed August 2025) insert a water services economic regulation regime into Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986, making the Commerce Commission the economic regulator for water services and giving it responsibility for the consumer protection regime, with information disclosure requirements and revenue thresholds; the first information disclosure rules apply from 27 February 2026. That is the 'something very similar put in its place' Webb predicted — the same regulator and substantially the same economic regulation plus consumer protection functions, relocated from a standalone Act into the Commerce Act.

statement: You’ll have to come up with a whole new framing of it which does fundamentally the same thing.
criterion: The legislative record for the 54th Parliament; true if a Government bill is enacted or introduced that establishes economic regulation and/or a consumer protection framework for water services performing substantially the functions of the repealed Act, false if the term ends with no such replacement regime legislated.
reasoning: The Water Services Acts Repeal Act 2024 (in force 17 Feb 2024) repealed the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023. The Government then introduced and enacted a replacement regime: the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 (No 42, Aug 2025), whose Commerce Act amendments make the Commerce Commission the economic regulator for water services and give it responsibility for the consumer protection regime (information disclosure rules in force 27 Feb 2026, plus powers for complaints-process regulations and a service quality code). That is a Government bill, enacted within the 54th Parliament, performing substantially the economic-regulation and consumer-protection functions of the repealed Act under a new framing — precisely what the criterion requires.

statement: Now, as it turns out, the Far North District Council—we estimate that without water services reforms, by 2051, every ratepayer there will end up paying another $8,690.
criterion: Far North District Council water charges in 2051 against the DIA water services reform modelling on which the figure rests: true if the average Far North ratepayer's annual water cost in 2051 is around $8,690 above the reform-scenario figure; false if the eventual cost is materially below that.
reasoning: The criterion is an outcome in 2051 (resolve by 2051-06-30) — twenty-five years away, so no evidence can settle it now. Searching for the $8,690 figure also found no published DIA per-ratepayer 2051 modelling line for Far North online, and the reform scenario the figure was calculated against was itself repealed in February 2024 (Far North instead joined a Northland-wide water entity), so the comparison baseline no longer exists in the form assumed. Neither of those makes the prediction wrong; the date simply has not passed.

statement: I guarantee that the councils in that proposed cluster won’t want to have a bar of Tararua, a region with only 12,000 rating units— $600 million they need to spend over 30 years.
criterion: The water services delivery arrangements agreed by Horizons-region councils; false if Tararua District Council is accepted into a joint water services entity or council-controlled organisation with other Manawatū-Whanganui councils, true if the other councils decline and Tararua is left to go it alone.
reasoning: The directional call held: Tararua is not in a joint entity with other Manawatū-Whanganui councils. Palmerston North, Horowhenua and Rangitīkei formed Central Districts Water (DIA-approved Nov 2025) without it; Whanganui/Ruapehu/Rangitīkei pursued their own grouping; Manawatū DC withdrew because its own modelling showed higher charges. But the prediction's substance — that the cluster wouldn't have a bar of Tararua, leaving it stranded — is materially overstated. The record shows Tararua resolved to exit the Manawatū-Whanganui model itself (65% of local submitters favoured a regional model) and was welcomed as an equal shareholder in Waitī Waters with Masterton, Carterton and South Wairarapa: joint WSDP submitted 29 Aug 2025, approved by DIA, CCO legally established by 1 July 2026 and taking over services 1 July 2027, with ~12% forecast savings. So neither criterion branch is satisfied cleanly — Tararua was not accepted into a Manawatū-Whanganui entity (so not false), but it was not left to go it alone either (so not fully true), and I found no evidence that the Horizons councils declined Tararua over its 12,000 rating units or $600m programme.

statement: So the $180 million waste that he’s talking about was actually an establishment, going towards fixing that problem, and the waste that that Government will deliver to New Zealanders is that during a cost of living crisis we will see Kiwis having to pay double, triple, quadruple rates for what would have been achieved through having a simple solution.
criterion: Council long-term plans and adopted water charges/rates for the councils affected by Local Water Done Well, compared against pre-reform baselines: true if water-related charges in a substantial number of councils rise by 100 percent or more over the period covered; false if typical increases remain well below a doubling.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-06-30; today is 2026-09-26, and only the first one to two years of the LWDW charge ramp have actually been set. Adopted increases so far are well short of a doubling: the Taxpayers' Union 2026 Rates Dashboard puts the average total cost increase for the fourteen councils newly facing separate water charges at 15.88% for 2026/27 (6.14% headline rates plus the new water charge), lifting the national average cost increase from 6.9% to 9.0%. Ten-year projections in the priced water services delivery plans are genuinely split rather than uniformly doubling. On the supporting side: Tiaki Wai (Wellington, Porirua, Lower Hutt, Upper Hutt) projects an average bill of ~$2,418 in 2026/27 rising to ~$6,206-$6,831 by 2035/36, roughly a tripling; New Plymouth ~$1,200 now to ~$2,700 by 2033 (+125%); Hastings ~$1,400 in 2024/25 to ~$2,200 in 2026/27 and ~$3,100 in ten years (+121%). On the disconfirming side, which I went looking for: Hamilton forecasts +28% and Waikato District +14% over the next decade, and Auckland's Watercare bills rise 7% this year. So 'water-related charges in a substantial number of councils rise by 100 percent or more' is not established, and 'typical increases remain well below a doubling' is not clearly established either. 'Triple' is reached only in Wellington at the far end of a ten-year horizon; nothing I found supports 'quadruple'. The criterion should be re-run after the resolve-by date against adopted charges rather than forecasts.

statement: What they are going to replace it with will not be as affordable.
criterion: Compare average household/ratepayer water charges projected under the repealed Affordable Water Reforms (DIA and WICS modelling published 2022-23) with the charges actually set under Local Water Done Well once councils' water services delivery plans are priced; true if LWDW charges are materially higher for most ratepayers, false if equal or lower.
reasoning: The criterion asks for a specific comparison: DIA/WICS 2022-23 modelling of household charges under the repealed Affordable Water Reforms versus charges actually set under Local Water Done Well once water services delivery plans are priced. The LWDW half of that now exists (all WSDPs submitted by September 2025, approvals from November 2025, first separate bills issued by Tiaki Wai in August 2026). The Affordable Water Reforms half does not exist in a comparable form: the published 2022-23 figures were savings against a 'no reform' counterfactual (the Government's claim of $2,770-$5,400 per household per year by 2054), not a per-household charge series that can be set beside today's adopted charges, and the underlying WICS aggregation modelling was itself contested. I searched for any official or independent like-for-like comparison - DIA, Commerce Commission, Auditor-General, Infrastructure Commission, RNZ, Newsroom - and found none. What exists is contested assertion on both sides: Local Government Minister Watts says LWDW has proved more affordable; Labour's Tangi Utikere and sector commentators argue 42 entities forgo the scale efficiencies, noting councils' water plans came in at ~$49.7bn, about $9bn above their own earlier long-term plans (though AWR was separately forecast at $120-185bn over 30 years, a different horizon and basis). S&P declined to call it either way. Rising LWDW bills alone do not settle the criterion, because the counterfactual entity would also have had to fund the same infrastructure deficit. The comparison as written cannot be made from available evidence.

statement: There is no way that Canterbury will join them—no one will.
criterion: Water services delivery plans and joint water services CCO arrangements established under Local Water Done Well: prediction true if no Canterbury territorial authority has joined a joint water services entity with West Coast councils by the resolve-by date; false if at least one has.
reasoning: The resolve-by date (2026-06-30) has passed. The joint water services entity formed by the West Coast councils under Local Water Done Well is Coast Waters Ltd, owned by Buller, Grey and Westland district councils only. Their joint water services delivery plan was approved by the Department of Internal Affairs in November 2025, the establishment board (chair Darin Cusack, with James Ryan and Onno Mulder) was appointed in 2026, and the CCO stands up by July 2027. No Canterbury territorial authority is a shareholder or has joined. I checked the disconfirming side specifically: the Canterbury councils all made separate arrangements - Hurunui and Kaikoura formed their own two-council joint water services CCO (Hurunui voted 8-3 on 13 May 2025; DIA approved it among the first ten plans), Waimakariri chose an in-house business unit, and Christchurch retained in-house control in May 2025. The 'Canterbury water coalition' reported in 2025-26 is a Canterbury-only grouping with no West Coast participant. So no Canterbury TA had joined a joint water services entity with West Coast councils by the resolve-by date.

statement: As LTPs have rolled out this year, I’ve got absolutely no doubt there will be more money put in by councils right across the board to do that.
criterion: The 2024–34 council Long-Term Plans adopted during 2024, compared with the previous (2021–31) LTPs: true if the large majority of councils budgeted increased capital spending on water infrastructure; false if increases were confined to a minority of councils or water budgets were held flat or cut across the board.
reasoning: The Auditor-General's report on the adopted 2024-34 long-term plans found the 58 councils covered plan to spend $38.6 billion on three waters assets over the decade, a 57% increase on their 2021-31 long-term plans (total capex $91.9b, +34%). Councils cite population growth, infrastructure deficits, cost escalation and service-level improvement; the post-repeal directive to fund water across all ten years (rather than years 1-2 only) pushed water back into every plan. Individual provincial councils confirm the pattern — Clutha attributed $12m of a required $15m rates increase to three waters expenditure. Disconfirming check: a handful of councils cut or deferred water work (Horowhenua slashed capex; Manawatu was recommitting to previously deferred renewals), and the OAG flagged deferral of renewals beyond the 10-year window as an audit concern, so 'right across the board' is not literally universal. But the criterion's false condition — increases confined to a minority, or water budgets flat/cut across the board — is plainly not met. Note the direct evidence is the aggregate +57%, not a per-council tally.

statement: They’re suddenly realising that, actually, the people they represent out in the rural areas are going to be hit with bigger rates bills because of the National Government’s irresponsible approach.
criterion: Rates increases adopted in rural/provincial councils' 2024/25 and 2025/26 annual plans and long-term plans (Local Government NZ / DIA rates data); true if average rates rises in predominantly rural districts are substantially above prior-year levels with council documents attributing part of the rise to retained water services, false if rural rates rises are flat or in line with earlier years.
reasoning: Rates in predominantly rural/provincial districts rose far above prior-year levels in 2024/25, and the councils themselves attribute a large share to retaining three waters after the repeal — which is exactly what the criterion asks. LGNZ's analysis of 48 draft long-term plans put average rises at ~15% for 2024/25, against a prior norm nearer 6%. Provincial districts sat at the top: Clutha adopted ~20.97% in year 1 (its own consultation says 'the need for the continued provision of three waters services to our communities, following the recent repeal of three waters legislation, is having a significant financial impact' and that $12m of a $15m increase is attributable to three waters; the unsmoothed water-driven rise would have been 45%); Tararua 16.29%. In 2025/26 rises moderated but stayed elevated — 8.39% national average (Taxpayers' Union) against 2.5% inflation, with Clutha still at 16.59%. Disconfirming evidence, which the criterion does not test but which qualifies the literal word 'rural': water-driven increases fall on reticulated properties, so within districts town ratepayers often bore more than rural ones — Central Hawke's Bay put town households near 12% and 'those rural areas without water services... around 5 per cent'. Cost escalation in construction was also a driver alongside the retained water services, but the criterion only requires councils to attribute part of the rise to water.

statement: Double-digit rates increases, year after year—that is what’s coming, folks, and in many cases we will not see the progress that is needed towards cleaning up our waterways, delivering safe drinking water for our communities, and futureproofing our cities against the floods that we will increasingly see as a result of climate change.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Stats NZ local authority rates data and adopted council long-term plans for the 2024/25 and 2025/26 rating years. True if the average territorial authority rates increase exceeds 10 percent in each of at least two consecutive years after the repeal; false if the average increase falls below 10 percent in either year.
reasoning: The criterion requires the average rates increase to exceed 10% in each of at least two consecutive years after the repeal, and is false if it falls below 10% in either year. Stats NZ CPI (which captures rates once a year in the September quarter) shows local authority rates and payments up 12.2% in the year to the June 2025 quarter — the 2024/25 rating year, the highest in decades — but only 8.8% annually in the September 2025 quarter, i.e. the 2025/26 rating year. The Taxpayers' Union's independent dashboard agrees: an 8.39% average for 2025/26 against 2024/25's 'over 14%'. So the double-digit rise happened once and then stepped down; 'year after year' did not eventuate on the measure the criterion names. Disconfirming check: the second year is still roughly three times CPI inflation (2.5-3.0%) and cumulative three-year rises are ~34.5%, so the substance of a rates shock holds — but the criterion's explicit numeric test fails on the second year.

statement: That cumulative $2,000 that people will lose over the period of four years will result in higher debts, less ability to engage in their communities, more toxic stress in those families, and more children growing up in poverty—all to be able to afford tax cuts for the rich.
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship and after-housing-costs 50% median measures) and MSD hardship assistance / recoverable assistance grant volumes for the years to June 2028; true if child poverty rates and beneficiary debt rise over the period, false if they fall or are flat.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2028-06-30; today is 2026-09-26, and the criterion asks for child poverty and MSD hardship/debt data 'for the years to June 2028'. Two further Stats NZ releases (YE June 2026 and 2027) fall inside the window. Interim evidence is mixed rather than confirming: child material hardship rose from 13.5% (YE June 2024) to 14.3% (YE June 2025, ~169,300 children) — a 10-year high and a significant rise from 10.6% in 2022 — but Stats NZ records no statistically significant annual change 2024-to-2025, and both income measures moved slightly the other way (BHC50 12.7%->12.6%; AHC50 fixed line 18.2%->17.8%). MSD debt data is too stale to judge the beneficiary-debt limb: the most recent published series ends at June 2021 ($980m owed, 66% of main-benefit recipients), with aggregate figures of ~$1.26b overpayment and ~$1.2b recoverable assistance to March 2024. Not enough to settle either limb, and the date has not passed.

statement: However, by the end of the forecast period in 2028, the rate is expected to be $18.15 less per week than if it was indexed to net average wage growth.
criterion: MSD/Treasury benefit rate tables for the jobseeker support rate (single, 25+) at the end of the 2028 forecast period, compared against the counterfactual rate produced by net-average-wage indexation over the same period. True if the CPI-indexed rate is roughly $18 per week lower; false if the gap is materially smaller, absent, or reversed.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2028-12-31; the criterion requires the jobseeker (single 25+) rate at the end of the 2028 forecast period against a net-average-wage counterfactual, and two annual adjustments (1 April 2027 and 1 April 2028) have not happened. Interim track, from official rate tables: jobseeker single 25+ went $337.74 (1 Apr 2023) -> $353.46 (1 Apr 2024, CPI 4.66%) -> $361.31 (1 Apr 2025, CPI 2.22%) -> $372.55 (1 Apr 2026, CPI 3.11%). The counterfactual has not moved consistently against beneficiaries: Work and Income states that for the 1 April 2026 adjustment CPI rose 3.11% while average wage growth rose 2.91%, so main benefits received the LARGER adjustment that year, narrowing rather than widening the gap; 2025 went the other way (CPI 2.22% vs a wage-linked NZ Super rise of just over 3%). I could not locate the source document behind the specific $18.15 figure; a contemporaneous report gives the parallel sole-parent figure as $31.27/week lower by 2028 ($542.19), which is consistent with the claim being a legitimate departmental projection rather than invented. Direction of travel is genuinely open, and the date has not passed.

statement: The savings the Government supposedly will make by lowering benefit increases will be incurred in costs by people needing to get hardship grants and people needing to take on more debt just to survive.
criterion: MSD hardship assistance statistics (special needs grants, advances and recoverable assistance) across the forecast period following the indexation change: true if the number and value of hardship grants and recoverable assistance debt rise materially after the change relative to the pre-change trend; false if hardship assistance volumes and beneficiary debt are flat or fall.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2028-06-30; the criterion asks for hardship assistance volumes and recoverable-assistance debt 'across the forecast period following the indexation change', which runs to 2028. Interim evidence does not support the claim and points at a confound the criterion does not handle. Food-grant applications were essentially flat across the change (1,387,359 in 2023; 1,359,171 in 2024; 1,401,600 in 2025), while the decline rate rose from 3.96% to 6.33% (a ~60% relative increase) and 66% more special-needs-grant applications of all categories were declined than two years earlier — MSD attributes this to restored manager-approval requirements from December 2023. More than 318,000 people applied for food grants in 2025 (~1.4m applications, >$130m paid). So the volume of assistance actually PAID may be flat or falling even if underlying need rises, which would read as 'false' on the criterion as written for a reason unrelated to indexation. The recoverable-assistance-debt limb is not yet checkable: the most recent published MSD debt series ends at June 2021, with aggregates of ~$1.2b recoverable assistance to March 2024 and total MSD debt over $2b. Date has not passed.

statement: In the short term, New Zealanders enduring the cost of living crisis can expect that main benefit rates will remain broadly similar.
criterion: MSD's published main benefit rates effective 1 April 2024, compared with the rates net-average-wage indexation would have produced for the same date; true if the CPI-indexed rates are within roughly 1 percent of that counterfactual, false if materially lower.
reasoning: The 1 April 2024 Annual General Adjustment increased main benefits by 4.66 percent (CPI, year to December 2023) — Jobseeker Support single 25+ moved from $337.72 to $353.46 net per week. The net-average-wage counterfactual for the same date was 5.2–5.3 percent (5.3 percent was the wage-growth figure cited in the February 2024 debate; MSD's regulatory impact statement on indexing main benefits to inflation gives CPI ~4.7 percent against wage ~5.2 percent). The resulting rate difference is roughly 0.6 percent (about $2/week at the JSS single rate), inside the criterion's 'within roughly 1 percent' band. So for the April 2024 adjustment the rates were indeed broadly similar to what wage indexation would have produced. The criterion is explicitly short-term; long-run divergence is real (contemporaneous analysis put Jobseeker around $50/week lower by 2030 under CPI indexation, and Herald analysis put disabled beneficiaries $2,300/year lower by 2028) but is not what this criterion tests.

statement: And here we have a Government who are now reversing that change and putting us at risk for having increased numbers of children living in poverty moving forward.
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship rate and the after-housing-costs 50% of median measure) for the years to June 2027 against the June 2024 baseline; true if the number or rate of children in poverty rises beyond sampling error, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion is written against Stats NZ child poverty statistics for the year to June 2027, measured from a June 2024 baseline, with a resolve-by date of 31 March 2028. Today is 26 September 2026; the year-to-June-2027 release will not appear until around February 2028, and even the year-to-June-2026 figures are not yet published. The most recent data available (year ended June 2025, released 26 February 2026) shows no statistically significant movement on either nominated measure against the year ended June 2024 — material hardship 14.3 percent of children, AHC-50 (fixed-line) 17.8 percent — so the claim is neither borne out nor refuted so far. Nothing in the criterion can be settled yet; no score.

statement: The cost of living is actually quite high and therefore beneficiaries will be better off under our changes.
criterion: MSD published main benefit rates at the April 2025 adjustment compared with the rates that wage indexation would have produced (Stats NZ average ordinary time weekly earnings). True if CPI-indexed rates are at or above the wage-indexed counterfactual; false if below.
reasoning: At the 1 April 2025 adjustment MSD raised main benefits by 2.22 percent, the CPI movement from the December 2023 to the December 2024 quarter (Jobseeker single 25+ $353.46 → $361.32 net). Over the same period wages grew materially faster: Stats NZ QES average ordinary-time hourly earnings rose 4.2 percent in the year to the December 2024 quarter, and — the decisive check against the criterion — NZ Superannuation and Veteran's Pension were lifted by just over 3 percent at 1 April 2025 specifically so they would remain at 66 percent of the net average wage (NZ Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, s 16). That wage-floor top-up is a direct reading of net average wage growth, and it sits about 0.8+ percentage points above the CPI adjustment applied to main benefits. So the CPI-indexed rates were below the wage-indexed counterfactual, not at or above it: beneficiaries were worse off under the change at the April 2025 adjustment. Cumulating both post-change adjustments (4.66% then 2.22% = 6.99%, versus roughly 5.3% then just over 3% under wage indexation) leaves the same direction, so this does not rescue a partly_correct reading. The premise Bidois relied on — cost of living running ahead of wages — had reversed by 2025.

statement: And mark me, this will probably be the next thing to go; we’ll see abatement thresholds come down as a way of decreasing and getting more money carved off to the side to fund tax cuts that were unaffordable when they first did their numbers.
criterion: Legislation, regulation or Budget decisions affecting main benefit abatement thresholds: true if the thresholds are lowered before the end of the parliamentary term, false if they are left unchanged or increased.
reasoning: MSD's current main-benefit income abatement threshold table is still the one effective 1 April 2021 — $160 gross/week for Jobseeker Support (70c abatement), $160/$250 for Sole Parent Support and Supported Living Payment. No change was made across Budgets 2024, 2025 or 2026. Budget 2025 moved in the opposite direction on the adjacent Working for Families threshold, raising it from $42,700 to $44,900 from 1 April 2026 (rate to 27.5%). Budget 2026's benefit savings came from cutting the Temporary Additional Support maximum rate from 30% to 25% of main benefit rates and from parental income testing of 18–19-year-olds for Jobseeker Support (Social Security (Jobseeker Support and Accommodation Supplement) Amendment Bill), plus an increase — not a decrease — in the Accommodation Supplement entry threshold for some homeowners. None of these is a main benefit abatement threshold. Searched for the disconfirming case (any bill, regulation or Budget line lowering abatement thresholds) and found none. The criterion says false if the thresholds are left unchanged or increased; they were left unchanged. Caveat: the term does not end until 7 Nov 2026, but the final Budget of the term has been delivered and no relevant bill is before the House.

statement: We know they won’t be better off in the future—in fact, they’ll be demonstrably far worse off in the future—but we can’t make those calculations accurately unless we have an understanding (a) that it is CPI, (b) what period of time that is for, and then we move to the ability to make an accurate comparison.
criterion: Compare the main benefit rates set by CPI indexation from 1 April 2027 (MSD benefit rate tables) with the rates that would have resulted from indexation to net average ordinary time weekly earnings over the same period (Stats NZ QES earnings series, net of tax and ACC earner levy): true if the CPI-indexed rates are materially lower; false if they are equal to or above the wage-indexed counterfactual.
reasoning: The criterion pins resolution to the main benefit rates set by CPI indexation from 1 April 2027, compared with a wage-indexed counterfactual. Today is 26 Sep 2026; the 1 April 2027 Annual General Adjustment has not been made or published (MSD's current rate tables run to 1 April 2026), so the CPI-indexed 2027 rates the criterion requires do not yet exist. The underlying policy change is confirmed: the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Act 2024 (Royal assent 21 Feb 2024) repealed s452A, which indexed main benefits to movement in average ordinary time weekly earnings, leaving adjustment under s453 by CPI. Officials at the time expected CPI indexation to give marginally higher rates than wage indexation in the short term for the 1 April 2024 adjustment, so the direction over the full period to 2027 is not settled by the legislation alone. Resolve-by is 2027-06-30; not a failing grade, just early.

statement: How can the Minister justify creating a $1.2 billion shortfall in the plan to decongest Auckland over the next four years, when congestion will cost us about $5 billion in productivity in the same period?
criterion: Published Auckland congestion-cost estimates (NZIER / Auckland Council / Ministry of Transport) covering 2024–2028: true if the cumulative estimated productivity cost of Auckland congestion over that four-year period is around $5 billion; false if the published estimates are materially lower or higher.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether published estimates put the cumulative productivity cost of Auckland congestion over roughly 2024–2028 at around $5 billion. The Ministry of Transport's published estimate is that congestion in Auckland costs the economy up to $1.39 billion annually in lost productivity — about $5.6 billion over four years, i.e. 'about $5 billion'. NZIER's earlier study put the weekday cost of congestion (the decongestion benefit at current network capacity) at $0.9–$1.3 billion a year, or $3.6–$5.2 billion over four years, which also brackets the figure. Checked for the disconfirming case — an estimate that would make $5 billion materially wrong. Auckland Transport's January 2025 cost-of-congestion white paper projects $2.6 billion a year by 2026 ($1.9b travel-time delay plus $0.7b macroeconomic cost), around $10 billion over four years; but that is total social cost, a broader measure than the productivity cost the criterion names, and its macroeconomic component ($0.7b/yr) is lower than MoT's productivity figure. On the productivity measure the criterion specifies, ~$5 billion over four years is inside the published range rather than an outlier. Note the four-year window does not close until 2028, so this is confirmed against published estimates, not against realised outturn.

statement: This proposal that we are debating today is going to mean that we have more children in poverty.
criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics for the years following the 1 April 2024 change: true if the primary measures (particularly material hardship and the after-housing-costs 50% measure) show a rise in the number of children in poverty over that period; false if they show a fall or no change outside sampling error.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Stats NZ child poverty statistics for the years following the 1 April 2024 indexation change, resolving by 2027-03-31. Only one full post-change year has been published (year ended June 2025, released Feb 2026); the year-ended-June-2026 release is due Feb 2027, inside the window. On the interim data Stats NZ's own headline is 'No annual change': material hardship 13.4% (156,600 children) -> 14.3% (169,300), AHC 50% fixed-2018 line 17.7% (208,000) -> 17.8% (210,600), BHC 50% 12.7% (149,900) -> 12.6% (148,700). Numbers rose on two of the three primary measures but no change was statistically significant, and the survey source changed from HES to HILS in July 2024, which weakens the year-on-year comparison. So the predicted rise is not yet evident, but the criterion's period is not complete. Note the longer-run rise from 2022 (material hardship 10.6% -> 14.3%, statistically significant) largely predates the 1 April 2024 change.

statement: This bill will continue to make it harder and our whānau worse off.
criterion: Compare main benefit rates as actually adjusted under the CPI indexation this bill restores against the rates that would have applied under the previous wage-indexation formula, using MSD benefit rate tables; true if recipients' rates are materially lower under CPI indexation than the wage-indexed counterfactual, false if they are equal or higher.
reasoning: The criterion compares main benefit rates as actually adjusted under the restored CPI indexation against the previous net-average-wage formula.
