The MSD Annual General Adjustment Cabinet papers state both figures each year: 1 April 2024 CPI 4.66% vs net average wage 5.28%; 1 April 2025 CPI 2.22% vs net average wage 3.51%; 1 April 2026 CPI 3.11% vs average wage growth 2.91% (the one year CPI ran ahead). Compounded, main benefits rose 10.3% over the three adjustments against 12.2% under the wage-indexed counterfactual, i.e. rates are about 1.7% lower than they would have been, a gap that widened in two of the three years. Disconfirming check: the 2026 adjustment favoured CPI, and the realised shortfall so far (~$6-7/week on a typical main benefit) is far smaller than the ~$45/week figures quoted during the 2024 debate. Direction nonetheless matches the criterion's 'true' condition unambiguously; rates are lower, not equal or higher.

statement: We all look forward to this Budget to see what kind of disaster will be wreaked upon the rest of New Zealand, what times of deep Public Service cuts we will see with a 6.5 to 7.5 percent cut right across all our public services.
criterion: Budget 2024 documents and agency baseline-savings decisions: true if the Budget applies savings targets in the 6.5–7.5 percent range broadly across public service agencies and delivers substantial reductions in public service spending/staffing; false if the Budget applies no such range, or if cuts are confined to a small number of agencies.
reasoning: The criterion requires savings targets in the 6.5-7.5% range applied broadly across public service agencies plus substantial reductions. In January 2024 the Finance Minister gave nearly 40 public service departments a baseline savings target of exactly 6.5% or 7.5% (7.5% for agencies that had grown more than 50% since 2017), targeting $1.5b in annual operating savings. Budget 2024 confirmed the target was met (~$1.57b/yr) and was accompanied by roughly 3,900 public service role reductions (~2,750 filled roles plus ~1,150 vacancies). Named examples span the range and multiple agencies: Justice 6.5% ($80.8m), MSD 6.5% ($119.4m), Transport 7.5% ($38.5m), MBIE 7.5% ($234m). Disconfirming check: the targets were not literally universal - frontline health, police and schools were largely exempt - so 'right across all our public services' is somewhat overstated, but the criterion's test of breadth across public service agencies and substantial cuts is met.

statement: They’re simply pushing back onto councils the water crisis that we have in New Zealand and the result is going to be very simple: ratepayers, Kiwi families will pay more—and those rates increases will start very soon.
criterion: Territorial authority annual plans and long-term plans adopted for the 2024/25 rating year, and Stats NZ / LGNZ figures on average rates increases: true if average residential rates rise materially above the prior year's average increase in 2024/25, false if increases are flat or below trend.
reasoning: Stats NZ recorded a 12.2% annual rise in local authority rates and payments in the September 2024 quarter — the rating year beginning 1 July 2024 — described as the largest since 1990 and the single largest upward contributor to annual CPI. The comparable prior-year figure was 9.8% (year to December 2023 quarter), so 2024/25 was materially above the previous year's average increase, satisfying the criterion's 'true' branch. The Taxpayers' Union 2024 Rates Dashboard independently put the average district council hike for 2024/25 at over 14%. The 'start very soon' element also holds: rates struck in the 2024/25 annual and long-term plans took effect 1 July 2024, about four and a half months after the statement. Caveat: the criterion tests only the size and timing of the increase, not Hipkins's attribution of it to pushing water costs back onto councils; 2024/25 increases reflected broad long-term-plan cost pressures (interest, insurance, construction, and water infrastructure among them), and I did not resolve the causal share.

statement: The Western Bay of Plenty is one of the fastest growing regions of New Zealand and is expected to be the home of more than 250,000 people by 2050.
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Western Bay of Plenty sub-region (Tauranga City plus Western Bay of Plenty District). True if the usually resident population exceeds 250,000 at or before the 2050 estimate; false if it remains at or below 250,000.
reasoning: The criterion names Stats NZ subnational usually-resident population estimates for the Western Bay of Plenty sub-region (Tauranga City plus Western Bay of Plenty District) at 2050, with a resolve-by date of 2050-06-30. That evidence cannot exist for another 24 years, so the claim is not yet settleable on the terms written down. Supporting context only: SmartGrowth — the Tauranga City / Western Bay of Plenty District / Bay of Plenty Regional Council partnership that does the sub-region's growth planning — projects 258,000 residents in the western Bay of Plenty by 2050, against an existing sub-regional population over 200,000. So the 'is expected to be' framing accurately reflects the official planning projection in circulation at the time, and the sub-region is genuinely among New Zealand's fastest growing. But a projection is not the outcome the criterion asks for, and substituting it would be answering an easier question.

statement: That might seem innocuous, but the appalling consequence of it is that 7,000 children will move into poverty.
criterion: Treasury/MSD regulatory impact and child poverty modelling for the CPI-indexation change, read against Stats NZ child poverty statistics; true if the official estimate of additional children in poverty attributable to the change is of the order of 7,000 by 2027/28, false if materially lower or if no such increase is estimated.
reasoning: The criterion's primary test is whether official modelling of the CPI-indexation change estimates additional children in poverty of the order of 7,000 by 2027/28. It does. The officials' supplementary analysis report (regulatory impact analysis) accompanying the reversion of main-benefit indexation from average wage growth to CPI gave a central estimate of 7,000 additional children in poverty by 2027/28 on the AHC50 measure (range 3,000–11,000) and also 7,000 on BHC50 (range 1,000–13,000), alongside Crown savings of $669.5m over four years and weekly losses of $18.15–$35.11 per recipient by 2028. Russell's 7,000 is the official central figure, not an inflation of it. The one thing she did not signal is the uncertainty band — officials gave a point estimate with wide variance, and she stated it as a settled consequence. Read against outcomes so far, Stats NZ child poverty statistics for 2024/25 move in the same direction: AHC50-fixed rose to 17.8% (210,600 children), a statistically significant increase on 2021–22, and material hardship rose to 14.3% (169,300 children). The portion of that attributable specifically to the indexation change cannot be isolated from the published statistics, so the modelling estimate — which is what the criterion asks for — is the basis for this verdict.

statement: The numbers are only going to increase. That means that the Māori seats will increase.
criterion: The Representation Commission's determination of Māori electorate boundaries following the next census and Māori Electoral Option; true if the number of Māori electorates exceeds seven, false if it stays at seven or falls.
reasoning: The criterion's named test — the Representation Commission's determination following the next census and Māori Electoral Option — has already returned an answer, and it is seven. Stats NZ announced on 25 Oct 2024 (post-2023-census, post-Option) that North Island general electorates fall from 49 to 48 while Māori electorates stay at seven; the Commission's final 2026 boundaries (8 Aug 2025) kept seven. Henare's premise held — the Māori roll grew (≈305,000 on the Māori roll vs ≈257,000 Māori on the general roll by Apr 2026; net switching gains each option period) and Te Pāti Māori says the roll has justified an eighth seat since Jan 2025 — but no eighth seat eventuated. Checked for a later increase inside the resolve-by window: there is no 2028 census (scrapped, admin data from 2030) and the Electoral (District Boundaries) Amendment Bill (Justice Committee, submissions closed 15 Apr 2026) would move the next review from 2029 to 2032, fixing Māori seats at seven for the 2026 and 2029 elections. So the claim fails the criterion as written and cannot be met by 2029-12-31.

statement: Looking ahead, while business confidence has picked up, a prolonged period of pressure on household budgets means growth is expected to remain weak, and high migration means GDP per capita is expected to continue to decline.
criterion: Stats NZ real GDP per capita series for the quarters following February 2024; true if GDP per capita records further declines across 2024, false if it returns to sustained growth.
reasoning: Stats NZ real GDP per capita fell in each of the three quarters after the statement: −0.3% in the March 2024 quarter (sixth consecutive fall; −2.4% annual), −0.5% in June 2024, and −1.2% in September 2024 (eighth consecutive fall). It rose 0.4% in the December 2024 quarter — the first quarterly rise in two years, released 20 March 2025 — which is a turning point, not the 'sustained growth' the criterion sets as the falsifier. Growth also remained weak: total GDP contracted 1.1% in the September 2024 quarter, putting NZ back in recession. One mechanism caveat that does not affect the criterion: Willis attributed the per-capita fall to 'high migration', but annual net migration collapsed from 128,300 (Dec 2023 year) to 27,100 (Dec 2024 year), so the continued per-capita decline came from shrinking output, not population growth.

statement: Put it this way: I think it is highly unlikely that the full set of forecasts in May will deliver any upside surprises.
criterion: Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update, 30 May 2024, compared with HYEFU 2023; true if the growth, revenue and OBEGAL tracks are unchanged or worse, false if the May forecasts revise the fiscal or growth outlook materially upward.
reasoning: The Budget Economic and Fiscal Update of 30 May 2024 was worse than HYEFU 2023 on every track the criterion names. Growth: trend GDP at the end of the forecast period was nearly 2% lower than the Half Year Update (weak productivity), with real GDP forecast to contract 0.2% in the year to June 2024. Revenue: core Crown tax revenue was lower than the Half Year Update across the whole forecast period — $119b for 2024/25 against $122b in December. OBEGAL: weaker in all years, especially 2024/25 (a deficit of ~3.1% of GDP), with the return to surplus pushed out a year to 2027/28 at just 0.3% of GDP; the bond programme rose $2b for 2024/25 (+$12b over four years) and net core Crown debt stayed at 41.8% of GDP in 2027/28, above the target band. Looking for the opposite: the only arguably better line was inflation returning below 3% during 2024, and Westpac's Budget review identified no upward revisions of substance — so no material upside surprise.

statement: Without three waters, without water infrastructure legislation, we can see that rise up to 25 percent that Aucklanders will be paying in their water rates in the coming years.
criterion: Auckland Council and Watercare published water charge decisions for the years following February 2024: true if an annual water price increase approaching 25 percent is adopted within that period; false if increases stay near the roughly 9 percent of the preceding year.
reasoning: Criterion: true if an adopted annual water price increase approaching 25% appears after Feb 2024; false if increases stay near the ~9% of the preceding year. Watercare's adopted increases were 7.2% on 1 July 2024, 7.2% on 1 July 2025 and 7.2% on 1 July 2026 — the falsifying branch. The 25.8% figure was genuine as a proposal in Auckland Council's draft long-term plan, but it was averted in May 2024 by the Local Water Done Well arrangement and the Watercare Charter, i.e. by the water infrastructure legislation whose absence Halbert's claim was conditioned on. Checked the disconfirming side: no year in the window adopted anything above 7.2%, and no Watercare/Council decision approaching 25% was ever adopted. Settled, not pending, since the last price decision before the 2027-07-01 resolve-by (1 July 2026) is published.

statement: It’s the Māori Health Authority that soon will be on the chopping block.
criterion: The legislative record for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if a bill disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora is enacted and the authority ceases to exist; false if the Māori Health Authority is still operating as a statutory entity at the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Criterion: true if a bill disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora is enacted and the authority ceases to exist by 2024-12-31. The Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill was introduced under urgency on 27 February 2024 — 13 days after Henare spoke — passed 28 February, received Royal Assent 5 March 2024, and the Māori Health Authority was disestablished on 30 June 2024, its functions moving to Health New Zealand and a Hauora Māori Advisory Committee. Disconfirming check: the authority was not still operating as a statutory entity at the resolve-by date; board and executive members marked its end on 1 July 2024. 'Soon' is well supported by the two-week gap to introduction.

statement: While it will almost certainly get voted down by the Government, we can use it as an opportunity to reset and to resist the Government’s anti-Māori and anti-Tiriti agenda, and push our Toitū Te Tiriti kaupapa.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Electoral (Entrenchment of Māori Seats) Amendment Bill; true if the bill was voted down with the governing parties (National, ACT, NZ First) opposing, false if it proceeded to select committee.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the first-reading division record of an Electoral (Entrenchment of Māori Seats) Amendment Bill by 2024-03-31. No such bill was before the 54th Parliament in that window: the only Māori-seats entrenchment bill of this term is Hūhana Lyndon's Green member's bill, announced 23 January 2026 (members' ballot), and the similarly named Tirikatene bill belongs to the 52nd Parliament, where it passed first reading with NZ First's support in 2018 and was defeated later. The division record the criterion points to therefore does not exist. Nor can the referent of Waititi's 'it' be established from the public record — 14 February 2024 was the all-stages urgency debate on the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill, and no Te Pāti Māori Tiriti-related bill or motion from that day is documented. The nearest real event, Waititi's GST-off-food member's bill defeated at first reading on 22 March 2024 with only Te Pāti Māori in support, is consistent with the general expectation but is not what the criterion names, so it cannot settle the verdict.

statement: Speaking to the question and, also, as it relates to the primary, the cellphone ban for Wainuiomata will have similar impacts to every other school that I’m hearing from, in that students are interacting more with each other, focusing on their learning, not getting distracted, and, very soon, we are going to have evidence and data to show that this policy is working.
criterion: Publication, by the Ministry of Education or an independent evaluator, of New Zealand data or evaluation evidence on the school cellphone ban: true if such evidence is published and reports a positive effect on student engagement or achievement, false if no such evidence is published by the resolve-by date or if what is published shows no effect.
reasoning: The Education Review Office published "Do not disturb: A review of removing cell phones from New Zealand's classrooms" on 20 November 2025 (data collected Term 2 2025), inside the resolve-by window. It reports positive effects on engagement and achievement: ~83% of secondary leaders and 79% of teachers say the policy improved students' ability to focus, ~61% of teachers and 58% of leaders report improved achievement, 77-78% report better classroom behaviour, and 69% of secondary leaders report less bullying. Criterion satisfied: NZ evaluation evidence published by the resolve-by date reporting a positive effect. Caveats (not disqualifying under the criterion as written): the evidence is self-reported survey data rather than measured achievement data; ERO's evaluation centre head said achievement changes cannot be directly attributed to the ban given other concurrent changes; students identifying as disabled or having learning needs reported worse outcomes (~23-28%); and in 2024 the Ministry of Education had advised the government the supporting evidence was 'marginal'. Disconfirming check: international work (Stanford/NBER 2025) finds little short-run achievement gain, but the criterion asks about NZ evidence specifically. Stanford's 'very soon' was generous - the evidence arrived ~21 months later - but the criterion set the deadline at 2025-12-31.

statement: Of course, having heard Carmel Sepuloni speak, it may well be that if the Amendment Paper isn’t withdrawn, we’ll need another amendment bill a bit later on to extend it further.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register and Parliament's bills record: true if, after the two-year amendment is enacted, a further bill extending the section 13 experience pathway deadline is introduced on or before the shortened expiry date of 27 February 2026; false if no such bill is introduced by then (or if the amendment was withdrawn, leaving the antecedent unsatisfied).
reasoning: The antecedent was satisfied: the Amendment Paper was not withdrawn. The Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 20 February 2024 with the shortened two-year extension (to 27/28 February 2026) rather than the four years to February 2028 originally proposed - a Cabinet paper confirms agreement to shorten the delay of the repeal by two years. The predicted consequent did not occur: no further bill extending the section 13 experience pathway was introduced by 27 February 2026. SWRB's 19 December 2025 and 12 February 2026 newsletters mention no extending legislation, only reminders that applications close 27 February 2026, and section 13 of the Act was repealed at 12am on 28 February 2026 (applications lodged by 11:59pm 27 February 2026 still processed). Disconfirming check: searched the legislation/bills record and SWRB news for any 2025-2026 amendment bill or member's bill extending s13 - none found, and the repeal took effect as scheduled, which it could not have if an extension had been enacted.

statement: We anticipate that this will support experienced Māori practitioners to register as social workers through the experience pathway over the next two years.
criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration statistics (annual reports 2024/25 and 2025/26) broken down by pathway and ethnicity; true if registrations of Māori practitioners via the experience pathway are sustained or rise over the two years to February 2026, false if they fall.
reasoning: The criterion names SWRB registration statistics broken down by pathway AND ethnicity in the 2024/25 and 2025/26 annual reports. That evidence does not exist in published form. The SWRB's 2025 Annual Social Worker Workforce Report gives pathway shares (85% NZ qualification, 12% overseas qualified, 3% - 115 survey respondents, 249 of 9,065 practising - via the section 13 experience pathway) and workforce ethnicity separately (24% Maori, 12% Pacific peoples), but explicitly provides no ethnicity breakdown by pathway and no year-on-year trend for s13. The 2024/25 Annual Report was only tabled in Parliament in early February 2026, and the 2025/26 annual report (year to 30 June 2026) is not yet published as at 26 September 2026, so the second of the two required data points does not exist. Best available proxy, offered as context rather than a verdict: the s13 share of the workforce rose from 2% (2023 workforce report) to 3% / 249 practitioners (2025 report), ~32% of s13 registrants identified as Maori in the 2023 data, and the pathway stayed open and accepted applications through 27 February 2026 - consistent with continued Maori registration via the pathway, but not the pathway-by-ethnicity series the criterion requires. Absence of this published breakdown is not evidence the prediction failed.

statement: I think we might have unanimous consent to just, all of a sudden, change the title of this bill, and I’m sure the Minister will be open to that.
criterion: The committee-stage and third-reading record for this Bill and the short title of the Act as enacted: true if the title was amended by leave during the Committee of the whole House, false if the Bill retained the title 'Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill'.
reasoning: The Bill's title was never amended by leave or otherwise. In the Committee of the whole House on 15 Feb 2024 the title suggestions (Bidois's 'Back to Work Bill' / 'Mana in Mahi') were informal debate banter, and Minister Bayly said a title change at that stage was unlikely. The only Amendment Paper in committee (AP 16, Ricardo Menendez March) amended clause 10 and inserted a new clause 11, and was voted down. The Bill passed all three readings 68-55 under urgency and received Royal assent on 21 February 2024 as the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Act 2024 - the identical title clause 1 carried at introduction. That is the criterion's 'false' branch.

statement: And the reverse is clearly true in the material that’s on the Table and was discussed in the House today—that this bill will push 7,000 kids back into poverty.
criterion: The official child poverty impact analysis for the bill and subsequent Stats NZ child poverty statistics releases: true if the official estimate of ~7,000 additional children in poverty attributable to the indexation change is borne out in the published projections and the measured child poverty rate rises consistently with it; false if the official analysis carries a materially smaller number or the measured outcome shows no such increase attributable to the change.
reasoning: The criterion is conjunctive and only its first limb can be checked today (2026-09-26); the resolve-by date is 2028-06-30. First limb holds: MSD's regulatory impact statement on indexing main benefits to inflation gave a central estimate of 7,000 additional children in poverty by 2028 on the AHC50 measure (range 3,000-11,000), and also 7,000 on BHC50 (much wider range, 1,000-13,000), so Robertson's account of the material on the Table is accurate rather than inflated. Second limb is unsettleable: the projected effect accumulates to 2027/28 and the latest Stats NZ release (year ended June 2025, published 26 Feb 2026) reports no statistically significant annual change, with AHC50 at 17.8 percent. Two further HILS years are outstanding, and no increase is yet attributable to the indexation change either way. Absence of a measured rise this early is not evidence the prediction failed.

statement: Over the longer term, New Zealand will gain from savings in benefit expenditure, while benefit recipients retain a consistent level of real financial resources—a simple way to put this is that it protects their purchasing power.
criterion: Treasury/MSD published benefit expenditure outturns against the pre-change baseline, plus MSD main benefit rate tables deflated by the Stats NZ CPI; true if cumulative benefit expenditure comes in below the wage-indexed counterfactual and the real (CPI-deflated) value of main benefit rates is no lower at the end of the period than in April 2024; false if there are no measurable expenditure savings, or if real benefit rates fall over the period.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Treasury/MSD benefit expenditure outturns against the pre-change (wage-indexed) baseline plus CPI-deflated MSD main benefit rate tables, judged over a period ending 2028-06-30 - a date that has not passed. What exists so far is forecast, not outturn: officials scored the switch from wage indexation to CPI indexation as saving the Crown about $669.52 million over four years, and annual general adjustments have proceeded on CPI (the 2026 adjustment used 3.11 percent). No published expenditure outturn measured against the wage-indexed counterfactual was findable, and the real-value limb ('no lower at the end of the period than in April 2024') is by construction only assessable at the end of the period. Commentary that wage growth outpaces CPI speaks to relative, not real, value and so does not settle either limb.

statement: Ten years from now, if no change occurs to fix this indexation mistake, then what we’ll have are benefits falling further and further behind. We’ll have more children living in poverty.
criterion: MSD main benefit rates as a percentage of the net average wage, compared 2024 vs 2034, plus Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics (before-housing-costs 50% median and material hardship measures) for the year to June 2034. True if the benefit-to-wage ratio has fallen and the child poverty rate is higher than 2024 outside sampling error, given CPI indexation was retained. False if the ratio holds or rises, or child poverty falls, under retained CPI indexation. Void if indexation is legislatively changed back in the interim, which the speaker's own condition excludes.
reasoning: The criterion requires MSD benefit-to-net-average-wage ratios for 2034 versus 2024 and Stats NZ child poverty figures for the year to June 2034. Today is September 2026; the resolve-by date is 2034-02-20. None of the required evidence exists yet, and the criterion also makes the prediction conditional on CPI indexation being retained through the whole period, which cannot be established in advance. No verdict is possible.

statement: But I’ll tell you right now: in four years’ time, what we will see is more families queuing up at Work and Income, needing hardship grants to make ends meet.
criterion: MSD hardship assistance statistics (Special Needs Grants and Advances, number of recipients and number of grants) for the year to June 2028 compared with the year to June 2024. True if both recipient numbers and grant volumes are higher in 2028; false if they are lower or flat.
reasoning: The criterion requires MSD hardship assistance statistics (Special Needs Grants and Advances, recipients and grant volumes) for the year to June 2028 compared with the year to June 2024. The resolve-by date is 2028-06-30 and today is September 2026, so the endpoint data does not exist. Interim MSD quarterly data through the March 2025 quarter in fact shows hardship payment volumes falling year-on-year (Sep 2024 quarter -10.4%, Dec 2024 quarter -8.0%, Mar 2025 quarter -4.0%), but that is two-plus years short of the window the criterion names and is not a verdict.

statement: There’s going to be increased whānau continuing to line up at our food banks, and increased whānau turning up at our marae requiring hardship grants.
criterion: MSD hardship assistance statistics (Special Needs Grants for food and other hardship assistance, by recipient ethnicity where published) and food bank demand reporting such as the New Zealand Food Network's annual figures, for the 12 months following February 2024 compared with the preceding 12 months. True if both measures rise; false if both are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires BOTH measures to rise over the 12 months after February 2024. Food bank demand rose: NZ Food Network's Food Security Snapshot (March 2025) reports over 500,000 individuals reached per month across Jul-Dec 2024, up from ~454,000 in Jan-Jun 2024, with distribution up from 12.3m to over 13m kg; NZFN separately reported a 42% rise in demand across 2024. MSD hardship assistance did NOT rise: total hardship payments fell year-on-year in every quarter of the window (Sep 2024 quarter 572,871, -10.4%; Dec 2024 quarter 553,575, -8.0%; Mar 2025 quarter 573,840, -4.0%), Benefit Advances fell 9-18%, and the value of hardship assistance fell 21-28%. Special Needs Grants for food were roughly flat to slightly down: 322,395 (-5.0%), 331,296 (-1.5%), 330,555 (+0.6%) -- a ~2% fall over the three quarters combined, consistent with OIA data showing food grant applications at 1,387,359 in 2023 versus 1,359,171 in 2024. Checking for disconfirmation on the grants side: the fall is driven partly by tightened approvals rather than reduced need -- food grant decline rates rose from 3.96% (2023) to 6.28% (2024) after manager sign-off requirements returned in December 2023. So the underlying hardship Kemp described did grow, but the specific indicator she named (whanau receiving hardship grants) moved the other way. One of two measures rose, which the criterion's 'both rise' test does not meet, and the substance holds only under a reading (unmet need rather than grants issued) that the speaker did not signal. No ethnicity-disaggregated MSD hardship series was published for this window.

statement: The problem is that with this bill, they’re actually going to get less money in the long run.
criterion: MSD's published main benefit rates after successive 1 April adjustments, compared with the rates the repealed wage-indexation formula (net average ordinary time weekly earnings, Stats NZ QES) would have produced over the same period. True if the CPI-indexed rates are materially lower by April 2027; false if they are equal or higher.
reasoning: The criterion runs to April 2027 and today is 2026-09-26, so the determining data point does not exist: the April 2027 adjustment will be set from CPI for the year to December 2026, which Stats NZ does not publish until January 2027. Three of the four adjustments in the window have occurred. Main benefits moved to CPI indexation from the 1 April 2024 AGA (the bill under debate on 2024-02-20). Jobseeker Support, single 25+, net weekly: $337.74 (Apr 2023) -> $353.46 (Apr 2024, +4.66%) -> $361.32 (Apr 2025, +2.22%) -> $372.55 (Apr 2026, +3.11%). Wage-growth comparators published alongside those adjustments: ~4.7% in 2024 (NZ Super couple rose $71.68 on $1,526.68 per fortnight), ~3% in 2025, and 2.91% in 2026. Cumulatively benefits are about 0.6pp behind the wage proxy — the direction Edmonds predicted, but far short of 'materially lower', and not monotonic: in the 2026 year CPI (3.11%) exceeded wage growth (2.91%), so CPI indexation paid more that year than the repealed formula would have. Genuine disconfirming evidence exists for the short run and the long run is not yet observable. Caveat on precision: the wage column uses the NZ Super/threshold wage-growth figures MSD and Work and Income quote, which track the net average ordinary time weekly earnings series but are not the repealed benefit formula itself; the MSD Annual General Adjustment cabinet papers that state the formula figures directly could not be text-extracted here.

statement: What we’re going to see now is that overall weekly benefit eroded over time.
criterion: MSD main benefit rates (Jobseeker Support and Sole Parent Support, net weekly) from April 2024 onward compared against Stats NZ average ordinary time weekly earnings; true if benefit rates fall as a share of the average wage over the period, false if they hold steady or rise relative to it.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve date is 2027-04-01 and today is 2026-09-26; the final adjustment in the comparison period has not happened. Two CPI-indexed adjustments plus the 2024 switchover year are observable. Jobseeker Support single 25+ net weekly went $353.46 (Apr 2024) -> $361.32 (Apr 2025) -> $372.55 (Apr 2026), i.e. +5.40% over the two adjustments since April 2024, against wage-growth comparators of ~3% (2025) and 2.91% (2026), about +6.0% compounded. So the benefit has slipped marginally as a share of the average wage — consistent with Boyack's direction — but the gap is roughly 0.6pp, and the 2026 year ran the other way (CPI 3.11% vs wage 2.91%), which is what one would expect to find if the prediction were wrong and is the disconfirming case. Erosion 'over time' cannot be settled from two adjustments, one of which favoured CPI. Same precision caveat as the Edmonds item: the wage figures are the NZ Super/threshold wage-growth numbers published with each AGA rather than the QES net average ordinary time weekly earnings series read directly.

statement: If this Government does manage to magic up some tax cuts—I’ve got no idea how they’re going to do that, but if they do—every single one of us in this room, those of us who are parliamentarians, will get a tax cut.
criterion: Legislated personal income tax changes announced in Budget 2024 and their effective date; true if income tax reductions took effect and applied to incomes at MPs' salary level (roughly $160,000+), false if no tax cut was delivered or if it was targeted so as to exclude that income band.
reasoning: Both halves of the criterion are satisfied. Budget 2024 legislated personal income tax threshold increases effective 31 July 2024: the 10.5% bracket top moved $14,000 -> $15,600, the 17.5% bracket top $48,000 -> $53,500, and the 30% bracket top $70,000 -> $78,100, with the 39% top threshold left at $180,000. Because the rates were unchanged and only the thresholds shifted, the saving accrues to every taxpayer above $14,000 and caps at $1,043 a year ($20 a week) for anyone earning $78,100 or more; there is no clawback or abatement on the threshold change at higher incomes. Checking the exclusion half of the criterion specifically: leaving the top threshold untouched means high earners got no extra cut, not that they were excluded from this one. Backbench MPs were on $163,961, rising to $168,600 during 2024 and $181,200 by the end of the term, all well above $78,100, so every parliamentarian received the full $1,043. The tax cut Boyack doubted would materialise did, and it applied to her own income band.

statement: I anticipate this will support experienced Māori practitioners to register as social workers through the experience pathway over the next two years.
criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration statistics by ethnicity and pathway for the period 20 February 2024 to 28 February 2026; true if registrations of Māori practitioners via the experience pathway rise relative to the preceding comparable period, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The pathway-level half of the prediction is confirmed, the ethnicity-specific half is not published. SWRB's Annual Report 2024-25 (p.12, 'New to Register by pathway') shows the experience pathway rose from 6% of 744 new registrants in 2023/24 to 10% of 583 in 2024/25 - roughly 45 to 58 people, a rise in both share and count, with 2024/25 falling wholly inside the extension window. So registrations through the pathway did increase over the extension, as Upston anticipated. However, the criterion asks specifically for registrations of MAORI practitioners via the experience pathway, and no SWRB publication disaggregates pathway by ethnicity: not the 2023-24 or 2024-25 Annual Reports, and not the 2025 Annual Social Worker Workforce Report, which reports ethnicity (25% Maori) and pathway (3% S13) only separately. The nearest figure is from the pre-extension 2023 Cabinet paper: of 292 people registered via the pathway over 13 years around a quarter identified as Maori, rising to 31% of S13 registrations in 2020-2022 - a trend that pre-dates the extension. Coverage is also incomplete: the latest annual report is 2024/25, so the final eight months to the 27 February 2026 closing deadline (the period most likely to show a rush of applications) are not yet reported, and SWRB's 2026 newsletters publish no S13 totals. Searching for disconfirming evidence, I found nothing showing the pathway or Maori participation in it falling. Verdict is partly_correct rather than correct because the measure the criterion names cannot be read off any published source, and partly_correct rather than uncheckable because the pathway-level statistics that do exist move in the predicted direction.

statement: I raised the point during committee stage, too, that if we find ourselves in a position 18 months from now where we still have the workforce shortages in the social work sector for qualified, registered social workers in 18 months’ time, there is a very strong chance, because of the urgent need to have social workers in these positions, that we’re going to end up back in this House, having to legislate, amend again for another extension when we could have just got it right the first time.
criterion: The New Zealand parliamentary legislation record for the Social Workers Registration Act s13 experience pathway: true if a further bill or amendment extending the experience pathway beyond the two-year period is introduced or passed before the pathway expires, false if the pathway lapses on the legislated two-year date with no further extension legislated.
reasoning: The criterion's false condition is met exactly: the pathway lapsed on the legislated two-year date with no further extension. SWRB confirms that applications closed at 11:59pm on Friday 27 February 2026 and that 'at 12am on Saturday, 28 February 2026, section 13 of the Act was repealed', with no new section 13 applications possible. Parliament did not return to extend it. Checking for the disconfirming case - a bill or amendment introduced but not passed, which the criterion would also count as true - the one piece of intervening legislation was the Social Workers Registration Amendment Bill (introduced 2024, first reading 27 August 2024, enacted as the Social Workers Registration Amendment Act 2025). Its content is 16 minor policy and technical amendments: broadening the grounds for interim suspension, transferring the power to obtain information about unauthorised practice from MSD to the Board, and ten technical fixes to inconsistencies created by the 2019 amendments. It did not extend the experience pathway, and SWRB's own guidance throughout 2025 and early 2026 told applicants the pathway would close on schedule. Note that the four-year option Sepuloni was arguing for existed in the original bill as introduced (repeal delayed to 28 February 2028) and was cut back to two years by amendment before passage - so the longer extension was considered and rejected in 2024, not revisited afterwards. Her prediction was hedged ('a very strong chance'), but the event she predicted did not occur.

statement: As we know, social workers provide a really important service to our most vulnerable, and, as we’ve heard in debates earlier in the House this afternoon, with 7,000 more children likely to be in poverty from one single action of this Government this afternoon, we know that Māori are impacted in many of the areas that require social work services, and so I am disappointed that the Minister did not heed the request and advice of these organisations and extended it out to the four years.
criterion: Treasury/MSD regulatory impact and child poverty modelling for the benefit indexation change passed in February 2024, checked against Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics releases for the years the modelling covers. True if the official estimate and subsequent measured outcome show roughly 7,000 or more additional children in poverty attributable to that change; false if the attributable figure is materially smaller or the modelling shows no such effect.
reasoning: The criterion requires two things - the official estimate AND the subsequent measured outcome - and sets a resolve-by date of 30 June 2028. Today is 26 September 2026, so the second half cannot yet be checked. On the first half, the 7,000 figure is confirmed and correctly quoted: officials advising on the change from wage indexation to CPI indexation of benefit rates (passed under urgency in February 2024, effective 1 April 2024) estimated an increase of 7,000 children in poverty over four years to 2028 on the AHC50 measure, with a range of 3,000 to 11,000, and 7,000 on the BHC50 measure with a range of 1,000 to 13,000. So Prime's '7,000 more children likely in poverty' matches the central official estimate for that single measure, and the word 'likely' is consistent with the ranges. What is not yet available is the Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics outturn for the years the modelling covers, which runs to 2027/28 and will not be published until 2028 - and even then, attributing a measured change to this one policy will be difficult, since the official estimate was explicitly conditional on no offsetting income-support measures. Returning not_yet_due rather than partly_correct because the criterion's true/false test turns on the measured outcome, which does not exist yet; absence of that data is not evidence against the claim.

statement: As I said, the experience pathway was always going to be a temporary measure, and now it is also going to be a temporary measure, but this extension of allowing people to use the experience pathway for another two years will allow some last-minute social workers, those who are out there and are considering getting registered as social workers, to really seriously consider and come on board and get their registration done.
criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual reports / registration statistics for the years to 28 February 2026; true if registrations granted under the experience (competence-without-qualification) pathway during the extension period exceed the pre-extension annual run-rate, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether experience-pathway (s13) registrations during the extension exceeded the pre-extension annual run-rate. SWRB annual reports give the 'new to the Register by pathway' split: 2022/23 = 4% of 650 new registrants (~26), 2023/24 = 6% of 744 (~45), 2024/25 = 10% of 583 (~58). The two-year extension ran from 28 Feb 2024 to 27 Feb 2026, so 2024/25 falls entirely inside it and is roughly double the last wholly pre-extension year (2022/23), with 2023/24 (which straddles the original 27 Feb 2024 repeal date) already elevated. Registrations therefore rose rather than stayed flat or fell, and people did use the extension to complete registration, as Parmar predicted. Caveat: SWRB's financial year ends 30 June, so the final stretch of the extension (Jul 2025 - 27 Feb 2026, including the closing rush before s13 was repealed on 28 Feb 2026) is in the 2025/26 annual report, which is not yet published; the criterion is nevertheless already met on published data. Percentages are rounded, so the counts are approximate (+/- ~3), but the gap is far larger than the rounding.

statement: Now, the Minister has said that this will be unlikely to impact the supply of methamphetamine in New Zealand.
criterion: ESR national wastewater methamphetamine consumption estimates and NZ Police/Customs data on domestic clandestine laboratory detections, comparing the period after pseudoephedrine returns to over-the-counter sale with the preceding baseline. True if there is no sustained rise in domestically manufactured methamphetamine or in pseudoephedrine-based clan-lab busts attributable to the reclassification; false if clan-lab detections and pseudoephedrine diversion rise materially after the change.
reasoning: Pseudoephedrine cold-and-flu medicines returned to pharmacist-only over-the-counter sale on 20 May 2024. On the criterion's own measures: NZ Police clandestine-lab detections (OIA IR-01-25-22265) were 26 in May-Dec 2023 (~3.3/month), 53 in calendar 2024 (~4.4/month) and 18 in Jan-May 2025 (~3.6/month) - a bump in 2024 followed by a return close to the earlier rate, i.e. no sustained rise. Pseudoephedrine diversion from pharmacies has not been shown to rise materially: one pharmacy burglary for the product was reported in the first two months, and the pseudoephedrine seized in 2026 lab busts was imported precursor brought in by an overseas-based syndicate, not pharmacy stock. Methamphetamine consumption itself did rise sharply over the period (ESR/Police wastewater: 36.6 kg/week in Q1 2026, 15% above the prior four quarters, records in April 2026), but seizure and Customs data point to imported finished product (cartel shipments, a 25-fold rise in imported pipe/bong seizures) rather than domestic manufacture. So on the criterion as written - no sustained rise in domestic manufacture or pseudoephedrine-based clan-lab busts attributable to the reclassification - the Minister's expectation holds. Caveat: lab-detection counts reflect enforcement effort as well as underlying activity, no official evaluation of the reclassification has been published, and if 'supply' is read broadly rather than as domestic manufacture, NZ meth supply plainly did increase over this period.

statement: We’re also concerned that the introduction of this legislation will retrigger the crime rates at pharmacies, as we saw in the late 2000s.
criterion: NZ Police recorded burglary and robbery offences at pharmacies for the 24 months after over-the-counter pseudoephedrine sales resume, compared with the 24-month baseline before resumption; true if pharmacy-targeted offences rise materially (roughly 25% or more) above that baseline, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The resolve-by date (31 Dec 2026) has not passed, and the specific measure the criterion names - NZ Police recorded burglary and robbery offences at pharmacies, 24 months after over-the-counter sales resumed (20 May 2024) against the 24-month baseline before - is not published. policedata.nz and the Police retail-crime releases do not break victimisations out by premises type such as 'pharmacy', so the comparison would require an OIA to Police; no such release covering the post-May-2024 window was findable. What is on the record is anecdotal and points both ways but is not the named measure: a Motueka pharmacy was burgled for pseudoephedrine within a week of the product's return (May 2024), and a Pharmacy Today review in July 2024 counted only that one burglary in the first two months; pharmacists reported more drug-seeking behaviour and called for a national sales register. No published source documents a roughly 25%-or-more rise (or a fall) in pharmacy-targeted offending.

statement: We could very well get back to the situation again where people who can’t afford P—and despite the fact we are awash with the stuff, it is actually relatively expensive still, and if it becomes a cheap option to go and get hold of your pseudoephedrine to make this product again locally, we will actually have the cycle starting again.
criterion: NZ Police / ESR clandestine laboratory detection statistics and pharmacy pseudoephedrine diversion reporting for the period after pseudoephedrine returns to pharmacy sale; true if clandestine lab detections or seizures of pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine rise materially above the 2023 baseline, false if clan-lab detections remain flat or fall and the meth supply stays import-dominated.
reasoning: The prediction window has fully elapsed: Medsafe approved 11 pseudoephedrine products on 12 April 2024 and they were confirmed on pharmacy shelves by 20 May 2024, over two years before the 2026-06-30 resolve-by date. Going to the source the criterion names (NZ Police clandestine-lab detection statistics), OIA response IR-01-25-22265 (18 August 2025) gives monthly clan-lab detections by district. Reconstructing matched 12-month windows around the return: Jun 2023-May 2024 = 44 labs; Jun 2024-May 2025 (first full year after return) = 51 labs. That is +16% on counts small enough to be roughly one Poisson standard deviation - not a material rise - and the like-for-like same-months comparison actually fell (Jan-May 2024 = 20 vs Jan-May 2025 = 18). On the criterion's second limb, pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine diversion did not rise: Reckitt's September 2026 Medsafe reclassification application records that the Pharmacy Guild and New Zealand Police have reported only a small number of isolated pseudoephedrine-related thefts from pharmacies since the products returned, against 285,802 packs (6.36m doses) sold in the 12 months to 15 March 2026. Supply stayed firmly import-dominated: Customs seized an estimated 976kg of methamphetamine in Jan-May 2025 alone, and the 2026 lab busts that did occur involved offshore operators (Chinese and Taiwanese nationals alleged to have entered specifically to manufacture) and bulk imported precursors, not pharmacy pill-shopping. Checking for disconfirming evidence, meth consumption IS up - 36.6 kg/week in Q1 2026, 15% above the prior four quarters - but that cuts against O'Connor rather than for him, because the mechanism he specified was conditional on meth being expensive ('we are awash with the stuff, it is actually relatively expensive still') so that pharmacy pseudoephedrine would become 'a cheap option'. The opposite happened: Massey's NZ Drug Trends Survey has the price falling from $563/g in 2017 to $334/g in 2025 ($253/g inflation-adjusted, a 55% real drop) with record lows in Auckland, Bay of Plenty and Waikato on new Mexican cartel supply. Rising use is being met by cheap imports, so the economic trigger for a return to local pseudoephedrine cooking never arrived. Both branches of the criterion's false condition are satisfied. Limitation: published clan-lab counts run only to May 2025, so the final year of the window (Jun 2025-Jun 2026) is not directly covered; import dominance and flat pharmacy diversion are, however, confirmed through September 2026.

statement: This bill, sadly, will mean there are more victims of crime, because the drivers of crime are not addressed and offenders reoffend.
criterion: Ministry of Justice reoffending statistics (12-month reconviction and reimprisonment rates) for cohorts sentenced after the Legal Services Amendment Act's commencement, compared with the immediately preceding cohorts. True if reoffending rises materially above the pre-commencement trend; false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion sets a resolve-by date of 2027-06-30, which has not passed (today is 2026-09-26), and the evidence it names does not yet exist. The Legal Services Amendment Act 2024 received Royal assent on 7 March 2024 and commenced 22 March 2024, removing legal aid funding for s 27 Sentencing Act reports. The criterion asks for Ministry of Justice 12-month reconviction and reimprisonment rates for cohorts sentenced after commencement, compared with the immediately preceding cohorts. No such cohort comparison has been published. Ministry of Justice criminal conviction and sentencing tables (most recent to 31 December 2024) and Corrections' reconviction research report aggregate reconviction and reimprisonment following release from prison (around 56.5% reconvicted and 35.8% reimprisoned within 2 years), but neither is cut by sentencing cohort relative to the Act's commencement, and neither identifies whether an offender had a s 27 report. The Equal Justice Project's one-year review of the defunding (covering to March 2025) explicitly reports that it could find no empirical data on sentences, appeals or demographic outcomes since defunding began, only practitioner concerns. Under the stated rule that absence of evidence is not evidence of falsity, and with the resolve-by date still roughly nine months away, this is not yet due rather than uncheckable - the data series required does exist in principle and should become reportable once post-March-2024 sentencing cohorts have a full 12-month follow-up published.

statement: Unilaterally, removing funding means a greater risk of unfair and ineffective sentences, a higher rate of sentence appeals, and will create a situation where those who can afford to privately pay for these reports will be more advantaged—and we Māori will be disadvantaged yet again.
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing and appeal statistics for the two years following the Act's commencement; true if the rate of sentence appeals rises measurably above the pre-change trend, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion asks for sentencing and appeal statistics for the two years following the Act's commencement (22 March 2024), true if the rate of sentence appeals rises measurably above the pre-change trend. The High Court of New Zealand Annual Report 2025 (published May 2026) breaks new criminal appeals out by type, which is the only published series that isolates sentence appeals. Sentence appeals filed in the High Court: 465 in 2023 (pre-change), 408 in 2024 (the commencement year - a 12% FALL), 650 in 2025 (a 59% rise, which the Court itself singles out as 'of particular note', and 40% above the 2023 pre-change level). So within the two-year window the measure moved against her prediction in year one and sharply in favour of it in year two, ending materially above baseline. Three things stop this being a clean 'correct'. First, the criterion asks for a rise above the pre-change TREND, and that trend was already climbing steeply before the Act: the same report notes conviction-and-sentence, conviction-only and sentence-only appeals to the High Court rose 82% since April 2023 - roughly eleven months BEFORE commencement - with criminal appeals at record highs in 2023, 2024 and 2025 alike. Second, checking for disconfirming evidence, the appellate picture is not uniform: Court of Appeal criminal appeals filed fell across the same window, 449 (2023) to 436 (2024) to 429 (2025). Third, no source attributes the 2025 sentence-appeal spike to s 27 defunding, and a large competing cause landed in exactly that year - the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 came into force on 17 June 2025, with previous strikes reactivated and third-strike sentencings moving to the High Court. Her further limbs - unfair or ineffective sentences, and Maori specifically disadvantaged relative to those who can pay privately - are outside the criterion as written and remain unmeasured; no published series breaks post-change sentence appeals or s 27 report use by ethnicity or by funding source. Partly correct: the outcome she named did materialise, a year later than implied and against a trend that was already rising for reasons that predate and postdate the Act.

statement: Information on the offenders’ background will continue to be presented to the court through other sources, such as their lawyer, the pre-sentence reports that the Department of Corrections prepares, or other reports that may be appropriate, such as alcohol and drug assessments or psychologists’ reports, and through letters of support from family and friends and letters from rehabilitation programme providers.
criterion: Sentencing practice after the Act's commencement, as recorded in sentencing notes, Law Society or Ministry of Justice commentary, or published review of section 27 material. True if courts continued to receive offender background material through counsel submissions, Corrections pre-sentence reports, health assessments and letters of support at a comparable rate. False if the removal of legal aid funding is documented to have left sentencing courts without that background material in a substantial share of cases.
reasoning: Judged against the criterion as written: the 'false' condition (removal of legal aid funding documented to have left sentencing courts without background material in a substantial share of cases) is not met, and the named channels demonstrably carried the material. Legal aid spending on psychiatric reports rose from ~$200,000 in April 2024 to over $470,000 by mid-2025, and on alcohol/drug addiction reports from $17,000 to over $222,000 in the same period. AUT law professor Kris Gledhill describes the effect as 'displacement from one part of the legal aid pot to another' and says courts are not receiving less background material overall. The Law Association notes the amendment does not prohibit legal aid disbursement funding for background information supplied for s8(i) purposes, and Corrections pre-sentence reports are untouched. Caveats: no published count establishes a strictly 'comparable rate'; defence lawyers report the burden shifted to unpaid counsel work and that some judges are reluctant to hear cultural evidence absent an independent report writer (Snelgar), and Bar Association/Law Society warned reports would remain available only to those who can pay privately — an equity effect, not an absence of material. One material development falls AFTER the 2025-12-31 resolve-by date and so does not change the verdict but qualifies its durability: in March 2026 MoJ's new Approved AOD Report Writers Service issued template guidance that reports 'should not include information on personal, family, whanau, community and cultural background relying on section 27 Sentencing Act 2002' — narrowing one of the very substitute channels Goldsmith named.

statement: They have written across social media and across media, and they have been very clear: all that removing the funding for cultural reports will do is entrench further discrimination in a justice system that already is trying to resolve its own discrimination.
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing and imprisonment statistics broken down by ethnicity, comparing the two years before and the two years after the funding change takes effect; true if the Māori share of custodial sentences, or the Māori/non-Māori gap in custodial sentencing rates for comparable offending, widens; false if it is flat or narrows.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific instrument: MoJ sentencing and imprisonment statistics broken down by ethnicity, comparing the two years before and the two years after the funding change (effective April 2024). The post-change window closes around April 2026, but the most recent published criminal conviction and sentencing statistics are for the June 2025 fiscal year; no June 2026 fiscal-year release exists, so the two-years-after half of the comparison is not yet publishable. Searching for the trend directly (rather than for confirmation of either direction) returned only point-in-time disproportionality analyses, not before/after series. What is available: Maori were 52.3% of prisoners by primary ethnicity at 30 November 2025 (56% counting all reported ethnicities) and ~52.6% in 2025 — roughly flat, but that is prison muster, not the Maori share of custodial sentences the criterion specifies, and it does not span the window. MoJ's wahine Maori analysis (year to June 2025) shows 7% of Maori women in court in 2024 were sentenced to prison vs 3% of non-Maori women, with over half the disproportionality unexplained by offence seriousness or history, and the Borrin/AUT report (Nov 2025) finds Maori more likely than comparable NZ European offenders to receive a more severe sentence — both establish a gap exists, neither establishes whether it widened or narrowed after April 2024. Resolve-by is 2027-06-30, still in the future. Not finding the comparison is not evidence the prediction failed.

statement: This bill will only increase incarceration rates and will increase poverty and will increase violence by not being able to have in place systems that allow for healing and the involvement of the broader community within the operations of our justice system.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster and sentencing statistics for the period following the Act's commencement, alongside Stats NZ material hardship figures; true if the prison population and average sentence lengths rise over the two years following commencement, false if they hold steady or fall.
reasoning: The criterion's measurement window (the two years following commencement, ~March/April 2024 to ~March/April 2026) has elapsed and the data exist, so this is resolvable ahead of its 2027-02-20 resolve-by. Incarceration leg: CONFIRMED and large. The prison population was 9,294 in February 2024 and 11,240 in February 2026 — a rise of about 21% — with the remand population up from 4,132 to 4,677 and the sentenced population up from roughly 5,162 to 6,563. MoJ's June 2026 Justice Sector Projections state the sentenced prison population has been increasing since June 2023 and that new policy settings are 'resulting in an increasing rate of imprisonment and longer sentences', which supports the average-sentence-length half, though no published average-sentence-length series covering 2024-2026 was findable (the Law Society's figures stop at 2017). Checking for the opposite, as required: the other two legs of the claim do not hold. Poverty — Stats NZ child poverty statistics for the year to June 2025 (released 26 Feb 2026) show material hardship at 14.3% with NO statistically significant change from 2024, so no measurable rise over the window (it is elevated against 2022, but that predates commencement). Violence — the NZ Crime and Victims Survey shows violent-crime victimisation fell significantly, 3% of adults in 2025 against 4% in both 2024 and 2018, about 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime, the lowest since the survey began. Attribution is also against the speaker: MoJ and commentators attribute the prison rise to the reinstated three strikes regime, the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act, the Crimes Amendment Bill and higher police/prosecution volumes — not to the cultural reports bill. So the substance (more incarceration) holds emphatically while the poverty and violence claims are unsupported or contradicted, and the causal link to this bill is unestablished.

statement: Then, with the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, our whaea Tipa Mahuta will lose that position, and we are left with one.
criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora board membership as published by the Ministry of Health after the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Act commenced: true if Tipa Mahuta no longer holds the position and only one Māori member remains; false if she retained a board position or more than one Māori member remained.
reasoning: Tipa Mahuta held her Health NZ – Te Whatu Ora board seat by virtue of chairing Te Aka Whai Ora; when Te Aka Whai Ora was disestablished on 30 June 2024 the seat ended and she was farewelled from the board (NZ Doctor). The Health NZ 2023/24 annual report lists the board as at 30 June 2024 (Levy, Ferguson, Adams, Lowe, Mahuta, Stoddart, Walker, Jarrold); of these, Mahuta and Dr Curtis Walker (Ngāti Porou/Whakatōhea) were the Māori members, so her departure left one, as predicted. Neither falsifier occurred: she did not retain a position, and more than one Māori member did not remain. Caveat in her favour rather than against: Walker declined to renew his term and on 24 July 2024 the entire board was replaced by Commissioner Lester Levy with deputy commissioners Jarrold, Whelan and Clegg, none Māori — so the 'one' lasted only weeks before becoming zero.

statement: Then, finally, how much worse is Māori health going to get over those five years—and I think it might be unlikely that he will still be the Minister of Health in 2029.
criterion: The official Ministerial List as published by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet during 2029. TRUE (prediction correct) if Shane Reti does not hold the Minister of Health portfolio at any point in 2029; FALSE if he holds it.
reasoning: The criterion names the Ministerial List as published during 2029; today is September 2026, so the resolving document does not exist yet and the prediction cannot be settled. Available evidence points the speaker's way — Shane Reti lost the Health portfolio to Simeon Brown in the 19 January 2025 cabinet reshuffle and was moved to Universities plus Science, Innovation and Technology — but holding the portfolio 'at any point in 2029' remains open, since a future reshuffle or government could restore it.

statement: Well, it’s pretty late, there’s no select committee process, this will be done by tomorrow, and the very mechanisms in this legislation to make it work, to deliver pae ora for all will be gone.
criterion: Parliament's bills record for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if the bill completed its third reading on or before 28 February 2024; false if it was still before the House after that date.
reasoning: The Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill was introduced under urgency on 27 February 2024 and taken through all three readings in one sitting with no select committee stage; it passed its third reading 68–54 on 28 February 2024 and received Royal assent on 5 March 2024. The criterion (third reading completed on or before 28 February 2024) is met exactly, and the speaker's 'done by tomorrow', said on 27 February, resolved as stated.

statement: Smoking rates are going to continue to fall under the existing legislation that we’re going to readopt.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for survey years after 2023/24; true if the rate is lower than the 2022/23 figure of 6.8%, false if it is flat or higher.
reasoning: The criterion tests NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for survey years after 2023/24 against the 2022/23 figure of 6.8%. The 2024/25 NZHS puts adult daily smoking at 6.8% (95% CI 6.2–7.4) — identical to 2022/23, and statistically unchanged from 6.9% in 2023/24. Ministry of Health and Smokefree.org.nz both describe the rate as plateaued: 'for the first time since the NZHS started, daily smoking prevalence remained virtually unchanged for three consecutive years', and the Smokefree 2025 goal of <5% was not achieved. The criterion says false if the rate is flat or higher; it is flat. Disconfirming check: MoH's own headline stresses the long-term decline from 16.4% (2011/12), which is real but is not the comparison the criterion specifies.

statement: Does the Minister accept that this Government’s breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi will lead to further claims before the Tribunal and further court litigation, or will he just simply do the right thing and remove his bill?
criterion: Waitangi Tribunal claim register and court filings in the year following 27 February 2024. True if one or more new claims and at least one court proceeding are filed concerning the repeal of the Māori Health Authority or related Crown action; false if no new claim or litigation is filed in that period.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied within the year after 27 February 2024. Tribunal claims: after the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill was introduced on 27 Feb 2024 and passed 5 March 2024, the Tribunal granted a priority inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora within Wai 2575 on 8 May 2024, reporting Hautupua Part 1 on 29 November 2024; 2024 also saw a record number of urgent claims (MHA disestablishment, s7AA repeal, Māori wards, te reo in the public sector), all arising from coalition-agreement policy. Court litigation on related Crown action: the Crown brought judicial review in the High Court over the Tribunal's summons of Minister Chhour in the s7AA inquiry (Isac J set the summons aside on 24 April 2024), and the Court of Appeal overturned that decision on 13 May 2024. Noted caveat: the court proceeding was Crown-initiated and concerned the s7AA repeal rather than the MHA repeal itself, which the criterion's 'or related Crown action' wording expressly permits.

statement: Let’s be clear—and the Minister knows this—this will lead to more people in jail for longer; people who, if they had the money to pay for such a report, a judge would know all the facts and wouldn’t have imprisoned them in the same way.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster and Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics for the two years after the Act's commencement, alongside any published evaluation of the funding change; true if custodial sentencing rates and average custodial sentence lengths rise and analysis attributes part of the rise to reduced access to section 27 reports, false if custodial rates and sentence lengths do not rise or the change is attributed elsewhere.
reasoning: The Legal Services Amendment Act 2024 (Royal Assent 7 March 2024) removed legal aid funding for s27 reports. In the two years since, imprisonment clearly rose: the prison muster hit a record 11,255 in March 2026 (from roughly 10,000 in early 2024), and MoJ/Corrections analysis states people who would previously have received home detention or intensive supervision are now more likely to be imprisoned and for longer, with the sentenced population projected up 26% by 2036. So the direction of Webb's claim holds. The criterion's third limb fails, however: no published evaluation attributes any part of the rise to reduced access to s27 reports. Law News' account of the MoJ Justice Sector Projections lists 'ending public funding for Section 27 reports' among the legislative drivers, but the quantified drivers are the 40% cap on mitigating discounts (RIS: ~1,350 more prisoners), reinstated three strikes, the Gangs Act and new offences. Law professor Kris Gledhill said in August 2025 that the displacement effect 'would be impossible to ever truly know' and called for a MoJ investigation that has not been done; the Equal Justice Project's one-year review relies on lawyer interviews, explicitly not on sentencing or imprisonment data. Substance holds, causal attribution to s27 remains unmeasured and is largely credited elsewhere.

statement: Yes, they’ll be doing it, but they’ll be doing it after the event.
criterion: The publication date of the Waitangi Tribunal's report on the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority, compared with the commencement of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Act: true if the report is released after that commencement date; false if the Tribunal reported before the Act took effect.
reasoning: The Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora was vacated when the Crown introduced the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Maori Health Authority) Amendment Bill on 27 February 2024; the Bill passed 28 February, received Royal Assent 5 March 2024, and Te Aka Whai Ora was disestablished on 30 June 2024. The Tribunal did not report until 29 November 2024, when it released 'Hautupua: Te Aka Whai Ora (Maori Health Authority) Priority Report, Part 1' in pre-publication format, finding breaches of tino rangatiratanga, partnership, active protection and redress. On the criterion as written, the report was released after the Act's commencement on any reading of that date (6 March or 30 June 2024), so Jackson's prediction that the Tribunal would act 'after the event' holds. Part 2, on the Crown's alternative plans for Maori health, was still to come.

statement: You are politicians on the eve of legacy parties, and you will not come back. You will not get a second chance at doing this.
criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission; true if National, ACT and NZ First do not together form the next Government, false if the coalition parties are returned to government.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against the result of the next New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission. That election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026 (advance voting from 26 October, enrolment closing 25 October; regulated period 7 August to 6 November 2026). Today is 26 September 2026, so the election has not been held and there is no declared result to judge against. The criterion's own resolve-by date of 2026-12-31 has not passed. No verdict on whether National, ACT and NZ First are returned to government can be reached yet.

statement: Dr Reti has said he is focused on priorities and targets. The statistics in health for Māori clearly state a case, then, that there will be increased funding from this Government for Māori health outcomes.
criterion: Vote Health estimates of appropriations for 2024/25 and 2025/26 compared with 2023/24: true if appropriations directed to Māori health outcomes rose in nominal terms under this Government, false if they were held flat or reduced.
reasoning: The criterion tests whether Vote Health appropriations directed to Maori health outcomes rose in NOMINAL terms in 2024/25 and 2025/26 against 2023/24. They did. The 'Delivering Hauora Maori Services' appropriation transferred from Te Aka Whai Ora to Health New Zealand on 1 April 2024 and received a $39m cost-pressure uplift, bringing it to $749.424m in 2024/25; the 2025/26 Estimates show $773m and the 2026/27 Estimates $811m. Funding to Maori health providers reached $1,093.4m in 2024/25, up from $584.8m in 2020/21. I checked the disconfirming side: provider funding fell as a share of Vote Health (4.4% in 2023/24 to 4.2% in 2024/25); ASMS's Budget 2025 analysis puts the increase to Maori services at under 1%, a real-terms cut; over $300m was cut from Maori-specific initiatives in Budget 2024, including the Maori Health Authority itself. So the rise is real but marginal, and both real-terms value and share of the Vote fell. Because the criterion specifies the nominal test, the verdict is correct rather than partly_correct. Caveat on evidence: Treasury, budget.govt.nz and health.govt.nz blocked direct fetches and PDF text extraction was unavailable, so the 2023/24 base for this appropriation (~$710m) is inferred from the Ministry of Health disestablishment memo's description of the $39m uplift rather than read directly off the Estimates table.

statement: There will be 8,000 deaths—8,000 deaths—from dumping smoke-free amendments.
criterion: Peer-reviewed modelling and Ministry of Health / Stats NZ smoking-attributable mortality data following the repeal of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022; true if the additional deaths attributable to the repeal are estimated at or above roughly 8,000, false if materially lower (e.g. an order-of-magnitude or half that figure).
reasoning: The criterion accepts peer-reviewed modelling estimates. Ait Ouakrim, Wilson, Waa et al. (Tobacco Control, 2023), the simulation study of the Smokefree Aotearoa Action Plan that underpinned the repealed Act, projects the measures would have reduced smoking deaths by 8,150 over 20 years (95% UI 6,450-9,890; 2,811 among Maori) and by 1,170 within 10 years. Repealing all three measures (smokefree generation, denicotinisation, retail reduction) forgoes that gain, so the estimated additional deaths attributable to the repeal are ~8,150 - at or above the ~8,000 threshold the criterion sets. Disconfirming check: I looked for lower official estimates and for arguments that vaping-driven decline would substitute; the Ministry's repeal options paper and critical commentary do not produce a materially lower modelled mortality figure, and no source contradicts the 8,150. Caveats that stop short of changing the verdict: the number is a 20-year modelled projection, not observed mortality (the 10-year figure is only 1,170), and Jackson signalled no timeframe; observed smoking-attributable mortality cannot settle this until well after 2040.

statement: Those strong Māori health providers will still be working for Māori health, and everybody in the health system will be doing the same.
criterion: Health NZ / Te Whatu Ora commissioning and contract records for providers formerly commissioned by Te Aka Whai Ora; true if those providers broadly retained contracts and continued delivering Māori health services after the disestablishment, false if a material share lost funding, had contracts discontinued, or closed.
reasoning: On the contracts half, the criterion is broadly met: all Te Aka Whai Ora contracts, assets and staff were transferred to Health NZ on a 'lift and shift' basis into a new Hauora Maori Services directorate; Minister Reti extended existing Hauora Maori and Budget 2022 contracts for a further year to July 2025; the Hauora Maori Services appropriation rose ~$39m to $749.4m, and total funding to Maori health providers reached $1,093.4m in 2024/25 (up 87% from 2020/21). I searched specifically for the disconfirming case - providers losing contracts, closing, or having funding discontinued - and found no evidence that a material share of former Te Aka Whai Ora providers did so by the 30 June 2025 resolve date. (The three Whanau Ora commissioning agencies did lose their contracts from 30 June 2025, but those were commissioned by Te Puni Kokiri, not Te Aka Whai Ora.) What does not hold is the degradation and the second clause. Providers moved from multi-year to 12-month contracts and absorbed the churn of reversing 18 months of transfers (Te Oranganui, 185 staff), losing dedicated relationship managers and national forums. And 'everybody in the health system will be doing the same' is contradicted: Health NZ proposed cutting its Director and Chief Advisor Maori Health roles, the Maori renal health taskforce was disbanded, Iwi-Maori Partnership Boards were left without a clear role and competing for limited funding, and the Waitangi Tribunal's Hautupua reports (Part 1, Nov 2024; Part 2, 2026) found the Crown breached Treaty principles and that the arrangements put in place after disestablishment were deficient. Substance of the provider-continuity claim holds; the systemwide claim is materially overstated.

statement: If those trends continue without any additional measures, New Zealand will hit the headline smoke-free goal of less than 5 percent of the population smoking daily by 2025.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 reporting year; true if below 5.0%, false if 5.0% or above.
reasoning: The criterion names the New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 reporting year: true if below 5.0%. The 2024/25 NZHS reports adult daily smoking at 6.8% (95% CI 6.2-7.4%), about 294,000 people - well above 5.0%. Costello's prediction also depended on the existing downward trend continuing; it did not. Daily smoking was 6.8% in 2022/23, 6.8% in 2023/24 and 6.8% in 2024/25 - the first time since the survey began that the rate held within 0.1% for three consecutive years - and current smoking has sat at 8.3-8.4% for three years. The goal as stated by government is under 5% for all population groups, and Maori (15.0%), Pacific peoples (10.3%) and the most deprived quintile (12.9%) are far above it. Disconfirming check: I looked for any measure or subgroup on which the target was met and for a later survey reading; the only sub-5% groups are Asian (4.5%) adults, and the 2025/26 survey is not yet published, but no plausible single-year fall from 6.8% to below 5.0% is in evidence - researchers analysing the 2024/25 results state the goal will not be achieved.

statement: Look, smoking rates have been falling consistently for some time, and that trend will continue under our Government.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence, annual releases from 2024/25 onward: true if the rate falls in each release through the term, false if it flattens or rises.
reasoning: Criterion: false if the NZHS adult daily smoking rate flattens or rises in releases from 2024/25 onward. It flattened. Adult daily smoking was 6.8% (2022/23), 6.9% (2023/24), 6.8% (2024/25).
