No annual report or investment announcement discloses a controlling (>50%) interest in an operating or infrastructure entity, and the Guardians have publicly framed control as 'an additional tool in the toolbox, rather than the target investment state'. But the criterion's resolve-by date is 30 June 2029, nearly three years away, and Willis's claim was explicitly about what would happen 'in future'. Absence of a controlling stake in the first two years does not make the prediction wrong yet.

statement: This funding means that many medicines that would have been at risk of delisting will continue.
criterion: Pharmac's Pharmaceutical Schedule changes over the following 18 months; true if no material set of existing funded medicines is delisted for funding reasons after the funding boost, false if Pharmac delists existing medicines citing budget constraints.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether Pharmac delisted existing funded medicines for funding reasons in the ~18 months after the boost (to 31 Dec 2025). It did not. The $1.774b package (incl. a $604m uplift, taking the four-year budget to $6.294b) was explicitly sized to cover cost pressures on existing listings, and Pharmac went on to make 64 investment decisions in 2024/25 and fund new medicines from 1 March 2025. The delistings that did occur in the window were not budget-driven: efavirenz 600mg (global supplier discontinuation of the original product, with transition time to funded alternatives), the Ibrance brand of palbociclib (a tender brand change — palbociclib stayed funded), iron as sucrose (supply running out), and routine tender brand switches. Pharmac's budget-pressure actions in 2025 targeted the *waiting list* of unfunded applications, not existing listings — and it abandoned even the broader cull of low-ranked applications after negative consultation feedback. Disconfirming check: searches for patients losing funded treatments to Pharmac budget cuts in 2024-25 returned only waiting-list and brand-change stories, no removal of a material set of funded medicines.

statement: Over the next few months, the Māori Affairs Committee will continue to hear and consider submissions for this bill.
criterion: The Māori Affairs Committee's submission record and report on Te Pire mō Ō-Rākau, Te Pae o Maumahara/Ō-Rākau Remembrance Bill on the Parliament website; true if submissions were called for and heard within roughly six months of 30 April 2024, false if the bill was not referred, no submissions were taken, or the process did not occur in that period.
reasoning: Te Pire mō Ō-Rākau, Te Pae o Maumahara/Ō-Rākau Remembrance Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Māori Affairs Committee on 30 April 2024 — the day Potaka spoke. The committee opened public submissions on 1 May 2024 with a closing date of midnight 14 June 2024, received and considered 55 submissions from groups and individuals, and heard oral evidence from 16 submitters at hearings held at Parawera Marae (22 July 2024) and in Wellington. That is squarely 'over the next few months' and well inside the criterion's roughly-six-month window from 30 April 2024. The bill was reported back and completed its second and third readings on 18 February 2025, with royal assent on 23 February 2025.

statement: We cannot wait to come and visit you, and then I cannot wait to stand in your presence again, several months from now, when this House passes this bill into law.
criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Ō-Rākau bill read a first time on 30 April 2024: true if it received the Royal assent within roughly a year of the statement; false if it was still before the House, lapsed or defeated at that point.
reasoning: Parliament's bill record shows Te Pire mō Ō-Rākau, Te Pae o Maumahara / Ō-Rākau Remembrance Bill had its first reading on 30 April 2024 (the day of the statement), second and third readings on 18 February 2025, and Royal assent on 23 February 2025 (Wikipedia's acts table gives 24 February; either way the same week). It was not still before the House, lapsed or defeated — it became the Ō-Rākau Remembrance Act 2025 roughly 10 months after the statement, inside the criterion's 'roughly a year'. Fleming's 'several months from now' is on the long side of that phrase but the criterion as written is satisfied.

statement: So the question is about productivity, and I am pleased to inform the member that the Treasury will actually very shortly be publishing a working paper on productivity and its analysis of what’s been going so badly wrong with productivity in the New Zealand economy in recent years.
criterion: The Treasury's published papers list: true if the Treasury publishes a working paper or analytical note on New Zealand productivity within roughly eight months of 30 April 2024; false if no such paper appears in that period.
reasoning: Treasury published 'The productivity slowdown: implications for the Treasury's forecasts and projections' (Treasury Paper TP 24/01, number assigned retrospectively in November 2024) on 3 May 2024 — three days after the 30 April statement, well inside the eight-month window, and matching 'very shortly'. Its content matches what Willis described: it analyses New Zealand's productivity slowdown and its likely drivers (lower productivity benefits from innovation, weak investment relative to employment growth, slowing international trade and connections) and the resulting forecast downgrades since mid-2023. The only gap is the series label — it is a 'Treasury Paper' rather than a 'Working Paper' — but the criterion explicitly admits 'working paper or analytical note', and Treasury has continued publishing on the same topic (e.g. Analytical Note AN 25/11 on industry structure and the labour productivity slowdown). Checked for the disconfirming case (no productivity publication in the window) and found the opposite.

statement: Of concern is that two-thirds of GPs are going to be retiring in New Zealand over the next decade, and we expect Health New Zealand to be doing all it can to be ready to tackle those problems.
criterion: Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners workforce survey / Medical Council workforce data over 2024–2034: true if roughly two-thirds of the GPs practising in 2024 have retired by 2034, false if the proportion is materially lower.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether roughly two-thirds of the GPs practising in 2024 have in fact retired by 2034; that decade has not elapsed (resolve-by 2034-04-30), so no workforce dataset can settle it yet. Context on where the number comes from: RNZCGP workforce surveys measure stated retirement *intentions*, which have risen steadily — 41% intending to retire by 2025 in the 2015 survey, 49% within 10 years in 2020, 55% in 2022, reported in 2023 coverage as 'nearly two thirds' planning to retire within 10 years. So Uffindell's figure tracks a real published statistic, but an intentions figure is not the realised-retirement measure the criterion names, and intention historically overstates actual exit. No verdict on truth is available before 2034.

statement: Now, it’ll probably get over the hurdle. It’ll probably get through tonight, and onward we’ll go.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill's reading on 10 April 2024: true if the reading was agreed to that sitting, false if it was defeated or not voted on.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the reading was agreed to at the 10 April 2024 sitting. Hansard (Final Daily, Wednesday 10 April 2024, p. 2795) shows the second reading debate ended with "Debate interrupted. The House adjourned at 9.57 p.m." — the question was never put that night, so on the criterion's literal test ("false if it was defeated or not voted on") the 'tonight' element fails. The substance of Webb's prediction did hold: when the debate resumed on 8 May 2024 the bill was read a second time by personal vote, Ayes 101 / Noes 21 (Hansard, 8 May 2024, p. 3251), and it went on to committee, third reading (31 July 2024) and Royal assent (1 August 2024). So: right about the hurdle being cleared and the bill going onward, wrong about it happening that sitting — the outcome was delayed four weeks by the House rising and by the April recess.

statement: It may well be the first time that the class of 2023 needs to see a personal vote in a couple of weeks, so I’m very much looking forward to that.
criterion: Hansard's division record for the second reading of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill; true if that reading was decided by a personal vote and no earlier personal vote had been held in the 54th Parliament, false if it was a party vote or a personal vote had already occurred in this Parliament.
reasoning: The criterion's first leg is confirmed directly from the division record: Hansard (Final Daily, Wednesday 8 May 2024, p. 3251) reads "A personal vote was called for on the question, That the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Bill be now read a second time." Ayes 101, Noes 21; motion agreed to. It was a personal vote, not a party vote. Immediately before it (p. 3250) the Assistant Speaker (Teanau Tuiono) said "I have determined that the subject of this vote will be treated as a conscience issue... This is the process we are going to follow: I am going to put the question, and I'm going to announce the result. At that stage, any member can ask for a personal vote" — a from-first-principles explanation consistent with this being the Parliament's first. Todd Stephenson on 10 April likewise said "This is obviously going to be, at the appropriate time, a conscience vote. I think it's now called a personal vote in the Standing Orders." I found no record of any earlier personal vote in the 54th Parliament (the bill's earlier personal vote, 105-9 on 1-2 August 2023, was in the 53rd Parliament), though I did not exhaustively scan every sitting day from December 2023, so that second leg is strongly supported rather than proven. Meager's timing was off: he said "in a couple of weeks" and the vote came four weeks later, on 8 May, because of the April recess. The claim was hedged ("It may well be") and the substance holds.

statement: Inflation has been falling since then, and the monetary policy committee is confident that inflation will return to within the 1 to 3 percent band in this calendar year.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation prints for the June, September and December 2024 quarters; true if any 2024 quarterly annual rate falls within 1-3%, false if all four remain above 3%.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether any 2024 quarterly annual CPI rate fell within 1-3%. Stats NZ reported annual inflation of 2.2 percent in the September 2024 quarter (release headlined "Annual inflation at 2.2 percent"), the first time back inside the Reserve Bank's 1-3% target band since 2021, and 2.2 percent again in the December 2024 quarter. The earlier 2024 prints were 4.0% (March) and 3.3% (June), so inflation was indeed falling and did return to within the band inside the 2024 calendar year, as Willis said the Monetary Policy Committee expected.

statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link, and it’s soon going to be completed, and that is $5 billion of investment into our rail network in Auckland, which is going to unlock significant opportunities for Aucklanders wanting to use public transport.
criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport announcements: true if the CRL is completed and opened for passenger services by the end of 2026, false if completion slips beyond that date.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether the CRL is completed and opened for passenger services by the end of 2026. It was: the City Rail Link formally opened on Friday 13 September 2026 (PM Christopher Luxon attending), with public passenger services running that weekend and the first weekday timetable from Monday 14 September; Auckland Transport reported roughly 70,000 boardings on the first day and Railway Gazette independently reported the opening to passengers. Brown spoke in May 2024 saying it was 'soon going to be completed' and it opened ~16 months later, inside the window. Checked for disconfirming evidence of a slip past 2026 and found none — the opening is reported as having happened, not as scheduled. Outside the criterion: the final project cost is generally reported nearer $5.5b than the $5b he cited, and the CRL was initiated under the Key government with the funding agreement signed in 2017, so the attribution limb is defensible; neither limb is what the criterion tests.

statement: It’s great to see this bill getting through its second reading, and I’m sure that it will progress further through the House and end successfully in due course.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bill record for the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill; true if it passes its third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, withdrawn or still not passed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion asked for the parliamentary record of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill: true if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent. It did. Hansard records the second reading on 11 April 2024, committee stage 7 May 2024, and the third reading on 9 May 2024; it was enacted as the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Act 2024 (No 16), Royal assent 4 June 2024, in force 1 July 2024, and it appears on the list of acts of the 54th Parliament. Checked the opposite case — no record of defeat, withdrawal or lapse. Russell's prediction that it would 'progress further through the House and end successfully in due course' was borne out about five weeks after she said it, far inside the 2025-12-31 resolve-by.

statement: During the 2020s, almost a quarter of a million more New Zealanders will reach 65 and over and will be claiming that super, and so, by the late 2050s, they’re predicting that we’re going to see that one in every four New Zealanders will be 65 or older.
criterion: Stats NZ population estimates for the late 2050s (and, for the first limb, the change in the 65+ population over 2020-2029); true if roughly 250,000 more New Zealanders pass 65 during the 2020s and the 65+ share reaches about 25% by the late 2050s, false if the 65+ share is materially below one in four at that point.
reasoning: The criterion's second limb — that the 65+ share reaches about one in four 'by the late 2050s' — cannot be observed until the late 2050s, and the resolve-by is 2060-12-31, so the prediction is not yet settleable. What is checkable now supports the claim rather than undercutting it. First limb: Stats NZ puts the 65+ population at about 0.79 million in 2020 and projects it to pass 1 million by 2028-29, so on the order of a quarter of a million more New Zealanders cross 65 during the 2020s — 'almost a quarter of a million' is a fair reading. Second limb as a report of what is predicted: Stats NZ's national population projections state that by the 2050s people aged 65+ could make up one-quarter of the population (with the 65+ count reaching about 1.5 million in the early 2050s), so Wedd accurately relayed the official projection. I looked for projections showing the 65+ share materially below 25% in that period and did not find any; the trend across successive Stats NZ projection bases (2020, 2022, 2024) is consistent. The claim is therefore an accurate restatement of current projections whose outcome is still three decades out.

statement: As my colleague Catherine Wedd said in her speech earlier, from the electorate she’s representing in Tukituki—the fruit bowl, as she often refers to it—by the late 2050s, over a quarter of New Zealand’s population will be aged over 65, and that is very stark.
criterion: Stats NZ national population estimates/projections for the years 2055–2059; true if the 65+ share of the resident population exceeds 25 percent at any point in the late 2050s, false if it remains at or below 25 percent through 2059.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the 65+ share of the resident population in 2055-2059; that period is 29-33 years away and no actual estimates exist. The admissible projections straddle the 25% threshold rather than settling it: Stats NZ's 2024(base)-2078 projections put the 65+ share at 17% in 2024, with a 90% probability of 21-24% in 2051 and 25-33% in 2078, and note the 65+ count (874,000 in 2024) roughly doubling by around 2059. Treasury's long-term fiscal work projects 65+ exceeding a quarter of the population by 2060. So a late-2050s crossing of 25% sits at the early edge of the central projection - plausible, marginally overstated on timing, but genuinely unresolved. No score.

statement: The Indonesian imports will continue to grow for as long as there is uncertainty in the gas industry—worsened by the naivety over there, and, sadly, aided and abetted by my erstwhile colleagues on the other side of the House.
criterion: Stats NZ / NZ Customs coal import volumes from Indonesia (and MBIE energy statistics) for the years following May 2024; true if imported Indonesian coal tonnage rises year-on-year, false if it falls or plateaus.
reasoning: The growth held for two years and then reversed inside the criterion's window (resolve by 2026-06-30). MBIE: coal imports rose 311% from 5.39 PJ (2023) to 22.15 PJ (2024) after Genesis announced in May 2024 it would resume importing sub-bituminous coal for Huntly amid gas-supply uncertainty; imports rose a further 29% (+6.44 PJ) in 2025, sub-bituminous up 38%, lifting the Huntly stockpile to 1.16 million tonnes by end-2025, the highest since March 2012. Most of that coal is Indonesian - MBIE and RNZ both identify Indonesia as the source for Huntly. But in the June 2026 quarter coal imports fell 94% to their lowest level since December 2011, with renewables at 92% of generation, and Genesis had signed a two-year 240,000 t domestic supply deal with BT Mining, cutting reliance on imports. Substance correct for 2024-2025, contradicted by the end of the window.

statement: But, in saying that, I’m sure that given the support that looks likely across the House, it will come to the Justice Committee and we look forward to considering it then.
criterion: The House's referral record for the Privacy Amendment Bill after its first reading: true if referred to the Justice Committee, false if referred to any other committee (e.g. Governance and Administration) or not referred.
reasoning: The Privacy Amendment Bill had its first reading on 2 May 2024 - the day Meager spoke - and was referred to the Justice Committee, exactly the committee named. The committee called for submissions closing 14 June 2024, considered 55 submissions, and recommended the bill be passed; it received Royal Assent on 23 September 2025. No source indicates referral to any other committee (e.g. Governance and Administration).

statement: That is why ACT will be supporting this bill, and we trust that it will get a good hearing at the Justice Committee and that parties across the House will continue to support it until it’s passed into law.
criterion: The division records for the Privacy Amendment Bill's subsequent readings and its royal assent: true if the bill passes into law without any party voting against, false if any party votes against at a later reading or the bill fails to pass.
reasoning: The bill Court spoke to at first reading on 2 May 2024 (Privacy Amendment Bill 2023 No 292, new IPP 3A) was referred to the Justice Committee as he predicted, and passed into law as the Privacy Amendment Act 2025, royal assent 23 September 2025 — inside the 2026-06-30 window. At the third reading on 18 September 2025 the Hansard record shows 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time.' with no division figures recorded, and speakers from National, ACT, NZ First, Labour and the Greens all supported or commended the bill; no party opposition is recorded at any later reading. Looking for the disconfirming case: I searched for a division or party vote against at second/third reading and found none, and no party issued an opposing position. IPP 3A came into force 1 May 2026.

statement: We’re now seeing in Australia an increased use of knife crime, and this is probably going to arrive on our shores too, and this Government’s going to get ahead of the problem and make sure that we actually deal with it.
criterion: NZ Police victimisation statistics for offences involving a knife or other cutting weapon; true if national counts rise materially above the 2023-24 baseline by the resolve-by date, false if flat or falling.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 2026-12-31, which has not passed (today is 2026-09-26), and the national weapon-type series it names is published only through the policedata.nz interactive reports, which I could not read directly; no 2025 or 2026 national count of knife/cutting-weapon victimisations is available in published reporting. The most recent published figure is for the year to December 2024: 1,639 incidents involving a stabbing or cutting weapon in serious assaults and aggravated robberies, a 1.7% DECREASE on the prior year, against the ~4.5%-over-five-years rise that was the current figure when Mitchell spoke in May 2024. Police reported only anecdotal local upticks (Auckland CBD, Napier/Hastings) and more machete use in robberies. So the evidence available so far points against the prediction of a material national rise, but the criterion's measurement window is still open and the decisive 2025-26 counts are not yet on the record.

statement: We’ve not shared any details of the Budget with the OECD, but it is safe to say that after 30 May, they will find that the Budget is entirely consistent with this advice.
criterion: Budget 2024 documents (BEFU 2024) and subsequent OECD commentary; true if the Budget's tax package is fully funded by offsetting savings/revenue and the deficit track continues to narrow as previously planned, false if the tax package is debt-funded or the forecast deficit path deteriorates against the plan the OECD endorsed.
reasoning: The criterion's false branch fired on both legs. BEFU 2024 (30 May 2024) deteriorated against the HYEFU 2023 path the OECD's May 2024 advice was framed on: the OBEGAL deficit widened to a forecast $13.4b in 2024/25 (3.1% of GDP), the return to surplus slipped a year to 2027/28 (a 0.3%-of-GDP surplus), net core Crown debt peaked higher, and bond issuance was raised by $12b over four years with a $38b 2024/25 programme — i.e. the tax package was delivered while overall borrowing rose, not while the deficit track narrowed as planned. On the OECD's own subsequent commentary, the OECD's position was that New Zealand should not borrow to fund tax cuts and that 'delaying tax cuts' would make credible consolidation easier; when the cuts took effect on 31 July 2024 this was reported as the government proceeding despite OECD advice, which is the opposite of 'entirely consistent with this advice'. The one leg that partly holds is the government's accounting claim that the $2.57b/yr package was met from identified savings, reprioritisation (departmental baselines, Climate Emergency Response Fund, closed programmes) and new revenue (commercial building depreciation, waste levy, immigration levies, online casino duty); the OECD's December 2024 Outlook later urged full implementation of Budget 2024's ~1.2ppt-of-GDP structural consolidation. That does not rescue 'entirely consistent', given the deficit path clearly worsened against the plan.

statement: Its debt is forecast to peak at $28.9 billion in 2033.
criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports and Treasury forecasts through 2033: true if reported total debt peaks in 2033 at approximately $28.9bn, false if the peak occurs in a different year or at a materially different level.
reasoning: The claim is about a debt peak in 2033; that year has not arrived, and the criterion asks for reported total debt at the peak, which cannot exist yet. The $28.9bn/2033 figure is real and correctly quoted: it comes from a leaked Ministry of Housing and Urban Development briefing (dated 17 June) reported by the NZ Herald, comparing 2022 economic models against 2018 assumptions, up from an earlier $20.9bn peak. Since the statement, the trajectory has been deliberately changed — Kāinga Ora's 2023 board-approved budget had debt reaching $24.8bn by 2026/27, and the February 2025 turnaround plan targets trimming borrowings by ~$1.78bn to about $20.5bn by 2027 via divestment. That makes a $28.9bn peak look less likely, but a revised forecast is not an outcome: the criterion names Kāinga Ora annual reports and Treasury forecasts through 2033, and the resolve-by date is 2034-06-30. No score.

statement: Well, this Government has clearly said that we’re putting public safety at the heart of what we’re doing. That means that we anticipate that there probably will be an increase in numbers coming into our corrections system, and that’s why we made this announcement around capacity.
criterion: Department of Corrections quarterly prison population (muster) statistics; true if the total prison muster is higher in mid-2025 than at May 2024, false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the total prison muster was higher in mid-2025 than at May 2024. It was, substantially. Corrections was managing 10,783 prisoners at 30 June 2025. Around the time of the statement the muster was materially lower: World Prison Brief records 9,638 for 2024 (up from 7,728 in 2022), and reporting cites 9,294 in February 2024 — so an increase of roughly 1,100-1,500 over the period, about 12%. The trend continued rather than reversing: the population hit a record 10,881 in September 2025, exceeded operational capacity of 10,633, and reached 11,256 at 30 June 2026, outstripping both the 2022 and 2024 justice sector projections. I checked for the opposite case — a flat or falling muster, or a one-off spike since unwound — and found none; every series (Corrections quarterly statistics, Stats NZ, World Prison Brief) shows the same direction, and the government has publicly owned the rise as a consequence of its sentencing and gang policies. Note the prediction was a weakly hedged one ('probably will be an increase'), and the outcome exceeded it.

statement: We have rejected the last Government’s policies when it comes to interest deductibility and restored a principled approach to tax policy which taxes profit, not revenue, and so that will be wound back and that will put downward pressure on rents.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and Trade Me median weekly rent series): true if annual rent inflation over the 12 months to April 2026, after deductibility is fully restored, is materially lower than the 12 months to April 2024; false if annual rent growth is the same or higher.
reasoning: The criterion's precondition is met — interest deductibility went to 80% from 1 April 2024 and 100% from 1 April 2025, so it was fully restored well before April 2026 — and both named series show annual rent inflation materially lower in the 12 months to April 2026 than in the 12 months to April 2024. Trade Me median weekly rent: $600 (Apr 2023) to $650 (Apr 2024), +8.3%; then $630 (Apr 2025) to $625 (Apr 2026), -0.8%. Stats NZ CPI actual rentals for housing: peaked at about 4.8% annual in Q2 2024, fell to 1.2% in the year to March 2026 (the smallest annual increase in 16 years) and 0.5% in the year to June 2026. I looked for disconfirming evidence — a series showing rents still rising at 2024 rates — and found none; interest.co.nz's Trade Me-derived series also shows year-on-year falls. One caveat the criterion does not test: the deceleration is attributed by Trade Me and market commentators mainly to rental supply up ~27% year-on-year and a sharp migration slowdown, not to the tax change, so the outcome test passes while Bishop's causal mechanism is not established by this evidence. Judged against the criterion as written, it is correct.

statement: But it is my ambition for that facility to be opened both as soon as possible but most definitely in this calendar year, and I would hope that it’s in the second half of the calendar year.
criterion: Health NZ announcements and news reporting on the opening of the North Shore Hospital expansion building; true if the facility opened between 1 July and 31 December 2024, false if it opened earlier than that window or not until 2025 or later.
reasoning: The North Shore Hospital expansion building is Tōtara Haumaru, the $317m 150-bed surgical facility. On 30 April 2024 it was complete but unopened (no operating budget/staff; Reti was then saying "likely June"). Reti officially opened it on Sunday 30 June 2024 and it took its first 13 surgical patients on Monday 1 July 2024, with Health NZ/Beehive later dating the opening to 1 July 2024. That falls in the criterion's 1 July–31 Dec 2024 window and matches both parts of his prediction (this calendar year, hoped second half). Only nuance: the ribbon-cutting ceremony was 30 June, one day before the window; the facility became operational 1 July, so the criterion is met on the operational date and the substance is met either way.

statement: I think it will come as no surprise to the House that it’s likely that those changes will relate to clauses 37 and 25.
criterion: The Supplementary Order Paper(s) and Hansard record of the committee stage of the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill; true if the Government amendments moved address clauses 37 and/or 25, false if the amendments concern other clauses or none are moved.
reasoning: The criterion names the Amendment Paper/SOP and the committee-stage Hansard for the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill (Bill 222), and I could not retrieve either: parliament.nz and hansard.parliament.nz return 404 or a JS-only error shell to every route tried (including a text-extraction proxy), legislation.govt.nz and nzlii return 403, and web.archive.org is blocked in this environment. No search index surfaces an "In Committee" Hansard page for this bill at all. Context is confirmed: clauses 37 and 25 were exactly the contested provisions (the select committee amended cl 37 and made consequential changes to cl 25 to give Representative Māori Organisations a role in appointing Te Ohu Kai Moana directors; National dissented; the Minister deferred the committee stage to consult). Indirect evidence leans against the prediction: after consulting, Shane Jones accepted the select committee's recommendation, and the enacted s 37 (amending s 44 of the 2004 Act) keeps RMO voting — 58 votes for MIO/RIO and 7 for RMOs — so no government amendment altering cl 37/25 was carried; meanwhile the committee-of-the-whole-House change I can find described concerns a different subject, extending the annual catch entitlement lease term from five to ten years. That last attribution comes only from search summaries of the third-reading Hansard, and another summary places the same change at select committee, so it is not solid enough to return "wrong". Verdict is uncheckable pending direct access to the Amendment Paper and the committee-stage Hansard.

statement: Mark my words: regardless of the likely inevitable removal of section 7AA, Te Pāti Māori will one day build a mokopuna Māori authority which will outshine this shameful moment in history, just like we did with Whānau Ora, by Māori for Māori and of Māori.
criterion: The New Zealand statute book and Parliament's bills record; true if a Bill repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 passes third reading and receives Royal assent, false if the repeal is abandoned, defeated or still unenacted by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Judged against the criterion as written (a Bill repealing s 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 passing third reading and receiving Royal assent by 31 Dec 2025): the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill was introduced 13 May 2024, first reading 21 May 2024, second reading 12 February 2025, passed its third reading on 3 April 2025 and received Royal assent on 7 April 2025 as the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act 2025. So the repeal Kapa-Kingi called "likely inevitable" did happen, well inside the resolve-by date; the repeal was not abandoned or defeated (Te Pāti Māori's late appeal to the Governor-General did not stop assent). Caveat on scope: the criterion only tests the 7AA half of the quote. The other half — that Te Pāti Māori will "one day" build a mokopuna Māori authority — carries no date and is not falsifiable on this criterion, so nothing here speaks to it.

statement: So I’m confident that with the recruitment work that the police can do over the next three years, that will quite comfortably meet our targets around that.
criterion: Police workforce reporting against the coalition target of 500 additional frontline police: true if the target is met within the stated three-year horizon; false if Police numbers fall short of the target at that date.
reasoning: The criterion's test date is 2027-05-07, which has not passed, so the three-year horizon is still open. Tracking as of 26 Sept 2026 is poor, however: the coalition's own two-year deadline (27 Nov 2025) passed without the 500 being reached; Treasury's revised estimate of ~September 2026 has also slipped; and the PM stated on ~15 Sept 2026 that 366 of the 500 had been delivered, with 300+ in training, the government conceding the full 500 will not arrive before the 7 November 2026 election (it now says 'before the end of the year'). Reaching 500 by May 2027 remains plausible, so the criterion cannot yet be settled, but the 'quite comfortably' framing is already contradicted by a deadline missed by more than a year.

statement: By police turning up to tangihanga in this way, which is completely disrespectful and culturally inappropriate, this will cause further pressure and distrust between mana whenua and police.
criterion: NZ Police annual Trust and Confidence (Public Perceptions) survey results for Māori respondents in the years following May 2024: true if Māori trust/confidence in police falls materially from the 2023/24 baseline; false if it holds steady or rises.
reasoning: The criterion requires the Māori-respondent series from the Police trust-and-confidence (NZCVS Police Module) survey for the years after May 2024. That breakdown is not published: Police issued 'summary results by demographic' tables only up to the 2023 cycle; the 2024 and 2025 releases, infographics and data tables report national figures only, and the March 2026 release (Cycle 8, Oct 2024–Oct 2025) carries no ethnicity disaggregation. The only Māori-adjacent measurement found is an RNZ-Reid Research poll (15–22 Jan 2026) showing 48.2% of Te Pāti Māori supporters have little or no trust in police — a party-support cut with no 2023/24 baseline, so it cannot show direction of change. The national series does not support a material fall (67%→69% to Oct 2024, then steady at 69% to Oct 2025), and the earlier 'stable including Māori' line traces to a June 2023 release that predates the claim, so it speaks to the baseline, not the follow-up. Judging the claim on the national proxy would substitute an easier question, so the criterion as written cannot be resolved.

statement: My question’s around strategic intent, and it follows the Minister and the Prime Minister, along with the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown, announcing the Local Water Done Well policy, an agreement unanimously reached by Auckland councillors that will avoid a 25.8 percent water rates increase on water users in and around Auckland this coming financial year.
criterion: Watercare/Auckland Council's adopted water charges for the 2024/25 financial year: true if the adopted increase is materially below 25.8 percent, false if a rise of about 25.8 percent or more is applied.
reasoning: Watercare confirmed on its own site that water and wastewater prices rose 7.2% on 1 July 2024, against the 25.8% increase in the draft Long-term Plan, following the Local Water Done Well agreement announced 5 May 2024 between the Government and Auckland Council. 7.2% is materially below 25.8%, satisfying the criterion's true condition; no evidence was found of any later 2024/25 charge revision back toward 25.8%.

statement: So the question to my right was a very clever question, and given that we will be addressing the uncertainty around the permits associated with aquaculture, you will find there will be a greater level, percentage-wise, of wealth coming from aquaculture over the next 5 to 10 years.
criterion: Aquaculture NZ / MPI seafood export revenue breakdown; true if aquaculture's share of total New Zealand seafood export revenue is higher in the 2029-2034 window than in 2024, false if its share is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion measures aquaculture's share of total NZ seafood export revenue in the 2029-2034 window against 2024; that window has not opened and the resolve-by date is 2031-05-07. Nothing published yet can settle it. For context only, MPI's June 2026 SOPI reports seafood export revenue dipping 3% to $2.2b in the year to 30 June 2026 partly on slightly lower aquaculture production, with a 2% recovery forecast in 2026-27 driven by improved aquaculture — but this is inside the interim period the prediction does not cover.

statement: There are members who have contributed to this piece of legislation who will be proud today to have reached the second stage in the legislation, and who will be looking forward to the third reading, when it will pass into law.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register and Hansard third-reading record; true if the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Bill receives Royal assent, false if it lapses, is voted down or remains unpassed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Bill did pass into law: third reading 13 May 2026, Royal assent 18 May 2026, now the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Act 2026 (2026 No 19). The criterion's substantive test — Royal assent, versus lapsing or being voted down — is met, and the quote attached no deadline to 'when it will pass into law'. The only qualification is timing: assent came about two years after the speech, past the criterion's bookkeeping resolve-by date of 2025-05-07, so the claim was unresolved rather than false at that point.

statement: I look forward to the bill’s further progress and, ultimately, to third reading and passing it in the not too distant future.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Ngāti Tara Tokanui Claims Settlement Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading within roughly a year of 7 May 2024, false if it had not passed third reading by then.
reasoning: The bill did reach third reading and pass — 13 May 2026, Royal assent 18 May 2026 (Act 2026 No 19), alongside two other Hauraki iwi settlement bills — so the substance of Simpson's prediction held. But the criterion as written required third reading 'within roughly a year of 7 May 2024' and the bill had not passed third reading by May 2025; it sat for two years after its 28 May 2024 second reading. 'Not too distant future' was therefore materially overstated: right outcome, wrong horizon.

statement: In some councils around New Zealand, I expect they will vote to retain those Māori wards, and in other councils they may not.
criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held alongside the 2025 local body elections; true if at least one council's voters vote to retain and at least one votes to remove, false if the results are uniform in one direction.
reasoning: The Māori ward polls held alongside the 2025 local elections split exactly as predicted: of the 42 councils polling, 18 voted to retain their Māori ward/constituency and 24 voted to remove it (e.g. Wellington City 64.6% keep, Porirua 66.8% keep; Stratford 58.9% remove, Taupō 57.0% remove). Nationally 542,134 votes to keep vs 467,923 to remove. The criterion's test — at least one council retains and at least one removes, false only if uniform — is satisfied. Checked for the disconfirming case (a sweep in one direction) and it did not occur.

statement: Whether a council retains its Māori ward because the voters in that community decide they want it, or they don’t, I am confident that more and more Māori will get elected to local councils up and down this country.
criterion: DIA/LGNZ counts of Māori elected members after the 2025 local elections compared with 2022; true if the number rises, false if it falls or is flat.
reasoning: LGNZ's own count of Māori elected members rose after the 2025 local elections: its 8 December 2025 release states 'over 160 Māori elected members this term, up from 145 members in 2022' — its largest-ever number — comprising 64 Māori ward councillors across 37 local councils and 13 Māori constituency members across 5 regional councils. The criterion asks for an LGNZ/DIA count and calls it true if the number rises; it rose. Caveat: this is the Te Maruata network tally, not an ethnicity field on a DIA return — LGNZ's 2025 Elected Members' Census does not appear to be published yet and DIA's 2025 local authority election statistics do not report member ethnicity, so no independent census figure is available to cross-check. Disconfirming check: the 24 councils voting to remove Māori wards do not reduce seats this term, as removals take effect only at the 2028 elections, so there is no offsetting fall.

statement: So I understand that our seafood exports are going to increase, hopefully, to around $2.3 billion by 2024.
criterion: Stats NZ / MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries seafood export revenue figures for the year to 2024; true if seafood export earnings reach approximately $2.3 billion, false if materially below that.
reasoning: MPI's SOPI series records seafood export revenue of NZ$2,141 million for the year ended 30 June 2024 (wild capture $1,568m, aquaculture $573m), up 2% from $2,097m in 2023, and $2,224m in the year to June 2025. So the increase Wedd predicted did happen, and she was faithfully relaying the December 2023 SOPI forecast of '$2.3 billion in the year to 30 June 2024' — but that forecast was not met: the actual came in roughly 7% ($160m) short of $2.3b, and even the June 2024 SOPI had already revised the expectation down to $2.2b. A calendar-2024 reading falls between $2,141m and $2,224m, also short. Substance (growth) holds; the $2.3b level is materially overstated, and $2.3b had still not been reached by the year to June 2025.

statement: Less natural gas will mean more coal being used to firm our electricity grid, as Genesis confirmed this morning.
criterion: MBIE quarterly electricity generation statistics: true if coal-fired generation (GWh) in calendar 2024 is higher than in calendar 2023; false if coal-fired generation is flat or lower.
reasoning: MBIE's Energy in New Zealand 2025 (2024 calendar year) reports coal-fired electricity generation rose 118% on 2023 to 2,243 GWh, taking coal from 2% to 5% of generation; coal energy input for electricity rose from 5.68 PJ (2023) to 18.47 PJ (2024), +225%. The criterion's test — 2024 coal GWh higher than 2023 — is met decisively. MBIE attributes the rise to a combination of unfavourable hydro inflows AND lower gas supply, so the gas mechanism Brown named is one of two drivers rather than the whole story, but the criterion does not require sole attribution. Consistent with Genesis resuming coal imports in May 2024 (imports +311%) to rebuild the Huntly stockpile, which is the confirmation Brown referred to. Checked for the opposite: no source shows coal generation flat or lower in 2024; renewables share fell from 88.1% to 85.5%.

statement: That means that we’re going to see many of our centres, I think, including Dunedin and some others, across the country, who are going to lose those services and who will no longer be able to provide access to that support to their people who are experiencing increased interest rates, cost of living hikes, their incomes are not keeping up with the cost of living, and they’re struggling to pay for food.
criterion: MSD building financial capability/budgeting service provider contracts and local reporting; true if budgeting services in Dunedin and other named centres ceased or lost the ability to provide services within the following year, false if the services continued operating.
reasoning: The funding side of the prediction held: MSD's Building Financial Capability core funding fell from $22.3m to $19.5m from 1 July 2024 and MSD stopped funding 44 of the 132 budgeting services it had funded the previous year. Dunedin Budget Advisory Service, the centre Sepuloni named, lost its ~$228,000 MSD contract, called the decision 'devastating' and cut its provision to about half; other centres lost funding too (Whanganui Budget Advisory Service), and Budget Service North Canterbury closed. But the strong form of the claim — that named centres 'will no longer be able to provide access to that support' — did not hold in Dunedin. Disconfirming evidence: an ODT report of 11 June 2025 (within the criterion's one-year window) shows DBAS still operating with two staff from the Rakiatia / Catholic Social Services hub in South Dunedin, administering the $160,000 DCC Consumer Electricity Fund, and Presbyterian Support Otago remained an MSD-funded BFC provider covering Dunedin. So capacity was materially cut and some services nationally did cease, but Dunedin did not lose access to budgeting services.

statement: Auckland households will not be hit with huge water rate increases any more, and that’s thanks to this Government.
criterion: Auckland Council/Watercare adopted water charge increases for the 2025/26 and 2026/27 years; true if annual increases stay in single digits or well below the previously signalled path, false if households face increases of a comparable magnitude to those said to have been averted.
reasoning: Watercare had signalled water charge increases of up to 25.8% per year to stay inside Auckland Council's borrowing limit. The Local Water Done Well agreement announced 5 May 2024 (Luxon, Simeon Brown, Mayor Wayne Brown) gave Watercare financial separation, and the increase for 2024/25 was set at 7.2% instead. Both years the criterion asks about are now known and both are single-digit and far below the averted path: 7.2% from 1 July 2025 (Watercare's first year as a financially independent company), and 7.2% confirmed from 1 July 2026 under the new regulated funding framework, with ~5.5% signalled for 2027. Counter-evidence considered: the increases are not nominal — 7.2% a year compounds and is above CPI, and Infrastructure Growth Charges rose 20% from 1 July 2026 — but IGCs fall on new development rather than household bills, and the criterion's test (single digits, or well below the previously signalled path) is satisfied on both limbs. Attribution to 'this Government' is reasonable: Watercare itself credits the regulated funding framework introduced following the Government-enabled financial separation.

statement: It’s been lauded in London, it’s been lauded in France, it’s been lauded everywhere, and this Government took the opportunity to get rid of that smoke-free legislation guaranteeing that thousands—thousands—more people will die.
criterion: Peer-reviewed modelling and Ministry of Health/Stats NZ smoking-attributable mortality and smoking prevalence data following the repeal; true if published estimates attribute thousands of additional deaths to the repeal relative to the retained legislation, false if prevalence and smoking-attributable mortality track the pre-repeal projected path.
reasoning: The criterion's true-limb — published estimates attributing thousands of additional deaths to the repeal relative to the retained legislation — is met. Ait Ouakrim et al. (Tobacco Control, Otago/Univ. Melbourne) modelled the repealed endgame package (denicotinisation, retailer reduction, smokefree generation) as averting 8,150 smoking-related deaths over 2020-2040 (95% UI 6,450-9,890; ~1,170 by 2030, ~6,990 in 2031-40) and 594,000 HALYs over the 2020 population's remaining lifetime; Otago researchers and Chris Bullen (~8,000 lives) restate this publicly. Even the lower uncertainty bound is thousands, so the magnitude Jackson used matches the peer-reviewed modelling. Disconfirming check: NZ Health Survey daily smoking has plateaued at 6.8-6.9% for three consecutive years (2022/23-2024/25) and the <5% goal will be missed — but a 2026 Lancet Regional Health-Western Pacific paper shows that plateau predates the repeal and attributes it to the composition of the remaining smoking population, so it neither confirms nor refutes the repeal's effect. The false-limb (prevalence and smoking-attributable mortality tracking the retained-legislation path) is not established. Caveats: the deaths are modelled counterfactuals, mostly falling after 2030, so observed smoking-attributable mortality cannot test this before ~2035, and 'guaranteeing' overstates the modelling's uncertainty.

statement: It is predicted that we need to generate twice the amount of renewable electricity we produce today to meet the 2050 demand forecast.
criterion: MBIE / Transpower / Climate Change Commission electricity demand and generation projections; true if actual (or, before 2050, officially projected) 2050 demand requires approximately twice 2024 renewable generation, false if the required increase is materially less or more than double.
reasoning: MBIE's Electricity Demand and Generation Scenarios (July 2024) projects electricity demand rising from 39.6 TWh in 2024 to 71.7 TWh in 2050 (+80.9%), with renewables supplying 92.1% by 2035 and 96.3-98.3% by 2050. Against 2024 actuals (43.9 TWh generated, 85.5% renewable, i.e. ~37.5 TWh of renewable generation), meeting 2050 demand implies roughly 70-75 TWh of renewable generation — about 1.9-2.0 times today's, i.e. approximately double. Transpower's Whakamana i te Mauri Hiko independently projects a 68% demand increase to ~70 TWh / 22 GW of electrified demand by 2050 at ~100% renewable, which is ~1.8x current renewable output. Both of the sources named in the criterion put the required increase at approximately double rather than materially less or more, so the officially projected path supports the statement as made in May 2024.

statement: Importantly, the other one thing I will mention, because it is really important, is we won’t be seeing the McLean Institute trust before this House again, because this makes it clear that the High Court will have the power to make trust variations, which will be a much more efficient process and quite possibly a lot cheaper.
criterion: The Parliament bills register: true if no further McLean Institute private bill or trust-variation bill is introduced by the resolve-by date, false if any such bill appears before the House.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on whether any further McLean Institute private bill appears by 2031-12-31, so it cannot be settled yet. Status as at 2026-09-26: no further McLean Institute bill has been introduced in the ~2.4 years since the statement, and the mechanism Webb relied on is real — the McLean Institute (Trust Variation) Act 2024 (assented 1 August 2024) applies Part 3 of the Charitable Trusts Act 1957 to the trust deed, giving the High Court jurisdiction over future variations, which removes the need for another private bill. Two qualifications worth recording: the same bill did come back before the House after 8 May 2024 for its third reading on 31 July 2024 (the bill completing passage, not a new bill, so not a falsifying event under the criterion's 'further ... introduced' wording); and under a broad reading of 'or trust-variation bill', a different private trust-variation bill — the Trust Horizon (Trust Variation) Bill — was introduced 26 February 2026 and passed 2 September 2026, showing the High Court route has not ended such private bills generally, though Webb's statement was specifically about the McLean Institute trust.

statement: As I read well—well, it is important that they would last another hundred years, because this is the last time that Parliament will have to look at this, as it moves through this process now and then is taken outside Parliament.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills register; false if any further bill to vary or amend the McLean Institute trust or its governing Act is introduced after this bill's passage, true if no such bill appears and variations proceed via the trustees/courts.
reasoning: The McLean Institute (Trust Variation) Act 2024 received Royal assent 1 August 2024 and repealed the McLean Institute Act 1934 (which had amended the 1909 and 1930 Acts), moving the trust's terms into a trust deed. The mechanism Costley relied on is real: the first-reading debate records that the difficulty was that 'the court was being asked to amend a legislative trust', so putting the terms in a deed hands future variation to the trustees/courts. Checking the bills register and the 54th Parliament's list of Acts, no further bill to vary or amend the McLean Institute trust or its governing Act has been introduced as at 26 September 2026 — Parliament has passed three other trust-variation private Acts since (Carter Trust, Otautahi Community Housing Trust, Trust Horizon), none about McLean. So the evidence for the first two years is entirely consistent with the prediction, but the criterion's window runs to 2034-05-08 and cannot be closed yet.

statement: I understand it virtually stopped—well, obviously, it stopped and even immediately following COVID, but it has slowly started to build up again, so this is not a theoretical piece of legislation; it is a very real piece of legislation which actually will be used.
criterion: NZ Police / Department of Corrections reporting or an OIA response on the number of registered offenders subject to the new overseas-travel reporting requirements after commencement; true if at least a handful of cases are recorded, false if the provisions record no use.
reasoning: The legislation is the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Act 2024 — Royal assent 4 June 2024, in force 4 September 2024 — which requires registrable offenders to name each country they intend to stay in for more than 48 hours and the addresses where they will stay. The criterion asks for a Police/Corrections count of registered offenders subject to those new requirements after commencement, or an OIA response giving one. No such figure is published: I checked the Police CSO register pages and FAQ, the CSO Register Evaluation (which covers Oct 2016-Oct 2019 only), the Police annual reports for 2024 and 2025, the Regulatory Impact Statement, the associated Cabinet papers, and FYI.org.nz OIA requests. Supporting context exists — Police describe the travel-notification process in operative terms (7 days' notice, destination law enforcement informed), and a February 2025 ministerial decision gave CSO Register staff direct access to the Customs border system to manage travelling offenders — but none of that is a count, so the criterion cannot distinguish 'a handful of cases' from 'no use'. Absence of a published number is not evidence the provisions went unused.

statement: The economy is in a recession, we have a budget deficit of over $9.4 billion, and we know we’re going to be in deficit until 2027.
criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government OBEGAL out-turns for the fiscal years to 2026/27; true if every year to and including 2026/27 records a deficit, false if a surplus is recorded in any of those years.
reasoning: The criterion requires Treasury Financial Statements of the Government OBEGAL out-turns for every year to and including 2026/27. Two of those years are settled and both are deficits: 2023/24, and 2024/25 with an OBEGALx deficit of $9.3b (~2.1% of GDP), slightly wider than 2023/24. The 2025/26 out-turn is not yet published — the year-end statements for 30 June 2026 are normally released in October, and as at 26 September 2026 the latest data is the interim statements for the nine months to 31 March 2026, which show a $7.8b OBEGALx deficit (i.e. a full-year deficit is close to certain but unaudited). The 2026/27 fiscal year does not end until June 2027; BEFU 2026 forecasts a 2.4% of GDP OBEGAL deficit in 2026/27 with a return to surplus only in 2028/29, so the direction of travel supports Doocey and if anything the deficit runs longer than 'until 2027' implies. But the final year the criterion names cannot be checked before the resolve-by date of 2027-10-31.

statement: The review will report back within six weeks on the short-term measures required to stabilise the system, with the second phase of the review making recommendations on longer-term policy and funding settings.
criterion: Date of delivery of the first-phase report of the independent review of the disability support system (Ministerial announcements / Whaikaha publications); true if the first-phase report was delivered by roughly mid-June 2024, false if it was delivered materially later or not at all.
reasoning: The Independent Review of Disability Support Services Phase One Report is dated and was delivered 28 June 2024 — about seven weeks after the 9 May statement and ~8.5 weeks after the review was announced (30 April 2024), rather than the six weeks promised or the 'roughly mid-June 2024' the criterion set. The predicted substance did happen: a first-phase report on short-term stabilisation measures was delivered, its seven recommendations were accepted, and DSS transferred to MSD from mid-September 2024; a second, longer-term phase was part of the commission as described. The miss is confined to the timeline, and it is a slip of roughly one to two weeks past the criterion's threshold rather than a failure to deliver — hence partly_correct rather than correct or wrong.

statement: It’ll be great to see the Aotearoa sailing down to Antarctica this summer and able to head into the Southern Ocean, but we have struggled to put ships near or in sea ice over recent years.
criterion: NZDF operational reporting and media releases for the 2024-25 Antarctic season: true if HMNZS Aotearoa deployed to Antarctica or the Southern Ocean between November 2024 and March 2025, false if it did not deploy in that season.
reasoning: HMNZS Aotearoa departed Devonport Naval Base on 17 January 2025 on Operation TIO, the Antarctic resupply mission for Scott Base and McMurdo Station, transiting via Geelong and arriving at McMurdo on 8 February 2025, returning 27 February 2025. The voyage ran 16 January – 27 February 2025, inside the criterion's November 2024 – March 2025 window, and it did enter Southern Ocean sea ice: the Antarctic Treaty Initial Environmental Evaluation covers a Ross Sea voyage, and the ship rendezvoused with USCGC Polar Star at the ice edge for ice-breaking and lead-through support. Both halves of the criterion (deployment to Antarctica, and into the Southern Ocean/sea ice) are satisfied.

statement: So the Defence capability plan that’s going to be released in the coming months is going to be a critical part.
criterion: Publication date of the New Zealand Defence Capability Plan on defence.govt.nz / Beehive releases: true if released by around the end of 2024, false if release slipped into 2025 or later.
reasoning: The Defence Capability Plan 2025 was launched by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Defence Minister Judith Collins on 7 April 2025 — eleven months after the 9 May 2024 statement that it would be 'released in the coming months', and well past the criterion's 'around the end of 2024' threshold. The criterion is explicit that a slip into 2025 or later counts as false. The plan was released, so the event occurred; but the criterion is about timing, and by that measure the prediction missed. I checked for an earlier 2024 publication of a capability plan and found none — capability planning pages and Beehive releases place the release in April 2025, with the previous plan being the 2019 Defence Capability Plan.

statement: There are very few bills that go to Parliament that go to a select committee that don’t come back with sensible refinements to improve the legislation. I’m sure that will be true of the fast-track bill.
criterion: The Environment Committee's report back on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if the committee recommends amendments to the bill as introduced, false if it recommends the bill proceed unamended or does not report back.
reasoning: The Environment Committee reported back on the Fast-track Approvals Bill on 18 October 2024 and recommended it pass with amendments, after 26,855 submissions and 66 hours of hearings. Recommended changes included restructuring the approvals process, requiring expert panel members with environmental expertise and one qualified in te ao Maori, extended comment timeframes at referral and panel stages, more comprehensive Treaty-obligation reporting, and replacing the final ministerial decision-making power with decisions delegated to expert panels. The criterion's true-condition (committee recommends amendments to the bill as introduced) is met; it neither recommended the bill proceed unamended nor failed to report back.

statement: So the reverse is true: by them bringing it back, there won’t be new builds; there will be competition on existing stock, house prices will go up, new homebuyers will be locked out, and rents will go up.
criterion: Stats NZ residential building consents, REINZ House Price Index and Stats NZ rental price index for the two years after May 2024; true if new-build activity falls while house prices and rents rise, false if house prices and rents are flat or falling over that period.
reasoning: Measured on the three series the criterion names, over the two years after May 2024: (1) Consents rose rather than fell - Stats NZ recorded 34,851 new dwellings consented in the year ended May 2024 and 39,737 in the year ended May 2026, up 19% on the year to May 2025 and the highest since 2023. (2) House prices did not rise - the REINZ House Price Index was -0.6% year-on-year in May 2026, -1.7% over three months, and has been broadly flat since mid-2023, still around 16% below peak. (3) Rents did not meaningfully rise - Stats NZ's actual rentals for housing index rose just 0.5% in the year to the June 2026 quarter, the smallest annual rise since 2001, with Trade Me's national median rent flat at $620 and Auckland (-1.5%) and Wellington (-0.8%) asking rents falling. The criterion's explicit false-condition (house prices and rents flat or falling) is satisfied. Disconfirming evidence checked: residential building work put in place did continue to fall even as consents rose, which partially supports the 'no new builds' leg, but the criterion names building consents, and the price and rent legs both failed outright.

statement: It is the very thing they will do, because it’s the very thing they did last time.
criterion: Kāinga Ora and HUD announcements and annual reports before the 2026 general election; true if more than around 1,000 State houses are transferred or sold to community housing providers or comparable organisations, false if no such large-scale transfer programme occurs.
reasoning: A large-scale state house divestment did occur this term: Kainga Ora's turnaround plan set sales of around 900 homes a year, its 2024/25 annual report planned 1,007 divestments in 2025/26, and by around May 2026 roughly 777-800 homes had been sold raising about $330m, with ministerial sign-off for batches such as 171 Ormiston properties. But it is not the transfer the criterion specifies. Homes are offered on the open market to private buyers and developers to maximise price, each sale is offset by a replacement new build so the portfolio stays near 78,000, and the only first-refusal right in play is iwi right of first refusal under Treaty settlement legislation, not a social-housing stock transfer. Community housing provider involvement this term is funding for roughly 1,500-2,000 additional NEW social houses plus the Flexible Fund, not acquisition of existing state houses. I found no announcement or report of more than around 1,000 state houses being transferred or sold to CHPs or comparable organisations, so the criterion's true-condition is unmet and its false-condition (no such large-scale transfer programme) is met; the substance of the prediction - state houses being sold at scale - nevertheless holds. The window formally closes at the 7 November 2026 election, and no programme of that scale is announced with six weeks remaining; the May 2026 social housing reform announcement only commits to targeted discussions with iwi and CHPs in the second half of 2026.

statement: But there is one thing that you cannot get away from in this report, and that is the elephant in the report: this is nothing more than priming the public up for the fact that (a) next week there will be no new income-related rent subsidy for housing in the Budget, and (2) it is a softening up for once again the sell-off of State houses in New Zealand.
criterion: Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) Vote Housing and Urban Development documents; true if no new income-related rent subsidy places are funded, false if the Budget funds additional IRRS-supported social housing places.
reasoning: The criterion tests limb (a): whether Budget 2024 funded additional IRRS-supported social housing places. It did. Treasury Report T2024/904, Table 1, lists under 'Additional New Spending' in the Budget 2024 package '$140m of additional 1500 public housing places being delivered by CHP's', with new operating funding of $17.5m in 2025/26, $52.5m in 2026/27 and $70m p.a. from 2027/28 — the ongoing per-place subsidy for social housing tenants, funded by winding down First Home Grants. HUD's own Budget 2024 page confirms '$140 million of new funding ... for a total of 1500 new social housing places'. The package was announced on 22 May 2024, the day after Woods spoke, and carried into the 30 May Budget. Disconfirming check: no new Kāinga Ora places were funded (Treasury recommended deferring that to Budget 2025) and ~$1b of Kāinga Ora expenditure was cut, so a narrow 'no new money for *state* houses' reading survives — but the criterion asks about IRRS places, and 1,500 were funded. Separately, the second limb of her quote (softening up for a state house sell-off) was borne out: Kāinga Ora began selling ~900 homes a year from July 2024. The criterion as written settles against her on limb (a).

statement: We won’t see more additional funding for public and State housing.
criterion: Budget 2024 (delivered 30 May 2024) Vote Housing and Urban Development documents; false if the Budget contains any new operating or capital appropriation for public/State/social housing above the previous baseline, true if no such new funding appears.
reasoning: The criterion is false if the Budget contains any new operating or capital appropriation for public/State/social housing above baseline. Budget 2024 contained one: $140m of new operating funding for 1,500 additional public housing places delivered by Community Housing Providers ($17.5m 2025/26, $52.5m 2026/27, $70m p.a. thereafter), recorded in Treasury Report T2024/904 Table 1 as 'Additional New Spending' and confirmed on HUD's Budget 2024 page. It was announced 22 May 2024, the day after Halbert spoke. Disconfirming check performed and it is substantial: Vote Housing was a net savings package (~$443.6m net savings at Budget Ministers 4), Kāinga Ora had ~$1b stripped from forecast expenditure with no new state-house places funded, and $174.5m was cut from the Emergency Housing Review/Homelessness Action Plan. So on 'State housing' narrowly — Kāinga Ora — he was right. But the criterion covers public/social housing too, and the $140m/1,500 places was the government's headline housing initiative, not a marginal line, so the claim as tested fails.

statement: Pātai tuarua: what is the Minister’s response to the fact that this effective cut to the minimum wage will increase child poverty rates, given that 64 percent of families in poverty are in work?
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship and the after-housing-costs 50% of median measure) for the year ended June 2025 compared with June 2024; true if the rates rise beyond the published sampling error, false if they hold steady or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires the Stats NZ rates for year ended June 2025 to rise beyond sampling error versus June 2024. They did not. Stats NZ published the release on 26 February 2026 under the headline 'No annual change in child poverty rates for year ended June 2025'. Material hardship: 13.5% (2024) to 14.3% (2025, ~169,300 children) — Stats NZ states 'there was no statistically significant change to the rate from the year ended June 2024'. After-housing-costs below 50% of median: moving-line 12.7% to 12.6%; fixed-line (2017/18 base) 18.2% to 17.8% — both flat or slightly down, neither significant. Direction of travel on material hardship was upward (+0.8pp), which is the direction Kemp predicted, but it sits inside the sampling error the criterion explicitly named, and the AHC50 measure moved the other way. Caveat on comparability: the survey changed from HES (Dep-17 index) to HILS (MH-18) over this window; Stats NZ nonetheless published the annual comparison and found no significant change, and CPAG — a critic of the measurement change — reports the same figures. I could not load stats.govt.nz or rnz.co.nz directly (403); the figures come from the Stats NZ release text mirrored at miragenews.com and CPAG's tabulation, which agree with each other and with the Stats NZ headline.

statement: In fact, what is clear is that the policy changes that this Government has made will decrease and disincentivise and lead to fewer houses being built.
criterion: Stats NZ new dwelling consents series; true if annual new dwelling consents in the two years after May 2024 fall below the year-to-May-2024 level, false if they hold steady or rise.
reasoning: Criterion is the Stats NZ new dwelling consents series, false if consents hold steady or rise after May 2024. Baseline year ended May 2024 was ~34,850 (Stats NZ reports 33,530 for the year ended May 2025, down 3.8% from the year ended May 2024). Year ended May 2025 dipped modestly below baseline (33,530, -3.8%), but the year ended May 2026 was 39,737 — up 19% year-on-year and ~14% ABOVE the pre-prediction baseline, explicitly ending three consecutive years of May-year declines. Summed over the two-year window, 73,267 consents vs ~69,700 for two baseline years, i.e. more homes consented, not fewer. Checked for disconfirming evidence: the value of building work put in place did keep falling over this period (so 'fewer houses being built' is arguably true on a completions/activity measure), but the criterion as written names the consents series, and on that series the prediction fails.

statement: I’ll close by saying this: renters deserve better and I have no doubt that they will rise up and kick this Government out in two years’ time for these actions.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission result of the next New Zealand general election; true if the National-ACT-NZ First coalition loses office (i.e. does not form the next Government), false if it is returned to government.
reasoning: Criterion is the official Electoral Commission result of the next NZ general election. That election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 (advance voting from 26 October; enrolment deadline 25 October). Today is 26 September 2026, so the election has not been held and no official result exists. No verdict is possible either way yet; the criterion's own resolve-by date (2026-12-31) has not passed.

statement: The Minister of Housing, Chris Bishop, claims that the changes to the Act will encourage landlords back into the rental property market.
criterion: Tenancy Services bond-lodgement data and MBIE active-bond/rental-stock series for the private rental market; true if the number of active private rental bonds/tenancies rises after the amendments take effect, false if the stock is flat or continues to decline.
reasoning: Criterion is MBIE/Tenancy Services active-bond data: true if active private rental bonds rise after the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 takes effect (staggered from 30 January 2025). I read the published monthly series directly (detailed-monthly-region CSV, location_id -99 = ALL NZ). National active bonds: 462,198 (May 2024, date of the speech); 481,704 (Jan 2025, commencement); 501,423 (Oct 2025); 523,449 (Jul 2026, latest). That is +8.7% from commencement and +13.3% from May 2024 — a rise, not flat or declining, so the embedded prediction resolves correct on the criterion as written. Two caveats that do not overturn it: (1) Tenancy Services flags the series as provisional during migration to a new bond system, which added 17,550 active bonds for definitional reasons, and closed-bond counts fall anomalously (5,106 in Nov 2025 vs a ~11,000 norm), suggesting under-recorded closures inflate the stock from late 2025 — but the May 2024 to Oct 2025 stretch (+8.5%) predates that artifact, so the rise survives the adjustment. (2) Disconfirming check: active bonds were already rising ~20,000/year through 2023 (433,383 in Jan 2023 to 453,393 in Dec 2023), so the post-amendment rise continues a pre-existing trend and does not establish the amendments caused it. Note also the quote relays Bishop's claim rather than asserting the speaker's own prediction. Trade Me/realestate.co.nz listing counts give mixed regional signals, but those measure vacant listings, not tenancy stock, and are not the named source.

statement: I understand quite a few of the recommendations have already been closed out and the remainder are well on track to be met by the end of this year.
criterion: WorkSafe's public reporting (annual report / board updates / OIA) on implementation of the review recommendations: true if all outstanding recommendations are recorded as closed by 31 December 2024, false if any remain open at that date.
reasoning: The quote does not name the review, and no source satisfying the criterion exists publicly. Candidate reviews of WorkSafe: the Laurenson review of WorkSafe's performance of its regulatory functions re Whakaari/White Island (published 22 Oct 2021; the Minister's required action date was 30 June 2022, so not a review 'on track for end of 2024'), MBIE's targeted review of the adventure activities regulatory regime, and WorkSafe's internal adventure activities regulatory health check. WorkSafe's published response pages describe completed workstreams (NZ Adventure Activities Certification Scheme v4.1 fully in force 1 April 2024; amended Adventure Activities Regulations in force 1 April 2024) but publish no recommendation-by-recommendation open/closed register, and neither WorkSafe's annual reporting nor MBIE's review pages record an implementation status as at 31 December 2024. I also could not obtain the 21 May 2024 Hansard text (the Hansard daily PDF is not text-extractable via the tools available, and the site's search is JS-driven), so the review could not be pinned down. Per the criterion, the required WorkSafe public reporting does not exist, so this cannot be resolved either way — absence of that reporting is not evidence the claim was false.

statement: Why would industry be seeking to invest in such an activity, given that the Government is going to take two years since the election to actually reintroduce the legislation, never mind actually reintroducing the practice?
criterion: Parliament's bills register; true if a bill reinstating live animal export by sea was not introduced until 2025 or later, false if such a bill was introduced during 2024.
reasoning: No bill reinstating live animal export by sea was introduced to Parliament during 2024, satisfying the criterion. In November 2024 the Government announced only that Cabinet had agreed to *draft* an Animal Welfare Amendment Bill, to be introduced 'in 2025', with select committee consideration expected that year. In April 2025 Animal Welfare Minister Andrew Hoggard said he expected the legislation to reach Cabinet 'within months', blaming a Parliamentary Counsel Office drafting backlog. In March 2026 Hoggard announced he could not get Cabinet agreement to overturn the ban and the plan was abandoned — the bill was never introduced at all. Boyack's prediction of a two-year delay in reintroducing the legislation therefore holds, and if anything understated the delay.

statement: So, ultimately, when it comes to fixed-term tenancies and the 90-day notices, we are incentivising landlords back into the market to put downward pressure on rents—that’s a good thing.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and MBIE tenancy bond median rents) for the 12 months following commencement of these provisions in early 2025: true if annual rent growth is materially lower than in the 12 months before commencement, false if rent growth is flat or accelerates.
reasoning: The fixed-term tenancy and 90-day no-cause notice provisions of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 commenced 30 January 2025. Rent growth in the 12 months after commencement was materially lower than in the 12 months before, as the criterion requires. Before: CPI actual rentals for housing rose 3.7% in the year to the March 2025 quarter — which Stats NZ noted was the first sub-4% annual rent rise since 2021, following a peak near 4.8% in mid-2024. After: rent rose just 1.2% in the year to the March 2026 quarter, the smallest annual rent increase in 16 years. On the flow measure from MBIE tenancy bond data (HUD's rental price index), new-tenancy rents were down 0.1% y/y in July 2025 and down 0.4% y/y in September 2025, with Wellington down ~6%. Stats NZ's standalone Rental Price Index is on pause, so the HUD/MBIE bond-based index is the equivalent series. Caveat the criterion does not test: HUD attributes the slowdown to easing net migration and a high level of dwelling completions rather than to the tenancy law changes, so the direction Bishop predicted occurred but his causal mechanism is not established by this evidence.

statement: It’s not true that this kind of legislation, which would see more people out on the street, which would see more vulnerable families displaced from their houses and will ultimately increase homelessness, is the answer to rents.
criterion: Ministry of Housing and Urban Development housing register and emergency-housing figures, and Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates, for the period after the 90-day no-cause termination provisions take effect: true if measured homelessness/severe housing deprivation rises materially against the pre-commencement trend; false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The 90-day no-cause provisions commenced 30 Jan 2025, so ~20 months of post-commencement data exist. The criterion's instruments split. (a) MHUD/MSD housing register: 19,002 applicants at 30 June 2026, down 0.6% on June 2025 and far below the ~25,000 level of late 2023 — flat to falling, which the criterion scores as false.
