(d) A motorcyclist in his 50s wearing a non-listed club's patch was stopped, with no action taken. (e) The Wellington High Court found the insignia ban inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act (July 2026), and a Mongrel Mob member's charge over a Lower North Bulldogs rugby league jersey was withdrawn, showing the ban being applied to non-gang clothing. Police publish no breakdown of charges, stops or notices by gang-membership status, so the criterion's 'material number' threshold cannot be confirmed from data; what is documented is a small number of individual instances, not a volume. The criterion's two-year window does not close until 21 Nov 2026.

statement: On the advice I have received to date, I can be very confident that the cost of delivering new ferries will be less than the projected cost of the failed and flawed project iReX, even when sunk costs are taken into account.
criterion: Final/updated Crown cost estimates for the replacement Cook Strait ferry programme (Ferry Holdings / Treasury) including landside works and iReX sunk and cancellation costs, compared with the last published iReX projected cost (~$3b); true if the replacement total is lower, false if it equals or exceeds it.
reasoning: The criterion asks for final/updated Crown cost estimates for the replacement programme including landside works and iReX sunk and cancellation costs, against iReX's last published ~$3b. Updated estimates exist and currently favour Willis, but no final cost does: the ferries are contracted from Guangzhou Shipyard International (signed 15 Nov 2025) for delivery in 2029, and the resolve-by date is 2030-12-31. State of the evidence as at Sept 2026: total programme estimated $1.86b (ferry build $596m, Picton infrastructure $531m, Wellington infrastructure $325m, management and contingency $415m), with taxpayer contribution stated as under the $1.7b allocated; iReX's final sunk and cancellation cost was confirmed by KiwiRail in Aug 2025 at $671m, including $222m to Hyundai Mipo Dockyard. $1.86b + $671m = ~$2.53b against iReX's ~$3.0-3.1b at cancellation (Treasury had warned of up to $4b), so on today's numbers the claim is tracking correct even with sunk costs counted. Countervailing evidence that could still flip it: the $1.867b estimate already exceeds the $1.7b Crown-tagged contingency Cabinet approved in March 2025 by ~$167m; the Picton wharf needs full replacement and Wellington a dual-level linkspan that were not in the original plan; and the programme relies on council-owned port contributions whose amounts were unapproved, with final scope and funding deals not settled until mid-2026. Three years of construction risk remain against a ~$470m margin.

statement: The internal combustion engine is not going anywhere in a hurry. No doubt, we will see a slow growth in electrical vehicles, the growth of which will be determined by investment in the electricity system, and work is under way to ensure that our electricity system does not contain any deficiencies that might impede competitiveness.
criterion: NZTA motor vehicle registration statistics for the light fleet, 2024–2026; true if annual EV/PHEV new registrations grow slowly or decline and EVs remain a small minority of the light fleet, false if EV registrations grow rapidly (e.g. more than doubling annually) or EVs reach a substantial share of new registrations.
reasoning: The criterion's true condition requires both slow growth or decline in EV/PHEV new registrations and EVs remaining a small minority of the light fleet; its falsifier is rapid growth (e.g. more than doubling annually) or a substantial share of new registrations. The fleet half holds: the EV fleet was 116,355 in Jan 2025 and passed 100,323 new BEV+PHEV registered by early March 2026, still only around 2-3% of a light fleet of roughly 4.5m, so the internal combustion engine is indeed not going anywhere in a hurry. The registrations half is falsified. 2024 matched Jones: BEV sales fell 74% from 21,611 (2023) to 6,748, with 6,542 new BEVs and 3,484 PHEVs registered after the Clean Car Discount ended 31 Dec 2023 and RUC exemption ended 1 April 2024. 2025 was flat-to-modest: BEV 7,706 (5.6% share), PHEV 6,885 (up from 2.7% to 5.0%). 2026 broke the prediction: BEV share was 16.2% in March 2026 vs 5.4% a year earlier; June saw BEV+PHEV at 38.2% of new passenger registrations vs 18.4%; July 2026 recorded 1,195 BEV + 1,479 PHEV, 29.8% of all new registrations and 36.7% of passenger registrations (vs 11.8% in July 2025); year to date BEV+PHEV was 28.5% of passenger registrations, more than double 2025's 12.8%. That is both more-than-doubling growth and a substantial share of new registrations, the criterion's explicit falsifier. Reporting attributes the surge mainly to fuel price volatility and model availability rather than to the electricity-system investment Jones named as the determinant.

statement: I actually think that the legislation we’re debating right now will do the complete antithesis of what the criteria say. It is going to increase reoffending, particularly for gang members, to the point where you’re seeing those numbers go.
criterion: Ministry of Justice / Department of Corrections reoffending statistics and prosecution data for gang insignia offences in the period after the Act commenced (21 November 2024); true if reoffending rates among gang members rise relative to the pre-commencement baseline, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires Corrections/MoJ reoffending statistics for gang members covering the period after commencement (21 Nov 2024), compared to a pre-commencement baseline. No such series has been published: Corrections reports reconviction on 12/24/48-month follow-up cohorts with long publication lags, and gang-affiliation breakdowns appear only in occasional research (e.g. the 2009 Nadesu work and the 'twice the rate' action-plan figure), not in a post-2024 time series. A 24-month post-commencement reoffending window does not close until November 2026, and the item's own resolve-by date (2026-11-30) has not yet passed. A Police OIA request specifically covering gang-policy effectiveness and dispersal notices remains unanswered. Proxy data run against the prediction — ministers report 38,000 fewer serious-violent-crime victims over the term and NZCVS violent-offence victims fell 23% between Oct 2024 and Aug 2025 — but these are population victimisation counts, not gang-member reoffending rates, and police acknowledged difficulty drawing a nexus to the Act. Not gradeable against the criterion as written yet; if the gang-broken-down series is never published it becomes uncheckable rather than false.

statement: Will this happen in our communities? And we know it will.
criterion: NZ Police reporting or OIA-released data on dispersal notices issued under the Gangs Act 2024 after commencement (21 November 2024), broken down by ethnicity: true if dispersal notices are issued to Māori and disproportionately so relative to population share; false if no notices are issued, or if Māori are not over-represented among recipients.
reasoning: Dispersal notices have been issued, so the criterion's 'no notices issued' false branch does not apply — but they have been used sparingly and no ethnicity breakdown of recipients has been published. The first notice came on 12 March 2025, nearly four months after commencement, to six Head Hunters members and associates at an Auckland motorway on-ramp; police did not state their ethnicity. Neither the Police Gangs Act page, the ministers' one-year release (21 Nov 2025), nor any OIA response located reports dispersal-notice counts or recipient ethnicity. The disproportionality the criterion looks for is documented for the adjacent insignia power: in the first three months (21 Nov 2024 – 18 Feb 2025) police charged 222 people, 184 of them (83%) Māori, against a Māori population share of 17.8%; by Nov 2025 there were 856 insignia charges. So the substance of the prediction — this enforcement landing on Māori communities — is borne out in the Gangs Act charge data, but the specific dispersal-notice-by-ethnicity evidence the criterion names is not available, and dispersal notices themselves turned out to be a rarely used power.

statement: Inflation is dropping but continues to sit above the 3 percent target, meaning a prolonged wait for mortgage-holders as interest rates stay high in order to beat inflation down.
criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions after 7 August 2024; true if the OCR was held at 5.5% through the remainder of 2024 with no cut, false if the RBNZ began cutting the OCR within the following months.
reasoning: The descriptive half was accurate on 7 August 2024: annual CPI was 3.3% in the June 2024 quarter, above the top of the RBNZ's 1–3% band. The predictive half failed immediately. The criterion's false branch — the RBNZ began cutting within the following months — is what happened: the OCR was cut from 5.50% to 5.25% on 14 August 2024, seven days after the speech and the first cut in over four years, then by 50bp to 4.75% on 9 October and by 50bp to 4.25% on 27 November 2024. It was never held at 5.5% for the remainder of 2024. Retail banks cut floating and fixed mortgage rates after each decision, so there was no 'prolonged wait for mortgage-holders'. Inflation was back inside the band at 2.2% by the September 2024 quarter, removing the premise of a prolonged fight to 'beat inflation down'.

statement: I’m sure there’s many other regions around the country which members will want to raise through the course of this debate as we get into the night on this legislation, and what that means for ratepayers around the country.
criterion: The Hansard record of the committee of the whole House stage on the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill; true if other members raise water-related rates impacts for regions beyond those Woods listed during the remainder of the committee stage, false if no such contributions are made.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether other members raised water-related rates impacts for regions beyond those Woods listed during the remainder of the committee stage. They did, repeatedly. In the same In Committee debate on 7 August 2024 (Part 1), Ingrid Leary (Labour—Taieri) raised Clutha District Council, where residents faced an up-to-20 percent rates increase and where she argued lower rates would leave water infrastructure unfixed and the council 'orphaned'; the debate also canvassed rates increases attributed to water for Ashburton (11.5%), Auckland (~25%), Gisborne (11.4%), Hamilton (25.5% then 14.1%), Hutt City (16.9%), Wellington (13.8–15.4%) and the Far North. When the committee stage resumed on 20 August 2024, Tangi Utikere (Labour—Palmerston North) said he had 'questions that relate to my specific area of Palmerston North City Council and the rates rises that have already been announced' (Part 3), and Arena Williams pressed the Minister on the Auckland/Watercare arrangements and consumers (Parts 3 and 4). Caveat on method: parliament.nz serves these Hansard pages via JavaScript and blocked every direct fetch I attempted (404s to WebFetch, a 'Loading…' shell via a text proxy, and no Wayback snapshot for the debate page), so this rests on search-engine extraction of the text of those exact Hansard URLs rather than a transcript I rendered myself. The content returned is specific, attributed and internally consistent (it reproduces Woods' own Westport passage verbatim), so I treat it as reliable, but a direct read of the Hansard pages would be a stronger check.

statement: It is a broad term which is deliberately used, but it is something which—ultimately, our expectation as a Government is that all councils will follow the law and will put forward a water service delivery plan on how they’re going to manage and deliver water services in their community.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs records of water services delivery plan submissions under the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act; true if all territorial authorities submitted a plan by the statutory deadline, false if any failed to submit.
reasoning: Under the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act 2024, every territorial authority had to submit a water services delivery plan to the Secretary for Local Government by 3 September 2025 (with a limited extension mechanism, requests due 3 August 2025). Local Government Minister Simon Watts announced after the deadline that every council required to submit by 3 September had done so, thanking 'all councils who have submitted their plans'; contemporaneous reporting describes councils as having met the deadline, and no report of a council failing to submit surfaced in searches specifically aimed at finding one ('did not submit', 'missed the deadline', 'not accepted'). Follow-through also holds: by July 2026 every mainland council had an approved plan, the last being Waitaki's amended plan. The one edge case is the Chatham Islands Council, which is off-mainland and outside the 'all mainland councils' announcement — but it did submit, and was directed to provide an amended plan in two stages (asset condition assessment by 30 June 2026, delivered; amended plan by 30 June 2028) pending funding decisions. So it is a case of a plan not yet accepted, not a failure to submit. Against the criterion as written — all territorial authorities submitted a plan by the statutory deadline — the prediction holds.

statement: Over three years, the ratepayers in Westport could see water charges rise from $2,300 to over $4,000 in just four years from now, under the provisions that we’ve got in front of us.
criterion: Buller District Council long-term plan / annual plan schedules of water and wastewater charges for Westport ratepayers; true if the per-household water charge exceeds $4,000 by the 2028/29 year, false if it remains materially below that.
reasoning: The criterion tests the per-household Westport water charge in the 2028/29 year against a $4,000 threshold, with a resolve-by date of 7 August 2028. Today is 27 September 2026, so the outcome year has not arrived and no annual plan sets the 2028/29 charge yet. Buller District Council adopted its 2025–2034 Long-Term Plan on 30 June 2025 and has since adopted the 2026/27 annual plan; those documents contain the funding impact statement and targeted-rate schedules, but the published material I could reach does not state a 2028/29 per-household water figure, and out-years in an LTP are forecasts that later annual plans revise. Context that bears on it but does not resolve it: Westport water and wastewater charges are already the subject of large targeted-rate movements (a 539% targeted-rate rise was reported for Westport in April 2024, Buller was cited in the same debate at a 31.8% rates increase, and the LTP commits $32.41m to drinking water over nine years plus a new Westport/Carters Beach stormwater-wastewater separation targeted rate rising annually from 1 July 2026). Resolve this against BDC's 2028/29 annual plan rating schedule when it is adopted, in mid-2028.

statement: So within four years, people living in Westport would be facing $4,000 worth of water charges because they didn’t have that ability to join forces with another council.
criterion: Buller District Council annual plan / long-term plan rating schedules for the 2027/28 or 2028/29 year; true if the average household water/wastewater charge is at or above roughly $4,000, false if it remains materially below that.
reasoning: The four-year horizon runs to 2028 and neither the 2027/28 nor the 2028/29 Buller rating schedule has been adopted; 2027/28 charges will further be set amid the transition to the joint West Coast water CCO from 1 July 2027. Best current evidence: Buller's Annual Plan 2026/27 (year 2 of the 2025-2034 LTP) sets the Westport single-residential water supply targeted rate at $1,474 and the Westport/Carters Beach sewage disposal targeted rate at $1,663 (both GST inclusive), i.e. $3,137 combined per connected household, with stormwater funded from general rates. That is below $4,000 but on a rising path, so the criterion is not yet settled either way. Note also that the quote's premise is contradicted by events: Buller did join forces with Grey and Westland, adopting a joint water services delivery plan and a jointly-owned WSCCO (approved by the Government in November 2025, operative July 2027).

statement: This is going to be important that it gets into the Hansard, because this is going to be interpreted by lawyers and in the courts when it turns out that councils have not gazed into crystal balls correctly, when they have not anticipated regulations because they couldn’t know.
criterion: New Zealand court or tribunal decisions (NZLII/judicial decisions database) concerning the water services delivery plan provisions of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act; true if at least one proceeding turns on a council's compliance with the 'anticipated future regulatory requirements' requirement, false if no such litigation has arisen by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2030-12-31, more than four years away. As at September 2026 no New Zealand court or tribunal proceeding could be found concerning the water services delivery plan provisions of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act 2024, and none turning on a council's compliance with anticipated future regulatory requirements. Searches of NZLII, the legislation site and legal-update coverage of Local Water Done Well return commentary and the statutes themselves, but no case law. The one serious dispute over a plan so far was resolved administratively rather than judicially: Waitaki District Council's standalone plan was rejected by DIA and the council accepted the appointment of a Crown facilitator rather than challenging the decision. The prediction therefore remains open.

statement: Otherwise, I do believe the Minister is going to get many applications for extensions and even the process of making the application is a certain amount of time and resource that’s taking away from actually getting the water service delivery plan done and the infrastructure in place.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / ministerial records of applications for extension of the water services delivery plan deadline under the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act 2024; true if a substantial number of councils (say 10 or more) applied for an extension, false if only a handful or none did.
reasoning: Far fewer than 10 councils applied for an extension of the water services delivery plan deadline. The Government announced on 4 September 2025 that every council required to meet the 3 September 2025 deadline had submitted its plan. Only one extension is identifiable as granted on the merits: Tasman District Council, extended to 1 October 2025 because of the winter storm emergencies (its plan was adopted 25 September 2025 and later approved). The Chatham Islands Council appears on the DIA/MCERT decisions table with an amended plan due 30 June 2026, a separate special case. Applications that were refused are individually reported and few: Southland District Council applied and was declined, and the Minister told the southern councils grouping in writing there would be no extension. That matches the criterion's false branch ('only a handful or none'). Caveat on completeness: DIA publishes decisions on plans, not a register of extension applications, so the count rests on the grant record plus press coverage of individual refusals; it is possible a few more quiet applications were made, but nothing suggests a figure approaching 10.

statement: I think, ultimately, the Government’s very clear message here is our expectation is that councils will work, either themselves or collaborate with other councils, to put forward these plans within the time frame and that they will put them forward, that they’ll be accepted, and that they will implement them and then they will deliver against them.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Secretary for Local Government records of water services delivery plan submissions under the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act; true if substantially all territorial authorities submitted a plan by the statutory deadline (3 September 2025) and those plans were accepted; false if a material number of councils missed the deadline or had plans rejected.
reasoning: The Government confirmed that all councils required to meet the 3 September 2025 statutory deadline submitted a Water Services Delivery Plan to DIA — no material number missed it. Acceptance was staged (only ~20% approved by 19 September 2025, with the Secretary for Local Government making the final call after panel moderation), and two councils had plans not accepted at first pass: Waitaki (told to resubmit by end of June 2026) and Mackenzie (resubmitted 26 March 2026). Both were subsequently approved, and by 1 July 2026 every mainland council had an approved plan, with five new council-controlled water organisations operating. Two initial non-acceptances out of ~66 territorial authorities is not a material number of rejections under the criterion. The quote's further limbs (councils implementing and delivering against the plans) fall outside the criterion as written and remain in progress.

statement: The challenging economic situation we have inherited inevitably means that job seeker numbers were expected to increase until January 2025, before decreasing.
criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly benefit fact sheets for jobseeker support recipients; true if the recipient count peaks around January 2025 and declines thereafter through 2025, false if numbers continue rising past that point.
reasoning: MSD's benefit statistics show Jobseeker Support recipients continued rising well past January 2025, not peaking there. The count was 209,838 at the March 2025 quarter and 216,009 at the June 2025 quarter (up 6,171, or 2.9%), and reached 223,512 at the December 2025 quarter — the highest figure in five years. MSD's own HYEFU December 2025 benefit forecasts put the expected peak at around 221,900 in January 2026, a full year later than the prediction. The June 2026 quarter (218,481) is the first clear step down from the December 2025 high, so any decline began roughly a year after the predicted turning point. The criterion's falsifying condition — numbers continuing to rise past January 2025 — is squarely met.

statement: I’m sure—the Minister said it’s absolutely fine to hear this as well—we will hear many out-of-scope submissions which are talking about things which are more than just the time table, but they will be valuable.
criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's submissions and final report on the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if the report or the published submissions record a substantial body of submissions on matters outside the bill's scope (e.g. the wider earthquake-prone building regime, NBS ratings), false if submissions were confined to the timetable provisions or the committee records no out-of-scope material.
reasoning: The evidence I could reach supports the direction of the prediction but not its scale. The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the bill (presented 5 November 2024) and parliament.nz's published submission list are behind a bot wall and could not be retrieved, so the committee's own record of out-of-scope material is unverified. Of the two published submissions to the committee I could obtain, both go well beyond the bill's deadline timetable: LGNZ's 26 August 2024 submission to Foster as chair explicitly says 'while this legislation has a relatively narrow focus, it goes hand in hand with the Government's wider work programme around seismic strengthening' and then sets out four asks about the wider seismic review (proportionality to risk, affordability, reasonable timeframes, staging by risk). Inner City Wellington's 23 August 2024 submission is almost entirely about the wider EPB regime — the cost-benefit basis of the whole system, the NBS linkage constraining new knowledge, GST and funding/incentive settings, and the scope and urgency of the MBIE seismic risk review — with an appendix on cost-per-life-saved. That is exactly the 'valuable out-of-scope' material Foster forecast, but two submissions do not establish the 'substantial body' the criterion asks for, and the committee's record of it could not be checked.

statement: But what evidence has he seen that longer sentences—which will inevitably come through a bill like this—actually lead to people exiting gangs in the first place?
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics comparing average custodial sentence length for offenders with the gang-membership aggravating factor applied before and after the provision's commencement; true if average sentence lengths rise measurably, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion names MoJ sentencing statistics comparing average custodial sentence length for offenders with the gang-membership aggravating factor applied, before vs after commencement (21 Nov 2024). No such breakdown is published: Stats NZ/MoJ criminal conviction and sentencing releases (latest available is the June 2025 fiscal year) do not flag whether the gang aggravating factor was applied, and MoJ has published no evaluation of the Sentencing Amendment Act 2024's effect on sentence lengths. The only forward-looking official figures are the June 2026 justice-sector projections, which attribute a rising prison population to recent sentencing reform as a package (~1,350 additional prisoners) without isolating the gang factor. The resolve-by date is 2027-06-30 and has not passed. Caveat for a later pass: because the gang-aggravating-factor flag does not appear in any published series, this item may end up uncheckable rather than resolvable even after the date. Note also that the criterion tests something narrower than the quote — the quote asks for evidence that longer sentences cause gang exit, the criterion only asks whether sentences got longer.

statement: We have to cut to the chase, cut to the root of the problem. Just taking their patches is not going to make communities any safer; it’s got to be a bit more than that.
criterion: NZ Police recorded-crime and NZ Crime and Victims Survey figures for gang-related and violent offending, plus any official evaluation of the Gangs Act 2024 (patch ban in force from 21 November 2024), covering the two years after commencement. FALSE if an official evaluation or the crime/victimisation series shows a reduction in gang-related offending or improved perceived community safety attributed to the patch ban; TRUE if no such improvement is identifiable.
reasoning: Twenty-two of the criterion's twenty-four months have elapsed (patch ban in force 21 Nov 2024). The TRUE side is well supported: no official evaluation of the Gangs Act 2024 has been published (MoJ's gang-legislation page reports no monitoring data); the National Gang List grew by more than 700 between Oct 2024 and Aug 2025 to 10,242 by Nov 2025; gang leaders and members report unchanged recruitment and describe the ban as optics; MoJ chief executive Andrew Kibblewhite attributed a rise in cannabis/meth possession charges (disproportionately Maori) to the ban's extra search powers rather than to any safety gain; and in July 2026 the High Court found the insignia prohibition inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act. But the criterion's FALSE branch is partly triggered: NZ Police (Asst Commissioner Paul Basham, six months to 14 May 2025) stated fear and intimidation from gangs had 'significantly reduced' and that intelligence suggested the ban had de-escalated some gang confrontations, and the Government's one-year release attributed large NZCVS falls in serious violent victimisation (147,000 victims in the year to Aug 2025; 38,000 fewer than on taking office) to the gang laws. Those are unquantified official assertions and a package-level attribution — NZCVS does not measure gang-related offending and cannot isolate the patch ban — so they do not establish that patches alone made communities safer, but they are official claims of improved perceived community safety attributed to the ban, which the criterion treats as disconfirming. Hence partly correct rather than correct; the two-year window does not close until 21 Nov 2026.

statement: Those are a really good example of orders that will never be made, just like non-association orders which already exist under the Sentencing Act and are pretty much never used because they’re not useful, they’re not effective, they don’t have any actual criminal justice purpose.
criterion: NZ Police / Ministry of Justice records of non-consorting orders applied for and granted under the Gangs Legislation Amendment Act after its commencement; false if any material number are made, true if effectively none are.
reasoning: The criterion's named source yields one direct datapoint, and it supports Webb: NZ Police's own enforcement release covering 21 Nov 2024 to 19 Feb 2025 states that while 337 insignia charges and 3,037 other charges were filed and 76 patches seized, 'No dispersal notices, non-consorting charges or prohibition orders have been issued.' Beyond that three-month window neither Police nor MoJ publishes a count of non-consorting orders applied for or granted — MoJ's non-consorting orders page is procedural only, the Police Gangs Act page carries no enforcement statistics, and no District Court or High Court judgment and no news report of any order being made could be found in the ~22 months since commencement, a period in which the Act has had close media scrutiny (the first dispersal notice, three months in, warranted its own police press release). So the substance holds on the evidence that exists, but 'never' is stronger than the published record can confirm: the full applied-for/granted series the criterion asks for is not public, so zero use across the whole period is inferred from one official three-month count plus silence.

statement: Now, we see inflation is tracking down to 3.3 percent and heading lower, and last week brought more good news for every Kiwi with a mortgage, with the first cut to the official cash rate in 4½ years.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual rate for the September 2024 and December 2024 quarters: true if the annual rate prints below 3.3%, false if it holds at or rises above 3.3%.
reasoning: Criterion asked for Stats NZ CPI annual rates for the Sept 2024 and Dec 2024 quarters vs the 3.3% baseline. Both printed 2.2% annual (Sept 2024: CPI +2.2% y/y, +0.6% q/q; Dec 2024: +2.2% y/y), i.e. below 3.3% and inside the RBNZ 1-3% band for two consecutive quarters. The premise that inflation was 'tracking down to 3.3 percent' matches the June 2024 quarter print, and the OCR cut he refers to (14 Aug 2024) was indeed the first in 4.5 years. Prediction that it was 'heading lower' is confirmed on both required prints.

statement: That’s driving inflation down, thankfully—and I would hope the member is joining us in great celebration with the lower interest rates that came through last week—and from that will flow economic growth and, ultimately, more employment opportunities for people.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and Household Labour Force Survey; true if real GDP returns to sustained growth and employment rises (unemployment rate falling) over the following year or so, false if GDP contracts and unemployment continues rising through that period.
reasoning: Criterion required BOTH sustained real GDP growth AND rising employment/falling unemployment over the following year or so for 'true'. GDP: -1.1% (Sept 2024 qtr), +0.5% (Dec 2024), +0.9% (Mar 2025), -0.9% (June 2025 - Stats NZ noted GDP had 'fallen in 3 of the last 5 quarters', GDP per capita -1.1%), +1.1% (Sept 2025, +1.4% annual), +0.2% (Dec 2025). So growth resumed but was not sustained - a sharp contraction one year after the statement. Employment: the opposite of predicted. Unemployment rose every quarter from 4.6% (June 2024 qtr, the print current when he spoke) through 5.1% (Mar 2025), 5.2% (June 2025), 5.3% (Sept 2025) to 5.4% (Dec 2025), the highest since 2015; Stats NZ recorded the Dec 2025 quarter's +15,000 as the first quarterly employment increase since the June 2024 quarter. I looked specifically for any quarter of falling unemployment in the window and found none. Growth half weakly vindicated, employment half not - materially overstated.

statement: What’s more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.
criterion: RBNZ official cash rate decisions through 2027; true if the OCR declines steadily and sits at approximately 3 percent during 2027, false if it is materially above or below that level by then.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on RBNZ OCR decisions through 2027 and asks whether the OCR sits at approximately 3 percent during 2027; today is 2026-09-27, so no 2027 decision exists yet. Context for a later pass: the realised path is not the 'steady decline' described - the OCR fell well below 3%, to 2.25% (held at the February and May 2026 MPS and the April 2026 review), then tightening resumed after inflation hit 4.1% in the June 2026 quarter, with hikes to 2.50% (July 2026) and 2.75% (2 September 2026). The RBNZ's current published track implies a peak around 3.25% by mid-2027, so the 2027 level could still land near 3 percent despite the route there differing from the August 2024 forecast track. Re-resolve after the 2027 OCR decisions.

statement: The Reserve Bank’s latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the September 2024 quarter; true if annual inflation printed at approximately 2.3% and within 1-3%, false if materially different or outside the band.
reasoning: Stats NZ's CPI release for the September 2024 quarter (published 17 October 2024) recorded annual inflation of 2.2% — inside the RBNZ's 1–3% target band and within 0.1pp of the 2.3% Willis cited from the Bank's August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement, which did project a return inside the band in the September quarter. The criterion's 'approximately 2.3% and within 1-3%' is met.

statement: For sectors like banking, this change will make it easier for consumers to switch providers or for innovative and disruptive new players like fintechs to enter the market and compete.
criterion: Status of the consumer/customer data right regime for banking and MBIE/Commerce Commission reporting: true if the regime is in force for banking with accredited requestors operating and evidence of increased consumer switching or new fintech entrants; false if the regime is not in force for banking, or is in force with no accredited entrants and no measurable switching effect.
reasoning: The criterion's conditions are satisfied. The CDR regime is in force for banking: the Customer and Product Data (Designations for Banking and Other Deposit Taking) Regulations 2025 bound ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac from 1 December 2025 (Kiwibank from June 2026), and MBIE's Register of Participants listed 14 accredited requestors as of July 2026, 8 of them accredited after 12 May 2026. New fintech entrants are operating and competing: June 2026 saw $114.5m across 362,869 open-banking payments (+24% on May) from ~199,000 unique customers, with providers such as BlinkPay pricing against cards. The criterion's alternative limb — increased consumer switching — is NOT evidenced: Consumer NZ's 2025 survey still found only 3% switching in a year and I found no measured post-December-2025 change, and the Commerce Commission's market study treats easier switching as requiring further measures beyond the data right. Because the criterion is disjunctive on that limb, the verdict is correct; note the formal resolve-by (2026-12-31) has not yet passed, so the switching evidence could still develop.

statement: On the matter of new section 165ZFHI, “Power to undertake review”, when the review is undertaken—and they will be very, very few in number, because this is not really a troublesome industry.
criterion: Count of reviews of coastal permit conditions initiated under the new section 165ZFHI (as enacted) reported by MPI / regional councils: true if fewer than roughly five reviews are initiated nationally in the first five years of the provision's operation, false if reviews are initiated routinely (dozens, or a substantial share of extended permits).
reasoning: The Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024 came into force 3 September 2024, and s165ZFHI originally required any review to be commenced within two years, i.e. by 3 September 2026. That window was extended from two to six years by s52 of the Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act 2025 (replacing '2' with '6' in s165ZFHI(3)(a)), so councils may still initiate reviews until September 2030. The criterion's five-year observation period and its 2030-06-30 resolve-by both lie in the future. No review by any regional council has been publicly reported to date and no MPI/council count has been published — consistent with Jones's prediction, and consistent with the practical brakes on reviews (Director-General concurrence under s165ZFHL, cost constraints in s165ZFHI(4)) — but absence of reporting is not the reported count the criterion asks for, and the window is still open.

statement: I’m very sorry to see the likelihood that this Government will pass this piece of legislation.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; false if it is defeated, withdrawn, or still not passed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion asks the parliamentary record for this specific bill. The Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill completed its third reading and became the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024, Public Act 2024 No 32, receiving Royal assent in late August 2024 (commentary and the legislation database date enactment to 27 August 2024; Wikipedia's list of 54th Parliament acts records 2 September 2024). Either date is within days of the 20 August speech and far inside the 2024-12-31 resolve-by date. It was not defeated, withdrawn or stalled. Disconfirming check: I looked for any report of the bill being pulled or lapsing at select committee and found the opposite — the Act is in force and automatically extends ~1,200 marine farm coastal permits by 20 years (not beyond 2050).

statement: We have stopped the wasteful spending, we’ve stopped loading costs up on businesses, and we’re getting spending under control. That’s driving inflation down, thankfully—and I would hope the member is joining us in great celebration with the lower interest rates that came through last week—and from that will flow economic growth and, ultimately, more employment opportunities for people.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and Household Labour Force Survey; true if real GDP growth turns positive and sustained and the unemployment rate falls below its August 2024 level within the following 18 months, false if growth remains negative or flat and unemployment continues to rise over that period.
reasoning: The criterion requires BOTH sustained positive real GDP growth AND unemployment falling below its August 2024 level within 18 months (i.e. by roughly February 2026). Only the first half came good, and late. Stats NZ quarterly real GDP: the economy contracted further through 2024-25, including -0.9% in the June 2025 quarter, before rebounding +1.1% (revised ~+0.9%) in September 2025, +0.5% in December 2025 and +0.8% in March 2026 — three consecutive positive quarters, but the run only begins ~13 months after the statement. The labour market half fails outright: the HLFS seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 4.6% in the June 2024 quarter (the reading current in August 2024) and rose steadily thereafter — 5.2% (Jun 2025), 5.3% (Sep 2025, a nine-year high), 5.4% (Dec 2025), 5.3% (Mar 2026), 5.6% (Jun 2026, highest since 2015). It never fell below 4.6%; it continued to rise across the whole window, and underutilisation reached 13.8%. So the 'true' branch is not satisfied and the 'false' branch is only half satisfied (unemployment kept rising, but growth did not remain negative/flat). Substance partly holds — growth returned — but the 'more employment opportunities' consequence was materially wrong over the stated horizon.

statement: What’s more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.
criterion: RBNZ official cash rate series during 2027; true if the OCR sits at approximately 3 percent (within about 0.5 percentage points) in that year, false if materially above or below.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against the RBNZ official cash rate series during calendar 2027, with a resolve-by date of 2027-12-31. Today is 2026-09-27, so no 2027 OCR observation exists yet and the claim cannot be graded. Context, not a verdict: the OCR bottomed in the 2.25-2.50% region and has been raised twice in 2026 — to 2.50% in July and 2.75% at the 2 September 2026 decision — as inflation proved persistent (4.1% in the June 2026 quarter, on fuel costs), with the Committee signalling it may need to go further. A 2027 OCR near 3% is therefore currently plausible rather than clearly off track, but the criterion's window has not opened.

statement: It will result in legislative changes, but then they will go through an exhaustive select committee process and will then be reported back to this House for debate, for further consideration, and, ultimately, for ratification.
criterion: The Parliament bills register; true if a Government bill amending the earthquake-prone building provisions of the Building Act arising from the seismic risk review is introduced and referred to select committee by 31 December 2026, false if no such bill has been introduced by that date.
reasoning: The criterion required a Government bill amending the Building Act's earthquake-prone building provisions, arising from the seismic risk review, to be introduced and referred to select committee by 31 December 2026. The Report of the Seismic Risk Management Review was delivered June 2025; the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill (238-1) was introduced 9 December 2025, passed first reading and was referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee with submissions closing 16 February 2026. The committee reported back 16 June 2026, second reading 30 June 2026, committee of the whole House, and the bill passed its third reading unanimously on 18/19 September 2026. Every element Brewer named — select committee process, report back, debate, further consideration, ratification — occurred, well inside the deadline. I looked for the disconfirming case (review shelved, or changes made by regulation/Order in Council rather than a bill) and found the opposite: primary legislation was the vehicle.

statement: This could potentially be the first of several different extensions, and before we know it we will be no further ahead and we will be regretting that decision.
criterion: New Zealand legislation and MBIE announcements on earthquake-prone building remediation deadlines after the August 2024 bill; true if at least one further statutory extension or deferral of those deadlines is enacted or announced after this bill, false if the deadlines set by this bill stand without further extension.
reasoning: The criterion: true if at least one further statutory extension or deferral of the remediation deadlines is enacted or announced after the August 2024 bill; false if the deadlines that bill set stand without further extension. They did not stand. The Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill, passed unanimously on 18/19 September 2026 (new system commencing 1 July 2027), lets earthquake-prone building owners apply to their territorial authority for extensions of time to complete seismic work on one or more occasions up to a cumulative maximum of 15 years, and applies retrospectively to owners whose deadlines expired on or after commencement. It also removes roughly 55% of earthquake-prone buildings (~2,900, including all of Auckland, Northland and the Chatham Islands) from the system entirely, extinguishing their deadlines. Disconfirming check: the 2024 Act's own one-off Order in Council power to add up to 2 years (usable until 2 April 2028) does not appear to have been exercised, and the 2026 reform leaves nominal deadlines in medium/high seismic zones unchanged — so the deferral is application-based and system-wide rather than another automatic blanket extension. That is a different mechanism from the one McLellan pictured, but the criterion's condition ('extension or deferral ... enacted or announced') is met. Resolve-by is 2028-12-31, but the evidence is already in.

statement: They’ll be substantive submissions backed by evidence.
criterion: The submissions published on the Parliament website for the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill: true if the bulk of submissions come from organisations and professionals (engineers, lawyers, councils, property bodies) and cite evidence or technical analysis; false if most are short individual opinion submissions without supporting evidence.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific source — the submissions published on the Parliament website for the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill — and asks whether the bulk came from organisations and professionals citing evidence, versus short individual opinion pieces. That list is not retrievable: parliament.nz, www3.parliament.nz, bills.parliament.nz and selectcommittees.parliament.nz all return a JavaScript error shell ('An unhandled error has occurred') or 404 to a fetcher; the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report/commentary is not indexed in any accessible mirror; legislation.govt.nz returns 403; web.archive.org is blocked in this environment. Partial evidence exists and leans Webb's way — submissions closed 26 August 2024 with oral evidence heard 29 August 2024, and confirmed submitters include Local Government New Zealand (organisational, addressed to chair Andy Foster), Property Council New Zealand (written and oral, drawing on member feedback), plus at least one further organisational PDF submission. But confirming named organisations submitted does not establish what the bulk of submissions were, and the two-and-a-half-week window means I cannot rule out a large volume of short individual submissions I simply cannot see. Not findable is not the same as false.

statement: With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent, and future charges are also expected to be lower than they would have been.
criterion: Watercare's adopted price increase for the year following this statement, and its price path in subsequent years compared with the pre-separation Auckland Council proposal; true if the increase lands at approximately 7.2 percent and later increases run below the pre-deal projected path, false if the increase materially exceeds that or later charges track at or above the pre-deal path.
reasoning: Watercare's adopted price change for the first year after financial separation (1 July 2025) was exactly 7.2% for water and wastewater (~$7/month for an average household), against the 25.8% rise Auckland Council/Watercare had signalled pre-deal under council borrowing limits. Later charges have tracked below that pre-deal path: 7.2% again from 1 July 2026, and 5.5% projected for 2027, with no revision upward found despite the Huia treatment plant cost blowout ($420m to $1.12bn). Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. Caveat: the 'lower than they would have been' counterfactual is not directly observable and rests on the 25.8% baseline plus the Crown/Watercare claim of ~$899m saved over four years; infrastructure growth charges separately rose 20% from July 2026.

statement: I’m very sorry to see the likelihood that this Government will pass this piece of legislation.
criterion: The Parliament of New Zealand bill record for the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Bill: true if it passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; false if it is voted down, lapses, or is not passed.
reasoning: The bill passed and is now law: the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024, Public Act 2024 No 32, enacted 27 August 2024 — a week after Abel spoke. It automatically extends aquaculture coastal permits by 20 years (not beyond 2050) and came into force the day after Royal assent. Checked for the disconfirming case (voted down, lapsed, or still before the House) and found none; multiple independent legal commentaries report it as enacted.

statement: This shows steady reductions from the current rate of 5.25 percent to a 3 percent OCR by mid-2027.
criterion: The RBNZ official cash rate as set at the monetary policy review nearest mid-2027; true if the OCR is at or below approximately 3.0%, false if it remains materially above 3.0%.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the OCR at the monetary policy review nearest mid-2027; today is 2026-09-27, so that review has not happened and the resolve-by date (2027-07-31) has not passed. Current state for context: the RBNZ raised the OCR 25bp to 2.75% on 2 September 2026 — its second consecutive hike after tightening resumed in July — following June-quarter inflation of 4.1%, with the published track signalling a hold in October and a further hike to 3.00% in December 2026. So the descent Willis described ('steady reductions') did not hold: the OCR went below 3% and is now rising back toward it, meaning the mid-2027 level could satisfy the criterion from above rather than via a steady glide. The criterion scores only the level, not the path, so it remains open.

statement: Currently, the market is pricing in a faster pace of interest rate cuts and expecting that the OCR will reach 3 percent in February 2026.
criterion: The RBNZ official cash rate in effect after the February 2026 Monetary Policy Statement; true if the OCR is at or about 3.0% at that date, false if materially above or below.
reasoning: At the February 2026 MPS (18 Feb 2026) the RBNZ held the OCR at 2.25%, unanimously — not 3.0%. The directional substance of the quote verified strongly: cuts came faster than the pricing she described, with the OCR hitting 3.00% in August 2025 (six months early), 2.50% in October and 2.25% in November 2025. But the specific level named for the specific date is 75bp too high, which the criterion treats as materially off. Mixed rather than wrong: the 'faster pace of cuts' clause held, the 3%-in-February figure did not.

statement: They will be doing everything they can to reintroduce dangerous weapons back into New Zealand, to take apart the regulations that control our shooting ranges, and to make our front line at risk of dangerous weapons in the hands of criminals.
criterion: Arms Act amendments and firearms regulations enacted before the end of the 54th Parliament; true if military-style semi-automatic firearms prohibited in 2019 are re-legalised or the shooting range regulatory regime is repealed, false if the prohibition and range regime remain in place.
reasoning: Neither limb of the criterion was met. The 2019 prohibition survives: the Arms Act 2026, which repealed and replaced the Arms Act 1983 and came into force 23 September 2026, expressly retains the ban on military-style semi-automatics and high-capacity magazines, retains universal firearms registration, and tightens licensing criteria and penalties (RACS, which lobbied to keep these, records them as retained). Nothing found re-legalises any prohibited category. The shooting-range regime was restructured, not repealed: the Arms (Shooting Clubs, Shooting Ranges, and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2025 defines and regulates pistol and non-pistol clubs separately, moving non-pistol clubs/ranges toward enrolment while keeping certification, appeal rights, reporting and inspection, and new clubs-and-ranges regulations are in force. I checked specifically for the disconfirming case (a repeal of the range regime or an A-category re-legalisation) and found only liberalising administrative change within a regime that still exists. Although the criterion's resolve-by date is 2026-11-30, it is already settled: Parliament adjourned for the final time on 23 September 2026 and dissolves on 1 October ahead of the 7 November election, so no further Arms Act amendment can be enacted in the 54th Parliament.

statement: But here we are, and so I am pleased that we are going to get this bill sorted once and for all.
criterion: The Parliament bills register for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it lapses, is discharged, or is defeated.
reasoning: The Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill passed its third reading and received Royal assent on 16 September 2024 as the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Act 2024 (2024 No 35) — well inside the 2025-12-31 horizon. It did not lapse, was not discharged and was not defeated; the three-year minimum gift-card expiry took effect 18 months after assent, on 16 March 2026.

statement: Lowering the official cash rate will lead to lower interest rates across the economy; in fact, this process has already started.
criterion: RBNZ published average mortgage and business lending rates; true if average floating and two-year fixed mortgage rates in August 2025 are below their August 2024 levels, false if they are the same or higher.
reasoning: Criterion asked whether average floating and two-year fixed mortgage rates in Aug 2025 were below Aug 2024 levels. Both were, substantially. Floating: median carded floating 8.39% at 1 Sep 2024 vs ANZ floating 6.29% from 21 Aug 2025. Two-year fixed: median 24-month 6.165% at 1 Sep 2024 vs ANZ two-year special 4.75% on 27 Aug 2025 (Kiwibank 4.95%). RBNZ's own series corroborates: floating stock yield peaked 6.99% in Aug 2024 and was 5.63% by Mar 2025; all-mortgage yield peaked 6.39% Oct 2024 and fell to 5.17% by Nov 2025. The OCR itself went 5.50% -> 3.00% over the window. The 'already started' clause also holds: banks were cutting carded fixed rates ahead of the 14 Aug 2024 OCR cut. Disconfirming check: no evidence of any bank raising floating or two-year rates over this window; the only rate rises found are from 2026, outside the criterion's date. Caveat: rbnz.govt.nz returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches, so the B20/B6 tables are cited via reporting that quotes them rather than read off the spreadsheet.

statement: The Reserve Bank’s latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the September 2024 quarter; true if annual inflation prints at about 2.3% and within the 1-3% band, false if outside the band or materially away from 2.3%.
reasoning: Stats NZ's CPI release for the September 2024 quarter printed annual inflation of 2.2 percent (quarterly rise 0.6 percent). That is inside the RBNZ's 1-3 percent target band and 0.1 percentage points from the 2.3 percent figure Willis attributed to the Reserve Bank's August 2024 forecast, so it satisfies 'about 2.3% and within the band' as the criterion required. Disconfirming check: no revision or alternative Stats NZ figure for that quarter outside the band was found.

statement: In actual fact, we know that water rates in Auckland will actually go up—I think the projection is by about 8 percent.
criterion: Watercare's published price schedule / Auckland Council's adopted water charges for the year following this statement; true if the headline water price increase is approximately 8 percent (say 7–9 percent), false if materially outside that band.
reasoning: Watercare's own release dated 1 July 2025 states: 'Today (July 1, 2025), our water and wastewater prices increase by 7.2 per cent.' That is inside the criterion's 7-9 percent band for 'about 8 percent'. The same 7.2 percent increase applied from 1 July 2024 and again from 1 July 2026, so the verdict does not depend on which year after the 20 Aug 2024 statement is taken as 'the year following'. Disconfirming check: higher figures do exist in the record - Auckland Council's draft 2024-2034 long-term plan projected 14.6 percent for 1 July 2025 and Watercare had earlier proposed 25.8 percent - but those were proposals superseded by the water services charter; the adopted and charged increase was 7.2 percent.

statement: I believe, at some point, there will be some piece of legislation that will come through, which will include something on this in the future.
criterion: The register of bills introduced to the House; true if a bill containing provisions on the treatment of employer KiwiSaver contributions under total remuneration arrangements (the subject matter of this bill) is introduced before the resolve-by date, false if no such bill is introduced.
reasoning: No bill containing provisions on the treatment of employer KiwiSaver contributions under total remuneration arrangements was introduced to the House between 21 Aug 2024 and the resolve-by date. The two KiwiSaver-touching government bills of the term do not address it: the Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2025 (assent 29 May 2025) raised minimum employer/employee rates to 3.5% then 4% and amended KiwiSaver Act ss 18-26 but left s 101B (the total remuneration carve-out) untouched; the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2025-26, Compliance Simplification, and Remedial Measures) Bill (introduced 21 Aug 2025) has KiwiSaver clauses (e.g. cl 103, extending the Budget 2025 rate rises to complying superannuation funds) but its departmental disclosure statement does not mention total remuneration or s 101B. The Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026 (bill introduced 15 July 2025) contains nothing on KiwiSaver. Disconfirming evidence was checked specifically: National stated that phasing out total remuneration 'is not part of the policy National announced', only that it was 'open to considering' it, and Labour's ban on total remuneration contracts is a 13 Sep 2026 election policy, not a bill before the House. The resolve-by date (7 Nov 2026) is nominally ~6 weeks away, but Parliament adjourned on 23 Sep 2026 and dissolves 1 Oct 2026 ahead of the 7 Nov election, so no bill can be introduced in the remaining window — the criterion is settled rather than pending. Note the prediction as spoken was open-ended ('at some point... in the future'); it fails only against the term-bounded window the criterion imposes.

statement: In a time of rising unemployment, in a time when people are kind of getting a bit desperate to get a job, in a time when unemployment is predicted to rise, and in a time where employers—businesses—are not creating extra jobs, then the employer has the advantage, and the employer can discriminate against workers.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate: true if the rate in any quarter between September 2024 and December 2025 exceeds the June 2024 quarter rate (4.6%) by more than sampling error; false if the rate is flat or falls across that period.
reasoning: Stats NZ HLFS seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 4.6% in the June 2024 quarter (up from 4.4% in March 2024 and 3.6% in June 2023). It then rose continuously: 4.8% in the September 2024 quarter, and by the December 2025 quarter it reached 5.4% (165,000 unemployed), up from 5.3% in September 2025 and the highest rate since the September 2015 quarter. That is a sustained 0.8 percentage-point rise over five quarters, far beyond HLFS sampling error, and the opposite of 'flat or falls'. The criterion tests only the unemployment-rate leg of the quote, and that leg is satisfied; the quote's further claims about employer bargaining advantage and discrimination are not tested by the criterion as written.

statement: I’m sorry, but it seems that Dr McLellan’s bill will not pass.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of Tracey McLellan's KiwiSaver member's bill on 21 August 2024; true if the bill was defeated, false if it passed its first reading.
reasoning: The Employment Relations (Protection for KiwiSaver Members) Amendment Bill, a member's bill in the name of Dr Tracey McLellan, was defeated on 21 August 2024 on a party vote of 49 Aye, 68 No, 0 Abstain, 6 Absent — so White's prediction, made during that debate, held. One correction to the criterion's framing: 21 August 2024 was the bill's SECOND reading, not its first; the first reading passed on 30 August 2023 by 109 to 10, and the bill then went to select committee, whose majority did not agree it should pass. The criterion's substantive test (was the bill defeated on 21 August 2024) is answered yes regardless of the stage mislabel.

statement: I can’t wait for the final reading of this legislation, when we table this completely, and we can actually stand up and celebrate that that will no longer happen to any other victim of domestic violence.
criterion: The Parliamentary record for the Family Proceedings (Dissolution for Family Violence) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, lapses, or is still awaiting a third reading at the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The bill, retitled the Family Proceedings (Dissolution of Marriage or Civil Union for Family Violence) Amendment Bill, passed its third reading on 16 October 2024 and received Royal assent on 17 October 2024, becoming Act 2024 No 42 (in force 17 October 2025). The criterion's true branch — third reading plus Royal assent before the 2026-11-07 resolve-by date — is satisfied; it is not not_yet_due because the passage already occurred.

statement: The Reserve Bank is confident that after three long years, inflation is now expected to fall back within the 1 to 3 percent target band in the September quarter.
criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation for the September 2024 quarter; true if the annual rate is between 1.0% and 3.0%, false if it is outside that band.
reasoning: Stats NZ reported annual CPI inflation of 2.2% for the September 2024 quarter (release headlined 'Annual inflation at 2.2 percent'; quarterly rise 0.6%). 2.2% is inside the 1.0-3.0% target band, so the criterion's true condition holds. Checked for disconfirmation: no later revision moved the September 2024 annual rate outside the band; the 3.0% print is the September 2025 quarter, a different period.

statement: Then a new, three-party coalition is elected, fiscal restraint comes on board, inflation comes down, interest rates come down, and soon growth will revive—there’s your story.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series; true if real GDP returns to positive quarterly growth on a sustained basis (at least two consecutive quarters) by the end of 2025, false if the economy is still contracting or flat over that period.
reasoning: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP (revised): March 2025 positive, June 2025 -0.9%, September 2025 +0.9% (revised down from +1.1%), December 2025 +0.2%. That is two consecutive quarters of positive growth by the end of 2025 (and an earlier pair in Dec 2024/Mar 2025), so the criterion's threshold for 'sustained' is met and the 'still contracting or flat' false branch does not hold. Caveat worth recording: the revival was interrupted by a -0.9% contraction in mid-2025 and annual average growth for calendar 2025 was only 0.2%, so under a stricter reading of 'soon' and 'sustained' this would be partly_correct; scored against the criterion as written.

statement: I don’t think it’s going to quite have the impact of turning the justice system from being the quite sluggish, very slow system it is now—a very careful use of words—to something that is going to race our defendants and speed justice up, because it simply won’t do that.
criterion: Ministry of Justice court timeliness statistics (median time from first appearance to disposal, District Court criminal cases) for the two years after the Act commences; true if no material reduction in median disposal times occurs, false if a substantial speed-up follows commencement.
reasoning: The bill under debate on 22 Aug 2024 was the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill; it received Royal assent 2 Sept 2024, with most provisions commencing 3 Sept 2024 and clause 7 on 2 March 2025. The criterion asks for Ministry of Justice median time from first appearance to disposal (District Court criminal) across the two years after commencement — that window closes Sept 2026/March 2027 and MoJ has not published that series for it. The available proxy metric (share of District Court criminal cases disposed within Timely Access to Justice thresholds) moved from 81% in early 2024 to 85% by June 2026, with backlog down 26.7% from the Jan 2022 peak, improvements credited to the Criminal Process Improvement Programme rather than remote participation. That is directionally consistent with his claim of no dramatic speed-up but is not the named statistic, and the window is incomplete.

statement: The bill is due to come back to the House by 18 October, and it is the Government’s intention to pass it into law by the end of the year so we can get on and rebuild this economy.
criterion: The Environment Committee's report-back date for the Fast-track Approvals Bill on the Parliament bills register, and the date of Royal assent; true if reported back on or before 18 October 2024 and enacted on or before 31 December 2024, false if either date slips.
reasoning: Both dated elements hold. The Environment Committee reported back on the Fast-track Approvals Bill on 18 October 2024, the exact date Bishop named. The bill passed its third reading on 17 December 2024 and the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (2024 No 56) received Royal assent on 23 December 2024 — inside 'by the end of the year'. No slip on either date.

statement: It’s a pleasure to rise as the chair of the Social Services and Community Committee that will be hearing submissions on this bill after it passes its first reading, which I speak on today.
criterion: The Parliamentary record for the Social Workers Registration Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its first reading, was referred to the Social Services and Community Committee, and that committee called for and heard submissions; false if it failed the first reading, was referred elsewhere, or no submissions process occurred.
reasoning: The Social Workers Registration Amendment Bill (Government Bill 63) passed its first reading on 27 August 2024 — the day Mooney spoke — and was referred to the Social Services and Community Committee, which he chaired. That committee called for submissions and held a public hearing in the week of 11 November 2024 (the Social Workers Registration Board attended alongside MSD as advisers), then reported the bill back recommending it be passed (version 63-2). Second reading 6 March 2025; enacted as the Social Workers Registration Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 17), Royal assent 30 March 2025. Every element of the criterion — first reading passed, referred to that committee, submissions called for and heard — is satisfied.

statement: We’ve seen the impact that this Budget had on reducing the domestic work we were doing on climate change, which means we’ll be funnelling more and more money overseas to pay other countries to cut their emissions and to keep people in green jobs.
criterion: New Zealand government decisions and expenditure on offshore mitigation for the first Nationally Determined Contribution (Treasury/MfE reporting, Budget appropriations); true if the Crown commits or spends on international mitigation purchases and the projected cost rises after Budget 2024, false if no such purchases are committed or the projected offshore requirement falls.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against NDC1 (2021-2030) spending decisions, resolve-by 2030-12-31, and the decision is explicitly still open as of Sept 2026. Half the criterion is satisfied: the projected offshore requirement rose after Budget 2024 (Newsroom, Nov 2025: gap grew from 71.5 Mt when Labour left office to 84 Mt), and Treasury published a dedicated costing (TP 26/01, June 2026) estimating NZ$4.4-5.0b for NDC1 within a wider $3.3-23.7b uncertainty range. But the other half fails: no purchase has been committed or spent. Budget 2026 contained no money for Paris Agreement compliance, and Treasury declined to recognise any liability because there is 'no legal obligation' and the government 'had not committed to any purchases'; TP 26/01 states it 'does not reflect government decisions or intentions'. Only enabling arrangements exist (MOUs with the Philippines and Thailand, an ADB carbon market role); Watts says mechanisms are in place to 'pull the trigger' but no decision has been made, and Luxon/Willis say there are 'no current plans to send billions of dollars overseas'. Note also that Treasury's 2026 central cost estimate sits below the 2023 analysis ($3b-$24b, with an earlier $7.9-13.8b figure for a 102 Mt gap), because assumed unit prices fell - so the projected dollar cost has not clearly risen even though the tonnage gap has. Applying the 'no purchases committed' limb literally today would make the 2030 resolve-by date meaningless; the honest answer is that the decisive fact is undetermined.

statement: In terms of our emission reduction budgets, we are currently consulting on a plan that will see us achieve the emission reduction goal set out in the zero carbon Act in the second campaign period, and we’re on track to achieve those in the first period.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission reporting on the first emissions budget period (2022–2025); true if net emissions over the period fall at or below the legislated first emissions budget, false if the budget is exceeded.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether net emissions over 2022-2025 fall at or below the legislated first emissions budget of 290 MtCO2e. The Climate Change Commission's 2025 monitoring report (25 July 2025) found 'the first emissions budget is likely to be met', with the Government's central projection at 284.1 MtCO2e, about 6 Mt under. The Commission's 2026 monitoring report restates this with a larger margin: 'Projections show the first emissions budget (290 MtCO2e) is likely to be met with a 7.7 MtCO2e buffer.' The April 2026 Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2024) supplies actual data for three of the four budget years, with 2024 net emissions of 54.8 Mt, down 2% on 2023, so only 2025 remains projected. Disconfirming evidence checked and recorded rather than ignored: the Commission attributes the pass partly to accounting rather than abatement - inventory methodology improvements effectively cut the first budget's requirement by about 7 Mt, and forest planting ran higher than assumed when the budget was set, so 'the budget can now be met with less effort than it originally required'; gross emissions reductions also stalled in 2024 on dry-year coal generation. Formal confirmation waits on the 2025 inventory (published 2027). On the criterion as written, the budget is met. (The second half of Willis's statement, about the second budget period, is outside this criterion; the 2026 monitoring report finds EB2 met by only 3.6 Mt with more than half the planned reductions now at risk.)

statement: It would mean that for an organisation that has working in the community for 38 years, they will, effectively, close in April of next year without that funding now being in place.
criterion: Charities Register and public reporting on North Shore Women's Centre; true if the organisation ceased operating on or about April 2025, false if it was still delivering services after that date.
reasoning: The organisation did close and did attribute the closure to the lost Oranga Tamariki funding, and April 2025 was the correct decision point - but it was still delivering services for a further seven months, which is the criterion's explicit false branch. The centre's own news page records the Aug 2024 position Andersen was quoting ('Should the funding landscape remain unchanged in April 2025 then we will have no option but to look at wind-down/closure'), then an April 2025 item announcing permanent closure, which is what Labour's 29 April 2025 release ('today's confirmed closure') refers to. The closure itself came later: the centre's homepage and news page both state 'North Shore Womens Centre will be closing permanently on 28th November 2025', after 38 years, and RNZ reported in August 2025 that it would 'close its doors in November'. The $118,000/yr Oranga Tamariki contract (~30% of its budget) was cut in June 2024 as part of the cancellation of 330+ provider contracts. So the substance (this organisation closes without that funding) is confirmed and the '38 years' detail is accurate, but the date on which it ceased operating was November 2025, not April 2025 - the only quantitative element of the prediction is materially wrong.

statement: But he failed short of making that promise, because he knows, in his heart of hearts, that rates will continue to go up, because the advice that he has received is that this approach by this Government will still result in rates increasing.
criterion: Stats NZ local authority rates data / LGNZ annual rates surveys for the 2025/26 and 2026/27 financial years; true if average territorial authority rates increases remain positive and materially above CPI in both years, false if average rates are flat or fall.
reasoning: Criterion: average TA rates increases positive and materially above CPI in both 2025/26 and 2026/27. Taxpayers' Union Rates Dashboard (the nationwide TA rates survey) put 2025/26 at 8.39% average against CPI of 2.5%, and 2026/27 at 6.92% (7.23% including water-reform cost transfers) against inflation of 3.1%. Adopted council plans corroborate: Auckland 7.9%, Gisborne 8.49%, Waikato District 3.79% at the low end — still above CPI. Checked for the opposite (flat or falling average rates, or a binding 2-4% cap taking effect for 2026/27): the 2-4% cap was legislated for later years and 2026/27 averages still came in near 7%. Stats NZ annual local authority financial statistics for the year ended June 2026 are not published until May 2027, so the LGNZ/dashboard survey path in the criterion is the operative one.

statement: Then there’s this stage and then there’s another one, which was quite clearly signalled in this bill and that will come at the end of this year.
criterion: Parliament's bills register; true if a further Government water services bill (the successor to the Preliminary Arrangements Bill) was introduced to the House on or before 31 December 2024, false if introduction slipped into 2025 or later.
reasoning: Criterion: a further Government water services bill introduced on or before 31 December 2024. The Local Government (Water Services) Bill (Government Bill 108) was introduced on 10 December 2024 and had its first reading on 17 December 2024, then was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee. The legislation.govt.nz as-introduced version carries the date 2024-12-10 and the Department of Internal Affairs disclosure statement for Bill 108 was finalised 10 December 2024. Checked for slippage into 2025: none — the bill was reported back in 2025 and enacted as the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025, but introduction was in December 2024 as Foster said.

statement: The numbers that have been talked about there—the $180 billion to $185 billion—I’m confident, as a result of the three stages that we are going through, that it will be well, well south of that; much, much cheaper to deliver the water services.
criterion: Published aggregate long-run water investment estimates under Local Water Done Well (DIA, Treasury, or council water services delivery plans aggregated); true if the total estimated cost is materially below $180–185 billion, false if the aggregated estimates land at or above that range.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2027-12-31, which has not passed, and no DIA or Treasury long-run (30-year) aggregate water investment estimate under Local Water Done Well has been published. The only published aggregate is councils' Water Services Delivery Plans, assessed and announced 11 December 2025, totalling $47.9 billion over the next ten years. That is not comparable on its face with the $180-185 billion figure Foster cited, which came from the 2021 Three Waters case-for-change estimate of $120-185 billion needed over 30 years — annualised, $47.9b/decade does not sit 'well, well south' of that range. Disconfirming evidence checked and found: the aggregated plans came in roughly $9 billion HIGHER than councils' own previous long-term plans, which runs against the 'much, much cheaper' direction of the claim. Verdict should be revisited when a 30-year aggregate on a comparable basis is published.

statement: The public’s water will become lower quality. Rivers will become more polluted and sewage will keep contaminating our oceans and our beaches.
criterion: Taumata Arowai annual Drinking Water Regulation Report and Ministry for the Environment / LAWA freshwater and coastal water quality trend reporting for the years following commencement; true if drinking-water compliance rates fall and national river/coastal contamination indicators worsen relative to 2024 baselines, false if they hold steady or improve.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2028-08-27 and the operative Local Water Done Well entities only began 1 July 2026, so the post-commencement trend series the criterion names is not yet published. LAWA's latest national river state-and-trend analysis still uses data only to June 2024 — the baseline itself, not the years after it. The two limbs of the criterion currently point opposite ways: drinking-water compliance has IMPROVED (Taumata Arowai: large council supplies meeting or almost meeting requirements rose from 49% in 2023 to 77% in 2025; school E. coli detections down 16% and long-term school advisories down from 17 to 7 in 2025), which runs against the prediction, while the sewage limb has a strong supporting event in the Moa Point wastewater plant failure of Feb 2026 (~70 million litres/day of untreated wastewater to the ocean, described as the largest such discharge in modern NZ history). The criterion requires compliance to fall AND river/coastal indicators to worsen relative to 2024 baselines; one is currently false and the other is not yet measurable.

statement: I think that’s something that every New Zealander needs to understand: the fact that ratepayers are going to bear the burden of these reforms through their rates.
