criterion: Council long-term plans and annual plans for 2025/26–2026/27 and DIA reporting on funding of water services delivery plans; true if the cost of required water infrastructure upgrades is met from rates or council-set water charges with no material central government contribution, false if central government funds a substantial share.
reasoning: The evidence the criterion names is now available: every mainland council has an approved water services delivery plan, and DIA forecasts $47.9b of water services infrastructure spend in the 10 years to June 2034, met by councils through rates, council-set water charges and debt. Local Government Minister Simon Watts stated the reform was achieved 'with very little central Government funding'; the only central financial commitment identified is the LGFA emergency backstop doubled from $1.5b to $3b and extended to 2037, which is a liquidity facility rather than infrastructure funding, and the previous government's $1.5b 'Better Off' grant package was abandoned. Searching specifically for a disconfirming central contribution (Budget 2026, grants to councils for water) turned up housing-growth incentives, not water infrastructure grants. The mechanism is visible in the numbers: for the 14 councils whose water plans took effect 1 July 2026, the national average household cost increase rises from 6.9% (rates only) to 7.9% once council-set water charges are included. Note the criterion explicitly counts council-set water charges as well as rates, which covers councils that shifted water to CCOs.

statement: They’re going to have to borrow for this at expensive rates, and that is going to put up everybody’s rates.
criterion: Stats NZ local authority rates data and DIA/LGNZ average rates increase figures for the 2025/26 and 2026/27 rating years; true if average council rates rise materially above general inflation nationally, false if average rates increases track or fall below inflation.
reasoning: Both rating years the criterion names are in and both are materially above inflation. Stats NZ CPI shows local authority rates and payments up 8.8% in the 12 months to March 2026 and 8.8% again in the 12 months to June 2026, against headline CPI of 3.1% (March 2026) and 4.1% (June 2026) — roughly double to nearly triple general inflation. The Taxpayers' Union dashboards put the 2025/26 average rates increase at 8.39% against 2.5% inflation, and the 2026/27 average proposed increase at 6.9% against 3.1%, rising to 7.9% nationwide once the 14 Local Water Done Well councils' new water charges are counted. Caveat on scope: the criterion tests only the outcome (rates materially above inflation), not Brooking's stated mechanism, so this verdict does not establish that borrowing costs for water specifically caused the rise — rates increases have multiple drivers. The water-specific 6.9%→7.9% gap is the closest direct support for the mechanism.

statement: I’ll tell you what will be unpopular, and that will be the rates bills that are going to start arriving in people’s letterboxes, with the dramatically increased rates in order to pay for water services infrastructure.
criterion: Local authority rates data (Stats NZ local authority statistics / LGNZ rates survey) for the 2025/26 and 2026/27 rating years. True if average council rates increases run well above the long-run historical average with water services cited as a principal driver; false if average increases return to historical norms.
reasoning: Rates increases ran well above historical norms in both target rating years, with water services a repeatedly cited principal driver. Average council rates increase was 8.39% for 2025/26 (vs 2.5% annual inflation), and Stats NZ CPI records local authority rates up 8.8% annually in both the March 2026 and June 2026 quarters, against an average of ~7.3% over 2018-2025 (itself already elevated) and pre-2022 norms of 3-5%. For 2026/27 the average proposed increase is 6.92%, 7.23% including water costs and 7.9% nationwide once the 14 councils transitioning under Local Water Done Well on 1 July 2026 are counted. Water is specifically cited: Wellington water charges +14.7% (+$310) in 2025/26 with ~28% forecast for 2027/28 and a doubling by 2036; Auckland water bills +7% on top of an 8% rates rise; Hastings/Napier +$400/yr in each of 2025/26 and 2026/27 to ~$2,200; Whangarei water rates proposed to rise >20% in 2026/27 and 2027/28. The Government's announced 4% rates cap corroborates the 'unpopular' element. Disconfirming checks: increases have fallen from the ~12.2% peak in the September 2024 quarter, and water is one of several drivers (insurance, interest, roading) with the Taxpayers' Union noting councils have not published driver breakdowns; also, in Wellington, Auckland and Hawke's Bay part of the water cost moved off the rates bill into separate water charges, so the household increase partly arrived as a water bill rather than a rates bill. Neither undercuts the criterion: increases did not return to historical norms.

statement: I rise to support this bill because it is all about supporting our primary industries and our food producers, and it will enable us to drive more productivity and increase the value of our exports—double those exports in the next 10 years, by value.
criterion: Stats NZ / MPI published export values: true if total export value in the year to 2034 is at least double the 2024 value in the same terms; false if it is materially below double.
reasoning: The claim is that export value will double within 10 years of 2024, i.e. by about 2034, and the criterion's own resolve-by date is 2034-12-31. Nothing is decidable in 2026. For context only: total exports were $80.7b in the year ended December 2025, and the doubling goal is stated Government policy via MBIE's Going for Growth programme, so a target and a baseline exist but the window has nine years to run. Commentary (BERL, The Conversation) notes previous doubling targets were not met and that NZ's commodity concentration makes it difficult, but that is not evidence about the 2034 outcome.

statement: My expectation is that public wage growth will start to level off as inflation settles within the band and as implementation of the workforce policy statement influences pay decisions and bargaining.
criterion: Stats NZ Labour Cost Index, public sector annual change for quarters through 2025; true if the annual increase falls materially below the 6.9% recorded to June 2024, false if it holds at or above that level.
reasoning: The criterion's baseline is confirmed: public sector LCI wage inflation reached a series high of 6.9% annually in the June 2024 quarter. It then fell in every subsequent quarter through 2025 and beyond: 4.2% in the year to March 2025, 2.8% to June 2025 (Stats NZ notes this is down from last year's record high for the sector), ~2.4% to September 2025, ~2.2-2.5% to December 2025, and 1.7% to both March 2026 and June 2026. That is materially below 6.9%, which is what the criterion asked. Disconfirming check: the stated premise about inflation settling in the band held only loosely - CPI was 2.5% (Mar 2025) and 2.7% (Jun 2025) but 3.0% (Sep 2025), 3.1% (Dec 2025 and Mar 2026) and 4.1% (Jun 2026), i.e. at or above the top of the 1-3% band for most of the period. The criterion tests the LCI series, and public wage growth levelled off sharply regardless of the inflation path, so the prediction resolves correct.

statement: It’s returning to within the statutory band of less than 3 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ annual CPI inflation prints following the statement. True if annual CPI falls below 3 percent within the next two quarterly releases; false if it remains at or above 3 percent through those releases.
reasoning: At the time of the statement (28 Aug 2024) the most recent print was the June 2024 quarter at 3.3% annual CPI. The next quarterly release, the September 2024 quarter (published 17 Oct 2024), came in at 2.2% annual — below 3% on the first of the two releases the criterion allows. The following release, the December 2024 quarter (Jan 2025), also printed 2.2%, which Stats NZ described as the second consecutive quarter inside the Reserve Bank's 1-3 percent target band. Criterion satisfied on both releases. (His characterisation of 1-3% as a 'statutory band' is loose — it is set by the Monetary Policy Remit under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act rather than stated in statute — but the criterion tests only the CPI outturn.)

statement: Since then, our Minister of Transport has announced that legislation will be introduced this year to enable time of use schemes to reduce travel times on our busiest roads and boost economic growth.
criterion: The Parliamentary bills register for 2024. True if a bill enabling time-of-use (congestion) charging was introduced to the House on or before 31 December 2024; false if no such bill was introduced within the calendar year.
reasoning: The Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill — which enables time-of-use (congestion) charging schemes — was introduced to the House on 15 December 2024, inside the calendar year as predicted. Corroborating primary evidence: the bill's official citation is '113-1 (2024)', and NZ bill numbers carry the year of introduction; its disclosure statement, which is published on introduction, is dated 6 December 2024. Its first reading then followed on 4 March 2025 (117 ayes to 6; Te Pati Maori against), second reading 21 Oct 2025, third reading 11 Nov 2025, Royal assent 17 Nov 2025. Caution: several secondary sources (a Minter Ellison insight, Auckland Transport) state the bill 'was introduced and passed its first reading in Parliament on 4 March 2025', conflating introduction with first reading; on that loose reading the claim would fail, but the bills register records introduction in December 2024, and the criterion asks only about introduction, not first reading.

statement: By supporting this bill—and it’s great that all parties across this House will be supporting this bill—we reaffirm our dedication to creating a safer and more just society for New Zealanders.
criterion: The division records for the bill's subsequent readings; true if every party votes in favour (or it passes without opposition), false if any party casts votes against.
reasoning: The bill Arbuckle was speaking to (second reading, 28 Aug 2024, discussing the Justice Committee report-back) is the Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill. The Ministry of Justice records that the legislation 'received unanimous bipartisan support through all its parliamentary stages'; it passed its third reading on 13 February 2025 and received Royal assent on 17 February 2025 as the Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Act 2025. The NZ Bar Association independently states it 'received unanimous parliamentary support'. No source records any party voting against at any stage, and I checked specifically for opposition (including from Te Pati Maori, which did oppose the unrelated time-of-use charging bill) and found none. Sourcing caveat: parliament.nz returned 403/404 to every fetch attempt, so I could not read the division lines in Hansard directly; the verdict rests on the Ministry of Justice's all-stages statement, which satisfies the criterion's 'passes without opposition' branch rather than its named division-record branch.

statement: That figure will only grow as more people enter the trade, attracted in part because tax authorities have limited visibility of income derived through crypto-assets.
criterion: Global crypto market capitalisation (CoinGecko/CoinMarketCap) measured two years after the statement and converted to NZD; true if higher than the ~NZ$4 trillion figure cited on 29 August 2024, false if lower.
reasoning: Baseline confirmed: IRD/Watts material for the 2024 bill cited crypto-asset total market capitalisation "close to NZ$4 trillion" (>22,000 crypto assets). Measured two years on, global crypto market cap was US$2.72 trillion on 29 August 2026 (CoinStats daily market report; CoinGecko showed US$2.96T in late September 2026). With NZD/USD trading 0.57-0.62 through August-September 2026, that converts to roughly NZ$4.4-4.8 trillion, above the ~NZ$4 trillion baseline on any plausible rate, so the criterion is satisfied. The USD series also grew (US$2.03T at end-August 2024 to US$2.72T at end-August 2026, +34%), so the verdict does not rest on currency depreciation alone. Caveat not covered by the criterion: growth was not monotonic - the market peaked substantially higher during 2025 and CoinGecko records it down ~22% year-on-year - so "will only grow" holds at the two-year measurement point but not continuously. The second half of the quote (that limited tax-authority visibility is part of the attraction) is a causal claim the criterion does not test.

statement: That is going to double the capacity of the Auckland commuter rail network.
criterion: Auckland Transport / City Rail Link Ltd published network capacity figures (peak passengers per hour or trains per hour) before and after CRL opening: true if post-opening capacity is about double the pre-CRL figure, false if the increase is materially less.
reasoning: The criterion asks for AT/CRL Ltd published before-and-after capacity figures. AT's published figures are 19,000 peak passengers per hour through the city centre against a pre-CRL 12,000 per hour - "about a 50% increase" - delivered by 16 trains per hour in each direction. Crucially this is the FINAL timetable figure, not merely the transitional one, so waiting for the ramp-up does not change it: CRL opened to passengers on 13 September 2026 on a reduced timetable (most suburban stations 6 trains/hour at peak rather than the 8 tested, gaps up to 15 minutes), with AT committed to the full timetable within six months (~March 2027, inside the resolve-by date). So the increase in delivered network capacity is about 50-58%, materially less than double. Against that, CRL Ltd/project materials do publish a "at least double its capacity" claim, resting on ultimate infrastructure design (up to 48 trains/hour through-running, stations built for 54,000 passengers/hour) rather than any timetabled service - a distinction Brown did not signal. Hence partly_correct: a large real capacity gain, materially overstated as doubling, and true only on a design-capacity reading. A strict binary reading of the criterion's "false if the increase is materially less" would score this wrong.

statement: There’s also good news for commuters: the City Rail Link will soon be complete, and other major public transport projects are being progressed through this NLTP, including the Eastern Busway, Airport to Botany busway, Northwest Rapid Transit corridor, and upgrades to commuter rails in the Manawatū and Wairarapa.
criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport announcements: true if CRL construction is completed and the line opens to passenger service by the resolve-by date, false if completion or opening is still outstanding at that date.
reasoning: The criterion tests only whether CRL construction completed and the line opened to passenger service by 2026-12-31. Auckland Transport's media centre announced passenger services beginning with the formal opening in September 2026; the City Rail Link was formally opened on 11 September 2026 and passenger services began on Sunday 13 September 2026, with the three new underground stations (Te Waihorotiu, Karanga-a-Hape, Maungawhau) in service and about 70,000 boardings on day one. That is inside the resolve-by date, so the criterion is met. Two notes the criterion does not weigh: "soon" turned out to mean two years, and the line opened on a transitional rather than full timetable. The other projects named in the quote (Eastern Busway, Airport to Botany, Northwest Rapid Transit, Manawatu/Wairarapa rail) were only claimed to be "being progressed through this NLTP" and are outside the criterion as written.

statement: Is the independent team of specialist advisers, appointed to give advice on the future structure of vocational education, wrong when they advised that any structure that splits institutes of technology and polytechnics (ITPs) into some independent ITPs and some grouped ITPs would continue to run deficits of tens of millions of dollars until 2028?
criterion: Audited financial statements of the successor ITPs for the years to 2028; true if the disaggregated ITP network runs combined annual deficits in the tens of millions of dollars through to 2028, false if the network reaches surplus or deficits fall well below that scale before then.
reasoning: The criterion requires audited financial statements of the successor ITPs for the years to 2028. The disaggregated network only came into existence on 1 January 2026 (Te Pūkenga disestablished, 10 regional polytechnics created by the Oct 2025 VET legislation), so no audited year of the disaggregated network has been published yet — the first would appear around mid-to-late 2027, and the criterion runs through 2028 (resolve by 2029-06-30). Interim evidence currently leans toward the prediction rather than against it: the independent advisers' May 2024 report projected collective losses of $96.3m in 2026 falling to $50.3m by 2028 under exactly the some-standalone/some-grouped model Russell described, with the ITP sector forecast to run a cumulative deficit of over $400m across 2024-2028 and only 6 of 16 ITPs forecast to reach surplus by 2028. Post-split, the government has had to make transition injections (a $325m capital transfer, ~$80.8m to Ara, ~$24-27m to Otago Polytechnic in Feb 2026) and Te Pūkenga's residual four institutes budgeted a $16m deficit for 2026 on a 6% enrolment fall. None of that is an audited disaggregated-network result, so the test as written cannot be run yet.

statement: What I admit is that as we move to a regional model, Tairāwhiti will benefit from a shorter line of decision making to a regional deputy chief executive; it will improve recruitment and retention.
criterion: Health New Zealand Tairāwhiti workforce reporting (vacancy/turnover figures, or OIA releases) after the regional model takes effect; true if the district's senior medical officer vacancy rate falls materially below the ~30 percent baseline cited, false if it remains flat or worsens.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether Tairāwhiti's senior medical officer vacancy rate fell materially below the ~30% baseline after the regional model took effect, resolving by 2026-03-31. It did not, within that window. The rate was ~35-37% when Reti spoke in August 2024; by February 2025 Health NZ itself put it at 37% while Tairāwhiti doctors said 44%, and in April 2025 senior doctors wrote to the Prime Minister saying Gisborne Hospital was on the 'brink of collapse', with radiology, psychiatry and anaesthesia more than two-thirds vacant. It was still 37% in September 2025, when Gisborne senior doctors struck citing an exhausted, under-resourced workforce. So over the whole period to the resolve date the rate was flat-to-worse against the baseline — the criterion's explicit 'false' condition. Looking past the deadline for disconfirming evidence: by June/July 2026 the rate had fallen to 28% (22 of 57 FTE posts vacant), with Minister Simeon Brown forecasting 10% by December 2026. That is a real improvement, but it arrives more than a year after the resolve date and lands only marginally below the ~30% baseline, and the CMO attributes it to international recruitment, visa and medical-registration processing and staff arrivals — plus a $25,000 hard-to-recruit allowance — not to the regional model's shorter decision line. Against Reti's stated mechanism the evidence runs the other way: reporting found the requirement for regional deputy chief executive sign-off put decisions further from the vacancy (a Gisborne ED administrator post decided in Hamilton), and Health NZ's board agreed in October 2025 to devolve decision-making from regional back toward district level.

statement: I can confirm that that won’t be the case for a number of other bills in her name.
criterion: Hansard division records for bills in Nicole McKee's name introduced or progressed after 29 August 2024; true if two or more such bills are opposed by at least one party at any reading, false if her subsequent bills continue to pass with unanimous support.
reasoning: The criterion needs two or more bills in Nicole McKee's name, introduced or progressed after 29 August 2024, opposed by at least one party at any reading. At least two qualify, with recorded party votes. (1) Arms (Shooting Clubs, Shooting Ranges, and Other Matters) Amendment Bill, introduced by McKee 22 September 2024: party votes of 68-55 at first reading (26 Sep 2024), second reading (18 Feb 2025) and third reading (25 Mar 2025) — National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8 in favour; Labour 34, Greens 14, Te Pāti Māori 6 (plus Darleen Tana) against. (2) Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill, also McKee's: second reading 12 December 2024 (68-54) and third reading 13 December 2024 (68-43), both along the same coalition-versus-Labour/Greens/Te Pāti Māori lines — its progression falls after 29 August 2024. Checking for the disconfirming case — that her bills kept passing unanimously — several of her later bills did pass without a division (the Arms Bill's first reading on 9 December 2025 was agreed on the voices, and the AML/CFT amendment work drew cross-party support), but the criterion is met by any two bills opposed at any reading, not by all of them being opposed. For completeness the Arms Bill was later divided against at its second reading on 21 July 2026 (National 48, ACT 11, NZ First 8 for; Labour 34, Greens 15, Te Pāti Māori 4 against), a third qualifying bill, though that falls after the 2025-12-31 resolve date.

statement: Today, this legislation will pass.
criterion: The Hansard record and the Parliament bill page for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if the third reading was agreed to on 11 September 2024, false if the reading was adjourned, defeated, or not completed that day.
reasoning: The Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill was read a third time on 11 September 2024; a party vote was called and the motion was agreed to, 111 ayes to 11 noes (ACT opposed). The reading was completed that day, not adjourned or defeated, so the criterion is met.

statement: I’m pleased to support this bill, I’m pleased it will be the law soon, and I commend it to the House.
criterion: The legislation record on legislation.govt.nz and the NZ Gazette: true if the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent within roughly six months of 11 September 2024; false if it fails, is discharged, or remains unenacted by that date.
reasoning: The bill passed its third reading on 11 September 2024 and received Royal assent on 16 September 2024 as the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Act 2024 (2024 No 35) — five days later, far inside the ~six-month window the criterion allowed. (It commenced 18 months after assent, on 16 March 2026, but the criterion asked for enactment, not commencement.)

statement: The digital gift card industry alone is expected to reach $2,000 billion by 2027.
criterion: Published market-size estimates for the digital/e-gift card market (e.g. Grand View Research, Mordor, Allied Market Research) for calendar 2027: true if the digital gift card market is measured at or above ~$2 trillion, false if it is materially below.
reasoning: Calendar 2027 has not yet occurred, but the criterion resolves against published market-size estimates for 2027, which exist. Those put the digital gift card market at roughly $580-680bn in 2025-26 and about $620-740bn in 2027, reaching $1.5tn only around 2032 (Allied Market Research). Even the entire gift-card market (digital plus physical) was ~$1.1tn in 2024-25 and is forecast to reach $2.3tn only by 2030. I looked specifically for a source supporting ~$2tn for digital alone by 2027 — including whole-market and US-only series that might explain the figure — and found none. The claim is materially overstated, by roughly 3x.

statement: She’ll be standing up 11 votes in favour for the ACT Party and voting in support of this legislation, because it’s about the consumer, it’s about businesses in New Zealand, and it’s about ensuring that everyone that receives a gift card, whether it’s through the Rutherford Secret Santa roulette, whether it’s through birthdays, whether it’s just for someone who is leaving a business and moving on to a new opportunity—whatever experience or whatever undertaking they receive it in—has got adequate time to use it and spend it as it is intended.
criterion: The party vote record for the third reading of the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if ACT's 11 votes are recorded in favour, false if they are recorded against or abstaining.
reasoning: The third reading party vote on 11 September 2024 passed 111-11, with ACT New Zealand's 11 votes recorded as the only Noes (Ayes: National 49, Labour 34, Greens 14, NZ First 8, Te Pati Maori 6). Contemporaneous reporting confirms ACT was the sole party not to support the bill, arguing it would unnecessarily burden businesses. The criterion's false branch (ACT's 11 votes recorded against) is what the record shows.

statement: I am excited to see a health system in five to 10 years’ time that, because of a good strategy, will have addressed these barriers and will see less Kiwis taking their own lives and more Kiwis living with good mental health and wellbeing.
criterion: Coronial Services of New Zealand annual provisional suicide statistics (rate per 100,000) for the year ending June 2034 compared with the year ending June 2024: true if the suicide rate is lower, false if it is the same or higher.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Coronial Services of New Zealand provisional suicide statistics for the year ending June 2034, compared with year ending June 2024. Today is 2026-09-27, so the comparison year is roughly eight years away and no resolving evidence can exist yet.

statement: GDP results for the June quarter will come out next Thursday. These are also likely to be weak, with many forecasters picking a negative quarter.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP release for the June 2024 quarter (published 19 September 2024); true if seasonally adjusted quarterly real GDP change is negative, false if it is zero or positive.
reasoning: Stats NZ published June 2024 quarter GDP on Thursday 19 September 2024 - the 'next Thursday' Willis named - and seasonally adjusted real GDP fell 0.2 percent, following a 0.1 percent rise in the March 2024 quarter. Both the timing and the negative-quarter prediction hold. (The '0.9 percent fall' headlines in search results refer to the June 2025 quarter, not this one.)

statement: It will be delivered next year on time and on budget thanks to the provision of the former Labour Government ensuring that we paid for it; we were committed to it, we built it, it’s going to serve the communities of the Manawatū and the Tararua district so well.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project records and opening announcements for Te Ahu a Turanga; true if the road opened to traffic during the 2025 calendar year at or under its approved budget, false if it opened later than 2025 or the final cost exceeded the approved budget.
reasoning: The road did open during 2025: officially opened 7 June 2025 and open to traffic 11 June 2025, matching the "next year" and mid-2025 schedule. The budget limb of the criterion fails decisively — the approved cost was $620m and the final expected cost to complete was $824.1m, a roughly $200m (33%) overrun that was already public before Utikere spoke (it was raised in the House on 18 September 2024 and used to justify a tolling proposal). Wikipedia records an even earlier 2018 estimate of $350-450m. So "delivered next year" held, "on budget" did not.

statement: Phase 2 of the inquiry will begin very shortly with hearings as early as November.
criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned phase 2 public record; true if hearings were held in November 2024, false if the first phase 2 hearings occurred later.
reasoning: Phase 2 of the Royal Commission commenced on 29 November 2024, but no hearings were held then. The inquiry's own timeline records the first Phase 2 public hearings as the "pandemic perspectives" week in Tāmaki Makaurau beginning 7 July 2025, and RNZ covered that week as the first public hearings into New Zealand's Covid-19 response. A planned second hearing week was abandoned in August 2025 after former Ministers declined to give evidence. Checked specifically for any November or December 2024 hearing and found none — the November date appears to be the start of Phase 2 itself, not hearings.

statement: And finally, a report will be delivered in early 2026, and with this report, be it a lesson for future parliamentarians.
criterion: Publication date of the phase 2 report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned; true if delivered by roughly the end of the first quarter of 2026, false if delivered later or not at all.
reasoning: The Phase 2 report was submitted to the Governor-General on 26 February 2026 and the Phase 2 reports were made publicly available on 10 March 2026. Both dates fall inside the criterion's window of roughly the end of the first quarter of 2026, so "a report will be delivered in early 2026" holds on either the delivery or the publication date.

statement: There is a pause and a maintenance of the existing funding while a rapid review is undertaken to understand why residential care costs have gone up beyond the level of inflation. That rapid review will have answers by the beginning of early 2025.
criterion: Whaikaha/MSD publications and ministerial statements; true if the residential care pricing rapid review reported its findings by around March 2025, false if findings were still outstanding or delayed beyond that point.
reasoning: The rapid review did complete and produce answers, but later than 'the beginning of early 2025'. DSS's provider pages attribute the implementation decisions on the new residential pricing model to a March 2025 Cabinet paper ('Stabilising Disability Support Services-Funded Residential Care', SOU-25-MIN-0015), which is at the outer edge of the criterion's 'around March 2025' window — but that paper was Budget-sensitive and only released on 23 May 2025, and the findings and the resulting Community Group Home Pricing Model were not communicated publicly or to providers until Budget 2025 (22-23 May 2025). Downstream, the funding freeze Simmonds described was maintained to 30 June 2025 and lifted 1 July 2025, provider rates were subject to a validation process finalising around September 2025, and the new contracts took effect 1 December 2025 with first payment 20 January 2026. So the substance holds — the review ran, concluded, and produced a pricing answer — but 'answers by the beginning of early 2025' overstates the timing: the decision came in March at the earliest, was published in May, and nothing providers could act on existed until mid-to-late 2025. No evidence was found of a published review findings report by March 2025.

statement: It will only intensify the increasing market consolidation and dominance of a small number of large, private providers, and that will be at the expense of the small, local, community-based early learning centres.
criterion: Ministry of Education ECE licensed-service statistics (services by service type and by ownership/provider group) compared between 2024 and 2027; true if the number or share of large-private-provider centres rises while community-based/standalone centre numbers fall, false if community-based provision holds steady or grows relative to large private providers.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on a 2024-vs-2027 comparison of Ministry of Education licensed-service statistics by service type and ownership/provider group, with a resolve-by date of 2027-12-31; today is 2026-09-27, so the endpoint data does not exist. What is available does not resolve it either way: Education Counts shows total licensed services essentially flat between the 2024 and 2025 census weeks (4,408 to 4,390, -0.4%), and the Ministry's published ECE census outputs do not break services out by large-private versus community-based ownership in a form covering the post-repeal period. Sector reporting notes continued closures (443 centres between March 2022 and July 2025, closures rising again in 2026) and ongoing corporate consolidation (Evolve's 111 centres sold to private equity), but nothing that separates provider groups as the criterion requires. Not finding the evidence yet is expected, not disconfirming.

statement: It’ll make it so much easier, as we’ve heard, for big global businesses to monopolise and privatise the sector to the detriment not only of teachers but of our students.
criterion: Ministry of Education ECE licensing and service-provider data: true if the share of licensed ECE services owned by large corporate or overseas-owned chains rises materially after the repeal, false if that share is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the share of licensed ECE services owned by large corporate or overseas-owned chains rises materially after the network-approval repeal (agreed 25 September 2024), with a resolve-by date of 2028-12-31 — over two years away. The required series does not exist yet: Ministry of Education / Education Counts publishes licensed services by service type, not by corporate-chain ownership share, and the only post-repeal census comparison available (2024 to 2025) shows total licensed services roughly flat at -0.4%. Consolidation activity is visible in the market (Evolve's 111-centre portfolio sold to Anchorage Capital Partners) and closures continued through 2025-2026, but neither establishes a rise or a flat/falling chain share on the measure named. Uncheckable-for-now rather than wrong.

statement: Well, I can confirm that they are opposed to this particular bill. Members opposite can say whatever they like, but the reality remains that those two members will vote in opposition to this particular bill.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the remaining readings of the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2) 2024; true if the Labour Party vote (which includes Jackson and Henare) is recorded against the bill, false if either member's vote is recorded in support or if Labour votes for it.
reasoning: The bill before the House on 12 Sept 2024 was the Education and Training Amendment Bill (2024, bill 66 — the charter schools bill); its second reading was that day (68 ayes / 49 noes, the noes being Labour 34 + Greens 15). The remaining stages, including the third reading on 25 September 2024, passed with National, ACT and NZ First in support and Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori opposed. No Labour split vote or individual dissent is recorded, so Willie Jackson and Peeni Henare were covered by Labour's 34 votes against — exactly what Utikere predicted. Note the criterion mislabels the bill '(No 2) 2024' (the bill actually named '(No 2)' is a 2025 bill), but on that bill too Labour's 34 were recorded against at third reading on 11 Nov 2025, so the verdict is unchanged on either reading.

statement: This bill needs to progress now so that the changes I believe will have significant impact on reducing vaping come into force as soon as possible.
criterion: ASH Year 10 Snapshot and NZ Health Survey vaping prevalence for the survey years following commencement; true if youth (14-15 year old and 15-24) daily vaping prevalence falls materially below the 2024 baseline, false if prevalence is flat or rises.
reasoning: Costello was speaking to the first reading (12 Sept 2024) of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (No 2); royal assent 17 Dec 2024, with the disposable-vape ban and retail visibility restrictions commencing after a six-month delay in mid-2025. The two sources named in the criterion disagree. ASH Year 10 (14-15) daily vaping fell from 8.7% in 2024 to 7.1% in 2025, and regular vaping from 14.1% to 11.2% — a material fall. But NZ Health Survey daily vaping among 15-24s was flat: 15-17s went 10.3% (2023/24) to 13.6% (2024/25) and 18-24s ~24% to 23.0%, neither change statistically significant. Two further limits: the 2024/25 NZHS field period largely precedes commencement, and the Year 10 decline was already running from the 2021-22 peak (20.2% regular) years before this bill, so the fall is real but not attributable to it. The decisive post-commencement data (2025/26 NZHS, 2026 ASH snapshot) is not published as at Sept 2026. Substance partly holds in one named source, fails the other, and 'significant impact' is not established.

statement: You see lower levels of inflation, you’ve seen interest rate cuts, you’ve seen the highest level of business confidence we’ve had in 10 years—then we’ll get economic growth, then we’ll keep people in employment.
criterion: Stats NZ GDP series and HLFS employment for calendar 2025; true if annual GDP growth is positive across 2025 and employment does not fall, false if the economy fails to return to growth or employment declines.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are met only marginally. GDP: annual average growth for the year ended December 2025 was +0.2% — positive, and the first annual growth in over two years (+1.3% year-on-year in the December quarter) — but the path was not continuous growth: the June 2025 quarter contracted about 1.0% and the year ended September 2025 was -0.5%. Employment: the Parliamentary Library's Monthly Economic Review (Feb 2026) records annual employment +0.2% in the year to the December 2025 quarter, after a -0.7% annual fall in the year to September 2025; the December 2025 quarter was the first quarterly employment increase since June 2024, and the unemployment rate rose to 5.4%, the highest since September 2015. So the economy did return to growth and employment ended calendar 2025 fractionally up, satisfying the criterion literally, but 'then we'll keep people in employment' is materially overstated against a year of falling employment and a decade-high unemployment rate.

statement: What that did was signal a warning bell for the fact that, actually, what we are potentially looking at as a result of the intentional decisions made under this Government to wind back some of the most successful climate change and mitigation policies is that we are, potentially, going to be off track to meet emissions budget 1 out to next year—to 2025.
criterion: Final accounting of emissions budget 1 (2022–2025) against the New Zealand Greenhouse Gas Inventory, as assessed by the Climate Change Commission/Ministry for the Environment; true if net emissions over 2022–2025 exceed the emissions budget 1 allowance, false if they fall within it.
reasoning: The criterion requires the final accounting of emissions budget 1 (2022-2025) against the NZ Greenhouse Gas Inventory as assessed by the Climate Change Commission/MfE. EB1 ended 31 December 2025, but the final assessment has not been published: the Commission's 2026 monitoring report (22 July 2026) states that its end-of-budget report in 2027 will give the full assessment using final emissions data, and the current inventory (published April 2026) only covers 1990-2024. Resolve-by date is 2027-06-30, still in the future. Best available interim evidence runs against the prediction rather than for it: the Commission projects EB1 (290 MtCO2e) will be met with a 7.7 MtCO2e buffer, partly because inventory methodology changes mean the budget can now be met with less effort than when it was set. But that is a projection, not the final accounting the criterion names, so the item is not yet resolvable.

statement: I’d like to ask the Minister whether he sees that it is going to, potentially, be the case that we are going to see those ETS auctions fail out to the end of this calendar year and, as a result, all of those units ultimately cancelled—and, hey presto, look, he has been pretty effective as far as that goes, although probably not with that being his intention.
criterion: EPA published NZ ETS auction results for the September and December 2024 auctions and the year-end unsold-unit cancellation notice; true if no units were sold at the remaining 2024 auctions and the full 2024 auction volume was cancelled, false if any auction cleared.
reasoning: The criterion makes the prediction false if any remaining 2024 auction cleared. The final 2024 auction, on 4 December 2024, partially cleared: 4 million NZUs sold at the $64 price floor, roughly a third of the volume on offer (about 7 million units went unsold at that auction). The September 2024 auction, held 4 September (before this 17 September statement), was bidless, and June was bidless too, but March 2024 had already partially cleared at ~80% of its offer. Across the full year, 7.007 million units were sold against 14.1 million made available, so neither limb of the criterion holds: an auction cleared, and the full 2024 auction volume was not cancelled (only the unsold residue plus the Cost Containment Reserve was retired). Checked for the opposite too: the run of bidless auctions Swarbrick was extrapolating from is real and resumed in 2025 (all four 2025 auctions failed and 6 million units plus 7.1 million CCR units were cancelled), but that is the following year and outside what she predicted.

statement: Sadly, because our genetic engineering laws aren’t where they need to be yet—but Minister Collins is pushing that through fast—it’s being trialled in Australia in 2025, first up, but we look to bring that back into New Zealand.
criterion: Ruminant BioTech / AgriZeroNZ announcements and Australian regulatory (APVMA) records. True if trials of the bolus were under way in Australia at some point during calendar 2025; false if no Australian trial commenced in that year.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether trials of the Ruminant BioTech bolus were under way in Australia at some point during calendar 2025. The intent and funding are documented: in August 2024 Ruminant BioTech received an A$3.5m grant under the Australian Government's Methane Emissions Reduction in Livestock (MERiL) programme whose stated key activities were controlled cattle trials at the University of Sydney plus deployment of the bolus in commercial cattle backgrounding operations, with a commercially-ready bolus expected by the project's end in 2025 and an Australian commercial launch then targeted for October 2025. But I could find no announcement, published result, company statement or government record confirming that an Australian trial actually commenced or ran during 2025 — and the second source named in the criterion cannot settle it either, because the company states no Australian registration is required for the product, so there is no APVMA application or permit record to inspect. I also checked for disconfirming evidence: by 28 November 2025 trade coverage had the Australian launch slipping to 2026, cited only New Zealand (Lincoln University) research for the efficacy claim, and made no mention of Australian trials; February 2026 coverage likewise reports only NZ regulatory milestones. That is consistent with delay but does not establish that no Australian trial ran. Evidence is genuinely not findable either way. Separately, and outside the criterion: Watts attributed the hold-up to New Zealand's genetic-engineering laws, but this bolus delivers synthesised tribromomethane and is being registered by MPI under the ACVM Act, not gated on gene-technology reform.

statement: It will put more serious offenders in prison for longer to prevent them creating new victims.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics and Ministry of Justice sentencing data after the sentencing reform package takes effect: true if the number of people sentenced to imprisonment for serious violent/sexual offending and the average length of those sentences both rise relative to 2024; false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The sentencing package Goldsmith was speaking to (Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act; three strikes) only came into force 29 June 2025, so the first full post-reform sentencing year is the year ended 30 June 2026, whose MoJ/Stats NZ tables were published only this month (September 2026) and have not been broken out for the two quantities the criterion names — count of imprisonment sentences for serious violent/sexual offending and their average length — relative to 2024. The criterion's own resolve-by date is 2027-06-30. Directional evidence exists but cuts both ways: the prison population has climbed (11,240 in February 2026, projected +35% to 15,200 by June 2036) and MoJ explicitly attributes the growth to the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act and Crimes Amendment Bill meaning 'more people will receive prison sentences, and for longer terms'; the sentenced population is projected up 26%. Against that, the June 2026 Justice Sector Projections treat average imposed sentence length as broadly stable over the next decade, and the projected growth is driven more by remand (+48%) than by the sentenced population. Since the criterion requires BOTH the count and the average length to rise on realised data, and the realised post-reform sentencing data has not yet been analysed, this cannot be settled yet. Not finding the data is not evidence the claim failed.

statement: I think that’s a fantastic result and, no doubt, there’ll be more material and more positive news in due course when we deliver on the August numbers.
criterion: MSD monthly emergency housing / Priority One statistics for August 2024; true if the August release shows further households and children exiting emergency housing at or above the trend reported for 30 April–31 July, false if the August figures show no further improvement or a reversal.
reasoning: MSD's own month-end series (released under the OIA on 31 October 2024, Table 1 of the 26 September 2024 memo to Potaka's office) gives total EH households: Apr24 2,724; May24 2,463; Jun24 2,133; Jul24 1,707; Aug24 1,365. The 30 April-31 July trend is -339 households/month; August delivered -342, i.e. at or above trend. Children in EH: Apr 2,886; May 2,544; Jun 2,139; Jul 1,614; Aug 1,101 — the April-July trend is -424 children/month and August delivered -513, comfortably above trend. MSD's memo states outright that 'the most significant reduction of children in EH (32 percent) occurred between July and August 2024'. Priority One placements also continued: 645 households and 1,311 children housed between May and August 2024, rising to 726 households and 1,452 children by 30 September. EH grant spend fell from ~$31m in December 2023 to ~$11m in September 2024. Checking for the opposite: I looked for any August reversal or plateau and found none — the only contemporaneous criticism (Labour, Te Matapihi, Te Ao News) was that the improvement was produced by tightened eligibility and declined applications and that MSD could not say where the households went, which is a challenge to the cause and the merit of the fall, not to the fall itself. The criterion asks only whether the August release showed further exits at or above trend; it did.

statement: The department has advised me that if councils utilise this new model, it will deliver 11 percent lower prices than forecast in their long-term plans and 8 percent less than the Water Industry Commission for Scotland modelling which was produced under the previous Government.
criterion: Compare realised household water charges set by Local Water Done Well water service organisations against the price paths published in councils' 2024–34 long-term plans; true if average charges land about 11 percent below those forecasts, false if they land at or above the long-term plan price path.
reasoning: Councils did adopt the model — 44 handed water services to a separate company, 23 kept them in-house — so the conditional Brown attached is satisfied, and the first Local Water Done Well entities began charging on 1 July 2026. Against the councils' own long-term-plan price paths, realised charges have landed at or above them, not ~11 percent below. (1) DIA's analysis of the approved water services delivery plans found councils will spend nearly $9 billion MORE on water over the decade than their long-term plans estimated, ~$47.9b in total — the aggregate cost base moved the wrong way. (2) Wellington's Tiaki Wai, the flagship multi-council entity, set an average household charge of ~$2,418 for 2026/27 against the $2,124 in the delivery plan the same councils submitted in August 2025 (~14 percent above), prompting Local Government Minister Simon Watts to intervene over charges 'greater than what was initially presented to the Department of Internal Affairs and the regulator'; even after Tiaki Wai backed down the increase was 12.8 percent, and 2036 bills are forecast at ~$6,206. (3) Hamilton/Waikato charges rose $174 in the first year. (4) Selwyn households faced an ~18 percent rise. I checked the strongest disconfirming case: Auckland's Watercare is rising 7.2 percent rather than the 25.8 percent in the DRAFT long-term plan — but the adopted 2024-34 LTP incorporated the Watercare charter, so 7.2 percent IS the long-term plan price path, i.e. at it, not below. Caveat on coverage: only the first cohort of entities has set charges and the criterion's resolve-by is 2027-07-01, so this is one year of realised data rather than the full window — but no entity has delivered charges below its LTP path, which is the criterion's explicit false condition.

statement: Furthermore, the Nelson detailed business case at this point is looking towards the end of this year, so all the signals and all the indications for the Nelson hospital upgrade, I would have thought, are good.
criterion: Health NZ / Ministry of Health records and public reporting on the Nelson Hospital detailed business case; true if the detailed business case was completed by 31 December 2024, false if it was still outstanding or delayed into 2025.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the Nelson Hospital detailed business case was completed by 31 December 2024. It was not. Health NZ's published DBC documents are dated 20-02-2025 (Part 1 and Part 2, V1.4), released 26 May 2025 alongside Cabinet minute Exp-25-Min-0030. The end-of-2024 commitment Reti made in August 2024 (master plan and DBC to Cabinet by year end) was not met; as late as 1 April 2025 local reporting recorded the business case as only just having been given to the Minister, and Health NZ's own timeline had Ministers considering it in early 2025. Reti's wider point that 'the signals are good' for the upgrade did hold — Cabinet approved a $1.098b programme and Budget 2025 funded a new 128-bed inpatient building — but the dated prediction the criterion tests slipped roughly two months past the deadline, into 2025.

statement: I understand maybe 10 to 12 may be ready, and some may be a month or two later.
criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health records of iwi-Māori partnership board community health plan submissions; true if approximately 10–12 plans were received by 1 October 2024 and the balance within roughly two months, false if materially fewer or more arrived by the deadline or the remainder took substantially longer.
reasoning: The criterion turns on how many iwi-Māori partnership board community health plans were in hand at the 30 September / 1 October 2024 deadline, and that number is not in the public record. I looked for it in the Beehive announcements, Ministry of Health information releases and briefings on IMPBs, the October 2024 handover coverage, and parliamentary questions; none reports a count as at the deadline. What is on the record is consistent with the shape of the prediction but cannot confirm or falsify it: five or six Te Manawa Taki boards presented their plans at a Whakatāne hui on 3-4 October 2024 (described as 'a third' of the boards) and that region stated it met the 30 September deadline; the Minister then announced on 11 December 2024 that he had received all 15 plans. The full set therefore arrived about ten weeks after the deadline, roughly matching 'some may be a month or two later', but without the deadline-day figure the 10-12 claim itself is not verifiable either way.

statement: Now, if this committee is going to go and travel the country in the two weeks that the deputy chair has peremptorily set for submissions, well, good luck to them for that, because it’s highly unlikely.
criterion: The Health Committee's meeting records and hearing schedule for the vaping bill up to the 31 October 2024 report-back; true if no hearings were held outside the Wellington area, false if the committee met or heard submissions outside Wellington.
reasoning: Webb predicted the Health Committee was highly unlikely to travel the country given the two-week submission period. The committee's report commentary on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (No 2) records that it received 849 submissions and 'heard oral evidence from 41 submitters in Wellington and by videoconference' — no hearings outside Wellington. The timeline also matches his complaint: the bill was referred to the committee on 12 September 2024 with submissions closing 27 September 2024 and a report-back date of 31 October 2024. Although the House's first-reading motion gave the committee the usual authority to meet outside the Wellington area, it did not use it; the second-reading debate likewise refers only to written submissions and oral submissions heard by the committee, with no mention of regional hearings. Checking for the opposite — any record of a hearing in Auckland or elsewhere — turned up nothing.

statement: Well, do you want to be standing here in two years’ time debating the fact that our laws didn’t work because we didn’t take the time to get it right? That’s what’s going to happen if we don’t take time to hear from the people who hold the devices in their hands every day, who make the devices.
criterion: Parliamentary and regulatory record to September 2026; true if the disposable-vape provisions enacted from this bill were found to be circumvented by product redesign and required further amending legislation or regulation, false if the rules were in force and operating without such remedial change.
reasoning: The criterion has two limbs. Limb 1 (circumvention by product redesign) is confirmed: the disposable ban took effect 17 June 2025, and a Public Health Communication Centre briefing of 17 June 2026 documents the industry replacing disposables with near-identical ultra-cheap reusables — 89% of audited stores selling starter products at NZ$15 or less and two-thirds at NZ$10 or less, versus a single brand at that price in January 2024 — retaining the low cost, flavour range and convenience that made disposables appealing to youth; a Wellington compliance audit also found poor compliance with advertising/visibility and age-verification rules (few stores, though, still sold disposables). Limb 2 (required further amending legislation or regulation) is NOT met as at September 2026: no remedial amendment closing the redesign loophole has been enacted. The June 2026 briefing is still advocating minimum pricing, flavour restrictions, excise and seizure powers, which establishes they had not been introduced. The only regulatory change since the ban ran the opposite way — on 24 July 2025 the removable-battery requirement (introduced by Verrall in 2023) was revoked from 1 September 2025 after a court challenge by Mason Corporation/Shosha, a loosening rather than a remedial fix. Disconfirming check: searched legislation.govt.nz, the Ministry of Health 'recent changes' record, Beehive releases and 2026 news for any post-ban amending Act or regulation targeting low-cost/pod devices and found none; the responsible minister was reported as having paused regulatory work rather than legislating. So the substance of the prediction (the rules would be worked around) is borne out, but the specific remedial-change test written into the criterion is not.

statement: The Reserve Bank, in its August Monetary Policy Statement, is forecasting annual CPI inflation of 2.3 percent in the current quarter, thereafter declining to 2 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI release for the September 2024 quarter: true if annual CPI inflation prints at about 2.3%, false if materially above or below.
reasoning: Criterion names the Stats NZ CPI release for the September 2024 quarter. Stats NZ reported annual CPI inflation of 2.2 percent for the 12 months to the September 2024 quarter (CPI up 0.6 percent on the June 2024 quarter). The forecast Willis quoted from the RBNZ's August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement was 2.3 percent for the current quarter; the actual print was 0.1 percentage point lower, which is 'about 2.3%' and not materially above or below. Her characterisation of the MPS as forecasting a decline thereafter toward 2 percent is also consistent with that statement's published track.

statement: Businesses, as surveyed in the ANZ Business Outlook survey, expect inflation to be under 3 percent in a year’s time.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the September 2025 quarter: true if below 3.0%, false if 3.0% or above.
reasoning: Criterion: Stats NZ annual CPI inflation for the September 2025 quarter, true if below 3.0%, false if 3.0% or above. Stats NZ reported the CPI rose 3.0 percent in the 12 months to the September 2025 quarter (up from 2.7 percent to June 2025; +1.0 percent on the quarter), with electricity +11.3%, local authority rates +8.8% and rent +2.6% the largest contributors. 3.0% falls on the 'false' side of the line as the criterion was written, so the year-ahead expectation Willis cited did not hold — though only just: the outcome sat exactly on the threshold and at the top of the RBNZ's 1-3% target band, not materially above it. Disconfirming check: looked for a lower revised or alternative annual figure for that quarter and found none; the 3.0% print is the official release and was reported as such by RNZ and Westpac, and by the Minister herself as 'within target band'.

statement: What I’d say to the member is that we are on track to hit the first and second emissions budgets.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission final accounting for emissions budget 1: true if net emissions for 2022–2025 come in at or under the budget, false if they exceed it.
reasoning: The criterion names MfE/Climate Change Commission final accounting for emissions budget 1 (2022-2025). That does not exist yet: the Commission's 2026 monitoring report states its end-of-budget report in 2027 will give the full assessment using final emissions data, so the resolve-by date of 2027-12-31 has not been reached. Interim evidence leans Luxon's way on EB1: the 2026 report projects the 290 MtCO2e budget is 'likely to be met with a 7.7 MtCO2e buffer', and the 2025 report already said EB1 was likely to be achieved - but partly through GHG inventory method changes and higher-than-projected forest planting, i.e. 'the budget can now be met with less effort than it originally required' rather than through the reductions originally intended. The second half of his claim, outside this criterion, has moved against him: EB2 (2026-2030) is now rated at significant risk, with 12.4 MtCO2e of planned reductions at risk (electricity, agriculture, transport all elevated to significant risk, forestry no longer able to provide buffer).

statement: Another action of the Government is to introduce the sentencing reform package that will install real consequences for crime and, ultimately, will put more serious offenders, including gang members, in prison for longer to prevent them creating new victims.
criterion: Department of Corrections sentenced-prisoner statistics and average custodial sentence length for serious violent/gang-related offending, comparing the period after the Sentencing Amendment Act's commencement with 2024; true if the sentenced prison population and/or average sentence length for serious offenders rises, false if flat or falling.
reasoning: The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 came into force on 29 June 2025 (assent 29 March 2025). The criterion's true test is that the sentenced prison population and/or average sentence length for serious offenders rises after commencement versus 2024. On the Ministry of Justice's own projections series: Feb 2024 baseline 9,294 total prisoners with 4,132 on remand (~5,162 sentenced); Feb 2026 baseline 11,240 total with 4,677 on remand, i.e. 6,563 sentenced - a ~27% rise, and already above the 5,826 sentenced peak the pre-reform 2024 projections expected for Sept 2026. Post-commencement Corrections data agrees (6,350 sentenced of 10,732 onsite in Sept 2025). MoJ's June 2026 release attributes forward growth to the reforms directly: 'more people will receive prison sentences, and for longer terms' because of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act and the Crimes Amendment Bill, projecting sentenced numbers to 8,300 by 2036. Disconfirming evidence checked and worth flagging: gang-affiliated prisoners were 3,124 of 10,623 in Sept 2025 - the lowest absolute count since 2015, even though the share is a 12-year high - so the 'including gang members' limb is not borne out in counts; 2026 growth has been almost entirely remand (+319) rather than sentenced (+29); and no published average-custodial-sentence-length series for serious violent offending yet confirms the 'for longer' limb in outturn rather than projection. The criterion's population limb is nonetheless clearly met and not flat or falling, with data still accumulating to the 2027-06-30 resolve-by date.

statement: Just like the election, it’ll be a group of Aucklanders who depose Chris Hipkins for the second time: Phil Twyford from out west, Arena Williams from down south, Helen White from central Auckland, and Ingrid Leary from Waiheke Island.
criterion: Labour Party caucus leadership records and contemporary reporting; true if Hipkins ceases to be Labour leader by way of caucus pressure or a leadership challenge before the 2026 general election, false if he remains leader through to that election (or departs for unrelated reasons such as resignation after an election loss).
reasoning: Chris Hipkins has led the Labour Party continuously since 22 January 2023 and is still leader as of today (27 Sept 2026): he launched Labour's 2026 election campaign in South Auckland on 27 September 2026, with the general election set for 7 November 2026. No leadership challenge or caucus coup occurred during the 54th Parliament; reporting describes public signs of caucus infighting as largely absent from 2024 onward, and Kieran McAnulty - the name Luxon used as the supposed successor - repeatedly ruled himself out and took the 2026 campaign chair role instead. Poor polling (Labour at 25.9% in early Sept 2026) prompted commentary about whether Labour should roll him, but produced no challenge. The criterion's false condition is that he remains leader through to the 2026 election; strictly that closes on 7 Nov 2026, 41 days away, but the predicted event - deposal by a group of Auckland MPs - cannot occur in a window that begins after the leader has fronted the campaign launch, so I am calling it rather than deferring. Incidental to the criterion: Brown's list is also loose on its own terms, since Ingrid Leary is MP for Taieri in Dunedin, not Waiheke Island.

statement: Let me tell Te Pāti Māori that out there in the real world, where Māori work sometimes two or three jobs, they won’t be voting for you at the next election—be as certain as that—because out there they want the real things that people want in this country regardless of race: decent houses, a health system that delivers, education escalators, and First World jobs.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission results for the next general election; true if Te Pāti Māori's support among Māori voters falls materially — losing a majority of the seven Māori electorates it held going in, or a fall in its party vote; false if it retains or increases its Māori electorate seats and party vote.
reasoning: The criterion requires official Electoral Commission results for the next general election. That election is on 7 November 2026, six weeks after today's date (27 September 2026), so no results exist and the criterion cannot be applied. Pre-election polling is mixed rather than confirming: a Whakaata Maori poll released 17 September 2026 has Te Pati Maori LEADING the Maori-roll party vote on 29% to Labour's 27%, while another Maori-voter breakdown put them second on 18% and projected 4 electorate seats. Note also that the criterion's premise is slightly wrong: TPM won six of the seven Maori electorates in 2023 (Labour held Te Tai Tonga) and lost Tamaki Makaurau at the September 2025 by-election, so 'the seven it held going in' overstates its baseline.

statement: They are going to gut the plans to rebuild Nelson Hospital, which is disappointing the Nelson region considerably.
criterion: Health New Zealand / ministerial decisions on the Nelson Hospital redevelopment; true if the announced scope or budget is materially reduced or staged down from the plan as it stood in September 2024, false if the rebuild proceeds at or above the previously planned scope.
reasoning: A material scope reduction from the pre-2024 plan is documented: Labour's Cabinet-approved Option One ($1.098b, one large acute services building with 255 beds, eight theatres and a new ED, complete 2031) was replaced by a staged series of smaller builds anchored on a 128-bed inpatient building (41 net new beds), with no rebuild of ICU, ED or theatres and further phases' business cases deferred to 2033-34; Boyack and Verrall called this a 'downgrade' / 'half the money for half the hospital'. But the timing undercuts it as a prediction against the criterion's own baseline: Health Minister Reti announced the re-scope to smaller staged builds with the 128-bed figure in August 2024, a month BEFORE the 18 September 2024 statement, so the plan 'as it stood in September 2024' was already the reduced staged plan. Measured against that baseline the project then proceeded rather than being further gutted: Budget 2025 confirmed over half a billion dollars over four years for stage two, consent was granted, construction of the inpatient building began in early 2026 and completion is set for 2029, two years earlier than the original plan. So the substance (a materially smaller rebuild than previously planned) holds, but 'gut the plans' overstates the outcome relative to the September 2024 position.

statement: Then, in saying that, I don’t expect we’ll need anywhere near as much money to implement it, because we will be recognising a lot of the existing farm plans that are already out there that farmers are using to do a lot of great work on their farms.
criterion: Vote Environment appropriations for freshwater farm plan implementation once the revised system commences: true if the appropriation is materially below (say under half of) the pre-2024 implementation allocation; false if it is comparable to or above it.
reasoning: The criterion keys off Vote Environment appropriations 'once the revised system commences', and the revised freshwater farm plan system has not commenced. The enabling changes passed in the Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act on 20 August 2025; final policy decisions were only released on 19 August 2026 (risk-based certification, thresholds lifted from 20ha to 50ha, six-year re-certification, industry organisations able to certify); regulations are still being drafted, and Beef + Lamb NZ's August 2026 update states farmers get up to five years to complete a plan 'after the regulations are switched on next year' — i.e. commencement in 2027. Budget 2026 documents and the Beehive/MfE releases carry no freshwater farm plan implementation appropriation figure, and no published pre-2024 implementation allocation for the farm plan system surfaced either, so there is currently nothing on either side of the comparison. The earliest test would be the Budget 2027 Estimates, and even then a separately identifiable line may not exist (in which case the item would become uncheckable rather than resolved).

statement: Of course, the member asking the question is on the select committee working through the process of the Fast-track Approvals Bill at the moment, and nothing has come back yet. It’s due back in mid-October, and, so, I have no doubt that she will make fulsome input into the report that comes back from the select committee.
criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Fast-track Approvals Bill: true if the select committee reported the bill back to the House in mid-October 2024; false if the report-back fell materially outside that window (e.g. November or later).
reasoning: The Environment Committee reported the Fast-track Approvals Bill back to the House on 18 October 2024, which is within the mid-October window Simmonds named and well inside the criterion's fail line (November or later). The report-back deadline had been extended from 7 September to 18 October, and the bill's committee report is published as 'Fast-track Approvals Bill — As reported from the Environment Committee'. Her secondary implication (that the questioner would input into the report) is not part of the criterion as written.

statement: The number of people receiving a working-age benefit is forecast to peak in January 2025 at about 388,100, or 12 percent of the working-age population.
criterion: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets quarterly working-age benefit recipient counts through 2025: true if the January/March 2025 figure is near 388,100 and no later 2025 quarter exceeds it; false if recipient numbers continue rising past that level during 2025.
reasoning: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets show the main-benefit (working-age) count never peaked at ~388,100 / 12%. It was already 409,665 (12.7%) at the December 2024 quarter, before the forecast January 2025 peak; 398,163 (12.2%) at March 2025; 406,128 (12.5%) at June 2025; and 427,236 (13.2%) at December 2025 — a five-year high. It was still 413,691 (12.8%) at June 2026. Recipient numbers therefore continued rising well past the forecast peak level throughout 2025, which is the criterion's explicit false condition. I checked the opposite case (a later 2025 quarter falling back near 388,100) and no quarter does.

statement: The current forecast is that instead of 202,500 being on the jobseeker benefit in January 2025, it will peak at 214,000.
criterion: MSD monthly jobseeker support recipient statistics: true if the series peaks at approximately 214,000 (and then declines), false if the peak is materially higher or lower, or if numbers continue rising well past 214,000.
reasoning: The forecast level was roughly right but the peak claim failed. MSD Jobseeker Support counts: 213,321 (Dec 2024), 209,838 (Mar 2025), 216,009 (Jun 2025), 223,512 (Dec 2025 — the five-year high), 218,481 (Jun 2026). The series did not peak at ~214,000 in January 2025 and then decline; it dipped in March 2025 and then rose for roughly another year, overshooting 214,000 by about 9,500 (4.4%). MSD's own HYEFU 2025 forecast later put the peak at ~221,900 in January 2026, a year after Upston's date. Against the criterion as written, the overshoot is modest rather than 'materially higher', but numbers plainly continued rising past 214,000 through 2025 — so the magnitude holds approximately while the timing and the 'peak then decline' substance do not.

statement: Budget 2024 will lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
criterion: Treasury's Budget 2024 child poverty impact modelling and subsequent Stats NZ child poverty statistics: true if official estimates/outturn show a reduction of approximately 17,000 children in poverty attributable to Budget 2024 measures; false if the modelled or observed reduction is materially smaller or absent.
reasoning: The 17,000 figure is the government's intermediate target (17,000 fewer children in material hardship by 2026/27 vs 2023), not a Treasury estimate of Budget 2024's own impact. Treasury's Budget 2024 Child Poverty Report modelled a positive effect on AHC50 but no statistically significant effect on BHC50, and Treasury's model cannot forecast material hardship at all, so no official modelling attributes ~17,000 children to Budget 2024 measures. Outturn goes the other way: material hardship rose from 12.5% (144,100 children) in YE June 2023 to 13.4% (156,600) in 2024 to 14.3% (169,300) in 2025 — about 25,000 more children, with Stats NZ finding no statistically significant annual change 2024→2025. BHC50 moved only 12.7% to 12.6% (~500 children). Budget 2026's child poverty report states NZ is not on track for its 2028 targets. The final target-year data (YE June 2027) is not published until 2028, but as of the criterion's resolve-by date of 2026-06-30 the modelled and observed reduction attributable to Budget 2024 is absent, which the criterion defines as false.

statement: It outlines a 91 percent increase in funding for road maintenance on our State highways, a 50 percent increase in road maintenance on our local roads, a 40 percent increase in public transport services funding, a significant investment in completing the rail network rebuild of $159 million to complete the rail network rebuild, and Auckland’s ready for the City Rail Link, which will open in 2026, and, as the member for Upper Harbour, Cameron Brewer, says, the Northwest Rapid Transit, continuing progress on that critically important rapid transit program for West Auckland.
criterion: Public opening of the City Rail Link to passengers; true if services commence in calendar 2026, false if the opening slips to 2027 or later.
reasoning: The criterion covers only the City Rail Link opening. CRL opened to passengers on Sunday 13 September 2026 (formal ribbon-cutting 11 September with PM Luxon and Mayor Brown; first weekday timetable 14 September; ~70,000 boardings on opening day). Services commenced within calendar 2026, so the criterion is met. The quote's other claims (91%/50%/40% funding increases, $159m rail rebuild) fall outside the criterion as written and were not assessed.

statement: It will open in 2026.
criterion: CRL Ltd / Auckland Transport service records; true if passenger services through the City Rail Link commence at any point in calendar year 2026, false if the opening slips to 2027 or later.
reasoning: Passenger services through the City Rail Link commenced on 13 September 2026, within calendar year 2026. Auckland Transport's own media releases confirm the opening date and the start of passenger services, and independent reporting confirms first-day operation with roughly 70,000 boardings. No evidence of a slip to 2027.

statement: Well, I’ve already talked about alternatives and I’m happy to talk about the alternatives again because the last National Government started construction of the City Rail Link and it will open in 2026.
criterion: City Rail Link opening date as reported by City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport: true if passenger services through the CRL commence during calendar year 2026, false if the opening slips to 2027 or later.
reasoning: Auckland Transport confirms City Rail Link passenger services commenced Sunday 13 September 2026, with the first weekday timetable from Monday 14 September 2026; Railway Gazette independently reports the opening to passengers in September 2026. The criterion asked for passenger services commencing during calendar 2026, which happened with no slip to 2027. (The criterion did not ask about the separate 'last National Government started construction' clause, so it is not judged here.)

statement: As a result of making that decision, they will save $2.5 million of Kordia fees.
criterion: Whakaata Māori annual report / Te Māngai Pāho funding documents following the move off terrestrial transmission; true if the reported reduction in transmission (Kordia) costs is approximately $2.5 million per year, false if the realised saving is materially smaller or the fees continue.
reasoning: The predicate event occurred: Whakaata Māori moved the standalone Te Reo channel off terrestrial broadcast to online-only (MĀORI+) on 28 March 2025 as part of the Wai Whakaata realignment completed December 2024. But the criterion requires the realised reduction in Kordia transmission fees as reported in the annual report or Te Māngai Pāho funding documents, and no such figure is published. Whakaata Māori's website carries no FY2025 annual report; the FY2024 annual report PDF is a scanned image with no extractable transmission/Kordia line item; and the State Media Monitor profile of the broadcaster states explicitly that although it records the terrestrial-to-online transition and the wider funding drop (from ~$49m in 2024/25 toward ~$38m in 2026/27), it 'does not isolate savings attributable to discontinuing terrestrial transmission'. Searches aimed at both directions — for confirmation of a ~$2.5m saving and for evidence that Kordia fees continued or the saving came in materially smaller — returned nothing on either side. The $2.5m may well be accurate; it is simply not verifiable against the sources the criterion names, and absence of evidence is not evidence of falsity.

statement: That particular initiative, I expect, will activate a number of schools that are kaupapa Māori - focused, and potentially many schools, as he did many years ago with Raewyn Tipene and others in the North.
criterion: The Charter School Agency / Ministry of Education published list of approved and opened charter schools; true if two or more kaupapa Māori-focused charter schools are approved or operating, false if none are.
reasoning: The criterion's bar is two or more kaupapa Māori-focused charter schools approved or operating. As of February 2026, seven of the 20 charter schools approved nationwide are Māori-focused — more than a third — with more expected. Individually verifiable instances include Te Kāpehu Whetū–Tāmaki (gazetted as a charter school 10 August 2025, opened Term 1 2026, taught in te reo Māori and English) and Te Rito, Te Kura Taiao (NZ Gazette 2025-go4625), plus Te Kura o Ngāti Whātua ki Tāmaki and Te Aratika High School. Notably, Te Kāpehu Whetū is the He Puna Marama Trust school in Whangārei led by Raewyn Tipene — the specific northern precedent Potaka named — so the prediction was borne out by its own cited example. I checked for the disconfirming case (no approvals, or Māori sponsors declining to apply): coverage instead reports Māori communities continuing to back the model despite political controversy.

statement: Many of us suspected that, and here’s the point, really: the economy will be turned around.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts and Household Labour Force Survey: true if New Zealand records positive annual real GDP growth and an unemployment rate below its post-statement peak by the end of 2026; false if annual real GDP growth is still negative or unemployment is still at or above its peak.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2026-12-31, which has not passed (today 2026-09-27), and the criterion's two legs currently split.
