Leg 1 (positive annual real GDP growth) is MET: GDP was +1.3% y/y in the Dec 2025 quarter — the first annual growth in over two years — and +1.7% for the year ended June 2026 (quarterly: Dec 2024 +0.7%, Mar 2025 +0.8%, Jun 2025 -1.0%, Sep 2025 +1.1%, Dec 2025 +0.2%, Mar 2026 +0.8%, Jun 2026 +0.2%). Leg 2 (unemployment below its post-statement peak) is NOT met on the latest data: unemployment was 4.8% in the Sept 2024 quarter when Peters spoke and has risen since to 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter — an 11-year high, worst since Sept 2015 — so the post-statement peak IS the most recent print, not a level already passed. Checked the disconfirming side: no later labour data exists yet; the Sept 2026 quarter release is 4 Nov 2026 and the Dec 2026 quarter release falls in Feb 2027, after the resolve date. So only one more observation can land in time, and it could still take unemployment below 5.6%. On present trend the criterion leans toward its 'false' condition, but the deadline has not arrived.

statement: There will be a lag between interest rates reducing and growth picking up, but that will happen and the economy will start to grow again.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series; true if at least one quarter after September 2024 records positive quarterly GDP growth, false if the economy records only flat or negative quarters through the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion required at least one quarter after September 2024 with positive quarterly GDP growth, by 2025-12-31. Stats NZ recorded GDP +0.7% in the December 2024 quarter (published 20 March 2025, following the -1.1% September 2024 quarter), +0.8% in the March 2025 quarter, and +1.1% in the September 2025 quarter. The criterion's false condition — only flat or negative quarters through the resolve-by date — is plainly not what happened. Disconfirming check: the recovery was not monotonic (the June 2025 quarter fell 1.0%), so 'the economy will start to grow again' was bumpier than the phrasing implies, but the criterion as written asks for one positive quarter and several occurred well inside the window.

statement: The Gangs Bill and the Sentencing Amendment Bill are expected to pass today.
criterion: Hansard and the parliamentary bills record for 19 September 2024; true if both the Gangs Bill and the Sentencing Amendment Bill passed their third readings that day, false if either did not.
reasoning: Both bills passed their third readings on 19 September 2024, each 68-55 on party lines (National/ACT/NZ First for; Labour/Greens/Te Pati Maori against), and both received royal assent on 23 September 2024. They were the two halves of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill, split on 8 August 2024 — the Gangs Bill (gang insignia ban, dispersal and non-consorting orders) and the Sentencing Amendment Bill (gang membership as an aggravating factor, replacing s 9(1)(hb) of the Sentencing Act 2002) — which is why they moved through the House together. Disconfirming check: a 1News report of the day foregrounded only the gang-patch law, and a separate Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill was before the House around the same period and did NOT pass on 19 September; but the Sentencing Amendment Bill paired with the Gangs Bill did, and the Sentencing Amendment Act 2024 commenced alongside the Gangs Act 2024 on 21 November 2024.

statement: I expect this will lead to tougher sentences for gang members and send a strong message that the unlawful activities of gangs will not be tolerated.
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics comparing average custodial sentence length for offenders identified as gang members before and after the Sentencing Amendment Act 2024 commenced; true if average sentences for gang-affiliated offenders rise after commencement, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion names Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics comparing average custodial sentence length for gang-affiliated offenders before and after 21 November 2024. That breakdown is not published: Stats NZ's criminal conviction and sentencing statistics (2025 calendar year, June 2025 fiscal year) and MoJ's data tables carry no gang-affiliation variable, and I found no MoJ monitoring report or evaluation of the amended s 9(1)(hb). Goldsmith himself told RNZ before commencement that it would be 'impossible to know' the laws' effect, and the government's own one-year release (21 Nov 2025) reported insignia charges, patch and firearm seizures and convictions but said nothing about sentence lengths. Indirect evidence is consistent with the prediction but does not test it: the prison population hit successive record highs (10,860 at 30 September 2025, ~9 months ahead of forecast; 11,240 by February 2026) and roughly 35% of prisoners (3,124 of 10,623 in September 2025) are gang-affiliated, with Justice Sector Projections attributing growth to tougher sentencing generally rather than the gang factor specifically. Disconfirming check: I looked for reporting or case law showing measured gang uplifts, and for any published series that would let the comparison be made in either direction, and found neither. The failure here is structural (the data is not collected in that form) rather than merely temporal, though the resolve-by date of 2026-11-30 has also not yet passed.

statement: It will not increase public safety, but it will result in people being put into prison, and for longer, and to increase the length of those sentences due to their affiliations with gangs.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison population and sentence-length data, plus sentencing statistics on the gang-affiliation aggravating factor, for the two years after the Act's commencement, read alongside the NZ Crime and Victims Survey / Police victimisation statistics: true if imprisonment numbers and gang-related sentence lengths rise with no measurable improvement in victimisation or public safety measures; false if sentences and prison numbers do not rise, or if public safety measures improve over the period.
reasoning: The prediction has two limbs and the evidence splits them. Imprisonment limb: confirmed. The prison population reached an all-time high of 10,860 on 30 September 2025 — a level not projected until early 2030 — rose to about 11,240 by February 2026, and the June 2026 Justice Sector Projections forecast 35% growth to 15,200 by 2036, expressly attributing it to tougher sentencing law and new offences; roughly 35% of prisoners are gang-affiliated. Public-safety limb: contradicted by the very measures the criterion names. NZCVS Cycle 8, fielded October 2024 to October 2025 and published March 2026, found 28% of adults victimised, the lowest since the survey began in 2018, with interpersonal violence falling significantly below 2018 levels for the first time (5% vs 7%) and burglary at 9% of households vs 12%; MoJ's quarterly violent-crime releases through May 2026 show the government's violent-crime target still being beaten with about 38,000 fewer victims than the October 2023 baseline. Read literally, the criterion's falsifier ('false if ... public safety measures improve over the period') is therefore met. Disconfirming check on the other side: the improvement cannot be credited to this Act — Goldsmith conceded attribution was not something the Ministry measures, and criminologists (e.g. Trevor Bradley) caution against reading the survey as policy evaluation — so her scepticism about causation is not refuted, only her claim that the measures would not move. The gang-specific sentence-length limb is unmeasurable: no published series breaks sentence length out by gang affiliation. Hence partly correct rather than correct or wrong.

statement: This gangs legislation amendment will not make New Zealand safer, as far as we’re concerned.
criterion: Police recorded gang-related offending and NZ Crime and Victims Survey victimisation data for the two years after the Gangs Act's commencement (21 November 2024); true if gang-related offending and victimisation show no reduction over that period, false if official statistics and evaluation show a material reduction attributed to the legislation.
reasoning: Neither branch of the criterion is cleanly satisfied. Against the 'true' branch (no reduction in gang-related offending and victimisation): victimisation clearly did fall. NZCVS Cycle 8, covering October 2024 to October 2025, recorded the lowest victimisation rate since 2018 (28%), with violent offences at 3% and interpersonal violence at 5% vs 7% in 2018; the government's one-year gang-laws release (21 November 2025) reported 147,000 victims of serious violent crime in the 12 months to August 2025, about 38,000 fewer than the October 2023 baseline and a 23% fall in victims of violent offending between October 2024 and August 2025, and MoJ's May 2026 quarterly release shows the target still being exceeded. Against the 'false' branch (a material reduction attributed to the legislation): no such attribution exists in official statistics or any evaluation. There is no published evaluation of the Gangs Act; Goldsmith, asked how the drop was attributed to these policies, said only that the justice sector is 'a very complex organism' and that the overall policy mix was heading the right way; Victoria University criminologist Trevor Bradley advises treating such claims cautiously. Disconfirming evidence for Jackson's side is also present: gang membership grew rather than shrank — the National Gang List reached about 10,478 in February 2026, roughly 6.5% up year on year, after 9,270-plus in July 2025 — and the High Court found the insignia ban inconsistent with the Bill of Rights in July 2026. Enforcement output (182 patches, 643 insignia items and 178 firearms seized; 856 insignia-display charges, 188 convictions) measures activity, not safety. The two-year window closes 21 November 2026 and NZCVS Cycle 9 is not out, so the picture is incomplete, but the direction of the victimisation data already contradicts the unqualified 'will not make New Zealand safer' while leaving the causal claim unresolved.

statement: Look, I know that this legislation is going to pass, but all of the amendments were written in the great faith that this would actually improve the situation for this particular bill.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register and Hansard third reading division for the Education and Training Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading and received Royal assent, false if it was defeated, withdrawn or still not passed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The Education and Training Amendment Bill (charter schools, Govt Bill 66) had its second reading 12 Sep 2024 (68-49) and third reading 25 Sep 2024, receiving Royal assent in late September 2024 (Wikipedia's list of 54th Parliament acts gives 25 Sep; WhereTheyStand gives 30 Sep). It became the Education and Training Amendment Act 2024, with the charter school provisions in force from 1 October 2024. Tinetti spoke on 19 Sep 2024, during the committee of the whole House stage between second and third reading, which matches her reference to amendments. The bill passed and was assented well before the 2024-12-31 resolve-by date; it was not defeated or withdrawn.

statement: Kiwi dairy farmers, meat producers, and manufacturers will be able to sell more products at competitive prices to the people of the UAE, who will, in turn, benefit from greater choice and competition.
criterion: Stats NZ merchandise trade statistics for exports to the United Arab Emirates by commodity; true if dairy, meat and manufactured export values to the UAE rise in the first full year after the agreement enters into force compared with the year before, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The NZ-UAE CEPA entered into force 28 August 2025, so the first full year (to ~August 2026) is complete and the criterion is resolvable early. On the Stats NZ-derived figures cited by the Trade Minister on 28 Aug 2026, NZ goods exports to the UAE rose 7% to $1.4b in the first CEPA year, with dairy up 15% (+$128m, to $1b), sheep meat up 61% and wood products up 70% - so the dairy and meat legs of the criterion hold. The manufactured/industrial leg does not check out: no published figure exists for it, and the arithmetic points the other way - total export growth (~$92m on a $1.4b total up 7%) is smaller than the dairy gain alone, so once sheep meat and wood are added, the remaining categories - which include the ~$242m industrial-products basket - must have fallen. Substance holds for two of the three named commodity groups; the third is unconfirmed and probably negative, and I could not reach commodity-level Stats NZ UAE tables directly (Infoshare/CSV datasets are not web-searchable), so this rests on the ministerial release of those figures.

statement: Our Government inherited a situation where the last Government had charged up the credit card to the max, unsustainably, and we are now in the position of course correcting, and we had set a very clear plan that it will allow the books to return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2027/28.
criterion: The Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2028 (and Treasury forecasts leading to it): true if OBEGAL is reported in surplus for 2027/28, false if OBEGAL is in deficit for that year.
reasoning: The criterion names the Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30 June 2028, which do not exist yet - the 2027/28 fiscal year has not begun as of today (27 Sep 2026), and the resolve-by date is 2028-10-31. Forecast evidence for whoever revisits this: Budget 2026 (28 May 2026) has OBEGALx still in deficit in 2027/28 (deficit more than halved from 2.4% of GDP in 2026/27) and returning to surplus of $2.6b / 0.5% of GDP only in 2028/29 - a year later than Willis's 2027/28 claim, though a year earlier than HYEFU 2025 had it. On current forecasts the claim looks likely to resolve wrong, but the evidence the criterion demands is not yet available.

statement: We are strong together and I look forward to joining in what will be the biggest protest march in our city for a long, long time on Saturday, because on Saturday we march for our city, we march for our region, and we march for the Dunedin Hospital.
criterion: Contemporaneous media and police/organiser attendance estimates (Otago Daily Times, RNZ) for the 28 September 2024 Dunedin Hospital march: true if reported attendance exceeds that of any Dunedin protest march in the preceding decade or more; false if attendance is comparable to or smaller than recent Dunedin marches.
reasoning: The 28 September 2024 march drew a Dunedin City Council estimate of up to 35,000, reported by ODT, RNZ, NZ Herald and Crux. RNZ's headline and Mayor Jules Radich call it the biggest protest in Dunedin in decades; other coverage calls it the city's biggest march in more than a decade. Disconfirming check: the largest Dunedin protest march in the preceding decade was the 2019 climate strike at ~9,000 (organiser estimate), about a quarter the size; one contemporaneous quote calls it the biggest Octagon crowd of any kind since 1992. The criterion's bar (reported attendance exceeding any Dunedin protest march in the preceding decade or more) is met.

statement: Inflation is falling—forecast to fall further later this week.
criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index for the September 2024 quarter, released 16 October 2024: true if the annual inflation rate printed below the previous quarter's 3.3%, false if it was equal to or higher than that.
reasoning: Stats NZ released the September 2024 quarter CPI on 16 October 2024, the day after the statement: annual inflation 2.2%, following 3.3% in the June 2024 quarter, and inside the RBNZ 1-3% band for the first time since March 2021. The annual rate printed below the previous quarter's 3.3%, exactly as the criterion required.

statement: I would just point out to both the leaders of Labour and the Green Party that we have a fantastic new piece of legislation called fast track that will enable us to generate 30 percent of the current electricity generation in renewables, so I’d encourage you all to support it.
criterion: MBIE electricity generation statistics and the register of projects consented under the Fast-track Approvals Act; true if renewable projects approved under that regime add generation equal to about 30 percent of 2024 national generation, false if the built/consented total falls well short.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 2030-12-31 and today is 2026-09-27, so the claim cannot be graded yet. Progress as at mid-2026: the government's own releases put renewable projects approved under the Fast-track Approvals Act at more than 990 MW, described as more than five per cent of current national generation capacity, with 59 projects still progressing through the process. Well short of 30% so far, but the bulk of the claim rests on a pipeline that is still open within the criterion's window, so no verdict either way.

statement: The Reserve Bank has also signalled further reductions to come. Markets are anticipating another 50-basis-point reduction before the end of the year, then more gradual reductions in 2025.
criterion: RBNZ OCR decisions from the November 2024 Monetary Policy Statement onward; true if the final 2024 decision cut the OCR by 50bp and 2025 decisions were smaller increments, false if the November move was a different size or there was no further 2024 cut.
reasoning: First conjunct of the criterion holds exactly: the final 2024 decision, the 27 November 2024 MPS, cut the OCR by 50bp to 4.25%. The second conjunct fails in part. The next decision, 19 February 2025, was another 50bp cut to 3.75% — equal, not smaller — and 8 October 2025 was a third 50bp cut, to 2.50%, larger than most economists expected. The remaining 2025 moves were 25bp (April to 3.50%, May to 3.25%, August to 3.00%, November to 2.25%) with a July hold. So 'another 50-basis-point reduction before the end of the year' was right, but 'then more gradual reductions in 2025' is materially overstated: two of the seven 2025 decisions were the same 50bp size. Neither of the criterion's explicit false conditions (a different November size, or no further 2024 cut) occurred, so this is partly_correct rather than wrong.

statement: And as a result, we’ve made some minor changes, but 95 percent of the legislation, as introduced, will be put to Parliament and be approved with minor changes.
criterion: The Act as enacted compared with the bill as introduced: true if it passes with only minor changes (roughly 95% of the introduced text intact), false if it fails, is substantially rewritten, or does not reach a final vote.
reasoning: The legislation is the Hauraki Gulf / Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Bill (Potaka was Minister of Conservation; the same scored window contains questions about high protection areas). It reached a final vote and passed its third reading on 8 October 2025, becoming the Hauraki Gulf / Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Act 2025 (No 54), in force 25 October 2025 — every party voted for passage. The introduced text survived substantially intact: after nearly ten months the Environment Committee recommended passage with the protected-area boundaries unchanged and no substantive changes, only technical amendments (deleting cl 8(2)(b), inserting cl 21(aaa) and cl 30A on Takutai Moana rights and permit tests). The enacted Act carries the same 12 high protection areas, 5 seafloor protection areas and 2 marine reserve extensions as introduced. The one contested change was the late ring-net amendment Potaka had announced on 13 October 2024, two days before he spoke: limited commercial ring-net fishing for four species, vessels under 6 m, March-August, in 2 of the 12 HPAs — about 3% of the 800 km2 of HPA, reviewable after three years. Disconfirming check: critics (WWF 'hollow victory ... loophole', Forest and Bird 'dangerous precedent', Greenpeace, Democracy Action) argue that carve-out is substantive, not minor, because it grants exclusive commercial access inside areas meant to be fully protected. But the criterion's false conditions — fails, is substantially rewritten, or does not reach a final vote — none occurred, and roughly 95% of the introduced text did pass intact.

statement: I am confident that the evidence is clear: this will not result in an increase in harm from gambling.
criterion: Ministry of Health gambling-harm service data and any DIA post-implementation review of class 3 online lotteries covering the three years after the Act commences: true if help-seeking and harm indicators associated with class 3 / online lottery gambling show no increase, false if they rise measurably and the rise is linked to online class 3 lottery sales.
reasoning: The measure is the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Bill, which made permanent the temporary exclusion of class 3 lotteries from the remote-interactive-gambling prohibition; the permanent exemption took effect 1 November 2024. The criterion requires Ministry of Health gambling-harm service data and any DIA post-implementation review covering the three years after commencement — i.e. to about November 2027 — and the item's own resolve_by is 2027-10-31, which is after today's date of 2026-09-27. The evidence needed does not yet exist: MoH's published gambling-harm intervention services data still ends at 2023, with no 2025-26 client numbers released, and no DIA post-implementation review of class 3 online lotteries was found. The Ministry's Strategy to Prevent and Minimise Gambling Harm 2025/26-2027/28 in fact identifies class 3 (instant lotteries, housie) as a gap where the evidence base still needs building and where mobile-technology risks are unassessed, which is the opposite of a settled finding in either direction. Not findable yet is not evidence against the claim.

statement: I think it’s important today to acknowledge that around the House, while there might be some differing views at the edges, this bill looks set to be passed without amendment across the House.
criterion: The House's bill record and division records for the remaining stages of the Gambling Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes with no amendments made after the select committee stage and no party votes against, false if amendments are made at committee of the whole House or any party opposes at a later reading.
reasoning: Both limbs of the prediction hold. (1) No amendment: the latest published version of the bill on legislation.govt.nz remains 74-1, the version as introduced — no 74-2 (select committee amendments) or 74-3 (committee of the whole House amendments) print was ever produced, so the Act as enacted is the bill as introduced. (2) Passed across the House: 3rd reading 23 Oct 2024, Royal assent 24 Oct 2024, in force 1 Nov 2024. WhereTheyStand's bill record shows all three readings passed with no vote breakdown recorded for any of them, i.e. no party vote/division was called, and I found no party, press release or news report of any party opposing at a later reading. Recorded opposition came only from submitters (the Salvation Army), not from a party — consistent with Brewer's 'differing views at the edges'. Limitation: parliament.nz blocks automated fetching (404/Radware on every Hansard, daily-progress and bills-API path tried; web.archive.org unavailable to this tool), so the raw 23 October Hansard division record could not be read directly; the 'no party votes against' finding rests on the absence of any recorded division in the aggregator plus the absence of contrary evidence.

statement: On that, I’m pleased that the House is supporting this unanimously, because it will give that certainty to the likes of our charities who use this as a form of revenue gathering for their very, very important work.
criterion: The Hansard vote/division record for the remaining readings of the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Bill: true if it passed with all parties recorded in favour, false if any party voted against or abstained in opposition.
reasoning: The bill completed its remaining stages without any party recorded against. Second reading 15 Oct 2024 (the day of the statement), third reading 23 Oct 2024, Royal assent 24 Oct 2024. WhereTheyStand, which records party vote breakdowns for reading votes when a party vote is taken, shows all three readings passed with no vote breakdown recorded — meaning the motions were agreed without a division being called. No party statement, media report or select committee minority view opposing the bill could be found; the only recorded opposition was from a submitter (the Salvation Army), which the criterion does not cover. The certainty the bill gave charities also materialised: the class 3 online-lottery allowance became permanent from 1 November 2024, per DIA. Limitation: parliament.nz is inaccessible to automated fetching, so the Hansard division record itself could not be read; the verdict rests on the aggregated bill record and the absence of any disconfirming evidence of a party voting against or abstaining in opposition.

statement: Aside from the concerns that have been raised about the short time allowed for submissions, another tūpatotanga I want to put here today that I think we need to be prepared for is an influx of applications we’re going to have from charities who want to become eligible to raise funds in this manner.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs class 3 gambling licensing statistics for the period after the bill's commencement; true if the number of society/charity applications or licences for online lottery sales rises materially above the pre-commencement baseline, false if application volumes are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion names Department of Internal Affairs class 3 gambling licensing statistics as the source, and DIA does not publish that series. Its gambling statistics portal covers only class 4 gaming machines (GMP dashboard, venue and machine numbers, class 4 grants) and expenditure figures for class 4, TAB racing, NZ Lotteries and casinos — there is no class 3 licence or application count, by year or otherwise. The DIA class 3 pages (forms, rule-change guidance) carry no volume data, the 2024/25 annual report section on regulatory functions gives no class 3 licensing figures, and no dataset appears on data.govt.nz. I also searched for indirect evidence of a surge in charity applications since the 1 November 2024 commencement (news, sector coverage, OIA releases) and found none in either direction. Absence of the statistic is not evidence the influx did not happen, so this is uncheckable rather than wrong. Context worth noting: online class 3 lottery sales were already permitted under the temporary COVID-era exemption from 2020 until 31 October 2024, so the Act made an existing allowance permanent rather than opening a new one.

statement: For this side of the House, this is the news that you need to hear today: there is going to be less gang members in alleyways, because they’re going to be locked up, because police have got the tools to deal with that.
criterion: NZ Police and Corrections data on gang-affiliated people charged and held in custody in the 12 months following commencement of the Gangs Act (21 November 2024), compared with the preceding 12 months: true if the number of gang members in custody rises materially; false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The enforcement half happened: between 21 Nov 2024 and 19 Feb 2025 Police filed 3,374 charges against gang members (337 for insignia breaches), seized 76 patches and 67 firearms, and by March 2025 had laid 403 insignia charges and >4,000 charges against gang members overall; patches largely left public view, with Police reporting 'high levels of compliance' and no dispersal notices or non-consorting orders in that first period. The custody half is not demonstrated on the criterion's terms. No Police/Corrections pre-vs-post 12-month comparison of gang-affiliated people in custody has been published, and the one in-window Corrections count available (Sept 2025) is 3,124 patched members and associates of 10,623 prisoners — not materially above pre-Act levels (about 3,346 in 2023; 3,099 in 2017; 2,736 in Feb 2022). Insignia breaches carry up to 6 months/$5,000 and in practice drew fines and patch forfeiture rather than imprisonment, and courts have since ordered patches returned (Sept 2025) before the High Court reversed that (June 2026), with some convictions found to breach protected rights (July 2026). Disconfirming check on the opposite reading: gang numbers kept growing — the National Gang List rose 13% since Nov 2023 to 10,478 by Feb 2026, outnumbering police — and while the total prison muster hit records (11,255 in March 2026) with Corrections saying the gang-affiliated proportion is rising, that is not a measured rise in gang members held in custody in the specified window. So: fewer patches in public, but not the demonstrated lock-up effect the claim rested on.

statement: This Government has made decisions and funding cuts that will make that 20 percent reporting rate even lower in New Zealand.
criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey reporting rate for family violence offences in the cycles after 2024; true if the reported proportion falls below the rate prevailing at the time of the statement outside sampling error, false if it holds steady or rises.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 31 Dec 2027 and the criterion asks for the NZCVS family-violence reporting rate across cycles after 2024. Cycle 7 (2024) and Cycle 8 (fieldwork Oct 2024–Oct 2025, published 2026) are out, but MoJ's published summaries report prevalence and incident volumes rather than a family-offence reporting-rate series: adults experiencing family offences fell from 2.2% (2018) to 1.4% (2025) while family offence incidents rose from 207,000 to 256,000, and fewer than half of family violence victims seek any help (31% considered help unnecessary). The reporting-to-police breakdown sits only in the downloadable Cycle 7/8 'Sexual violence and family offences' data tables, and no published MoJ statement identifies a fall in the family-violence reporting rate outside sampling error relative to the ~20% prevailing when the statement was made; the overall all-crime reporting rate is reported around 26–28%. With later cycles still to come and no significant fall yet recorded, this is not yet resolvable either way.

statement: That is a different thing, and it’s very likely, I believe, that this provision would lead to considerable dispute and argument and litigation if it were passed as written.
criterion: Employment Relations Authority or Employment Court determinations, or reported union disputes, concerning the transfer of school support staff to charter school sponsors under the new section 119 'no less favourable overall' test: true if one or more such disputes or proceedings are recorded by the resolve-by date; false if no such dispute or proceeding is recorded.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 31 Dec 2027 and the triggering event has not yet occurred: as of 15 April 2026 no state or state-integrated school had completed a conversion to charter status (18 expressions of interest, 3 in contract negotiation, against a budgeted 35 for 2025–26; all 11 approved charter schools were new builds), so no support staff have been transferred to a sponsor under the section 119 'no less favourable overall' test and no ERA or Employment Court determination on it exists. Searching for the opposite (disputes already recorded) turns up argument but not proceedings: reporting identifies employment agreements as 'the real bottleneck' stalling conversions — translating decades of collectively bargained rights into bespoke arrangements while keeping staff no worse off — PPTA advice to principals lists entitlements it says cannot be carried across (centrally allocated sick leave balances, study awards, Kapa Haka/Polyfest relief) and notes staff move from collective agreements onto individual agreements, and the Support Staff in Schools' Collective Agreement 2026–2028 ratified in March 2026 added a clause recognising service for employees transferred under clause 119 of Schedule 1 who return to coverage. That is consistent with Twyford's direction but does not yet meet the criterion's threshold of a recorded determination or union dispute over an actual transfer, and 15 months remain.

statement: I was there, just last week, with our Minister for so many things the Hon Simeon Brown, and we were showing him their intentions there to build a floating wharf that will reduce their response time, in many instances, from the currently 45 minutes, while they get it off the boat trailer, to fewer than five minutes.
criterion: Coastguard New Zealand / Coastguard Manukau operational reporting once the Onehunga floating wharf is commissioned: true if reported typical response times after commissioning are under five minutes, false if the wharf is not built or response times remain materially above five minutes.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2028-12-31 and the wharf is not yet commissioned, so the criterion cannot be applied. Coastguard's Onehunga presence remains a temporary Eke Panuku lease after the Titirangi/French Bay base was destroyed in the 2023 Anniversary floods; $3.1m over four years was allocated in Oct 2024 toward the replacement base. Auckland Council's Onehunga Wharf project page, updated after NZTA's 9 July 2026 East West Link pause, mentions no pontoon, floating wharf or launching facility and gives no opening timeline, and no Coastguard operational reporting of post-commissioning response times exists. Absence of a built wharf in 2026 is not falsification of a 2028 horizon.

statement: We are going to see more degraded waterways, we’re going to see more contaminated drinking water, we’re going to see a more polluted marine coastal environment, we’re going to see more misery and suffering for animals, and we’re also going to see more destruction of biodiversity.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Stats NZ 'Our freshwater' and 'Our marine environment' environmental reporting, Taumata Arowai annual drinking water regulation reports, and MPI animal welfare compliance reporting through to end-2028; true if the national indicators for river water quality, drinking-water compliance and coastal water quality worsen relative to their 2024 baselines, false if they hold steady or improve.
reasoning: The criterion asks for national indicators to move against their 2024 baselines in reporting through end-2028, and that reporting does not yet exist. Our Freshwater 2026 (published 9 April 2026) analyses 2005-2024, so its data window ends at the baseline rather than after it: its findings (54% of river length with moderate/severe organic pollution or nutrient enrichment, 44% of river length unsuitable for swimming, 53% of lake sites worsening for nitrogen, nitrate rising at 39% of groundwater sites, E. coli above the drinking-water limit at 45% of groundwater sites) describe the state Abel was predicting from, not change since. Our Marine Environment 2025 (Oct 2025) is largely pressure and climate-risk framing, not a post-2024 coastal water-quality comparison. The one leg with genuine post-2024 data runs the other way: Water Services Authority reporting to end-2025 has large council supplies meeting or nearly meeting requirements rising 49% to 77% between 2023 and 2025, protozoal barriers 76% to 90%, school long-term advisories falling 17 to 7 and school E. coli detections down 16%, which disconfirms the drinking-water clause as it stands. Mixed and mostly unmeasurable; checkable again after the 2028 reporting round.

statement: I think the biggest threat for the sheep milking is that soon wool will be so valuable that they probably won’t want to be bothered milking them, but for those who do want to persist with the sunset industry that would be sheep milking, ahead of the pending wool boom, there are some opportunities for them.
criterion: New Zealand strong wool auction indicator prices (PGG Wrightson / NZ Wool Services auction data) compared with the October 2024 level; true if average strong wool prices rise substantially (say 50% or more) above the October 2024 level at some point before the resolve-by date, false if prices remain flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion's 50% threshold was cleared well before the 2026-10-15 resolve-by. Strong wool sat around $3.00-3.67/kg clean in Oct-Nov 2024. By the 29 May 2026 sale, good-style crossbred fleece passed $7.00/kg clean, a level not reached since about 2011, with the Fusca coarse fleece indicator at $7.52/kgCL against $3.08/kgCL a year earlier, more than double; North Island wool hit a 30-year high at Napier in July 2026 and the national indicator, though eased to $6.03 at the 24 Sep 2026 sale, remains roughly 65-100% above the October 2024 level. Drivers were a contracting national flock and tight supply against strong natural-fibre demand. Checked for the disconfirming case (prices flat or falling) and found the opposite. Note the criterion tests only the wool-price leg, not his separate aside about sheep milking being a sunset industry.

statement: As has been said before, this bill will encourage innovation, increase competition, and increase value returned to farmers.
criterion: MPI/MFAT dairy export quota allocation records for the first two allocation rounds after the Act commences; true if the number of distinct exporters allocated quota (including sheep and goat milk processors) exceeds the pre-amendment count, false if allocation remains confined to the same incumbent cow-milk traders.
reasoning: The Act (Dairy Industry Restructuring (Export Licences Allocation) Amendment Act 2025) commenced 1 May 2025, so only ONE of the two allocation rounds the criterion names has happened. That first round (2026 quota year, Gazette 2025-go5795, MPI Notice 1958) allocated licences to 6 distinct exporters — Fonterra, Open Country Dairy, New Zealand Grass Fed Products LP, Canary Enterprises, Westland Dairy Company, Synlait — against 4 in the last pre-amendment round (2025 quota year, Gazette 2024-go4857, MPI Notice 1868: Fonterra, Tatua, Open Country, Synlait). So 6 > 4 and three names are new: the criterion's 'false' arm (allocation confined to the same incumbent traders) is not met on round one, and the evidence so far runs in the claim's favour. But no sheep or goat milk processor appears in either notice, and the 2027-year allocation notice has not been gazetted as of 2026-09-27 (resolve-by 2027-06-30), so the two-round test the criterion specifies cannot be completed. Re-check after the 2027-year allocation notice publishes (expected late 2026).

statement: I’m sure the Minister will have many more things to say in the committee of the whole House.
criterion: Hansard for the committee of the whole House stage of the Contracts of Insurance Bill; true if the Minister in charge makes substantive contributions at that stage, false if the bill's committee stage passes without the Minister speaking to it.
reasoning: The Contracts of Insurance Bill's committee of the whole House stage ran on 22 October and 5-6 November 2024, and the Minister in charge, Hon Andrew Bayly (Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs), made substantive contributions throughout — speaking to clause 1 of Schedule 1 on 22 October, and in Parts 2 and 3 answering amendments: he defended the civil-law standard in replying to the Green Party's proposal to replace 'dishonestly' with 'fraudulently' in clause 14(2A) ('there are different tests between fraudulent and dishonest misrepresentation — one has criminal implications and one has civil implications'), and responded to Hon Dr Duncan Webb on the clause 70 'reasonable time' remedy ('it needs to be reasonable in the context'). The bill was also divided at this stage, which the Minister moves. The criterion's false arm — the committee stage passing without the Minister speaking to the bill — is not met. Resolve-by 2025-12-31 has passed; the bill was passed 14 November 2024.

statement: Inflation is now back within the Reserve Bank’s target range; the genie is back in the bottle; and the era of high, persistent, crushing price increases is over.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly annual CPI prints from December 2024 onward; true if every print stays at or below 3.0% through the resolve-by date, false if any annual print exceeds 3.0%.
reasoning: The criterion fails on any Stats NZ annual CPI print above 3.0% from December 2024 onward. Prints: Dec 2024 2.2%, Mar 2025 2.5%, Jun 2025 2.7%, Sep 2025 3.0%, Dec 2025 3.1%, Mar 2026 3.1%, Jun 2026 4.1%. Three prints exceed 3.0%, the June 2026 quarter by a wide margin — 4.1% annual (1.5% quarterly), above the RBNZ's 1-3% band, with petrol up 27.5% and diesel up 71% together contributing about two-thirds of the quarterly rise. Stats NZ noted the Dec 2025 print of 3.1% was already the highest annual rate since June 2024. Willis's narrower statement that inflation was back in the band was accurate on the day she said it (Sep 2024 quarter, 2.2%), but the forward-looking part — that the era of high price increases 'is over', tested here as staying at or below 3.0% — did not hold. The unexpired resolve-by date (2026-12-31) does not make this not_yet_due: the criterion's false condition has already triggered and cannot be undone by later prints.

statement: I stand by the statements I have made that around 100,000 households will be eligible for FamilyBoost, and I am pleased that the number of successful claims is growing every day.
criterion: Inland Revenue / Treasury FamilyBoost eligibility and uptake reporting; true if official estimates of eligible households remain around 100,000, false if the eligible population is later revised materially below that figure.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether official estimates of ELIGIBLE households stayed around 100,000. They did: the Beehive's July 2025 FamilyBoost fact sheet, describing the then-current $180,000/$75-a-week settings, states IRD estimates 162,000 families have children in ECE and 106,000 of those are entitled to some FamilyBoost payment if they apply. No downward revision of the eligible population below 100,000 is on record. What was revised was a different figure — IRD's estimate that 21,000 families would qualify for the FULL payment, against 249 who had claimed it by 9 April 2025 — which Willis conceded was wrong modelling, and first-year uptake (78,000 registered / 60,000 paid by mid-2025, i.e. fewer than half the eligible pool in Dec 2024 reporting). The second half of the quote also held: recipients rose to 97,500 with 115,000 registered by July 2026, though that is after the October 2025 widening (rebate 25%→40%, cap $75→$120, income threshold to $229,000), which added roughly 16,000–22,000 families. So: substance of the eligibility claim confirmed against the criterion as written, with the caveat that eligibility ≠ receipt and the sub-estimate for the maximum payment failed badly.

statement: By 2050, more than 10,000 homes of whānau in our biggest cities will become uninsurable.
criterion: Insurance Council of New Zealand / Reserve Bank or Treasury reporting on residential insurance retreat; true if more than 10,000 dwellings across New Zealand's largest cities are recorded as uninsurable (insurers declining cover) by 2050, false if the number remains materially below that.
reasoning: The prediction's horizon is 2050; nothing can yet be recorded as insurers declining cover on 10,000+ dwellings. The figure's provenance checks out: the Helen Clark Foundation / WSP report 'Premiums Under Pressure' (2024) estimates around 10,000 coastal properties in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin could become uninsurable by 2050 from coastal erosion and inundation, with partial insurance retreat beginning around 2030 in Wellington and Christchurch and a few years later in Auckland and Dunedin. Willis's 'more than 10,000' matches RNZ's framing of that report but is at the top of its estimate. No ICNZ/RBNZ/Treasury dataset yet records realised uninsurability at that scale, so the criterion cannot be evaluated either way in 2026.

statement: They will increase deaths and serious injuries for Aucklanders.
criterion: Ministry of Transport / Auckland Transport deaths-and-serious-injuries (DSI) counts for the Auckland region; true if Auckland DSI over the 2024-27 NLTP period rises above the year-ending-July-2024 baseline, false if DSI remain flat or fall over that period.
reasoning: The criterion is Auckland DSI over the full 2024–27 NLTP period, which runs to June 2027 (resolve-by 2027-12-31); as of September 2026 the period is incomplete, so the verdict cannot be settled. Interim Auckland Transport safety performance reporting runs in the direction of the claim rather than against it: Auckland recorded 611 DSI in the 2024/25 financial year against 589 in 2023/24 (+22, ~3%), with fatalities up from 31 to 49 and serious injuries 563→567; calendar-year Auckland road deaths went 36 (2024) → 40 (2025). Disconfirming context exists too — 2024/25 DSI is still ~70 below 2022/23 and well below the 2017 peak of over 800, and AT's own evaluation attributes prevented harm to the lower limits now being reversed, so a longer-run decline could reassert itself before June 2027. Not resolvable yet.

statement: We simply need to change the law, and, today, I know that we’re going to do it so that, in cases where people have separated and where there is domestic violence, instead of waiting for too long and instead of waiting for two long years in which the victim remains tied to their abuser, a divorce can be obtained immediately.
criterion: Hansard / Parliament's bill record for the Family Proceedings (Dissolution of Marriage or Civil Union for Family Violence) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was read a third time and passed on 16 October 2024, false if the third reading was defeated, adjourned or not completed that day.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether the bill was read a third time and passed on 16 October 2024. Hansard's third-reading debate for the Family Proceedings (Dissolution of Marriage or Civil Union for Family Violence) Amendment Bill is dated 16 October 2024 (Hansard id HansDeb_20241016_20241016_28), Labour's 17 October release describes the third reading as completed, and the bill became the Family Proceedings (Dissolution of Marriage or Civil Union for Family Violence) Amendment Act 2024 (Public Act 2024 No 42). The third reading was not defeated, adjourned or left incomplete. Two facts sit alongside the verdict without defeating the criterion: the Act commenced 17 October 2025, not on passage, and the immediate dissolution route requires the applicant to be a protected person under a final protection order — so 'immediately' means 'without the two-year separation wait', which is what Russell was contrasting against.

statement: Today is a very satisfying day, because it’s really Parliament at its best and it’s Parliament coming together—I believe it’s going to pass unanimously, which is a wonderful thing—to fix a problem.
criterion: The Hansard vote/division record for the third reading of the Family Proceedings (Dissolution for Family Violence) Amendment Bill on or about 16 October 2024; true if the bill passed with all parties in favour and none opposed, false if any party or member voted against.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the third reading passed with all parties in favour and none opposed. RNZ's report is headed 'Ashley's law passes unanimously' and states the legislation 'passed with full cross party support this week in parliament'; independent legal commentaries (Simpson Western, McVeagh Fleming, Corban Revell) all describe unanimous support of all parliamentary parties. I searched specifically for a party or member voting against and found no such record in any source. Limitation on the evidence: parliament.nz returned HTTP 404/error on every attempt to retrieve the Hansard page the criterion names, so I could not read the division/motion text verbatim; the unanimity finding rests on consistent secondary reporting rather than the primary division record.

statement: I want to say, when the Labour Government is re-elected in 2026, you will know us by our actions, because we are the true party of working people.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it; true if Labour leads the resulting government, false if it does not.
reasoning: The criterion requires the official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it. The Electoral Commission and the Prime Minister's announcement both set election day as Saturday 7 November 2026, with voting opening 26 October 2026. Today is 27 September 2026, so no votes have been cast, no result exists, and no government has been formed. The claim's resolve-by date (31 December 2026) has not passed either. Nothing is scoreable yet; pre-election polling is not the evidence the criterion names.

statement: I want to acknowledge their advocacy throughout the submission process, their contributions, which have also led to progress in other areas of protection in the law, including stalking laws, which the Government has indicated it will be introducing later on this term.
criterion: The Parliament bills register; true if a Government bill creating a stalking offence is introduced before the 54th Parliament is dissolved, false if no such bill is introduced in that period.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a Government bill creating a stalking offence was introduced before the 54th Parliament dissolved. The Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Bill — Government Bill 107 (2024), per its legislation.govt.nz 'bill/government/2024/0107' registration — was introduced in late 2024 (first reading 12 December 2024, referred to the Justice Committee, submissions closed 13 February 2025). It creates a standalone stalking-and-harassment offence in the Crimes Act 1961 with a 5-year maximum. It went further than the criterion required: second reading 23 July 2025, third reading 19 November 2025, Royal assent 26 November 2025, in force 26 May 2026. Meager's statement that the Government 'has indicated it will be introducing [stalking laws] later on this term' is borne out.

statement: This amendment bill, as we see today, will pass its third reading unanimously, by the look, across the House.
criterion: The Hansard division/vote record for the third reading of the Family Proceedings (Dissolution of Marriage or Civil Union for Family Violence) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed with no party or member voting against, false if any party or member voted against.
reasoning: The Family Proceedings (Dissolution of Marriage or Civil Union for Family Violence) Amendment Bill ('Ashley's Law') passed its third reading on 16 October 2024, the same sitting day as the quote. The Hansard record of the third reading shows no division — the motion was agreed to on the voices — and post-passage reporting states directly that 'the law change was passed with the unanimous support of all parliamentary parties.' I searched specifically for disconfirming evidence (any party or member voting against, including the plausible dissenters NZ First and ACT) and found none; NZ First spoke in support during the debate. Caveat on the evidence: because the bill was agreed to on the voices, there is no division table to inspect, so 'no party voted against' rests on the absence of a called division plus contemporaneous reporting of unanimity. That is the strongest record available and it meets the criterion as written.

statement: Firstly, I’d just like to congratulate Ms Nimon on getting this bill through, and it looks like we’re going to have support around the House, which is certainly where I hoped we would get to.
criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Bill: true if it passes with the support of all or nearly all parties, false if any significant party votes against.
reasoning: Katie Nimon's Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 24 October 2024 and became the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Act 2024 (No 45). The Hansard record of the third reading ends 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time' with no division recorded, and the debate itself refers to the bill being about to pass unanimously and 'enjoying such strong support from all across the House'; WhereTheyStand records the third reading as passed with no vote breakdown (i.e. no division). National's own release of 24 October cites 'cross-party support'. No source reports any party voting against, so the criterion's 'support of all or nearly all parties' is satisfied. Same evidentiary caveat as the other vote item: agreed on the voices means no roll-call exists to inspect.

statement: I have no doubt that part of that strategy will be informing what workforce is required, how we enable that, how we support workforce development, and in the right areas as well.
criterion: The mental health and wellbeing strategy published by the Minister under the amended Act; true if it contains a section or substantive content on mental health workforce requirements and workforce development, false if the published strategy omits workforce content (or if no such strategy is published by the resolve-by date, the item is not yet due).
reasoning: The strategy required by the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Act was published as the Mental Health and Wellbeing Strategy 2026-2036, launched 6 August 2026 by Minister Matt Doocey. Workforce is one of its four stated priorities ('a supported and capable workforce'), with substantive content on what workforce is needed and how to develop it: improving recruitment and retention, developing a diverse workforce, strengthening planning and coordination for the Consumer/Peer Support/Lived Experience workforce, and building skills across health and social service workers. The accompanying three-year Implementation Plan carries concrete workforce-development actions (475 New Entry to Specialist Practice places a year for nurses, occupational therapists and social workers; 120 NZQCF Level 4 places a year for the peer/lived-experience workforce; a training programme for up to 40 psychology assistants a year from 2026/27). The criterion's true-condition — a section or substantive content on workforce requirements and workforce development — is met. The one part of Nimon's phrasing not directly verifiable from the summaries is 'in the right areas as well' (geographic/service distribution), but the criterion does not require it.

statement: I’m sure the ACT Party, who are property-mad, will support it, because the right to property is one of their foundation stones.
criterion: The Hansard division records for the second and third readings of the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill; true if ACT's votes are recorded in favour, false if ACT votes against.
reasoning: ACT voted against the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill, not for it. The bill's second reading was on 16 October 2024 — the day of Webb's statement — and passed 63 Ayes to 60 Noes; the third reading on 12 March 2025 passed on the same 63-60 split. Multiple independent accounts of the third reading state that National and ACT opposed the bill and that New Zealand First's support with the opposition parties (Labour, Greens, Te Pati Maori) carried it. The arithmetic confirms the party-vote composition at both readings: the 60 Noes are exactly National (49) plus ACT (11), and the 63 Ayes are Labour (34), Greens (15), Te Pati Maori (6) and NZ First (8). The Act received royal assent on 13 March 2025. Webb's prediction that ACT would support the bill because 'the right to property is one of their foundation stones' is contradicted by the recorded votes at both the second and third readings.

statement: We’ve gone through the select committee process, I think we’re going to get to the committee of the whole House process, and, hopefully, a successful third reading—but that’s all in the future.
criterion: Parliament's bill record and Hansard for the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill; true if it completed committee of the whole House and passed a third reading, false if it was defeated, withdrawn or still had not reached third reading by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill completed the committee of the whole House (concluded 20 November 2024) and passed its third reading on 17 December 2024, becoming the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Act 2024 (No 57) with royal assent on 22-23 December 2024. All three readings (20 March 2024, 6 November 2024, 17 December 2024) are recorded as passed. Stephenson's prediction that the bill would go through committee of the whole House and reach a successful third reading was borne out, well within the resolve-by date.

statement: The imminent apology that is going to result from the inquiry into the abuse in State care, I think, is a good example where that was a really painful process, a difficult process, and while some steps are being taken, we’re still falling well short of what is needed to address the harm that was caused in those circumstances where it was the State that was responsible.
criterion: Hansard and official Crown records; true if a formal Crown/Government apology for abuse in State care was delivered within roughly a year of 16 October 2024, false if no such apology had been delivered by that date.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether a formal Crown/Government apology for abuse in State care was delivered within roughly a year of 16 October 2024. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon delivered a formal and unreserved Crown apology in Parliament on 12 November 2024 — 27 days after the statement — accompanied by a government redress and response package (Ministry of Justice / Beehive records). Disconfirming check: there is no record of the apology being deferred, cancelled or postponed beyond that date; if anything it came sooner than 'imminent' implied. The second clause ('still falling well short of what is needed') is an evaluative judgement the criterion does not test, so it does not qualify the verdict.

statement: It is the second one of my colleagues that I’ve jealously had to congratulate tonight for having a member’s bill pulled in their first term and one which will, hopefully, have support of the House—and I think it does—and it will be seen all the way through.
criterion: The bill's progress record on parliament.nz: true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; false if it is defeated at any reading, discharged, or still has not passed by the end of the 54th Parliament.
reasoning: The bill being debated is identified from the source window's content — a member's bill restricting prisoner contact with victims and protection-order holders, back from the Justice Committee with 12 submissions, with Meager citing ~26,000 community-managed people and ~9,500 prisoners — as the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill, a member's bill of Rima Nakhle, a first-term National MP (Takanini), drawn from the ballot on 31 January 2024. Against the criterion (parliament.nz progress record): 1R 20 March 2024 passed unanimously, 2R 6 November 2024 passed, committee of the whole concluded 20 November 2024, 3R 17 December 2024 passed, Royal assent 22–23 December 2024 (WhereTheyStand records 22 December, Wikipedia's acts list 23 December). Disconfirming check: no reading was lost, and the bill was not discharged — the 'false' branch (defeated, discharged, or unpassed by the end of the 54th Parliament) does not apply. One dating caveat that does not change the verdict: Hansard shows no Corrections bill debate on 16 October 2024 — the second reading began 23 October and resumed 6 November — so the corpus window appears mis-dated by one sitting day.

statement: We expect this number will rise further due to the lagged effects of high inflation, high interest rates, and the recession on employment.
criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets; true if the number of jobseeker support recipients in any quarter up to June 2025 exceeds the September 2024 figure, false if the count declines from September 2024 onward.
reasoning: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets put Jobseeker Support at 204,765 at the end of September 2024 (up 12.8% on September 2023). Every subsequent quarter through the criterion's June 2025 cut-off is higher: December 2024 approx. 213,300, March 2025 = 209,838, June 2025 = 216,009 (up about 10% year-on-year and up 6,171 on March 2025). The criterion's 'true' condition — any quarter to June 2025 exceeding the September 2024 figure — is met in all three quarters. Disconfirming check: for 'false' the count would have had to decline from September 2024 onward; the March 2025 dip relative to December 2024 is the only fall in the series and it still sits above September 2024, so no quarter undercuts the baseline.

statement: The Budget update forecasts this to occur, although we know it is not a given and that many factors affecting this balance are outside the Government’s direct control.
criterion: Treasury's Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30 June 2028 (and intervening fiscal updates); true if a total Crown OBEGAL surplus is recorded for 2027-28, false if a deficit is recorded or the surplus forecast is pushed beyond 2027-28.
reasoning: The criterion is falsified if a deficit is recorded for 2027-28 OR the surplus forecast is pushed beyond 2027-28. The second leg is already satisfied. Willis was citing BEFU 2024, which forecast an OBEGAL surplus in 2027/28. Every Treasury update since has moved it out: BEFU 2025 (22 May 2025) forecast a $304m OBEGALx deficit in 2027/28 with surplus in 2028/29; HYEFU 2025 (Dec 2025) pushed the return to surplus to 2029/30; BEFU 2026 (28 May 2026) brought it back to 2028/29 at $2.6bn, explicitly 'a year earlier than was forecast at HYEFU' but still a year beyond 2027-28. The final Financial Statements for 2027-28 are not due until October 2028, so the 'deficit is recorded' leg remains open, but the forecast-slippage leg resolves the criterion now. Caveat: the headline measure changed from OBEGAL to OBEGALx (ACC excluded) at Budget 2025, so levels are not strictly comparable across updates — the surplus year moved out regardless of measure.

statement: I’m not sure what my schedule will be at that time; I have a funny feeling I might be overseas, but the point would be, very clearly, people are free to protest as long as it’s done legally and peacefully.
criterion: The Prime Minister's official diary and media reporting for 19 November 2024; true if he was overseas that day, false if he was in New Zealand.
reasoning: Luxon guessed he might be overseas when the hikoi reached Parliament; he was in New Zealand. Hikoi mo te Tiriti arrived at Parliament on 19 November 2024 (police estimate up to 42,000). Luxon's only overseas trip that month was the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Lima, Peru on 15-16 November (he met Xi Jinping there on 15 November); he was back in New Zealand before the 19th. On 19 November he personally answered oral questions in the House — Hansard/Scoop's Questions and Answers for that day records him fielding supplementaries on the hikoi, including from Tamatha Paul about why he did not front the crowd, to which he replied that National 'had a delegation from the National Party representing our position, receiving the hikoi.' He then discussed it on TVNZ Breakfast and the Mike Hosking Breakfast the next morning. So he was in Wellington at Parliament, not overseas. His prediction was hedged ('I'm not sure', 'a funny feeling I might be'), but the criterion is binary on location and resolves false.

statement: I can tell the Minister, I was at an EU event last night and this action was discussed. This was an informal meeting—an event I was at—but I would be very surprised if there are not substantial consequences for our farming communities because of this Government’s actions.
criterion: EU and MFAT records to 31 December 2026: true if the EU formally raised the freshwater changes as a compliance issue under the NZ–EU FTA, or restricted/conditioned market access for NZ agricultural products citing them; false if no such formal action or documented market-access loss occurred.
reasoning: The criterion's window runs to 31 December 2026 and today is 27 September 2026, so the date has not passed. Neither truth condition has occurred as of now. MFAT's NZ-EU FTA implementation page lists all committee activity through April 2026 (Trade Committee Oct 2025; Trade and Sustainable Development Committee May 2025; Sustainable Food Systems Feb 2025 and Apr 2026; Trade in Goods Apr 2025 and Apr 2026; SPS Feb 2025) with no dispute settlement or TSD consultation request on record, and nothing raising New Zealand's freshwater changes. The October 2025 Trade Committee joint press statement raises no freshwater compliance issue; its only agri-environment item runs the opposite way, with the EU agreeing to avoid undue impacts on New Zealand producers from the EU Deforestation Regulation and recognising that New Zealand's agriculture and forest production systems support sustainability outcomes. Bilateral trade was up 8%; no restriction or conditioning of NZ agricultural market access citing freshwater was found. Importantly the window is still genuinely open: the next Trade Committee is scheduled for the second half of 2026 in Brussels, which is the forum where such an issue would be formally raised. I checked for disconfirming evidence and found that the pressure to date has come from civil society (WWF-NZ arguing the deregulation programme breaches the FTA's TSD chapter, echoed by other environmental groups) rather than from the EU itself, which is not what the criterion requires.

statement: Of course, this law won’t have commenced by tomorrow, because it needs to have a third reading, which is not going to happen tonight, and then, of course, it needs Royal assent—also not going to happen tonight.
criterion: The Royal assent date recorded for the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2024 on New Zealand Legislation: true if assent fell after 23 October 2024, false if the Act was assented and commenced on or before that date.
reasoning: The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 23 October 2024 (not the night of 22 October), received Royal assent on 24 October 2024, and came into force on 25 October 2024. The criterion asks whether assent fell after 23 October 2024: it did (24 October), so neither assent nor commencement had happened by 'tomorrow' as Brooking predicted. Confirmed by the RMLA note ('received Royal Assent on 24 October and came into force the following day') and corroborated by the legislation.govt.nz listing and the Beehive third-reading release.

statement: This is all relevant to the commencement date, because the commencement is going to be retrospective—or not, if this item ends up on the agenda tomorrow, which is looking increasingly unlikely.
criterion: Otago Regional Council meeting agenda and minutes for 23 October 2024; true if the plan-notification item was not on the agenda or no vote to notify was taken that day, false if the item was restored and voted on.
reasoning: ORC's 23 October 2024 council meeting had a 1pm pLWRP decision paper scheduled, but on 22 October chief executive Richard Saunders announced he would withdraw it: 'there will be no vote taken.' This followed the Government's 22 October announcement of an RMA amendment barring councils from notifying freshwater plans until a new NPS-FM is in place. The meeting proceeded with the pLWRP notification item pulled, and no vote to notify was taken that day — which is the criterion's 'true' branch. Disconfirming check: reporting on the day (NZ Herald/Newstalk ZB, Newsroom) describes the vote as pulled/disrupted, not held; ORC did not vote on notify-vs-pause on 23 October.

statement: One of them will have to be in the House correcting their answer.
criterion: Hansard record of corrections of answers to the House; true if either Christopher Luxon or Andrew Bayly lodges a correction to their statements on this matter, false if no such correction appears by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The one correction on this matter in the House is Andrew Bayly's, made just before 10pm on Tuesday 22 October 2024 — the night BEFORE Hipkins spoke. Bayly amended his 2.50pm answer to Arena Williams on whether he had drunk alcohol at the beer garden or winery: 'for the avoidance of any doubt, after the incident and at the end of the day, I had a small wine tasting.' Reporting states that this correction is what led to Hipkins' further questioning of Luxon in the House 'the next day' (23 October), i.e. Hipkins was predicting a FURTHER correction arising from the conflict between Luxon's answers and Bayly's account. I found no correction lodged by either Luxon or Bayly on this matter after 23 October 2024 and before 31 December 2024; the story was heavily covered (including an OIA release of Bayly's texts in November 2024) and no such correction is reported, and Bayly's next major development was his February 2025 resignation over an unrelated incident. Note on the criterion as literally written (no start date): Bayly's 22 October correction does sit inside the window, so a purely literal reading could be satisfied — but crediting a prediction with an event that preceded and prompted it would be back-dating, so I grade the predicted event as not having occurred. Confidence is moderate rather than high: parliament.nz blocked direct fetching of Hansard, so the absence rests on press coverage rather than a Hansard sweep.

statement: We’re dealing with the country’s health and education systems, and because of us alone, we will, in New Zealand, reach the smoke-free target in 2024, not some time in the distant future.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2024 reporting period: true if the rate is below the 5 percent Smokefree Aotearoa threshold for the adult population in 2024; false if it remains at or above 5 percent.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2024 reporting period fell below the 5% Smokefree threshold. It did not: 6.9% in 2023/24 and 6.8% in 2024/25 (~294,000 adults), a plateau of 6.8-6.9% across 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25. PHCC's briefing on the 2024/25 survey states explicitly that the goal of under 5% daily smoking for all population groups will not be achieved; Maori are at 15.0%, Pacific peoples 10.3%, most-deprived neighbourhoods 12.9%. Under either reading of 'the 2024 reporting period' (2023/24 or 2024/25) the rate is comfortably above 5%, so the prediction that New Zealand would reach the smokefree target in 2024 is wrong. I checked for a disconfirming reading — some sub-population or redefined target that had been met — and found none; the inequities run the other way.

statement: The roll-out of the confirmation of payee service will begin next month and will be in place across 13 banks by Easter 2025.
criterion: New Zealand Banking Association / participating bank announcements on confirmation of payee availability; true if the service is live across 13 banks on or before 20 April 2025, false if fewer than 13 banks have it live by that date.
reasoning: Both limbs hold. The rollout began the month after the statement: NZBA member banks started Confirmation of Payee on 28 November 2024. The participating set is exactly 13 banks — ANZ, ASB, Bank of China, BNZ, CCB, The Co-operative Bank, Heartland, ICBC, Kiwibank, Rabobank, SBS, TSB, Westpac — and the criterion asks whether the service was live across all 13 on or before 20 April 2025 (Easter Sunday). I specifically hunted for a bank that missed it, since the smaller banks were the risk. Every late go-live date I could find precedes the deadline: ICBC from end of March 2025, Bank of China from 2 April 2025, CCB for Internet Banking on 15 April 2025. obconnect/Raidiam's August 2025 retrospective states ten banks went live initially and then thirteen, covering over 95% of consumer bank accounts — consistent with the three Chinese-owned banks being the last of the 13, all live by 15 April. No source reports any of the 13 missing Easter. Two residual caveats, neither enough to downgrade against the criterion as written: no single document certifies 'all 13 live as at 20 April 2025', and CCB's 15 April launch was for Internet Banking specifically, so per-channel (mobile app) completeness at some banks may have trailed the bank-count milestone. A separate 30 November 2025 date appears in payments-regulation coverage, but that is the Code of Banking Practice anti-scam commitment coming into force, not the technical rollout.

statement: I think most members of Parliament will support that.
criterion: The division record for the remaining stages and third reading of the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Bill; true if a majority of members vote in support, false if it fails or a majority votes against.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a majority of members voted in support at the remaining stages and third reading of the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Bill. Boyack spoke on 17 October 2024 during the committee stage (Hansard for that day records the House in committee on this bill, with Boyack taking a short call). The bill then passed its third reading on 23 October 2024 and received Royal Assent on 24 October 2024 as the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Act 2024 — so a majority necessarily supported it. WhereTheyStand records all three readings as passed with 'no vote breakdown recorded', which is what you see when a stage is agreed on the voice rather than a party vote being called; that is consistent with, not contrary to, broad support. I could not retrieve explicit Ayes/Noes totals (parliament.nz blocks automated fetching), so the majority is established by passage and assent rather than by quoted division numbers. The bill was a narrow measure making permanent a charitable-lottery exemption that was due to lapse on 31 October 2024; the Salvation Army made a critical submission, but nothing indicates a party voted the bill down.

statement: I watched Andrew Hoggard, one of the true farmers of this Parliament—one of the few true farmers of this Parliament—announce that significant natural areas, those violations of farmers’ property rights, are having the pause button pushed, and then they too will be gone.
criterion: Statute and national direction as at the end of the parliamentary term: true if the significant natural area (SNA) obligations in the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity / RMA are repealed outright, false if they are only suspended or remain in force.
reasoning: The criterion is explicit: true only if SNA obligations in the NPS-IB/RMA are repealed outright, false if merely suspended or still in force. They are suspended, not repealed. The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) amendment suspended the NPS-IB provisions on identifying and notifying new SNAs for three years (until 25 October 2027) and extended other SNA implementation timeframes to 31 December 2030; the suspension expressly does not affect obligations for SNAs already in plans or proposed plans, and councils must still give effect to the rest of the NPS-IB 2023, which remains in force. Seymour's antecedent observation (Hoggard announcing the pause) was already public by 14 March 2024, so the predictive content is 'then they too will be gone.' Checking for the disconfirming case — a repeal via the RMA replacement — the Natural Environment Bill and Planning Bill passed third reading on 23 September 2026 with staged commencement to about 2030, and the Bills provide for significant natural areas to be identified in spatial plans, with a regulatory-relief test where controls fall on private land. That retains SNAs in a new form rather than removing them. As at the end of the parliamentary term, no repeal.

statement: The era of crushing prices is over.
criterion: Stats NZ annual CPI inflation prints from Q4 2024 through Q4 2025; true if annual inflation remains at or below roughly 3 percent across that period, false if it rises materially back above the RBNZ 1-3% target band.
reasoning: Stats NZ annual CPI prints across the criterion's window: December 2024 2.2%, March 2025 2.5%, June 2025 2.7%, September 2025 3.0%, December 2025 3.1%. The criterion's false condition — inflation rising materially back above the 1-3% RBNZ band — did not occur, so the claim's substance (no return to the 2022-23 price shock) holds. But it holds only at the margin and only on the 'roughly 3 percent' reading: inflation rose in every single print across the window rather than falling, and the final observation breached the top of the target band at 3.1%, the highest annual rate since June 2024, with electricity up 12.2%, local authority rates up 8.8% and international air transport up 7.2% in the quarter. Checking beyond the window for disconfirmation, the March 2026 print was also 3.1%, so the band-edge level persisted. Prices were still rising at the ceiling of the band, which makes 'the era of crushing prices is over' materially overstated rather than wrong.

statement: I’d like to speak about this Government’s kamikaze lawmaking, to get its own way, that will result in Otago’s rivers being less swimmable, if swimmable at all, over the next 30 years, through a kamikaze amendment and a process that is worrying and that in some ways feels sinister and Machiavellian.
criterion: LAWA / Otago Regional Council river water-quality monitoring, swimmability (E. coli attribute state) grades for Otago monitored river sites: true if the proportion of Otago sites graded swimmable is lower than the 2024 baseline over the following decades; false if it is the same or higher.
reasoning: The criterion measures the proportion of Otago monitored river sites graded swimmable on the E. coli attribute state against a 2024 baseline 'over the following decades', with a resolve-by date of 2054-10-23. Only about two years have elapsed, and LAWA's long-term swim grade is itself a rolling five-bathing-season aggregate, so no post-2024 grade yet reflects a period distinguishable from the baseline, let alone a 30-year trajectory. The precipitating event in the quote is verified: the Government introduced an eleventh-hour RMA amendment in October 2024 blocking councils from notifying freshwater plans until a new NPS-FM is in place, which disrupted the Otago Regional Council's scheduled vote on its proposed Land and Water Regional Plan, and that plan remains paused pending the new legislation and national direction. That confirms the mechanism she described but says nothing about the predicted outcome. Not finding decidable evidence here is a function of the horizon, not of absent data: ORC monitors more than 30 swim sites and LAWA publishes the grades, so the criterion will be checkable when the time series exists.
