statement: That’s going to decline very quickly over the next 30 years, and once they’re not swimmable, it’s really hard to get them back.
criterion: LAWA / Ministry for the Environment swimmability reporting for Otago river sites: true if the share of sites meeting swimmability standards falls materially (outside monitoring variability) below the ~85% baseline by 2054; false if the share holds steady or improves.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on LAWA/MfE Otago swimmability reporting by 2054; only ~2 of the 30 years have passed. LAWA publishes current Otago river-quality and summer swim-site monitoring, but no measurement of the ~85% baseline's trajectory to 2054 exists, and the national picture (~70% of rivers/lakes swimmable now, 90%-by-2040 target) does not resolve the Otago share. Absence of a 2054 figure is not evidence against the prediction.

statement: It means that the four-lane expressway is actually going to happen 12 to 15 months faster than scheduled.
criterion: NZTA project completion records for the Hawke's Bay expressway compared with the delivery date scheduled as at October 2024; true if opened 12 or more months ahead of that schedule, false if the saving is materially smaller or the project runs to or beyond the original date.
reasoning: The criterion requires NZTA completion records compared with the delivery date scheduled as at October 2024, resolvable by 2030-06-30. The project is mid-build, not complete: NZTA approved >$600m in August 2025, construction started November 2025, stage one is due 2028 and later stages 2030/2034, so no completion date can be compared yet. Supporting but non-resolving evidence: NZTA and Wedd both state that using the 2025/26 construction season brought construction forward 12-15 months, enabled by early ground improvement with Cyclone Gabrielle silt. That is an accelerated start, not a delivery date beaten by 12+ months, which is what the criterion tests.

statement: I’m sure restricted practices will be a critical topic of discussion and of high importance to submitters and the select committee.
criterion: The Health Committee's submissions and final report on the Mental Health Bill: true if restricted practices/seclusion are addressed by a substantial share of submissions and receive dedicated treatment or recommended amendment in the committee's report; false if the topic is largely absent from submissions and the report.
reasoning: The Health Committee reported the Mental Health Bill back on 17 April 2025 after 384 submissions from 358 submitters and 89 oral hearings. Restricted practices featured heavily among submitters: the Chief Ombudsman submitted in his OPCAT detention-monitoring role, the Disabled Persons Assembly was 'extremely concerned' at retention of restraint, seclusion and forced medication, Te Hiringa Mahara sought a sunset clause ending seclusion, and Mana Mokopuna addressed the under-18 seclusion ban. The committee's report records 'differing views on complex issues such as the use of seclusion in hospitals', and Te Hiringa Mahara's critique refers to 'the Committee's proposed amendments, particularly those regarding seclusion' as not going far enough - so the topic received both dedicated treatment and amendment, satisfying the criterion. I checked the disconfirming reading (topic largely absent from submissions or the report) and it fails; the consistent complaint is insufficiency, not silence. Caveat: parliament.nz and legislation.govt.nz blocked direct fetching, so the report's contents are established via Te Hiringa Mahara's summary rather than the commentary text itself.

statement: Thank you to my committee colleagues from across the House for listening to the submissions and making the necessary changes to enable this day and the inevitable—dare I say, the inevitable—passing of what will soon be known as the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Act; 42 years in the making.
criterion: The New Zealand statute book and Parliament's bill progress record. True if the bill receives Royal assent as the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Act; false if it is defeated, lapses, or is still not enacted by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The bill received Royal assent on 25 November 2024 under exactly the predicted name, the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Act 2024, after a unanimous third reading on 20 November 2024. The Governor-General's own record confirms the assent, and the statute book carries the Act. The '42 years' framing also checks out against the 1982 Act it reverses. No evidence of the bill being defeated, lapsing, or being renamed.

statement: I’m sure that there will be widespread agreement around the House, so I won’t take too much of our time, but just to say that, undoubtedly, the locals in the North Shore will be greatly appreciative of the House’s support in allowing them to use this local asset—once a proud part of their history—to update it, upgrade it, and make sure it’s fit for 2024 purposes.
criterion: The Hansard record of the first reading vote on the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Act Amendment Bill: true if the bill was read a first time with no party voting against; false if any party opposed or the reading failed.
reasoning: The Hansard record of the 23 October 2024 first reading of the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Act Amendment Bill shows the motion agreed to on the voices — no party vote was called and no party voted against. Speakers from all six parties (National, Labour, Green, ACT, NZ First, Te Pati Maori) spoke in support, and the bill was referred to the Governance and Administration Committee. It later became the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Amendment Act 2025, consistent with unopposed passage.

statement: I’m sure all parties will be supporting this unanimously.
criterion: The Hansard/House record of the first reading vote on the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Act Amendment Bill; true if the bill was read a first time with the agreement of all parties (no party voting against), false if any party opposed.
reasoning: Same record as the companion item: the bill was read a first time on 23 October 2024 with the motion agreed to on the voices, no party vote and no party opposing. Every party represented in the debate — National, Labour, Green, ACT, NZ First and Te Pati Maori — spoke in favour, so Court's 'all parties supporting this unanimously' holds as written.

statement: I know that the Governance and Administration Committee will look forward to opening submissions shortly on this bill.
criterion: The Parliament NZ select committee record for the Governance and Administration Committee: true if a public call for submissions on this local bill opened within roughly five months of 23 October 2024; false if no call for submissions had opened by then.
reasoning: The bill under debate was the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Act Amendment Bill (the Takapuna Boating Club local bill, land at 17 Sir Peter Blake Parade, Bayswater). The Governance and Administration Committee issued a call for public submissions on 25 October 2024 — two days after the 23 October speech — with submissions closing 11.59pm Wednesday 13 November 2024. Six submissions were received and three submitters were heard orally; the committee reported the bill back recommending it be passed. This is comfortably inside the criterion's ~five-month window, so the prediction resolves correct.

statement: The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Bill, which we’re about to pass unanimously, reflects our commitment to building a healthier and more resilient future for all New Zealanders.
criterion: The Hansard division/voice-vote record for the third reading of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Bill on 23 October 2024; true if the bill passed with every party voting in favour, false if any party or member voted against.
reasoning: The third reading debate (Hansard HansDeb_20241023_20241024_20, begun 23 October 2024 and concluding in the early hours of 24 October) ends with "Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time." — a voice vote with no division called and no party vote recorded, which is the form an uncontested passage takes. Speakers from National, Labour, the Greens, ACT, NZ First and Te Pati Maori all spoke in support; no party or member is recorded voting against. Te Hiringa Mahara (Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission) independently reported on 29 October 2024 that "the Bill was passed into law with unanimous support from MPs"; royal assent followed on 24 October 2024. Checked for disconfirming evidence (any party opposition or a division on the third reading) and found none.

statement: I congratulate my colleague Katie Nimon—it looks like this is going to pass through unanimously—and I want to thank all of the people who have contributed today for their contributions.
criterion: The third reading vote record in Hansard for the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Bill; true if it passed with the support of all parties, false if any party voted against.
reasoning: Same evidence base as the companion item: the Hansard third-reading record for the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Bill closes with "Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time." with no division and no party recorded against, after support speeches from all six parties in the House. Te Hiringa Mahara reported it "passed into law with unanimous support from MPs"; royal assent 24 October 2024. WhereTheyStand records the third reading as passed with no vote breakdown, consistent with an unopposed voice vote. So Uffindell's forecast that it would pass unanimously holds.

statement: I have been assured by Minister Matt Doocey that all New Zealanders, including all ethnic and migrant communities, will have the opportunity to contribute to this Government’s mental health policy direction, both now and in the future.
criterion: Ministry of Health / Minister for Mental Health records of the consultation process for the mental health and wellbeing strategy required by the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (Improving Mental Health Outcomes) Amendment Act: true if a public consultation or submission process open to all New Zealanders was run on the strategy or the Government's mental health policy direction, with targeted ethnic/migrant community engagement; false if the strategy was developed without any public consultation opportunity.
reasoning: The Ministry of Health ran a full public consultation on the draft Mental Health and Wellbeing Strategy 2026-2036 (the strategy required under the Pae Ora amendment) from 8 April to 18 May 2026 on its Citizen Space portal, explicitly open to members of the public as well as the sector; around 900 people and organisations contributed. Participation options included facilitated consultation sessions, lived-experience hui and 'sessions for specific communities', NZSL feedback, and the consultation Summary was issued 'in accessible formats and multiple languages' with translated resources - the ethnic/migrant-access limb of the criterion, albeit evidenced indirectly, since I could not retrieve health.govt.nz pages naming ethnic- or migrant-specific engagement events (403 to automated fetching). The draft strategy itself names Asian peoples, migrants and people with a refugee background among communities to be included in decision-making. The falsifying condition - a strategy developed with no public consultation opportunity - did not occur; the strategy was launched by Minister Doocey after that consultation.

statement: What will he say to the predicted 50,000 people, many of whom will be supporters of Ihumātao, who will march against the Government on 18 November in protest over this Government’s anti-Treaty agenda?
criterion: Contemporaneous police and media crowd estimates for the hīkoi/march against the Government in mid-to-late November 2024; true if a march took place on or about 18 November with participation in the order of 50,000, false if it did not occur or drew an order of magnitude fewer participants.
reasoning: Hikoi mo te Tiriti marched on Parliament on 19 November 2024 - one day after the date Jackson named, which satisfies the criterion's 'on or about 18 November'. Wellington District Commander Superintendent Corrie Parnell put the crowd at 42,000, revised up from an initial police estimate of 35,000; independent and partisan estimates ranged from 40,000 to 100,000 (Te Pati Maori's Rawiri Waititi said 100,000, NZ First's Winston Peters said 22,000). 42,000 is of the order of the predicted 50,000, and commentators described it as possibly the largest protest in New Zealand's history - the opposite of the order-of-magnitude shortfall that the criterion sets as the falsifying condition. Checked for disconfirmation: the lowest contemporaneous figure cited by anyone (22,000, from a political opponent) is still the same order of magnitude.

statement: The child protection amendment bill is part of a raft of legislation that the Government is enabling, including the gangs legislation which has passed, which will be enacted by mid-November.
criterion: The commencement provisions and Royal assent date of the Gangs Act 2024 on legislation.govt.nz; true if the Act was in force on or before about 15 November 2024, false if commencement fell later.
reasoning: The Gangs Act 2024 received Royal assent on 23 September 2024 (so 'the gangs legislation which has passed' was accurate), but its commencement date was 21 November 2024 - the gang patch ban and other provisions came into force then, not by mid-November. Against the criterion as written ('true if in force on or before about 15 November 2024, false if commencement fell later'), the timing claim fails, by six days. I record partly_correct rather than wrong because the substance held - the Act did take effect in November 2024, in the window he was gesturing at - and the miss is a fortnight-boundary one rather than a failed prediction; a strict application of the criterion returns wrong.

statement: So with those caveats, we do support this to first reading, and I look forward to the many submissions that we will get.
criterion: The Health Committee's record of submissions on the Mental Health Bill; true if the committee received a large public response (100+ submissions), false if the submission count was small (under 100).
reasoning: The bill was referred to the Health Committee at first reading on 23 Oct 2024; written submissions closed 20 Dec 2024. The committee reported back on 17 April 2025 having received 384 submissions from 358 unique submitters, with 89 submitters heard orally. Te Hiringa Mahara independently describes 'over 300 submissions'. The criterion's threshold was 100+, so Leary's expectation of 'many submissions' is confirmed by the committee's own record.

statement: The next part is to acknowledge that there will be a lot of submissions. I expect those submissions to come forward to the Health Committee when this bill is up for consideration.
criterion: The Health Committee's record of submissions on the Mental Health Bill (submission tables and the committee's report to the House): true if the committee received a substantial volume of written submissions (on the order of 100 or more), false if submissions were sparse (a few dozen or fewer) or if the bill did not reach select committee consideration.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion hold. The bill did reach select committee consideration: the Health Committee ran a public submission process (closing 20 Dec 2024) and reported to the House on 17 April 2025 recommending amendments. Volume was substantial, not sparse: 384 written submissions from 358 unique submitters, of whom 89 appeared to give oral evidence — well above the 'order of 100 or more' the criterion set.

statement: I’m really looking forward to seeing this bill unanimously supported through the rest of its stages.
criterion: Hansard division records for the bill's committee stage and third reading; true if every party voted in favour (or it passed without opposition), false if any party voted against.
reasoning: The bill completed its remaining stages with no reported opposition. After stalling through 2025, it was progressed under urgency from Tuesday 30 June 2026, passed its third reading (reported 30 June, announced 4 July) and received Royal assent on 9 July 2026 as the Mental Health Act 2026. On party positions, the ODT's health reporter (10 July 2026) states that all parties planned to vote for the bill and that Doocey used his second-reading speech to call for bipartisanship; no source reports any party voting against at committee stage or third reading, and I searched specifically for that disconfirming evidence. Caveat on strength of proof: I could not reach the Hansard division text the criterion names — parliament.nz's 2026 Hansard day pages and the bills.parliament.nz history tab are JS-rendered and returned 404/unhandled-error to every URL pattern tried, and health.govt.nz and RNZ returned 403. So the verdict rests on the ODT account plus the absence of any reported dissent rather than on the division record itself.

statement: I just want to acknowledge the Sarjeant Gallery, or what will become known as Te Whare o Rehua Sarjeant Gallery when it reopens after a huge redevelopment, on 9 November.
criterion: Sarjeant Gallery / Whanganui District Council announcements and news coverage; true if the gallery reopened to the public on 9 November 2024 under that name, false if the reopening was delayed past that date or the name differs.
reasoning: The gallery reopened to the public on 9 November 2024 (dawn ceremony from 4.30am, doors open 9.30am) under the name Te Whare o Rehua Sarjeant Gallery, after a four-year, ~$70m redevelopment. 1News reported the public opening on the day itself, and the gallery's own opening-weekend page and the Whanganui District Council announcement both give 9 November 2024. No delay, and the name matches what Bates said.

statement: If we kick this can down the road, we will be back in 10 to 15 years and it won’t be $1 billion—it will be $2 billion or it will be $3 billion.
criterion: Health NZ / Treasury costings for a full Nelson Hospital rebuild published between 2034 and 2039; true if a full rebuild is again under active consideration and costed at $2 billion or more, false if the rebuild has been completed under the current programme or is costed materially below $2 billion.
reasoning: The criterion requires Health NZ/Treasury costings for a full Nelson Hospital rebuild published between 2034 and 2039; today is September 2026, so that window has not opened and neither the true nor the false condition can be tested. Current state for context only: the 2023 Labour-era plan was ~$1.098b over 10 years; in May 2025 the government rescoped to ~$500m over four years (five-storey, 128-bed inpatient unit, energy centre, seismic upgrades plus refurbishment), with an $11m ED expansion completing early 2026 and main construction expected to begin around end-2026. Whether a further full rebuild is reconsidered at $2b+ in the 2030s is unknowable now.

statement: It was about cheering them on and championing them, because I have a vision that as National comes in and as our Government builds this new road—it starts construction next year, from Ōtaki to Levin, with four lanes all the way.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project updates for the Ōtaki to north of Levin (O2NL) highway: true if main construction is under way at any point during the 2025 calendar year, false if the start of construction slips beyond 31 December 2025 or the project is cancelled or descoped from four lanes.
reasoning: Main construction on the Ōtaki to north of Levin (Ō2NL) highway began on 23 September 2025, within the 2025 calendar year Costley predicted — PM Luxon and Transport Minister Bishop turned the sod, and NZTA material dates main construction to spring/October 2025 with completion in late 2029. The highway is four lanes across its full 24 km. I specifically checked the descoping risk: the cost-driven cuts announced in early 2025 and reinstated in June 2025 concerned the Tararua Rd grade-separated interchange (briefly reduced to a roundabout), the Taylors Rd southbound onramp and the Manakau Heights bridge — the lane count was never reduced from four.

statement: The Reserve Bank, for example, is expecting a negative GDP result in the previous quarter—the September quarter—but a positive result in the current quarter and a steadily growing economy in 2025 and beyond.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases: true if the September 2024 quarter records a fall in real GDP and the December 2024 quarter records a rise, with positive growth continuing through the 2025 quarters; false if either quarter moves in the opposite direction or 2025 growth is not sustained.
reasoning: Both specific quarter calls were right: Stats NZ recorded a 1.0% fall in Sept 2024 quarter real GDP (later revised to -1.1%) and a 0.7% rise in the Dec 2024 quarter (later revised to +0.5%). But the criterion also requires positive growth continuing through the 2025 quarters, and it did not: Mar 2025 +0.8%, Jun 2025 -0.9% (a sharp, broad-based contraction across 10 of 16 industries, well below forecast), Sep 2025 +1.1% (revised to ~+0.9%), Dec 2025 +0.2%. Stats NZ itself noted at the June release that GDP had fallen in 3 of the last 5 quarters. The near-term forecast held; the 'steadily growing economy in 2025' half did not.

statement: That will not continue for ever, however, and unemployment is expected to come down next year.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate: true if the rate for the December 2025 quarter is lower than the December 2024 quarter rate; false if it is the same or higher.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the HLFS unemployment rate for the Dec 2025 quarter is lower than the Dec 2024 quarter. It is higher: 5.1% (Dec 2024) vs 5.4% (Dec 2025), the highest rate since the Sept 2015 quarter. Checking for the disconfirming case — any point in 2025 where the rate fell — the series instead rose steadily through the year (5.1 -> 5.2 -> 5.3 -> 5.4), with unemployed people up 5,000 over the Dec 2025 quarter alone, so no reading of 'came down next year' survives.

statement: And on the 19th, I think we’ll get to see that a little bit more closely outside on the grounds.
criterion: News reporting and Parliamentary Service records for 19 November 2024; true if a large protest/hīkoi assembled on Parliament grounds that day, false if no such gathering occurred.
reasoning: Hikoi mo te Tiriti, organised by Toitu te Tiriti against the Treaty Principles Bill, reached Parliament on 19 November 2024 after a nine-day march. Police estimated about 42,000 participants; Parliament grounds reached capacity with thousands spilling onto surrounding streets. Contemporaneous reporting from RNZ, 1News and Newsroom all date the Parliament-grounds gathering to that day, so the criterion's 'large protest/hikoi assembled on Parliament grounds on 19 November 2024' is met directly.

statement: This framework will also enable the implementation of significant changes and improvements through provisions coming into force by regulation over the next two to three years.
criterion: The New Zealand Gazette / legislation.govt.nz record of regulations made under the amended Policing Act relating to police vetting; true if such regulations are made and in force by late 2027, false if no vetting regulations have commenced by that date.
reasoning: The criterion asks for regulations made under the amended Policing Act relating to police vetting, in force by late 2027. The Policing (Police Vetting) Amendment Bill has not been enacted: it passed first reading 5 Nov 2024, the Justice Committee reported back 1 April 2025 recommending it pass, and it is still awaiting second reading; it does not appear in the list of Acts of the 54th Parliament. With no Act, there can be no regulations under it. The resolve-by date (2027-11-05) has not passed, so this is undue rather than false — though the bill's stall since April 2025 makes the two-to-three-year timeline she described look unlikely. Disconfirming check: police vetting fee regulations DO exist under the Policing Act 2008, but via the separate cost-recovery amendment lineage that predates this bill, so they do not satisfy the criterion as written.

statement: To be perfectly honest, at this stage of the debate, in my view, there’s not a great deal more to say, although I’m sure my colleague Tracey McLellan will have much more to say.
criterion: The Hansard record of the first reading of the Policing (Police Vetting) Amendment Bill on 5 November 2024: true if McLellan speaks in the debate at greater length/substance than Webb's contribution, false if she does not speak or offers only a brief formal contribution.
reasoning: Tracey McLellan did speak in the same 5 Nov 2024 first reading debate on the Policing (Police Vetting) Amendment Bill, and her contribution was substantive rather than formal: she noted her surprise at the volume of police vets conducted, that the service had been well embraced and well used despite the absence of a regulatory framework, and that following the review it made sense to put a statutory framework in place. That rules out the criterion's false branch (does not speak, or brief formal contribution). I could not verify the comparative clause — that she spoke at greater length/substance than Webb — because the full Hansard transcript was not retrievable: parliament.nz returns 403/404 to automated fetches, hansard.parliament.nz serves a JS-only shell, and the Wayback mirror is unreachable from this environment. Webb's own recorded contribution was short and descriptive (he called it an uncontentious bill with the core issue being privacy against public safety, and said the framework was largely already adopted by police), which is consistent with his prediction but not proof of the comparison.

statement: One thing that the select committee did not consider, because it was out of the scope of this bill, but it might be considered in the review and what happens next, should the extension pass—which it probably will—is looking at how we can make this more achievable for people.
criterion: Parliamentary record for the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, withdrawn or still not passed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Genter predicted the earthquake-prone building deadline extension would probably pass. The Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill completed its passage and received Royal assent on 25 November 2024 as Act 2024 No 49, commencing 26 November 2024 (the day after assent) — three weeks after she spoke. Confirmed independently by the legislation.govt.nz Act record, the Wikipedia list of Acts of the 54th Parliament (2024/49, assented 25 November 2024), and MBIE's Building Performance notice describing the four-year deadline extension plus a one-off power to extend by up to two further years. Disconfirming check: no record of the bill being defeated, withdrawn or lapsing.

statement: Stop the conflation, stop the hyperbole, and actually protect the sector in which, we maintain on this side of the House, we’re going to see a doubling of export revenue inside of the next 10 years.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries food and fibre export revenue series; true if annual export revenue by the year ending 2034 is at least double the level reported for the year ending 2024 (roughly $55bn to $110bn), false if it falls materially short.
reasoning: Criterion resolves on MPI SOPI food and fibre export revenue for the year ending 2034; resolve-by is 2034-12-31, eight years away. Baseline (SOPI June 2024) ~$54.3bn, so the target is ~$108-110bn. Latest actual/forecast is a record $64.3bn for the year to 30 June 2026 (+6%), but MPI forecasts 2026-27 to ease 3%. Reaching $110bn would need ~7%/yr sustained growth, which MPI's out-year track does not currently show. No grade possible yet.

statement: When the Minister talks about the disarray and the appetite for new investments, as he mentioned, that’s just not going to happen, because we look at the evidence from the Government officials—that 2014 was the last time it was done.
criterion: NZ Petroleum & Minerals block offer / exploration permit award data and company investment announcements: the prediction is correct if no new petroleum exploration permits are taken up and no new exploration investment is announced following the repeal; incorrect if new exploration permits are awarded and exploration investment announced.
reasoning: The criterion makes the prediction incorrect if new exploration permits are awarded and exploration investment announced after the repeal. Both occurred before the resolve-by date. On 29 July 2026 NZP&M granted EnZed Energy a 12-year offshore petroleum exploration permit over ~546 km2 of the Taranaki Basin (Kaheru prospect), the first since the ban was reversed; further applications entered the competitive process (a fourth and a fifth bid) and Monumental Energy advanced a Taranaki permit. On 24 September 2026 the Government announced $21.5m of Crown equity into the ~$71m Kaheru exploration programme (EnZed raising the remaining $49.5m) plus the first Gas Security Fund loans of up to $23.5m to Todd Energy for two Taranaki wells, with a refreshed exploration data pack. Caveat worth noting but not exculpating under the criterion as written: the investment is modest in scale and substantially Crown-underwritten, so a narrower claim about private appetite would fare better than the one he made.

statement: This Government has total magical thinking on this, and it’s going to hurt the economy in the long run because we’re not going to have those trade agreements that we’ve signed up to at the moment when countries realise that we are doing nothing.
criterion: MFAT records and trading-partner statements: true if a trade agreement New Zealand had signed as at Nov 2024 (e.g. the NZ–EU FTA) is suspended, has benefits withheld, or has climate-related trade measures applied against New Zealand on climate-performance grounds; false if all such agreements remain in force with no climate-based restriction applied by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2029-12-31. As at September 2026 the NZ-EU FTA (in force 1 May 2024) remains fully in force, no benefits have been withheld, and no climate-related trade measure has been applied against New Zealand, so the criterion's trigger has not fired. Related pressure exists but falls short of the criterion: MFAT advised ministers in 2024 that repealing the offshore exploration ban would likely breach the deal, the EU's domestic advisory group discussed New Zealand's policy choices against the non-regression clause in May 2026, lawyers warned the LNG plans would breach trade deals, and the UK is reported to be examining New Zealand's oil and gas measures under its own FTA. No Commission consultation request or sanction was found. Searched for disconfirming evidence (suspension, withheld benefits, TSD consultations) and found none.

statement: The reversal of this foolish, dangerous, juvenile, puerile pursuit of climate purity will be reversed and we will now find ourselves in the clover-rich territory of many applications to develop our petroleum resource.
criterion: New Zealand Petroleum & Minerals block offer and permit-application records after the Crown Minerals Amendment Act comes into force; true if block offers attract multiple new exploration permit applications/awards, false if block offers attract no or negligible applications by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The reversal itself happened: the Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025 received royal assent on 5 August 2025, overturning the 2018 offshore exploration ban. Against the criterion's permit-application record, the true-branch threshold is met — six petroleum prospecting/exploration permit applications had been accepted by August 2026, and the first new offshore exploration permit was granted on 29 July 2026 to EnZed Energy (546 km2 in the offshore Taranaki Basin, Kaheru prospect). Three more sat in open-market competitive processes as of late 2026 (Taranaki Energy, Sunda Energy, CBX Energy in the Pegasus Basin). So this is not 'no or negligible applications'. But it is materially overstated on two counts. First, no Block Offer tender — the mechanism the criterion names — has been run since 2020; allocation shifted to the open-market competitive process, so the block-offer part of the prediction has simply not been tested. Second, six applications over roughly thirteen months, from junior explorers (Monumental's Tirua Point bid attracted no competing application at all), is a trickle rather than 'clover-rich territory of many applications'; over the same period proven and probable gas reserves fell 23% to 731 PJ, the lowest since records began. The resolve-by date is 2027-12-31 and more applications may follow, but the criterion's true condition is already satisfied at a level the quote's rhetoric overstates.

statement: The fast track will open up coalmines.
criterion: The list of projects approved under the Fast-track Approvals Act: true if at least one coal mining project receives approval under the regime; false if no coal mine is approved through fast track.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the list of projects approved under the Fast-track Approvals Act, with a resolve-by date of 2027-12-31. As at 27 September 2026 no coal mining project has been approved through the regime, but none has been finally declined either, so the criterion is not yet satisfied in either direction. The only coal project on the listed-projects schedule is Bathurst Resources / BT Mining's Buller Plateaux Continuation Project (Stockton/Denniston, ~20 Mt of coking coal over 25 years, listed by Order in Council). Its substantive application was returned by the EPA on 23 September 2026 for failing the completeness check — an outstanding wildlife approval and missing consent from the manager of a reserve, with Forest & Bird pointing to a lizard salvage rate under 1% against a DOC best-practice target above 80%. Bathurst says it will resolve both and resubmit, after which an expert panel would assess the merits. Stevenson Mining's unlisted Te Kuha coal referral was likewise returned for not meeting application criteria. The mining approvals granted so far are Waihi North (gold, 18 December 2025, the first mining project approved under the regime); the Taranaki VTM seabed project was draft-declined in February 2026 and withdrawn. Nothing found suggests a coal approval has been ruled out — the pathway was deliberately widened for Buller Plateaux — so the honest answer is that the prediction's window is still open.

statement: Nuclear is their biggest option, and nuclear power will be generating a record amount across the world in 2025.
criterion: IEA Electricity report / Ember global generation data for calendar 2025: true if global nuclear generation (TWh) in 2025 exceeds the previous all-time annual high; false if it falls below it.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether global nuclear generation in calendar 2025 exceeded the previous all-time annual high, judged on IEA / Ember-class global generation data. It did. The World Nuclear Association's World Nuclear Outlook Report 2026 reports that reactors worldwide generated 2,702 TWh in 2025, up 35 TWh on 2024's 2,667 TWh, 'setting a new annual record for global nuclear generation' and a record high for the second year running (2024 having already surpassed the earlier mid-2000s peak), supplying around 9% of world electricity. The IEA's Global Energy Review 2026 independently states that annual nuclear generation reached a record high, growing about 1.2% in 2025 on the back of Japanese reactor restarts, strong French output and new units entering service in several countries, and that it is set to keep rising through 2030. I checked for the disconfirming case — a generation dip masked by flat capacity — and found the opposite pattern is consistent across sources: global capacity was roughly flat at 420 GW end-2025 (3 GW added, 3 GW retired) while generation still rose on higher utilisation, which is exactly how a record year without a capacity build looks. Note the verdict covers only the checkable half of the quote; the accompanying assertion that 'nuclear is their biggest option' is an opinion the criterion does not test.

statement: I’m hoping that, while this is going to go through, no doubt, there is a better approach to what the energy solution for Taranaki should be that includes iwi and hapū and the knowledge and experience that they have.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Crown Minerals Amendment Bill; true if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, withdrawn or lapses.
reasoning: The criterion tests whether the Crown Minerals Amendment Bill passed. It passed its third reading on 31 July 2025 and received Royal assent on 5 August 2025, becoming the Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025 (Public Act 2025 No 40, in force 6 August 2025). It was not defeated, withdrawn or lapsed. Ngarewa-Packer's 'this is going to go through, no doubt' is borne out; the rest of the quote is a hope, not a prediction, and is outside the criterion.

statement: This bill will provide confidence. It will provide the ability to plan our transition to renewable energy.
criterion: MBIE petroleum exploration permit statistics and announced exploration investment following the Act's passage. True if new exploration permit applications/grants and announced exploration investment materially increase over the pre-Act baseline by the end of 2026; false if they remain flat or decline.
reasoning: The criterion measures permit applications/grants and announced exploration investment 'by the end of 2026'; today is 27 September 2026, so the window has not closed. Interim evidence is mixed and does not settle it either way. Upward: four petroleum permit applications have entered the process since the Act (EnZed Energy offshore South Taranaki in October 2025 — the first since the 2018 ban; Monumental/3TCF/NZEC PEP61554 covering ~245 km2 in northern Taranaki in May 2026; plus two others), against a pre-Act baseline of effectively zero outside onshore Taranaki since Block Offer 2020; one onshore exploration permit has been granted; a Gas Security Fund investment and an updated Petroleum Exploration Data Pack were announced 24 September 2026. Flat/downward: only two companies have signalled exploration interest since June 2026, EnZed holds its block with no drilling plans and needed public co-investment to raise capital for the Kaheru prospect, and Pohokura/Maui/Kapuni continue to decline. Whether this is a 'material' increase in announced investment should be judged after 31 December 2026.

statement: Inevitably what will be said by the Minister in the third reading is that this is a piece of law which benefits consumers and fairly benefits them in regards to their interests being balanced with those of the insurers, who have much more power in these situations than they do.
criterion: Hansard for the third reading of the Contracts of Insurance Bill; true if the Minister's third-reading speech claims the bill benefits consumers or balances consumer and insurer interests, false if no such claim is made in that speech.
reasoning: The third reading took place on 14 November 2024 and both the Contracts of Insurance Act 2024 and the Contracts of Insurance (Repeals and Amendments) Act 2024 received Royal assent on 15 November 2024. I could not open the third-reading Hansard page itself — every parliament.nz URL returned 404 from this environment, including pages search results confirm are live — so the named source is unread. All retrievable evidence points one way: Minister Andrew Bayly's own statement on passage ('Safeguarding Kiwis with modern insurance law') claims Kiwis will have confidence they are treated fairly by insurers; his consistent framing was that the bill balanced 'customer protection with providing certainty for the market', i.e. consumer benefit balanced against insurer certainty — the exact framing Williams predicted; and his first- and second-reading Hansard statements make the consumer-benefit claim directly. Graded correct on that basis, with the caveat that the third-reading speech text itself was not directly verified.

statement: Now, there are clear indications that the economy has turned upwards, but even so, I would expect the unemployment rate to rise a bit further before beginning to fall.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate in the quarters after September 2024: true if the rate rises above 4.8% and then turns down from a peak; false if it falls immediately from 4.8% without rising, or if it is still rising with no peak by the resolve date.
reasoning: The HLFS seasonally adjusted unemployment rate did rise above the 4.8% of the September 2024 quarter — 5.1% (Dec 2024), 5.1% (Mar 2025), 5.2% (Jun 2025), 5.3% (Sep 2025), 5.4% (Dec 2025), 5.4% (Mar 2026, revised 5.3%) — but it then rose again to 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter, the highest in about 11 years. There is no peak followed by a turn down by the 2026-06-30 resolve date, which is exactly the criterion's stated false condition. The 'rise a bit further' half was right (and the rise was far more than 'a bit'); the 'before beginning to fall' half has not happened.

statement: This expanded package in Wellington will result in significant travel time savings during peak times, reducing travel times from the northern suburbs to the CBD, hospital, and airport by around 10 minutes to boost productivity and enable Wellingtonians to get where they need to go quickly and safely.
criterion: NZTA post-implementation travel time monitoring once the expanded package is open: true if measured peak journey times on that corridor fall by approximately 10 minutes against the pre-project baseline; false if the saving is materially smaller, or if the package is cancelled or not delivered.
reasoning: The criterion requires NZTA post-implementation travel-time monitoring once the expanded package is open. The package (second Mt Victoria Tunnel, duplicate Terrace Tunnel, Basin Reserve grade separation) is not built: NZTA confirmed the preferred option in Nov 2024, unveiled a design in Nov 2025 costed at $2.9–3.8b, and the fast-track consenting application began in Aug 2026 with no confirmed funding or construction start. So no measured post-implementation data exists. The false branch does not fire either — the package has not been cancelled, it is still being progressed. The ~10-minute figure is NZTA's own forecast as stated in the Nov 2024 announcement, so the quote reports the official forecast accurately; whether it is realised is unresolvable until the corridor opens. Resolve date 2035-12-31.

statement: Well, if the Opposition parties at second reading vote against it like the National Party will, it won’t become law.
criterion: The division record for the second reading of the Treaty Principles Bill: true if, with National and the Opposition parties voting against, the bill is defeated and does not pass into law; false if the bill proceeds to enactment notwithstanding those votes.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11. ACT's 11 votes were the only ones in favour; National (49) voted against alongside Labour (34), the Greens (15), NZ First (8) and Te Pati Maori (6). The bill did not proceed and did not become law, exactly as the criterion's true condition specifies.

statement: That is a chance for the public to engage with the process; then it will come back to this House for a second reading, at which point it’ll be voted down.
criterion: The division record for the second reading of the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill; true if the bill is defeated at second reading, false if it passes second reading or never returns for one.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill returned to the House and was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 — 112 votes against, 11 for (ACT alone). That is before the 2025-08-31 resolve-by date, and neither failure condition in the criterion (passing second reading, or never returning for one) occurred.

statement: They’ve cut things like the upgrade of the Interislander—watch this space, though, for Nicola Willis to come back to the House and say that she got it wrong and that maybe, actually, the ferry deal that she said was so bad wasn’t such a bad deal after all.
criterion: Hansard record of Nicola Willis's statements in the House: true if she states that she got the ferry decision wrong or that the cancelled iReX deal was not a bad deal; false if no such concession appears on the record by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The resolve-by date is 2026-11-07 and today is 2026-09-28, so the window is still open. No concession has appeared so far: at the December 2024 replacement announcement Willis said 'I've delivered' and defended the cancellation, and when the $1.86b cost of the replacement programme was published in November 2025 the government's framing was that it had saved $2.3b against iReX, not that the original deal was sound. The only admission of error on the record runs the other way — Hipkins himself said Labour's two mega ferries 'wasn't the wisest decision'. Evidence trends against the prediction, but per the criterion it cannot be marked false until the date passes.

statement: We have a Government that is afraid as our people activate and consolidate and unite as we prepare for the biggest hīkoi that this country will ever see—bigger than any other hīkoi in history.
criterion: Police and media attendance estimates for the Toitū Te Tiriti hīkoi arriving at Parliament in November 2024, compared with estimates for previous hīkoi (the 1975 Land March and the 2004 foreshore and seabed hīkoi). True if the 2024 hīkoi's estimated numbers exceed those of every earlier hīkoi; false if an earlier hīkoi is estimated larger.
reasoning: Police estimated 42,000 at the Hikoi mo te Tiriti arriving at Parliament on 19 November 2024 (initial estimate 35,000); experienced crowd counter Grace Millar counted 50,500 passing Lambton Quay. The 2004 foreshore and seabed hikoi — the previous benchmark, 'the largest in a generation' — is reported at 15,000-20,000 arriving at Parliament, and the 1975 Land March at about 5,000. Checking the disconfirming case: some 2004 activists claim up to 50,000, which would close the gap, but that is an outlier against contemporaneous reporting, and commentators who covered both called 2024 'the most people who have ever marched on parliament'. The forward-looking half of the quote ('will ever see') is not testable, but the criterion as written asks only whether 2024 exceeded every earlier hikoi, and it did.

statement: This is just to put in practice as a member’s bill to codify the responsibilities on the chief executive and prison managers and the expectations that victims can have, too—so they can go back to the statute, they can seek advice, and say, “What are my actual rights here? Where do I stand with this unwanted communication?” and it will all be explicitly written down in statute and passed through the third reading in a matter of days, if not weeks.
criterion: The Parliamentary bills record for the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill; true if the third reading is completed by roughly mid-February 2025 (i.e. within weeks of 6 November 2024), false if the third reading falls materially later or the bill does not pass.
reasoning: The Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill (Nakhle, member's bill 11-1) completed its committee of the whole House stage on 20 November 2024, passed its third reading on 17 December 2024 and received royal assent on 22 December 2024. That is roughly six weeks after the 6 November 2024 statement — within the criterion's 'by roughly mid-February 2025' window, and the bill did pass. Checked the opposite case (bill stalling or lapsing on the members' order paper) and found no evidence of it: Parliament's own record shows it awaiting third reading after 20 November, and legislation.govt.nz lists it as an enacted public Act amending the Corrections Act 2004.

statement: Well, ACT is going to support it, so I think there’s a good chance it’s going to be supported by the Justice Committee.
criterion: The first reading division record for the Evidence (Giving Evidence of Family Violence) Amendment Bill (McLellan): true if the bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Justice Committee; false if it was defeated at first reading or not referred to that committee.
reasoning: The Evidence (Giving Evidence of Family Violence) Amendment Bill (Tracey McLellan, member's bill 30-1) passed its first reading on 6 November 2024 with cross-party support and was referred to the Justice Committee on that date. The committee called for submissions closing 19 December 2024, heard the member in charge on 20 February 2025, and reported back on 19 May 2025; the bill was later enacted on 25 August 2025. So it was neither defeated at first reading nor sent to a different committee.

statement: There’s a lot of work to do, and I look forward to 19 November when this whole place will be receiving many, many Māori—wāhine Māori, children, whānau, hapū, iwi—to come and show their disappointment at what’s going on in the House.
criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting and Parliamentary Service crowd estimates for 19 November 2024; true if a large Māori protest march reached Parliament grounds on that date, false if no such gathering occurred on 19 November 2024.
reasoning: Hīkoi mō te Tiriti reached Parliament grounds in Wellington on 19 November 2024, the exact date named. Police initially estimated 35,000 on the final leg and later revised the figure to more than 42,000; Te Pāti Māori put it higher and NZ First lower, but every source agrees a very large Māori-led march arrived at Parliament that day in protest at the Treaty Principles Bill and related policy. The disconfirming case — no gathering, or one on a different date — is contradicted by same-day reporting from 1News, Newsroom, RNZ, NZ Herald and Te Ao Māori News.

statement: Like I say, I’m really excited to hear from people and do implore, when we go through the select committee process and this gets opened—and I’m sure that will be in the sort of coming days or weeks—that we do get a good, broad number of contributions because we don’t just want to hear from businesses, we don’t just want to hear from the unions, and we don’t just want to hear from women, we don’t just want to hear from Pasifika.
criterion: The Parliament select committee record (call for submissions notice) for the pay-transparency member's bill referred at this first reading; true if submissions opened within roughly six weeks of 2024-11-06, false if the committee did not call for submissions until materially later.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the select committee called for submissions within roughly six weeks of 2024-11-06. The Education and Workforce Committee opened submissions on 13 November 2024 — seven days after the first reading — closing 23 January 2025. Nimon said it would be 'in the sort of coming days or weeks'; it was seven days, comfortably inside the window. Her further hope for a broad range of contributors is not part of the criterion, but is consistent with the outcome: 225 submissions were received and 16 submitters heard orally.

statement: It’s great to hear that bill looks like it’s destined to be heard at the select committee where it can have that more precise looking-over, which will involve submitters coming to the select committee to really give their perspectives on this bill.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Employment Relations (Employee Remuneration Disclosure) Amendment Bill on 6 November 2024: true if the bill was read a first time and referred to a select committee, false if the first reading was defeated.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the bill was read a first time and referred to a select committee on 6 November 2024, false if defeated. The first reading passed 104–19 on a party vote (National, Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori for; ACT and NZ First against) and the bill was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee. Tuiono's further expectation that submitters would appear before the committee also held: 16 submitters were heard orally at hearings in Wellington and by videoconference, with the member in charge appearing on 12 February 2025.

statement: This time, you do not need our support, so it’s still going through to the select committee and I do congratulate you on that.
criterion: The first reading division record for Camilla Belich's Employment Relations (Employee Remuneration Disclosure) Amendment Bill; true if the bill was read a first time and referred to a select committee, false if the first reading was defeated.
reasoning: Criterion: true if Belich's bill was read a first time and referred to a select committee. It passed 104–19 and went to the Education and Workforce Committee. Patterson's embedded premise — that NZ First's support was not needed — also holds: NZ First voted against (with ACT), and the bill still carried by 104 to 19 because National joined Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori.

statement: We’re going to meet the emission reduction plan.
criterion: Climate Change Commission and Ministry for the Environment reporting on delivery of the first emissions budget (2022–2025) and Emissions Reduction Plan; true if official reporting records the budget as met, false if reported emissions exceed the budget.
reasoning: The criterion requires official Climate Change Commission / Ministry for the Environment reporting to record the first emissions budget (2022-2025) as met. As of September 2026 no such final reporting exists: the Commission's 2026 monitoring report (published 22 July 2026) says projections show the first emissions budget (290 MtCO2e) is 'likely to be met with a 7.7 MtCO2e buffer', and explicitly defers judgement — 'the Commission's end-of-budget report in 2027 will give a full assessment using final emissions data.' The resolve-by date (2027-06-30) has not passed and the final 2025 inventory is not yet in. Direction of the evidence favours the prediction (helped partly by GHG inventory methodology improvements and higher-than-projected forest planting, which lowered the effort needed rather than by extra abatement), but per the criterion as written this cannot be scored yet.

statement: To demonstrate our commitment to change, this afternoon a bill that will introduce a range of measures to improve the safety of children and vulnerable adults in State care will have its first reading here in Parliament.
criterion: Hansard and the Order Paper for 12 November 2024; true if a bill concerning the safety of children and vulnerable adults in State care had its first reading that afternoon, false if no such first reading occurred that day.
reasoning: The Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill (Government Bill 97, 2024) was introduced on 12 November 2024, the same day as the Crown's formal apology to survivors of abuse in care, and had its first reading in the House that day — first-reading speeches from that debate (e.g. Chlöe Swarbrick, Kahurangi Carter) are on the record. Its contents match the description given: removing strip searches of children in care, new search powers at youth justice facilities, stronger restrictions on people working with young children, better agency record-keeping, and amending the Crimes Act to include disability in the definition of 'vulnerable adult' — i.e. measures on the safety of children and vulnerable adults in State care. No disconfirming evidence found; contemporaneous news reporting on 12 November explicitly pairs the apology with the bill's introduction and first reading.

statement: This week, tens of thousands—in the largest mobilisation that our country has seen in living memory—are marching to this place to demand that we not only change but transform this system, demanding, as many survivors have, that we honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi me te He Whakaputanga, that we ensure that our people get the systems and the services that they deserve, and that we care not just in words but in action for each other and the planet that we all share.
criterion: Police and media crowd estimates for the hīkoi's arrival at Parliament in November 2024; true if credible estimates put the crowd at 20,000 or more, false if estimates fall materially below that.
reasoning: Hīkoi mō te Tiriti reached Parliament on 19 November 2024. Wellington District Commander Superintendent Corrie Parnell put the crowd in the parliamentary precinct and surrounding streets at approximately 42,000 by mid-afternoon (police had said 35,000 earlier in the day); RNZ, 1News and other outlets reported the same figure. That clears the criterion's 20,000 threshold by a wide margin. I checked for lower counter-estimates: Winston Peters said 22,000 and crowd-counting analyses noted the figures are contested (Te Pāti Māori's Rawiri Waititi claimed 100,000), but even the lowest credible estimate is above 20,000, so the criterion is satisfied on any reading. Note the quote's 'this week' was loose — the hīkoi set out from Te Rerenga Wairua on 11 November and arrived at Parliament the following week — but the criterion tests crowd size, not timing.

statement: Is it important to democracy to support a piece of proposed legislation that will have a cost to racial disharmony and will not proceed anywhere past the second reading?
criterion: The Parliament bills register and Hansard division records for the Treaty Principles Bill; true if the bill was defeated at or before its second reading and never proceeded to committee of the whole House or third reading, false if it advanced past second reading.
reasoning: Said 2024-11-07, a week before the bill's first reading. The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi (Treaty Principles) Bill passed first reading 68-54 on 14 Nov 2024, went to the Justice Committee (300,000+ submissions; report 4 April 2025), and was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with ACT the only party in support. It never proceeded to committee of the whole House or a third reading. Checked for disconfirming evidence (reintroduction, revival, a later stage): none - Seymour said only that ACT would 'reveal next steps before the 2026 election', with no further legislative stage recorded. Criterion satisfied as written.

statement: It seems obvious, it seems axiomatic, that if you remove any of the incentives, any promise of a forthcoming pricing regime, any sort of backstop, those emissions are going to start increasing again.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment New Zealand Greenhouse Gas Inventory, agricultural emissions series; true if reported agricultural emissions rise across consecutive years following the removal of the backstop, false if they remain flat or continue to fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires reported agricultural emissions to rise across consecutive years FOLLOWING removal of the backstop. The backstop was removed by the Climate Change Response (Emissions Trading Scheme Agricultural Obligations) Amendment Act, in force 26 November 2024. The MfE Inventory runs 16 months behind: the latest edition (April 2026) covers 1990-2024 only, so no full post-removal year is yet reported, let alone consecutive rising years. The one data point near the boundary runs the other way - Agriculture fell 0.14 Mt CO2e (-0.3%) between 2023 and 2024, driven by ongoing sheep-flock decline (-333 kt) outweighing increased dairy enteric fermentation (+177 kt) and agricultural soils (+71 kt) - but 2024 is a pre-removal year and one year is not a trend. Resolve-by is 2029-12-31.

statement: It is important to work a market-led approach, and as I’ve stated, as outlined in our draft emissions reduction plan, the market is already, in conjunction with the industry, on track to meet targets in regards to emissions reduction by 2030.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Climate Change Commission monitoring reports for the 2030 biogenic methane target (10% below 2017 levels); true if the 2030 target is met, false if the reported 2030 figure falls short.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the reported 2030 biogenic methane figure against the 10%-below-2017 target; 2030 has not occurred and the inventory reporting lag means the figure will not exist before roughly 2032 (resolve-by 2032-06-30). Interim evidence is disconfirming but is a projection, not an outturn: the Climate Change Commission's 2026 Monitoring report: Emissions reduction (22 July 2026) concludes the 2030 biogenic methane target will not be met, citing government estimates of a 7.9% reduction against the 10% target, notes agricultural emissions pricing has been removed from the emissions reduction plan, judges planned policies 'insufficient to deliver the required reductions', and finds evidence that the NZ ETS 'is not efficiently driving emissions reductions now' - directly against the 'market-led... on track' claim. Flagged for re-resolution, but not scoreable yet under the criterion as written.

statement: No. I’ve repeated over and over again that nothing will change when it comes to partnership agreements with hapū and iwi around the country, but I will wait for the select committee to finish their deliberation of this bill and will commit to carefully considering their report once it’s tabled in the House.
criterion: The status of Oranga Tamariki strategic partnership agreements with iwi and hapū after the section 7AA repeal takes effect; true if existing partnership agreements remain in force with no reduction in number or scope, false if agreements lapse, are not renewed, or partners publicly withdraw citing the repeal.
reasoning: The Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act 2025 received Royal assent 7 April 2025. Against the criterion's false-conditions, none occurred: no iwi or hapū partner has publicly withdrawn from a strategic partnership agreement citing the repeal, and Oranga Tamariki's strategic-partnerships page still lists the same nine partner entries (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāpuhi, Waikato-Tainui, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa Rangatira & Te Āti Awa, Tūhoe, Eastern Bay of Plenty Iwi Provider Alliance, Māori Women's Welfare League, Te Kahu Oranga Whānau) against the 10 agreements recorded under s 7AA before repeal. Chhour also did the second thing he promised: the Social Services and Community Committee recommended retaining the partnership duty, and the final Act inserted a new s 7 requiring the chief executive to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations. But 'nothing will change' is materially overstated. The repeal removed the mana tamaiti / whakapapa / whanaungatanga duties and the mandatory annual public reporting that gave the agreements their statutory content; the new s 7 is markedly less prescriptive, and OT's own s 7AA reporting page has carried a 'we will update this page in due course' notice since April 2025 with no replacement reporting regime. No authoritative post-repeal enumeration of the agreements has been published, so 'no reduction in scope' cannot be confirmed positively — only that no agreement is known to have lapsed. Disconfirming check: searched specifically for iwi withdrawals, terminations and lapses (Ngāi Tahu, Waikato-Tainui, Ngāti Toa, National Iwi Chairs Forum) and found strong pre-repeal opposition but no post-repeal exit. The 2024-25 OT provider funding cuts hit Māori service providers but are service contracts, not strategic partnership agreements, so they fall outside this criterion.

statement: A majority of Parliament tomorrow will vote in favour of the Treaty principles bill.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the Treaty Principles Bill's first reading: true if the ayes exceed the noes; false if the bill is defeated or the vote does not proceed.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill's first reading was held on 14 November 2024, the day after Hipkins spoke. The division was 68 ayes to 54 noes: National 49, ACT 11 and NZ First 8 in favour; Labour 34, Green 15 and Te Pāti Māori 5 against. Ayes exceeded noes and the bill proceeded to the Justice Committee, satisfying the criterion's true-condition exactly. (The bill was later defeated at second reading on 10 April 2025, but the criterion is explicitly about the first reading.)

statement: I tell you what: for those in the northern part of the electorate—and, to be fair, for all of us—we just look forward to the next phase, the next stage, Ōtaki to north of Levin, all the way to the north of Levin, construction starting next year.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project updates for Ōtaki to north of Levin: true if main construction is under way at any point during calendar 2025, false if construction had not commenced by 31 December 2025.
reasoning: Costley spoke on 13 November 2024, so 'next year' means calendar 2025. NZTA signed project alliance agreements with the two delivery alliances in July 2025 (Downer/McConnell Dowell/Beca/Tonkin+Taylor south of the Ōhau, Fulton Hogan/HEB/WSP/Aurecon north), and main construction on the 24 km Ōtaki to north of Levin (Te Pae o Tararua) expressway started on 23 September 2025 with a sod-turning attended by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport, with completion scheduled for late 2029. NZTA's own October 2025 project information boards and flyover design update confirm works under way. Main construction was therefore under way within calendar 2025, meeting the criterion's true-condition.

statement: Moving to models of care that avoid institutional environments would take significant time to achieve and cannot be addressed through these amendments, but I expect that the overall impact of these changes to be a reduction in the intrusive search practices.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki reporting on searches in secure residences (Section 7AA/annual residence reporting, Children's Commissioner or Independent Children's Monitor reviews, or Ministerial answers): true if the recorded number/rate of hands-on and strip searches after commencement is lower than the pre-amendment baseline, false if intrusive searches hold steady or rise.
reasoning: The amendment did take effect: the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 57) commenced 25 October 2025, and Oranga Tamariki's residence search guidance was updated 30 October 2025 'following the passing of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill and the removal of strip searches', leaving only scanner search, pat-down search and mail inspection as permitted methods. But the criterion asks for recorded numbers/rates of hands-on and strip searches AFTER commencement compared with a pre-amendment baseline, and no such post-commencement reporting has been published. Oranga Tamariki's Annual Report 2024/25 and the Independent Children's Monitor's Experiences of Care in Aotearoa 2024/25 both cover the year to 30 June 2025, entirely before commencement; the Monitor's youth justice residence monitoring visits reported to date were August-November 2024. The first reporting period that could test the prediction (2025/26) is not published as at 28 September 2026, and the stated resolve-by date of 31 December 2026 has not passed. Note also that the abolition of strip searches drives that category to zero by law, but whether total intrusive (hands-on) searching fell is exactly what the unpublished data would show.

statement: These services are currently being established, and I understand they’ll be in place in the middle of next year.
criterion: Whaikaha / Ministry of Social Development announcements, annual report or service listings for the People for Us initiative; true if the service was operating with disabled peer staff in residential services by around mid-2025, false if it had not been stood up by then.
reasoning: People for Us does exist and is staffed by disabled people, tangata whaikaha Maori and Pacific disabled people, visiting adults in DSS-contracted residential services (community group homes), delivered by People First NZ, Te Ahi Kaa and Vaka Tautua and funded by MSD. But it was not in place by mid-2025 as Upston expected. The Disability Support Services page for the service states it 'was designed back in 2024 with significant input from the disability community and the sector' and that 'since its soft launch in September last year, People for Us have visited more than 330 disabled people in community group homes up and down the motu' — written around the official launch on Monday 31 August 2026, so the soft launch was September 2025. DSS provider newsletters through June and July 2025 make no mention of the service being live. So the service was stood up, with disabled peer staff, in residential services — roughly a quarter later than the predicted middle of 2025, with national coverage and the formal launch only in 2026. The substance holds; the timing was overstated.

statement: I expect those forecasts will show a strengthening economy, lower interest rates, and reducing unemployment over the next few years.
criterion: The Treasury Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update 2024 published 17 December 2024: true if its central forecasts show real GDP growth strengthening, 90-day/interest rate track declining, and the unemployment rate declining across the forecast horizon; false if any of the three is forecast to worsen over that horizon.
reasoning: Checked against the Treasury Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update published 17 December 2024. Two of the three legs hold. Strengthening economy: real GDP forecast to grow 0.5% in 2024/25 then accelerate to 3.3% in 2025/26 before settling around 2.4-2.5% late in the horizon. Lower interest rates: the 90-day bank bill rate track declines, assumed to fall to a low of about 2.9% (implying an OCR low near 2.75%). The third leg does not hold as stated: unemployment was NOT forecast to decline across the horizon. It was forecast to rise from the last actual print of 4.8% (September 2024 quarter, published 6 November 2024) to a peak of 5.4% in the first half of 2025 before easing toward roughly 4.3% late in the forecast — the Budget 2025 economic outlook confirms the peak was '5.4 per cent in the first half of 2025 — the same as at HYEFU — before easing over the rest of the forecast period'. The criterion says false if any of the three is forecast to worsen over the horizon, and unemployment was forecast to worsen for the first two to three quarters. Read over 'the next few years' as a whole the net direction is down, so this is overstated rather than simply wrong.

statement: Once that reading is done tomorrow, we’ll have to endure thousands of submissions from people like Hobson’s Pledge. This is what they want, this is their wish, and National Party members who vote tomorrow are giving in to them and giving them what they want.
criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill, and Parliament's published submission count. True if written submissions received number in the thousands or more; false if fewer than one thousand submissions were received.
reasoning: The Justice Committee received over 307,000 written submissions on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill — the most-submitted-on bill in NZ parliamentary history — plus ~16,000 requests for oral submissions. The criterion's threshold (thousands or more) is cleared by two orders of magnitude. Halbert's framing attributed the volume to Hobson's Pledge-aligned submitters, and the composition ran the other way (90% opposed, 8% supportive), but 8% of 307,000 is still tens of thousands, and the criterion as written turns on count, not alignment.

statement: Taranaki don’t want this, those who care about our mokopuna don’t want this, but, instead, what we have, unfortunately, is a Government that is executing this so damned fast—so fast—that what you don’t realise is you’re fast tracking your way out of Parliament, and let this be a one-term Government, for all we can do.
criterion: Result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and subsequent government formation: true if the National-led coalition does not return to government, false if it forms a government for a second term.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the 2026 general election result and subsequent government formation. The election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026 and, as of today (28 September 2026), has not been held; no government formation has occurred. Nothing in the criterion can be evaluated yet, though it should resolve before the 31 December 2026 resolve-by date.

statement: Without social licence, we will see development tied up in courts.
criterion: Court records for projects approved under the Fast-track Approvals Act. True if one or more fast-track-listed or fast-track-approved projects becomes the subject of judicial review or other court proceedings brought by communities, iwi/hapū or councils; false if no such proceedings are filed against any fast-track project by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion is met: fast-track projects have been the subject of judicial review brought by iwi/hapū and community parties. In Ngāti Kuku Hapū Trust v EPA [2025] NZHC 2453, Ngāti Kuku Hapū Trust (a hapū of Ngāi Te Rangi) and the trustees of Ngā Hapū o Ngā Moutere Trust successfully reviewed the EPA's acceptance of Port of Tauranga's Stella Passage application; the High Court held it was out of scope of Schedule 2, the expert panel due to convene on 1 September 2025 was halted, and the Government responded by amending the Act. Jones v EPA [2026] NZHC 1872 (30 June 2026) is a second instance, over the Kings Quarry Expansion Stage 2 project at Waitoki. I checked for the disconfirming possibility that the Act's narrowed appeal rights had foreclosed such challenges; practitioner commentary documents the opposite — judicial review remains available to commenters and limits the effectiveness of the appeal restriction.

statement: Thinking of Masterton Town Hall is probably going to have to be demolished.
criterion: Masterton District Council records and local news reporting on the fate of the Masterton Town Hall building; true if the building is demolished (or a council decision to demolish is taken and acted on), false if it is retained, strengthened or remediated instead.
reasoning: The Masterton Town Hall was demolished, not retained or strengthened. Masterton District Council resolved in its Long-Term Plan 2024-34 to demolish the Town Hall and Municipal Buildings including the facade (budget capped at $25m); an independent commissioner granted resource consent for demolition in May 2025; demolition began 5 January 2026, the bulk of the buildings were down by 22 January 2026, the site was backfilled and levelled in May 2026, and a temporary pop-up park/activation space opened on the cleared site in June-July 2026. The council decision existed before the 2024-11-13 quote and has now been acted on, satisfying both limbs of the criterion.

statement: Banning disposable vapes will ensure that these products are removed from New Zealand’s retail market.
criterion: Post-commencement compliance/enforcement reporting by the Ministry of Health and Customs, plus retail availability surveys; true if disposable vapes are no longer sold at legal retail after the ban commences, false if they remain available through retailers.
reasoning: The ban on manufacture, distribution, sale and supply of disposable vapes commenced 17 June 2025. A post-commencement compliance audit published in Tobacco Control visited 87 specialist vape retailers in metropolitan Wellington (98% of stores in the region) and found disposables had largely left legal retail, but 4 stores (5%) were still observed selling disposable vapes, and 52% of stores were non-compliant with at least one assessed measure. The audit also found the market adapted rather than closed: ultra-low-cost reusable starter kits at NZ$15 or less were available in 89% of stores with similar youth-appealing attributes. Police have separately seized thousands of illicit vape products outside legal retail. So the substance holds -- disposables are mostly gone from legal retail shelves -- but the absolute claim that the ban 'will ensure that these products are removed from New Zealand's retail market' is materially overstated against a criterion whose false branch is 'they remain available through retailers'.

statement: It also will incentivise those enforcement officers out there to go out there and take that enforcement action. At the moment, they are weighing it up against the cost of the enforcement, but this does further incentivise them to do that.
criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health smokefree and vaping enforcement statistics (infringement notices issued, investigations and prosecutions of retailers) for the two years after the Act's commencement compared with the two years before; true if enforcement actions rise materially, false if they remain flat or fall.
reasoning: Enforcement action rose materially after commencement (penalties increased 18 December 2024; visibility rules and the disposables ban 17 June 2025). Health NZ reported on 4 March 2026 that more than 4,500 controlled purchase operations were carried out in the past year, up from around 2,000 the year before, and that 489 infringement fines were issued compared with 198 the year before -- roughly a 2.5x increase. The Ministry of Health's compliance monitoring page records that infringements issued under the Smokefree Act increased significantly again in the January-March 2026 quarter, attributed to increased monitoring of the June 2025 visibility restrictions. Prosecutions of repeat-offender retailers have also begun, with $36,000 in fines in initial sentencings. Two caveats: the criterion's full two-year post-commencement window does not close until December 2026, so the comparison is based on roughly the first 1.75 years (the magnitude of the rise nevertheless rules out the 'flat or fall' branch); and the increase is at least partly driven by 18 newly recruited compliance officers and the new visibility offences rather than solely by higher penalties changing officers' cost-benefit calculus, which is the mechanism the speaker asserted. The criterion as written tests the trend, and the trend is clearly up.

statement: We’re going to reach our target of Smokefree 2025 next year, but there is more work to be done in the vaping space.
