criterion: The New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2024/25 (or 2025/26) year, the official Smokefree 2025 measure; true if daily smoking prevalence is reported below 5% for the adult population, false if it remains at or above 5% (and materially false if the Māori and Pacific rates, against which the goal is also assessed, remain well above 5%).
reasoning: The criterion's named source — the New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for 2024/25 — reports 6.8% (95% CI 6.2–7.4%, ~294,000 adults), well above the 5% Smokefree 2025 threshold, and unchanged for three consecutive survey years (6.8–6.9% since 2022/23), an unprecedented plateau in the series. The criterion's 'materially false' condition also fires: Māori daily smoking is 15.0% and Pacific 10.3%, roughly three times and twice the target, with the most deprived quintile at 12.9%. PHCC's briefing on the 2024/25 survey states the government's goal of under 5% for all population groups 'will not be achieved', and RNZ reported on why the target was missed. No plausible disconfirming reading exists: I checked for any official claim that the goal had been met on an alternative measure and found none — the Ministry of Health's own release frames the finding as a long-term decline, not attainment. Rutherford's prediction that the target would be reached 'next year' (2025) is wrong.

statement: We’ve heard from landlords that the changes made to tenancy terminations in 2020 increased risk and costs, and discouraged them from renting to tenants who, for example, do not have perfect references or a steady job. The changes in the bill will address the concerns of landlords and encourage landlords back into the market.
criterion: MBIE/Tenancy Services bond data on the number of active private residential tenancy bonds (and Stats NZ rental dwelling stock) in the 12–18 months after the termination provisions come into force; true if active private rental tenancies rise relative to the pre-commencement trend, false if the count is flat or continues to decline.
reasoning: The termination provisions of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 commenced 30 January 2025, so the criterion's 12–18 month window is roughly Feb–Jul 2026. On the flow measure drawn from MBIE bond data, private tenancy activity clearly rose rather than stayed flat or declined: HUD's Housing Market Update (March Quarter 2026) shows seasonally-adjusted new private tenancies at about 14.4K/month in Feb 2026 (raw 16.5K), up from roughly 12.5K through 2022–24; interest.co.nz reports 13,326 bonds received in Nov 2025 (+10.7% YoY) and 15,246 in July 2026 (+12.5% YoY, a 10-year high for July). HUD also states 'rental supply has lifted, and tenant demand has dropped'. Three things stop this being a clean pass. (1) The criterion's actual named measure — the count of ACTIVE private bonds — cannot be read: Tenancy Services flags the Bond Hub migration as leaving data 'in a provisional state', 'not directly comparable with earlier periods', with '17,550 more active bonds because the two systems recorded the information differently'. (2) The rise sits on a pre-existing upward trend that began before commencement, so 'rise relative to the pre-commencement trend' is not established. (3) Looking for disconfirming evidence: HUD attributes the supply lift to elevated dwelling completions and subdued net migration, not landlords re-entering; Trade Me new rental listings were down 5% YoY in Feb 2026 and 8% YoY in July 2026; and rents for new tenancies fell 0.4% in the year to March 2026 with landlords 'facing increased competition' and poor returns. The substance (more rental tenancies in the market) holds, but the mechanism Potaka claimed is not supported and the criterion's stock measure is unreadable.

statement: Where this relates to the bill is that we will have higher levels of homelessness and higher levels of competition for rental markets.
criterion: Official homelessness measures (HUD/MSD homelessness insights reporting, transitional and emergency housing demand, and severe housing deprivation estimates) for 2025–26; true if measured homelessness is higher than at the time of the statement, false if it falls or is flat.
reasoning: On the criterion's homelessness limb the prediction holds. Against the November 2024 baseline, official and provider measures rose: HUD's June 2025 insights report put people living without shelter at 10.1 per 10,000 (up from 7.8 in 2018), Auckland provider counts rose from 426 in September 2024 to 809 (+90%), Christchurch +73% and Wellington rough sleeping +23%; emergency housing applications declined rose from 4% (March 2024) to 32% (March 2025) and 33.2% over Oct 2025–Mar 2026 on 12,207 applications; and transitional-housing entries by households living without shelter rose to 23.5%/291 people in March 2026 from 19.0%/248 in March 2025. Checking for disconfirming evidence: HUD's report to 31 March 2026 says numbers 'may have begun to stabilise', with Auckland (586, down from a Sept 2025 peak of 940), Christchurch, Rotorua and Palmerston North decreasing, and the social housing register down to 19.7K from ~25K in 2024; HUD also states explicitly it cannot conclude whether homelessness overall has changed since the 2023 Census, and no new severe housing deprivation estimate exists. Even so, Auckland at 586 in March 2026 remains well above the Sept 2024 figure, most councils HUD engaged reported increases over the preceding six months, and Te Matapihi reports Māori homelessness increasing. The second limb of the quote fails outright: rather than higher competition for rentals, rents for new tenancies fell 0.4% in the year to March 2026, existing-tenancy rent growth hit its lowest level on record, rental supply lifted and tenant demand dropped with longer vacancy periods.

statement: I want to go back to the fact that this bill is supposed to lead towards a greater supply of rental housing, and I’m just going to reiterate and make sure it’s on record that this bill will not lead to that, nor will any of the other actions that the Government are taking.
criterion: MBIE active bond / tenancy bond data and Stats NZ rental dwelling stock for the two years following the bill's commencement; true (prediction correct) if the number of private rental dwellings/active bonds does not rise above its level at commencement, false if rental stock rises materially over that period.
reasoning: The criterion's falsifying branch has already triggered, so the two-year window ending 30 Jan 2027 cannot rescue the prediction. MBIE's national active-bond series (location_id -99 in the monthly region CSV) stood at 478,893 at commencement (Jan 2025), 519,207 at Jan 2026 (+8.4%) and 523,449 at Jul 2026 (+9.3%). The criterion says the prediction is correct only if active bonds do NOT rise above the commencement level; they rose materially and cannot plausibly fall ~45,000 back below 478,893 by Jan 2027. Corroborating: HUD's March 2026 Housing Market Update says 'landlords are facing increased competition as rental supply has lifted, and tenant demand has dropped', with rents for new tenancies falling 0.4% in the year to March 2026. Important caveat the criterion does not test: this is an outcome test, not a causal one. Active bonds have grown every year on trend (+5.2% in 2023, +5.0% in 2024), and HUD attributes the supply lift to dwelling completions and subdued migration rather than the Act, so the rise does not itself show the bill produced it. Sepuloni's causal claim is therefore not disproved on its own terms — but against the criterion as written, the rental stock rose materially and the verdict is wrong.

statement: No-cause evictions will increase homelessness, no-cause evictions will lead to more people in emergency housing, no-cause evictions will widen the gap between Māori and the rest of us and will be a breach of Te Tiriti obligations by the Crown by failing to provide housing for people.
criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Report emergency housing (special needs grants / motel placements) counts and the Stats NZ–HUD homelessness insights reporting, comparing the period after terminations without cause became available (30 January 2025) with the preceding period; true if homelessness measures and emergency housing numbers rise after commencement, false if they fall or remain flat.
reasoning: The criterion requires BOTH emergency housing numbers AND homelessness measures to rise after terminations without cause became available on 30 January 2025. Emergency housing clearly did not rise: households in emergency housing fell from 2,880 (Jan 2024) to 498 (Dec 2024) and have been largely static or lower since — 471 in mid-2026 and 413 at 2026 Q1 — while quarterly EH grant spend fell from about $36m (Sep 2024 quarter) to $9.64m (Sep 2025 quarter) and 2025 saw 23,421 applications with 34% declined, against 103,920 with ~3% declined in 2023. That fall is driven by the separate August 2024 gateway tightening, but the criterion asks about levels, and the levels fell. Homelessness measures, by contrast, did rise over the year following commencement: Auckland rough sleeping counted by the Salvation Army went from 426 (Sep 2024) to 940 (Sep 2025), Auckland Council outreach counted 653 in Jan 2025 rising to 706 in Jan 2026, people on post-release orders with no fixed abode rose 23.7% (430 in Mar 2025 to 532 in Mar 2026), NHI 'no fixed abode' records rose from 929 (Jun 2024) to 1,037 (Jun 2025), and the share of households entering transitional housing because they were living without shelter rose from 19.0% (Mar 2025) to 23.5% (Mar 2026). By March 2026 HUD reports the without-shelter numbers 'may have begun to stabilise' (Auckland down to 586), while council staff in most areas still reported increases over the prior six months; the social housing register fell from ~25.8k to 19.7k. So one half of the criterion fails outright and the other holds for 2025 but is softening — partly_correct. Note also that HUD states explicitly it 'is not possible to tell whether changes described in this report... are attributable to policy changes', and neither source tests the Māori-gap or Te Tiriti-breach elements of the quote, which the criterion does not cover.

statement: We see landlords now that will come back into the market and will be prepared to put their asset up for rent—an asset that they have worked hard to earn their whole life, to finally buy a rental property to try and get a bit of extra investment, and put that back into the market now with these changes.
criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services active bond counts / rental stock series for the 12 months after the Act's provisions commenced; true if the number of active rental bonds rises materially from the level at commencement, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion is MBIE Tenancy Services active bond counts over the 12 months after commencement (30 January 2025), correct if they rise materially and wrong if flat or falling. Reading the national row (location_id -99, 'ALL') of MBIE's monthly-by-region rental bond CSV: active bonds were 478,893 in Jan 2025 and 519,207 in Jan 2026, a rise of 40,314 (+8.4%); by Jul 2026 they were 523,449. That is faster than the two preceding years (+5.2% in the year to Jan 2024, +5.0% in the year to Jan 2025). New tenancies (seasonally adjusted bonds lodged) also ran at ~14.4k/month by Feb 2026 against ~12.8k in early 2024, and HUD's March 2026 Housing Market Update records that 'rental supply has lifted' with longer vacancy periods and falling new-tenancy rents. Disconfirming checks: Trade Me listing stock was down 5% year-on-year in April 2026 and realestate.co.nz national rental listing stock fell 0.9% in April 2026 — but those are listing flows, not the stock of tenancies, and Crockers separately reports NZ rental supply at a record high. One data caveat: closed-bond counts for Nov 2025 (5,106) and Dec 2025 (6,666) are roughly half the normal ~11,000, consistent with the Bond Hub migration MBIE warns makes recent data provisional; adjusting for that still leaves ~+7% growth, comfortably material. Attribution caveat the criterion does not test: the active-bond series has risen every year regardless of tenancy law, and HUD credits dwelling completions and weak demand, so this does not establish that the Act brought landlords back — only that the supply measure the criterion names rose.

statement: Interest rates falling, and what will happen on 27 November—what will happen on 27 November? We don’t know; we don’t know, but we know it’s heading in the right direction—we know it’s heading in the right direction—and the introduction of pet bonds.
criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement of 27 November 2024 and subsequent OCR decisions through 2025; true if the OCR was cut on 27 November 2024 and the OCR track continued downward over the following year, false if the OCR was held or raised on that date or reversed upward.
reasoning: RBNZ cut the OCR by 50bp to 4.25% at the 27 November 2024 Monetary Policy Statement, and the OCR track continued downward through the following year without reversal: 3.75% (Feb 2025), 3.25% (May), 3.00% (20 Aug), 2.50% (8 Oct), 2.25% (26 Nov 2025). Both limbs of the criterion's true condition are met (cut on that date; continued downward track), and the false limbs (hold, raise, or upward reversal) did not occur at any point in the window.

statement: It’s going to increase the homelessness that we experience in our largest city in this country, that we’re already struggling with.
criterion: HUD homelessness insights reporting and Auckland rough-sleeping/emergency housing counts for the period after the Act commences; true if measured Auckland homelessness rises above the level at commencement, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 commenced 30 January 2025 (pet provisions 1 December 2025). Auckland rough-sleeping counts: 426 (Sept 2024), 653 (Jan 2025, i.e. at commencement), 809 (May 2025), 940 (Sept 2025 peak), and 706 in January 2026 per Auckland Council data cited in HUD's homelessness insights report to 31 March 2026 — still above the 653 commencement level at the resolve date. The criterion's true branch (measured Auckland homelessness rises above the level at commencement) is met; the false branch (flat or falls relative to commencement) is not. Disconfirming evidence checked: Auckland counts did fall from the September 2025 peak and HUD reports Auckland Housing First numbers down from 169 to 86, but the level never returned to or below the commencement figure. Caveat outside the criterion: the criterion tests the level, not causation — providers, HUD and commentators attribute most of the rise to emergency-housing eligibility changes rather than to this Act, so Halbert's attribution is not itself verified here.

statement: Nevertheless, we are going to have whole classes of vulnerable people in New Zealand for whom insurance will be a privilege because the places in which they live are vulnerable to climate change.
criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand, Treasury, ICNZ or Stats NZ reporting on insurance retreat; true if by the resolve date there is documented material withdrawal of cover or unaffordable premiums affecting identifiable groups of residential properties in climate-exposed New Zealand locations, false if cover and pricing in those locations remain broadly available and comparable to the national market.
reasoning: The resolve date (2030-12-31) has not passed, but the criterion's true condition is already partly documented, so not_yet_due would understate the evidence. Documented withdrawal affecting an identifiable group of climate-exposed residential properties: AA Insurance wrote to the Buller District Mayor at the end of 2025 halting new home, business and landlord cover in the 7825 postcode (Westport, Carters Beach, Cape Foulwind) after its internal flood-exposure limits were reached. RBNZ's May 2026 Financial Stability Report put insurance affordability on its financial stability risk register for the first time, naming affordability, underinsurance and geographic retreat from high-hazard areas, with the national average domestic-buildings premium ~$2,900 rising faster than CPI since ~2009 and NHC estimating ~60,000 uninsured homes. Disconfirming evidence, which is why this is not 'correct': the same RBNZ report states residential insurance coverage 'currently remains high'; the Westport action is one insurer, new business only, existing policies unaffected, and stated as temporary; and the 60,000 uninsured homes figure is national, not specific to climate-exposed locations. So retreat is documented at identifiable margins, but Russell's 'whole classes of vulnerable people' is not yet established, and the window to 2030 remains open.

statement: Forecasts indicate that by 2030 more than 2.8 million people will be living within 80 kilometres of Tīkapa Moana.
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates/projections for 2030 aggregated over the territorial authorities lying within 80 km of the Hauraki Gulf (Auckland, Thames-Coromandel, Hauraki, Waikato district and adjacent areas) — true if the total exceeds 2.8 million, false if it falls short.
reasoning: The line is a real pre-existing published forecast (it appears verbatim in Sea Change / Hauraki Gulf Marine Spatial Plan material, e.g. Forest & Bird's Sea Change pamphlet), so Potaka was relaying an existing projection. Checked against the criterion's named source, Stats NZ 2023-base subnational projections (medium series): Auckland region 1,886,100 (2028) and 2,003,800 (2033), so about 1.93m in 2030; Waikato region 552,200 (2028) and 584,700 (2033), so about 0.57m. Auckland plus the entire Waikato region is only about 2.50m, and Waikato's inland districts (Taupo, Waitomo, South Waikato, much of Waipa) lie outside 80 km. Aggregating just the TAs the criterion names (Auckland, Thames-Coromandel, Hauraki, Waikato district and near neighbours incl. Hamilton and Matamata-Piako) gives roughly 2.1-2.4m, short of 2.8m. A generous 80 km buffer of the Marine Park (which runs Mangawhai to Waihi Beach, bringing Whangarei and Tauranga inside the radius) gets to roughly 2.7-2.9m, so the threshold is straddled depending on how the buffer is drawn. The Hauraki Gulf Forum's own State of our Gulf 2023 describes the 14,000 km2 Gulf region as home to 'around 2 million people', and the older Sea Change-era figures (Auckland 1.6m today to 2.5m by 2041) rest on a pre-2020 trajectory. Substance holds - a very large and fast-growing population adjacent to the Gulf - but the specific 2.8m threshold is not confirmed by current Stats NZ projections under the criterion's aggregation, and the 2030 estimate itself will not exist until 2031.

statement: E taku iwi [To my Māori people]: 35,000 people marched yesterday across that bridge, and they will arrive here, at Parliament.
criterion: News reporting of the Toitū Te Tiriti hīkoi's arrival at Parliament grounds in Wellington; true if the march reaches Parliament, false if it disperses or is stopped before arriving.
reasoning: The Hikoi mo te Tiriti reached Parliament grounds in Wellington on 19 November 2024, five days after Waititi spoke. Police estimated about 42,000 participants; Parliament grounds reached capacity and crowds spilled onto surrounding CBD streets, and police described the event as peaceful. It was neither dispersed nor stopped before arriving, so the criterion is met. One caveat on the quoted number: police estimated about 5,000 people crossed the Auckland Harbour Bridge on 13 November (organisers claimed a higher total), so the '35,000 across that bridge' figure is well above the police estimate for the bridge leg - though the final Wellington turnout did exceed 35,000. The criterion judges the arrival, which happened.

statement: As I said at the start, I’m very confident that the Chief of Defence Force and his team will work constructively in good faith.
criterion: PSA and NZDF bargaining records and any Employment Relations Authority proceedings arising from this dispute; true if bargaining continued and reached a settlement without a good-faith breach being alleged and upheld against NZDF, false if a bad-faith claim against NZDF was upheld or NZDF withdrew from bargaining.
reasoning: Bargaining continued and settled, with no good-faith breach upheld against NZDF. Timeline: bargaining from August 2024, PSA industrial action from September, mediation on 28 November 2024, a 21-day strike from 8am 18 December 2024 to 6pm 8 January 2025, then two days of Employment Relations Authority facilitation in January 2025 producing a settlement that PSA members ratified in late February 2025 with pay increases for every member covered by the collective agreement. NZDF did not withdraw from bargaining. On the good-faith limb: the only relevant adjudication is Chief of New Zealand Defence Force v NZ PSA [2024] NZEmpC 251 (full Court, 16 December 2024), which arose from the earlier bargaining round; the Court found NZDF passed on union-negotiated rates intending to deter union membership but held that s 59B(2) requires both intention and effect, and since the union accepted there was no undermining effect, there was no breach of good faith - and no unlawful preference. So a good-faith claim was alleged in the prior round but not upheld, and none was upheld arising from this dispute. Caveat on the spirit rather than the criterion: the process was adversarial - a zero-percent opening offer held through two mediations, sustained strike action, and the Minister of Defence invoking powers unused since 2001 to have military personnel cover struck civilian work - so 'work constructively' is a generous description of how the settlement was reached, even though the criterion's test is satisfied.

statement: Now, the Government hasn’t confirmed this, but chances are Parliament’s going to knock off on Wednesday, 18 December of that week.
criterion: The 2024 parliamentary sitting record / Hansard: true if the House's last sitting day before the summer adjournment was Wednesday 18 December 2024; false if the House sat later (e.g. 19 December) or rose earlier.
reasoning: 18 December 2024 was a Wednesday and was the House's final sitting day of 2024. Hansard for 18 Dec 2024 contains the end-of-year debate 'Adjournment and Sittings of the House', in which the PM moved adoption of the 2025 sitting programme (House to resume 28-30 January 2025). Corroborated by Luxon's 18 Dec 2024 post describing his 'final speech to Parliament for the year', RNZ's 'Oral Questions for Wednesday 18 December 2024', and RNZ's report on the extra members'-bills morning added to the final sitting day. No Hansard record exists for 19 or 20 December 2024, so the House did not sit later.

statement: Otherwise, we’re just going to be sitting here in maybe—well, I think the original motion was meant to be 14—we’re going to be sitting here again on 14 February with the Ministry of Defence again asking for this motion to be extended.
criterion: Hansard and the Order Paper for February–March 2025: true if a further Government notice of motion under section 9 of the Defence Act authorising NZDF personnel to cover striking Ministry of Defence civilian staff was moved on or about 14 February 2025; false if no such extension motion was brought because the dispute settled or the cover lapsed.
reasoning: The 19 November 2024 Ministerial Statement/motion extended the section 9 authorisation from 2 December 2024 until 14 February 2025, deliberately chosen to cover the whole period of strike action. The strike ran 18 December 2024 to 6pm 8 January 2025 and then ended; a settlement was agreed after two days of Employment Relations Authority facilitation in January 2025 and ratified in the week of 27 February 2025. No further extension motion was moved on or about 14 February 2025 - the authorisation simply ran its term. The Government's 2025 Defence (Workforce) Amendment Bill rationale refers only to the December 2024 industrial action as the occasion on which Parliament had to be asked, and no Hansard item, Order Paper entry or news report of a February/March 2025 re-authorisation exists. This matches the criterion's explicit 'false' branch: no extension motion because the dispute settled.

statement: No doubt the good-faith negotiations that are taking place now will be resolved as soon as possible. We hope and expect that this will take place by late January or, if not by then, then mid-February.
criterion: PSA and NZDF public statements / collective agreement settlement records: true if the NZDF civilian collective bargaining dispute was settled on or before mid-February 2025; false if the dispute remained unresolved (or strike action continued) after that date.
reasoning: Strike action ended at 6pm on 8 January 2025 and a settlement was agreed after two days of Employment Relations Authority facilitation during January 2025, so the negotiations did move to an in-principle resolution inside Penk's window and no strike action continued past mid-February. But the dispute was not actually settled by mid-February: PSA members voted to ratify the new collective agreement in the week of 27 February 2025, which is when both the PSA and NZDF announced the dispute settled - roughly two weeks past his stated outer bound. Substance holds, timing materially overstated.

statement: It’s true—I wasn’t invited to speak. But my message to the general audience at the hīkoi is the same: we will not support the bill beyond first reading, and therefore it won’t become law.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill; true if the bill was defeated or lapsed without becoming law, false if it passed third reading and received Royal assent.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was defeated or lapsed without becoming law. The parliamentary record shows the bill passed first reading 68–54 on 14 Nov 2024, was reported back by the Justice Committee recommending it not proceed, and was defeated at second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11 (only ACT in favour). National voted against, as Luxon said it would. There was no third reading and no Royal assent, so the bill never became law. Checked for disconfirming evidence (a later revival, a restored bill, or assent) and found none — ACT said it would set out 'next steps' before the 2026 election, but no bill of this kind has passed.

statement: That is why the National Party won’t be supporting the bill beyond first reading and it won’t become law, unless the Opposition support it.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Treaty Principles Bill; true if the bill fails to pass into law (defeated at or before second reading, or lapses at the end of the 54th Parliament), false if it receives Royal assent.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the Treaty Principles Bill fails to pass into law (defeated at or before second reading, or lapses at the end of the 54th Parliament). It was defeated at second reading on 10 April 2025, 112–11, with only ACT's 11 members supporting it; National voted against, and the Opposition did not support it either, so the speaker's escape clause ('unless the Opposition support it') was never triggered. No Royal assent. Both limbs of the prediction — National not supporting it beyond first reading, and the bill not becoming law — are borne out by the record.

statement: That is what we really need to consider this afternoon, and just simple things like making sure that punctuation is correct so that it actually is in order, so that once it’s all—because I’m assuming, unless members across the floor choose to come and join us on this side, this will eventually pass.
criterion: The Hansard record of the vote on the Government notice of motion No. 1 in the sitting of 19 November 2024; true if the motion was agreed to, false if it was defeated or lapsed.
reasoning: The motion in question is identified in Hansard as 'Motions — Defence Act 1990—Extension of Authorisations' (19 Nov 2024): Government notice of motion No. 1 extending the authorisations of 5, 11 and 18 November 2024 for armed forces personnel to do the work of striking NZDF civilian staff (RNZAF Base Auckland firefighting, security at Defence House/Pipitea House, camps and bases, and Kauri Point) from 2 December 2024 out to 14 February 2025. The record of that sitting day shows the motion under s 9(8) of the Defence Act 1990 was agreed to, so Bennett's forecast that 'this will eventually pass' holds. Caveat on sourcing: parliament.nz served bot-protection pages to the fetch tool and its Hansard pages render client-side, so the outcome comes from the search-indexed text of the Hansard segment and the day's daily-progress record rather than a page I rendered directly. Disconfirming checks found nothing: no report of the government losing the vote or of the authorisations lapsing, military backfill continued through the December 2024 strike, and the 2025 Defence (Workforce) Amendment Bill was justified as removing the requirement for such House debates rather than as fixing a failed extension.

statement: Does he recognise, then, that this approach to cracking down on gangs and locking them up in prison is not going to achieve the reduction in gang membership that he says he wants?
criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership numbers; false (i.e. the prediction was wrong) if recorded gang membership falls materially between November 2024 and the end of 2026, true if membership is flat or higher over that period.
reasoning: Criterion: wrong if recorded gang membership falls materially Nov 2024 → end 2026; correct if flat or higher. Every National Gang List reading in the window rises. Nov 2024 ≈ 9,460 (Mitchell's written answer put it 190 above the ~9,270 of Nov 2023 / the 2023 election). 10 July 2025: 10,009 — first time above 10,000 and a record, which the Police Minister called 'highly concerning'. Early Nov 2025: ~10,242–10,368. Feb 2026: 10,478 (+13%, +1,208, on the 2023 election), at which point gang members narrowly outnumbered sworn police (10,475). That is ~+1,000 (~11%) on the Nov 2024 baseline, so the crackdown had not produced a reduction. Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for a reported fall. The only downward pressure on the series is a 2024/25 'sanitising' of the list (which Luxon and Mitchell said they would not claim as success) and criminologist Jarrod Gilbert's argument that the patch ban now causes an undercount — both would understate growth, not hide a fall. Caveat on timing: the criterion's window closes 31 Dec 2026 and the most recent published figure I can find is February 2026, so the final ~7 months are unobserved; reversing the verdict would need a drop of more than 1,000 in that time.

statement: Well, as I've said, the bill is being introduced at first reading, it won't be supported at second reading, and therefore it won't become law.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill: true if the bill is defeated at or before second reading and does not receive Royal assent; false if it passes second reading or becomes law.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill is defeated at or before second reading and gets no Royal assent. The bill was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025, 112 votes to 11 — only ACT's 11 members supported it, while National, NZ First, Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori all voted against. National voting it down at second reading is exactly what Luxon said would happen. The bill did not proceed to a third reading, received no Royal assent, and is not law; I found no revival of the bill after April 2025 (Seymour said ACT would keep campaigning on the issue, and commentators noted a citizens-initiated referendum remains theoretically possible, but neither is this bill passing).

statement: Because we have a coalition agreement—we’re supporting the bill to first reading. We honour our commitments and our agreements to each other in this coalition Government, and we’re saying we’re not supporting it at second reading. It won’t become law unless the Opposition parties vote for it.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill: true if the bill fails to pass into law (defeated or lapsed); false if it is enacted.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the bill fails to pass into law. It was voted down at second reading on 10 April 2025, 112–11, and was never enacted; the resolve-by date of 31 Dec 2025 has passed with the bill dead. The specifics of Luxon's statement also hold: National supported it to first reading under the coalition agreement and then voted against at second reading, and the opposition parties (Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori) all voted against, so no opposition votes rescued it. Only ACT's 11 votes were in favour.

statement: Around 2,000 claimants per year will experience improved access to justice as a result of this bill.
criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal case statistics for the first full year after the raised jurisdiction takes effect: true if roughly 2,000 (order of magnitude, say 1,000–3,000) additional claims per year are filed in the $30,000–$60,000 band; false if the number of claims in that band is materially below that range.
reasoning: The Disputes Tribunal Amendment Act 2025 raised the Tribunal's financial jurisdiction from $30,000 to $60,000 with effect from 24 January 2026 (three months after royal assent in October 2025). The criterion requires Ministry of Justice case statistics for the first full year after commencement, i.e. the year to 24 January 2027 (or FY2026/27). As at 28 September 2026 that year is not complete and MoJ has published no statistics on claims filed in the new $30,001-$60,000 band; its jurisdiction page still carries only the forward-looking 'about 2,000 claims per year could see improved access to justice' modelling that Goldsmith was quoting. No evidence either way is available yet, so this is not a failing grade.

statement: We’ve heard from the Minister that she’s planning to bring some new legislation into the House next year, and the question this begs is: why has it been separated out?
criterion: The Order Paper / Parliament's bills register for 2025. True if a further Government vaping or smokefree-environments bill is introduced during 2025; false if no such bill is introduced in that year.
reasoning: Searching the subject (NZ smokefree/vaping legislation 2025) rather than the direction: no further Government vaping or smokefree-environments bill was introduced to the House during 2025. The legislative activity in 2025 was implementation of the December 2024 Act — the disposable-vape ban and retail visibility rules commencing 17 June 2025 — plus secondary legislation (Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Product Safety Requirements for Vaping Products) Amendment Regulations 2025, SL 2025/152), not a new bill. Disconfirming check: the promised broader reform of vaping, smokeless tobacco and oral nicotine regulation was still pre-legislative at the end of 2025 — Cabinet had agreed only 'in principle' (May 2025), and at the health select committee on 3 December 2025 Costello said the advisory group's recommendations were 'still being considered', with no bill before the House. Searches of legislation.govt.nz's Government bill series for 2025 return no Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products bill. Caveat on attribution: the prediction embedded here is the Minister's plan as reported by Leary, not Leary's own forecast; judged against the criterion as written, the bill did not appear in 2025.

statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I stand by my full statement, which was, “we had set a very clear plan that it will allow the books to return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2027-28. If we had stuck to the spending plans of the last Government, that date would have been pushed out until 2031, an unacceptable outcome.” In answer to the second part of the question, no.
criterion: The Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2028 (and intervening Treasury forecasts): true if OBEGAL is in surplus for 2027/28 on the measure referred to; false if OBEGAL is in deficit for that year or the forecast surplus date has been pushed beyond 2027/28.
reasoning: The forecast return to OBEGAL surplus has been pushed well beyond 2027/28, which the criterion explicitly makes a falsifier. At HYEFU 2024 (17 December 2024, a month after this answer) Treasury pushed the surplus out and the Government adopted the ACC-excluding OBEGALx measure. Budget 2026 (28 May 2026) forecasts an OBEGALx deficit of $5.1b in 2027/28, with the first surplus of $2.6b in 2028/29 — which Willis presented as the surplus date coming forward a year relative to HYEFU 2025, i.e. it had slipped to 2029/30 in the interim. On the unadjusted OBEGAL measure that Bishop's quoted statement named, surplus is not forecast until 2029/30 ($2.3b). Disconfirming check: no post-2024 Treasury forecast restores a 2027/28 OBEGAL surplus, and Treasury itself puts only a 50-60% probability on reaching surplus within the forecast period. The 2027/28 outturn is not final until the Financial Statements of the Government are published in late 2028, but the criterion admits intervening forecasts as decisive on the push-out.

statement: I think the GCC and, particularly, Saudi Arabia, who have a great desire for the food that we produce and the lamb that we grow in New Zealand, will actually replace what Iran was, so that we can sell more.
criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade data for sheepmeat exports: true if Saudi Arabia/GCC sheepmeat export volumes rise to a share of NZ lamb exports comparable to Iran's historical peak; false if GCC sheepmeat exports remain a minor share.
reasoning: The criterion's horizon runs to 2029-12-31 and the mechanism the prediction rests on has barely begun: the NZ-GCC FTA was concluded 31 Oct 2024 but MFAT still lists it as "concluded but not in force", with tariffs on 99% of exports eliminated only over ten years. Interim evidence does not yet support the claim: NZ shipped ~16,000 t of lamb to Persian Gulf markets in the year to 30 Sep 2025 (Saudi Arabia about half), and sheepmeat to Saudi Arabia was worth ~NZ$85m in 2024, against total red meat to the GCC of ~NZ$245-298m — a minor share. Iran's historical peak was far larger: a 200,000 t four-year contract from 1979, and Iran/Iraq together taking about a third of NZ lamb exports in 1980-81, roughly one lamb in four. So on today's numbers the "false" branch is where the data sits, but the prediction was explicitly forward-looking and its resolve-by date is more than three years away, so it cannot be graded yet. Checked for the opposite too: no evidence found of a step-change in GCC sheepmeat volumes since the FTA was concluded.

statement: As we say in politics, it’s best not to count your chickens before they’re in the umu, but I am confident that there will be enough support—hopefully, unanimous support—for this bill to get through its third reading.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading, false if it was voted down. The 'unanimous' element is true only if no party voted against.
reasoning: Both elements of the criterion hold. The Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 20 November 2024 — the same sitting day as the quote — and it passed with unanimous support: no party voted against. The National Party, which had opposed the bill at its first reading on 10 April 2024, switched to support after select committee amendments, with Cameron Brewer confirming National's support during the third reading debate. Looked specifically for a dissenting party (National, NZ First or ACT voting against, or a split vote) and found none reported in any account of the third reading; multiple independent outlets describe it as unanimous, and the Act received Royal assent on 25 November 2024 as Act 2024 No 48.

statement: Going forward, yes, the process will start very, very soon. After five days, all those individuals who will be eligible after this bill goes through will be able to apply to reclaim their citizenship.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / NZ Legislation commencement record for the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Act 2024; true if applications could be lodged within about five days of the bill passing/Royal assent, false if the opening of applications came materially later.
reasoning: The commencement record matches the five-day figure. The bill passed its third reading on Wednesday 20 November 2024, received Royal assent on Monday 25 November 2024 (five days later), and the Act came into force the day after assent — 26 November 2024. The Department of Internal Affairs' release of 26 November 2024 announces the Act as law and states that individuals can apply directly to DIA, and applications were being lodged immediately: DIA had approved 49 applications by early December 2024. Contemporaneous confirmation from the same debate: National's Cameron Brewer told the House that, assuming the Governor-General signed on the Monday, people could apply from the Tuesday. Six days from the statement, one day from assent — within the criterion's "about five days"; no evidence found of a materially later opening (no separate Order in Council or deferred application window).

statement: I think there’s going to be a lot more Chinese EVs that are very cheap and are hitting Europe about now and we will get them at some point anyway. They will be more than cost-competitive, so we don’t need a fringe benefit tax for EV uptake.
criterion: NZTA / Motor Industry Association new and used vehicle registration data and advertised NZ retail prices: true if Chinese-brand EVs (e.g. BYD, MG, GWM) rise materially as a share of NZ EV registrations and at least one model is priced at or below a comparable petrol model; false if Chinese-brand EV share is flat or falling and no Chinese EV reaches price parity with a comparable ICE vehicle.
reasoning: Both legs of the criterion hold. Share: Chinese brands rose from ~10.3% of NZ new vehicle registrations in Aug 2025 to 18.7% in Aug 2026 (21.6% of the passenger market in April 2026, six Chinese brands at 1,536 units vs 683 a year earlier); BYD went from 51 registrations in May 2025 to 471 in May 2026 and third overall (7.1%) in July 2026; Chinese-brand models now top the BEV charts (BYD Atto 3 #1 with 107 in Aug 2026, MG S5 #3, BYD Sealion 7 #4), and Dongfeng entered as the third-largest BEV brand from a standing start. Price parity: the BYD Atto 1 Essential launched at NZ$29,990 — identical to the Mazda2 ($29,990) and Suzuki Swift RSC ($29,990) and below the Toyota Yaris (from $33,490); the Dongfeng Box matched at $29,990, and motoring press describe the Atto 1 as the first EV to reach full price compatibility with an internal-combustion car in NZ. Checked the disconfirming case (flat/falling Chinese EV share) and found the opposite — BYD NZ sold out with 90-day waits. Only caveat: the entry Atto 1 is $3,000 above the cheapest comparable Swift variant (GLZ, $26,990), so parity is at the segment level rather than a universal undercut, which the criterion's 'at or below a comparable petrol model' still satisfies.

statement: I’m sorry that it won’t be passing, but we support it.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Income Tax (Clean Transport FBT Exclusion) Amendment Bill: true if the motion was not agreed to; false if the bill proceeded to select committee.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the first-reading motion was agreed to. It was not: the Income Tax (Clean Transport FBT Exclusion) Amendment Bill (Julie Anne Genter, Members' Bill 35-1 2024) was negatived at first reading on 20 November 2024, the same sitting day as the quote, on a division of 55 ayes to 68 noes with no abstentions. It did not proceed to select committee and will not become law. Williams' prediction that it would not pass was therefore right. Note on sourcing: parliament.nz's Hansard and bill pages are behind a bot-protection wall and could not be fetched directly; the division figures come from WhereTheyStand's bill record, corroborated independently by Deloitte NZ's tax-developments roundup (bill 'read and terminated at the first reading') and the bill's own legislation.govt.nz record.

statement: Oh, it’s OK—this bill will be running for several months, but thank you, Mr Speaker.
criterion: The Parliament bill record for the Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill: true if the bill is still before the House or the Justice Committee at least three months after 20 November 2024; false if it is discharged, defeated or completed its passage before 20 February 2025.
reasoning: The criterion is whether the Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill was still before the House or the Justice Committee three months after 20 November 2024. It was. The bill (Greg Fleming, Members' Bill 36-1 2024, introduced 21 March 2024) passed its first reading in mid-December 2024 and was referred to the Justice Committee, which called for submissions closing 13 February 2025 and was due to report on 16 June 2025. So on 20 February 2025 it was live before the committee — not discharged, defeated, or through its passage. Records as of mid-2026 still show it 'in progress', awaiting second reading. Checked the disconfirming possibility that it had been killed or fast-tracked to completion before 20 February 2025 and found no such record. Minor discrepancy in secondary sources on the exact first-reading date (17 vs 18 December 2024); immaterial to the criterion.

statement: It’s a day when this Parliament does what no other Parliament has done over that 42 years, despite several requests to take action; and it’s a day when this Parliament will be unanimous—I’m confident we’ll be unanimous, Teanau—in supporting this legislation to correct that wrong, which was done 42 years ago when that House was unanimous in creating the wrong in the first place.
criterion: The Hansard division/voice-vote record for the third reading of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Bill; true if it passed with all parties in support and no party voting against, false if any party or member opposed.
reasoning: The Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 20 November 2024 with unanimous support from all parties — no party or member voted against. National, which had opposed at first reading (party vote 74–49, 10 April 2024), confirmed support at third reading via Cameron Brewer; the Greens, Labour, ACT, NZ First and Te Pāti Māori also supported. The '42 years' arithmetic (1982 Act to 2024) is also right. Caveat: I could not open the Hansard transcript itself (parliament.nz/legislation.govt.nz returned 403/404 to the fetcher), so whether the question was put as a voice vote or a recorded party vote is unverified; unanimity and passage are corroborated by RNZ, NZ Herald, PMN, the Greens' release and Wikipedia.

statement: It is the unity of our Samoan community that has led to what will be a successful passing of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Bill here today.
criterion: Hansard third-reading record for the Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading on 20 November 2024, false if it is voted down, adjourned or not completed that day.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether the bill passed its third reading on 20 November 2024. It did: the third reading was completed that sitting (Wednesday 20 November 2024) and the bill passed with unanimous support; royal assent followed on 25 November 2024 and the Act commenced 26 November 2024. It was not voted down, adjourned or left incomplete. (The speaker's causal framing — that community unity produced the result — is not part of the criterion and is not tested here; note that RNZ later reported divided community opinion about the Act's scope, particularly its exclusion of descendants.)

statement: When this bill passes in a few minutes and she submits her application on Monday, her mother Alofa will again be a citizen of Niu Sila.
criterion: Hansard third-reading record for the Restoring Citizenship Removed by Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Bill on 20 November 2024: true if the bill passed its third reading that sitting and the resulting Act restores citizenship, on registration/application, to Samoan-born people of Alofa Toma's cohort who lost it under the 1982 Act; false if the bill did not pass or if the restoration route does not cover a person born in 1940 applying in this way.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion hold. The bill passed its third reading that sitting (20 November 2024, unanimous), received royal assent 25 November and came into force 26 November 2024. The resulting Act restores New Zealand citizenship, on application to the Department of Internal Affairs, to people born in Western Samoa between 13 May 1924 and 1 January 1949 (plus limited spouse/children cases) whose citizenship was removed by the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 — so a person born in 1940 is squarely inside the eligible cohort, and citizenship comes as of right rather than through standard residency/citizenship processes. The route demonstrably works: over 2,000 people have had citizenship restored under it. Two small slips the criterion does not test: applications opened Tuesday 26 November, not the Monday Fleming named (National's Cameron Brewer told the House 'people can apply from Tuesday'), and citizenship takes effect on the grant rather than on submitting the form.

statement: However, as a consequence of quota allocation decisions, not the least of which is a massive expansion of the catchable amount of snapper in New Zealand, I imagine that the value of fish is going to shrink.
criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index / Food Price Index fish and seafood subgroup, comparing the index level at November 2024 with subsequent quarters; true if fish prices fall below the November 2024 level, false if they are flat or higher.
reasoning: The premise held — snapper catch limits for SNA 2, 7 and 8 rose 28% from 1 October 2024 — but fish prices did not shrink. Stats NZ's fresh-fish weighted-average retail price was NZD 44.95/kg at November 2024 and then 44.78 (Mar 2025), 44.64 (Jun 2025), 47.11 (Sep 2025), 46.61 (Dec 2025), reaching 49.46 by June 2026: two quarters essentially flat (-0.4%/-0.7%) followed by clear increases, ~3.7% above the November 2024 level by the resolve-by date. The wider FPI meat/poultry/fish group rose 5.4% in the year to May 2025 and 8.9% in the year to January 2026. The criterion treats flat-or-higher as false, so this fails on both the flat quarters and the subsequent rise. Checked the opposite case: no Stats NZ series or release shows a fish/seafood price fall below the November 2024 level in any subsequent quarter.

statement: Banks have agreed to implement confirmation of payee, which will be in place by Easter next year, and I’m working with them on a compensation scheme for scam victims.
criterion: NZ Banking Association and individual bank announcements on the confirmation of payee rollout; true if the service was live across participating retail banks on or before Easter (20 April) 2025, false if the rollout was still incomplete at that date.
reasoning: The CoP rollout began 28 November 2024 across 13 participating retail banks with a stated completion target of Easter 2025, and the individually datable late entrants all went live before 20 April 2025: Bank of China (January 2025), ICBC (end of March 2025) and CCB New Zealand (15 April 2025, internet banking). No NZBA, media, Consumer NZ or Banking Ombudsman source in the following year reports the Easter target being missed, and the infrastructure provider records 13 banks live covering over 95% of consumer accounts. Caveats: I found no single dated 'all banks live' announcement at Easter, CCB's launch covered internet banking only, and Raidiam's 'six months and twelve days' phrasing could imply the last of the 13 landed after Easter — so the verdict rests on dated per-bank go-lives plus the absence of any reported slip rather than one confirming statement. The second half of the quote also materialised: NZBA announced a voluntary scam reimbursement scheme in April 2025, in force from 30 November 2025.

statement: Food and fibre export revenue is expected to reach $54.6 billion this year and will hit a record $66.6 billion in 2028.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for the Primary Industries actual food and fibre export revenue for the year to June 2028: true if it reaches approximately $66.6 billion or more and is a record, false if materially below that figure.
reasoning: The criterion asks for MPI's actual food and fibre export revenue for the year to June 2028, which has not occurred (today is 28 September 2026) and will not be reported until late 2028. Only forecasts exist. For context, SOPI June 2026 puts the year to 30 June 2026 at about $64.3 billion, well above the $54.6 billion Bayly cited for 2024, so the 2028 figure is not obviously off-track — but nothing in the criterion can be resolved yet.

statement: I’m looking forward, actually, to the apology that comes from the other side of the House when the figures are released shortly that show agriculture is already meeting its targets.
criterion: Emissions figures released after 21 November 2024 (NZ Greenhouse Gas Inventory / MfE emissions projections); true if those figures show agricultural biogenic methane emissions already at or below the legislated 2030 target trajectory of 10% below 2017 levels, false if they show agriculture short of that trajectory.
reasoning: The figures released after 21 Nov 2024 do not show agricultural biogenic methane at or below the 10%-below-2017 target. The Greenhouse Gas Inventory 1990–2023 (released 15 April 2025) showed only a 2% drop in agricultural emissions in 2023; the Climate Change Commission's 2025 monitoring report puts the agriculture sector 6.0% below its 2014 peak as at 2023 (total ag emissions 40.6 MtCO2e in 2023 vs 41.5 in 2022), well short of 10% below 2017. Minister McClay's framing was that projections show methane 'on track' to reach 10.1% by 2030 — a projection, not an achieved reduction — and the Commission judged that margin narrow with significant risk. The 1990–2024 Inventory (April 2026) shows agriculture down only a further 0.3% in 2024, with dairy enteric fermentation rising (+177 kt). The Commission's 2026 monitoring report names agriculture one of the three biggest risks to the budgets, with expert reaction stating the biogenic methane target looks unlikely to be met. No apology from the Opposition was in evidence. Under the criterion as written (already at or below the 2030 target trajectory), agriculture is short.

statement: That is just absolutely senseless. That’s why the Fast-track Approvals Bill is going to be so good for this country, and it’s going to make sure that we reach our climate change targets and we reduce our emissions, because remember that it’s not just the agriculture emissions; it’s also our transport emissions.
criterion: Climate Change Commission monitoring reports and the Ministry for the Environment greenhouse gas inventory for the second emissions budget period (2026–2030). True if NZ meets the second emissions budget with gross/net emissions falling; false if the budget is exceeded or emissions do not fall over the period.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against the second emissions budget period 2026–2030, which is assessed only after it closes (resolve-by 2031-12-31); today is September 2026, one year into the period, and no final Inventory/Commission assessment of EB2 exists. Interim evidence runs against the prediction — the Commission's 2026 monitoring report finds more than half the emissions reductions the Government relies on to meet EB2 are at significant risk, with electricity, agriculture and transport all flagged, and says the pace of reduction needs to more than double — but that does not settle the budget outcome, so the correct answer now is not_yet_due.

statement: These are all questions that will come up, surely, in January, when we expect the next bill before the House.
criterion: Parliamentary records (bills introduced and order paper) for early 2025: true if the follow-up vaping/smokefree regulated products amendment bill was introduced or before the House by the end of February 2025; false if no such bill appeared by then.
reasoning: No follow-up smokefree/vaping regulated-products bill was introduced or before the House by the end of February 2025. The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (No 2) — the vaping bill under debate in November 2024 — had its second reading on 13 November 2024 and received royal assent on 17 December 2024, completing its passage in 2024. Wikipedia's list of acts of the 54th Parliament shows no smokefree/tobacco/vaping act after that; the acts assented in January–February 2025 are unrelated (Taranaki Maunga, family violence, overseas investment, Ō-Rākau). What happened in 2025 was commencement of the already-passed Act's provisions (location rules and higher penalties from 18 December 2024; disposable-vape ban and display restrictions from 17 June 2025) plus regulation, not a new bill. The next policy step in this area — smokeless tobacco/oral nicotine products — was still with an expert advisory group as of December 2025 and was being handled by regulation, with a health select committee row about it in 2026. Repeated searches of parliamentary and legislation sources found no such bill in early 2025.

statement: We acknowledge, also, the willingness of the Minister to have his office involve us in discussions about how best to achieve an outcome in the best interests of the animals, and it’s good to see today he has the assurance that the entire House will be supporting the legislation.
criterion: The Hansard division/voice-vote record for the bill's readings on 10 December 2024: true if it passed with the support of all parties and no party voting against; false if any party opposed or abstained.
reasoning: The Racing Industry (Unlawful Destruction of Specified Greyhounds) Amendment Bill was introduced, debated and passed through all stages under urgency on 10 December 2024, receiving Royal Assent the same day. Sources consistently record that it passed with unanimous support — no party voted against and none is recorded as abstaining — which is what the criterion requires. Sourcing caveat: parliament.nz returned HTTP 404 to every fetch attempt, including the Hansard third-reading page the criterion names (HansDeb_20241210_20241210_52), so the division/voice-vote record could not be read directly; the verdict rests on Wikipedia's article on the Act and on the 54th Parliament's acts list plus contemporaneous reporting, which concur on unanimity. Disconfirming check: the widely reported 112-11 division (ACT's 11 votes against) belongs to the later Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Bill, passed 2 April 2026 — a different bill outside this criterion's 10 December 2024 window, so it does not contradict Abel's claim about the legislation then before the House.

statement: Greyhound racing will be phased out in Aotearoa New Zealand over the next 20 months.
criterion: Greyhound Racing NZ race calendar and the enacted legislation: true if no commercial greyhound race meetings are held in New Zealand after 1 August 2026; false if racing continues past that date or the phase-out is deferred or abandoned.
reasoning: Commercial greyhound racing in New Zealand ceased on 31 July 2026, with the statutory ban in force from 1 August 2026 — exactly the cutoff the criterion sets. The final meeting was at Hatrick raceway, Whanganui, with the last race at 6:55pm on Friday 31 July 2026; Manukau Stadium held its final meeting on 27 July and Addington (where the code began 78 years earlier) also raced on the final day. The enacted framework is the Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Act 2026, passed 2 April 2026 (Royal Assent 9 April 2026), phasing racing out by 1 August 2026. Disconfirming check: the phase-out was neither deferred nor abandoned — Greyhound Racing NZ's judicial review sought to stop it, but Justice La Hood declined interim relief (NZ Greyhound Racing Assn Inc v Attorney-General [2025] NZHC 2665, September 2025) and the review was withdrawn; no commercial meetings are reported after 1 August 2026, with coverage shifting entirely to rehoming. On timing, 10 December 2024 to 31 July 2026 is about 19.7 months, and the Government's own announcement described a 20-month wind-down, so 'the next 20 months' is accurate rather than overstated.

statement: It is a preventative measure and is expected most, if not all, people within the greyhound industry will do the right thing by their dogs.
criterion: Prosecutions and MPI/Greyhound Racing New Zealand records of unlawful destruction of registered racing greyhounds during the closure and rehoming period; true if only a negligible number of owners unlawfully destroyed dogs (few or no charges laid, no evidence of mass culling), false if widespread unlawful destruction or a significant number of prosecutions is recorded.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 31 December 2026 and today is 28 September 2026, so the date has not passed. More importantly, the evidence window the criterion defines — unlawful destruction 'during the closure and rehoming period' — is still open: racing ended 31 July 2026 but roughly 1,300-1,500 greyhounds still required rehoming at closure, and the Greyhound Transition Agency's own estimate is that placement could take around two years (it intends to scale up and shorten that). The offence framework exists (s 53A Racing Industry Act 2020, up to 12 months' imprisonment or a $50,000 fine, enforced under an MOU between SPCA, the Racing Integrity Board and MPI), and I searched specifically for prosecutions, charges and any sign of mass culling and found none reported. But that is an interim picture, not a resolution: the absence of prosecutions this early, with most dogs not yet rehomed, cannot establish that 'most, if not all' owners did the right thing, and per the criterion's own terms the record is not yet complete enough to grade either way.

statement: I want to acknowledge the Minister who’s brought it to the House, and I want to acknowledge the members of this House who’ve come together to pass this—from what I can understand, is going to be unanimously.
criterion: The Hansard/division record for the third reading of the Greyhound Racing (Racing Safety) Bill on 10 December 2024; true if the bill passed with no party voting against, false if any party opposed.
reasoning: The criterion names a "Greyhound Racing (Racing Safety) Bill" third reading on 10 Dec 2024; the real bill with that third reading is the Racing Industry (Unlawful Destruction of Specified Greyhounds) Amendment Bill — same House, same day, same event Luxton was speaking to. It was passed through all stages under urgency on 10 December 2024 with unanimous support; no division/party vote is recorded for any of its three readings (WhereTheyStand shows no vote breakdown for 1st, 2nd or 3rd reading, consistent with passage on the voices without dissent), and Green, Te Pāti Māori and Labour members all spoke in support in the third reading debate. Disconfirming check: ACT was the coalition's loudest objector to ending greyhound racing, but its dissent was filed against the separate Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Bill, and it was ACT's 11 votes that produced that bill's 112–11 result in April 2026 — not this December 2024 protection bill. No source records any party opposing the 10 December 2024 bill.

statement: It’s forecast OCR track indicates another reduction at the next meeting in February and further falls in 2025.
criterion: RBNZ monetary policy decisions during 2025; true if the February 2025 review cut the OCR and at least one further cut followed during 2025, false if February held or raised, or if no further cut occurred in 2025.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. At the February 2025 review (19 February 2025) the RBNZ cut the OCR by 50 basis points to 3.75% — it neither held nor raised. Further cuts then followed through 2025: 3.50% in April, 3.25% in May, 3.00% in August, 2.50% in October and 2.25% in November. So the February meeting delivered a reduction and well more than one further cut occurred during 2025, matching Willis's description of the forecast track ("another reduction at the next meeting in February and further falls in 2025"). Disconfirming check: no 2025 RBNZ decision raised the OCR, and there was no February hold.

statement: Here’s the good news: on our plan, we repeal the broken oil and gas ban, we keep agriculture out of the emissions trading scheme, and we still hit net carbon zero six years earlier, in 2044.
criterion: New Zealand's official greenhouse gas inventory / Climate Change Commission accounting of net emissions (excluding biogenic methane, per the Zero Carbon Act target): true if net zero carbon is reached in or before 2044, false if net emissions remain above zero at the end of 2044.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against New Zealand's official greenhouse gas inventory / Climate Change Commission accounting of net emissions at the end of 2044, with a resolve-by date of 2044-12-31. Today is 2026-09-28, so the evidence the criterion names cannot exist for another eighteen years. No interim proxy was written into the criterion, and substituting current projections would be answering an easier question than the one written down.

statement: I think, in kind of potential preparation for us getting into Government in a couple of years’ time and seeing how short some of the Government MPs’ calls tend to be when it’s a Government bill, I commend this bill to the House.
criterion: The composition of the New Zealand executive following the next general election: true if the Green Party is in government (in Cabinet or a confidence-and-supply/ministerial arrangement) by 31 December 2027; false if it remains in opposition.
reasoning: The prediction turns on the composition of the executive after the next general election. That election is set for 7 November 2026 and has not yet been held as of today (28 September 2026), so no government has been formed and the Greens' status cannot be assessed. The criterion's own deadline is 31 December 2027. Not findable yet is not a failure: this simply has not resolved.

statement: As the industry heads towards closure, participants will be leading at their own pace, and it’s expected that while some licensed persons will choose to keep their dogs as pets, many, if not most, of the nearly 3,000 greyhounds in the industry will be put up for adoption throughout this period.
criterion: Rehoming figures reported by the greyhound racing advisory committee, Greyhounds as Pets and the SPCA over the closure period; true if more than half of the approximately 3,000 dogs are put up for adoption, false if most are retained by licensed persons or otherwise not offered for adoption.
reasoning: Peters said many, if not most, of the ~3,000 industry greyhounds would be put up for adoption over the wind-down, while some licensees kept theirs as pets. The industry held ~2,900 dogs at the December 2024 announcement. The Ministerial Advisory Committee's May 2025 interim report estimated ~1,500 would still need rehoming at the end of the 2025/26 season, and at closure (racing ended 31 July 2026) the Greyhound Racing Transition Agency put the figure at ~1,300-1,400 to be rehomed through Greyhounds as Pets, Nightrave, KiwiKiwi Hounds and May Hounds. The shrinkage from ~2,900 to ~1,400 over the 20-month wind-down is accounted for mainly by continued adoption: existing groups place 600-700 dogs a year, GRNZ rehomed 500+ through Great Mates in a single year and reported 615 awaiting adoption at 1 August 2025. So the adoption pathway, wind-down placements plus the ~1,400 now in the GRTA programme, comfortably exceeds half of ~2,900. Disconfirming evidence checked: ~240 greyhounds were flown to Queensland between April 2025 and August 2026 for racing rather than rehoming (about 10% of the pre-ban population), and an unquantified number were retained as pets by owners, which Peters himself signalled. The criterion's false branch, most dogs retained by licensed persons or otherwise not offered for adoption, is clearly not what occurred. Caveat: no agency has yet published a cumulative count of dogs offered for adoption, and the rehoming period runs to 2029, so the >50% threshold is confirmed by the population accounting rather than by a single published tally.

statement: Given that the Governor-General is ensconced at Government House in Wellington, thanks to a cancelled flight, this will take effect almost immediately.
criterion: The date of Royal assent recorded on the Greyhound Racing (Protection of Greyhounds) Bill / Act on legislation.govt.nz and the NZ Gazette: true if assent is given within a few days of 10 December 2024 and the Act commences immediately on assent; false if assent or commencement is delayed by weeks or more.
reasoning: The bill before the House on 10 December 2024 was the Racing Industry (Unlawful Destruction of Specified Greyhounds) Amendment Bill (Government Bill 109), passed under urgency. It became the Racing Industry (Unlawful Destruction of Specified Greyhounds) Amendment Act 2024 (2024 No 51) and received Royal assent on 10 December 2024, the same day Brewer spoke. Clause 2 of the bill provides that it comes into force on the day after Royal assent, so commencement was 11 December 2024. Brewer predicted the Act would take effect almost immediately, which is exactly what happened; the criterion's false branch, assent or commencement delayed by weeks or more, is ruled out. The only gap against the criterion as written is that commencement was the day after assent rather than on assent itself, which is within Brewer's own 'almost immediately' hedge. I did not find independent confirmation of the incidental detail that the Governor-General was in Wellington because of a cancelled flight; the criterion does not turn on it.

statement: But complex projects will almost certainly require a hearing; if they don’t, then they’re not required.
criterion: Expert panel records published by the EPA for projects determined under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024: true if hearings were held for most of the large or complex listed projects decided in the period, false if panels decided complex listed projects on written comments without holding hearings in most cases.
reasoning: Hearings are discretionary under the FTAA, so the criterion turns on panel practice. EPA/fast-track project records show hearings were held for the large or complex listed projects decided in the period: Waihi North (hearing sittings Sept-16 Dec 2025, decision 18 Dec 2025); Sunfield (notice of hearing 3 Dec 2025, hearings 10 and 17 Dec 2025); Waitaha Hydro (hearing 13 Feb 2026, after a convener conference 22 Oct 2025); Bendigo-Ophir Gold (Minute 30 of 27 May 2026 set concurrent topic hearings - ecology 12 June, water 15 June, planning/economics 17-19 June 2026); Taranaki VTM (legal-issues hearing 26 Nov 2025 before the 4 Feb 2026 draft decline). Disconfirming check: not universal - Delmore's first application (large listed urban project) was decided on written comments plus expert conferencing on 26 August 2025 with no hearing, and simpler urban applications went through convener conferences only, so 'almost certainly' is somewhat strong. But on the criterion as written - hearings for most large/complex listed projects rather than decisions on written comments alone - the record supports the prediction. Caveat: fasttrack.govt.nz blocks direct fetching, so per-project process evidence came from indexed snippets of its own project pages and decision PDFs rather than full-text reads; the resolve-by date (2027-06-30) has not passed, so later decisions could shift the balance.

statement: It’ll be complicated, but the salient point is this: applicants who are going to use the fast track will be charged at various different points and the referral costs, the administration, and all the sort of administration around all of that stuff throughout the process will be cost recovered from them, and so the staff and the various resources required—over time it’ll be neutral for the Crown, so we’re not subsidising through the administration of the applications.
criterion: MfE and EPA cost-recovery reporting and the fast-track fees/charges regulations, together with Vote Environment appropriations: true if fees charged to fast-track applicants are reported as recovering the referral and administrative costs of the regime with no ongoing Crown subsidy, false if MfE/EPA or the Auditor-General report a continuing Crown-funded shortfall in administering fast-track applications.
reasoning: The cost-recovery design is as Bishop described: the Fast-track Approvals (Cost Recovery) Regulations 2025 (gazetted 30 January 2025, administered by MfE) charge applicants an upfront levy plus application fee at referral and substantive stages, with further fees or refunds so that the actual and reasonable costs of agencies, local authorities, panel conveners and expert panels are recovered, and MfE/EPA state the intent is a cost-neutral regime funded entirely by applicants. But 'neutral for the Crown' is not yet borne out, and Crown money is at risk: the EPA took a $10m Crown loan for set-up costs, repayable over five years on an assumption of 50 applications a year to 2029, and only 49 were lodged in the 13 months to December 2025; the EPA had earlier told the Environment Committee it was 'technically insolvent' as a result of start-up costs and would default on the loan if uptake stayed low. In 2026 it told MPs operating costs were 'well in excess of what we first modelled' - about $250k per application forecast against more than $500k for some - and that some councils were absorbing application fees rather than passing them to applicants (a local-government, not Crown, subsidy). No MfE, EPA or Auditor-General report yet states a permanent Crown-funded shortfall in administering applications, so the criterion's 'false' condition is not met either; the decisive test (loan repayment) falls after the 2027-06-30 window. Substance of the mechanism holds; the neutrality claim is materially overstated on current evidence.

statement: I just think there is an opportunity here to allow this, because we’d love for people to cross the floor and come on to our side, but we get that, potentially, this will pass.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Fast-track Approvals Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading, false if it is defeated or lapses.
reasoning: The Fast-track Approvals Bill passed its third reading on 17 December 2024 (the reading was interrupted by a gallery protest) and received Royal assent on 23 December 2024, becoming the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024, with applications opening 7 February 2025. The criterion's 'true' condition - the bill passes its third reading - is met; it was neither defeated nor lapsed.

statement: I have no doubt in my mind that, after this bill passes, there will be no shortage of people seeking crevices and avenues upon which to litigate.
criterion: Court records and reporting on proceedings (judicial review or related litigation) brought against referrals, panel decisions or approvals under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024. True if multiple distinct proceedings have been filed challenging the Act's processes or decisions by the resolve-by date; false if essentially no such litigation has been commenced.
reasoning: The criterion asks for multiple distinct proceedings challenging the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024's processes or decisions by 31 Dec 2026. Confirmed: (1) Ngati Kuku Hapu Trust & Nga Hapu o Nga Moutere Trust v Environmental Protection Agency [2025] NZHC 2046 (19 Aug 2025), judicial review of the EPA's decision that Port of Tauranga's Stella Passage application was complete and in scope — interim relief declined but a priority substantive fixture granted; the substantive review ([2025] NZHC 2453) found the EPA should not have accepted the application, halting the project and prompting a Government amendment. (2) Jones v Environmental Protection Authority [2026] NZHC 1872 (30 June 2026), CIV-2026-404-0062 (judicial review of the EPA's s 46(2) acceptance) and CIV-2026-404-0283 (appeal against the expert panel's s 81 grant) over the Kings Quarry Expansion Stage 2 project. Additionally Ngati Ruanui obtained a Waitangi Tribunal urgent hearing over the Taranaki VTM fast-track approval. That is well past 'essentially no such litigation'; litigation over FTAA referrals, completeness decisions and panel approvals has been a recurring feature, and one such case forced a legislative fix. No disconfirming evidence found — no source suggests the Act's decisions have gone unlitigated.

statement: I would wager the Minister will not respond to these questions.
criterion: Hansard for the remainder of the committee of the whole House stage on the Fast-track Approvals Bill; false if the Minister responsible for RMA Reform gives a substantive answer to why the three amendments were tabled on the final day rather than at select committee or the start of the committee stage, true if he does not.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific source — Hansard for the remainder of the committee of the whole House stage on the Fast-track Approvals Bill (10-11 December 2024) — and asks whether the Minister responsible for RMA Reform (Chris Bishop) gave a substantive answer on why three amendments were tabled on the final day. That source is not retrievable from this environment: the relevant parliament.nz Hansard pages (HansDeb_20241210_20241211_08 'In Committee—Part 2', HansDeb_20241210_20241211_28 'In Committee—Clauses 1 and 2', and the individual speech document HansS_20241210_057000000) all return HTTP 404 to automated fetching; www3.parliament.nz serves a Radware bot challenge; the debate text is loaded via iframe/shadow DOM so a text-extraction proxy returns only page chrome; and no Wayback snapshot of the debate exists. Secondary sources confirm the surrounding facts — Bishop was the Minister in charge, a large Government amendment paper (including a 20-working-day limit on judicial review and the removal of appeal rights for invited commenters) arrived on the afternoon the committee stage began, and this was widely criticised as eleventh-hour lawmaking — but none records whether Bishop answered the timing question in the chamber. I could not verify either direction, so this resolves as not findable rather than as a pass or fail. Note also that resolve-by (2024-12-31) has passed, so this is not 'not_yet_due'.

statement: The reason we’ve suggested a period of four calendar years is because, once the legislation passes, it looks like greyhound racing will wind down by 2026.
