criterion: Official records (Racing Minister's announcements, Greyhound Racing NZ, the commencement date in the enacted prohibition legislation); true if commercial greyhound racing in New Zealand has ceased by 31 December 2026, false if racing meetings are still being held after that date.
reasoning: The criterion is true if commercial greyhound racing in New Zealand ceased by 31 December 2026. It did. Racing Minister Winston Peters announced the ban on 10 December 2024 (the same day as the quote) with an end-date of 2026; Parliament passed the Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Act 2026 on 2 April 2026, setting the phase-out for 1 August 2026; the final commercial race meeting was held at Hatrick Raceway, Whanganui on 31 July 2026 (last race ~6.55pm), with Manukau and Ascot Park clubs finishing in the days before, and the prohibition took effect 1 August 2026. Checked for disconfirming evidence — no reporting of racing meetings continuing after 1 August 2026 or of the commencement date being deferred. McAnulty's forecast that the industry would 'wind down by 2026' matches the outcome with about five months to spare.

statement: The pet-bond system won’t be operational until probably late 2025, early 2026.
criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services records / commencement of the pet bond provisions of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024: true if the pet bond system became operational between roughly October 2025 and March 2026; false if it was operational earlier than late 2025 or later than early 2026.
reasoning: The pet bond and pet consent provisions of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 were brought into force by commencement order on 1 December 2025, and MBIE's Tenancy Services bond system supported pet bond lodgement, top-ups and refunds from that date. RNZ reported 1,708 pet bonds registered by 7 February 2026, confirming the system was genuinely operational, not merely legally in force. 1 December 2025 falls inside the criterion's roughly-October-2025-to-March-2026 window, and matches Bishop's 'late 2025, early 2026' hedge.

statement: Whether this is in or not, we’re still going to be facing the same problem, but we’re certainly going to be facing it in greater numbers from early 2026 onwards as the industry starts to wind down.
criterion: Greyhound Racing NZ / Greyhounds as Pets / SPCA rehoming intake figures: true if greyhounds entering rehoming from Q1 2026 onwards exceed the comparable 2025 monthly rates, false if intake stays flat or falls.
reasoning: The substance holds — a large increase in greyhounds entering rehoming did arrive in 2026, far above the 600-700/year that existing groups normally place — but the timing is materially overstated and the criterion's specific comparison cannot be verified. No monthly or quarterly intake figures from GRNZ, Greyhounds as Pets or SPCA are published for Q1 2026 versus 2025; the Greyhound Transition Agency and rehoming groups have released only aggregate estimates. What is documented points to the surge coming at the END of the wind-down rather than from early 2026: approximately 1,300-1,500 dogs were still in the industry at the final race on 31 July 2026, and the 'kennels full, hundreds of applications, foster-home shortage' reporting dates from August-September 2026. The last published pre-2026 figure runs the other way: GRNZ recorded 615 greyhounds awaiting adoption at 1 August 2025, down from 662 a year earlier, showing no early acceleration. So greater numbers, yes, but from roughly August 2026, not early 2026, and the underlying intake series the criterion names is not public.

statement: Will there be tribunal cases as a result of the pet laws? Of course there will.
criterion: Published Tenancy Tribunal decisions after the pet provisions commence; true if one or more decisions turn on the new pet bond, pet consent or pet damage liability provisions, false if no such decision exists by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Tenancy Tribunal Principal Adjudicator Brett Carter issued a decision on 1 May 2026 — reported as the first under the new pet rules that commenced 1 December 2025 — holding a Christchurch landlord's refusal of consent for a Labrador puppy unreasonable, permitting the pet subject to a two-week pet bond and conditions. The decision turns directly on the new pet consent and pet bond provisions and sets out a framework for future cases, satisfying the criterion well before the 2027-12-31 resolve-by date. Checking the other direction: the earliest reporting (February 2026) recorded no pet-bond disputes yet, so the absence of cases held only for the first five months.

statement: The view is that changes will increase supply, and whilst that might come as a surprise to our colleagues on the other side of the Chamber, it is our view that the changes that are being proposed—in the context that they’re being proposed, and together—will increase supply at the margins by giving landlords greater flexibility to rent to tenants and to a broader suite of tenants.
criterion: MBIE tenancy bond lodgement data on the number of active private rental tenancies, and Stats NZ rental stock estimates, for the two years after the Act's termination provisions commenced; true if private rental supply rises relative to the pre-Act trend, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion asks for MBIE bond-lodgement and Stats NZ rental-stock data covering the TWO YEARS after the Act's termination provisions commenced. Those provisions commenced 30 January 2025 (Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024; pet provisions later, 1 December 2025), so the window closes 30 January 2027 and the stated resolve-by date of 2027-01-31 has not passed. Separately, the named source cannot currently answer the question even for the elapsed portion: Tenancy Services states that rental bond data migration to the new Bond Hub system is ongoing, that the data 'remains in a provisional state', that figures are drawn from both legacy and new systems, and that there are '17,550 more active bonds because the two systems recorded the information differently' — explicitly warning users to 'exercise caution when comparing recent data releases with earlier periods'. A trend break of that size is larger than any plausible policy effect 'at the margins', so no active-tenancy comparison against the pre-Act trend is defensible today. I found no published Stats NZ rental-stock series or MBIE analysis isolating a post-Act supply effect. Not findable yet is not a failing grade for Potaka; the claim is still open.

statement: Kāinga Ora isn’t going to be building houses in the future.
criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports for 2025/26 and 2026/27 new-build completions; true if new-build completions fall to essentially zero, false if Kāinga Ora continues to complete new homes at a material rate.
reasoning: The criterion's false branch — 'Kāinga Ora continues to complete new homes at a material rate' — is met, and by a wide margin. Kāinga Ora completed 3,456 new homes in 2024/25 against a target of at least 3,400 (following 4,864 in 2023/24). Its FY26 Q3 report (1 January – 31 March 2026) states it is on track to meet or exceed all financial targets and that 'build costs continue to trend down as housing delivery activity increases' — i.e. delivery rising, not stopping. The February 2025 turnaround plan, the very policy McAnulty was attacking, commits Kāinga Ora to roughly 1,900–2,000 construction events per year from 2026/27 onwards, about 1,500 of them new-build homes plus 400 retrofits. I deliberately checked the disconfirming case: Kāinga Ora's stock IS shrinking — forecast 78,027 homes at 30 June 2026, a fall of 177 against an expected growth of 420, with ~1,000 properties to be sold in 2025/26. But that is net stock falling through sales, demolitions and lease expiries, not new-build completions falling to zero; Housing Minister Chris Bishop's response to exactly that stock figure was that Kāinga Ora 'are continuing to build right around the country'. Caveat on completeness: the 2025/26 annual report was not yet published or indexed as at 28 September 2026, and the 2026/27 report cannot exist before late 2027. I did not return not_yet_due because the criterion is a zero-versus-material test and the elapsed record already settles it decisively in one direction — nothing in the 2026/27 report could bring completions retrospectively to essentially zero.

statement: We know that there’s probably going to be more cases going to the Tenancy Tribunal because of the changes that the Government is making.
criterion: MBIE/Tenancy Services published Tenancy Tribunal application and case-lodgement statistics: true if annual applications lodged in the year following commencement of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 changes exceed the 2024 baseline outside normal year-to-year variation; false if lodgements are flat or fall.
reasoning: I totalled landlord + tenant applications from the Tenancy Services quarterly Dispute Resolution statistics (the source the criterion names). Calendar 2024 baseline: Q1 6,315+1,188; Q2 6,025+1,286; Q3 6,091+1,205; Q4 6,093+1,089 = 29,292 (matching the independently reported 'more than 29,000'). Calendar 2025: 7,861 + 7,201 + 7,386 + 7,515 = 29,963, a rise of just 2.3%. The termination provisions commenced 30 January 2025, so the criterion's window (Feb 2025 – Jan 2026) works out at roughly 30,300, about +3.3%. The direction is up, so the criterion's false branch ('flat or fall') is not cleanly met — but neither is the true branch, which requires the rise to sit OUTSIDE normal year-to-year variation. It does not: the same series rose 14% from 2023 to 2024 and 43% from 2022 to 2024, so a 2–3% rise is in fact a sharp deceleration against trend. What supports Hernandez on the mechanism he had in mind: termination/possession disputes specifically rose from 10,556 in 2024 to 11,182 in 2025, and then to 3,543 in Q1 2026 alone, up 21.8% on Q1 2025. Volumes have also climbed since the criterion window closed — 8,756 in Q1 2026 and 8,061 in Q2 2026, putting the 12 months to June 2026 at 31,718, or +8.3% on 2024. That later rise is outside the window the criterion set, and causal attribution to the Act is not established in any of these sources: rent arrears remain the dominant dispute type throughout (57–62% of applications), and the December 2025 pet provisions are a separate confounder.

statement: Specifically, it’s saying that that information needs to be supplied within five days, and the commentary back from the select committee is saying we should be making that five working days, which I’m sure will be seen as a sensible change by all.
criterion: The enacted Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Act and the Hansard division record for its remaining stages: true if the 'five working days' wording is adopted and no party opposes that change, false if the amendment is rejected or is voted against by any party.
reasoning: The select committee's 'five working days' wording was enacted: MBIE's Building Performance guidance on the amended Building Act states standalone BCAs must provide the s238A information to the territorial authority 'within five working days' of the date of decision or acceptance. The bill passed third reading 21 Nov 2024 and got royal assent 24 Nov 2024. On opposition, only Labour voted against at first reading (89-34); RNZ's The House reported that after the select committee amendments all parties supported the bill, and no division was taken against the working-days change. Both limbs of the criterion are met.

statement: When they got in, in 2009, they kept it in place because it was the only tool that we had to meet our international obligations, to provide some market signals for our economy and participants in our economy to reduce our emissions over time, because if we don’t, we’re going to be writing out cheques for billions of dollars under the Kyoto and the Paris accords.
criterion: New Zealand government accounts and Treasury/MfE reporting on the cost of meeting the first Nationally Determined Contribution (2021–2030), including offshore mitigation purchases; true if the Crown commits or pays NZ$1 billion or more for international units/offshore mitigation to meet the NDC, false if the cost is below that or no such payment is required.
reasoning: The criterion's window (NDC1, 2021-2030, resolve by 2031-12-31) has not closed. As of Budget 2026 the Crown has committed no money: Treasury's 2026 budget documents state the Government 'has not communicated a sufficiently specified plan to purchase offshore mitigation... to create a valid expectation... that it will do so', and the Prime Minister has said the Government will not spend billions overseas. Treasury's June 2026 technical annex nonetheless models offshore mitigation for NDC1 at roughly NZ$4.4-5.0bn (earlier estimates spanned $3.3-23.7bn), so the magnitude O'Connor asserted is consistent with official costings — but the NZ$1bn commitment or payment the criterion requires has not occurred and cannot yet be judged.

statement: I’m pleased to announce that you will be able to buy cool wool rugs by Christmas.
criterion: Bremworth's product listings and press releases; true if a 'cool wool' rug product is on sale to the public on or before 25 December 2024, false if no such product is available by that date.
reasoning: I checked the source the criterion names — Bremworth's rug product listings and collections — and found no product marketed as a 'cool wool' rug, by 25 Dec 2024 or since; nor does any other identifiable NZ maker or retailer sell one under that name. But the attribution to Bremworth is the extractor's inference, not anything in the quote. The speech was on the Climate Change Response (ETS Agricultural Obligations) Amendment Bill, about biogenic methane, so 'cool wool' most plausibly refers to wool from B+LNZ's low-methane Cool Sheep(R) genetics programme, which has no consumer rug line I can trace under any brand. Because I cannot pin down the referent, a negative search cannot distinguish 'never went on sale' from 'went on sale under a name I cannot identify', and marking it false would rest on an unverified assumption about which company he meant.

statement: I’ll leave these for the consideration of the Minister in the hope that we can look towards making sure that the scope of this bill—and the fact is it’s going to continue through the House—actually reflects the lives of our people and not simply the bubble of Parliament.
criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill before the House on 2024-12-10: true if it advances past the committee stage to a third reading (and/or receives royal assent); false if it is defeated, withdrawn or left un-progressed.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill advanced past committee stage to a third reading and/or royal assent. Parliament's bill record shows it passed its third reading on 10 December 2024 (the same sitting day as the quote) and received royal assent on 16 December 2024 as the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 (2024 No 52). It was not defeated, withdrawn or left un-progressed. Checked for the disconfirming case (a bill stalled at committee or discharged at term's end) and found the opposite: the Act is in force, with tranches commencing 18 Dec 2024, 30 Jan 2025, 20 Mar 2025, 1 Dec 2025 and 16 Apr 2026.

statement: I’m advised that it will be late 2025, but, rest assured, I say to the member, I’m putting the heat on the good team at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to get on with the job and make sure we get it in as quickly as possible.
criterion: The commencement date of the pet bond provisions of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 as recorded in the Act/Order in Council on legislation.govt.nz: true if they came into force in the last months of 2025, false if they commenced in 2026 or later (or materially earlier).
reasoning: Bishop said he was advised the pet bond provisions would be in place in late 2025. The criterion asked whether they commenced in the last months of 2025. The pet consent and pet bond provisions (new s 18AA, inserted by the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024) were brought into force by Order in Council on 1 December 2025, a date Cabinet locked in around late October 2025, and Tenancy Services confirms 'these provisions took effect on 1 December 2025'. That is within late 2025, so neither a slip to 2026 nor a materially earlier commencement. The Act's later methamphetamine tranche (16 April 2026) is a separate provision and does not bear on the pet bond date.

statement: Thank you for doing this no-cause evictions mahi, because I think renters will actually recognise their power in numbers and utilise that, and this is going to be a one-term Government—not just because of all of this but because of everything else that the Government has decided to do.
criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election; true if the National/ACT/NZ First coalition loses the ability to form a government, false if any of those parties return to government after that election.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the result of the next New Zealand general election. The Prime Minister set that election for Saturday 7 November 2026, with advance voting opening 26 October 2026 and enrolment closing 25 October. Today is 28 September 2026, so no result exists and the National/ACT/NZ First coalition remains in government. Checked whether the government had already fallen or an early election been called — it had not; the date was announced by Luxon as sitting PM. The item's own resolve-by date of 2027-01-31 is after the election, so this is pending rather than unresolvable.

statement: Next week’s changes to fiscal forecasts are almost entirely driven by changes to revenue and expense forecasts—they are not driven by discretionary fiscal decisions.
criterion: The Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update published 17 December 2024 and its fiscal-track reconciliation: true if the reconciliation attributes the bulk of the change since Budget 2024 to revenue and expense forecast revisions rather than to new discretionary policy decisions; false if new policy decisions account for a substantial share of the change.
reasoning: HYEFU 2024 was published 17 December 2024 as predicted. Its Table 2.10 ("Movements in OBEGALx since the Budget Update", p.45) is exactly the reconciliation the criterion names, and it attributes the entire $18.3b deterioration over the forecast period to forecast revisions: core Crown tax revenue -$13.0b (Table 2.9 attributes this to GST -$5.8b, source deductions -$5.0b, net other persons -$1.1b, corporate -$0.9b, driven by "the weaker economic outlook and the impact of weaker tax outturn for some tax types"), net finance costs -$1.6b, expense phasing changes -$1.7b, education forecasting and depreciation -$1.4b, Health NZ results -$1.3b, benefit expenses -$0.2b, other +$0.9b. The table contains no line for new discretionary policy decisions, and the narrative (p.43) states "The key factor influencing the weaker outlook is slower economic activity and a deterioration in recent tax outturns, which have reduced the forecast for tax revenue" and (p.45) "The change in the outlook for OBEGALx is largely driven by the changes in core Crown tax revenue and core Crown expenses." Disconfirming check: the only discretionary decision visibly moving the forecasts is the new annual capital allowance framework set in the 2025 Budget Policy Statement, which added $2.2b of forecast capital investment (p.46) — but that sits on the capital/debt side, is offset by a $2.1b reduction in NZ Super Fund contributions, and is immaterial against the $18.3b operating and $18.7b debt movements. The prediction holds as stated.

statement: Today’s report shows New Zealand’s high quality, sustainable, and environmentally food and fibre exports are forecast to hit $56.9 billion by 30 June 2025 and climb to a record $58.3 billion the following year, demonstrating the farming and primary sector’s significant contribution to the New Zealand economy.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries actuals (and Stats NZ trade data) for the years ended 30 June 2025 and 30 June 2026: true if food and fibre export revenue reaches at least $56.9b in 2024/25 and at least $58.3b in 2025/26; false if either year falls materially short of the stated figure.
reasoning: Both figures were beaten. The December 2024 SOPI, which McClay was quoting, forecast $56.9b for the year to 30 June 2025 and $58.3b for the year to 30 June 2026. Actual food and fibre export revenue for the year ended 30 June 2025 was a record $60.4 billion, confirmed in MPI's December 2025 SOPI and the accompanying 16 December 2025 ministerial release ("this year's record-setting $60.4 billion") — $3.5b above the stated $56.9b. For 2025/26, MPI's June 2026 SOPI (released 11 June 2026) puts export revenue at a record $64.3 billion for the year to 30 June 2026, up 6 percent, with dairy $28.6b, meat and wool $14.1b, horticulture $9.5b — $6b above the stated $58.3b. Caveat on the second year: the $64.3b is MPI's estimate made three weeks before year end rather than a closed-out actual (the final figure lands in SOPI December 2026), and the intermediate December 2025 forecast for 2025/26 was $62b, also well above $58.3b. Neither reading comes close to falling materially short, so the caveat does not change the verdict.

statement: Despite all of that, we cannot support this bill, because it makes it easier for landlords to dismiss tenants, and in the wider context of the housing situation in this country, we fear that this will lead to higher levels of homelessness, and—more importantly—the termination of tenancies outlined in Part 2 of this bill will not achieve the stated aims of the Government.
criterion: Official homelessness measures for the period after the 30 January 2025 commencement — Stats NZ / HUD severe housing deprivation and rough-sleeping counts, and MSD emergency/transitional housing demand: true if measured homelessness rises materially in the 18 months following commencement; false if it is flat or falls over that period.
reasoning: The no-cause termination provisions commenced 30 January 2025, so the criterion's window runs to about July 2026; official data currently reaches 31 March 2026 (HUD's homelessness insights reports are six-monthly and the next is not yet out), so roughly 14 of the 18 months are observable. The criterion's most robust named measure is unavailable: severe housing deprivation comes only from the five-yearly Census, and both the September 2025 and March 2026 HUD reports still cite the 7 March 2023 figures (112,500 severely housing deprived, 4,965 without shelter) with no update. HUD states explicitly: "We cannot draw any conclusions as to whether the numbers of those sharing someone else's private dwelling, living in uninhabitable housing, or homelessness overall have increased, decreased, or remained stable since the March 2023 Census." On the measures that do exist the picture splits. Rises: Auckland outreach-engaged rough sleepers went from 653 in January 2025 to a peak of 940 in September 2025 (the Salvation Army's comparable count was 426 in September 2024); transitional-housing entries by households living without shelter rose from 19.0% / 248 people in March 2025 to 23.5% / 291 in March 2026; people on post-release orders with no fixed abode rose from 430 to 532 (+23.7%); NHI 'no fixed abode' records rose 790 (Jun 2023) to 929 (Jun 2024) to 1,037 (Jun 2025), a trend already running before commencement; Napier and New Plymouth providers reported increases. Falls or flat: Auckland fell back to 706 in January 2026 and 586 in March 2026, below the pre-commencement January 2025 level; the social housing register was broadly stable (+~400 households March 2025 to March 2026) and its 'without shelter' entry category was flat (2,232 to 2,274); children in transitional housing fell 5,607 to 5,141 with adults flat; Housing First households not yet housed fell 1,102 to 1,031; homelessness-recorded hospitalisations fell 1,003 to 884. HUD's March 2026 key point is that numbers living without shelter "may have begun to stabilise, with some large and small centres beginning to see a decrease," though council staff in most areas reported increases over the preceding six months. So a material rise did occur during the window but was not sustained to its end, and the aggregate measure the criterion leans on cannot be read at all. Disconfirming check on the mechanism: HUD outreach clients cite eviction as a factor in 14% of cases, well below housing affordability (35%), family breakdown (29%) and lack of social support (22%), and HUD says twice that "it is not possible to tell whether changes described in this report reflect existing trends and broader economic and social contexts or are attributable to policy changes" — the more commonly cited proximate driver over this period is the August 2024 tightening of emergency housing access (declined applications rose from 4% in March 2024 to 33.2% for October 2025 to March 2026), not the tenancy-termination change. The second limb of the quote, that the Part 2 terminations would not achieve the Government's stated aims, is outside what the criterion asks and is not assessed here.

statement: It will only drive more and more young New Zealanders overseas, because they regard this country as being backwards.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for New Zealand citizens aged under 35: true if the annual net outflow in the years ending December 2025 and December 2026 is higher than the year ended December 2024, false if it falls.
reasoning: The criterion requires the NZ-citizen net outflow in BOTH the December 2025 and December 2026 years to exceed the December 2024 year, and states it is false if it falls. It fell. Stats NZ: net migration loss of New Zealand citizens was 47,100 in the December 2024 year (the largest for any calendar year, 72,000 departures vs 24,900 arrivals), and 40,000 in the December 2025 year (66,300 departures, down 1%; 26,300 arrivals, up 12%). The trend continued down into 2026: net loss of 36,500 in the March 2026 year and 37,700 in the June 2026 year, both below the 2024 figure. On the young-adult cut the criterion is aimed at, Stats NZ does not publish a net under-35 series, but gross 18-30-year-old NZ-citizen departures also fell, from 27,200 (38% of 71,800) in the June 2025 year to 24,700 (39% of 63,900) in the June 2026 year. The December 2026 year is not published until February 2027, but because the criterion requires both years to be higher, 'true' is already unreachable, and every available proxy moves in the falling direction. Caveat recorded: the age-restricted net series named in the criterion was not directly retrievable, so the verdict rests on the all-citizen net series plus the 18-30 gross departure series.

statement: Whilst you might want to congratulate yourself on the other side of the House, Mr Brewer, I challenge you to check the numbers in three years’ time, because they will have gone back up.
criterion: NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2027/28 year compared with the 2023/24 figure; true if the rate is higher, false if it is the same or lower.
reasoning: The criterion names the 2027/28 New Zealand Health Survey, whose results are not collected until mid-2028 and are typically published late in the following calendar year, so the deciding figure does not yet exist. Baseline and interim data, for context only: adult daily smoking was 6.9% in 2023/24 (95% CI 6.3-7.6, ~300,000 adults) and 6.8% in 2024/25 (95% CI 6.2-7.4, ~294,000 adults) - the Ministry of Health notes the rate has been flat within 0.1% for three consecutive years. So the rate has not gone back up as at the latest published year, but the criterion's comparison year is four survey cycles away and cannot be graded now.

statement: These legislative changes are critical components of the Government’s efforts to increase exits into employment and have 50,000 fewer people on jobseeker support by 2030, which is forecast to save the country $2.3 billion in welfare payments.
criterion: MSD quarterly benefit statistics for 2030 compared with the 2024 baseline of roughly 200,000 jobseeker support recipients; true if the 2030 count is at least 50,000 lower, false if the reduction is materially smaller or numbers rise. Treasury/MSD welfare expenditure forecasts for the corresponding savings figure.
reasoning: The prediction targets 2030 and the criterion compares MSD quarterly benefit statistics for 2030 against the ~200,000 jobseeker baseline; that data is four years away. Interim evidence, for context only and not a grade: jobseeker support recipients were around 218,000 in the June 2026 quarter - higher than the 2024 baseline, not lower - and MSD's own benefit forecasts for Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2026 (finalised 10 April 2026) project a fall to roughly 194,000 by June 2030, about 24,000 below the June 2026 level and well short of a 50,000 reduction. That points against the claim but does not resolve it, since the forecast is not the outcome and the resolve-by date has not passed.

statement: The risk is this: if we lessen the time frames and afford greater freedom and eviction processes to landlords, we will absolutely see drastic increases in homelessness and reliance on social housing, and already 25,000 people are on the social housing waiting list.
criterion: MSD Housing Register / emergency housing and MHUD homelessness statistics for the two years following December 2024; true if homelessness measures and the social housing register rise substantially from their December 2024 levels, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires both homelessness measures and the social housing register to rise substantially from December 2024. Homelessness did rise sharply: Auckland's count of people living without shelter more than doubled in the year to September 2025 (426 to 940), January 2026 was 706 vs 653 a year earlier, and Community Housing Aotearoa's May 2026 report found homelessness at record levels; emergency housing access was cut hard (motel households 3,141 in Dec 2023 to 471 two years later; grant value down 88% on March 2023) and officials and advocates link the narrowed gateway to rising rough sleeping. But the social housing register fell rather than rose: 19,002 applicants at 30 June 2026 (-0.6% year on year), down from ~25,483 in late 2023 and ~19,431 at September 2025 — flat to falling since December 2024, and below the 25,000 she cited. So the harm she named appeared in homelessness but the indicator she cited moved the other way. MSD's register is also contested as an understatement of need (officials warned people are discouraged from applying), but the criterion names the register as written.

statement: They are going to be providing less public housing over the next few years and that will leave communities across the country far more vulnerable to landlords of expensive rentals who will actually put them into more financial hardship.
criterion: Kāinga Ora and MHUD public housing stock/placement figures for 2025-2027; true if net public housing places delivered fall relative to the 2024 baseline, false if they continue to grow.
reasoning: The criterion is met on the evidence available to mid-2026: net public housing places delivered fell relative to the 2024 baseline. Kāinga Ora and CHPs delivered 2,787 additional places in 2024/25; in 2025/26 Kāinga Ora's stock instead fell by 177 (to 78,027) against a planned +420, with about 1,000 properties sold, and CHPs delivered only 200 of the Budget 2024 tranche of 500 by 30 June 2026. The Budget 2026 top-up (1,800-2,250 Flexible Fund homes) does not begin delivering until 2028/29, outside his window. The final year of the 2025-2027 window is not yet reported, but reversing the direction would require an implausible swing. His second clause — tenants left more vulnerable to expensive rentals and greater hardship — is not part of the criterion and in fact ran the other way, with rents flat to falling through 2025-26.

statement: I think there’s been a number of provisions laid out—sensible, pro-tenant changes to the Residential Tenancies Act, which, along with the introduction of interest deductibility, will increase the supply of rental housing and make landlords more willing to enter into arrangements.
criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE rental bond and tenancy bond lodgement data plus the Census-based rental stock series: true if the number of rental dwellings available nationally rises measurably in the two years after the bill's commencement; false if the rental stock is flat or falls over that period.
reasoning: Measured on the sources the criterion names, rental supply did rise measurably after the Act's main changes commenced on 30 January 2025, then stalled. National bonds lodged rose from 159,494 in 2024 to 169,509 in 2025 (+6.3%), with 102,798 in Jan-Jun 2026. Available rental stock on realestate.co.nz was up 21.2% year on year in October 2025 and 17.4% in November 2025, and rents fell to their lowest since 2023. But 2026 reversed: Trade Me new listings were down 5% nationally in February 2026 with Auckland supply down 10%, Auckland bonds lodged fell about 10% for the year to April 2026, and a record 37-38% of surveyed landlords planned to sell. Two caveats: the bond series is provisional during MBIE's system migration (reclassification alone added 17,550 active bonds), and analysts attribute the 2025 abundance mainly to record emigration cutting tenant demand and landlords re-letting rather than selling, not to the tenancy changes or restored interest deductibility. The rise happened but did not hold through the two-year window (which closes January 2027), and the mechanism he asserted is unsupported.

statement: There will simply not be a situation under this Government where there will be as many jobs as there are unemployed people.
criterion: Stats NZ job vacancies measures (Jobs Online / Business Employment Data vacancies) compared with HLFS unemployed persons for each quarter of the 2023–2026 term; true if vacancies remain below the number of unemployed in every quarter, false if vacancies equal or exceed unemployed persons in any quarter before the term ends.
reasoning: Criterion caveat: the named measure does not exist as a count. MBIE's Jobs Online (not Stats NZ) is an index of online ads on four job boards; Stats NZ's Business Employment Data counts filled jobs, not vacancies — NZ has no official vacancy count. On every available measure the claim holds by a wide margin for every quarter of the term: HLFS unemployed rose to 171,000 (5.6%, an 11-year high) in the June 2026 quarter, while the Jobs Online vacancy index was 154 in Q2 2026 against an all-time high of 313 in Q3 2022, with ads still ~26% below 2019 levels. Infometrics' read is that job ads are 'not keeping pace with the number of people wanting work'. Disconfirming check: ads have grown for four straight quarters (+7% in the year to June 2026) after 11 quarters of falls, but that recovery is off a deep low and nothing puts advertised vacancies within an order of magnitude of 171,000. Only the Sept 2026 quarter remains unpublished before the term ends 7 Nov 2026, and it cannot close a gap of that size, so the falsifying condition is out of reach.

statement: I also note that keeping these repeat offenders off the streets will contribute to this Government’s commitment to 20,000 fewer victims of violent crime by 2029.
criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey (Ministry of Justice) victimisation counts for violent offences: true if the number of victims of violent crime in the 2029 reporting year is at least 20,000 below the stated baseline year; false if the count is flat or higher.
reasoning: The criterion measures the NZCVS 2029 reporting year against the stated baseline (185,000 victims of violent crime, October 2023; target 165,000 by 2029). That measurement is over three years away, so the criterion cannot be settled. Interim readings run strongly in the claim's favour and the government has already declared the target surpassed: 157,000 in the year to Feb 2025 (28,000 below baseline), 156,000 to May 2025 (29,000 below), and roughly 136,000 to Oct 2025 — 49,000 below baseline and the lowest since the survey began in 2018. Disconfirming evidence exists and matters for a 2029 reading: the sexual-assault component is above its own baseline (76,000 in Oct 2023 to 78,000 by May 2025), Canterbury recorded a 43% jump in violent-crime victims between Feb and May 2025, and NZCVS estimates carry wide confidence intervals, so the aggregate can move materially over three years. Separately, the causal half of the quote — that keeping repeat offenders in prison is what contributes to the reduction — is not testable against this criterion, since NZCVS victimisation counts cannot be attributed to a single sentencing regime.

statement: What we will see is that we will see an increased number of prisoners in our prisons.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics and the Ministry of Justice/Corrections forecast for the bill: true if the total prison muster is higher two years after commencement than at commencement, consistent with the official impact estimate for the regime; false if the muster is flat or lower.
reasoning: The bill is the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill (the second-reading debate began 10 Dec 2024 in the combined Hansard document HansD_20241210_20241212 and concluded 12 Dec; royal assent 17 Dec 2024), which commenced 17 June 2025 — matching the 2027-06-30 resolve date. Corrections managed 10,783 prisoners at 30 June 2025, thirteen days after commencement; the total was 11,256 at 30 June 2026, an increase of 473 (+4.4%). The muster passed the previous 2018 record of 10,820 in September 2025 (10,881), about 3.5 years earlier than the 2024 justice-sector projections expected, and the June 2026 projections put it at 15,200 by 2036. The formal two-year checkpoint is June 2027 and growth has plateaued since early 2026 (11,240 in Feb, 11,256 in June), but a false verdict would require the muster to fall below 10,783 within nine months, against every official forecast and a legislative pipeline (Sentencing (Reform) Act, Crimes Amendment Bill) expected to push it up. Attribution caveat the criterion invites: the increase is dominated by remand growth (43% of the population in 2025, up from 20% in 2014) and the wider sentencing package rather than the three-strikes regime itself, which bites only at second and third strike sentencing and so contributes little by 2027.

statement: This is an example of a Government implementing, as we’ve heard, a policy on the basis—only on the basis—that it suffices a coalition agreement, and what a shaky ground on which to put something into legislation, something that we know didn’t work last time, that we know won’t work this time.
criterion: Ministry of Justice / Department of Corrections evaluation of the reinstated three-strikes regime, measured on the two tests the speaker sets out in the same speech — deterrence of serious violent reoffending, and public perception of safety. True if neither a statistically detectable deterrent effect on qualifying offending nor an improvement in public perceptions of safety is found; false if either is demonstrated.
reasoning: The criterion requires a Ministry of Justice / Corrections evaluation of the reinstated regime measured on deterrence of serious violent reoffending and public perceptions of safety. The regime commenced 17 June 2025 and no such evaluation has been published as at September 2026; the Act contains no statutory review/evaluation requirement. Only operational volume data exists (182 strikes in the first year to 30 June 2026, one third-strike offender), which speaks to usage, not deterrence, and no post-commencement public-perception measure was found. The pre-enactment MoJ advice (no NZ evidence of general deterrence or increased public confidence) supports the speaker's direction but concerns the 2010-2022 regime, which the criterion as written does not accept as the test. Resolve-by date is 2030-06-30, so the prediction is not yet due.

statement: Once this bill is passed, there will be many people with one or two strikes, as we’ve said, who simply won’t know the conditions they now face.
criterion: The Act as enacted and Ministry of Justice/Corrections implementation material; true if the enacted regime carries strikes from the previous regime forward with no statutory or administrative requirement to notify affected individuals, so that a substantial number of people hold strikes without being informed; false if a notification process to those people was provided for and carried out.
reasoning: The enacted regime is retrospective: the select committee reversed the Minister's original 'not retrospective' position, and warnings given under the former law between 1 June 2010 and 16 August 2022 are reactivated where they meet the new thresholds (12 months for a first strike, 24 for later ones). Roughly 9,350 of 14,687 first strikes were reactivated. Ministry of Justice implementation material provides no notification to those people: to find out whether you hold a reactivated warning you must write to your local court asking for a Criminal and Traffic History Report, and 'a judge will then decide about giving them a copy'; MoJ states expressly that this cannot be obtained through a criminal record check. Otherwise a person learns of it from counsel only when next before the court. No statutory or administrative duty to notify was found in the Act or in MoJ/Corrections material, so a substantial number of people hold strikes without being informed - the criterion's 'true' branch.

statement: The Ministry of Justice are confident: not only are there no mistakes in the system; they don’t expect there to be any mistakes in the system going forward—not with the six-month implementation that they have.
criterion: Ministry of Justice, Police or court records, Official Information Act releases, or reported court decisions after the regime commences: false if any wrongly recorded, wrongly issued or wrongly counted strike warning or strike is identified in the first year of operation; true if no such error is documented.
reasoning: Searching MoJ releases, legal press, OIA-based reporting and court coverage for the first year of operation (17 June 2025 - 17 June 2026), I found no documented instance of a wrongly recorded, wrongly issued or wrongly counted strike warning or strike. The criterion's 'true' branch is therefore met. Two caveats limit the evidential weight, and I checked specifically for disconfirming material: Julie-Anne Kincade KC told practitioners in January 2026 that MoJ was reassessing strikes imposed under the previous framework and that 'there is no clear process for challenging incorrect classifications', so an individual error would be hard to surface publicly; and the large-scale recalculation of historic strikes (all 25 three-strike offenders reduced, ~half of 700 second strikes and 36% of 14,700 first strikes extinguished) was by design under the new thresholds, not error. MoJ's forecast of ~1,200 first strikes a year against 182 actual is a modelling miss, not a records error of the kind the criterion names. Verdict is 'unfalsified' rather than independently verified.

statement: I look forward to the third stage of this, which will be repealing this bill in 2026, and I look forward to being able to do that and introduce a justice system that works for victims, that actually delivers outcomes for New Zealand’s justice system, and that’s not just a bunch of cowboys looking tough.
criterion: The NZ statute record and Hansard third-reading divisions; true if the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 is repealed by an Act passed during calendar year 2026, false if it remains in force at 31 December 2026.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on 31 December 2026, which has not passed (today is 28 September 2026). Current state of the record: the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 received Royal assent 17 December 2024, its three-strikes provisions commenced 17 June 2025, and it remains in force with no repeal bill introduced. The general election is 7 November 2026 and Labour has not committed to repeal (justice spokesperson would only say she would 'be very surprised if that was a law that we continued to support'). A repeal Act passed in calendar 2026 would have to clear all stages in the few sitting weeks after the election, so the evidence points strongly toward the claim failing, but the resolution window is still open and absence of a repeal today is not yet the criterion's 'in force at 31 December 2026'.

statement: I’ve got a prediction: I think that they will, obviously, repeal the Therapeutic Products Act, they will work on an alternative, the alternative, as we know, will be split across a couple of different bills, and where we’ll end up landing will be pretty much where we would have been all along.
criterion: The replacement therapeutic products/natural health products legislation introduced by the Government: true if the replacement is introduced as two or more separate bills and its regulatory regime (risk-proportionate approval of medicines and medical devices, therapeutic-claim rules) is materially similar to the Therapeutic Products Act 2023; false if a single replacement bill is introduced, or if the resulting regime departs substantially from the repealed Act's framework.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on 30 June 2027 and turns on replacement legislation that has not been introduced. The repeal itself happened (Therapeutic Products Act Repeal Act 2024, assent 17 December 2024). On the 'split across a couple of different bills' half, the evidence so far matches: Cabinet agreed in September 2024 that natural health products would be regulated under a standalone bill, with medicines and medical devices in a separate Medical Products Bill. But as of the May 2026 official update, drafting was only expected to begin in 2026 with introduction to Parliament 'anticipated in 2027, subject to decisions after the upcoming election'. With no bill text, the criterion's second and decisive half — whether the regime is materially similar to the repealed Act's risk-proportionate approval and therapeutic-claim framework — cannot be tested.

statement: As a result of this legislation, as I understand it, there will then be a void in terms of any oversight over issues that relate to surgical mesh.
criterion: Medsafe / Health New Zealand publications after the repeal takes effect: false if surgical mesh remains subject to the existing pause, device notification and guideline development under the Medicines Act 1981 and its regulations; true if no oversight mechanism for surgical mesh is in force.
reasoning: The criterion is explicit: false if surgical mesh remains subject to the existing pause, device notification and guideline development under the Medicines Act 1981. It does. The Therapeutic Products Act 2023 had never commenced (its statutory date was 1 September 2026), so repealing it left the prior regime untouched: Medsafe continues as device regulator under the Medicines Act 1981, Medicines Regulations 1984 and the Medicines (Database of Medical Devices) Regulations 2003, which mandate WAND notification for devices including mesh. The disease-specific oversight also continued past the repeal: the August 2023 Director-General pause on mesh for stress urinary incontinence is still in force, Health NZ's mesh exception process (multidisciplinary panel review of every request) page was last updated 26 August 2026 after an April 2026 review, the Surgical Mesh Roundtable met in April 2026 and agreed to publish its minutes, an Interim High Vigilance Guideline is published, and the national mesh registry is under construction as the fourth safety condition that must be met before the pause can lift. I checked for the opposite — a gap, a lapsed pause, or a regulatory void after the repeal — and found none; there was no oversight to lose because the repealed Act had never taken effect. The reasonable reading of Utikere's claim is materially wrong, not merely overstated.

statement: I’m sure that, on reflection and after we go through them in detail, she will, but there is one thing I’d say first.
criterion: The committee-of-the-whole-House record for the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill; true if the Minister indicates support for, or the committee adopts, any of Duncan Webb's tabled amendments, false if every one is opposed and none is agreed to.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the Minister indicated support for, or the committee adopted, any of Webb's tabled amendments to the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill. The committee-of-the-whole-House Hansard (In Committee—Part 1, HansDeb_20241210_20241212_68, sitting block beginning 10 Dec 2024, committee stage taken 12 Dec under urgency) records Associate Minister Nicole McKee going through Webb's tabled amendments one by one and declining each: the first tabled amendment (12.15 p.m.) was refused on the ground that 'permanent' is consistent with other statutory language about the court record; the 12.52 p.m. and 12.53 p.m. amendments were likewise not supported; and of the commencement amendment tabled at 7.54 p.m. she said 'we will not be supporting this amendment. There's no need to delay the commencement.' No Opposition amendment was agreed to. Two independent checks on the final text confirm this: the Act commenced 17 June 2025, exactly the six-months-after-assent date the bill already provided (so the delayed-commencement amendment plainly failed), and the 'permanent' record wording survived into the Act. Wikipedia's account of the passage likewise records no Labour amendments being adopted; the bill moved from committee straight to a third reading passed 68-43 on party lines. Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for any amendment the government accepted at committee stage and for a 65-3 version reflecting Opposition changes, and found none — the only committee-stage changes traceable to the final Act are the Minister's own. Caveat on method: parliament.nz returns 404 to this environment's fetcher and legislation.govt.nz returns 403, so the Hansard text above was extracted via the search index reading those pages rather than a direct read of the transcript.

statement: I remind Dr Webb that, last night, we indicated that we also didn’t support the amendments, and I’ve checked with my colleagues in the ACT Party and New Zealand First, and they won’t be supporting the amendments either—just to give Dr Webb some assurance that this side of the Chamber won’t be supporting the amendments the Minister has already well and truly covered off.
criterion: The committee-stage voting record for the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill; true if ACT and New Zealand First voted against the Opposition amendments (including Webb's tabled amendment to new section 86KA), false if either party supported any of them.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether ACT and New Zealand First voted against the Opposition amendments at committee stage, including Webb's amendment to new section 86KA. Every Opposition amendment failed: the committee-stage Hansard shows Minister McKee (ACT) rejecting each of Webb's tabled amendments in turn, and no Opposition amendment appears in the bill as passed — the Act retains the select committee's 86KA appeal-court warning provision and the 'permanent' court-record wording, and commenced on the bill's own 17 June 2025 date. The arithmetic closes the case on NZ First: the House was 123 members, the government bloc 68 (National, ACT, NZ First) against 54-55 for Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori on the same day's second-reading division (68-54). Had either ACT (11) or NZ First (8) crossed, any Opposition amendment they backed would have carried. None did, so both parties must have opposed. Disconfirming check: I searched for any committee-stage amendment the government side supported, and for any NZ First speech or vote departing from the coalition line on this bill, and found none. Caveat: the amendments appear to have been negatived without party votes being called, so there is no division-by-division record naming ACT and NZ First; the verdict rests on the amendments' failure plus the seat arithmetic rather than on printed vote tallies for each amendment.

statement: It’s a sad day for justice when we’ve got a bill which cuts across constitutional principle, intentionally imposes disproportionate sentences, doesn’t have the effect of reducing the number of victims, and, in fact, if anything, it will have the likely effect of increasing crime in our communities in the long term, and, as I was saying, the regulatory impact statement says it won’t have any good effect but it will detrimentally affect many families, including families of Māori.
criterion: Police recorded violent-crime statistics and the NZ Crime and Victims Survey for the years following the regime's commencement in mid-2025; true if violent offending rises materially above the pre-commencement trend and evaluations attribute it in part to the regime, false if offending falls or is flat relative to trend.
reasoning: The criterion requires police recorded violent-crime statistics and NZCVS results for the years following commencement, plus evaluations attributing any rise to the regime. The regime commenced 17 June 2025, about fifteen months before today's date of 28 September 2026, and the criterion's own resolve-by date is 31 December 2030. The regime has barely operated: Ministry of Justice figures released to the NZ Herald under the OIA show roughly 10 first strikes imposed in the law's first five months, with no second or third strikes at all, so the mechanism Webb says will increase crime in the long term has had almost no exposure. The Ministry of Justice has committed to a post-implementation review but has not reported, and the Ministry's own evidence brief notes there is no substantial international or New Zealand evidence on the effect of three-strikes laws on crime either way. The NZCVS violent-crime releases continue (most recent factsheet May 2026) but no release or evaluation attributes any movement in violent offending to this regime. Disconfirming check: I searched for evidence that offending has fallen or is flat relative to trend, which would make the claim false rather than pending, and found no evaluation making that attribution either. Absence of a verdict here is the correct answer, not a failing grade for the claim.

statement: Instead, we have 12,000 fewer construction sector workers because this Government, based on these numbers, based on more cuts to come, will not be building houses.
criterion: Government housing delivery through 2025: true if no new public/social housing build programme is funded and new public housing completions fall away to negligible levels, false if the Government funds and delivers new public houses (e.g. new social housing places announced in Budget 2025).
reasoning: The criterion's false branch is satisfied: the Government both funded and delivered new public housing through 2025-26. Budget 2025 committed $128m over four years for at least 550 (550-600) new social homes in Auckland, on top of Budget 2024's $140m for 1,500 CHP social housing places running 1 July 2025 - 30 June 2027; the Housing Flexible Fund's first tranche delivered 820+ new social and affordable homes across nine locations. HUD's monthly delivery dashboard as at 30 April 2026 records 446 of those Budget 2024/2025-funded homes already delivered (211 + 235), and Kainga Ora plus CHPs delivered 2,787 additional places in 2024/25. Completions did not fall to negligible levels, and no new-build programme was withdrawn. Disconfirming evidence checked and partly found for her wider point but not for the criterion: Kainga Ora's own build programme was cut back under its turnaround plan and it sold ~800 state homes for $330m from July 2025, so net stock growth is far slower than gross additions suggest; construction sector activity was also weak through 2025 before recovering (construction up 2.7% in the June 2026 quarter, the largest rise since June 2023). Those qualify the severity but do not make 'will not be building houses' true as written.

statement: After several years of growth jumping along the bottom, in and out of recession, we are now able to forecast confidently a sustained period of economic growth.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP (production measure) for the calendar quarters of 2025; true if growth is positive across the period with no further technical recession (two consecutive quarterly contractions), false if the economy contracts again or growth stalls near zero.
reasoning: Stats NZ production-measure GDP for the 2025 calendar quarters: March +0.9%, June -0.9%, September +0.9% (first reported +1.1%, revised), December +0.2%. Annual average growth for the year ended December 2025 was just +0.2%. Both of the criterion's false conditions occurred - the economy contracted again (a sharp -0.9% 'June swoon', more than twice the fall economists forecast), and growth then stalled near zero (+0.2% in the December quarter, +0.2% annual average). Disconfirming evidence checked: there was no second technical recession, since the June 2025 contraction was a single quarter followed by a 0.9-1.1% rebound in September, and growth has continued into 2026 (+0.9% March 2026, +0.2% June 2026, +1.7% for the year to June 2026). So a recovery did eventually arrive, but the 'sustained period of economic growth' he said could be forecast confidently was interrupted within two quarters and averaged near zero across 2025, which is what the criterion tests.

statement: It is to defund public services to failure, to watch them fail, point that out to the public, and then say, “Hey, we should privatise that.” Mark my words: that is the next thing on the agenda.
criterion: Government announcements and Budget/manifesto documents through the end of the parliamentary term; true if the Government proposes or legislates the sale or privatisation of a public service or state asset, false if no such proposal is made by the end of the term.
reasoning: The criterion's true branch is met, so this resolves now rather than not_yet_due even though the term runs to 7 November 2026. The Government has proposed partial privatisation of a state asset: Cabinet approved Kiwi Group Capital raising up to $500m of private capital for Kiwibank, with Willis saying investors could later sell on the NZX 'should a future Government decide to float the bank', and in May 2026 State-Owned Enterprises Minister Simeon Brown's letter of intent to KGC explicitly asked Kiwibank to revisit partial privatisation after the bank had shelved it in December 2025. Kainga Ora has also sold ~800 state homes for $330m since July 2025 under a programme targeting 900-1,000, and Treasury ran an SOE 'ownership purpose' review while Brown demanded turnaround plans from NZ Post, Landcorp and Kordia. Disconfirming evidence, which is why this is only partly correct: the Government repeatedly reconfirmed it would not sell assets this term; the Kiwibank raise returns no capital to the Crown, keeps Kiwi Group Holdings at least 51% government-owned, and Willis said an IPO would not proceed without an electoral mandate; National's campaign chair said in September 2026 that National is 'not going to the election campaigning on asset sales' and its 2026 pledge card omits them; and no public service was proposed for privatisation. Swarbrick's specific mechanism - defund a public service to failure, then propose privatising it - is not what the record shows; a commercial SOE capital raise and state-house churn is a materially weaker version of her claim.

statement: Let me guess, they’ll probably say, “before the next election”—we will all wait until then and probably not see it.
criterion: The legislative record on legislation.govt.nz and Parliament's bills register; true if no replacement therapeutic products/medicines regulatory regime has been enacted by the 2026 general election, false if replacement legislation is passed before that election.
reasoning: Criterion: true if no replacement therapeutic products/medicines regulatory regime has been enacted by the 2026 general election (7 Nov 2026). No such Act exists. The Therapeutic Products Act 2023 was repealed (Therapeutic Products Act Repeal Act 2024, royal assent 17 Dec 2024). Its intended replacement, the Medical Products Bill, was still at Cabinet policy stage on 7 April 2026, was never introduced to the House, and MoH material says it would commence 'around 2030'. No medicines/medical/therapeutic products Act appears in the 54th Parliament's 2026 enactments. The one enacted change, the Medicines Amendment Act 2025 (in force 19 Nov 2025), amends the Medicines Act 1981 (overseas-approval verification pathway, pharmacy ownership) rather than replacing the regime, so it does not satisfy the criterion's 'replacement regime'. Although the resolve date has not literally arrived, the outcome is determined: the House adjourned on 24 September 2026 and Parliament dissolves 1 October 2026, so no further legislation can be enacted before the election. Disconfirming check: searched the legislation/acts register and bill register for a Medical Products Act or Natural Health Products Act 2026 and found none.

statement: Well, I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries.
criterion: Public record of the Cook Strait ferry replacement programme: true if two rail-compatible ferries procured under this decision are in operational service during 2029; false if they are not in service by the end of 2029 or the rail-compatible specification is abandoned.
reasoning: Criterion resolves on whether two rail-compatible ferries are in operational service during 2029; resolve-by 2029-12-31, over three years away. Interim status (not a verdict): Ferry Holdings signed a NZ$596m fixed-price contract with Guangzhou Shipyard International for two 200m rail-enabled ferries, named KUPE and COOK; KiwiRail was confirmed as operator at Parliament on 17 July 2026; Picton (Waitohi) and Wellington port works are underway; ship design is in final stages with construction due to start May 2027; the programme is still stated as entering service in 2029 within the $1.7bn Crown funding envelope. The rail-compatible specification has not been abandoned. Nothing yet decides the claim either way.

statement: Does he agree with the Child Poverty Action Group that his decision to put the wellbeing of landlords over the wellbeing of tamariki will put 20,000 more children into poverty by the time his term is up?
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics releases through to the year ending June 2026: true if the number of children in poverty on the primary measures rises by approximately 20,000 or more over the term; false if the count is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion is explicitly tied to Stats NZ child poverty statistics through to the year ending June 2026, which is not published until around February 2027 (resolve-by 2027-02-28). Two of the term's three years are in. Baseline YE June 2023: material hardship 12.5% (143,700 children); BHC50 12.6%; AHC50 17.5% (202,100). YE June 2025 (released 26 Feb 2026): material hardship 14.3% (169,300) — roughly +25,600 on 2023; AHC50-fixed 17.8% (210,600); BHC50 12.6% (148,700), essentially flat. So one primary measure has already risen by more than 20,000 while another is flat and Stats NZ reported no statistically significant annual change from 2024 to 2025. Disconfirming consideration: the Household Income and Living Survey replaced the Household Economic Survey from 2024/25, creating a break in series that weakens direct term-start-to-term-end comparison. The final year's data decides it.

statement: Under those conditions, I’m confident we will see a turn-around that will keep these people far away from any levers of power for a generation to come.
criterion: General election results and government formation from 2026 onward; false if Labour/Greens/Te Pāti Māori form a government at the next election, true if they remain out of office well beyond it.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the next general election and subsequent government formation. The 2026 New Zealand general election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026, which has not yet occurred as of 28 September 2026. No result and no government formation exist to judge against, and the claim's stated horizon ('a generation to come') extends far past the 2026-12-31 resolve-by date in any case. Not findable because it has not happened, not because evidence is missing.

statement: Be afraid, be very, very afraid, of Budget 2025 and what it is going to bring. It is going to bring more cuts.
criterion: Budget 2025 documents (delivered May 2025): true if the Budget announces further baseline savings, programme reductions or departmental cuts beyond those already in place; false if it contains no new savings or reductions.
reasoning: Budget 2025, delivered 22 May 2025, announced substantial further savings and programme reductions beyond those already in place, exactly as the criterion requires. The operating allowance was reduced from NZ$2.4b to NZ$1.3b; roughly NZ$5.3b of savings offset NZ$6.7b of new operating spending. Named cuts include the NZ$375m Kahui Ako programme (disestablished), NZ$36.1m from kaupapa Maori/Maori-medium education, NZ$32.5m from Maori housing supply, NZ$36m from the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, NZ$18m over four years from RNZ, and a NZ$20m reduction to the Maori Development Fund; the pay equity threshold change was booked at ~NZ$12.8b over four years. Most departments received no cost-pressure funding and had to absorb wage increases. Treasury's own Budget 2025 baseline savings reports confirm a formal baseline savings exercise. Woods' prediction of 'more cuts' is borne out; nothing found suggests the Budget was savings-neutral.

statement: What is positive to note is that the outlook going forward is going to be better. We know that the economic growth forecast for next year is increasing.
criterion: Stats NZ real GDP series; true if annual real GDP growth for calendar 2025 exceeds that for calendar 2024, false if it is equal or lower.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether annual real GDP growth for calendar 2025 exceeds calendar 2024. Stats NZ reported GDP fell 0.5 percent over the year ended December 2024. For 2025 the series turned positive: Stats NZ recorded +0.2 percent in the December 2025 quarter following +0.9 percent in September 2025, with the economy growing 1.1 percent over the second half of 2025 and annual growth to the December 2025 quarter of about 1.3 percent; TradingEconomics' full-year series puts calendar 2025 at +0.2 percent against -0.3 percent for 2024. On every series checked, 2025 growth exceeds 2024, so the criterion is satisfied. Disconfirming check: 2025 was not a smooth recovery (a June 2025 quarter contraction, and Westpac noted the 1.3 percent annual result undershot its 1.6 percent forecast and was too weak to move unemployment), and growth came in far below the forecasts Watts was citing in December 2024 — but the criterion is a comparison of 2025 against 2024, not against forecast, and 2025 clears it.

statement: There will be protests, and that will lead to uncertainty, and my advice to applicants is to not use this process.
criterion: Media and police records of public protest action directed at projects listed under the Fast-track Approvals Act: true if organised protests against one or more listed projects are reported during 2025, false if no such protest activity occurs.
reasoning: The criterion asks only for media/police records of organised protest against Fast-track-listed projects during 2025. Abundant and dated: ~700-1,500 people at Ruakākā Beach plus a 50+ vessel flotilla on 16 March 2025 against the McCallum Bros Bream Bay sand-mining fast-track proposal; 70 people occupied the Denniston Plateau mine site on 20 April 2025 with at least nine charged with wilful trespass; two activists occupied Bathurst's Stockton aerial ropeway for 23 days in July-August 2025 explicitly against its fast-track application to mine the Denniston Plateau, and appeared in court; beach protests and paddle-outs against Trans-Tasman Resources' South Taranaki seabed mine on 10 June 2025. Checked for the disconfirming case (a quiet year, no project-specific action) and found the opposite across mining, seabed mining and sand extraction. Note the criterion tests only the protest half of the quote, not the 'applicants should not use this process' advice.

statement: Now, they have the opportunity to do that and it’s highly likely that they will proceed in some form or other, and that is a disgrace.
criterion: Decisions of expert panels under the Fast-track Approvals Act on applications from listed projects that had previously been declined consent (for example previously declined mining or subdivision proposals): true if a majority of those previously declined listed projects obtain fast-track approval and proceed, false if most are declined or do not advance.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-12-31 and the set of previously-declined listed projects is still part-decided, with no majority determinable either way as at 2026-09-28. Against the prediction: Te Kuha (declined by the Environment Court and Supreme Court) had its fast-track referral returned as non-compliant on 7 March 2025 and the mine is recorded as cancelled; Trans-Tasman Resources' Taranaki VTM (2017 consent quashed by the Supreme Court in 2021) received a draft decision to decline on 4 February 2026 and the applicant withdrew on 19 February 2026. For the prediction: Maitahi Village (Nelson) and Sunfield were approved (Sunfield's March 2026 approval is under High Court appeal by Auckland Council), and Delmore was approved on a relodged application after its first was draft-declined and withdrawn in September 2025. McCallum Bros' Bream Bay application, lodged January 2026 after the company's Pākiri consents were refused and lost in the Environment Court, is undecided. Around 30-plus approvals have issued overall, but the previously-declined subset the criterion names has outstanding cases that could swing the majority.

statement: I can assure you that they have nothing to worry about, because the Māori Party won’t be here at the next election. If the Serious Fraud Office doesn’t drive them out, the people who voted them in will turn their backs on them, because this bill actually embeds genuine statutory engagement and participation rights for Māoridom.
criterion: The Electoral Commission official result for the next New Zealand general election: true if Te Pāti Māori returns no members to Parliament; false if it wins any electorate or list seat.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the Electoral Commission official result for the next general election, which is scheduled for 7 November 2026. As at today (28 September 2026) the election has not been held, so no official result exists. Te Pāti Māori currently holds 4 seats in the 54th Parliament (down from 6 at the 2023 election through mid-term attrition), and it is contesting the 2026 election, but neither fact resolves the criterion as written.

statement: On the other side of the House, we see the people who say “No, no, no” to all of those things, and the people of New Zealand will say no to them at the 2026 election.
criterion: The official result of the 2026 New Zealand general election as declared by the Electoral Commission. True if the Opposition parties fail to win enough seats to form a government; false if they are able to form the government.
reasoning: The criterion names the official 2026 general election result declared by the Electoral Commission. The election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026 (announced by PM Luxon; advance voting from 26 October, enrolment deadline 25 October). Today is 28 September 2026, so no vote has been held and no result declared. No evidence either way can exist yet; this is pending, not false.

statement: They will extend the life and extent of coalmines.
criterion: Decisions of expert panels under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024: true if one or more coal mining projects extending the life or footprint of an existing mine are approved under the Act, false if no coal mine extension is approved by the resolve date.
reasoning: The criterion requires an expert-panel approval under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 of a coal project extending an existing mine's life or footprint, by 2027-12-31. As of late September 2026 no coal project has been approved: the only coal project in Schedule 2, Bathurst's Buller Plateaux Continuation Project (25-year extension, ~6,500 ha across the Stockton and Denniston plateaux, 20 Mt to 2055), was lodged 21 August 2026 and returned as incomplete by the EPA around 25 September 2026 (lizard mitigation; reserve-manager consent). Bathurst plans to resubmit and expects a decision in 2027, inside the resolve window. Disconfirming check: the first and only mining approval under the Act to date is Waihi North (gold, 18 Dec 2025), and the Taranaki VTM ironsands application was draft-declined then withdrawn — so no coal approval has been missed. Directional context that does not meet the criterion as written: an Order in Council amended Bathurst's fast-track listing to enable a larger West Coast coal project, which is consistent with the claim's direction but is not a panel approval.

statement: Kia kaha, kia hāneanea tō noho mō te rua tau. Ka mutu te rua tau, kua ngaro noa atu koutou.
criterion: The result of the New Zealand general election due in 2026 and the government formed after it; true if the National–ACT–New Zealand First coalition does not return to government, false if it is returned to office.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the 2026 general election result and the government formed after it. The election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 and has not been held as of 28 September 2026, so no government formation has occurred and the National–ACT–NZ First coalition's return or defeat is undetermined.

statement: What this does mean for New Zealanders and their families is this: New Zealanders will have better access to more effective cancer treatments, such as CAR T-cell therapy—if they want to.
criterion: Medsafe approvals and Pharmac funding decisions plus Te Whatu Ora service records for CAR T-cell therapy; true if CAR T-cell therapy is approved and available to New Zealand patients through the health system (beyond clinical-trial-only access) by the resolve date, false if access remains trial-only or requires treatment overseas.
reasoning: Resolve date is 2028-12-31, two years away. As of September 2026 CAR T-cell therapy is still not available in New Zealand outside clinical trials — no Medsafe approval and no Pharmac funding decision for any CAR T product could be found, and the therapy is not offered publicly or privately. The Malaghan Institute's ENABLE-2 phase 2 trial is past its midpoint with patient treatment expected to complete in early 2027; Prof. Weinkove's stated ambition is public-system availability 'in 2027 – subject to results and regulatory approvals and funding'. Engagement with Medsafe, Pharmac and Health NZ is at the stage of defining how CAR T therapies should be assessed, not a decision. The criterion (approved and available through the health system beyond trial-only access) is therefore not yet met, but the date has not passed, so this is pending rather than wrong — the trajectory is consistent with the claim.

statement: Our GE regime is going to change.
criterion: The statute book and Parliament's bill record; true if legislation replacing or materially amending the HSNO 1996 controls on new organisms (the Gene Technology Bill or a successor) is enacted, false if the regime is unchanged by the resolve date.
reasoning: Resolve date is 2026-12-31, three months after today. The Gene Technology Bill has not been enacted: first reading December 2024, referred to the Health Committee, which reported back on 10 October 2025 with a revised draft; the second reading then slipped repeatedly (the PM: 'it's complicated'), was reported as stalled in mid-2026 with inter-party negotiations ongoing, and was back on Parliament's agenda the week of 22 July 2026. September 2026 coverage still describes it as proposed legislation before Parliament. No Gene Technology Act appears on the statute book and HSNO 1996 still governs new organisms, so the criterion's 'true' condition (enactment of legislation replacing or materially amending the HSNO controls) is not yet satisfied — but nor has the resolve date passed, and a general election falls on 7 November 2026. Pending, not wrong.

statement: The credit rating agencies have said, because of this bill and because this Government repealed affordable water, councils’ credit ratings will go down.
criterion: S&P Global Ratings' published New Zealand local government rating actions; true if multiple territorial authorities are downgraded or shifted to negative outlook in the period following the bill, false if council ratings are broadly affirmed or upgraded.
reasoning: Both halves of the claim check out against the criterion. The attribution is real: S&P's Martin Foo said in November 2023 that repealing the Affordable Water Reforms without a workable alternative 'could add to recent downgrade pressure on the 25 councils we rate in New Zealand' (three councils — Marlborough, Hastings, Whangarei — had already been cut, five more on negative outlook). The outcome occurred: on 18 March 2025 S&P downgraded 18 councils (Christchurch, Dunedin, Greater Wellington, Hamilton, Hastings, Hutt, Kapiti Coast, Marlborough, Nelson, New Plymouth, Palmerston North, Porirua, South Taranaki, Tasman, Taupo, Waimakariri, Wellington City, Whanganui) plus three CCOs, and separately shifted 15 councils and two CCOs from stable to negative outlook. An October 2025 S&P report ('New Zealand Water Reforms Don't Guarantee Rating Relief For Local Councils') found the replacement regime 'may not ease the financial burden... our ratings on some may continue to face downward pressure', because water-entity debt is still counted as a council contingent liability — 'off the books doesn't always mean off the hook'. Disconfirming check: the only reversal found is Wellington City's outlook returning to stable in September 2026 — one council against 18 downgrades, so ratings were not 'broadly affirmed or upgraded'.
