Nuance worth noting: S&P's stated drivers for the March 2025 round were the revenue/expenditure mismatch and higher structural debt, with policy volatility ('quick passage and repeal of several key laws') a contributing factor rather than the water bill specifically — the causal weight McAnulty implied is stronger than S&P's own rationale, but the criterion as written asks only whether multiple territorial authorities were downgraded or moved to negative outlook following the bill, and they were.

statement: This bill doesn’t fix the problem and it will cost ratepayers more.
criterion: Council long-term plan and annual report data on average household water charges/rates under the new regime, plus Water Services Authority monitoring; true if average household water charges rise in real terms across councils following implementation, false if they hold flat or fall in real terms.
reasoning: The criterion resolves by 2028-06-30 and requires council long-term-plan/annual-report data on average household water charges plus Water Services Authority monitoring across councils following implementation. Implementation has barely begun: the Local Government (Water Services) Act 2025 came into force 27 August 2025 and the first water organisations were only established on 1 July 2026 (e.g. Tiaki Wai, Wellington). No post-implementation annual reports or WSA charge-monitoring series exist yet, so the named evidence base cannot be read. Early direction leans toward the cost half of the claim: the Taxpayers' Union 2026 dashboard puts the average proposed 2026/27 rates rise at 6.9% against 3.1% inflation and 7.9% nationwide once new water charges are included, and for the 14 councils transitioning on 1 July 2026 reporting puts a headline 6.14% rise at 15.88% total cost once water charges are counted. That is a single year from an advocacy source, not the LTP/annual-report/WSA evidence the criterion names. The 'doesn't fix the problem' half is not operationalised by the criterion.

statement: This legislation is expected to be passed in mid-2025, with the first permits being considered at the end of next year.
criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill and MBIE permit announcements: true if the bill received Royal assent around the middle of 2025 and the first permit applications were under consideration by 31 December 2025; false if passage slipped materially beyond mid-2025 or no permits were being considered by the end of 2025.
reasoning: Both halves of the criterion fail. Passage slipped materially beyond mid-2025: the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill passed its third reading on 30 June 2026 and was signed into law on 9 July 2026 as the Offshore Renewable Energy Act 2026 — about a year later than predicted. On permits, feasibility-permit and cost-recovery regulations were only made once the Act was in force in mid-2026, and as of July 2026 officials were still to advise on the timing of the first application round, with summaries of proposed developments to be published only after an application round closes. No permit applications were under consideration by 31 December 2025.

statement: I suspect it will get support around the House, and I see no reason to delay it on that process.
criterion: The Hansard vote record for the next reading of the Crimes (slavery offences penalties) Amendment Bill; true if it passed with the support of all parties, false if any party voted against it.
reasoning: The support half holds so far: Greg Fleming's Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill passed its first reading on 17/18 December 2024 with no party vote breakdown recorded and no party reported as voting against, consistent with 'support around the House'. But the criterion points at the vote record for the next reading, and that vote does not exist: the select committee report was due 16 June 2025 and the bill is still awaiting its second reading as of September 2026, well past the 31 December 2025 resolve date. So the all-party vote Webb anticipated cannot be confirmed, and 'I see no reason to delay it' did not hold in practice. Note the Crimes Amendment Bill that reached a third reading in August 2026 is separate government legislation (opposed by Labour and the Greens), not Fleming's member's bill.

statement: She’s going to see her bill passed today, and the bill has a good foundation in what is seeks to achieve.
criterion: Hansard record for 17 December 2024; true if the bill's third reading was agreed to that day, false if it was not put or was defeated.
reasoning: The bill in question is Rima Nakhle's Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill (member's bill, National). Its legislative history shows: introduced 31 Jan 2024, first reading 20 Mar 2024, second reading 6 Nov 2024, committee of the whole House concluded 20 Nov 2024, and THIRD READING 17 DECEMBER 2024 — PASSED, with royal assent days later (22–23 Dec 2024) as the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Act 2024. The criterion (third reading agreed to that day) is satisfied. Disconfirming check: no source indicates the reading was deferred or defeated, and the existence of the assented Act plus the 11-3 (third reading) bill print rules that out. Webb's added clause about the bill having 'a good foundation' is an opinion, not a falsifiable prediction.

statement: They have willingly listened and heard, and they will subsequently continue to monitor and to report back on the safeguards available to protect those victims where their offenders are serving community-based sentences.
criterion: Department of Corrections annual reports and Justice Committee annual review/Estimates responses after 2024; true if Corrections reports on safeguards for victims of community-managed offenders, false if no such monitoring or reporting appears.
reasoning: Checked the sources the criterion names. The Justice Committee's 2023/24 annual review of the Department of Corrections (March 2025, hearing 5 Dec 2024) contains no discussion of safeguards for victims of community-managed offenders — 'victims' appears only as a generic core responsibility ('providing information to the courts, the NZ Parole Board, and registered victims') and as a Justice Cluster objective ('better outcomes for victims'). The Justice Committee's 2025/26 Estimates for Vote Corrections report (July 2025) likewise has nothing: its only 'victims' references are staff who are victims of assault by prisoners. No 2024/25 annual review report was locatable before the 2026-06-30 resolve-by date. On the other hand, Corrections does continue to monitor and report victim-related measures in its Annual Report: Vote Corrections 2025/26 specifies 'Percentage of victims who are notified as per New Zealand Parole Board requirements' (target ≥98%, est. actual 88–93%) and 'Number of justified complaints about notification services received from registered victims' (Nil), plus a funded component 'Information and Administrative Services to Victims', and the 'Public Safety is Improved' appropriation covers offenders on community-based sentences 'in a manner so as to improve the safety of offenders, staff, victims and the public'. But those victim measures are anchored to the Parole Board/judicial process, and the 'Sentences and Orders Served in the Community' category's only measures are sentence completion and non-compliance accountability — no victim-safeguard measure. So the general commitment to keep monitoring and reporting on victims holds, but the specific report-back Brewer promised, on safeguards for victims whose offenders are on community-based sentences, does not appear in the named accountability documents. Caveat: corrections.govt.nz returns 403 to my fetches, so the full 2024/25 Annual Report PDF was read only indirectly (via the Estimates measures it reports against and search snippets indicating the victim-notification measure was 'achieved').

statement: Having public select committee hearings will enable us to put the spotlight on post-natal care in New Zealand, it will enable us to raise any concerns, and it will provide the opportunity for those who want to share their stories.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament Health Committee record for the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill; true if the committee called for and received public submissions and held oral hearings on the bill, false if the bill did not reach committee or the committee took no public submissions.
reasoning: The Health Committee's report on the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill (37—1, June 2025) states in its Committee procedure appendix: 'The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill was referred to the committee on 17 December 2024. We called for submissions with a closing date of 17 February 2025. We received and considered submissions from 123 interested groups and individuals, and heard oral evidence from 20 submitters.' That satisfies both limbs of the criterion (public submissions called for and received; oral hearings held). The report's body also records concerns being raised by submitters on both sides and personal/organisational perspectives on postnatal care, matching Wedd's three predicted outcomes. The committee recommended the bill be passed without amendment. Disconfirming check: there is no indication the bill failed to reach committee or that submissions were not taken.

statement: Well, I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries.
criterion: Public records of the Cook Strait ferry replacement (Ferry Holdings / KiwiRail / Minister for Rail announcements); true if two rail-compatible ferries are in commercial operation on the Cook Strait during calendar 2029, false if they are not in service by 31 December 2029.
reasoning: Resolve date is 2029-12-31; the ferries cannot be in commercial operation yet. As of mid-2026 the programme is proceeding: two 200m rail-enabled ferries (Kupe and Cook) contracted to Guangzhou Shipyard International under a fixed-price deal (~$596m ships within a $1.7b envelope), ship construction to begin 2027, port infrastructure works underway in Wellington and Picton, and Ferry Holdings' July 2026 update states the vessels remain on track to enter service in 2029 (one arriving earlier, one by end of 2029). No slippage announced, but nothing confirms operation in 2029.

statement: Does he agree with the Child Poverty Action Group that his decision to put the wellbeing of landlords over the wellbeing of tamariki will put 20,000 more children into poverty by the time his term is up?
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics releases covering the years to 2026/27; true if the number of children in poverty on the primary measures rises by approximately 20,000 or more over the term, false if the count is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on Stats NZ child poverty releases covering years to 2026/27 (resolve-by 2027-02-28); today is 2026-09-28 and the latest release is year ended June 2025, published 26 Feb 2026. Interim evidence runs in the predicted direction but is not the required release: material hardship rose from 10.6% (~125,300 children) in 2022/23 to 14.3% (169,300) in 2024/25, and AHC50-fixed from 14.6% (2022) to 17.8% (210,600) — increases well above 20,000 children — though the June 2025 annual change was not statistically significant and the survey changed from HES to HILS from July 2024, which Stats NZ and CPAG both flag as a comparability caveat.

statement: After several years of growth jumping along the bottom, in and out of recession, we are now able to forecast confidently a sustained period of economic growth.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP series for 2025 and the first half of 2026: true if New Zealand records consecutive quarters of positive growth through that period with no further technical recession; false if GDP contracts for two consecutive quarters at any point before mid-2026.
reasoning: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP (production): Mar-25 +0.8%, Jun-25 -0.9%, Sep-25 +1.1% (revised to about +0.9%), Dec-25 +0.2%, Mar-26 +0.8%, Jun-26 +0.2% (annual +1.7% to June 2026). The criterion's falsifier — two consecutive contracting quarters before mid-2026 — never occurred, so there was no further technical recession. But the criterion's truth condition of consecutive positive quarters through 2025 and H1 2026 also failed: the June 2025 quarter fell 0.9%, a broad-based contraction that at the time made three falls in five quarters. Growth since has been positive but slow. Substance (no recession, growth resumed) holds; 'confidently forecast a sustained period of growth' overstates what followed.

statement: This is the austerity playbook. It is to defund public services to failure, to watch them fail, point that out to the public, and then say, “Hey, we should privatise that.” Mark my words: that is the next thing on the agenda.
criterion: Government announcements and Cabinet papers to the end of the parliamentary term; true if the coalition Government proposes the sale or privatisation of a public service or state asset, false if no such proposal is advanced.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the coalition Government proposes the sale or privatisation of a public service or state asset before the term ends. Concrete moves after December 2024 satisfy it in letter: Health Minister Simeon Brown's March 2025 Letter of Expectations directed Health NZ to give private hospitals 10-year elective-surgery outsourcing contracts (~10,600 surgeries, $50m announced), which is privatised delivery of a public service; Kainga Ora began a ministerially signed-off programme selling ~900 state homes a year for $400-500m (730 sold by March 2026, including Bishop's sign-off on 171 Ormiston properties); and in July 2025 Cabinet approved Kiwi Group raising up to $500m of private capital, with the Crown to retain at least 51% and an IPO explicitly deferred pending an electoral mandate — after that raise collapsed, Newsroom reported in May 2026 that a partial sale was back on the menu. Groundwork was also laid: Treasury's November 2025 Investment Statement urged a formal capital-recycling programme, Deputy PM Seymour commissioned ownership-purpose statements for 10 SOEs (Pamu/Landcorp, Kordia, QV, TVNZ, NZ Post, Kiwibank, the gentailers), and Luxon publicly floated taking asset recycling to the electorate. But the stronger reading she signalled — the coalition moving to privatise services it had defunded — was not borne out within the term: the Government insisted the Kiwibank raise was 'not a state asset sale', repeatedly ruled out asset sales this term, NZ First opposed, Willis said in September 2026 that asset sales are off the table while she is finance minister and 'not our policy at the election', and campaign chair Simeon Brown then confirmed National would not campaign on asset sales in 2026. Substance holds, materially overstated.

statement: Under those conditions, I’m confident we will see a turn-around that will keep these people far away from any levers of power for a generation to come.
criterion: New Zealand general election results and subsequent government formation; true if neither Labour nor the Greens is in government after the 2026 and 2029 elections, false if either enters government at either election.
reasoning: The criterion requires the results of both the 2026 and 2029 general elections and the governments formed after them. Luxon announced the 2026 general election for Saturday 7 November 2026 (advance voting from 26 October); as of today, 28 September 2026, it has not been held, so no post-2026 government exists to test, let alone the 2029 one. No disconfirming event is available either — neither Labour nor the Greens has entered government since the claim was made in December 2024. Earliest partial resolution is after 7 November 2026 government formation; full resolution not before the 2029 election.

statement: Five more years of deficit means five more years of pōharatanga—of austerity and pain for our people.
criterion: Treasury fiscal updates and the Crown's annual Financial Statements for the years 2025 through 2029: true if OBEGAL (or OBEGALx) remains in deficit in each of those years, false if a surplus is recorded before 2029.
reasoning: The criterion needs OBEGAL/OBEGALx outturns for 2025 through 2029, and only 2025 is settled. The audited Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 record an OBEGALx deficit of $9.3bn (~2.1% of GDP), wider than the prior year — a deficit, consistent with the prediction. The FY2026 year-end statements are not yet published (the eleven-month interim to 31 May 2026 came out 2 July 2026; the annual accounts are normally released in October). Budget 2026 (28 May 2026) forecasts an OBEGAL deficit of $11.9bn (2.6% of GDP) in 2025/26 and $11.4bn (2.4%) in 2026/27, with the first OBEGALx surplus at $2.6bn (0.5% of GDP) in 2028/29 — described by Willis as the first surplus in a decade — and the traditional OBEGAL measure not reaching surplus ($2.3bn) until 2029/30. So on current forecasts no surplus is recorded before 2029, which would make the claim correct, but 2027, 2028 and 2029 are forecasts rather than outturns and the forecast first surplus falls on the 2029 boundary the criterion draws. Not resolvable until the FY2029 accounts.

statement: Be afraid, be very, very afraid, of Budget 2025 and what it is going to bring. It is going to bring more cuts.
criterion: Budget 2025 documents (Budget Economic and Fiscal Update and the savings/reprioritisation summary) delivered May 2025: true if the Budget announces further savings or spending reductions beyond those already in place, false if it contains no new cuts.
reasoning: Budget 2025, delivered 22 May 2025, was funded by an average $5.3b/yr of savings, reprioritisation and revenue measures (~$21b over four years) inside a $1.3b operating allowance, the lowest in a decade. New reductions announced in that Budget include narrowing the pay equity regime (~$12.8b over the forecast period), halving the government KiwiSaver contribution from $521 to $260.72 and removing it above $180k income (~$0.6b/yr), full income-testing of Best Start (~$211m/4yr), and $5.2b of reprioritised savings across 116 initiatives. The criterion asked for further savings or spending reductions beyond those already in place; Budget 2025 announced several, so the prediction of 'more cuts' resolves true.

statement: We are in a turn-round, and the actions that this Government has taken, on this side of our House, are setting the foundations for a successful future in this country which will see increased economic growth, increased value, and increased benefits for hard-working Kiwis.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts: true if annual average real GDP growth for calendar 2025 exceeds that for calendar 2024; false if growth is equal to or lower than 2024.
reasoning: On the criterion's stated measure (Stats NZ national accounts, annual average real GDP), growth for the year ended December 2025 was +0.2 percent, versus a fall of 0.5 percent for the year ended December 2024. Stats NZ/RNZ noted the December 2025 quarter release marked the first annual growth in more than two years, which independently confirms 2024 was negative. 2025 therefore exceeds 2024 and the criterion resolves true. Checked the disconfirming side: no revision puts 2024 above 2025, and the following quarter (March 2026, +0.8%) continued the expansion. Noted for the record that the margin is small - growth off a contraction rather than strong growth - but the criterion asked only whether 2025 exceeded 2024.

statement: I can assure you that they have nothing to worry about, because the Māori Party won’t be here at the next election.
criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the next general election after December 2024; true if Te Pāti Māori returns no members of Parliament, false if it wins any electorate seat or crosses the party-vote threshold.
reasoning: The criterion requires Electoral Commission official results for the next general election after December 2024. That election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 (announced January 2026 by the Prime Minister); writ day is 4 October 2026, Parliament dissolves 1 October 2026, advance voting opens 26 October and the writ returns by 3 December 2026. As of today, 28 September 2026, the election has not been held and no official results exist, so the criterion cannot be evaluated. Te Pati Maori currently holds 4 seats (down from 6 in 2023, after the 2025 Tamaki Makaurau by-election), but interim caucus size is not the evidence the criterion names and was not substituted for it.

statement: It’s going to be supported across the House.
criterion: The Hansard vote record for the first reading of the Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill; true if it passed with every party voting in favour, false if any party voted against.
reasoning: The bill did pass its first reading on 17/18 December 2024 and was referred to the Justice Committee, so it was not defeated. But the criterion names the Hansard vote record, and that record is not retrievable from here: the parliament.nz Hansard page for the debate (HansDeb_20241217_20241218_04) is indexed by search engines but returns 404 or a Radware block, has no Wayback snapshot, and renders content only via JavaScript. WhereTheyStand, which mirrors divisions when they exist, states 'No vote breakdown is recorded on WhereTheyStand for this reading.' No secondary source (World Vision, Salvation Army, NZ Law Society, news coverage) reports either unanimity or any party opposing. So the 'every party voting in favour' element is unverified in either direction — absence of a recorded division is not proof it was unopposed.

statement: At that stage, there will be a raft of amendments brought to make that section 98 even more robust.
criterion: The Justice Committee's report back on the bill (Parliament's bills page / select committee report): true if the committee recommends multiple amendments to the clauses amending section 98 of the Crimes Act; false if the bill is reported back unamended or with only minor/technical changes, or if it does not reach report-back.
reasoning: The criterion's false branch ('or if it does not reach report-back') is what happened. As of September 2026 the latest version of the Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill on legislation.govt.nz is still 36-1 (2024) — no 36-2 'as reported from the Justice Committee' version exists, which is what a report-back with recommended amendments would produce. The committee's report was due 16 June 2025; in January 2026 the bill was still publicly described as 'currently before Select Committee', it never reached a second reading, and it appears in no list of enacted legislation of the 54th Parliament. The section 98 / 98AA strengthening Fleming predicted did occur, but through the Government's separate omnibus Crimes Amendment Bill (third reading 4 August 2026, Royal assent 7 August 2026), which aligned penalties across the slavery and trafficking regime and removed prosecution barriers. So the substance was delivered by a different vehicle, not by the select-committee stage of his own bill that the criterion names.

statement: I want to talk about that a little bit later, about some of the things that I think we can do to follow up this bill, which looks set to pass.
criterion: The Hansard third-reading record and the Parliament bills register for the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading on or about 17 December 2024 and received Royal assent, false if it was defeated, withdrawn or left unpassed.
reasoning: The Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill (member's bill, Rima Nakhle) passed its third reading on 17 December 2024 — the same sitting — and received Royal assent on 23 December 2024, becoming the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Act 2024 (Public Act 2024 No 57); it came into force 17 June 2025. It was neither defeated, withdrawn nor left unpassed, which satisfies the criterion (the 'on or about 17 December 2024' third reading and Royal assent both hold).

statement: There will be protests, and that will lead to uncertainty, and my advice to applicants is to not use this process.
criterion: Mainstream New Zealand media reporting and police/council records of organised public protest (marches, occupations, blockades) directed specifically at projects listed in or approved under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024; true if such protest action is documented, false if no protest against a fast-track project is recorded by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Protest directed specifically at projects listed under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 is documented in mainstream NZ media. ~1,500 people rallied at Ruakākā Beach (Oct 2025), a sandcastle protest by Bream Bay Guardians and local hapū against McCallum Bros' Bream Bay sand-extraction proposal, one of the 149 listed projects; NZ Herald reported it as 'expected to be first of many against fast-track projects'. Greenpeace occupied mining-lobby offices over the Trans-Tasman Resources fast-track seabed bid, Taranaki iwi served a trespass notice on the applicant, and an activist was arrested after a five-day tree occupation blocking Bathurst's fast-track Denniston/Cypress coal expansion. The criterion's test (documented organised protest against a fast-track project) is met.

statement: That is true that they can be declined, but it’s very unlikely that they will be declined once they’re on this list because of how the bill is written—that is, the primary focus of decision makers has to be on that purpose, which is to facilitate the projects—and these applications can be for things that are prohibited under the Resource Management Act, which means that it is not possible to get a resource consent.
criterion: Decisions published by expert panels under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024; true if fewer than roughly 10 percent of substantive applications decided by the resolve-by date are declined, false if a substantial share are declined.
reasoning: As of Sept 2026, 34 projects have been granted fast-track approval (Stella Passage / Port of Tauranga was the 34th, 7 Sep 2026). No substantive application has been finally declined by a panel: the two that received draft declines (Delmore housing, Taranaki VTM seabed mine) were both withdrawn by the applicant before a final decision. Six applications were returned for incompleteness, which is a lodgement failure rather than a decline. Decline rate is therefore roughly 0–6%, inside the criterion's 'fewer than roughly 10 percent' threshold. Disconfirming evidence checked: the TTR draft decline shows panels will decline on adverse effects despite the Act's facilitative purpose, so the mechanism Brooking named is weaker than she claimed, but the rate she predicted holds. Interim read — the criterion's window runs to 2027-06-30 and remains open.

statement: On the other side of the House, we see the people who say “No, no, no” to all of those things, and the people of New Zealand will say no to them at the 2026 election.
criterion: The official 2026 New Zealand general election result declared by the Electoral Commission: true if the parties opposing this bill (Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori) fail to form a government, false if they collectively win enough seats to form the government.
reasoning: The 2026 New Zealand general election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026, with voting opening 26 October 2026. Today is 28 September 2026, so no Electoral Commission result exists and the criterion cannot be evaluated. Resolve-by date (2026-12-31) has not passed.

statement: They will extend the life and extent of coalmines.
criterion: Decisions of expert panels under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024: true if at least one coal mine extension or expansion is approved through the fast-track process; false if no coal mining project is approved under it by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion names decisions of expert panels under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024, resolve-by 2027-12-31. As of 2026-09-28 no coal project has been approved (or declined) by a fast-track panel. Only one coal project is on the listed schedule: Bathurst/BT Mining's Buller Plateaux Continuation Project (Stockton + Denniston, ~20 Mt coking coal over 25 years), whose listing was amended by Order in Council around June 2026. Bathurst lodged its substantive application 21 Aug 2026; the EPA returned it as incomplete circa 25 Sep 2026 over a wildlife approval (lizard/invertebrate salvage far below DOC's 80% best practice) and reserve-manager consent, so it has not yet reached a panel. Bathurst guides investors to a panel decision in 2027. Disconfirming check: the earlier Te Kuha Coal Project referral was returned non-compliant in March 2025 and never reached a minister or panel; the only substantive panel approvals to date are Waihi North (gold/silver, 18 Dec 2025), Homestead Bay (housing) and Ayrburn Screen Hub, and the Taranaki seabed ironsands project drew a draft decline. So the pathway Parker described exists and is being used for a mine-life extension, but no approval has issued and the resolve-by date has not passed.

statement: Kia kaha, kia hāneanea tō noho mō te rua tau. Ka mutu te rua tau, kua ngaro noa atu koutou.
criterion: The official result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it; true if the National/ACT/NZ First coalition does not form the next government, false if it is returned to office.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the official result of the 2026 general election and the government formed after it, resolve-by 2027-02-28. The election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026 (advance voting opens 26 October; enrolment deadline 25 October), announced by PM Christopher Luxon. As of 2026-09-28 the election has not been held, no result exists, and the National/ACT/NZ First coalition remains in office, so neither the true nor the false branch of the criterion can be evaluated yet.

statement: What this does mean for New Zealanders and their families is this: New Zealanders will have better access to more effective cancer treatments, such as CAR T-cell therapy—if they want to.
criterion: Pharmac funding decisions and Medsafe/gene-technology regulator approvals: true if CAR T-cell therapy is publicly funded or routinely available to New Zealand patients outside clinical trials by the resolve-by date, having not been so at the time of the statement; false if access remains confined to clinical trials or private self-funding.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether CAR T-cell therapy is publicly funded or routinely available to NZ patients outside clinical trials by 2027-12-31. As of 2026-09-28 it is not: reporting confirms CAR T-cell therapy is available neither publicly nor privately in New Zealand (unlike Australia, the UK and much of Europe), with patients facing US$500k-$1m to be treated overseas; there is no Pharmac funding decision and no Medsafe approval of a CAR T product. The baseline the criterion assumes also holds — it was unavailable outside trials when Collins spoke in December 2024. Progress is real but unfinished: the Malaghan Institute's phase 2 ENABLE-2 trial passed its midpoint (30th of a target 60 patients) and is tracking to complete dosing by end-2026, with clinical/manufacturing data being prepared for Medsafe review and a stated ambition of public-system availability in 2027, subject to results, regulatory approval and Pharmac/Health NZ funding. Since the resolve-by date is over a year away and the decisive Medsafe/Pharmac steps are pending, the prediction is not yet due rather than wrong.

statement: Which is to say, the burden of remaining GMO-free—as every current producer in this country is, whether you’re an animal producer, a fruit or a vegetable producer, or a crop producer—will now fall on those producers to prove their non-GMO status.
criterion: The Gene Technology Act regime as enacted and its implementing rules, plus documented certification arrangements once GMO releases are approved: true if GMO-free certification costs are borne by non-GMO producers seeking that status, false if the regime places segregation/certification costs on GMO developers or releasers.
reasoning: The criterion requires "the Gene Technology Act regime as enacted and its implementing rules, plus documented certification arrangements once GMO releases are approved." None of those exist. The Gene Technology Bill never got past its Health Committee report (10 Oct 2025); NZ First refused support, Winston Peters said in June 2026 it "will not be put forward this term", and the bill lapsed when the 54th Parliament rose on 23 September 2026 ahead of the 7 November election. There is no Act, no regulator, no implementing rules and no approved GMO release, so there is nothing yet that could allocate segregation or certification costs to either side. Resolve-by is 2028-12-31. Looking for disconfirming evidence: I checked whether the reported-back bill placed costs on developers/releasers instead — submitters and commentary consistently report the opposite, that the bill contains no liability or coexistence framework at all and leaves contaminated non-GMO producers to seek compensation through the courts, which is directionally consistent with Abel's claim. But that is a reading of an unenacted bill, not the enacted regime the criterion names, so it cannot settle the verdict.

statement: Our GE regime is going to change.
criterion: The NZ statute book; true if legislation amending or replacing the HSNO 1996 regime for gene technology (e.g. the Gene Technology Bill) is enacted, false if the regime is unchanged at the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion: true if legislation amending or replacing the HSNO 1996 regime for gene technology is enacted by 2026-12-31, false if the regime is unchanged. It is unchanged. The Gene Technology Bill had its first reading on 17 December 2024 and the Health Committee reported back on 10 October 2025 recommending changes, but it never reached a second reading. Coalition partner NZ First withheld support, calling it "too liberal, beyond our key trading partners"; talks failed through 2026, and in June 2026 Winston Peters said "this legislation will not be put forward this term and it will become an election issue." The 54th Parliament sat for the last time on 23 September 2026 with more than 60 bills lapsing unfinished; Parliament was dissolved on 1 October for the 7 November general election. The Gene Technology Bill was not among the final-week passages (the two RMA replacement bills, the Agricultural Compounds and Veterinary Medicines Bill, and a postnatal-stay bill). Disconfirming check: I looked for any other enacted change to the gene technology regime. The Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Amendment Bill (304-1), which would amend new-organism approvals, was still in select committee (submissions closed mid-2026) and lapsed as well; I found no HSNO regulation or other statute changing the gene technology settings. The formal resolve date is three months away, but the outcome is determined: the bill is dead in this Parliament, and a Parliament elected 7 November could not reinstate and pass contested gene technology legislation through three stages before 31 December.

statement: This is going to lead to higher rates—the credit rating agencies have said it.
criterion: Stats NZ local authority rates data / LGNZ average rates increases for the 2025/26 and 2026/27 rating years alongside council long-term plan rates forecasts; true if average council rates rises accelerate relative to pre-bill forecasts with water costs cited as a driver, false if rates growth is flat or lower than pre-bill projections.
reasoning: Both rating years the criterion names are now set, so this is largely resolvable. What supports McAnulty: household water-and-rates costs have risen sharply with water explicitly the driver. The 2025/26 average rates increase was 8.39% against 2.5% inflation, and Stats NZ's June 2025 CPI identified local authority rates as the largest single contributor to annual inflation, up 12.2%. For 2026/27, the 14 councils transitioning to new water entities under Local Water Done Well on 1 July 2026 show an average headline rates rise of 6.14% but an average total cost increase of 15.88% once separately billed water charges are counted (Hutt City 59.79%, Upper Hutt 32.33%); the national equivalent including water charges is reported as 9.0%. In metro Wellington, Tiaki Wai's first-year average household water charge is about $2,390, roughly $5.60/week above what households were paying through rates. On the rating-agency half of the claim: S&P put 15 councils on negative outlook after the Three Waters repeal, said council incomes were not rising fast enough to cover infrastructure responsibilities, and projected 18 of its 24 rated councils would raise rates above 4% per year from 2025 to 2029 — so that part is substantially borne out, though S&P's warnings attach to the repeal and the broader framework rather than to this specific bill. What cuts against it, and why this is not a clean 'correct': the criterion's test is acceleration relative to pre-bill forecasts, and headline rates growth decelerated, 8.39% in 2025/26 to 6.9% in 2026/27. Individual councils have come in under their pre-bill long-term-plan forecasts — Tauranga struck 7.2% for 2026/27 against 10.4% projected in its 2024-34 LTP. Much of the 2026/27 jump is also a reclassification: water costs moved out of rates into separate charges, which raises total household cost without raising rates. And the 2024-34 LTPs already priced in large water-driven rises following the Three Waters repeal, so an increment attributable to this bill cannot be cleanly isolated. Caveat on sourcing: the only all-council series is the Taxpayers' Union dashboard, an advocacy source whose own page (7.9%) and press release (9.0%) give different national water-inclusive totals; Stats NZ local authority data for 2026/27 is not yet published, which is why the criterion allows until 2027-06-30.

statement: Tasman’s probably going to go with Marlborough and possibly going to go with Buller, so we’ll have the top of the South but no Nelson.
criterion: The water services delivery plans submitted to and accepted by the Department of Internal Affairs (due September 2025); true if Tasman's plan is a joint arrangement with Marlborough and/or Buller and Nelson's is standalone, false if Nelson and Tasman submit a joint plan or Tasman goes alone.
reasoning: Tasman District Council voted unanimously on 12 June 2025 for a standalone in-house business unit, with no joint arrangement with Marlborough or Buller, and adopted its own Water Services Delivery Plan on 25 Sept 2025 (updated plan to DIA mid-Oct, approved Dec 2025). Nelson also stayed standalone (plan adopted 7 Aug 2025), so the 'no Nelson' half held, but the criterion names Tasman going alone as an explicit falsifier: there is no 'top of the South' grouping.

statement: This legislation is expected to be passed in mid-2025, with the first permits being considered at the end of next year.
criterion: The Royal assent date of the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill on the New Zealand legislation register, and MBIE records of the first feasibility permit applications considered. True if the bill was enacted around the middle of 2025 and the first permits were under consideration before 31 December 2025; false if enactment slipped materially past mid-2025 or no permits were considered in 2025.
reasoning: The Offshore Renewable Energy Bill passed its third reading on 30 June 2026, was signed into law on 9 July 2026 and came into force 10 July 2026 — enactment slipped a full year past 'mid-2025'. Consequently no feasibility permit applications were or could be considered before 31 Dec 2025; the feasibility/commercial permit pathway and the Offshore Renewable Energy Regulations 2026 only became operative after July 2026. Both limbs of the criterion fail.

statement: I suspect it will get support around the House, and I see no reason to delay it on that process.
criterion: The vote record for the first reading of Greg Fleming's member's bill aligning penalties for slavery offences under the Crimes Act; true if it passes with support from all or nearly all parties, false if any party votes against it or it fails.
reasoning: Greg Fleming's Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill passed its first reading on 17/18 December 2024 and was referred to the Justice Committee (submissions closed 13 Feb 2025). No party is recorded anywhere as voting against it, and no division breakdown exists — consistent with the motion being agreed on the voices, i.e. no party vote called. Caveat on sourcing: I could not reach the Hansard transcript or bills.parliament.nz directly (both behind bot protection), so the per-party division record is unverified; WhereTheyStand records the reading as passed with 'no vote breakdown recorded'. Neither failure condition in the criterion (a party voting against, or the bill failing) is supported by any evidence found. Separately, the other half of Webb's sentence — 'no reason to delay it' — did not hold: the select committee report was due 16 June 2025 and the bill still has no second reading as of Sept 2026. That is outside the criterion as written.

statement: I want to talk about that a little bit later, about some of the things that I think we can do to follow up this bill, which looks set to pass.
criterion: The Hansard third reading record for the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill; true if the bill was read a third time and passed, false if it was defeated or failed to pass.
reasoning: The Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill (Rima Nakhle, member's bill 11-3 (2024)) passed its third reading on 17 December 2024 — the same sitting day Stephenson spoke — and received Royal Assent on 22–23 December 2024. It is listed among the acts of the 54th Parliament. The criterion's true-condition (read a third time and passed) is satisfied.

statement: Jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022 and are expected to peak in January 2025. The forecast has always been for the numbers to get worse before they get better.
criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly benefit statistics for jobseeker support through 2025. True if the jobseeker count reached its high point in January 2025 and declined thereafter across the year; false if numbers continued rising past January 2025.
reasoning: The January 2025 peak was the HYEFU 2024 forecast (214,000, the third upward revision after 202,500 at Budget 2024 and 197,400 at PREFU 2023) and it did not occur. MSD figures show the caseload continued rising past January 2025: 209,838 in the March 2025 quarter and 223,512 by the December 2025 quarter — a record and the highest since the 2013 reforms, up 18% from 190,000 in December 2023. MSD's HYEFU 2025 forecast moved the peak to January 2026 (~221,900), and Upston herself later identified December 2025 as the peak. Checking the disconfirming case: there was a genuine monthly decline from January to March 2025, which the Government highlighted, but that is the usual summer seasonal fall — the caseload resumed rising and ended 2025 at a twelve-year high, so the criterion's required 'peaks in January 2025 and declines thereafter across the year' fails. The first half of the quote (numbers rising steadily since 2022) is accurate, but the predictive claim the criterion targets is not.

statement: As I said in my answer to the primary, the jobseeker numbers were expected to peak in January 2025.
criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly jobseeker support benefit numbers through 2025; true if the caseload peaks in January 2025 and declines thereafter, false if the caseload continues rising past January 2025.
reasoning: Same evidence as the companion claim. The MSD jobseeker caseload did not peak in January 2025: it was 209,838 in the March 2025 quarter and reached a record 223,512 in the December 2025 quarter, the highest since the 2013 welfare reforms. MSD's HYEFU 2025 forecast subsequently placed the peak at ~221,900 in January 2026, and the Q2 2026 figure of 218,481 remains above every 2025 quarter before December. The January–March 2025 monthly dip is seasonal, not a peak. The criterion's false-condition (caseload continues rising past January 2025) is what the record shows.

statement: What does she say to the New Zealanders who will be accessing welfare support this Christmas, Christmas 2026, Christmas 2027, Christmas 2028, and Christmas 2029, given the economic outlook is so bleak that the unemployment rate will not even be back to 2023 levels by 2029?
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for 2029 compared with the 2023 annual average (~3.7%); true if the 2029 rate remains above the 2023 level, false if it has returned to or below it.
reasoning: The criterion requires the Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for 2029 compared with the 2023 annual average (~3.7%, consistent with 2023 quarterly prints of 3.4-4.0%). Today is September 2026, so the 2029 outturn does not exist. Interim evidence points the same way as the prediction but cannot resolve it: the seasonally adjusted rate was 5.4% in the December 2025 quarter, and Treasury's HYEFU 2025 forecasts a fall only to about 4.3% by the end of its forecast horizon - still above 2023 levels. A forecast is not the measured 2029 rate, so no verdict is available until HLFS data for 2029 is published.

statement: And here’s the best present of all: next year we will deliver a growing economy with more opportunities and more choices for New Zealanders.
criterion: Stats NZ GDP series for calendar 2025; true if annual average real GDP growth for the year to December 2025 is positive, false if it is zero or negative.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether annual average real GDP growth for the year to December 2025 was positive. Stats NZ's December 2025 quarter release (published 19 March 2026) shows GDP up 0.2% in the quarter and, on an annual average basis, growth of 0.2% for the year ended December 2025 - the first annual growth recorded in more than two years. Positive, so the criterion is met. It is a thin pass: the first half of 2025 was broadly flat with all growth in the second half (+1.1% over the final six months), and the Q4-on-Q4 comparison was +1.3%. I checked for the disconfirming case (a negative annual average, which would have been reported as a continued recession) and found the opposite across Stats NZ, RNZ, 1News and Westpac.

statement: I expect the commission to have finalised the new caps for card fees by mid-2025 so it can be implemented soon thereafter.
criterion: Commerce Commission publications on interchange fee caps: true if the Commission issued its final decision setting the new caps on or before 30 June 2025; false if the final decision was issued after that date.
reasoning: The Commerce Commission's Final Decision and Reasons Paper on interchange fee regulation for the Mastercard and Visa networks is dated 17 July 2025, and the final network standard was published the same day. That is after the criterion's 30 June 2025 cut-off, by 17 days, so the criterion's bright line for 'finalised by mid-2025' fails. The second half of the prediction held: the revised caps took effect 1 December 2025 for domestic cards and 1 May 2026 for foreign-issued cards, i.e. implemented soon thereafter, cutting fees by roughly $90-100m a year. I looked for an earlier final decision that would satisfy the criterion and found only the draft decision preceding 17 July, plus a separate 2026 process for commercial credit cards. Strictly against the written 30 June date this is wrong; under the speaker's own looser 'mid-2025' wording 17 July is arguably inside it, hence partly_correct rather than wrong.

statement: We’ve seen it with the fast track last week, and then it seems like we’re going to see this with this bill when it’s in committee stage.
criterion: Hansard for the committee of the whole House stage of the Hauraki Gulf Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill and the Amendment Papers register; true if the Minister introduced substantive amendments (including the high protection area fishing change) at committee stage without a further select committee referral, false if the changes were instead referred back to select committee or not made.
reasoning: The Environment Committee reported the bill back recommending it pass with no substantive change. The Minister (Tama Potaka) subsequently brought a government amendment allowing commercial ring-net fishing in two of the high protection areas (Kawau Bay, and around Rangitoto/Motutapu) — the amendment surfaced in July 2025 and was made at the committee of the whole House on 22 August 2025, with no further select committee referral. Opposition speeches at the third reading (7-8 Oct 2025) explicitly characterised it as an 11th-hour change made after select committee. Checked for the disconfirming possibilities named in the criterion: the bill was not referred back to select committee, and the change was made (it is in the enacted law, subject to a three-year review). Both branches of the criterion therefore resolve in favour of the prediction.

statement: They’ve made it clear—or they haven’t made it clear but everyone else has made it clear, including the Commissioner of Police—that they’re not going to hit their target for recruiting more police.
criterion: NZ Police / Government reporting on constabulary officer numbers against the 500 additional police commitment: false (i.e. the prediction fails) if 500 additional officers were confirmed recruited by the Government's stated deadline; true if the deadline passed without the target being reached.
reasoning: The National-NZ First coalition agreement committed to 500 additional constabulary officers within two years, i.e. by 27 November 2025. Commissioner Richard Chambers said publicly in May 2025 that the target would more likely be reached in 'the early part of 2026' and that he would not lower standards to hit the date; Police Minister Mark Mitchell said the Government was not 'hung up on an arbitrary date'. The deadline passed in November 2025 with roughly 361 additional officers, and the target date was then pushed successively to June 2026, August 2026 and September 2026. Disconfirming check: no reporting shows 500 additional officers confirmed by the November 2025 deadline, so the criterion's 'false' branch does not apply. (That the target may have been reached later in 2026 is outside the criterion, which turns on the stated deadline.)

statement: If the estimated 100,000 people that this Government has managed to mobilise against their attacks on Te Tiriti o Waitangi tell us anything, it is that your power, Mr Prime Minister, will be fleeting.
criterion: Result of the next New Zealand general election and Christopher Luxon's tenure as Prime Minister; true if the National-led coalition is not returned to government at that election (or Luxon ceases to be Prime Minister before it), false if the coalition is returned to office with Luxon as Prime Minister.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the result of the next general election or Luxon ceasing to be Prime Minister before it. Luxon announced on 21 January 2026 that the election will be held on 7 November 2026, which has not yet occurred (today is 28 September 2026). Checked the early-departure branch too: Luxon faced a National caucus leadership challenge on 12 August 2026 and survived the vote, and he was still serving as Prime Minister at post-Cabinet press conferences on 14 and 21 September 2026. Neither branch of the criterion has resolved, so the prediction is not yet due.

statement: I want to acknowledge Mr Fleming for getting this bill drawn and getting it to the House and for having this first reading, at which it looks likely to pass, given the indications from the other members this morning.
criterion: The Hansard division/voice-vote record for the first reading of the Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed first reading, false if it was defeated.
reasoning: The Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill (Greg Fleming, member's bill 36-1) passed its first reading in the sitting of 17/18 December 2024 and was referred to the Justice Committee, which opened submissions closing 13 February 2025 with a report-back date of 16 June 2025. WhereTheyStand records the first reading as 'Passed'; contemporaneous NGO coverage (World Vision, via Scoop, 19 Dec 2024) reports the bill 'passed its first reading'. Stephenson's prediction that it looked likely to pass at first reading is borne out.

statement: This is a great bill. It’s a good bill. It’s going to be supported across the House.
criterion: The Hansard first-reading vote record for the Crimes (Increased Penalties for Slavery Offences) Amendment Bill; true if every party voted in favour, false if any party voted against.
reasoning: The criterion requires the per-party first-reading vote record. I could not retrieve it: Parliament's Hansard (hansard.parliament.nz) and bills.parliament.nz are client-rendered apps that return only an error shell to a fetcher, the legacy HansDeb_ URLs 404, and legislation.govt.nz blocks automated fetches. WhereTheyStand, which does publish party-vote breakdowns, states none is recorded for this reading. Indirect evidence is consistent with Meager's claim — the bill passed first reading and went to select committee, and no source I found (news, NGO commentary critical of the bill for not going far enough, or submissions) records any party voting against — but 'every party voted in favour' cannot be confirmed without the division record, and absence of a recorded division is not the same as a recorded unanimous vote. Not findable, so no verdict against the criterion as written.

statement: At that stage, there will be a raft of amendments brought to make that section 98 even more robust.
criterion: The Justice Committee's report back on the trafficking member's bill sponsored by Greg Fleming: true if the committee recommends substantive amendments to section 98 of the Crimes Act 1961, false if the bill is reported back without amendment (or not reported back) by the due date.
reasoning: By the 2026-06-30 due date there is no sign the Justice Committee reported the bill back with substantive amendments to section 98. legislation.govt.nz still carries only version 36-1 (2024) as 'latest' — no 36-2 'as reported from the Justice Committee' exists, which is what a committee recommending amendments would produce. WhereTheyStand, synced 31 May 2026, shows the bill 'In progress' with the second reading still pending and no committee report. What did happen instead: the Government's own Crimes Amendment Bill carried the trafficking/slavery penalty reforms (subpart 2), reaching third reading on 4 August 2026, with Minister James Meager acknowledging Fleming's advocacy — i.e. the policy advanced through a different vehicle, not through 'a raft of amendments' to section 98 at the select committee stage of Fleming's own bill. Under the criterion (false if reported back without amendment or not reported back by the due date), this resolves against the prediction. Caveat: the inference rests on the absence of a reported-back version and on WhereTheyStand's status, since the Parliament bill/committee pages could not be read directly.

statement: Māori people will take you out of this place because they, more than anyone I know, when they go on the marae, they respect the traditions.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission results for the next general election (due 2026): true if Te Pāti Māori loses the Māori electorate seats it held in 2023 and is materially reduced or removed from Parliament; false if it holds or increases its seats.
reasoning: The criterion requires official Electoral Commission results for the next general election, which is scheduled for 7 November 2026 with official results declared 27 November 2026 — both after today's date of 28 September 2026. No Maori electorate results or Te Pati Maori seat count exist yet. Opinion polling and seat projections are available but are explicitly not the evidence the criterion names, so they cannot substitute. Resolve-by date of 2026-12-31 has not passed.

statement: Now, you got to say their high point came this year. You watch the next election, and that goes for Te Pāti Māori sitting on the left-hand side of them as well.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission results for the next general election: true if both the Green Party's party vote falls below its 2023 share (11.6%) and Te Pāti Māori's falls below its 2023 share/seat count, false if either party improves on its 2023 result.
reasoning: The criterion requires official party-vote shares for both the Green Party (vs 11.6% in 2023) and Te Pati Maori from the next general election. That election is 7 November 2026, with official results declared 27 November 2026 — after today (28 September 2026). Party-vote shares do not exist until votes are counted, and pre-election polling is not the source the criterion names.

statement: Interest rates are falling—falling—and the Reserve Bank is forecasting that more relief is on the way very, very shortly.
criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions following 28 January 2025: true if the OCR is reduced at the February 2025 Monetary Policy Statement; false if the OCR is held or raised.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether the OCR was reduced at the February 2025 Monetary Policy Statement. On 19 February 2025 the RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee reached consensus to lower the OCR by 50 basis points, from 4.25% to 3.75% — a reduction, not a hold or rise. The supporting claims also hold: this was the fourth consecutive cut, 175bp cumulative easing since August 2024 ('interest rates are falling'), and the Committee said it had 'scope to lower the OCR further through 2025', with the projected track revised down to roughly 3.00% by end-2025 ('more relief on the way'). Checked for the disconfirming case (a hold or hike in Feb 2025) and found none; a 50bp cut was widely expected in advance and delivered.

statement: Our prediction is this will be a one-term Government because this year we will continue to use our influence, our political platform, to unite this nation, to leave no one behind, to make sure that the spirit of Te Tiriti and indeed the honour of being tangata whenua is realised and felt by all.
criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election (due 2026): true if the National-led coalition (National, ACT, NZ First) does not form the government after that election; false if it returns to government in any configuration.
reasoning: The next NZ general election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 (date announced by PM Luxon on 21 January 2026) and has not been held as of 28 September 2026 — no results exist, and the National–ACT–NZ First coalition is still the incumbent government. The criterion depends on who forms the government after that election, so it cannot be resolved before the resolve-by date of 31 December 2026.

statement: We’ve got the bill coming up—Seymour’s bill—in May.
criterion: Parliament's records for the Treaty Principles Bill: true if the select committee reported back, or the bill was next debated in the House, during May 2025; false if that stage occurred in a different month.
reasoning: The Justice Committee's statutory report-back deadline for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was 14 May 2025, which is presumably the basis of the claim, but the committee reported back early — on 3–4 April 2025, recommending the bill not proceed — and the bill's next House stage, its second reading, was held on 10 April 2025, where it was defeated 112 votes to 11. Both the report-back and the next debate occurred in April, not May, which the criterion specifies as false.

statement: This year, we know that the Government is going to further weaken how they measure child poverty.
criterion: Child Poverty Reduction Act measures and targets as set by the Government during 2025; true if primary measures or targets are changed, removed or replaced, false if the measurement framework is unchanged at 31 December 2025.
reasoning: The Child Poverty Reduction Act measurement framework was unchanged at 31 December 2025: the four primary measures (material hardship, BHC50, AHC50 fixed line, persistent poverty), the ten-year 2027/28 targets, and the 2024/25–2026/27 intermediate targets all stood as set before 2025. The less ambitious intermediate targets were set in June 2024, the revised child poverty related indicators in October 2024 and the persistent-poverty target in December 2024 — all before the quote. The one substantive measurement change, replacing the DEP-17 index with MH-18, was made by the Government Statistician (an independent statutory officer, not ministers) and published on 19 January 2026, applying from the February 2026 release. Checking for the opposite: I looked for 2025 removals, replacements or legislative amendments to the Act's measures or targets and found none (the only 2025 amendment to the Act was a cross-reference fix in the Public Service Amendment Bill). The MH-18 change also did not flatter the government — hardship came out at a ten-year high, and CPAG welcomed two added items while objecting to respondent selection.

statement: And let’s put this on the record, because the Treaty principles bill, yeah, it’s going to die, but there are other bills that this Government has signed up to and agreed to legislate within their coalition agreement—the holy coalition agreement—that will impact our laws, which will remove Te Tiriti as a lawmaking principle within this country.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill — true if the bill is defeated (e.g. voted down at second reading) or otherwise fails to become law; false if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was defeated at second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11 (only ACT's 11 MPs in favour). It did not pass a third reading and received no Royal assent, so the bill 'died' exactly as the criterion specifies. The criterion covers only the bill's fate; the quote's further claim that other coalition-agreement bills will remove Te Tiriti as a lawmaking principle is outside it and was not tested here.

statement: Of course, our dairy industry will be able to produce more dairy for exactly the same number of cows as they had last year, but they will produce more, and that makes the country richer.
criterion: DCANZ / Fonterra / LIC-DairyNZ New Zealand Dairy Statistics for the 2024/25 season against 2023/24. True if total milksolids production rose while the national herd was flat or smaller; false if production fell, or if any rise was accompanied by a larger herd.
reasoning: LIC/DairyNZ New Zealand Dairy Statistics 2024/25: total milksolids production was 1.94 billion kg, up 2.9% on 2023/24, while the national herd fell 0.5% to 4.68 million cows and per-cow output hit a record 414 kg MS (up 14 kg). Production rose on a herd that was slightly smaller, not larger — which is what the criterion requires ('rose while the national herd was flat or smaller'). His phrasing 'exactly the same number of cows' is loose (the herd shrank marginally), but that falls inside the criterion's allowance rather than against it.

statement: There are a number of changes which will be litigated.
criterion: New Zealand court records / law reports and media coverage of challenges to the roadside oral-fluid testing and detention provisions of the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act; true if at least one court proceeding challenging or turning on these new provisions is brought by the resolve-by date, false if no such litigation is recorded.
reasoning: The resolve-by date is 2028-01-28, sixteen months after today (2026-09-28). The Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 only commenced on 15 December 2025, with roadside oral-fluid testing rolling out from Wellington and reaching nationwide coverage around mid-2026, so the provisions have been operating for well under a year. I searched for court proceedings challenging or turning on them and found none: the Spinoff's six-month statistical review of the regime records no legal proceedings, and NZDSOS/Justice Watch NZ (July-August 2026) describe a challenge as something they are lobbying for rather than something filed. Per the rules, that absence within an open window is not evidence the prediction is wrong.

statement: This is an important piece of legislation that will significantly improve the safety on our roads.
criterion: Ministry of Transport road safety statistics for the two full years following commencement of roadside oral fluid testing, compared with the two years preceding it: true if road deaths and serious injuries involving drivers with drugs in their system fall materially; false if they are flat or rise.
reasoning: The criterion requires Ministry of Transport road-safety statistics for the two full years following commencement of roadside oral fluid testing, against the two years before. Roadside oral fluid testing only began in December 2025 in the Wellington region under the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025, with nationwide rollout through mid-2026. Two full years of post-commencement data will not exist until late 2027 at the earliest, and published MoT figures not until 2028. As of 2026-09-28 there is nothing to compare; the item's own resolve-by date is 2028-06-30.

statement: As it continues its journey through the House, I’m sure that it will continue to be supported by many members.
criterion: The division records for the committee of the whole House and third reading of the Privacy Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes with support from multiple parties beyond the governing coalition, false if it is opposed by most non-government parties or fails to pass.
reasoning: The Privacy Amendment Bill completed its third reading on 18 September 2025 and received royal assent on 23 September 2025 (Privacy Amendment Act 2025 No 53). No division was called at any stage: the Hansard record ends 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time.' Speeches in support came from Labour (Duncan Webb, Glen Bennett, Vanushi Walters, Kieran McAnulty) and the Greens (Tamatha Paul) as well as all three coalition parties, so the bill passed with support from multiple parties beyond the governing coalition — the criterion's 'true' branch. The 'false' branch (opposition from most non-government parties, or failure to pass) did not occur.

statement: I don't think that this is a particularly simple area of law; it's evolving and it's going to have unintended consequences and they're going to crop up and we are going to have to change the law fairly frequently if we're going to keep abreast of a situation.
criterion: New Zealand legislation record (legislation.govt.nz / Parliament bills database) for amendments to the Privacy Act 2020: true if one or more further amendment Acts or Government privacy amendment bills are introduced or enacted in the three years after January 2025; false if the Act is left unamended over that period.
reasoning: The criterion's window is the three years after January 2025, i.e. to January 2028, which has not elapsed. The only Act amending the Privacy Act 2020 enacted in the window so far is the Privacy Amendment Act 2025 (assent 23 September 2025) — the very bill White was debating, so it is not a 'further' amendment in the criterion's sense. I found no further Government privacy amendment bill introduced or enacted as of September 2026; post-2025 activity has been secondary instruments rather than statute (Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025 in force 3 November 2025, Amendment No 1 in March 2026 aligning it with IPP 3A). The 'false' branch requires the Act to be left unamended across the whole three years, which cannot yet be determined.

statement: I believe we will look back in a few years’ time and regard this move in a similar way to the way in which we regard blood-alcohol testing, which is a perfectly normal part of life: controversial when first introduced, amongst some, but actually par for the course.
criterion: State of roadside oral-fluid drug testing in New Zealand by early 2030: true if the regime is operating routinely and no party represented in Parliament holds a policy to repeal it; false if the regime has been repealed, suspended, or remains a live subject of party-political opposition.
reasoning: The criterion's horizon is the state of roadside oral-fluid drug testing in early 2030; today is 2026-09-28, so the resolve-by date has not passed. Interim evidence: the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 came into force 15 December 2025, testing started in the Wellington District and scaled toward nationwide coverage through 2026, so the regime is neither repealed nor suspended. But the criterion also requires that no party in Parliament holds a repeal policy, and the Greens and Te Pati Maori voted against the enabling bill on privacy and rangatahi Maori grounds; whether that hardens into live opposition or fades cannot be judged before 2030.

statement: The Consumer Data Rights Bill will be coming before the House, hopefully, in the next three weeks for the second reading, but we’re targeting to have open banking in place by the end of this year.
criterion: Hansard's record of the second reading of the Customer and Product Data Bill; true if the second reading debate occurred on or before about 19 February 2025, false if it occurred later or not at all.
reasoning: Bayly said on 2025-01-29 that the bill would come before the House for its second reading 'hopefully, in the next three weeks', which the criterion bounds at about 19 February 2025. The Customer and Product Data Bill (the Consumer Data Right legislation he was referring to) actually had its second reading on 6 March 2025, when the House accepted it as amended by the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee — roughly five weeks after the three-week window he named. The criterion states this is false if the second reading occurred later. The bill did progress and received Royal assent later in 2025, so the delay was modest, but the criterion as written is about the date and only the date.

statement: While David Seymour recognised in his 15-minute spiel the likelihood of his bill being voted down—I’d say yes to that—he highlighted that once an idea is put forth in motion, it cannot be undone.
criterion: The division record for the Treaty Principles Bill's next reading after this statement; true if the bill is defeated, false if it passes that reading.
reasoning: The criterion is the division record for the Treaty Principles Bill's next reading after 2025-01-29: true if defeated. The bill was voted down at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with ACT the only party in support and National, NZ First, Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori all opposed. Checking for the opposite — that it survived to a third reading or committee stage — finds nothing; the vote ended the bill.

statement: According to the Reserve Bank—who, suddenly, the Government wants to claim all the credit for—business investment will be lower at the end of this year than at the end of our last Labour Government.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts / RBNZ published series for real business investment: true if the December 2025 quarter level is below the December 2023 quarter level; false if it is at or above it.
reasoning: Criterion: real business investment, Dec 2025 quarter level vs Dec 2023 quarter level. OECD/Stats NZ real gross fixed capital formation (constant prices, seasonally adjusted; FRED series NAEXKP04NZQ659S, year-on-year growth) shows -5.557% in the year to 2024-Q4 and +0.216% in the year to 2025-Q4. Compounded, the Dec 2025 quarter is ~5.3% BELOW the Dec 2023 quarter (0.94443 x 1.00216 = 0.9465). Levels corroborate: real GFCF was 17,049-17,203 NZDm (chained 2009/10, SA) in 2025-Q4, having fallen from 17,429m in 2025-Q3; the nominal series peaked at its all-time high of 26,697 NZDm in Dec 2023 and was 25,984 NZDm in Dec 2025. Disconfirming check: because residential construction fell hard over the same period, total GFCF could in principle overstate a fall in BUSINESS investment specifically. It does not reverse the sign. Stats NZ's own December 2025 GDP release attributes the annual GFCF decline (average annual -2.1%) to plant, machinery and equipment and transport equipment -- business assets, not housing -- and reports GFCF down 2.2% in the quarter 'as businesses invested less in physical fixed assets'. Westpac likewise reports business investment fell in the December quarter. Arithmetically, even on a generous assumption that residential (~22% weight) fell ~13-15% over the two years, the non-residential remainder is still down ~3%. Caveat worth stating: I could not read a Stats NZ/RBNZ series labelled 'business investment' in isolation (RBNZ's M3 pages and Stats NZ's data files returned 403 to automated fetching), so the verdict rests on total real GFCF plus Stats NZ's own attribution of the decline to business asset types. Both point the same way. Note the criterion does not require verifying Hipkins' attribution of the forecast to the Reserve Bank, only the level comparison.

statement: Now, he’s telling us that he’s going to take privatisation to the next election, which means that this Government, right now, is currently managing our country’s assets and wellbeing with a mind to selling those things off in the not-too-distant future.
criterion: National Party policy documents and campaign announcements for the 2026 general election: true if National campaigns on a privatisation or asset-sales policy (including partial sell-downs of state assets); false if no such policy is part of its 2026 platform.
reasoning: Criterion: National's 2026 policy documents and campaign announcements -- true if National campaigns on a privatisation or asset-sales policy (including partial sell-downs); false if no such policy is part of its 2026 platform. Resolve-by is 2026-11-30; the election is 7 November 2026 and today is 28 September 2026, so the platform is not yet complete. Evidence as at today cuts both ways and the decisive document does not exist. AGAINST: National's campaign chair Simeon Brown said (reported 15 Sept 2026) the party was 'not going to the election campaigning on asset sales', and the 10-point pledge card Luxon launched on 27 September 2026 contains no asset-sales or privatisation plank (its items are growth/jobs, no new taxes, school results, crime, healthcare, infrastructure, surplus, compulsory KiwiSaver, paid parental leave, supermarket competition). FOR: finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis explicitly separated Kiwibank from Brown's statement and said National WILL release a Kiwibank policy before the 7 November election; she has previously said she is open to private capital in Kiwibank and an NZX listing provided she has an electoral mandate, and she declines to classify diluting the Crown's stake as an 'asset sale'. She also cites the Chorus securities sale as precedent for 'asset recycling'. Swarbrick's antecedent was sound -- Luxon did publicly hint in 2025 that a 2026 win would be the mandate for asset sales next term -- but whether a privatisation policy ends up in the 2026 platform turns on a Kiwibank announcement that has not been made. Not finding it yet is not evidence it will not come.

statement: Even if, which I still doubt, this bill does not pass in this Parliament, I believe that sooner or later a bill very much like it will pass into law, because, ultimately, a House divided cannot stand.
criterion: The New Zealand statute book and parliamentary voting record: true if an Act defining the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi in statute in substantially the terms of the Treaty Principles Bill is passed into law by the resolve-by date; false if no such Act has been enacted by then. The subsidiary claim resolves against the division record for the Treaty Principles Bill in the 54th Parliament.
reasoning: Criterion: true if an Act defining the Treaty principles in statute in substantially the terms of the Treaty Principles Bill is passed into law by the resolve-by date (2030-12-31); false if no such Act has been enacted by then. That date is more than four years away, so the main prediction ('sooner or later a bill very much like it will pass into law') cannot resolve yet. No such Act is on the New Zealand statute book as at September 2026, but the criterion asks about the position at 2030, not now -- absence today is exactly what a 'sooner or later' prediction would look like mid-flight, and mapping it to 'wrong' would be reading the criterion against its own terms. The subsidiary claim IS resolved and went against Seymour: he said 'I still doubt this bill does not pass in this Parliament', and the Treaty Principles Bill was voted down at second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with only ACT's 11 members in favour and National, Labour, NZ First, the Greens and Te Pati Maori all opposed. Disconfirming check on the main claim: ACT's own August 2026 election constitutional policy drops both the bill and the referendum, substituting new Constitution Act principles, property rights in the Bill of Rights Act, limits on judicial use of tikanga, and a Cabinet Treaty-interest disclosure requirement. That is evidence the specific vehicle has been abandoned and makes the prediction look less likely, but it does not enact or foreclose anything by 2030.

statement: Now, once we pass that Gene Technology Bill, we can plant trees that will grow fruit within a year.
criterion: New Zealand gene technology regulator approvals and Plant & Food Research / industry reporting: true if, following enactment, gene-technology fruit trees are approved for field planting in New Zealand and are documented as bearing fruit within about a year of planting; false if no such approval exists by the resolve-by date, or if the approved trees take substantially longer than a year to fruit.
reasoning: The criterion requires, following enactment, a NZ gene-technology approval for field planting of GM/gene-edited fruit trees documented as fruiting within about a year, judged by 2028-12-31. As of 2026-09-28 the Gene Technology Bill has not been enacted: it was reported back from the Health Committee on 10 Oct 2025, then stalled because NZ First refuses to support environmental release of GMOs, and by mid-2026 NZ First said the overhaul is unlikely to pass before the election, with the bill possibly carried into the next parliamentary term. With no Act and no Gene Technology Regulator standing up, no approval can exist yet, and the resolve-by date is more than two years away. Background: the science Nimon gestures at is real but containment-based — Plant & Food Research's FT-like/MADS-box fast-flowering apple and pear lines flower and fruit within roughly a year, used to speed breeding cycles, not as orchard plantings.
