statement: In about 12 months’ time—maybe less—the Government’s going to tell us the system is broken; we need to sell it.
criterion: Ministerial statements, Cabinet papers and Budget 2026 documents to 29 January 2026; true if a Minister publicly proposes sale or privatisation of a state department, ministry or SOE on the grounds the system is broken, false if no such proposal is made in that period.
reasoning: Within the window (to 29 Jan 2026) ministers did publicly propose selling state assets, so the prediction's substance landed, but the specifics are overstated. Confirming: by Nov 2025 David Seymour, as shareholding minister for 20 SOEs, had sought advice on why the Crown owns each and had ~10 SOEs effectively on a sales list (QV, Pamu Landcorp, AsureQuality, Kordia, Kiwibank, Mercury/Meridian/Genesis, TVNZ, NZ Post), arguing the state should not own what has a commercial competitor and that 'the government is hopeless at owning things'; Luxon called for a 'mature' conversation on asset sales after Treasury's 2025 Investment Statement urged formal 'capital recycling', and the Government said it was open to selling Kiwibank; Housing Minister Chris Bishop's April 2025 Kainga Ora turnaround plan began selling ~900 state houses a year on the grounds the agency's finances (debt $2.3b to $16.5b, deficit $568m) were unsustainable — the closest thing to 'the system is broken, so sell it'. Disconfirming/qualifying: no minister proposed selling a government department or ministry; the Government ruled out sales this term and framed privatisation as something to seek an electoral mandate for in 2026, with Willis saying Kiwibank would not be listed without a mandate; and the stated grounds were ownership rationale and returns ('capital recycling'), not a declaration that a system is broken. Also weakening it as a forecast: Seymour was already publicly pushing privatisation on 24 Jan 2025, five days before Rurawhe spoke, so the 'in about 12 months' framing described a trend already visible.

statement: Only the other day, we had the man who will be the next Deputy Prime Minister raising the prospect of privatisation of the public health system.
criterion: Official record of who holds the office of Deputy Prime Minister after the scheduled 31 May 2025 handover. True if Seymour is sworn in as Deputy Prime Minister; false if the handover does not occur.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether the scheduled 31 May 2025 handover of the Deputy Prime Ministership to David Seymour occurred. It did: Seymour was sworn in as Deputy Prime Minister at a ceremony at Government House, Auckland, at midday on 31 May 2025, succeeding Winston Peters under the 2023 coalition arrangement that split the term 18 months each. The appointment is recorded by the Governor-General's office and reported by NZ Herald, RNZ/ODT and international wires. No evidence of any postponement or substitution.

statement: There’s also good news ahead, with business confidence for consumers and businesses on the rise, and growth is expected to rise to a healthy level this year.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts for calendar year 2025; true if annual real GDP growth for 2025 is at or above 2.0%, false if it is below 1.0%.
reasoning: Stats NZ national accounts for calendar 2025: real GDP rose 0.2% in the year ended December 2025 (annual average basis) vs the year ended December 2024, and 0.2% in the December 2025 quarter. That is below the criterion's 1.0% false threshold. Even on the more flattering through-the-year measure (Dec 2025 quarter vs Dec 2024 quarter, +1.3%) growth was well short of the 2.0% needed for 'true'. It was the first annual growth in over two years, so the direction MacLeod described was right, but 'a healthy level' was not reached on any reading: commentary at release called the economy 'still fragile' with private demand lacking.

statement: Either the Minister listens now or this Government knows that, in 20 years’ time, there will be another apology for another stolen generation of Māori tamariki, for the Minister not listening.
criterion: Official Crown/Government records of formal apologies relating to children in State care; true if a formal Crown apology is made by 2045 covering Māori children taken into State care in the period following this repeal, false if no such apology is made by that date.
reasoning: The prediction's horizon is 20 years from 2025-01-29, with a resolve-by date of 2045-01-29. No Crown apology covering Māori children taken into State care after the repeal of section 7AA could exist yet, and none does: the November 2024 Crown apology responded to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care and concerns historical abuse, predating the repeal (the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act passed in 2025). Checked for disconfirming evidence — no post-repeal formal apology of the kind the criterion specifies, which is expected this early and is not evidence either way. Unresolvable for ~19 more years.

statement: While it’s a difficult time for those who are looking for work, we are cautiously optimistic that the labour market is on the verge of a revival, following years of low growth and rising unemployment that began in 2022.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate and Monthly Employment Indicator filled jobs over calendar 2025: true if unemployment peaks and falls during 2025 and filled jobs grow over the year; false if unemployment continues to rise through 2025 and filled jobs keep contracting.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion's false condition are satisfied. HLFS unemployment rose in every quarter of 2025 — 5.1% (March), 5.2% (June), 5.3% (September), 5.4% (December, the highest since the September 2015 quarter) — up from 5.1% in the December 2024 quarter; it did not peak and fall during 2025. The first fall came in the March 2026 quarter (5.3%), after the criterion window. Monthly Employment Indicator: actual filled jobs in December 2025 were 2.38 million, down 1,505 (0.1%) on December 2024, so filled jobs contracted rather than grew over the year. Disconfirming evidence does exist and is worth naming: HLFS employment rose 15,000 in the December 2025 quarter, the first quarterly rise since June 2024, and seasonally adjusted filled jobs edged up in June, July, August and November 2025 — the turn arrived right at the edge of the window. But over calendar 2025 as the criterion specifies, unemployment kept climbing to a decade high and filled jobs ended the year lower.

statement: We won’t wait 16 years and we’ve started to deliver some progress well within 16 months: growth, forecast to reach over 2 percent in 2025; business and consumer confidence rising, with average mortgage interest rates falling for the first time in over three years; and whānau seeing key reforms in housing, infrastructure, health and safety laws, and planning rules that will drive productivity and empower local businesses.
criterion: Stats NZ GDP series for calendar year 2025: true if annual (annual-average or annual-actual) real GDP growth for 2025 is above 2.0 percent; false if it comes in at or below 2.0 percent.
reasoning: Criterion: true only if annual (annual-average or annual-actual) real GDP growth for calendar 2025 exceeds 2.0%. Stats NZ's December 2025 quarter release (19 March 2026) reports GDP up 0.2% in the December quarter, 1.3% higher than a year earlier, and 0.2% on an annual-average basis for calendar year 2025. Both of the measures the criterion allows are well below 2.0%, so the forecast the speaker cited did not eventuate. (Growth only reached ~2.6% year-on-year by the June 2026 quarter, i.e. after the window.)

statement: Today, with the passing of this bill, the highly regarded and treasured lands of Taranaki will be granted legal personhood status.
criterion: The Hansard third-reading record and Royal assent date for Te Pire Whakatupua mō Te Kāhui Tupua / Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading on 30 January 2025 and conferred legal personhood, false if it did not pass that day or the personhood provisions were removed.
reasoning: Te Pire Whakatupua mo Te Kahui Tupua / Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Bill passed its second and third readings on 30 January 2025, the day of the statement, with MPs unanimously commending it; no party opposed. The Act confers legal personhood on Te Kahui Tupua — Taranaki Maunga together with Panitahi, Patuha, Kaitake and Pouakai — giving it the rights and responsibilities of a legal person, with the surrounding national park (Te Papa-Kura-o-Taranaki) jointly managed by the Crown and the eight iwi. It received Royal assent on 1 February 2025 as Te Ture Whakatupua mo Te Kahui Tupua 2025 / Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act 2025 (2025 No 1). The personhood provisions were not removed. Checked for disconfirming evidence (a deferred reading, or personhood stripped at committee of the whole) and found none.

statement: And it’s good to see that Labour and the Green Party will also be supporting the legislation.
criterion: The division record for the Māori Purposes Bill's subsequent readings in the House. True if both Labour and the Green Party are recorded voting in favour; false if either party votes against or abstains.
reasoning: The reading in question is the Maori Purposes Bill's first reading, begun 30 January 2025 (the day Marcroft spoke) and resumed 12 February 2025. The Hansard record shows Labour and the Green Party both speaking in support — Labour with a caveat about scrutinising the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act amendments at select committee, the Greens welcoming the modernisation — alongside National, NZ First, ACT and Te Pati Maori; Waatea reports 'Labour, the Greens, NZ First, ACT, and Te Pati Maori all supported the bill.' The motion was agreed to and the bill referred to the Maori Affairs Committee on 12 February 2025, which later recommended it be passed with all amendments recommended unanimously. One caveat on the criterion as written: because no party opposed, the reading was agreed to without a division, so there is no division tally to cite — the evidence is the recorded speeches plus unopposed passage. Neither party voted against or abstained. I searched for a subsequent second/third reading where support might have been withdrawn and found no record of the bill progressing past select committee as of 28 September 2026.

statement: That’s why it was actually really great to see the Tairāwhiti mill is set to reopen in the coming months under new owners, adding value and creating quality jobs in our regional economy.
criterion: Company or regional news reporting on the Tairāwhiti (Gisborne) mill; true if the mill resumed operation under new owners by the end of 2025, false if it remained closed or the sale/reopening did not proceed.
reasoning: The mill Luxon referred to is the former Juken Nissho sawmill at Matawhero, Gisborne, shut down by Juken in late 2023/March 2024. Australian-owned Millari Group (via True Blue Timber) agreed to buy it and settled in February 2025 — announced 10-12 February 2025, immediately after Luxon spoke. It resumed production in 2025: an Innovatek report of 5 November 2025 (also carried by NZ Herald/Gisborne Herald) says the mill had by then been open and operational for around five months as Millari Mill, with 110 jobs created, 109 of them local, processing locally grown logs across its plywood, LVL and sawmill lines, and targeting 24/7 operation by year-end. A March 2026 Timber Trader News piece confirms the reopening and the 110 roles. I checked for the disconfirming case — a collapsed sale or a mill still idle — and found none; every source after February 2025 reports the sale completing and the mill running. The criterion (resumed operation under new owners by end of 2025) is met.

statement: Infometrics has estimated that by the end of this year, households will have another $45 million to spend every week due to lower mortgage interest costs.
criterion: RBNZ aggregate household mortgage interest payment data comparing end-2025 with early-2025, or Infometrics' own follow-up estimate; true if the weekly reduction in aggregate mortgage interest costs is around $45 million, false if materially smaller.
reasoning: The attribution is accurate: Infometrics did estimate (reported by NZ Herald in early 2025) that the boost to household spending from lower mortgage interest would reach about $45 million a week by the end of 2025 — roughly 1% of private consumption — up from about $8 million a week at the time, as fixed mortgages repriced. On the outcome, RBNZ C32 shows quarterly interest charged on residential mortgages peaked at $5.804b in the December 2024 quarter, fell to $5.571b in the March 2025 quarter, $5.4b in the June 2025 quarter and $4.8b by the June 2026 quarter. RBNZ mortgage-book yield data puts the average rate on all outstanding mortgages at 5.07% in December 2025, down from a 6.39% peak in October 2024, on a book of roughly $390b; Stats NZ's household living-costs indexes recorded a 17.3% fall in average-household interest costs across calendar 2025. Those imply a December-2025 quarterly interest bill of roughly $5.0b, i.e. about $43-51 million a week less than early 2025 and materially more than that against the October-2024 peak Infometrics used as its baseline. Caveat: I could not retrieve the December-2025 C32 quarterly total directly (RBNZ's own pages returned 403), so that figure is reconstructed from the yield and debt-stock series either side of it; the reconstruction has ample margin before the reduction would be 'materially smaller' than $45m. Disconfirming check: the OCR actually fell further than Infometrics assumed (2.25% by November 2025 versus their 3.25% mid-2025 forecast), which pushes the saving up, not down. A separate caveat the criterion does not ask about: the interest saving was realised, but consumer spending stayed weak into 2026, so the money freed up did not all show up as extra spending.

statement: Well, let’s make sure they don’t get back for another parliamentary term, because I’ll bet that we will be seeing the sale of those assets and I’ll bet that there is a privatisation agenda.
criterion: Government announcements and Treasury records of State-owned asset sales in the parliamentary term following the 2026 general election; true if a sale of a State-owned enterprise or a stake in one is announced or completed, false if no such sale occurs by the end of that term (including where the government does not return).
reasoning: Leary's bet is about the parliamentary term following the 2026 general election. That election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 and has not yet been held (today is 28 September 2026), so the term in question has not begun and no government of that term has announced or completed anything. The criterion's own resolve-by date is 31 December 2029. As at the campaign, National had ruled out asset sales in the current term and announced no privatisation policy, with Luxon saying 'we haven't announced any policies on that' while leaving the door open for the future; ACT is openly in favour and NZ First opposed. None of that resolves the prediction either way.

statement: Our plan shows that we can grow the economy and deliver our climate commitments—effective policies that can lay the foundation to meet net zero targets as early as 2044.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission official greenhouse gas inventory and net zero accounting; true if New Zealand's net long-lived greenhouse gas emissions reach zero on or before 2044, false if net zero is not achieved by the end of 2044.
reasoning: The claim resolves against the official GHG inventory / net zero accounting no earlier than end-2044, 18 years away. The underlying plan statement is accurate as a projection: New Zealand's second emissions reduction plan (Dec 2024, amended Jan 2026) says the plan 'sets the foundation to meet our net zero 2050 target as early as 2044' for net long-lived gases (biogenic methane excluded). Whether emissions actually reach net zero by 2044 cannot be checked now.

statement: I don’t trust this Government to back CCDM; I think they’ll scrap it.
criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health programme documentation and nursing union (NZNO) statements; true if CCDM is formally discontinued, defunded or replaced before the resolve-by date, false if it remains a funded, operating programme.
reasoning: CCDM has not been scrapped and remains a funded, operating programme — the criterion's false condition. Health NZ's 25 Sept 2026 announcement of 380 new frontline roles came out of its annual CCDM staffing calculations, and the April 2026 NZNO/Health NZ terms of settlement state the CCDM FTE calculation methodology will not be discontinued or changed without the agreement of both parties. An independent 2026 review found data consistency/quality problems and Health NZ is developing a business case on nurse-to-patient ratios, but that is due in 2027 — after the 7 Nov 2026 resolve-by date — and the stated approach is not to discard existing tools without an agreed alternative. Disconfirming evidence exists for the distrust but not the prediction: Health NZ removed safe-staffing commitments from a 2025 pay offer and NZNO says FTE calculations were paused from October 2024. That is friction, not discontinuation.

statement: Now, the election is supposed to be at the end of next year, but let’s see if we even make it that far.
criterion: Whether a general election is held on its ordinary 2026 timetable with the coalition Government intact; false if the scheduled election proceeds without the Government collapsing or an early election being called, true if an early election occurs or the coalition falls before then.
reasoning: No early election was called and the National-ACT-NZ First coalition is intact and campaigning as of 28 Sept 2026. The election is on the ordinary timetable: 7 November 2026, Parliament dissolving 1 October 2026, writ day 4 October, official results 27 November. Caveat: election day is still about six weeks away, so the criterion's false branch ('the scheduled election proceeds') is not literally complete; but the substance of the prediction — the Government not surviving to the scheduled election — is settled, since the coalition reached dissolution on the normal three-year timetable and after dissolution there is no Parliament in which a coalition could fall.

statement: In respect of the purpose of our Regional Infrastructure Fund, I want to assure New Zealanders that not only is it well run but it is going to deliver concrete opportunities to improve local infrastructure, whether it be water or community energy, as was announced, and I want to say to Māoridom as well that the bill which you are jumping up and down over will never pass.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill: true if the bill is defeated or lapses without becoming law, false if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill passed first reading on 14 Nov 2024 (68-54) but was defeated at second reading on 10 April 2025 by 11 votes to 112, with only ACT's 11 MPs in support. It never reached a third reading and never received Royal assent; Wikipedia records its status as 'Not passed'. Checked for the disconfirming case (revival/reintroduction) and found the opposite: ACT's August 2026 election constitutional policy omits both the bill and the referendum. Jones's prediction that it 'will never pass' holds on the criterion as written.

statement: With inflation now under control and interest rates coming down, and wages rising faster than inflation, we expect the unemployment rate to start to decrease.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate; true if the seasonally adjusted rate records a decline from its peak in any quarter up to and including Q4 2025, false if it is still at or above its Q4 2024 level and has not declined by then.
reasoning: The criterion's baseline is the Q4 2024 seasonally adjusted HLFS unemployment rate of 5.1 percent. Every quarter to the cutoff rose or held, never declined: March 2025 5.1 percent, June 2025 5.2 percent, September 2025 5.3 percent, December 2025 5.4 percent (highest since September 2015). No decline from a peak was recorded in any quarter up to and including Q4 2025, and the rate finished above its Q4 2024 level -- exactly the criterion's stated false condition. Uffindell's expectation that the rate would 'start to decrease' did not eventuate in the window.

statement: We’ve brought back interest deductibility for residential rental properties, which will ease the pressure on rents.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index / MBIE mean weekly rent series: true if annual rent inflation in the two years after this statement is materially lower than the rate at the time it was made; false if annual rent inflation is flat or higher.
reasoning: Rate at the time of the statement: Stats NZ CPI actual rentals for housing was up 3.7 percent annually in the March 2025 quarter (about 4.2 percent at the December 2024 quarter, the reading current in February 2025). Outcome: 1.2 percent in the year to March 2026 (smallest in 16 years) and 0.5 percent in the year to June 2026 (smallest since the December 2001 quarter). MBIE/HUD's new-tenancy series went negative (nationwide -0.1 percent in July 2025; Wellington -6 percent). That is materially lower, not flat or higher, so the criterion's true condition is met. Two caveats: the criterion's window runs to February 2027 so roughly 19 of 24 months are observed, but the deceleration is far too large for the remaining quarters to reverse, which is why this is not returned as not_yet_due; and the criterion tests only the rent index, not causation -- commentary attributes the slowdown to abundant rental supply and collapsed population growth rather than to interest deductibility, so this verdict does not endorse the causal mechanism Luxton asserted.

statement: Dairy prices are looking like they’re going to be at record levels.
criterion: Fonterra's final farmgate milk price for the 2024/25 season (and the Global Dairy Trade price index over 2025); true if the final payout exceeds the previous nominal record per kgMS, false if it falls short.
reasoning: Criterion: true if Fonterra's final 2024/25 farmgate milk price exceeds the previous nominal record per kgMS. Fonterra's final 2024/25 Farmgate Milk Price, confirmed with its FY25 annual results on 25 September 2025, was $10.16/kgMS. The previous nominal record was $9.30/kgMS for 2021/22 (the next highest prior seasons were well below: 2013/14 $8.40, 2023/24 $7.83). $10.16 exceeds $9.30 by 86c, so the payout test is met. Disconfirming check on the criterion's secondary indicator: the GDT index itself was NOT at record levels over 2025 and in fact trended down through the year (index −4.3% at the 11 Dec 2025 event, butter −12.4%), and Fonterra's later 2026/27 forecast was cut to $9.25. So the auction index does not support 'record levels'; the criterion's decisive true/false rule is the final payout, which clears the record, hence correct rather than partly_correct.

statement: This is all leading to one inevitable outcome: the next thing they will do—and the Prime Minister said not this time, but next, maybe—is privatise our public health system.
criterion: Legislation, Cabinet decisions or announced policy up to the end of the next parliamentary term: true if a National-led government enacts or formally announces transfer of public hospital/health service ownership or delivery to private ownership; false if no such measure is introduced.
reasoning: Criterion window runs 'up to the end of the next parliamentary term' with a resolve-by of 2029-12-31. As at 28 September 2026 the general election (7 November 2026) has not been held, so the 'next term' the claim points at has not begun, let alone ended. On the substance so far: no National-led government measure enacts or formally announces transfer of public hospital or health service OWNERSHIP to private ownership. National's campaign-launch pledges (26 Sept 2026) list 'faster healthcare and more medicines' with no privatisation component. Confirming-direction evidence exists but falls short of the criterion: Health NZ awarded a national Outsourced Clinical Services – Ophthalmology panel on 1 July 2026 (27 suppliers, ~$45m/yr, ~$450m over a ten-year arrangement), described by critics as the first country-wide public hospital clinical service put out to private providers, alongside directed 10-year elective-surgery contracts with private hospitals; Luxon has also signalled asset sales as a 2026 campaign item and has not ruled out health. That is contracted-out service DELIVERY under continued public ownership and funding, not the ownership transfer the criterion requires, and none of it is the post-election step the quote predicts. Verdict therefore pending, not false.

statement: In the Regulatory Standards Bill, to be passed later this year, it states that no law should be passed without showing what the problem is that is being solved, whether the benefits outweigh the costs, and who pays the costs and who gets the benefits. It seems like the ACT Party has contradicted its own legislation between this bill and the one to be passed later in the year.
criterion: The NZ Parliament bill record for the Regulatory Standards Bill; true if it receives Royal assent on or before 31 December 2025, false if it is still before the House, defeated or withdrawn at that date.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the Regulatory Standards Bill receives Royal assent on or before 31 December 2025. The Ministry for Regulation states the Regulatory Standards Act 2025 was enacted on 18 November 2025 and came into force on 1 January 2026, with Part 2 requirements from 1 July 2026. The bill (Government Bill 155, introduced by David Seymour on 19 May 2025) passed its third reading on 13 November 2025 by 68-55 along coalition/opposition lines, and received Royal assent five days later. Disconfirming check: no evidence the bill was defeated, withdrawn or still before the House at 31 December 2025 — it is a commenced Act with a Regulatory Standards Board operational from 1 July 2026. Andersen's 'to be passed later this year' is therefore borne out. Note the scoped criterion tests only the passage timing, not her characterisation of the bill's cost-benefit requirements or the contradiction she alleges.

statement: I think that is a comfortable place to sit, and I would suggest that in 12 to 15 years’ time, if there ever comes a change of Government, that will not change and that will be a long-lasting change, because it’s one that makes sense.
criterion: Administration of the Arms Act policy function as shown in Cabinet/ministerial portfolio allocations and departmental responsibility schedules: true if policy responsibility still sits with the Ministry of Justice in 2037-2040; false if it is transferred back to Police or another agency before then.
reasoning: The criterion's window is 2037-2040, 11+ years out, so the claim cannot yet be resolved. Checked for the criterion's early-falsification branch (transfer back to Police or another agency) and found the opposite: as of September 2026 firearms/Arms Act regulatory stewardship and policy still sit with the Ministry of Justice, which is leading the reform programme, and the September 2026 restructure moved the operational regulator (Firearms Safety Authority) further from Police into a new independent body monitored by Justice rather than back to Police. No change of Government has occurred either (the 2026 general election had not been held at the time of checking), so the conditional the speaker set up has not been tested.

statement: That is entirely a decision for the committee, but the market and most economists are expecting a 50-basis point reduction in the OCR. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates, lower mortgage rates, which in turn will support a growing economy.
criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Monetary Policy Statement and OCR decision of 19 February 2025; true if the OCR was cut by 50 basis points to 3.75%, false if the cut was a different size or the rate was held.
reasoning: The RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee cut the OCR by exactly 50 basis points to 3.75% on 19 February 2025, matching both the size and the resulting level Willis named. The Committee reached consensus on the 50bp reduction and signalled scope for further cuts through 2025. Willis framed it as market/economist expectation rather than her own forecast, and that expectation was borne out.

statement: So the New Zealand economy may be conceived as a quiver of arrows and each arrow must strike a target. Consequently, the $3 billion target that has been set for this sector—clear and measurable—will achieved by 2035, but it will only be achieved as we operationalise fast track, an idea that is driven by growth, prosperity, and embraced and improved, based upon the model of the Labour Party.
criterion: MBIE / official minerals sector export or revenue statistics for the year ending 2035 measured against the $3 billion target defined in the Minerals Strategy; true if the sector reaches or exceeds $3 billion by 31 December 2035, false if it remains below.
reasoning: The criterion measures minerals sector exports against the $3 billion target at 31 December 2035, roughly nine years away, so no resolving statistic exists. The target itself is confirmed as stated: the January 2025 Minerals Strategy for New Zealand to 2040 sets doubling mineral exports to $3 billion by 2035 (revised up from $2 billion after Stats NZ export data revisions). Interim trajectory is running toward it — around $1.46b in 2023 to about $2.5b in 2025 — but that is progress, not resolution, and nothing found contradicts the target's existence or measurability.

statement: In other words, the gap between average wages and benefit levels will cumulatively increase year on year.
criterion: MSD published main benefit rates against Stats NZ average weekly earnings (QES); true if the benefit-to-average-wage ratio declines in each year from April 2024 through April 2027, false if the ratio holds steady or rises in any of those years.
reasoning: The criterion requires the benefit-to-average-wage ratio to decline in each year through the April 2027 adjustment; that adjustment has not been made (it is set each Feb/Mar for 1 April, and the item's resolve-by is 2027-06-30). Evidence to date is consistent with the prediction but does not complete it. Main benefits moved from wage indexation to CPI indexation from 1 April 2025. Jobseeker Support single 25+ net weekly: $353.46 (1 Apr 2024), $361.32 (1 Apr 2025, +2.22%), $372.55 (1 Apr 2026, +3.11% CPI). Stats NZ QES average weekly earnings, FTE incl. overtime: $1,588 (Dec 2023 qtr, +6.1%), $1,651 (Dec 2024 qtr), $1,712 (Dec 2025 qtr, +3.7%), $1,716 (Mar 2026 qtr). Ratio: 22.3% -> 21.9% -> 21.8%, i.e. a decline in each observed year, so nothing has falsified it yet. Two caveats on the 2026 step: the margin is narrow (3.11% vs ~3.7%), and MSD's own net-average-wage measure for that adjustment was 2.91%, below the 3.11% CPI benefits received — so on a net-wage basis the gap narrowed that year, and the verdict depends on the QES series the criterion names.

statement: That’s why we’ve brought in the targets, and already from the front line we’ve seen that is turning around the deliveries and that will drive down waiting times.
criterion: Health NZ published mental health and addiction waiting-time reporting against the new targets — true if median/target-band waiting times for primary and specialist mental health services fall relative to the 2024 baseline, false if they are flat or rise.
reasoning: Health NZ's published target-band reporting shows waiting times falling for both services named in the criterion, relative to the 2024 baseline. Baseline Q1 2024/25 (Jul-Sep 2024, first quarter reported): 80.8% of people accessing primary mental health/addiction services via Access and Choice seen within 1 week; 80.4% of specialist referrals seen within 3 weeks. Q1 2025/26: 83.4% and 82.2% (a like-for-like year-on-year comparison published by the Minister). Q3 2025/26: 83.7% and 82.2%. Q4 2025/26 (Apr-Jun 2026, the resolve-by quarter): over 83% primary and more than 82% specialist. Disconfirming check: the independent monitor Te Hiringa Mahara's June 2026 system performance report agrees — 'good progress has been made on improving wait times' and the targets 'are being met for the total population' — so this is not just the Minister's own framing. Caveats that fall outside the criterion as written: young people are now facing LONGER waits for specialist services (youth first reported Q4 2025/26 at 77.5% primary / 78.7% specialist, both below the 80% target), people with the highest needs are not sharing the gains, and the ED 6-hour target remains far off (70.8% against 95%). On the primary/specialist aggregate the criterion specifies, the prediction holds.

statement: I’ll tell you what, we won’t hear them do it this term, because they know their socialism failed their Government, but most importantly failed this country.
criterion: Hansard for the 54th Parliament up to its dissolution; true if no Labour MP describes themselves as a socialist in the House over that period, false if any does so on the record.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific source — Hansard for the 54th Parliament up to dissolution — and asks for a universal negative over it. The window is now closed (the House rose on 23 September 2026 after the adjournment debate; dissolution 1 October, election 7 November), so the period is complete, but I could not run the search the criterion requires: hansard.parliament.nz serves its search as a client-side app that returns 'an unhandled error has occurred' to a fetch, its /api/search endpoint is behind a Radware browser-verification WAF, the daily PDFs are Flate-compressed and unreadable to the fetch tool, and general web search does not do reliable exact-phrase matching over three years of transcripts. Absence of hits from a search I could not properly execute is not evidence the negative holds, so I am not scoring this as correct. What I did establish: no reported instance of a Labour MP self-describing as a socialist in the House during this term surfaced in any search. The nearest evidence points the other way but fails the criterion's 'in the House' test — Chris Hipkins accepted the label in an RNZ interview on 12 November 2025 ('Social democrat, democratic socialist, variants of the same thing: people who believe there is a more active role for the state'). The famous Kieran McAnulty line, 'Yes, I am a socialist, and I'm proud of it', is from 2021 — the 53rd Parliament, outside the window — and a September 2026 blog post recycles it as current with no date or Hansard citation, which is the trap a keyword search would fall into. This item is settleable offline by grepping the project's own Hansard corpus for 'socialis' and cross-referencing speakers against the Labour roster.

statement: The tide is turning and we will make history by making this the first one-term National Government.
criterion: The official result of the 2026 New Zealand general election; true if National does not form a government after that election, false if a National-led government is returned.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the official result of the 2026 NZ general election. That election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 (announced by PM Luxon; advance voting from 26 October). As of today, 28 September 2026, the election has not been held and no result exists, so the claim that National will be a one-term government cannot yet be graded. Not-yet-due, not a failure; the resolve-by date of 2026-12-31 remains appropriate.

statement: Speaking of the economy and boosting all good things, I’m so excited that Hamilton Airport is going to be having international flights from July.
criterion: Hamilton Airport and airline (Jetstar) schedules and news reports; true if scheduled international passenger services commenced from Hamilton Airport during July 2025, false if they did not start by then or were cancelled/deferred.
reasoning: Scheduled international passenger services did commence at Hamilton Airport (NZ) and were operating in July 2025: Jetstar's first Sydney-Hamilton flight ran Monday 16 June 2025 and the first Gold Coast-Hamilton flight on Wednesday 18 June 2025 (4x and 3x weekly respectively), the first trans-Tasman services from Hamilton in 13 years. Checked for the disconfirming case - no cancellation or deferral; RNZ reported in December 2025 that the routes had performed strongly over their first six months. The criterion's false leg ('did not start by then or were cancelled/deferred') is therefore not met. The only inaccuracy is the month: services began mid-June, about two weeks earlier than 'from July', and the June start had already been publicly announced when he spoke - an understatement of timing, not an overstatement.

statement: What about in Kawerau, where next month a large processor will celebrate a $20 million investment into switching a massive manufacturing and processing entity from natural gas to geothermal steam.
criterion: Company or Bay of Plenty regional announcements during March 2025; true if a Kawerau processing plant publicly marks a gas-to-geothermal conversion of approximately $20 million in that month, false if no such event occurs by then.
reasoning: Essity publicly marked the completion of its gas-to-geothermal conversion at the Kawerau paper mill on Wednesday 12 March 2025 - the month predicted ('next month' from 12 February 2025). The event was the official unveiling of upgraded tissue machine PM3, described as the world's first tissue machine drying on 100% geothermal steam instead of natural gas, a NZ$20 million investment by Essity with industrial co-funding from EECA and steam supplied by Ngati Tuwharetoa Geothermal; more than 100 guests attended. Amount, location, technology switch and month all match the criterion. The underlying conversion work had been reported since mid-2024, so the March 2025 date is the celebration/launch event rather than the start of the project - which is exactly what she predicted ('will celebrate').

statement: I am confident that with us on their side, the economy will grow, and the Treasury backs me up on that, the Reserve Bank backs me up on that.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases covering calendar 2025; true if annual GDP growth for 2025 is positive, false if the economy contracts over the year.
reasoning: Criterion: true if annual GDP growth for calendar 2025 is positive. Stats NZ's December 2025 quarter release reports GDP +0.2% in the quarter, +1.3% versus the December 2024 quarter, and +0.2% on an annual-average basis for the year ended December 2025 — described as the first annual growth in over two years. Westpac's release-day note independently confirms +0.2% q/q and +1.3% y/y (both below its own and market forecasts). The economy grew rather than contracted, so the criterion is satisfied. Disconfirming check: I looked for a contraction reading and found none — no measure of calendar-2025 annual growth is negative. Worth noting the margin is thin on the annual-average measure (0.2%) and the outturn undershot the Treasury/RBNZ forecasts Willis invoked, but the criterion as written asks only whether growth was positive.

statement: I’ll guarantee you that the Labour Party—TBC—will oppose it, and I guarantee you that Te Pāti Māori will oppose it.
criterion: Division records for the first readings of the Government's RMA reform/replacement bills introduced from 2025, plus party statements: true if Labour and Te Pāti Māori both voted against, false if either supported.
reasoning: Criterion: true only if Labour AND Te Pāti Māori both voted against the Government's RMA reform/replacement bills; false if either supported. The Planning Bill and companion Natural Environment Bill were introduced 9 December 2025 and passed first reading on 16 December 2025. The Hansard division on the Natural Environment Bill records Ayes 102 (National 49, Labour 34, ACT 11, NZ First 8) and Noes 21 (Greens 15, Te Pāti Māori 4, plus Ferris and Kapa-Kingi). Labour voted FOR the bills, sending them to the Environment select committee; Wikipedia's account of both bills gives the same line-up. So Bishop was right about Te Pāti Māori (they opposed, citing lack of explicit Treaty protection) and wrong about Labour — and under the criterion as written, Labour's support makes the prediction false. Note Bishop hedged his own Labour guarantee in the quote ("TBC"), and Labour's vote was to send the bills to committee rather than an endorsement of the final scheme, but the division record is what the criterion names.

statement: His policy means that there will be no increase in State houses.
criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD public housing stock figures; true if the net number of State houses at 30 June 2026 is at or below the level at February 2025, false if net stock increases over that period.
reasoning: Criterion: true if net State houses at 30 June 2026 is at or below the February 2025 level; false if net stock increased. Baseline from Kāinga Ora's own managed-stock statistics at 31 March 2025 (closest quarter to February 2025): State Rentals 72,276, total managed properties 77,259. At 30 June 2025 those were 73,147 and 78,204. AAP FactCheck (7 July 2026), working from Kāinga Ora data, reports total stock of 77,609 at March 2026 and Kāinga Ora-managed state houses reaching 73,325 by 30 June 2026 — "the highest number on record". Both the state-rental measure (+~1,050) and the total managed measure (+~350 on the March 2026 actual) are above the February/March 2025 baseline, so net stock increased. Disconfirming check: there is a genuine competing reading — total managed stock dipped from its June 2025 peak of 78,204 (a September 2025 forecast had it ending FY26 at 78,027, down 177 year-on-year), so "stock fell" is true against a June 2025 baseline. It is not true against the February 2025 baseline the criterion specifies. Caveat on sourcing: I could not retrieve the FY2025/26 Kāinga Ora annual report or a June 2026 stock PDF directly (the site blocks automated fetching and no June 2026 PDF resolved), so the 30 June 2026 figure rests on AAP's citation of Kāinga Ora data, corroborated by the March 2026 actual which is already above the baseline.

statement: They’re going to sell our prized assets, but they’re cagey.
criterion: Government announcements, Budget documents and legislation through to the end of the parliamentary term; true if the Government announces or legislates the sale of a significant state-owned asset, false if no such sale is announced or enacted.
reasoning: Against the criterion as written, the Government did announce and enact the sale of a significant Crown-owned asset within the term: in October 2025 it announced it was considering divesting the Chorus UFB funding securities, in December 2025 decided to progress the early monetisation, and the transaction settled in August 2026 for ~$702m net (against $642m book value). Labour itself framed this as asset sales ("hock off the family silverware"). The "cagey" element also holds: Luxon has repeatedly signalled National would seek an election mandate to sell assets next term rather than announce sales before the 7 November 2026 election, Treasury ran a Crown asset review, and a partial Kiwibank sell-off returned to the agenda in May 2026. However, no state-owned enterprise or "prized asset" of the kind Webb signalled (power companies, Kiwibank, Air NZ, NZ Post, Landcorp, Kordia, AsureQuality) was announced for sale or legislated; asset sales were explicitly ruled out for this term while Nicola Willis is Finance Minister, and searching specifically for SOE divestment announcements in 2025-26 found none. So the criterion's literal true-condition is met by a non-SOE financial asset, but the substance of the claim is overstated relative to what the speaker meant.

statement: Our blue economy is an economy that can grow, and we can increase the sector to $3 billion by 2035.
criterion: Aquaculture New Zealand / MPI sector revenue figures for the year ending 2035; true if annual sector revenue is at or above $3 billion, false if materially below.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Aquaculture NZ / MPI sector revenue for the year ending 2035, and the resolve-by date is 2035-12-31 — nine years away. No 2035 revenue figure exists. For context only: the $3bn-by-2035 figure is the New Zealand Government's own official target, set in the 2019 Aquaculture Strategy and carried into the NZ Aquaculture Development Plan 2025-2030, and the sector was at roughly $760m annual revenue as at 2024, so the target requires ~$2.24bn of growth over the decade. That is context, not a verdict; the prediction cannot be graded yet.

statement: It has still projected to go further.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for quarters after February 2025: true if any quarterly print exceeds 5.1 percent, false if the rate peaks at or below 5.1 percent.
reasoning: The criterion is met: a quarterly Stats NZ HLFS unemployment print after February 2025 exceeded 5.1 percent, well inside the 2026-02-28 resolve-by window. Stats NZ reported 5.3 percent for the September 2025 quarter and 5.4 percent for the December 2025 quarter (released 4 February 2026) — the highest rate since 2015, and above market expectations, which had forecast the rate to have peaked at 5.3 percent. I checked for the disconfirming case (a peak at or below 5.1 percent) and it does not hold; the rate did not peak in that range, and continued above the threshold afterwards at 5.3 percent in the March 2026 quarter and 5.6 percent in the June 2026 quarter.

statement: I’m confident that police will apprehend the offenders of both instances, and I’m equally confident that when they do, they will face a tougher justice system with the sentencing reform laws that are going through Parliament right now.
criterion: Police statements and court/news records for the Birkenhead stabbing of early February 2025 and the armed robbery outside the Northcote MP's office on 11 February 2025: true if offenders were arrested and charged in both cases; false if either case remained unsolved with no charges laid.
reasoning: Both incidents named in the criterion ended in arrest and charge. Birkenhead Ave stabbing of 4 Feb 2025: a 26-year-old was arrested 22 Feb 2025 at a Northcote address under search warrant and charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, appearing in North Shore District Court with bail opposed. Armed robbery of an Armourguard cash-in-transit crew on Birkenhead Ave, Tuesday 11 Feb 2025 just before 2.30pm (a firearm was presented): following an overnight search in Northcote a 43-year-old was charged with aggravated robbery and commission of a crime with a firearm. Neither case remained unsolved, so the criterion's falsifier does not fire. Caveat beyond the criterion: the quote's second limb (offenders 'will face a tougher justice system with the sentencing reform laws') is not established — the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 received Royal assent 29 March 2025 and came into force ~29 June 2025, after both offences, so these particular offenders most likely were not sentenced under the new regime. The criterion asked only about arrest and charge.

statement: I do have a warning for New Zealanders, because we have heard very clearly in some of these headline statements that the Prime Minister has made at the beginning of this year that if New Zealanders do not chuck this Government out, as they should do at the next election, this Government is going to privatise New Zealand’s assets.
criterion: Government announcements and legislation after the 2026 general election; true if a re-elected National-led government announces or legislates the sale of a state-owned asset or a partial float of a Crown company, false if no such sale or float is initiated by the end of the following parliamentary term.
reasoning: The criterion is explicitly conditioned on government announcements and legislation after the 2026 general election, which is scheduled for 7 November 2026 — six weeks after today's date (2026-09-28). No post-election government exists yet, so neither the truth condition (a re-elected National-led government announcing or legislating an asset sale or partial float) nor the falsifier (no such sale initiated by the end of the following term) can be evaluated. The item's own resolve-by date is 2029-12-31.

statement: That will be the legacy of this one-term Government.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission result of the next New Zealand general election and the government formed after it. True if National does not lead the government formed after that election; false if National leads the incoming government.
reasoning: The criterion requires the official Electoral Commission result of the next general election and the government formed after it. That election is set for 7 November 2026 and has not been held as of 2026-09-28; the National-led coalition with ACT and NZ First formed after the 2023 election is still in office. There is no result to read, and the item's resolve-by date (2026-12-31) has also not passed.

statement: No one has seen a Government so far behind in the polls, but I’ve got some advice for the Government: keep doing what you’re doing, because you’re already way behind in the polls and it’s only going to get worse.
criterion: Major public polls (1News Verian and RNZ Reid Research) for the final quarter of 2025: true if combined National/ACT/NZ First support is materially lower than in the February 2025 polls, false if it is level or higher.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether combined National/ACT/NZ First support in Q4 2025 was materially lower than in February 2025. It was materially HIGHER. 1News-Verian (fieldwork 3-7 Feb 2025): National 34, ACT 9, NZ First 5 = 48%, projecting 60 seats for the right bloc against 61 for the left. 1News-Verian Q4 2025: 4-8 Oct = National 34, ACT 8, NZ First 9 = 51%; 29 Nov-3 Dec = National 36, ACT 10, NZ First 9 = 55%, giving the coalition 67 of 125 seats against the opposition's 58. RNZ-Reid Research published no February 2025 and no Q4 2025 poll (it resumed public polling in March 2025 and its nearest readings are 4-12 Sept 2025 and January 2026); the Sept 2025 poll showed a 60-60 deadlock, roughly level with its March 2025 result (National 32.9 + ACT 9.4 + NZF 7.2 = 49.5), so it shows no decline either. Looking for disconfirming evidence: no major public poll in the final quarter of 2025 showed the coalition below its February 2025 level. Jackson's prediction that it would 'only get worse' for the government fails on the criterion as written.

statement: On Monday, the Prime Minister and I announced we’ll be hosting an international investment summit in March, with about a hundred of the world’s highest-profile investors in super funds, construction companies, engineers, and business leaders coming.
criterion: Attendance and programme records for the New Zealand Government's international investment summit; true if the summit was held in March 2025 with approximately 100 international investors and business leaders attending, false if it did not occur in March 2025 or drew a materially smaller number of such attendees.
reasoning: The summit occurred exactly as predicted in timing and form: the New Zealand Infrastructure Investment Summit was held in Auckland on Thursday 13 and Friday 14 March 2025, hosted by Prime Minister Luxon and Infrastructure Minister Bishop. Treasury's official Outcomes Report (July 2025) records 122 delegates from 114 organisations across 16 countries, 80% chairs/CEOs, collectively managing over NZD $6 trillion, and describes 'over 100 senior executives from global and New Zealand infrastructure investor, financier, sponsor, construction, asset management and consultancy companies as well as senior representatives from a number of iwi investment companies.' The overstatement: only 70 of the 122 delegates were from global organisations. Bishop said 'about a hundred of the world's highest-profile investors ... coming', which holds only if domestic NZ and iwi delegates are counted in the hundred - a reading he did not signal. The criterion's threshold ('approximately 100 international investors and business leaders') is met at 122 total external delegates but not at 70 international ones, so the substance holds while the international headcount is materially overstated.

statement: Already we’ve seen a lift in sheep meat prices over recent months with December lamb prices exceeding the five-year average, record high cattle prices, and rising demand for key red meat markets that could see an additional $1 billion in export revenue for our farms this year.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries meat and wool export revenue for the year to June 2025 compared with the prior year; true if red meat export revenue rises by approximately $1 billion or more, false if the increase is materially smaller.
reasoning: The criterion names MPI's Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries meat and wool export revenue for the year to June 2025 versus the prior year. SOPI June 2025 reported meat and wool export revenue up 8 percent to $12.3 billion for the year to 30 June 2025, attributing the lift to tighter global beef and lamb supply and firm demand from Europe and the US - an increase of roughly $0.9 billion on the ~$11.4b prior-year base implied by that 8 percent. SOPI December 2025 independently confirms the outturn: it forecasts $13.2 billion for the year to June 2026, a 7 percent lift, which back-implies ~$12.3b actual for the year to June 2025. Disconfirming check: MPI's own December 2024 forecast, current when McClay spoke, had FY2025 meat and wool at only $11.4b (roughly flat), so the ~$1b lift was not already baked in - the June 2025 revision was a genuine upgrade. At ~$0.9b the increase is approximately, not materially below, the $1 billion claimed, so the criterion resolves true.

statement: Health New Zealand has advised me that surveillance colonoscopies in MidCentral will definitely recommence from Saturday, 15 February, now they have the patient pre-work issues sorted.
criterion: Health NZ MidCentral confirmation (or media/OIA reporting) that surveillance colonoscopies resumed on or from 15 February 2025; true if the service recommenced on that date, false if the restart slipped beyond it.
reasoning: Health NZ MidCentral did recommence surveillance colonoscopies in February 2025 — its own figures, reported in August 2025, say the service 'resumed in February', with extra Saturday lists at least twice a month, 95 patients seen and 187 given appointment dates since. No source reports the restart slipping past mid-February, so the substance of the prediction holds. But the criterion asked for confirmation of the specific date, and no Health NZ statement, media report or OIA response I could find pins the resumption to 15 February: the publicly announced restart date was Saturday 1 February (three sessions, 45 longest-waiting patients), which Doocey's own 13 February wording implies had already slipped over 'patient pre-work'. So the restart is confirmed for February, the 15 February date itself is not independently documented.

statement: It’s supported across the House, and it will pass.
criterion: The Parliament of NZ bills register and Hansard division record for the Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, lapses, or is not passed.
reasoning: The Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill was read a third time on 13 February 2025 (Hansard: 'Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill — Third Reading', 13 Feb 2025) and received Royal assent on 17 February 2025 as the Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Act 2025. The Ministry of Justice records that it had 'unanimous bipartisan support through all its parliamentary stages', and the NZ Bar Association likewise reports unanimous parliamentary support — so both halves of Meager's claim (supported across the House, will pass) hold.

statement: I’m really pleased that it’s gotten to this stage, that it will go through the House today with unanimous support.
criterion: The Hansard third-reading record for the Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill on 13 February 2025; true if the bill was read a third time that day and passed with no party voting against, false if it did not pass that day or any party opposed.
reasoning: The bill's third reading took place on 13 February 2025 — the day Russell spoke — per the Hansard record for that sitting, and the Beehive release announcing that the legislation 'has passed through Parliament'. Royal assent followed on 17 February 2025. On unanimity, the Ministry of Justice states the Act 'received unanimous bipartisan support through all its parliamentary stages', and the NZ Bar Association independently describes it as having 'received unanimous parliamentary support'; I found no record of any party voting against. I could not load the parliament.nz division table itself (the site returned 404/blocked to my fetches), so the no-party-opposed element rests on those two secondary sources rather than the division record.

statement: As, I think, Infometrics put it earlier this week, up to $45 million per week should be expected in lower interest rates by the end of this year, for people with mortgages up and down their country.
criterion: Infometrics' published commentary of early February 2025 plus RBNZ household mortgage data: true if aggregate weekly mortgage interest costs by December 2025 are around $45 million per week lower than at the time of the statement; false if the reduction is materially smaller.
reasoning: Brown's attribution to Infometrics is accurate: Infometrics (chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan) said in its late-January/early-February 2025 commentary that with the OCR forecast to reach 3.25% by mid-2025, "the boost to household spending will reach $45 million a week by the end of this year" (~1% of private consumption), measured against an October 2024 baseline, with ~$8m/week already freed up by early February 2025. The outcome exceeded that. The OCR fell further than Infometrics assumed (3.25% in May 2025, then 3.0% in August, 2.5% in October, 2.25% in November 2025). RBNZ's average yield on the existing stock of residential mortgages fell from its 6.39% peak (October 2024), and 6.29% at December 2024, to 5.07% at December 2025 — a fall of ~1.22-1.32 percentage points. Applied to a mortgage stock of $369.5bn (as at the February 2025 reporting) growing to roughly $385bn by December 2025, that is about $4.6-4.9bn per year, i.e. ~$85-95m per week on a constant-debt basis, and still ~$70m per week once the ~4% larger debt stock is netted off. The criterion fails the claim only if the reduction is "materially smaller" than $45m/week; it was materially larger, and Brown hedged with "up to $45 million per week should be expected," so the prediction was met and overshot. One caveat on framing rather than on the verdict: Infometrics' own $45m figure was a net boost to household *spending* (~1% of private consumption), a smaller and less directly observable quantity than the gross fall in aggregate mortgage interest costs that the criterion names.

statement: I think, to me, the way in which we can avoid this massive backlog which requires more District Court judges—and the way that we can avoid the big price tag that comes with these two bills that we are, basically, referencing and debating in the process not as one, but as part of the debate—is to actually make the necessary investments into adequate housing, into ending poverty, and into Tiriti justice so that then our District Court judges can focus on delivering genuine justice, and not dealing with a Government that is simply going to worsen the huge backlog that exists in the criminal justice system.
criterion: Ministry of Justice District Court criminal case statistics: true if active/pending criminal caseload or median time to disposal in the District Court is higher at the end of 2026 than at the time of this statement; false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion measures the District Court criminal caseload or median time to disposal "at the end of 2026"; today is 28 September 2026, so the measurement point has not arrived and the end-2026 figure does not exist yet. The interim record, however, runs clearly against the prediction, and I looked specifically for evidence the other way. Courts Minister Nicole McKee announced on 20 February 2026 the largest recorded fall in the District Court criminal backlog: 7,133 cases waiting at December 2024 down to 5,571 at December 2025, a 22% drop (1,562 fewer cases). The Ministry of Justice's Timely Justice Action Plan reports 85% of District Court criminal cases disposed of within agreed timeframes as at June 2026, up from 81% earlier in 2025, tracking toward a 90% target in 2027. Disconfirming evidence exists but is narrower in scope rather than contradictory: the Criminal Bar Association argued in June 2025 that the back-up jury trial system adjourns cases rather than clearing them (backlog cases down only 9% in that period against an 11% national headline), and judge-alone trial waits remained long, with 32% of cases taking four months or more to reach the trial stage as at November 2024. For the criterion to be satisfied the backlog would have to rise back above roughly 7,100 cases within three months, which nothing in the data suggests. So: formally not_yet_due, substantively on track to be wrong.

statement: I look forward to its unanimous support through the House, and I commend the bill to the House.
criterion: The Hansard voting/division record for the remaining stages of the bill before the House on 12 February 2025 that increases the District Court judge cap by one; true if it passed all remaining stages with no party voting against, false if any party opposed.
reasoning: The bill is the District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Bill (Government Bill 78-1), which raises the statutory cap on District Court judges by one, from 182 to 183 FTE — the bill the criterion describes. Its first reading party vote on 24/25 September 2024 was 123 ayes, 0 noes, 0 abstain, 0 absent: every party in the House, including the Greens, whose Ricardo Menendez March and Lawrence Xu-Nan criticised the surrounding policy context while their party supported the bill. The Justice Committee recommended it pass without amendment. Parliament's vote data, as republished by WhereTheyStand, records no party vote and no opposition at the second reading (12 February 2025), the committee stage, or the third reading (6 March 2025); the bill received royal assent on 11 March 2025 as the District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Act 2025 No 6. So Meager's prediction of unanimous support through the House holds. Two limitations I should state rather than paper over. First, the criterion assumes the remaining stages were taken on 12 February 2025; in fact 12 February was only the second reading, and the committee stage and third reading were taken on 5-6 March 2025 under urgency and extended sittings. Second, parliament.nz's Hansard and division pages block automated retrieval (404/Radware challenge on every route I tried, including the archive and text-proxy routes), so the later-stage divisions are evidenced through Parliament's vote data as mirrored by WhereTheyStand and through the Act's legislative history, not read off the Hansard division record directly.

statement: Decisions about the OCR are, of course, for the committee but the market and most economists are expecting a reduction in the OCR of 50 basis points.
criterion: The RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement and OCR decision of 19 February 2025: true if the OCR was reduced by 50 basis points to 3.75 percent; false if the cut was a different size or no cut was made.
reasoning: The criterion names the RBNZ MPS/OCR decision of 19 February 2025 and asks whether the cut was exactly 50 bp to 3.75%. RBNZ's own release and the February 2025 Monetary Policy Statement record that the Committee reached consensus on 19 February to lower the OCR by 50 basis points to 3.75 percent (from 4.25%), a two-year low, with scope to cut further through 2025. RNZ reported the same. Checked for the disconfirming outcomes the criterion specifies (a differently sized cut, or no cut) and found none; pre-decision commentary also had 50 bp as the consensus expectation, supporting Willis's characterisation of market and economist expectations.

statement: I’ve seen a report from Westpac that says that dairy incomes look set to hit record highs in nominal and, perhaps, real terms.
criterion: Fonterra's final farmgate milk price for the 2024/25 season and DairyNZ/MPI sector revenue estimates: true if 2024/25 dairy farm income is the highest nominal figure on record; false if it falls below a previous season's nominal income.
reasoning: Two parts both hold. (1) The attribution is accurate: Westpac's NZ Economic Overview, February 2025 states that dairy incomes look set to hit record highs in nominal and perhaps even real terms, citing lower interest rates and on-farm costs, a lower NZD and high world prices — the same hedge Willis used. (2) The criterion asks whether 2024/25 dairy farm income is the highest nominal figure on record. Fonterra's FINAL 2024/25 farmgate milk price was $10.16/kgMS — a nominal record — equating to $15.3bn paid to NZ farmers, up $3.8bn on the prior season. MPI's SOPI put 2024/25 dairy export revenue at a record $27.0bn (+16%). DairyNZ recorded owner-operator operating profit rising from $2,845 to $4,849/ha and cash operating surplus from $612k to $904k, with gross farm revenue up 21% per kgMS against a 4% cost rise. No prior season exceeds these nominal figures. Disconfirming check on the real-terms half: DairyNZ described 2024/25 as one of the strongest financial years recorded over the past DECADE rather than an all-time real record, so real terms is not established — but the speaker flagged that with 'perhaps', and the criterion tests only the nominal record.

statement: The next steps: the site, once this bill is passed, will transfer 21 working days after the Royal assent by our Governor-General, Cindy Kiro, which will provide for it to be vested before the 161st anniversary of this battle.
criterion: The date of Royal assent to Te Pire mō Ō-Rākau, Te Pae o Maumahara/Ō-Rākau Remembrance Bill and the Act's commencement/vesting provision: true if the site vested on or before 31 March 2025; false if vesting occurred after that date.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the date of Royal assent and the Act's vesting provision, and is true if the site vested on or before 31 March 2025. Te Ture mo O-Rakau, Te Pae o Maumahara 2025 / O-Rakau Remembrance Act 2025 (Public Act 2025 No 3) received Royal assent on 24 February 2025 and came into force the day after assent; s 5 defines the vesting date as 20 working days after commencement, which lands on 25 March 2025. LINZ's Landwrap (April 2025) independently confirms the outcome rather than just the schedule: 'The provisions of the Act took effect on the vesting date, 25 March 2025', with the 9.7 ha site vested in Nga Ahi e Toru for Maniapoto, Raukawa and Waikato, and the Registrar-General issuing registration guideline LINZ OP G 01312 to create the title. 25 March precedes 31 March 2025, the 161st anniversary of the battle (fought 31 March - 2 April 1864). Potaka's '21 working days after the Royal assent' is a slight restatement of the statute's '20 working days after commencement' but yields the same date, and the substantive prediction - vesting before the 161st anniversary - was met. Looked for evidence of deferral or a later vesting date and found none.

statement: In short, we know this will incarcerate more Māori, this doesn’t seem to show how it’s even going to help victims, but it gets to tick a box on your sheet of how you’ve tried to deliver restoring law and order.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics broken down by ethnicity; true if the number of Māori in prison rises in the two years following commencement of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act relative to the level at commencement, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion tests the Māori prison count over the two years following commencement of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025. The Act got Royal Assent on 29 March 2025 and commenced 29 June 2025, so the window closes 29 June 2027 — fifteen months after today's date (2026-09-28). No two-year comparison is possible yet. Interim evidence points the way Andersen predicted but does not settle it: the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement estimated the reforms would add ~1,350 prisoners; MoJ forecasts the muster rising 36% from 10,488 (early 2025) to ~14,230 by June 2035; Corrections' published quarterly musters for March and June 2026 show the population above 10,680; and Māori remain ~53% of imprisoned men, 67% of women and 81% of youth, so a rising muster mechanically raises the Māori count. Corrections' own June 2026 statistics page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the exact ethnicity-broken-down count at commencement vs now was not directly retrieved. Note the criterion covers only the first clause of the quote; the 'doesn't help victims' clause is not tested by it.

statement: Infometrics has previously estimated that by the end of this year, as a result of lower mortgage rates, households will have another $45 million to spend every week.
criterion: Infometrics / RBNZ estimates of the aggregate reduction in household mortgage interest payments over calendar 2025: true if the annualised saving is around $45 million per week (~$2.3bn a year) by December 2025, false if materially below or above that.
reasoning: The attribution checks out: Infometrics did estimate in January 2025 that falling mortgage payments were freeing up ~$8m/week at the time, rising to ~$45m/week by the end of 2025, on an assumption that the OCR would reach 3.25% by mid-2025. The predicted mechanism and direction both verified, and the threshold was reached — but the number was materially understated, because rates fell much further than assumed. The RBNZ cut the OCR to 2.25% by November 2025 (below the 3.25% assumption), and the effective mortgage rate actually paid by households fell 122 basis points, from a 6.39% peak in October 2024 (Infometrics' own baseline month) to 5.17% by late 2025. Against a housing debt stock of ~$388.5bn that is ~$4.7bn a year, or roughly $85–90m a week — about double the forecast. An independent route agrees: Stats NZ's household living-costs data shows average household interest payments fell 17.3% over 2025, which on a ~$21bn annual mortgage interest bill implies a reduction of ~$4.4bn a year (~$84m/week). No published Infometrics or RBNZ retrospective giving a single aggregate figure was findable, so these are derived from RBNZ/Stats NZ series rather than quoted. Caveat on the derivation: Infometrics' concept was cash 'freed up for additional spending', and BNZ's Mike Jones notes a chunk of the relief went to extra principal repayment rather than spending, so the spending-relevant figure is somewhat below the gross interest reduction. Even allowing for that, the realised saving sits above the criterion's band, so it cannot be scored `correct`; it failed on the conservative side, not by overstatement.

statement: The bank expects unemployment to peak at 5.2 percent, which is, of course, just a shade above where it is now—but very importantly, members, lower than what it was forecast to reach when the last people were in charge.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate series: true if the cycle peak print is 5.2% (± rounding), false if the peak is materially higher or lower.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date (2026-06-30) has passed and the June 2026 HLFS print is published, so this is checkable. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate did not peak at 5.2%: it was 5.3% in the September 2025 quarter, 5.4% in December 2025 (then the highest since September 2015), 5.3% as first published for March 2026 (shown as 5.4% in the June release's comparison), and 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter — 171,000 unemployed, an 11-year high and worse than the 5.4–5.5% economists expected. The rate was still rising at the latest print, so the cycle peak is at least 5.6% and has not yet been reached. That is 0.4pp above the forecast peak Willis cited, materially higher than rounding. I checked for the disconfirming case — a peak at or near 5.2% followed by sustained decline — and the only fall in the series (March 2026) was a single quarter that was promptly reversed. The forecast itself was accurately attributed to the RBNZ's February 2025 MPS; it is the forecast, not the attribution, that was wrong.

statement: Today, it is good news to have confirmed inflation is under control, and it is set to remain under control.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation prints for the quarters of 2025; true if every quarterly annual rate falls within the RBNZ 1–3 percent target band, false if any print falls outside it.
reasoning: Stats NZ annual CPI for the four 2025 quarters: March 2.5%, June 2.7%, September 3.0%, December 3.1%. Three of four prints fall inside the RBNZ 1-3% target band; the December 2025 print is outside it by 0.1pp (the highest annual rate since June 2024, and the RBNZ band is 1-3%). Applied literally, the criterion ('false if any print falls outside it') returns false. I record partly_correct because the breach is a single marginal 0.1pp overshoot in the final quarter rather than a loss of control, but the 'set to remain under control' half of the claim is the part that fails: inflation rose in every quarter of 2025 and continued past the band afterwards (3.1% to March 2026, 4.1% to June 2026). Checked for the disconfirming case that a later revision brought December back to 3.0% or below: Stats NZ still headlines the quarter at 3.1 percent.

statement: With that—here’s the piece of news that I was delighted to see—unemployment is forecast not to get as high as it was when they left office.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate; true if the peak rate after February 2025 stays at or below the December 2023 quarter rate (4.0%), false if it rises above it.
reasoning: The criterion's benchmark is confirmed: the seasonally adjusted HLFS unemployment rate was 4.0% in the December 2023 quarter. Every print after February 2025 is above it, and by a wide margin: 5.1% (March 2025), 5.2% (June 2025), 5.3% (September 2025, then a 9-year high), 5.4% (December 2025), 5.3% (March 2026), 5.6% (June 2026, the highest since September 2015, with 166,500 unemployed and underutilisation at 13.8%). The rate breached 4.0% in the first print after the statement and never returned. I looked for the disconfirming possibility that the series had been rebased or revised down toward 4% - it has not; the peak so far is 5.6% and the trend is still upward. The criterion is decided even though the series has not finished rising.

statement: We will see over the next 12 months and next year that New Zealand farmers, with the Government, are working hard to restore the economy and provide greater income, more jobs, and a better standard and quality of life for every New Zealander, because of the hard work that they do.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS total employment and Labour Cost Index / average weekly earnings adjusted for CPI, for the year to the March 2026 quarter, together with agricultural export receipts; true if employment rose and real incomes rose over that period, false if employment fell or real incomes fell.
reasoning: The criterion requires both employment and real incomes to have risen over the year to the March 2026 quarter. Employment: HLFS employment rose about 0.4% y/y to 2.889 million (2.885m in December 2025, +4,000 on the quarter), so the jobs leg holds weakly - but the tax-based filled-jobs series was flat to slightly down over the same year (men -0.3%/-3,746, women +0.1%/+1,035), the unemployment rate was 5.3% and rose to 5.6% by June 2026, and the employment rate slipped to 66.7%. Real incomes: annual CPI to March 2026 was 3.1% against LCI salary and wage rate growth of 2.0% (private 2.0%, public 1.7%) and QES average weekly earnings growth of 3.0% to $1,716. Both wage measures therefore fell in real terms - about -1.1pp on the LCI and -0.1pp on average weekly earnings. The criterion's 'false if real incomes fell' condition is met. The agricultural leg of the claim is the part that did come true and I checked it specifically as the disconfirming case: MPI's Situation and Outlook has food and fibre export revenue at a record $64.3b for the year to 30 June 2026, dairy $28.6b (+5%), meat and wool $14.1b (+14%). Record farm receipts did not translate into rising real incomes 'for every New Zealander' over the criterion's window.

statement: But, actually, when you’ve got a renewable energy mix at 85 to 87 percent, you need to keep the lights on and we’re not going to have the situation we had last winter.
criterion: Electricity Authority wholesale spot price and security-of-supply data for winter 2025 (June–September); true if there is no repeat of the winter 2024 gas-shortage episode — i.e. no sustained wholesale price spike of comparable magnitude and no industrial demand curtailment — false if a comparable or worse episode occurs.
reasoning: The price half of the criterion holds; the curtailment half does not. Transpower's Security of Supply Review - Winter 2025 (Nov 2025) reports that Winter 2025 average wholesale prices were "elevated but moderate relative to 2024," that prices "dropped from the shoulder season into winter in-line with improving hydro storage" after Contact and Genesis secured additional Methanex gas in May, and that peak demand of 7,015 MW on 25 July (third highest ever) was met with "fewer tight capacity situations than in recent winters." No conservation campaign or supply emergency was declared, and the Electricity Authority's Jan-June 2025 review confirms prices "fell during May and remained low into June." So there was no sustained spike comparable to winter 2024, when the seven-day rolling average hit roughly $800/MWh in August. However, the criterion also required no industrial demand curtailment, and that condition failed. Transpower states explicitly: "As was the case in Winter 2024, demand-side responses played a pivotal role. As hydro storage levels declined, large industrial electricity users - most notably the New Zealand Aluminium Smelter (NZAS) through its contract with Meridian - curtailed load to ease pressure on hydro reserves. Methanex on-sold gas supplies to generators, shutting down its own production for seven weeks from mid-May to the end of June."
