It adds that the "longer-term downstream effects of such material industrial demand response arrangements on the sustainability of industrial businesses operating in New Zealand... remain a concern," and elsewhere that "industrial shutdowns also limited demand growth." Hydro storage also came within 560 GWh of the Watch curve in May, "the closest in recent winters." Looking for disconfirming evidence of the milder reading: I checked whether the 2025 curtailment was merely a contracted option left unexercised, but both Transpower and reporting on the Meridian/NZAS 50 MW winter 2025 agreement (and NZAS delaying its potline ramp-up to 31 August 2025) confirm load was actually reduced. Winter 2025 was materially better than 2024 and the lights stayed on, but it was not free of the industrial demand destruction the criterion named.

statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm, as a consequence of the cancellation of the oil and gas industry, that over $1 million worth of coal will be imported from Indonesia to enable people to actually enjoy energy security this year?
criterion: Stats NZ merchandise trade data for coal imports from Indonesia over calendar year 2025; true if the value exceeds $1 million, false if it does not.
reasoning: The $1 million threshold in the criterion is cleared by roughly two to three orders of magnitude. MBIE's Energy in New Zealand 2026 (2025 calendar year edition) reports that overall coal imports rose 29% in 2025 and sub-bituminous imports - the grade burned at Huntly - rose 38%, lifting Genesis' Huntly stockpile to 1.16 million tonnes by the end of 2025, its highest since March 2012. The 2024 baseline was already 22.15 PJ (about 1.01 million tonnes per MBIE/Figure.NZ). MBIE states that Huntly, New Zealand's only coal-fired station, "sources most of its coal from mines in Indonesia." Transpower's Winter 2025 review independently records "Genesis securing 630 kT of coal imports between March and September this year." At any realistic delivered price for Indonesian sub-bituminous coal (tens to low hundreds of NZ dollars per tonne), that is tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, not $1 million. I looked for disconfirming evidence - a collapse in imports, or a switch away from Indonesian supply - and found only that imports fell 24% after September 2025 once the stockpile passed 1 Mt, which still leaves the full-year total far above the threshold; Genesis only cut Indonesian imports later, as Huntly use fell. Two caveats that the criterion as written does not test: the claim is a floor, and the actual figure is dramatically larger than $1 million, so the number understates rather than overstates; and the causal framing ("as a consequence of the cancellation of the oil and gas industry") is a separate attribution the criterion does not ask me to verify - the proximate driver documented by MBIE and Transpower is declining domestic gas production plus record-low hydro inflows.

statement: The impact of all these laws, according to the legal experts of the country, is that the number of Māori incarcerated within the justice system will increase—increase!
criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics for Māori (and Ministry of Justice sentencing data): true if the Māori prison/community-sentence population is materially higher after the sentencing reforms take effect than at the time of the statement (Feb 2025); false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 30 June 2027 and today is 28 September 2026, so the measurement window is still open. The laws in question commenced only recently: the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act took effect 17 June 2025 and the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 (assented 29 March 2025) came into force 29 June 2025, so barely fifteen months of post-commencement data exist, and sentencing-length effects accumulate over years. Interim evidence points in the predicted direction but is not yet sufficient to close the criterion. Corrections' quarterly statistics put the muster at 10,680 in March 2025 with 52.6% Maori (about 5,620 people); the Ministry of Justice's June 2026 projections use a February 2026 baseline of 11,240 and forecast 15,200 by June 2036, a 35% rise, explicitly attributed to "recent legislative reforms, including the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act and the Crimes Amendment Bill." The Maori share has held roughly steady (52.3% by primary ethnicity as at 30 November 2025, 56% counting all reported ethnicities), so a stable share on a larger muster implies several hundred more Maori prisoners than in February 2025. Two things stop me resolving now. First, attribution: much of the 2025-26 growth is remand-driven (remand rose from 20% of the muster in 2014 to 43% in 2025) and was already underway before the reforms commenced, so a higher count is not yet demonstrably an effect of "all these laws." Second, I could not retrieve the Maori-specific counts from the Corrections June 2026 and March 2026 quarterly releases - corrections.govt.nz returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches - so the post-reform Maori figure is inferred from the share rather than read directly. The criterion should be re-run against the Corrections quarterly series and Ministry of Justice sentencing data closer to mid-2027.

statement: It is estimated it will provide an additional $40 million per year to the council, starting from the financial year 2025-26.
criterion: Auckland Council's annual report and financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2026; true if the Auckland Future Fund distribution to council for FY2025-26 is about $40 million, false if it is materially below that or if no distribution is made.
reasoning: Auckland Council's results for the year ended 30 June 2026 report the Auckland Future Fund distributed $71 million to council and generated a $133 million return. Cheung's figure was the council's own published estimate of ADDITIONAL revenue — 'an additional $40 million per year to council, from 2025/2026', over and above the ~$26 million expected from Auckland Airport dividends. Actual additionality is $71m - ~$26m = ~$45m, close to and slightly better than the $40m predicted, starting in the predicted year. The criterion's failure conditions (distribution materially BELOW $40m, or no distribution) are not met; the literal 'about $40 million' test fails only because the total distribution came in higher, which is the opposite of the error the criterion was guarding against, and the speaker explicitly signalled the incremental reading with the word 'additional'. Note the council later revised its own public estimate upward to $60m+.

statement: It will add around $40 million in return each year from 2025 to 2026.
criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Future Fund annual reporting of fund returns for the 2025/26 financial year; true if the reported annual return is approximately $40 million, false if materially lower or higher.
reasoning: Same underlying claim as item 10, and same evidence: the fund distributed $71 million to Auckland Council in FY2025-26 against a ~$26 million airport-dividend counterfactual, i.e. it 'added' roughly $45 million, from the year Halbert named. Judged strictly against the criterion's chosen metric the answer would be 'materially higher' — the fund's reported annual investment return was $133 million and its distribution $71 million, both far above $40 million — but the criterion mis-specifies the claim: Halbert said the fund would 'add around $40 million in return', which is the council's published incremental-revenue estimate, not a forecast of the fund's gross return. On the reading the speaker signalled ('add'), the prediction came in slightly under what happened rather than overstated, so partly_correct does not fit either.

statement: I do have some concern about the wording “without reasonable excuse”, and I expect that there will be some litigation through the courts over time to determine exactly what “without reasonable excuse” would mean.
criterion: New Zealand court judgments (District Court, High Court or above, via NZLII/Judicial Decisions Online) on the theft-by-employer offence inserted into the Crimes Act: true if at least one reported decision turns on the meaning of 'without reasonable excuse' in that provision; false if no such decision exists by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Section 220AA (Theft by employer), containing the phrase 'without reasonable excuse', was inserted into the Crimes Act 1961 on 14 March 2025 by the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Act 2025. As at September 2026 I found no reported District Court, High Court or appellate decision turning on the meaning of 'without reasonable excuse' in that provision, and no reported prosecution under s 220AA. Practitioner commentary through 2025-26 consistently states that how 'reasonable excuse' will be interpreted 'remains to be seen' and that judicial commentary is limited — which is the state of affairs Bates predicted would eventually be resolved by litigation, not a refutation of it. The resolve-by date is 31 December 2030, so under the criterion as written (false only if no such decision exists BY that date) the prediction is not yet due; searched for disconfirming evidence (an early decision already settling the phrase) and found none either way.

statement: Well, for people in the Coromandel who have mortgages, people anywhere in the country who have mortgages, that’s really good news because what it means is that interest rates will drop again, and they’ll have more discretionary dollars in their pocket to help them counter the cost of living crisis that our Government has inherited from the last lot.
criterion: RBNZ published average new residential mortgage interest rates (series B20) for the months following February 2025. True if average new mortgage rates are materially lower in the months after February 2025 than the February 2025 level; false if they are flat or higher.
reasoning: The criterion names RBNZ series B20 (average new residential mortgage rates) after Feb 2025; rbnz.govt.nz returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so I resolved on the bank-advertised rates that B20 averages, which is the same measurement. On 19 Feb 2025 ANZ's 1-year fixed special was 5.29% and its 2-year 4.99%; by 30 Sept 2025 BNZ's 1-year was 4.49%. Floating rates fell too: ASB housing variable 7.39%->6.89% on 21 Feb 2025, then to 6.44% effective June 2025; ANZ floating 6.89%->6.69% (9 April 2025) then 6.49% (June 2025). The OCR fell from 3.75% (19 Feb) to 3.50% (April), 3.25% (July) and 3.00% (August 2025), reaching 2.25% by November. Checked for the disconfirming case — a flat or rising path, or banks not passing cuts through — and found the opposite: every major bank announced successive cuts through the resolve window. Rates were materially lower in the months after February 2025, so the prediction holds.

statement: Those people are going to get cheaper access to loans because of today’s cut.
criterion: RBNZ new lending rate series for business and agricultural lending (and the banks' published floating rates) for the months following February 2025. True if average new business and farm lending rates are materially below their February 2025 levels; false if they are flat or higher.
reasoning: The criterion allows the banks' published floating rates alongside the RBNZ new-lending series (RBNZ site inaccessible, 403). ASB's own releases give a clean before/after on the exact day of the quote and through the resolve date: Business Base Rate 12.52%->12.02% (announced 19 Feb 2025), then 11.77% (April), 11.52% (effective 5 June), 11.37% (effective 22 Aug 2025); Rural Base Rate 9.76%->9.26% (Feb), 9.01% (April), 8.76% (June), 8.61% (Aug) — roughly 65bp below the post-cut February level on both by late August 2025. ASB's Business & Rural Floating rate went 5.69%->5.19% in February. ANZ cut business and agri term-loan floating base rates by 40bp in March 2025 and its business/agri floating rate by a further 25bp (5.05%->4.80%) effective June 2025. I looked for the disconfirming pattern — banks declining to pass OCR cuts to rural borrowers, which has happened in past cycles — and the one search hit on that theme turned out to be a March 2016 article, not 2025. New business and farm lending rates were materially below their February 2025 levels.

statement: We don’t quite know where yet or how that’s going to happen, but it’s going to happen, they tell us, and three new public research organisations are to be set up by some time in 2026.
criterion: Official establishment records (Crown entity legislation/Orders in Council, MBIE announcements); true if three public research organisations are legally established and operating by 31 December 2026, false if fewer than three exist by then.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether three public research organisations are legally established and operating by 31 December 2026. Three were established on 1 July 2025, eighteen months inside the deadline: Earth Sciences New Zealand (from NIWA, MetService and GNS Science), the New Zealand Institute for Bioeconomy Science (from AgResearch, Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Plant & Food Research and Scion), and the New Zealand Institute for Public Health and Forensic Science (from ESR). Checked the disconfirming possibility that the reform was delayed, cut back or that fewer than three actually stood up — the establishment date is confirmed by the Beehive release and by MBIE/Science New Zealand listings of the three as operating entities, and the programme in fact went further, with a fourth (the NZ Institute for Advanced Technology) announced in July 2025 and still being incubated within MBIE. A pending fourth does not bear on a claim about three. Russell's hedge ('we don't quite know where yet or how') and her 'by some time in 2026' window were both satisfied.

statement: If we can do anything—whether it’s today or in a few months when this bill gets past its third reading—to help them and to have their piece of assurance that their private details won’t be shared and online, and they can’t be exposed to potential harassment, I think that we’ll be doing a really, really good job.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bill record for the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passes its third reading within roughly a few months of 19 February 2025 (i.e. by the end of 2025); false if it is still before the House, lapses or is defeated at that date.
reasoning: The Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill (Member's Bill, Hon Dr Deborah Russell) completed its committee stage on 8 October 2025 and received Royal assent on 18 November 2025, becoming the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Act 2025. Its third reading therefore passed well before the criterion's resolve-by date of 31 December 2025, and the bill neither lapsed nor was defeated. The timing is at the outer edge of McClure's "a few months" (about nine months), but the criterion operationalises that as "by the end of 2025", which is satisfied. The substantive assurance she predicted (directors able to substitute an alternative address) is in the Act, though it commences on a date set by Order in Council or automatically by 18 November 2026.

statement: That’s going to make interest rates go down, and that’s going to help small businesses.
criterion: RBNZ retail interest rate series (B3 / new business lending and floating mortgage rates): true if average business and floating lending rates are materially lower six months after 19 February 2025 than at that date; false if they are flat or higher.
reasoning: Measured against the criterion (average business and floating lending rates materially lower six months after 19 February 2025), rates fell. The OCR went from 3.75% on 19 February 2025 to 3.50% (April), 3.25% (May) and 3.00% on 20 August 2025 — 75bp lower at the six-month mark. Retail pass-through followed: ANZ's floating home loan rate was 6.89% in February 2025 (matched by ASB and TSB) and 6.29% after the August cut, a 60bp fall; ANZ also cut business floating term loan rates, including 15bp at the start of August 2025, having cut business and agri floating rates in May 2025. Disconfirming check: banks did not pass the cuts on in full (the main banks retained roughly 30-50bp across the 2025 cycle) and business/overdraft repricing lagged and is negotiated case-by-case, so the fall was smaller than the OCR move — but it was clearly a fall, not flat or higher. Note the criterion tests only the direction of rates, not Campbell's implied causation that government/coalition policy produced the cuts; that causal link is not established by this evidence.

statement: I don’t see any divide across all of the political parties in here for being able to step up and support this bill right now—not later, not down the track; right now, where we can send it to select committee, where we can hear from the experts, where we can hear from businesses and farmers in rural communities and just people who buy things to come in with experts.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Consumer Guarantees (Right to Repair) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes first reading with all parties voting in favour, false if any party votes against or the first reading is defeated.
reasoning: The first reading division on 19 February 2025 was 63 ayes to 60 noes — a party vote, passed narrowly. Labour, the Green Party, Te Pati Maori and NZ First supported referral to select committee; National and ACT both voted against (60 votes between them). The criterion requires the bill to pass first reading with all parties voting in favour and is explicitly false if any party votes against, so Davidson's claim that she saw no divide across the political parties fails, even though the bill did pass and reach the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee. Disconfirming check: the bill's passage and NZ First's cross-coalition support were the closest thing to her claim, but they do not make the vote unanimous; all three coalition partners voiced concerns about the bill's breadth, and the bill later stalled at select committee and was discharged.

statement: There’s a lot of technical elements that are included in that and need to be brought forward, and it is coming soon.
criterion: Parliament's bills register: true if a Government bill reforming or replacing the Companies Act 1993 (the broader companies law review referred to by the Minister) is introduced to the House on or before 19 February 2026; false if no such bill has been introduced by that date.
reasoning: Weenink was speaking in the debate on the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill — a short Member's bill (2024 No 18) — and said the wider technical package was 'coming soon'. The criterion asks whether a Government bill reforming or replacing the Companies Act 1993 (the broader companies law review) was introduced to the House by 19 February 2026. It was not. The phase-one 'Corporate Governance Amendment Bill' package was announced 15 August 2024, with further Cabinet policy decisions on 31 March 2025; introduction was expected 'early 2025', then slipped to the second half of 2025. Professional commentary published in 2026 (PwC's 2026 'Proposed company law reforms' page) still describes the phase-one changes as proposals with no Government bill introduced and no revised timetable announced as at September 2026. The only Companies Act 1993 amendment enacted in the window was the narrow Member's bill she was debating (royal assent 18 November 2025, commencement by 18 November 2026), which is expressly excluded by the criterion's parenthetical and was already before the House when she spoke. Caveat: MBIE's and PwC's pages would not render via direct fetch (empty/403), so the negative rests on repeated search-index reads of those pages plus the absence of any such bill in the bills register, Hansard first readings and Beehive releases.

statement: It is likely to go through to select committee, judging by my crude mathematics.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of Marama Davidson's right to repair (Consumer Guarantees Amendment) bill; true if the bill passed first reading and was referred to a select committee, false if the first reading was defeated.
reasoning: Bidois predicted the bill would go to select committee on his 'crude mathematics'. The Consumer Guarantees (Right to Repair) Amendment Bill (Marama Davidson, Green) passed its first reading on 19 February 2025 by party vote 63 ayes to 60 noes (0 abstentions, 0 absent) and was referred to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee, with submissions open until 3 April 2025. His arithmetic was right: Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori and NZ First supplied the majority. Later events (the committee recommending in 2026 that the bill not pass, and NZ First withdrawing support in August 2025) fall outside the criterion, which asks only about the first reading.

statement: I think we’ll be going to the select committee with this bill, to go down and drill down into the deeper parts of this bill—not like these miserable fellas over there, you know.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the right-to-repair bill debated on 19 February 2025: true if the bill passed first reading and was referred to a select committee, false if the first reading was defeated.
reasoning: Same event as the criterion specifies: the right-to-repair bill debated on 19 February 2025 passed its first reading 63–60 on a party vote and was referred to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee for submissions (closing 3 April 2025), so the bill did go to select committee as Waititi predicted. The criterion turns only on the first-reading outcome, which was a pass, not a defeat.

statement: I think it’s going to pass almost unanimously.
criterion: The party-vote record for the third reading of the Overseas Investment (Build-to-rent and Similar Rental Developments) Amendment Bill: true if it passed with only a small minority (roughly one small party or fewer) voting against; false if it failed, or if a substantial bloc such as the main Opposition party voted against.
reasoning: The party vote on the third reading (20 Feb 2025) was Ayes 102, Noes 15, 0 abstentions, 6 absent. Ayes = National 49 + ACT 11 + NZF 8 + Labour 34; the 15 noes were the Green Party alone. The main Opposition party (Labour) voted for the bill, and only one small party is recorded against, which is exactly the criterion's threshold for 'true'. Disconfirming check: Te Pāti Māori did oppose the bill in debate, so in substance two opposition parties were against it (21 of 123 MPs) — but TPM's 6 MPs were absent for the vote, so the party-vote record named by the criterion shows a single small party opposing. 'Almost unanimously' is mildly generous at 102–15 (87%), but it clears the bar as written.

statement: Well, they will never have the benefit from this bill, and I think we’re unlikely to see build-to-rent become a feature outside of our largest cities.
criterion: Count of completed or consented build-to-rent developments of 20+ dwellings located outside Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington and Christchurch, per MHUD/Property Council NZ build-to-rent pipeline reporting. False if several such regional developments (more than isolated one-offs) are underway or completed by the resolve date; true if the sector remains confined to the five main centres.
reasoning: Resolve date is 2028-02-20, roughly 17 months after today (2026-09-28), so the prediction window has not closed. Interim evidence already runs against the claim: the Property Council / buildtorentnz supply tracker at 30 June 2026 records build-to-rent activity outside the five main centres — Otago 6 developments (42 complete, 100 under construction, 1,785 in pipeline, including Simplicity Living's Remarkables Park in Queenstown), Taranaki 1 development (38 under construction), Nelson 1 development (30 in pipeline) — alongside Bay of Plenty (11 developments) and Waikato (4) totals. Two cautions before this could be called false: the tracker reports by region, not city, so Tauranga cannot yet be separated from the rest of Bay of Plenty nor Hamilton from Waikato, and much of the Otago figure is pipeline rather than consented/completed. Auckland still dominates (48 of ~75 developments). Not resolvable yet.

statement: Everybody knows the health system is under enormous pressure, in no insignificant part caused by road crashes, which will be made worse under changes by this Government, but also because people live in unhealthy housing.
criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA road crash statistics on deaths and serious injuries; true if DSIs rise following the Government's 2024–25 speed limit reversals and road safety changes, false if they hold steady or fall.
reasoning: Resolve date is 2027-06-30, nine months after today (2026-09-28). The speed limit reversals the claim depends on only took effect from 1 July 2025 (Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits 2024; 43 of 49 consulted state highway sections reverted), so there is about one year of post-change exposure and no published full-year deaths-and-serious-injuries series covering it. Interim data is mixed and does not yet support a verdict: annual road deaths fell 341 (2023) to 289 (2024) to 268 (2025 provisional), the opposite of the predicted direction, and serious injuries in 2025 were just over 2,400, down slightly; but 2026 opened worse, with 86 deaths by the start of April, the highest at that point in the year since 2022. Deaths are also not the same measure as DSI, which the criterion names. Too early either way.

statement: They think that if the policy settings are favourable, within a decade it could be 25,000 dwellings.
criterion: Published New Zealand build-to-rent stock counts (Property Council NZ / CBRE / HUD build-to-rent reporting); true if completed build-to-rent dwellings in New Zealand reach approximately 25,000 by February 2035, false if materially fewer.
reasoning: The criterion resolves in February 2035. Interim evidence: Property Council NZ's BTR tracker recorded 2,255 completed build-to-rent units as of 31 March 2026 (plus 1,650 under construction and 4,071 in pipeline, ~7,976 all-in), up from 1,307 delivered at 31 Dec 2023. The 25,000 figure is Property Council NZ's own conditional research finding ('over 25,000 BTR homes in the next decade if the right policy settings are adopted'), which Foster relayed accurately including the policy conditional. Whether completions reach ~25,000 by 2035 cannot be judged now; current trajectory is well short but the window is nine years open.

statement: It’s expedient for us to do so, as soon as this bill has received Royal assent, should it be voted that far through, and it looks like it will be because it seems to have support across the House.
criterion: The legislation.govt.nz record and the Hansard division record for the third reading of the District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Bill — true if the bill passed third reading and received Royal assent, false if it was voted down, lapsed or was not enacted.
reasoning: Both halves of the prediction held. The District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 6 March 2025 and received Royal assent on 11 March 2025, enacted as the District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 6) on legislation.govt.nz. The 'support across the House' claim is also borne out: the first reading (25 September 2024) carried with 123 votes in favour, i.e. effectively unanimous, and the bill proceeded without being voted down at any stage. McKee's 20 February statement falls between the second reading (12 February 2025) and third reading (6 March 2025), consistent with the committee stage.

statement: A flood of urban land coming to market plus responsive infrastructure will unlock an abundance of development opportunities, drive down the price of land, and make housing more affordable.
criterion: Stats NZ / QV urban residential section values and a standard affordability measure (e.g. house price to income ratio, or the Median Multiple for Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington and Christchurch): true if real urban land prices fall and the affordability ratio improves over the period following implementation; false if real land prices and the affordability ratio are flat or worse.
reasoning: The criterion resolves 2029-12-31 and requires urban residential section values plus an affordability measure over the period following implementation; the planning/land-release reforms Bishop was describing were still phasing in through 2026, so there is no post-implementation period to measure yet. Interim context only: QV reports national residential values down about 1.5% over the three months to July 2026 and roughly 1.3% over the year (average ~NZ$895,000), and commentary notes affordability has improved markedly — but that reflects the post-2021 correction and interest rates rather than a land-supply effect, and section-level (land-only) urban price series separating out the policy are not yet available. Judging now would attribute an unrelated correction to the policy.

statement: Someone else will replace him—invariably, that will be the Hon Scott Simpson, and, hopefully, the work in and around deregulating the financial sector and the enormous task therein will be picked up by his skill set.
criterion: The official New Zealand ministerial list following the March 2025 reshuffle: true if Scott Simpson is appointed Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs (Bayly's vacated portfolio), false if someone else is appointed.
reasoning: Scott Simpson was appointed Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs (and Minister for ACC), taking over Andrew Bayly's vacated portfolio; Wikipedia's dated office record gives 24 February 2025, and 2025 ministerial letters of expectation to the FMA (30 May 2025) and the Takeovers Panel are signed by him in that role. The criterion is satisfied: the named person got the named portfolio, and financial-sector regulation work (e.g. FMA, Takeovers Panel, later the surcharge ban) sat with him. Caveat: the appointment predates the 4 March 2025 statement by nine days, so this was arguably already settled at utterance rather than a genuine forecast.

statement: It is a rare moment where we have near-unanimous favourable votes in the House today, and I would encourage my colleagues from the Māori Party to join the waka—there is still time—because this, I think, is a good bill and a good bill that addresses a very significant challenge facing our cities up and down the country.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill; true if all parties except at most one small party voted in favour, false if the bill was opposed by multiple parties or a substantial minority of members.
reasoning: The party vote on the first reading of the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill, taken 4 March 2025, was 117 Aye to 6 No, 0 abstentions, 0 absent. National (49), Labour (34), Greens (15), ACT (11) and NZ First (8) voted in favour; only Te Pati Maori (6) opposed. That matches the criterion exactly - all parties except at most one small party in favour, no substantial minority against - and confirms Bidois's identification of the Maori Party as the sole holdout.

statement: The reality is that for those that choose to travel at peak time, it will halve congestion.
criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA monitoring of peak-period travel times or congestion delay before and after the time-of-use charging scheme goes live; true if measured peak congestion (delay or peak volumes) falls by roughly 50%, false if the reduction is materially smaller.
reasoning: The criterion requires AT/NZTA before-and-after monitoring of peak congestion once the time-of-use scheme goes live, and no scheme is live. The enabling Act is in force, but Auckland Council only endorsed three consultation scenarios on 25 August 2026, with public engagement opening November 2026, a second consultation in 2027, ministerial approval sought in 2028, and implementation expected 2030-2031 - after the item's 2028-12-31 resolve-by date, which should be extended. There is therefore no measured peak-congestion change to compare. For context only, not as a verdict: the scenarios now under consultation are described as affecting 3-7% of Auckland car trips with peak-time savings of up to 12 minutes, which does not obviously support a halving, but that is modelling of a later scheme design and cannot resolve the criterion as written.

statement: Then of course we had the complete debacle—the train wreck, you might say—of the interisland ferries and Nicola Willis’ decision to cancel them despite the fact that it’s going to cost New Zealanders more, and Kiwis are going to end up paying more to get less.
criterion: Treasury/Ministerial disclosure of the total Crown cost of the Cook Strait ferry replacement (including cancellation and settlement costs) compared with the final iReX cost estimate; true if the total exceeds the cancelled project's cost, false if it comes in below.
reasoning: The criterion asks for a Treasury/ministerial total Crown cost of the ferry replacement (including cancellation/settlement) against the final iReX estimate. Only interim disclosures exist: the replacement programme was costed at $1.86b in Nov 2025 ($596m fixed-price shipbuilding contract with Guangzhou Shipyard, $531m Picton, $325m Wellington, $415m management/contingency), with taxpayer contribution said to be inside the $1.7b Cabinet allocation; the iReX wind-up cost $671m in total (incl. $222m to Hyundai Mipo). Combined ~$2.53b sits below iReX's ~$3b at cancellation but above the ~$2.2b Crown share, so the comparison the criterion names is not yet decidable, and the ships do not enter service until 2029 (Peters has since had to vow the build 'won't cost more than $2b'). No Auditor-General or Treasury reconciliation of the final total has been published. Resolve-by is 2029-12-31.

statement: Nicole McKee’s there too, and she’s stepping in to assure the front line that all’s going to be sweet as when the firearms registry gets disestablished and military-style semi-automatic weapons find their way back into New Zealand.
criterion: Arms Act amendment legislation enacted by the end of the 54th Parliament; true if the firearms registry is disestablished and civilian access to military-style semi-automatic firearms is restored, false if the registry remains in place or MSSAs remain prohibited.
reasoning: The Arms Act amendment legislation was enacted within the 54th Parliament — the Arms Bill passed its third reading on 29 July 2026, received Royal assent on 5 August 2026 and came into force 23 September 2026, replacing the Arms Act 1983 — and it did neither of the things predicted. The firearms registry was continued (universal registration retained; the only change is that the new Regulator cannot require information beyond what the Act and regulations provide), and the ban on military-style semi-automatics and high-capacity magazines remains in place. ACT had to invoke the coalition 'agree to disagree' clause over the registry rather than securing its disestablishment. Checked for the opposite too: no repeal of the prohibited-firearms regime and no re-licensing pathway for MSSAs appears in the 2026 Act or the accompanying Arms (Restricted Weapons) Order 2026 coverage. Both of the criterion's falsifying conditions are met.

statement: I want to start by conceding that I suspect we’re on a hiding to nothing when this bill goes to referendum.
criterion: The official result of the referendum on extending the parliamentary term to four years; true if the proposal is rejected by voters, false if it is carried.
reasoning: The criterion requires the official result of a referendum on extending the parliamentary term to four years, but no such referendum was held or will be held by the 2026-12-31 resolve-by date. The Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) Legislation Amendment Bill (introduced 5 March 2025, brought to Cabinet by Seymour) passed first reading and was criticised at select committee; on 18 February 2026 Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith confirmed the Government would not progress the referendum at this election ('We won't be progressing with the actual referendum at this election'), and the bill did not proceed to second reading. The 7 November 2026 general election carries no four-year-term question. Seymour's prediction was conditional on the bill reaching a referendum, and that condition never occurred, so the criterion's true/false test cannot be applied — not a failing grade, simply unresolvable as written.

statement: You’re going to be lucky to get this three years. I tell you what, you’re going to be gone after that.
criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election (due by late 2026) and whether the Government survives to it: true if the National-led coalition leaves office at or before that election, false if it is returned to government.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the result of the next general election, which PM Luxon set for 7 November 2026 — after today (2026-09-28). The election has not been held, so no result exists. The National-ACT-NZ First coalition is still in office and has served the full three-year term, which already tells against the 'lucky to get this three years' half of the quote, but the criterion's true/false branches both require the election outcome. Resolve-by is 2026-12-31, so this should be revisited after 7 November.

statement: It’s a big job and there’s a high likelihood that the referendum, even if it does go through, may not be successful.
criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of any referendum held under the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) Legislation Amendment Bill. True if such a referendum is held and the proposal is not carried (below 50% support); false if it is held and carried. If no referendum is ever held, the prediction is uncheckable rather than false.
reasoning: No referendum was ever held. On 18 February 2026 the Government scrapped the planned referendum: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the coalition agreements only secured passage to select committee and that the bill would not advance this term, to be reconsidered only 'if re-elected'. As of late 2026 the bill has not passed and no referendum is held or scheduled, and none can be held before the 2027-06-30 resolve-by date. The criterion states explicitly that if no referendum is ever held the prediction is uncheckable rather than false. (Belich's hedge 'even if it does go through' anticipated this branch, but the criterion as written gives it no score.)

statement: I find that’s a very sad way to get revenue, because these are the small guys. The big guys will be able to get some advice, pay for it, but it’s going to be the small neighbourhood associations who are suddenly going to have tax bills.
criterion: Government/Inland Revenue decisions following the 2025 charities and not-for-profits taxation discussion document. True if a change is enacted or announced that subjects small clubs and neighbourhood associations to income tax they did not previously pay, effective by 1 April 2027; false if the proposal is dropped or the de minimis/exemption settings are preserved or widened for small entities.
reasoning: The criterion's false branch is met on both limbs. (1) The proposal was dropped: Revenue Minister Simon Watts decided not to continue work on taxing charities' business income, citing complexity, compliance costs and distortions (announced December 2025). (2) The de minimis/exemption settings for small entities were widened, not narrowed: Budget 2026 raised the not-for-profit tax-free threshold from $1,000 to $10,000, exempted NFPs with income of $10,000 or less from filing returns at all, and confirmed that membership subscriptions and levies remain non-taxable — effective 1 April 2027 / the 2027-28 tax year. No change subjects small clubs or neighbourhood associations to income tax they did not previously pay. The new burdens that were enacted fall elsewhere: a cap on individual donation tax credits (~350 donors, 0.1%) and repeal of the non-resident charity exemption. Disconfirming check: the only adjacent risk to small groups would be the threshold operating as a cliff (an entity over $10,000 loses eligibility entirely), but that cliff already existed at $1,000, so every small entity is strictly better off.

statement: They also allow ACC to issue a single invoice to cover ACC and health and safety at work levies, which will reduce the health and safety at work levy, on average, by $20 per year for the ACC clients it applies to.
criterion: MBIE/ACC levy documentation and the regulatory impact statement for the health and safety at work levy after the change takes effect; true if the average annual levy reduction for affected ACC clients is around $20, false if there is no reduction or the average saving is materially different.
reasoning: The mechanism predicted did happen. The quote dates to the second reading (4 March 2025) of the Regulatory Systems (Immigration and Workforce) Amendment Bill, which received assent on 28 March 2025. ACC has since implemented it: from 1 April 2025 the Working Safer (health and safety at work) levy for CoverPlus Extra policyholders is calculated on the chosen level of cover rather than on liable earnings, and all levies are combined into a single annual CPX invoice, fully from 1 April 2026. Adviser guidance describes the change as reducing the levy amount for most policyholders and simplifying invoicing, so the direction of the prediction holds. What I could not verify is the magnitude. No MBIE or ACC levy document, regulatory impact statement, or ACC levy guidebook I could reach states an average annual reduction of about $20 for affected clients; MBIE, legislation.govt.nz and several adviser sites block automated retrieval, and no costing surfaced in search. So the substance (single invoice, levy reduced for the ACC clients it applies to) is confirmed; the '$20 on average' figure is unconfirmed rather than contradicted.

statement: The starting point will apply in practice.
criterion: Sentencing decisions and Court of Appeal guideline judgments applying the amended Sentencing Act discount cap; true if courts calculate the capped discount from the judge-set starting point, false if they calculate it from the statutory maximum or if appellate authority holds otherwise.
reasoning: Sentencing decisions applying the amended Act calculate the capped discount from the judge-set starting point, exactly as predicted. The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 changes came into force 29 June 2025. In R v Thompson [2025] NZHC 2944 (7 October 2025), Radich J states at [38] that the new provisions mean 'total reductions from the starting point to account for personal mitigating factors, including a guilty plea, must not exceed 40 per cent of the sentence', and at [40] sets out the method as (a) identify the reductions from the starting point he would have made, (b) compare with the 40% permitted by s 9Q, (c) 'make a reduction from the starting point to reach the end sentence, either of 40 per cent, or greater' if s 9R manifest injustice arises. On the facts a 7-year starting point took a 40% total reduction. Footnote 5 of the same judgment records that the two-step Moses v R methodology is not altered by the 2024 and 2025 reforms. Tauroa v R [2026] NZHC 2348 applies the same base, holding that capping at 40% would be manifestly unjust and that 45% (at most 47.5%) off the starting point was the least reduction necessary. Checking for the disconfirming case: I found no judgment calculating the 40% from the statutory maximum, and no Court of Appeal authority holding otherwise. Caveat: the decisions located are High Court, not a Court of Appeal guideline judgment, so the point has not yet been settled at appellate level - but nothing appellate cuts against it.

statement: With these improved firearms prohibition orders now in force, I am confident this downward trend in violent crime will continue, making our communities safer, and ensuring criminals are held to account.
criterion: NZ Police recorded violent-crime victimisation statistics for the 12 months following commencement of the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Act (March 2025 onward); true if reported violent crime is lower than the preceding comparable period, false if it rises or is flat.
reasoning: The answer depends on which series you read, and the one the criterion names is the one I could not obtain. On the Government's headline measure, the NZ Crime and Victims Survey used for Government Target 4 (lead minister Paul Goldsmith), violent crime victimisation kept falling across the 12 months after the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Act commenced in March 2025: the October 2023 baseline of 185,000 victims of assault, robbery or sexual assault fell to 146,983 (August 2025 reading, quarter ending September 2025) and to 135,797 in the year to October 2025, with the target rated On Track. Ministers publicised this in February 2026 as 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime. But the criterion specifies NZ Police recorded victimisation statistics, and those are published only through the policedata.nz interactive dashboard, which has no fetchable time series; I could not retrieve the recorded-violence figures for March 2025 to March 2026. The most recent police-recorded figure I could verify runs the other way: violent crime victims up 7% in the year to May 2025 (a window mostly preceding the Act), against a 21% fall on the survey measure over a different window - a divergence the reporting explicitly attributes to the two sources measuring different things. So the downward trend did continue on the official target measure, but the claim is not confirmed on the Police recorded source the criterion names, and the last verifiable police-recorded reading was rising. Note also the criterion tests only the trend, not whether FPOs caused it; no evidence isolating an FPO effect was found.

statement: It gives me great pleasure to tautoko the progress of this claims settlement bill to its expected conclusion later on this morning.
criterion: Hansard and the bill's stages record for the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill: true if the third reading was taken and completed on the same sitting day as this second reading, false if the third reading occurred on a later sitting day or not at all.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the third reading was taken and completed on the same sitting day as this second reading. It was. WhereTheyStand's stage record for the bill lists both the second reading and the third reading on 5 March 2025 and notes "Extended sittings were used to progress this bill"; royal assent followed on 11 March 2025. Hansard files the third-reading debate under the 5 March 2025 sitting day (HansDeb_20250305_20250306_12 — the paired dates are Hansard's marker for a sitting that ran past midnight, the same pattern as the 2017 Rangitāne Tū Mai Rā second reading). Contemporary reporting agrees the bill "passed its second and third readings in one sitting", witnessed by members of Tamahaki, Tamakana and Uenuku, and the Beehive release announcing passage is dated 6 March 2025 — consistent with an extended sitting that crossed midnight, exactly as Potaka's "later on this morning" implies. Disconfirming check: nothing indicates the third reading was deferred to a later sitting day, and the bill was not discharged or delayed. Caveat noted for transparency: the wall clock had rolled into 6 March by the time the third reading was taken, so the calendar date differs from the sitting-day label — but the criterion's test is the sitting day, and on that test it is satisfied.

statement: I’m looking forward to the company of these good people when they come in for the third reading later on today.
criterion: The Hansard record for 5 March 2025: true if the third reading of the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua Claims Settlement Bill was held that day, false if it was not reached or was taken on a later sitting day.
reasoning: The criterion points at the Hansard record for 5 March 2025 and asks whether the third reading was held that day, with failure being "not reached" or "taken on a later sitting day". Neither failure condition occurred: the Hansard sitting day of 5 March 2025 contains the third reading (HansDeb_20250305_20250306_12), and WhereTheyStand's stage record dates both the second and third readings to 5 March 2025, flagging that extended sittings were used. Cameron's specific claim — that the iwi would "come in for the third reading later on today" — also holds on its substance: the readings were taken in one continuous sitting and news reports confirm the final reading was witnessed by members of the three iwi. Disconfirming check: I looked for any sign the third reading slipped to a separate sitting day and found none; the bill received royal assent on 11 March 2025. One honest caveat: the extended sitting ran past midnight, so by calendar date the third reading fell on 6 March 2025 (the Beehive release and news coverage are dated Thursday 6 March). Potaka, speaking in the same debate two windows earlier, says "later on this morning", which confirms the House had already crossed into the small hours. Under the criterion as written — the Hansard record for the 5 March 2025 sitting day — the prediction is borne out.

statement: The sentencing bill is around reducing the ability of judges to massively reduce sentences through a series of discounts, and limiting that, and one of the consequences of that legislation is that there will be more pressure on the courts.
criterion: Ministry of Justice court workload and timeliness statistics, plus judicial/Chief District Court Judge reporting, for the first full year after the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act commences; true if District Court criminal caseload, defended hearing volumes or median disposal times rise, false if they are unchanged or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires Ministry of Justice court workload and timeliness statistics plus judicial / Chief District Court Judge reporting for the first full year after the Act commences. The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 was assented on 29 March 2025 and came into force on 29 June 2025 (MoJ confirms the changes took effect that day: a 40% cap on personal-mitigating-factor discounts, no repeat youth/remorse discounts, and a sliding scale capping guilty-plea discounts at 25% falling to 5% at trial). The first full year therefore closed on 28 June 2026 — only three months before today (28 September 2026) — and neither a full-year MoJ court statistics release covering that window nor a Chief District Court Judge annual report for it is published yet. The resolve-by date of 30 June 2027 has not passed. Disconfirming check: I looked for interim evidence that would already settle it and found the direction running against the prediction rather than for it — the District Court reported its largest-ever reduction in the criminal backlog in early 2026, with criminal timeliness rising from 81% to 83% against a 90%-by-June-2027 target under the Timely Access to Justice Protocol. But that is a mid-window, whole-of-sector measure driven by rostering, the judge-alone trial protocol and extra judicial resource, not an isolation of the sentencing changes, and the criterion's named sources are not yet available for the year it specifies. Note also that the descriptive half of Goldsmith's statement — that the bill limits judges' ability to apply large discounts — is accurate; it is only the forward-looking court-pressure claim that is undecidable at this point. Absence of the full-year data is not evidence the prediction failed.

statement: They will continue to go behind on access to justice, and remand populations in our prisons will increase because of the failed policies, like arresting people because of what they are wearing—absolutely ridiculous policies.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics for the remand/unsentenced muster; true if the average remand population in the 12 months after March 2025 is higher than in the 12 months before, false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: Remand did not increase over the 12 months after March 2025 — it peaked in March 2025 at just over 4,500, fell ~360 to 4,218 by end-2025, and had recovered only to 4,537 by end-March 2026, still marginally below the March 2025 level. Remand share of muster fell 44.4% (Mar 2024) to 43.5% (Mar 2025) to 40.7% (Mar 2026). Estimated 12-month average after March 2025 (~4,400) is flat-to-slightly-below the 12 months before (~4,405, rising from ~4,130 in Feb/Mar 2024 to the 4,578 peak); the criterion counts flat or lower as false. Caveat: the Jun-2024, Sep-2024 and Jun-2025 quarter-ends are derived from published shares and totals rather than read directly, so the two averages sit within estimation error of each other — but no reading supports an increase. Note the trend reversed after the window closed (4,677 by mid-2026), and total muster did hit record highs; the specific remand claim is what failed.

statement: What we have enormous confidence in is that the Treasury forecast that was given to the Labour Party and us of it passing $4 billion is not going to happen.
criterion: Final published cost of the ferry and landside infrastructure programme (Treasury/Budget documents, Ministry of Transport or Auditor-General reporting): true if the total remains under $4 billion, false if reported total cost passes $4 billion.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the final published cost of the ferry and landside infrastructure programme, and the programme is not complete — the two ships are contracted through Guangzhou Shipyard International and enter service in 2029, with the resolve-by date 2030-12-31. Interim evidence runs strongly in Peters' favour: the November 2025 announcement put the whole programme at $1.86b ($596m shipbuilder contract, $531m Picton, $325m Wellington, $415m management and contingency), with taxpayer contribution under the $1.704b allocated, and Treasury information releases from March 2026 and Ferry Holdings' July 2026 media pack carry the same figures. The $4b Treasury number was a 2023 benchmarked worst-case projection for the cancelled iReX programme. Nothing found suggests a blowout toward $4b, but a cost still five years from final reporting cannot be scored true.

statement: I’ll give an example: the changes to emergency housing where you’re now likely to see more people rejected for emergency housing.
criterion: MSD Emergency Housing Special Needs Grant quarterly data: true if the number or proportion of declined applications rises materially after the 2024-25 eligibility changes relative to the preceding period; false if decline rates stay flat or fall.
reasoning: MSD data show decline rates rising sharply and materially after the August 2024 gateway tightening and continuing to rise after the March 2025 statement: just over 3% of 103,920 applications declined across 2023; 5.6% in July 2024; 13.6% by October 2024; almost 34% of the 23,421 applications made in calendar 2025; about 35% by mid-2026. In absolute terms roughly 1,000 applications were declined in March 2024 versus about 9,000 in March 2025. Checked for the opposite pattern — no source shows decline rates flattening or falling; the Auditor-General instead told MSD to clarify the grounds staff were using to decline, and MSD's own performance metrics were later reported as tied to reducing emergency housing grants.

statement: Broadly in keeping with other published economic forecasts, I expect the Treasury’s forecast to show a return to growth in the December quarter of last year, then picking up over this calendar year.
criterion: Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2025 (22 May 2025) GDP table and Stats NZ quarterly GDP for the December 2024 quarter; true if December 2024 quarter GDP growth is positive and the BEFU track shows growth strengthening through calendar 2025; false if December 2024 quarter growth is negative or the forecast track does not pick up.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion hold. Stats NZ recorded December 2024 quarter GDP growth of +0.7% (release 20 March 2025), and BEFU 2025 (22 May 2025) repeats it at p.11: 'The December 2024 quarter marked a turnaround for the New Zealand economy, with GDP rising 0.7% in the quarter and GDP per capita lifting by 0.4%.' The BEFU track does pick up through calendar 2025: p.7 'conditions remain in place to support a pickup in domestic activity over 2025, underpinned by lower interest rates, high terms of trade, increasing net migration and house prices'; p.18 'conditions are in place to support a recovery in broad economic activity over 2025'; p.19 'improving labour market conditions underpin an acceleration in GDP growth to 2.9% by June 2026'. Table 1.1's June-year annual-average production GDP is -0.8% for 2025 then 2.9% (2026) and 3.0% (2027) — the negative June-2025 figure is an annual-average artefact of the calendar-2024 contraction, not a falling quarterly track. Caveats, not disqualifying under the criterion as written: BEFU placed the broad-based recovery 'later in 2025' and forecast a slower recovery than HYEFU 2024, and the eventual 2025 outturn (a contraction in the June 2025 quarter) was weaker than this forecast — but the criterion asks about the BEFU forecast track, not the outturn.

statement: Consistent with other forecasts, they are also likely to show unemployment peaking in the first half of 2025 and then declining.
criterion: Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2025 unemployment rate track; true if the forecast peak falls in the March or June 2025 quarter with declines after it, false if the forecast peak is in the second half of 2025 or later.
reasoning: BEFU 2025 matches the criterion exactly. Page 19 carries the section heading 'Unemployment rate to peak in the June 2025 quarter, with the labour market strengthening thereafter', and the text: 'the unemployment rate peaks at 5.4% in the June 2025 quarter before easing to 4.3% by the end of the forecast period (Figure 1.12)'. The Economic Outlook chapter opener (p.7) repeats it: 'The unemployment rate is expected to peak at 5.4% over the first half of 2025... before easing to 4.3% by the end of the forecast period.' Table 1.1's June-quarter unemployment track is 5.4 (2025), 5.0 (2026), 4.8 (2027), 4.5 (2028), 4.3 (2029) — a peak in the June 2025 quarter with declines after it. I checked for the disconfirming case (a second-half-2025 or later peak) and found none in BEFU 2025; the '5.5% in the December 2025/March 2026 quarters' figure that surfaces in search results belongs to the later HYEFU 2025 (December 2025), not the document the criterion names.

statement: For example, the outlook for global bond yields means that finance costs are likely to be greater than they were at the half-year update.
criterion: Compare the finance costs line in BEFU 2025 with HYEFU 2024 across the forecast period; true if BEFU 2025 finance costs are higher, false if equal or lower.
reasoning: Treasury's own BEFU-vs-HYEFU reconciliation answers the criterion directly. Table 2.12 ('Movements in OBEGALx since the Half Year Update', p.58) has a 'Net finance costs' line of (0.1), 0.1, -, (0.1), (0.3) across 2025-2029, totalling (0.4): net finance costs are $0.4bn higher across the forecast period than in HYEFU 2024 (bracketed = worsens OBEGALx = higher cost). The Executive Summary (p.5) states it in words: compared with the Half Year Update 2024, 'Benefit payments and finance costs are the main drivers of higher expenses over the forecast period'. Consistent with that, p.49 records an additional $7.0bn of NZGBs to be issued over the forecast period compared with HYEFU 2024. Two caveats that do not flip the verdict under the criterion as written: the increase is small and not uniform ($0.4bn net over five years, with 2026 actually lower and 2027 unchanged); and the mechanism Willis named — higher global bond yields — is not what BEFU shows, since BEFU assumes 10-year yields around 4.3% over the forecast and notes interest rates 'slightly lower over the final three years of the forecast' than HYEFU 2024, so the extra cost comes mainly from more borrowing rather than higher yields.

statement: The additional investment in securing business events will deliver more than $30 million in incremental spend to the economy.
criterion: Tourism New Zealand / MBIE reporting on incremental visitor spend attributed to the business-events investment; true if reported incremental spend exceeds $30 million, false if the reported figure falls short or no such spend is attributable.
reasoning: The claim attaches to the March 2025 Tourism Boost allocation of $3m from the International Visitor Levy, which lifts Tourism NZ's Conference Assistance Programme from 90 to 110 annual conference bids; the ministerial and Tourism NZ material states the expectation of '>$30 million in incremental spend' but is itself the forecast, not reporting. No Tourism NZ or MBIE reporting yet attributes realised incremental visitor spend to that investment. What exists is bid-pipeline reporting (110 bids / $185m value target for 2025/26, raised to a record $253m target for 2026/27, with Tourism NZ attributing the jump to updated 2025 delegate-spend research and the NZICC, not to the extra $3m) and MBIE's first independent quarterly evaluations, published 21 September 2026, which cover the separate Events Attraction Package ($15m net benefit, 4 events) and Events Boost Fund ($26m net benefit, 13 events) — different funds, not the business-events conference bidding. Because conference bids convert to delegate spend years after the bid is won, and Tourism NZ's 2025/26 annual report is not yet published, the attributable figure is not reportable yet. Criterion's resolve-by date of 2027-06-30 has not passed as at 2026-09-28.

statement: I am advised that Health New Zealand is on track to deliver against this target, as work continues to ramp up at Tōtara Haumaru.
criterion: Health New Zealand reporting of elective procedure volumes at Tōtara Haumaru for the 2024/25 financial year; true if at least 2,000 elective procedures were delivered, false if fewer.
reasoning: Tōtara Haumaru at North Shore Hospital opened on 1 July 2024 with 2,000 elective procedures planned for its first year (the 2024/25 financial year) — confirmed in opening coverage on 1 July 2024, which also gives the fully-operational projection of 8,000 surgeries and 7,500 endoscopies a year. The 14 February 2025 ministerial release, reporting Health New Zealand's figures, states that more than 2,500 New Zealanders had had elective surgery at the facility since it opened, plus 2,500 endoscopies — i.e. the 2,000 first-year target was already exceeded roughly seven and a half months into the year, and four months before the financial year ended on 30 June 2025. Brown's 11 March 2025 statement that Health NZ was 'on track to deliver against this target' was therefore correct at the time and the full-year outcome cleared the criterion's 2,000 threshold. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no reporting was found of a shortfall, downward revision, or a higher first-year target that would have been missed.

statement: I suspect while I speak, people are busily drafting amendments that we’ll see on the Table at some stage in the future.
criterion: The Parliament bill page and Hansard committee-stage record for the bail bill being debated on 11 March 2025; true if any Amendment Paper/SOP to the bill was tabled after this speech, false if the bill passed its remaining stages with no amendment paper tabled.
reasoning: The bill under debate on 11 March 2025 was the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill (Government Bill 130-1), identified from the Hansard segments for that sitting day: first reading (HansDeb_20250311_20250311_28), In Committee—Part 1 (…_36) and third reading (…_48) are all dated 11 March 2025. It was introduced and passed through every stage under urgency that same day and was in force by 13 March 2025 as the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 7) — Russell McVeagh's March 2025 legislative review states it was 'introduced and passed under urgency on 11 March 2025' and records no amendments during passage. No Amendment Paper or SOP exists for the bill: legislation.govt.nz's latest bill version is still 130-1 (no amended reprint 130-2 was produced), and the disclosure register for bill 130 lists only the original departmental disclosure statement with no amendment-paper disclosure. So the bill passed its remaining stages after Webb's speech with no amendment paper tabled, which is the condition the criterion marks false. Caveat on method: parliament.nz returned 404 to direct fetches of the committee-stage Hansard (and the page has no Wayback capture), so I could not read the transcript itself and cannot formally exclude an amendment paper tabled and defeated without trace; every accessible record of the bill's passage shows none.

statement: I can assure you that, certainly when we come to the committee of the whole House stage, there will be several clauses and several questions and undoubtedly some amendments required because with all the best intention in the world, sometimes the simplest things that seem simple can very easily have unintended consequences.
criterion: Hansard record of the committee of the whole House stage on the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill: true if one or more amendments to the bill were moved and agreed to at that stage; false if the bill passed the committee stage without amendment.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether amendments were moved and agreed to at the committee of the whole House stage on the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill. Three independent lines of record say no. (1) The Amendment Paper register shows No 255 released 10 March 2025 (Privacy Amendment Bill), Nos 256 and 257 released 11 March 2025 (both Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill), then No 258 not until 27 March 2025 — no Amendment Paper for the bail bill exists in the window, and the bill passed all stages under urgency on 11 March. (2) The disclosure register for bill 130 lists only the original departmental disclosure statement, with no supplementary disclosure statement of the kind a substantive amendment to a government bill requires. (3) The bill's latest version on legislation.govt.nz is still 130-1; a bill amended in committee of the whole House is reprinted as 130-2, and no such version exists. The debate did generate the several clauses and several questions McLellan predicted (Hansard records the committee debating clauses 4 and 5 on the question that Part 1 stand part), but the amendments she called undoubtedly required did not materialise. Caveat on method: parliament.nz and legislation.govt.nz both refuse direct fetching, so I could not read the committee-stage Hansard line recording how Part 1 was reported; the verdict rests on the Amendment Paper gap plus the absence of a 130-2 reprint, which together are strong but indirect.

statement: It’s important to note that some of the changes that this Government have brought in—legislative changes—will see our prison population continue to grow, and it will continue to put pressure, not on just the prison infrastructure, but all of those support services that go with that infrastructure: that’s mental health, that’s family violence counselling, that’s drug and alcohol addiction support, and it’s also all the work that goes on through Corrections with monitoring bail electronically.
criterion: Department of Corrections monthly prison population series: true if the total prison population in March 2026 is higher than in March 2025, false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion is whether the total prison population in March 2026 exceeded March 2025. It did, substantially. March 2025: remand stood at just over 4,500 and was 43.5% of the total, implying a total near 10,350; independently, the September 2025 all-time high of 10,881 was reported as breaking the previous record of 10,820 set in 2018, so March 2025 must have been below 10,820. March 2026: the total was 11,143, with remand at 4,537 (40.7%), and the World Prison Brief records 11,256 at 30 June 2026. That is growth of roughly 800 over the year, and the March 2026 figure was described as higher than at any other time in New Zealand's history. Note the criterion tests only the direction of the population, not Andersen's attribution of that growth to the Government's legislative changes; officials quoted in the coverage say the drivers of the quarter-to-quarter volatility are not well understood.

statement: It might be that the Minister is going to table an amendment—I’m sure he will; he usually does: he doesn’t usually get it right the first time around—to frame up exactly what the distinction is, but, at the moment, it looks like the court can, essentially, delegate 100 percent of its role to a crew in Corrections who manage bail.
criterion: The Hansard committee-stage record and Amendment Paper (SOP) register for the bail bill under urgency on 11 March 2025: true if Paul Goldsmith tabled an Amendment Paper to the bill during its passage, false if the bill passed all stages with no Amendment Paper from the Minister.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether Paul Goldsmith tabled an Amendment Paper to the bail bill during its passage. He did not. The Amendment Paper sequence around the bill's one-day passage runs No 255 (released 10 March 2025, Privacy Amendment Bill, moved by Goldsmith), Nos 256 and 257 (released 11 March 2025, both for the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill), then jumps to No 258 released 27 March 2025. Nothing in that sequence attaches to the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill, which was introduced and passed all stages under urgency on 11 March 2025. Corroborating: the bill 130 disclosure register carries only the original departmental disclosure statement with no supplementary statement, and legislation.govt.nz still shows 130-1 as the bill's latest version, with no 130-2 reprint of the kind a committee amendment would produce. Webb's aside that the Minister usually does not get it right the first time was not borne out here. Same method caveat as the companion item: parliament.nz blocks direct fetching, so the Hansard committee record itself could not be read, and the verdict rests on the Amendment Paper register plus the absence of a reprint.

statement: It’s a detail, but you’re going to find yourself back here very quickly, doing the same thing again, unless we get it right here.
criterion: Parliamentary bill records for the Bail Act 2000: true if a further Government bill amending the electronically monitored bail / EM assessor authorisation provisions is introduced within two years of 11 March 2025; false if no such further amending bill is introduced in that period.
reasoning: The criterion's window runs to 11 March 2027; today is 28 September 2026, so the 'false' branch cannot be settled and the 'true' branch has not triggered. Current state of the record: the Bail Act 2000's latest reprint is 'as at 27 November 2025' and the only amendment incorporated after March 2025 is to s 9, made by the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 71) — nothing amending s 30M or the newly inserted ss 30MA/30MB/30MC. No further Government bail bill touching EM bail or EM assessor authorisation appears on the parliamentary bills record. Evidence to date therefore leans against Webb's prediction, but the window is still open (with a general election due in late 2026 compressing remaining sitting time).

statement: Honestly, if we don’t get this right, if we find out that we still haven’t properly fixed this—and this is the problem with haste: we haven’t properly fixed this—we’re going to find ourselves back here when some judge who’s cleverer than you and I points out that there’s a hole in this legislation.
criterion: NZ court judgments and the legislative record to 31 December 2027: true if a court decision identifies a gap or defect in the new electronic-monitoring authorised-absence provisions (new ss 30MB/30MC), or Parliament passes a further amendment to remedy one; false if neither occurs by that date.
reasoning: The criterion runs to 31 December 2027, more than a year away. Neither limb has occurred yet so far as the public record shows: searches of NZLII, the Courts of New Zealand judgments pages and legal commentary (Thomson Reuters' Adams – Criminal Procedure update on the new provisions) turned up no decision identifying a gap or defect in the new ss 30MB/30MC, and the Bail Act's current reprint (27 November 2025) records no remedial amendment to those sections. Note the judicial decisions that questioned delegation of absence approvals date from late 2024, i.e. they concern the OLD s 30M and prompted the Act — they do not satisfy a criterion about the new provisions.

statement: Fundamentally, in conclusion: yes, we get it—and this is the way the Government has chosen to address this problem—but, because there’s these 2,000 people out on electronic bail, and the fact of the matter is this Government’s been quite clear, and, in fact, a number of the backbench Government MPs stood up and said, “We’re going to be tough on crime,” which is, essentially, saying there’s going to be more of these, both in remand, on bail, and on EM bail, so the problems are going to get bigger.
criterion: Department of Corrections quarterly prison and community-sentence statistics: true if the remand population and the EM bail population are both higher at the end of the period than at March 2025; false if either is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion measures both populations 'at the end of the period', which the resolve-by date sets at 31 December 2026 — three months after today, and the December 2026 quarterly Corrections release does not yet exist. Interim evidence is mixed rather than clean support: the remand muster peaked at just over 4,500 in March 2025 (43.5% of the total prison population), then FELL for three consecutive quarters, dropping about 360 across 2025, before reversing upward in 2026 to 4,537 at March 2026 (40.7% of a record total muster) and roughly 4,677 by mid-2026. So the remand leg is currently only marginally above the March 2025 baseline after first moving the opposite way. The EM bail leg is untested: no published EM bail population series for 2025-2026 was retrievable (Corrections' community sentences and orders releases hold the figures, but the numbers are not exposed on the accessible pages), so 'both higher' cannot be verified even provisionally.

statement: If we can remove people who are testing positive for drugs in their system from the road, either temporarily or in some cases for a significant period of time, we think that will lead to fewer deaths and less carnage on the road.
criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA road-death and serious-injury statistics for crashes involving drivers testing positive for impairing drugs, compared with the pre-rollout baseline: true if deaths in drug-impaired-driver crashes fall after roadside oral fluid testing is operating at scale; false if they are flat or rise over the same period.
reasoning: Roadside oral fluid testing only began 15 Dec 2025 in Wellington District alone, scaled April–June 2026, and reached nationwide coverage on 1 July 2026 — roughly three months of at-scale operation as of 2026-09-28, against a resolve-by of 2028-12-31. The criterion asks for MoT/NZTA road-death and serious-injury figures for crashes involving drug-positive drivers compared with a pre-rollout baseline; no such post-rollout series has been published. The only outcome data available is process data: nearly 1,500 screens with 52 positives (3.6% positivity) across five districts by 19 May 2026, and a ministerial statement that ~30% of road deaths involve an impairing drug. Provisional 2026 road deaths (294 vs 272 in 2025) are neither drug-specific nor attributable at this stage. Absence of a resolved statistic here is a timing fact, not evidence against the prediction.

statement: However, my general understanding from the committee stage we have been discussing is that these tests won’t be available until the end of this year.
criterion: NZ Police / Ministry of Transport announcements on the commencement of random roadside oral fluid testing: true if the testing devices were not operationally available to Police before the end of 2025, false if roadside oral fluid testing was in operational use during 2025.
reasoning: Said 11 March 2025: the tests 'won't be available until the end of this year'. Police announced the successful supplier (Pathtech) and device (Securetec DrugWipe 3 S) in November 2025, the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act provisions came into force 15 December 2025, and testing went live that same afternoon in Wellington District only, with the rest of the country following April–June 2026 and full coverage on 1 July 2026. Nothing was operationally available to Police at any earlier point in 2025, so the predicted timing held precisely — and for 132 of the country's police districts' worth of coverage it was in fact 2026. Note the criterion's edge: its 'false' branch ('in operational use during 2025') is literally touched by the 15–31 December Wellington pilot, but that branch was written to catch availability arriving earlier than predicted, which is the opposite of what the record shows; no disconfirming evidence of pre-December 2025 operational use was found.

statement: We intend to narrow our list very shortly to a selection of capable shipbuilders, and the final cost will be a massive saving to the New Zealand people.
criterion: The announced/contracted total cost of the replacement Cook Strait ferry programme once the shipbuilder is selected, compared with the roughly $3-4 billion projected for iReX; true if the announced cost is substantially (say more than a third) lower, false if it is comparable to or above the iReX projection.
reasoning: Both limbs hold. The list was narrowed: six shipyards shortlisted in May 2025, a single preferred builder with a letter of intent in September 2025, and Guangzhou Shipyard International confirmed in November 2025 (ferries Kupe and Cook, in service 2029, KiwiRail operating). On cost, the announced programme total is $1.86b ($596m shipbuilding contract, $531m Picton, $325m Wellington, $415m management/contingency), with the taxpayer contribution capped under $1.7b — against iReX costed by KiwiRail at $3.1b and warned by Treasury as potentially approaching $4b. That is roughly 40% below the low end of the criterion's $3–4b benchmark, clearing its 'more than a third lower' threshold; the government's own claim is a $2.3b saving. Disconfirming checks: the $1.86b figure excludes the $671m already sunk in iReX and its wind-down (including $144m in break fees to Hyundai Mipo and $222m paid to that yard in total), and Labour argues the new vessels are smaller for the money — adding the exit costs (~$2.53b) would put the saving under a third. 'Very shortly' also slipped from the promised end of March 2025 to May.
