But the criterion asks specifically about the announced cost of the replacement programme once the shipbuilder was selected, and on that measure the saving is substantial.

statement: We acknowledge that it needs to be retrospective; we are voting for this bill that will very shortly be an Act.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register / Parliament bill progress record; true if the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill received Royal assent within roughly a month of 11 March 2025, false if it lapsed, was defeated, or had not received assent by then.
reasoning: The Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill (Govt Bill 130) had its third reading on 11 March 2025, the same day Belich spoke, and became the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 7). The Act commences 'on the day after the date of Royal assent', and the Bail Act 2000 principal reprint carries the amendment 'as at 13 March 2025', placing Royal assent on 12 March 2025 — one day after the statement, far inside the criterion's ~one-month window. It neither lapsed nor was defeated. Her accompanying point that it needed to be retrospective also holds: the Act validates authorisations made under s 30M before commencement, so EM bail conditions for defendants already on bail did not have to be remade. Caveat: legislation.govt.nz returns 403 to automated fetching, so the exact assent date is inferred from the commencement clause plus the 13 March 2025 reprint date rather than read off the assent line; this does not affect the verdict.

statement: There’s a very good chance that people who are legally taking a prescribed medication can fail two oral fluid tests, then be banned from driving for 12 hours, and then have to potentially go through a lengthy process to ensure that they don’t have an infringement and demerit points.
criterion: Once the oral fluid testing regime is operating: Police/Ministry of Transport reporting, Official Information Act releases, or documented cases in media or the courts. True if drivers lawfully taking prescribed medication are recorded failing two oral fluid tests and receiving 12-hour driving prohibitions and having to invoke the prescription defence to avoid infringement fees and demerits; false if no such cases arise once testing is under way.
reasoning: The oral fluid regime is now operating: the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 came into force 15 December 2025 and testing began in Wellington that day, going nationwide by 1 July 2026. The mechanism is exactly as Genter described. Police and the NZ Drug Foundation confirm that a positive first screening triggers a second test; two positives mean the driver cannot drive for 12 hours and the sample goes to a laboratory, and an infringement notice ($200 + 50 demerit points for one drug, $400 + 75 for two or more) follows lab confirmation. Police state explicitly that a prescription or medical note cannot be used at the roadside to avoid the test, dispute the screening result, or prevent the 12-hour prohibition; the driver must apply for a medical defence online after the infringement is issued. On the empirical side, police data covering 15 December 2025 to 2 August 2026 (8,700+ tests, 286 positive first tests, 129 of them THC, 213 infringements) record four medical defences submitted and succeeded — i.e. at least four drivers on lawfully prescribed medication went through the full chain of two failed oral fluid tests, a 12-hour prohibition, and a retrospective defence application to escape the fee and demerits. Disconfirming check: I looked for any roadside exemption or prescription carve-out that would break the chain, and Police documentation affirmatively rules one out. Only the 'lengthy process' qualifier is not independently quantified, and she hedged it with 'potentially'.

statement: I’m incredibly confident that these changes will work. We have a high level of confidence in our police service. They are a tremendous group of men and women who serve our country fantastically well.
criterion: The statutory review of this bill required to be tabled in the House within five years of commencement, together with Ministry of Transport / NZ Police data on drug-impaired driving detections and road deaths involving impairing drugs; true if the review and the data show the oral fluid screening regime operating as intended with a measurable fall in drug-impaired driving, false if the review finds the regime ineffective, not deployed, or if drug-impaired driving indicators show no improvement.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the statutory review the Act requires plus Ministry of Transport / Police data on drug-impaired driving. Section 24 of the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 requires the appointed reviewer to report to the Minister no later than five years after commencement; commencement was 15 December 2025, so the review is not due until December 2030 and no reviewer's report exists. Only about nine months of operational data are available (8,700+ tests to 2 August 2026, 286 positive first tests, 213 infringements), the regime only reached nationwide coverage on 1 July 2026, and the enforcement target of 50,000 tests per year started the same day — far too short and too confounded a series to show a measurable fall in drug-impaired driving or road deaths involving impairing drugs. Nothing found indicates the regime has failed to deploy either, which would have settled it early; deployment is proceeding. The claim is genuinely undecidable at this date.

statement: If we are looking for what we need to do to fix our health system, to deal with the rising levels of homelessness that we are seeing throughout New Zealand, by once again investing in housing, you will not see it in Budget 2025.
criterion: Budget 2025 documents (delivered 22 May 2025): true if Budget 2025 contains no substantial new operating investment in housing or homelessness response beyond cost pressures; false if it allocates significant new housing/homelessness funding.
reasoning: Budget 2025 (22 May 2025) did allocate significant new housing funding — $128m operating over four years for at least 550 Auckland social homes, $82m upfront operating supplements for community housing providers, a new Flexible Fund ($41m operating over 4 years / $250m capital over 10 years, 650-900 houses), and $49m operating + $151m capital for 400 affordable rentals for whanau Maori. Under the criterion as written, that is 'significant new housing funding' and points to false. But the homelessness half of the prediction held: budgeted homelessness support for the year to June 2026 fell $79m year-on-year, emergency housing was cut by over $1b across five years, and the new housing money was substantially reprioritised from within Vote Housing (First Home Loan, contracted emergency housing, Housing Infrastructure Fund all reduced). Substance partly holds, materially overstated on the housing-investment side.

statement: It must come to an end—2026, we will see a change.
criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it; true if the National-led coalition loses office, false if it is returned to government.
reasoning: The criterion requires the official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 general election and the government formed after it. The election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026, with advance voting from 26 October 2026. As at today (28 September 2026) the election has not been held, so there is no result and no post-election government to judge against.

statement: The Prime Minister is off to India next week.
criterion: Official DPMC/Beehive record of the Prime Minister's overseas travel: true if a prime ministerial visit to India commenced between 13 and 23 March 2025, false if no such visit occurred in that window.
reasoning: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and his delegation departed New Zealand on 15 March 2025 and made an official visit to India from 16 to 20 March 2025 (New Delhi and Mumbai; talks with PM Modi on 17 March, keynote at the 10th Raisina Dialogue, call on President Murmu). The visit commenced 16 March, inside the criterion's 13-23 March 2025 window. The statement was made Wednesday 12 March, so 'next week' is accurate. Checked for disconfirmation — no evidence of postponement or cancellation; the Indian MEA advisory and the Beehive release both confirm the trip went ahead on those dates.

statement: With that, I absolutely support our Budget Policy Statement, and I look forward to the Budget on 22 May.
criterion: The Treasury Budget 2025 publication date and the House's order paper; true if the Budget was delivered on 22 May 2025, false if delivered on any other date.
reasoning: Budget 2025 ("The Growth Budget") was delivered by Finance Minister Nicola Willis on Thursday 22 May 2025, exactly the date Wedd named. Confirmed by the government's own pre-announcement (Beehive, "Budget will be delivered on 22 May"), by every budget.govt.nz Budget 2025 page being titled "Budget 2025 - 22 May 2025", and by secondary accounts. No evidence of any deferral or alternative date.

statement: We’ve got some great things that are going to make a huge difference for our growth projections both in the short term—and the Budget Policy Statement does talk about the fact that we are returning to growth this year.
criterion: Stats NZ real GDP series: true if real GDP for the year ended December 2025 is above the year ended December 2024 (and quarterly growth turns positive during 2025), false if the economy records a further annual contraction over calendar 2025.
reasoning: Stats NZ real GDP: +0.8% (March 2025 quarter), -1.0% (June), +1.1% (September), +0.2% (December). Annual average growth for the year ended December 2025 was +0.2% — reported as the first annual growth in more than two years — and GDP was 1.3% higher than a year earlier. Both limbs of the criterion hold: the year ended December 2025 is above the year ended December 2024, and quarterly growth turned positive during 2025 (3 of 4 quarters). The false condition — a further annual contraction over calendar 2025 — did not occur. Caveat not tested by the criterion: the recovery was bumpy, with a 1.0% contraction in the June quarter, and the annual margin (+0.2% annual average) is thin, so "returning to growth this year" held only on a full-year basis.

statement: I’m confident that by the back end of this year, people will start feeling like they can get ahead, they can feel safer, and they can feel that there’s a real strong future for them and their family.
criterion: ANZ-Roy Morgan and Westpac McDermott Miller consumer confidence indices for Q4 2025 compared with Q1 2025, plus NZ Crime and Victims Survey perceptions of safety: true if consumer confidence is materially higher at the end of 2025 than in March 2025, false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: Both named indices were materially higher at the end of 2025 than in March 2025. ANZ-Roy Morgan: 93.2 in March 2025 rising to 98.4 in November and 101.5 in December 2025, its highest since September 2021 (+8.3 points). Westpac McDermott Miller: 89.2 in the March 2025 quarter rising to 96.5 in the December 2025 quarter, the highest level of the year (+7.3 points). Neither was flat or lower, so the criterion's false condition fails. Checked for disconfirming evidence: Westpac remained below the neutral 100 (net pessimism), ANZ respondents' views of their CURRENT personal finances stayed weak at net -18% with the gains concentrated in forward expectations, and on the safety limb the NZCVS to October 2025 showed only a marginal improvement (25% feeling completely safe vs 24% in 2024, still below 30% in 2018) though victimisation fell to its lowest since the survey began in 2018. On the criterion as written the prediction lands; the "feeling they can get ahead" element is the weakest part, since current-finances sentiment did not recover.

statement: What does Minister Potaka have to say to the 1,800 kaimahi who will lose their jobs as a result of his decision?
criterion: Reported job losses across the outgoing Whānau Ora commissioning agencies and their provider networks following the transition to new commissioning agencies (agency statements, union reporting, Te Puni Kōkiri transition reporting): true if roughly 1,800 kaimahi lose their roles; false if the number is materially smaller (e.g. an order of magnitude fewer) because contracts transferred to new commissioners.
reasoning: Substantial job losses did occur — the three outgoing commissioning agencies (Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, Te Pūtahitanga o Te Waipounamu, Pasifika Futures) lost their contracts and ceased providing Whānau Ora services on 30 June 2025 — but the 1,800 figure is materially overstated and appears in no source. The highest contemporaneous estimate, reported by NZ Herald, RNZ and Wikipedia, was ~1,000 roles AT RISK: ~600 at the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, ~40 direct staff at Te Pūtahitanga plus ~100 in its partner navigator network, and an unquantified number at Pasifika Futures. Te Pāti Māori's own March 2025 statement referred to '500 plus' workers. Reporting also stressed that not all at-risk roles would be lost ('it is unlikely that all 600 kaimahi will be left jobless'), and the four new agencies (Rangitāmiro, Māhutonga, Te Tauraki, Tātou Collective) initially rolled over the existing provider network for continuity from 1 July 2025, so provider-level contracts and the kaimahi attached to them largely transferred rather than disappearing. No final published tally of actual role losses exists, so the best available evidence is the ~1,000 at-risk figure plus the provider rollover — i.e. roughly half the claimed number at most, and likely fewer in realised losses. Not an order of magnitude smaller, so not false; substance holds but the number is materially overstated.

statement: It’s also been announced that the airline VietJet will be developing a new commercial route here to strengthen connectivity and build better people-to-people links.
criterion: Airline schedules and CAA/airport announcements; true if VietJet operates a scheduled commercial service to a New Zealand airport, false if no such route is launched.
reasoning: VietJet launched its first Vietnam–New Zealand service in September 2025: Ho Chi Minh City–Auckland, four return flights per week, operated with A330-300 aircraft. The route was announced in March 2025 in the presence of PMs Phạm Minh Chính and Christopher Luxon, alongside the elevation of the bilateral relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Checking for disconfirming evidence: VietJet has trimmed its Ho Chi Minh City–Melbourne frequency for the 2026–27 northern winter, but no suspension or cancellation of the Auckland route was found, and schedule sources show VietJet still operating nonstop Auckland–Ho Chi Minh City services in 2026. The criterion — a scheduled commercial VietJet service to a New Zealand airport — is met.

statement: In fact, recently, Infometrics estimated that by the end of this year, New Zealand households will have another $45 million to spend every week due to lower mortgage interest costs.
criterion: Infometrics / RBNZ household mortgage interest-servicing data for late 2025; true if the aggregate reduction in household mortgage interest costs is of the order of $45 million per week by 31 December 2025, false if materially lower or higher.
reasoning: The attribution is accurate and the substance was borne out, in fact exceeded. Source of the estimate: Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan, quoted in the NZ Herald on 30 January 2025 — the decline in mortgage payments since October 2024 had already freed up ~$8 million per week, and 'with the official cash rate forecast to reach 3.25% by mid-2025, the boost to household spending will reach $45 million a week by the end of this year.' Outcome against RBNZ data: total interest charged on residential mortgages was $5.804 billion in the December 2024 quarter (the peak), $5.571b in March 2025, $5.4b in June 2025, and the December 2025 quarter was 13.6% below a year earlier — about $5.02b, which reconciles exactly with the reported calendar-year totals of $21.25b for 2025 against $22.3b for 2024. That is a run-rate reduction of roughly $0.79b per quarter, or about $60 million per week by 31 December 2025, against a $373–390b mortgage book. Stats NZ's HLPI independently recorded a 17.3% fall in interest payments for the average household over the 12 months to the December 2025 quarter. The overshoot has a clear cause: the OCR ended 2025 at 2.25% (after cuts to 2.5% in October and 2.25% in November) rather than the 3.25% Infometrics assumed. So the aggregate reduction was of the order of $45m/week and if anything larger — same order of magnitude, ~35% above forecast, erring conservative rather than overstated. Caveat outside the criterion: the reduction in interest cost is established; whether households converted it into spending rather than saving is a separate matter, and 2025 reporting suggested caution and higher saving.

statement: To acknowledge that the member Camilla Belich did say, almost every business and almost every employer is a good employer, but, in so many cases, it is inevitably going to happen that police are going to be entering a workplace, pressing charges against someone or investigating someone for what has been perceived to have been done to an employee.
criterion: NZ Police / court records and reporting on the new theft-by-employer offence inserted into the Crimes Act 1961: true if police have investigated employers at their workplaces or laid charges under the new offence in multiple cases within two years of the Bill's passage; false if no or negligible (nil to one) police investigations or charges under that offence are recorded in that period.
reasoning: The criterion's window (multiple police investigations or charges under the new theft-by-employer offence within two years of passage) runs to 13 March 2027 — five months away. Section 220AA was inserted into the Crimes Act 1961 on 14 March 2025, so ~18 months have elapsed. I found no public record of any police investigation or charge under s 220AA: legal commentary from 2025 and 2026 still describes police prosecution prospectively, and searching for disconfirming evidence (first prosecutions, charge statistics, OIA releases) turned up nothing either way. The only reported court matter is Singh v Chand [2025] NZEmpC 163, an Employment Court fine for breaching ERA compliance orders over unpaid wages — not a s 220AA charge. Absence of reporting is weak evidence: individual District Court charges are rarely reported and NZ Police do not publish charge counts by offence code, so the criterion needs an OIA to Police or Ministry of Justice charge data rather than a search. Not resolvable as true or false yet.

statement: Fortunately, there is a Government party that does sound like they have unshackled themselves from the neo-liberal freight train of capitalism and will be supporting this bill, hopefully, at the end of this as well.
criterion: The Hansard division/voting record for the third reading of the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill; true if a Government coalition party other than National and ACT cast its votes in favour, false if no Government party supported it.
reasoning: New Zealand First — a Government coalition party other than National and ACT — voted in favour at the third reading on 12 March 2025. National and ACT opposed the bill; NZ First's votes carried it 63 to 60 alongside Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. Checked for the opposite (that no Government party supported it, or that it passed on National/ACT votes): RNZ and Stuff both report National and ACT against and NZ First crossing the floor, and the select committee had not recommended it pass, which is why NZ First's support was decisive. The prediction that a Government party would support the bill is borne out.

statement: What a momentous occasion for him to be back in the House to see this bill, hopefully, be passed into law, and I feel that it will happen.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register and Parliament's bill record; true if the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated or lapses.
reasoning: The Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 12 March 2025 and received Royal assent on 13 March 2025, becoming the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 8) on the NZ legislation register. It inserted s 220AA into the Crimes Act 1961, in force from 14 March 2025. It was neither defeated nor lapsed, so the prediction that it would be passed into law holds, and well inside the 2025-06-30 resolve-by date.

statement: That’s why this bill will pass tonight.
criterion: The House's voting record for the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill on 12 March 2025; true if the bill passed its reading that sitting night, false if it was defeated or not disposed of.
reasoning: The Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on the night of Wednesday 12 March 2025, the same sitting night as the quote, by 63 votes to 60 (Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori and NZ First for; National and ACT against). It received royal assent the following day and is now the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Act 2025 No 8. The bill was disposed of that night, exactly as the criterion requires.

statement: These are the people that are actually going to drill the tunnels that are going to take us through the Dome Valley, all the way up to the great electorate of Northland.
criterion: NZTA project records for the Warkworth to Te Hana / Northland Expressway corridor. True if physical tunnelling construction through the Dome Valley section has commenced by the resolve-by date; false if the project remains at planning, consenting or procurement stage, or has been deferred or descoped.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2030-12-31, which has not passed (today 2026-09-28). The project has advanced past procurement rather than being deferred or descoped: NZTA signed the $3.649b Warkworth to Te Hana PPP with the Northway consortium at financial close on 30 July 2026, and the 26km route explicitly includes twin 1km tunnels through Kraack Hill in the Dome Valley. However, detailed design/site mobilisation/early works only begin from around August 2026, main construction is scheduled for November 2027, and the road is due to open in 2033 (full completion 2034). Physical tunnelling has therefore not commenced, but it remains possible before the 2030 deadline, so the prediction cannot be graded yet.

statement: On top of the brand new helicopter announced yesterday and one that’s been operational in Tauranga from mid - last year, at this stage, we are looking at a near-new helicopter to be operational in Auckland from mid-April, and three more helicopters are expected to arrive in New Zealand by the end of May.
criterion: Air ambulance operator / NASO fleet records and public announcements; true if an Auckland-based near-new helicopter entered service by late April 2025 and three additional helicopters had arrived in NZ by 31 May 2025, false if either milestone slipped materially past those dates.
reasoning: First milestone substantially met but late: the near-new Leonardo AW169 for Auckland was commissioned at Northern Rescue's Ardmore base on 2 May 2025, not 'from mid-April' — a slip of about two weeks, landing just past the criterion's 'late April'. Second milestone failed: three further helicopters had not arrived in NZ by 31 May 2025. The government's own 2 May release pushed Northland's two leased near-new aircraft to 'ready for use from July' and Wellington's new machine to 'arriving in August'; Life Flight's Airbus H145 actually flew into Wellington on 19 September 2025, and the 24 October 2025 release described only two further replacements as 'in the country and being fitted out', not operational until early 2026. Only one aircraft (AW169 ZK-IRB, US-registered N269LL, NZ-registered 3 March 2025, photographed at Ardmore 12 May 2025) is documented in NZ in that window. Note the Beehive release version of this announcement said 'two further second-hand aircraft' arriving end of May, where the House quote says three. Substance (a replacement programme delivering aircraft) holds; the specific dates were overstated.

statement: By 2026, there will be 20,000 more New Zealanders on jobseeker support than there would have been otherwise.
criterion: MSD jobseeker support recipient counts for 2026 compared with the Budget 2024 (BEFU 2024) forecast track for benefit recipients; true if the 2026 count exceeds that forecast by roughly 20,000 or more, false if it comes in at or below the earlier forecast.
reasoning: MSD's Benefit Fact Sheets record 218,481 people on Jobseeker Support at end-June 2026 (216,009 June 2025; 223,512 in the December 2025 quarter). The BEFU 2024 forecast track had Jobseeker peaking at ~202,000 in January 2025 and declining to ~180,400 by June 2028, which puts the forecast for 2026 in the low 190,000s — actuals exceed that track by roughly 25,000, and exceed even the forecast peak by 16,500. The criterion's threshold (roughly 20,000 or more above the BEFU 2024 forecast) is met. Caveat: the criterion tests a forecast gap, not causation, so the 'than there would have been otherwise' attribution to government policy is not itself demonstrated — the labour-market downturn also drove the overshoot.

statement: The truth is that under the original OBEGAL measure, New Zealand will not reach surplus in its forecast period.
criterion: Treasury forecasts and subsequent Financial Statements of the Government for the BPS 2025 forecast years through to 2028/29; true if OBEGAL including ACC remains in deficit in every year of that period, false if a surplus on the original measure is forecast or recorded in any of those years.
reasoning: At HYEFU 2024 (the BPS 2025 basis) OBEGAL including ACC was forecast in deficit in every year to 2028/29, with ACC contributing roughly $3-4bn a year of deficit; only the new OBEGALx measure reached surplus. That still holds at the latest update: Budget 2026 forecasts OBEGALx returning to surplus at $2.6bn (0.5% of GDP) in 2028/29, but on the original OBEGAL measure including ACC a surplus is not reached until 2029/30 — one year beyond the BPS 2025 forecast period. Recorded outturns so far are deficits (2024/25 OBEGALx deficit $9.3bn; OBEGAL including ACC larger). Two of the five years are recorded; 2026/27-2028/29 rest on current Treasury forecasts and the 2028/29 margin is thin, so the verdict could change before the 2029-10-31 resolve date.

statement: Look, I understand that it’s likely that this bill will go through its third reading, as it passed the second reading, and so I am just acknowledging the nuances and reinforcing the very reasons that in the second reading, we did not support this bill, for the reasons that I will outline.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill; true if the third reading is agreed to, false if the bill is defeated or fails to complete its third reading.
reasoning: The Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill was agreed to at its third reading on 12 March 2025 — the same sitting in which Nimon spoke — by 63 votes to 60, with National and ACT opposed and NZ First supporting alongside the opposition parties. It received royal assent on 13 March 2025 as the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 8), in force 14 March 2025. The bill completed its third reading, so the criterion's 'true' condition is satisfied.

statement: But my colleague the Hon Deborah Russell, in a subsequent contribution, will come back and remind the Minister exactly what questions were being asked.
criterion: Hansard for the remainder of the committee stage of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2024–25, Emergency Response, and Remedial Measures) Bill; true if Deborah Russell speaks again and restates the questions on clauses 20/30, false if she does not return to them.
reasoning: Hansard for the remainder of that committee stage shows Deborah Russell speaking again immediately after Woods. In the project's scraped Hansard for 13 March 2025, Woods' remark is in window 2025-03-13#4; the next window (#5) contains Russell restating the deduction question to the Minister ('In order to deduct an expense, it has to be incurred either in the conduct of a business or because it's an earning income... You've got to have that nexus with income, and those are the actual words in the Income Tax Act') and the Minister (Simon Watts) replying 'this new section DB 69 inserted by clause 30, in regards to deduction, supplements the general provision which the member has noted'. Watts also remarks 'I actually said that twice when I got asked the same question in prior sessions on the same point', consistent with questions being re-put. Caveat: the live Hansard (hansard.parliament.nz / parliament.nz) is a JS app behind Radware bot protection — it returns 404/403 to automated fetch and its text is not in the search index — so the verification rests on the repo's scraped copy of that sitting day (attribute-extraction/hansard_scores_v3.jsonl, windows 2025-03-13#4 and #5). Clause 30 is directly evidenced; clause 20 is not separately evidenced in the extracted statements (clauses 21, 23, 30, 31/32, 53B and subpart FP are), so the 'clauses 20/30' pair is only half confirmed, but Russell did return and restate the questions.

statement: This legislation—what’s going to be formed later in 2025—is something this report will inform, so we’re really happy that the recommendations and the guiding principles and objectives that have been put forward will help that piece of legislation.
criterion: Parliamentary bills register (bills.parliament.nz) and Government legislation programme: true if a climate adaptation framework bill was introduced to the House during calendar 2025; false if no such bill was introduced by 31 December 2025.
reasoning: No climate adaptation framework bill was introduced to the House during calendar 2025. What 2025 produced was policy, not legislation: the National Adaptation Framework, a four-page document released by Climate Change Minister Simon Watts on 17 October 2025, which set out roles and responsibilities and signalled that the Climate Change Response Act would be amended later. The bill itself — the Climate Change Response Amendment Bill, which requires regional councils to identify priority areas and city/district councils to prepare 30-year adaptation plans — was introduced on 15 July 2026, more than six months after the criterion's 31 December 2025 cut-off (and the responsible minister said in July 2026 it was unlikely to pass before the election). Legislation had been signalled for 'early 2025' as far back as May 2024, so the slip is against the government's own stated timetable, not just Arbuckle's. Disconfirming check: the other 2025 bills in this space are not adaptation framework bills — the Natural Environment Bill and Planning Bill (introduced 9 December 2025) are RMA replacements, and the Climate Change Response (2050 Target and Other Matters) Amendment Bill concerns the emissions target.

statement: Ensuring that assets are priced according to the associated risk—really what we’re talking about here is physical assets; homes and businesses—and if I look at my electorate of Northcote, there are areas where the insurance premiums are going to go up. They’ve already gone up but they will go up to such a high rate that it makes them uninsurable.
criterion: Insurance Council of NZ / insurer disclosures and Reserve Bank insurance-retreat monitoring for flood-prone North Shore (Wairau Valley / Northcote) residential properties; true if by the resolve-by date insurers have withdrawn or priced out full flood cover for identifiable residential areas in the Northcote electorate, false if flood cover remains generally available at commercially normal premiums.
reasoning: The resolve-by date is 31 December 2032; today is 28 September 2026, so the prediction has more than six years to run and cannot be graded. State of play so far: insurance retreat is a live and worsening phenomenon in New Zealand — the Reserve Bank's May 2026 Financial Stability Report put insurance affordability, underinsurance and retreat from flood-exposed areas on its risk register, and AA Insurance halted new home/landlord policies for the Westport postcode (7825) at the end of 2025. But nothing found shows insurers withdrawing or pricing out full flood cover for identifiable residential areas in the Northcote electorate (Wairau Valley included); cover there still appears generally available, with premiums rising rather than withdrawn. So the specific condition in the criterion is not yet met, and the window remains open.

statement: But I’m really looking forward to this framework and the legislation that will be brought by Minister Simon Watts.
criterion: Parliamentary bills register: true if a climate adaptation framework bill is introduced by the Minister of Climate Change before the end of the 2023-2026 parliamentary term, false if no such bill is introduced by then.
reasoning: The Climate Change Response Amendment Bill was introduced to Parliament on 15 July 2026 with Climate Change Minister Simon Watts as the minister in charge. Watts said it "delivers one of the key actions under our National Adaptation Framework"; it requires councils to prepare 30-year adaptation plans for high-risk communities. Introduction happened before the end of the 2023-2026 term (7 Nov 2026), which is exactly what the criterion requires. Disconfirming check: no evidence another minister carried it, and no evidence the adaptation framework was abandoned. Outside the criterion, Watts has said the bill is unlikely to pass before the election and cost-sharing decisions are deferred to the next term, but the criterion asks only about introduction.

statement: Forecasters expect the economy to continue picking up over 2025, but the journey could be a little bumpy.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases for the four quarters of calendar 2025: true if annual growth over 2025 is positive and the quarterly path is generally stronger than 2024; false if the economy records renewed contraction such that 2025 annual growth is flat or negative.
reasoning: Stats NZ quarterly GDP for 2025: +0.9% (March), -1.0% (June), +1.1% (September), +0.2% (December). Year ended December 2025 was +1.3% on a year-earlier basis and +0.2% on an annual average basis - the first annual growth since the year ending September 2024 - against -0.5%/-0.6% annual average for 2024, whose path included -1.1% in September 2024. So annual 2025 growth is positive and the quarterly path is generally stronger than 2024: the criterion's true condition holds and its false condition (flat or negative 2025 annual growth) does not. Noting for the record that the "a little bumpy" hedge absorbed a lot: the June 2025 quarter's 1.0% contraction was well below market forecasts (~-0.3%), and the +0.2% annual average is only marginally above flat.

statement: Negotiators will have their first discussions this week and they will start to exchange texts in the coming months, and I expect the first in-person negotiations to take place in New Zealand next month.
criterion: MFAT negotiation round announcements and media reports: true if the first in-person negotiating round was held in New Zealand during April 2025; false if it was held elsewhere (e.g. New Delhi) or occurred outside that month.
reasoning: MFAT's own NZ-India FTA negotiation timeline records that April 2025 contained only virtual negotiator discussions plus McClay launching public consultation - no in-person round. The first in-person round was held in New Delhi from 5-9 May 2025, confirmed by Indian government and media reports of its conclusion. The first round hosted in New Zealand was round three (Queenstown, 15-19 September 2025). The criterion names precisely this outcome - held elsewhere (e.g. New Delhi) or outside April - as false. The earlier parts of the quote (virtual talks starting that week, text exchange in following months) did hold, but the specific prediction being scored - first in-person negotiations in New Zealand next month - did not.

statement: In fact, what we will see is again State house sell-offs, and I know because I’ve spoken to constituents who have had KO visiting them.
criterion: Kāinga Ora annual report / public announcements of housing asset disposals: true if Kāinga Ora sells State houses as a deliberate programme in the period following March 2025, false if no such sales programme occurs.
reasoning: Kāinga Ora ran an explicit state-house disposal programme in the period following March 2025. Newsroom (1 Apr 2025) reports CEO Matt Crockett saying exiting 900 houses in the coming year was "a quite explicit part of the reset", with proceeds redeployed to renewals, and sales already under way in Point Chevalier, Remuera and Ellerslie; Housing Minister Chris Bishop endorsed the approach. The programme formally ran July 2025 – June 2026 (~900 homes, est. $400–500m), and by May 2026 Kāinga Ora had sold about 777 homes for $330m, of which 256 ($179m) were in Auckland. No evidence of the programme being halted or reversed. The criterion's true leg — a deliberate sales programme after March 2025 — is squarely met.

statement: We expect Police to be ready to implement the bill by the end of this year, once it becomes an Act.
criterion: NZ Police and Ministry of Transport statements and the drug-driving regulations/device approval notices; true if Police were ready to commence (or had commenced) roadside oral fluid testing by 31 December 2025, false if readiness or roll-out slipped into 2026 or later.
reasoning: The Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 received royal assent 29 March 2025 and came into force 15 December 2025. Police procured devices (Securetec DrugWipe 3 S via Pathtech) and commenced random roadside oral fluid testing in the Wellington region on 15 December 2025 — i.e. Police had commenced testing before 31 December 2025, satisfying the criterion's true leg as written. The first driver failed a test in Wellington in December 2025. Caveat against the criterion's false leg: national availability was staged, with the roll-out reaching all of Police nationwide by mid-2026. That was the announced plan rather than slippage in readiness, and Bishop's claim was specifically that Police would be "ready to implement the bill by the end of this year" — in the same speech he noted procurement, device approval, lab services and officer training had still to happen "before it is rolled out". Readiness and commencement both landed inside 2025, so correct, with the staged national coverage noted.

statement: Some have been traversed tonight; some, I’m sure, will be brought up by other members.
criterion: Hansard record of the remainder of the third reading debate on the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill: true if subsequent speakers raise issues beyond those already canvassed, false if no further member raises such issues.
reasoning: Checked directly against the criterion's named source: the corrected daily Hansard for Tuesday 25 March 2025 (Volume 782), Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill — Third Reading, pp. 9777–9789. Luxton (ACT) spoke at p. 9782 and said the line in question. Seven members spoke after him before the debate was interrupted at 9.57pm: Andy Foster (NZ First), Ricardo Menéndez March (Green), Dan Bidois (National), Hon Ginny Andersen (Labour), Stuart Smith (National), Shanan Halbert (Labour) and Tom Rutherford (National). They raised issues beyond what Luxton had canvassed, including the 12-hour stand-down persisting even after a negative lab test and prescription medicines (Foster); medicinal cannabis returning positives with no impairment, and disproportionate targeting of Māori and Pacific communities (Menéndez March); ESR/lab funding, CBD and tramadol/opioid family detection, and effects on prescribing (Andersen); and impacts on Māori, Pasifika and young people plus the absent 20-minute detention limit (Halbert). Bidois explicitly acknowledged "there were many issues that have been raised in the last few speeches." The false leg — no further member raising such issues — is not met.

statement: This legislation passing—if not tonight, then tomorrow—will be a further step towards ensuring that roads are safe and that communities are protected.
criterion: The Hansard third reading record for the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passed its third reading on 25 or 26 March 2025; false if the third reading was not completed by 26 March 2025 or the bill was defeated.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill completed its third reading on 25 or 26 March 2025. Hansard records the third reading debate spanning the sitting of 25 March into 26 March 2025 (HansDeb_20250325_20250326_04), and 1News reported on 26 March 2025 that the bill passed its third reading with National, ACT, NZ First and Labour in support (Greens and Te Pati Maori opposed). It received assent as the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 12), in force from 29 March 2025. Utikere's 'if not tonight, then tomorrow' is exactly what happened.

statement: Those days are over, and anyone driving while impaired can expect to get caught and face the consequences.
criterion: NZ Police roadside oral fluid testing statistics for the first 12 months of operation; true if a substantial testing programme is running with impaired drivers regularly detected and penalised, false if testing is not rolled out, is minimal in volume, or detections are negligible.
reasoning: The criterion names NZ Police roadside oral fluid testing statistics for the first 12 months of operation. Testing started in the Wellington District on 15 December 2025 and only reached nationwide coverage on 1 July 2026, so the first 12 months of operation do not close until mid-December 2026 (and the 50,000-test annual requirement under the Road Policing Investment Programme runs to 30 June 2027); the resolve-by date is 2027-06-30. Interim police data for 15 Dec 2025 - 30 Jun 2026: 4,145 tests, 136 positive roadside screens (3.3% positivity), 126 lab-confirmed detections, 102 infringement notices for positive tests plus 37 for refusing a screening test and 16 for refusing a saliva sample. So the programme is rolled out and detections are non-negligible, but volume so far is roughly a tenth of the annual test target, and the criterion's 12-month window has not closed.

statement: So you’ve got yourself into a right bind here because that’s going to happen a lot and I’m wondering if that’s really why you’ve done this protection orders.
criterion: Ministry of Justice / Department of Corrections sentencing statistics on section 106 discharges without conviction: true if the number or rate of discharges without conviction rises materially (outside normal year-to-year variation) in the first full year after the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act's discount caps commence; false if the rate is flat or falls.
reasoning: The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 discount caps commenced 29 June 2025, so the first full year after commencement is the financial year ending 30 June 2026, and the Ministry of Justice published that release (including the named 'Discharge without conviction' data table) on 17 September 2026. I located the exact table (55Qg1l_Discharge-without-conviction_June-2026_v1.0.xlsx) but could not extract its values - it is a binary spreadsheet and this session had no spreadsheet/scripting tooling available - and no news, law-media or research source reports the FY2025/26 discharge-without-conviction count. The only readable evidence for that year is MoJ's narrative summary, which says sentencing outcomes were 'similar to last year' and the proportion of people convicted was 75% versus 76% the prior year (part of a slow multi-year drift from 79%); that proxy is far too coarse to detect a movement in roughly two thousand discharges out of 221,204 finalised charges, so it cannot decide the criterion either way. Note this is a tooling limit, not genuine unavailability: the figure is obtainable by opening the published MoJ table. Webb's underlying concern is on the record - he predicted the caps would push judges toward discharges without conviction.

statement: This sentencing reform bill is going to result in more people being funnelled into our prisons and it does not make our communities any safer.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster and the Justice sector prison population forecast after the Act's commencement; true if the muster rises materially above the pre-commencement trend, false if it is flat or falls. The safety leg resolves on Police victimisation / NZ Crime and Victims Survey violent-crime rates over the same period.
reasoning: Prison leg holds; safety leg is contradicted by the data the criterion names. The Act commenced 29 June 2025. Muster: 10,783 at 30 June 2025 → 11,256 at 30 June 2026 (World Prison Brief, from Corrections), a record, so not 'flat or falls'. The June 2026 Justice Sector Projections explicitly name the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act (with the Crimes Amendment Bill and three strikes) as meaning 'more people will receive prison sentences, and for longer terms', projecting 11,240 (Feb 2026) → 15,200 by June 2036, with sentenced up 26% to 8,300. Disconfirming check: the *rate* of muster growth actually slowed in the first post-Act year (+473, versus roughly +1,000/yr over the preceding two years — 9,294 in Feb 2024 to 11,240 in Feb 2026), and the growth was compositional (sentenced up, remand flat/slightly down), so 'materially above the pre-commencement trend' is only partly met. Safety leg fails as written: NZCVS (released 20 Mar 2026, covering Oct 2024–Oct 2025) has violent-offence victimisation at 3% of adults vs 4% in 2024 and 2018, and interpersonal violence 5% vs 7% in 2018 — the lowest since the survey began; the May 2026 quarterly violent-crime release puts victims at 156,000 in the 12 months to May 2026 against the 185,000 October 2023 baseline, 29,000 fewer. Attribution of that fall to the Act is not established (the decline predates commencement), but the criterion asks only whether rates fell over the period, and they did. Full post-Act NZCVS cycle lands in 2027; the prison leg is effectively settled.

statement: The IMF is forecasting growth in the New Zealand economy of 1.4 percent in 2025, rising to 2.7 percent next year.
criterion: Stats NZ annual real GDP growth for calendar 2025 and 2026 (and IMF WEO outturn estimates): true if 2025 growth lands near 1.4% and 2026 near 2.7% (within roughly half a percentage point); false if outturns are materially below or above those figures.
reasoning: Willis reported the IMF forecast accurately — the IMF's Staff Concluding Statement of the 2025 Article IV mission (12 March 2025) projected 'real GDP growth ... to rebound to 1.4 percent y/y in 2025 and 2.7 percent y/y in 2026'. But the criterion resolves on outturns, and the 2025 outturn is far below: full-year real GDP growth for calendar 2025 was 0.2% (up from −0.3% in 2024), and the IMF's 2026 Article IV (Aug 2026) states 'Real GDP is estimated to have expanded by 0.2 percent in 2025'. That is 1.2pp below 1.4%, well outside the criterion's ±0.5pp band, so the 2025 leg is false. The 2026 leg is not final until Stats NZ publishes the December 2026 quarter (March 2027), but it is tracking below the band too: quarterly growth was +0.9% (Mar 2026) and +0.2% (Jun 2026), annual growth 1.7% for the year to June 2026; a Middle East oil shock delayed the recovery, and the IMF now projects 2.0% average growth for 2026 (Westpac revised calendar 2026 to 1.9%), with 2.7% pushed out to 2027. Since the criterion requires both legs to land near the stated figures and one has already missed materially, it cannot resolve true.

statement: The Government is making great progress. Today the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill was passed. This piece of legislation will put more serious offenders in prison for longer, to prevent them creating new victims. It does this by a range of sweeping changes to the Sentencing Act, including the capping of total sentencing discounts to 40 percent, stopping repeated discounts for remorse, and the addition of new aggravating factors to restore real consequences for crime.
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics and Department of Corrections prison population data for offences sentenced after the Act commences; true if average custodial sentence length for serious violent and sexual offenders and/or the sentenced prison population rises measurably relative to the pre-Act trend, false if there is no measurable rise.
reasoning: The descriptive half is fully accurate: the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act passed third reading 25 March 2025, received Royal assent 29 March and commenced 29 June 2025, capping total discounts for personal mitigating factors at 40% (subject to manifest injustice), preventing repeat discounts for youth and remorse, and adding aggravating factors (victim vulnerability, digital sharing of offending, offences against lone workers). On the predictive half, one arm of the criterion is met and the other is not yet measurable. Sentenced prison population: rose over the first post-Act year (Corrections/WPB total 10,783 at 30 Jun 2025 → 11,256 at 30 Jun 2026 with remand at 41.0%, i.e. ~6,640 non-remand, against ~6,350 sentenced in late Sept 2025) while the remand population was flat or slightly down, and MoJ's June 2026 Justice Sector Projections attribute a 26% rise in the sentenced population (to 8,300 by 2036) to sentencing policy, naming this Act; the MoJ regulatory impact statement estimated ~1,350 more prisoners. The sentence-length arm cannot be tested yet: Stats NZ/MoJ criminal conviction and sentencing statistics run only to the June 2025 fiscal year, so no published average custodial sentence length exists for serious violent or sexual offences sentenced after commencement. Disconfirming evidence also matters: total muster growth decelerated in the first post-Act year rather than accelerating, and the reinstated three strikes regime commenced 17 June 2025 plus gang laws in the same window, so the rise cannot be attributed to this Act alone. Full resolution needs the FY2026 sentencing statistics, due before the 2027-06-30 deadline.

statement: The short-term and long-term effect will be more people in our prisons, which is a Petri dish for crime and criminal behaviour and gang membership.
criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster (total sentenced and remand population) for the two years following the Act's commencement: true if the muster rises materially above the level at commencement, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The Act commenced 29 June 2025. Corrections was managing 10,783 prisoners at 30 June 2025. The muster then hit an all-time record 10,881 on 24 September 2025 (beating the 2018 peak of 10,820), reached 11,240 in February 2026, and stood at 11,256 at 30 June 2026 — a rise of roughly 4.4% above the level at commencement, which clears the criterion's 'rises materially' bar. MoJ's June 2026 Justice Sector Projections explicitly name the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act (with the Crimes Amendment Bill and three strikes) as a driver, and project continued growth to 15,200 by 2036, so there is no plausible path to the muster falling back below 10,783 before the window closes. Caveat: the criterion's two-year window runs to 29 June 2027, so only the first year is observed; also, much of the increase is remand growth driven by court delay rather than sentencing length, and the criterion does not test the 'Petri dish for crime and gang membership' half of the quote, which remains unassessed.

statement: First and foremost, our reforms today, which will pass, will limit sentence discounts that judges can apply to 40 percent.
criterion: Hansard division record for the third reading of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill; true if the bill is read a third time and passes, false if it is defeated or not passed.
reasoning: The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill was read a third time on 25 March 2025 — the day Goldsmith spoke — and passed 68 Aye to 55 No (party vote, 0 abstain, 0 absent). It received royal assent on 28 March 2025 as the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 13), and the changes came into force on 29 June 2025. The substance he named also holds: new s 9Q caps total reductions for personal mitigating factors at 40% of the sentence. Noted but outside the criterion: the cap is not absolute — where 40% would make the sentence manifestly unjust the court must exceed it to the extent needed, so 'limit to 40 percent' is a slight simplification. The criterion asks only whether the bill was read a third time and passed, and it was.

statement: Now, if you’re going to make sentencing by definition excessive, by definition unjust, then recourse to discharges without conviction will increase.
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics on discharges without conviction. True if the number or rate of discharges without conviction rises materially after the sentencing discount cap takes effect relative to the preceding comparable period; false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion names Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics on discharges without conviction, and that source does exist: MoJ publishes a dedicated 'Discharge without conviction' data table, last updated 17 September 2026 covering the financial year to 30 June 2026. That is only the first full year after the cap took effect on 29 June 2025, and the criterion's resolve-by date is 31 December 2027. I could not obtain the actual counts — the spreadsheet was not parseable in this environment and no news report, Law Society item, Stats NZ release or court publication has published post-reform discharge-without-conviction figures or a pre/post comparison. Two further complications for the eventual comparison: the ANZSOC v2.0.0 offence recategorisation implemented from July 2025 cuts across the comparable-period requirement, and the long-run trend before the reform was strongly downward (3,263 in 2010 to roughly half that by the late 2010s), so a fair test needs a trend-adjusted baseline rather than a raw year-on-year step. Nothing in the reform blocks the mechanism Webb described — the Act's own amendment to s 106 (new s 106(2A), inserted by s 17) concerns only protection orders and does not tighten the discharge test. Absence of published figures here is a timing gap, not evidence the prediction failed.

statement: As the member may have heard me say earlier on, we’re expecting to see the regulations for banking before Christmas.
criterion: The New Zealand Gazette / legislation.govt.nz record of regulations made under the Customer and Product Data Act designating the banking sector; true if such banking regulations were made before 25 December 2025, false if the first banking designation regulations were made after that date.
reasoning: The Customer and Product Data (Designations for Banking and Other Deposit Taking) Regulations 2025 (SL 2025/228) were made by Order in Council and notified in the Gazette on 16 October 2025, with commencement 1 December 2025 (Kiwibank phased from 1 June 2026). Open banking went live for ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac on 1 December 2025. The criterion's true-branch — banking designation regulations made before 25 December 2025 — is satisfied; the false-branch (first banking designation regulations made after that date) is disconfirmed by the legislation record itself.

statement: That will lead to innovation, competition, and we expect that with the passing of this bill, there will be new entrants in the market.
criterion: MBIE/Commerce Commission registers of accredited requestors and secondary users under the open banking designation, plus RBNZ registered-bank and payments-provider listings; true if firms not previously operating in those data services are accredited and active by the resolve-by date, false if the register shows only incumbents.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 30 June 2027; today is 28 September 2026, so the window has not closed. Interim state: accredited-requestor applications opened 1 December 2025 and MBIE has approved a first group, now listed on its Register of Participants with an accreditation trust mark. But MBIE processed the initial tranches on the basis of firms' existing bilateral data-sharing agreements with banks — i.e. providers already operating in these data services — so the register so far does not establish the criterion's discriminating fact (firms not previously operating in those data services being accredited and active), nor does it show only incumbents. Judgement must wait for the register nearer the resolve-by date.

statement: This availability of data is going to make sure that that becomes a slick process and a more reliable one, where I can actually see what the best saving scheme is before I sign up to a term of maybe a couple of years of being locked in.
criterion: Regulations made under the Customer and Product Data Act and Powerswitch's stated data sources: true if by the resolve-by date the electricity sector has been designated and a comparison service such as Powerswitch can retrieve a consumer's actual consumption data under that regime; false if no electricity designation is in force or comparison services still rely on user-entered estimates.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 31 December 2027, over a year away. The retail electricity sector has been designated as the next sector under the Customer and Product Data Act (announced January 2026), with detailed regulations decided around mid-2026 and the designation commencing 1 July 2027 — inside the resolve window but not in force now. Consistent with that, Powerswitch still estimates annual consumption from user-entered bill details plus an average-profile algorithm adjusted for location, household size, heating and hot water, rather than retrieving actual metered consumption under a CDR regime. So the criterion's false-branch condition currently holds, but only because the enabling regulations have not yet commenced; the prediction cannot be scored until after 1 July 2027.

statement: We’ve heard—and we see in the report back from the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee—that the likely first two issues to go into force will be banking and electricity.
criterion: Orders in Council / regulations made under the Customer and Product Data Act designating sectors; true if banking is the first designated sector and electricity the second, false if some other sector is designated ahead of them.
reasoning: Banking is confirmed as the first designated sector: the Customer and Product Data (Designations for Banking and Other Deposit Taking) Regulations 2025 (SL 2025/228) commenced 1 December 2025 for ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac, with Kiwibank from 1 June 2026. Electricity retail was confirmed by Cabinet in December 2025 as the next sector to be designated, after MBIE consultation in Sept-Oct 2025; designation regulations were due mid-2026 with requirements expected in full effect around mid-2027. As at 28 September 2026 no electricity designation regulations are yet in force, so the second half of the prediction has not resolved. Checking for disconfirmation: no other sector has been designated ahead of electricity — open finance and other sectors are still at policy-exploration stage. So the ordering claim holds, but only one of the two has actually gone into force.

statement: I expect that this change will increase compliance.
criterion: Regulator (Te Tari Pūreke / Ministry of Justice) reporting on the number of non-pistol clubs and ranges enrolled and compliant after the new enrolment system commences, compared with approvals/certifications under the previous system; true if enrolment/compliance rises, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion requires regulator reporting on non-pistol clubs and ranges enrolled/compliant under the new system versus approvals/certifications under the old one. The Arms (Shooting Clubs, Shooting Ranges, and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2025 came into force on 29 June 2025, but its transitional provisions (Schedule 1, Part 4, cl 22-28) deem clubs and ranges already approved or certified to hold the new status, so the enrolment system only applies to first-time applicants or at renewal — the cohort has not yet turned over. Te Tari Pureke / the Firearms Safety Authority publishes a monthly Firearms Information Summary Report covering licence holders, endorsements and registry uptake, but I found no published series of club/range enrolment or compliance counts, and no before/after comparison. The resolve-by date (2027-12-31) has not passed, so this is pending rather than unverifiable in principle.

statement: It’s going to give them the opportunity to participate now, therefore also leading to doubling export value as is the goal of not only this current Government but also us here on this side of the House.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries / Stats NZ export revenue series; true if New Zealand export value has doubled against the 2023/24 baseline by the Government's ten-year target horizon, false if it has not.
reasoning: The Government's goal is to double the value of exports within ten years, i.e. by 2034, so the horizon is eight years away and the criterion's own resolve-by date is 2034-12-31. Interim evidence: MPI's SOPI June 2026 forecasts food and fibre export revenue at a record $64.3bn for the year to 30 June 2026, up 6%, building to about $70.1bn by 2030 — roughly 2% a year, well short of the ~7% compound growth doubling would require. Total goods and services exports are cited by the Government as having risen from $94.4bn to $114.1bn. Growth is real but nothing here resolves the doubling claim either way yet.

statement: The devil may be in the detail, indeed, but I do think that this particular bill is an example of what we should be trying to achieve on a number of pieces of legislation because, frankly, industry does not need the flip-flop of change of Governments—and we know this Government’s going to be gone in 18 months.
criterion: Whether a government not led by National is sworn in on or before 25 September 2026; true if the Christopher Luxon-led coalition has left office by that date, false if it remains in office (including where the general election has not yet been held or was won by the incumbent coalition).
reasoning: 18 months from 25 March 2025 is 25 September 2026. The Christopher Luxon-led National/ACT/NZ First coalition was still in office on that date: Luxon survived a National caucus leadership vote on 12 August 2026 and held post-Cabinet press conferences on 14 and 21 September 2026. The 2026 general election is set for Saturday 7 November 2026 — after the criterion's resolve-by date — so no election had been held, let alone a change of government. The criterion as written makes this false: 'false if it remains in office (including where the general election has not yet been held)'.

statement: The board intends to review suspension time frames again in its 2025 review, ensuring further refinement if needed.
criterion: The Social Workers Registration Board's 2025 review of the Social Workers Registration Act (or the Ministry of Social Development's publication of it); true if the review examines interim suspension timeframes, false if the review does not occur or does not address suspension timeframes.
reasoning: The SWRB's statutory s104 review of the Social Workers Registration Act 2003 did occur (engagement July–November 2025, report to the Minister December 2025, tabled in Parliament 7 April 2026), and it expressly examined the interim-suspension question. Paragraph 61 of the Final Report 2025: 'When considering the Social Workers Registration Amendment Act 2024 during its Committee stage earlier this year, the Social Services and Community Committee raised a question about the timeliness of investigations by PCCs in the context of considering a revision to the sections dealing with interim suspensions. As agreed with the Committee, this is another area we have looked at as part of the review.' Appendix One contains a dedicated entry for 'Section 57A Interim suspension of registration or practising certificate…' (noting s57A(2)(a) is overused because of the process required by 57A(2)(c), and suggesting a new 57A(2)(d)), and paras 62–65 analyse PCC timeliness including the legislative suggestion of 'setting out timeframes in the Act for dealing with matters'. Caveat for the record: the review did not recommend altering the ten-working-day extension period itself, but the criterion asks only whether the review examines interim suspension timeframes, which it does.

statement: This change will reduce delays in the registration processes for applicants seeking social worker registration and would free up the board’s appointed members to prioritise their responsibilities in governance.
criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual reports for the years following commencement (1 July 2025), comparing registration application processing times with the pre-2025 baseline; true if average/median time to register falls after delegation is in place, false if it is unchanged or longer.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against SWRB annual reports for the years following commencement on 1 July 2025, with a resolve-by date of 30 June 2027. As at 28 September 2026 the most recent annual report listed on the SWRB publications page is 2024–2025; the 2025/26 report (year ended 30 June 2026) has not yet been published or tabled, and the 2026 Onboard newsletters (June, July, September 2026) contain no registration processing-time figures. The delegation itself was also still being scoped at the time of the December 2025 review report ('We are currently working with the Board to consider areas where the Secretariat could progress registration applications to improve timeliness…'), enabled by the March 2025 amendments, so no post-delegation comparison against the pre-2025 baseline is possible yet.

statement: But when this legislation passes, we’re going to see products from overseas that are cheaper, more efficient, safer, provide a better quality of building, but also mean that New Zealand producers can access ideas overseas, bring them into New Zealand, innovate products, and actually test it out in New Zealand and come up.
criterion: MBIE records of overseas building product standards/certification schemes recognised under the Act, plus Stats NZ capital goods price index for residential building materials: true if recognised overseas products are demonstrably in use in New Zealand builds and building material prices for those product categories fall in real terms by 31 December 2027; false if no overseas schemes are recognised in practice or material prices show no such fall.
reasoning: Criterion resolves 31 Dec 2027; that date has not passed (today 2026-09-28), so no verdict is due. Interim state checked against both limbs: (1) Recognition is real — the Building (Overseas Building Products, Standards and Certification Schemes) Amendment Act 2025 passed April 2025, the Product Certification regulations created a 'Recognised Products Certified Overseas' pathway, and MBIE/the Minister have recognised the Australian WaterMark scheme, ~90,000 products in Oct 2025 plus ~38,274 more on 11 Feb 2026 across 54 recognition notices (~128,000 total). So the 'no overseas schemes recognised in practice' failure limb is NOT met. (2) The price limb is not met and shows no sign of being met: Stats NZ CGPI residential construction prices rose 1.4% in the June 2026 quarter, and BusinessDesk reported in April 2026 that the construction sector says the new import rules have made little difference to costs so far. Also relevant to the quote's scope: the recognitions so far are concentrated in plumbing, drainage, tapware and stormwater, not the structural/cladding categories implied by 'better quality of building'. On current evidence the claim is tracking toward partly_correct at best — recognition yes, cheaper materials no — but it cannot be graded until 2027-12-31.

statement: I think there will certainly be more competition, not less, as a result of the legislation.
criterion: Commerce Commission monitoring/market reporting on residential building supplies after the Building (Overseas Building Products, Standards, and Certification Schemes) Amendment Act takes effect; true if the Commission (or an equivalent official review) records increased supplier entry/competition in building products, false if it records competition unchanged or reduced.
reasoning: Criterion resolves 30 June 2028; that date has not passed. The criterion names Commerce Commission monitoring/market reporting on residential building supplies as the source, and no such post-Act report exists — the Commission's residential building supplies market study is the 2021-22 one (final report Dec 2022, government response May 2023), and there has been no equivalent official competition review published since the Act took effect. So the named evidence is not yet available and neither the true nor the false limb can be triggered. Interim signals are mixed: supply-side entry has become possible (Building Product Specifications from July 2025 cleared thousands of overseas products including multiple plasterboard brands; ~128,000 WaterMark-certified products recognised by Feb 2026), but the construction sector told BusinessDesk in April 2026 that the changes had made little difference to costs, and Gib still held ~97% of plasterboard sales. Increased recognition of products is not the same as recorded supplier entry, which is what the criterion asks for.

statement: I ask the question because Fletcher Building’s Clever Core prefab house-building factory in my electorate of Manurewa, in Wiri, will shut today, and it will be replaced next year by a PlaceMakers frame and truss plant.
criterion: Fletcher Building / PlaceMakers announcements and site records for the Wiri facility; true if a PlaceMakers frame and truss plant is operating (or under construction) at that site during 2026, false if the site is used otherwise or the plan is abandoned.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. Fletcher Building's Clever Core prefab factory at Wiri did close (announced early 2025, shutting by 30 June 2025), explicitly to be replaced by a PlaceMakers frame and truss plant on the same site — Fletcher said relocating frame and truss to Wiri let it fast-track the plant by about a year and redeploy Clever Core staff. Fletcher's 2026 annual report records that the new PlaceMakers Frame & Truss site at Cavendish Drive (the ex-Clever Core site), Wiri, became operational during FY26, with a ~40% uplift in finished product output per direct labour hour. Corroborating: in Feb 2026 Fletcher announced the unconditional sale of its Felix Street, Onehunga frame-and-truss property to Goodman Property Trust for $53.5m, stating this was a consequence of its decision to establish the PlaceMakers Frame & Truss plant at the ex-Clever Core Cavendish Drive site, settling end of May 2026. I looked for the disconfirming case — the site being repurposed otherwise or the plan abandoned — and found no such report; the Felix Street divestment is strong evidence the relocation actually happened rather than being shelved. Williams's 'replaced next year' (i.e. 2026) matches. Minor slip not covered by the criterion: the Clever Core closure date was end of June 2025, not 'today' (1 April 2025).

statement: That bill was reported back unanimously, just as this one has been, and yet we hear that there are going to be some changes that were not part of the select committee process.
criterion: The Amendment Papers / committee-of-the-whole-House record for the Hauraki Gulf (Tīkapa Moana) Marine Protection Bill: true if substantive amendments not recommended by the select committee were moved by the Government, false if the bill proceeded as reported back.
reasoning: The criterion is squarely met. The Environment Committee reported the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill back on 20 June 2024 with unanimous, cross-party recommendations, recommending enactment with no change to the protection areas. At the committee of the whole House the Government then moved three Amendment Papers in the name of Minister of Conservation Hon Tama Potaka (AP 260, AP 261 and AP 349, released 13 August 2025). AP 260 was substantive, not minor drafting: it permitted commercial ring-net fishing inside two of the High Protection Areas, a mechanism whose stated purpose was to prohibit commercial and recreational fishing. DOC officials had advised Potaka against it and he backed the change after lobbying from Seafood NZ; the exemption had already been ruled out during the select committee phase. Labour's Priyanca Radhakrishnan attacked precisely this at third reading, saying the select committee had unanimously recommended the bill pass with no substantive change and that the Government had watered down protections, and committing Labour to reverse it. So the bill did not proceed as reported back. Royal assent 10 October 2025, in force 25 October 2025 — comfortably inside the 31 December 2025 resolve-by date. I checked for the disconfirming case (that the bill passed unamended, or that the only APs were select-committee-recommended tidy-ups) and the opposite is documented.

statement: We need to be mindful, as the legislation is implemented, that future leaders in the bureaucracy maintain a sense of balance, because the fishing industry, as you well know, is a wildlife industry, and from time to time certain lapses do take place, but, by and large, I think all members of the committee realise that our reputation as a fishing nation, our reputation internationally, is second to none, and I see very little reason as to why our committee stage should be protracted.
criterion: Hansard for the committee stage of the Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if the committee stage is completed within a single sitting block without extended debate or divisions, false if it runs across multiple sittings or is materially protracted.
reasoning: The Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill was not protracted at any stage after Jones spoke. Russell McVeagh's Watching Brief published 20 March 2025 still lists it under 'Bills awaiting Second Reading'. Five days later the House took it through the rest of its passage inside one sitting block: the Hansard volume containing the third-reading debate is indexed HansDeb_20250325_20250327_36 (the 25–27 March 2025 volume), Shane Jones moved the third reading in it, and contemporaneous reporting dated 27 March 2025 says the bill 'passed its third reading in Parliament today'. WhereTheyStand records second and third reading both as passed in that same week and Royal assent on 28 March 2025 (it became Act 2025 No 18). So the committee stage was disposed of within the single 25–27 March sitting block and the bill was law three days after Jones's remark — the opposite of running across multiple sitting blocks or being materially protracted. One honest limitation: parliament.nz's Hansard is a JavaScript application and every fetch of the 'In Committee' transcript, the daily volume and the Hansard mirror returned 404 or an unrendered shell, so I could not read the committee-stage debate itself. The 'without extended debate or divisions' limb of the criterion is therefore inferred from the compressed timeline rather than read off the division record; the 'single sitting block / not protracted' limb is directly evidenced.

statement: The Commerce Commission is continuing its work to complete its wholesale inquiry, its analysis into land banking issues, in its second grocery report, and we can expect to hear more from the commission in the middle of the year.
criterion: Commerce Commission publications between May and August 2025; true if the Commission released its second annual grocery report or wholesale/land banking findings in that window, false if nothing was published until later.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the Commission released its second annual grocery report or wholesale/land banking findings between May and August 2025. Both of the first two landed in that window. The Wholesale Supply Inquiry Preliminary Findings Paper was published 5 June 2025, finding the wholesale market was not functioning well and that the regulated grocery retailers' buyer power limited rivals' ability to compete. The second Annual Grocery Report was published 6 August 2025 — the Commission's own media release of that date says 'has today published the second Annual Grocery Report' — reporting the majors' 82% national share, regional inequities, and Overseas Investment Act / RMA compliance as entry barriers. Willis said 'we can expect to hear more from the commission in the middle of the year', and that is what happened. Two qualifications that do not change the verdict under the criterion as written: the wholesale inquiry was not actually *completed* mid-2025 — its Inquiry Closure Report came 7 July 2026 — and land banking was not published as findings in the window, only carried forward as something the Commission planned to investigate further. Neither undercuts the criterion, which is disjunctive and which two separate publications satisfy.

statement: Nothing within this legislation will change that fact, and those wonderful things that the member spoke about will continue.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki strategic-partner listings and Mokopuna Ora programme reporting after the repeal commences; true if Waikato-Tainui remains a strategic partner and the programme continues operating, false if the partnership lapses or the programme ceases following the repeal.
reasoning: The Repeal of Section 7AA Amendment Act (royal assent 7 April 2025, in force 8 April 2025) was amended to retain the chief executive's obligation to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations (new s 7). ~17 months post-commencement, Waikato-Tainui is still listed among the nine current strategic partners on the Oranga Tamariki site, and Mokopuna Ora is still operating: Waikato-Tainui's own programme page describes active teams based in three Oranga Tamariki offices in the Waikato plus a strategy team in Hamilton, with current contact channels, under the $32.1m/five-year Oranga Tamariki funding. I looked specifically for the disconfirming case (partnership lapsing, funding cut, programme wound up post-repeal) and found no such report. Both limbs of the criterion hold.

statement: This bill will cause even more disparities.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki / Ministry for Children published care-and-protection statistics on the proportion of tamariki Māori in State care (and Māori share of entries into care) for the two years following commencement of the repeal; true if the Māori share or rate rises materially above the pre-repeal baseline, false if it is flat or falls.
