reasoning: The criterion requires Oranga Tamariki / Ministry for Children care-and-protection statistics covering the two years following commencement (8 April 2025), i.e. through roughly mid-2027. The most recent Māori-outcomes reporting available is Aroturuki Tamariki's second annual Māori outcomes report, published June 2026 but covering 1 July 2024 – 30 June 2025 — almost entirely pre-repeal, so it cannot show a post-repeal change. It confirms continuing overrepresentation (Māori ~27% of the child population but 57% of reports of concern) and worse outcomes on most measures, but that is the baseline the criterion asks to compare against, not movement away from it. Quarterly performance reporting to 31 March 2026 exists but does not yet give two post-repeal years of Māori share/rate of entries. No verdict is available until the 2026/27 figures are published; resolve-by 2027-07-01 remains correct.

statement: But, New Zealand, your lights will stay on because this side of the House realises coal and gas have a key role to play to ensure that we have sustainable flows of energy.
criterion: Transpower / Electricity Authority records: true if no forced load-shedding or rolling outages caused by an electricity supply shortfall occur in New Zealand through the winter following the statement; false if a grid emergency causes supply-shortage outages.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether forced load shedding or rolling outages from an electricity supply shortfall occurred through the winter following the 2 April 2025 statement. Transpower's Security of Supply Review – Winter 2025 (November 2025) records that the 2025 risk eased as hydro storage recovered above historic mean, and that generators locking in extra gas and coal buffered the system and stabilised prices through winter 2025; it reports no supply-shortage load shedding, and the Electricity Authority's January–June 2025 market review reports none either. I searched directly for the opposite case (grid emergency, rolling cuts, June–August 2025 shortfall outages) and found only forward-looking warnings plus the May 2025 storm, which caused lines/weather outages, not a supply shortfall, and is outside the criterion. Winter 2026, also inside the resolve window, saw record demand (7,141 MW late July 2026) and Customer Advice Notices on 5 August 2026, met with coal and diesel generation and explicitly no consumer outages or emergency load shedding. Note the criterion tests the outcome, not Jones's causal attribution to coal and gas — though the winter 2025 review does credit extra coal and gas cover.

statement: I fully expect, in a few months’ time, she’ll be rocking up to the House and saying that the sentencing bill is actually working better than she thought.
criterion: Hansard and public statements by Ginny Andersen to the end of 2025; true if she is recorded saying the sentencing legislation is working better than she anticipated, false if she makes no such concession.
reasoning: The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 took effect 29 March 2025, so Goldsmith's 'few months' falls inside 2025. No statement by Ginny Andersen conceding the sentencing legislation works better than she anticipated is recorded in her public record; Labour's position stayed oppositional, with Andersen attacking the coalition's crime package for not addressing causes and being unoperationalisable given police budget cuts, and Labour still attacking the sentencing reforms in mid-2026 over the projected 30%+ prison-population rise. Limitation: an exhaustive full-text Hansard query was not possible via search, so this rests on the absence of any such concession across searchable Hansard-linked and news coverage — which is exactly the criterion's stated false branch ('false if she makes no such concession').

statement: I won three seats, sunshine, and I’ve been around for decades. You’ll be gone next time!
criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the next general election; true if Mariameno Kapa-Kingi is not returned as an MP (loses her electorate and is not elected on a list), false if she returns to Parliament.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Electoral Commission official results for the next general election. That election is 7 November 2026, six weeks after today's date (2026-09-28), so no results exist. Kapa-Kingi left Te Pati Maori (reinstated March 2026) and on 11 May 2026 launched her own Te Tai Tokerau Party to contest the seat against Te Pati Maori's Aperahama Edwards, Labour's Willow-Jean Prime and the Greens' Huhana Lyndon, so she is standing and the outcome is genuinely open.

statement: We will enable them to have their berth extension and to do the dredging so that we can increase exports in this country, so that we can double them over the next 10 years.
criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise and services trade statistics: true if total New Zealand export value for the year to 2035 is at least double the year-to-2025 figure; false if it is less than double.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Stats NZ export values for the year to 2035, nine years away. Only interim data exists: total exports of goods and services were $32.5b in the June 2026 quarter, up from $28.5b in the June 2025 quarter (goods exports up ~14% on the quarter), against the government's stated aspiration to double export value in ten years. Far too early to judge the doubling.

statement: I have been working diligently behind the scenes with both the New Zealand Transport Agency and the Minister of Transport to see if we can get one or two of the off-ramps and on-ramps on the Pāpāmoa East Interchange opened early, and I have received good news that that is likely to happen a year in advance of the interchange opening.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project records and opening announcements for the Pāpāmoa East Interchange: true if at least one on- or off-ramp opened to traffic approximately a year before the full interchange opening; false if no ramp opened early or the gap is negligible.
reasoning: A ramp did open early, but by materially less than the predicted year. The eastbound off-ramp opened to traffic on Tuesday 26 August 2025, reported as nine months ahead of schedule; the full Pāpāmoa East Interchange opened before Easter 2026 (dawn blessing 30 March 2026). That is a gap of about seven months, not 'a year in advance of the interchange opening'. Only one ramp opened, not 'one or two' — the eastbound on-ramp was serving construction traffic and the westbound ramps depended on the bridge. Under the criterion, a ramp did open early and the gap was not negligible, so this is not false; but 'approximately a year' is not met.

statement: This legislation can’t come soon enough and will disincentivise those gross criminals from pursuing permanent name suppression and further destroying the lives of their victims.
criterion: Ministry of Justice / court statistics on applications for and grants of permanent name suppression by persons convicted of sexual offences, comparing the period after the Act's commencement with the period before: true if applications or grants fall measurably; false if they hold steady or rise.
reasoning: The Victims of Sexual Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) legislation commenced 30 October 2025 and applies to charges filed on or after that date, so permanent-suppression decisions under the new regime are only starting to appear as those cases reach conviction. The Ministry of Justice / court name-suppression data tables currently published run to 2025 (Figure.NZ mirror of the MoJ series, 2016–2025), giving at most two months of post-commencement coverage, and I found no published pre/post comparison of applications for or grants of permanent name suppression in sexual-offence cases. The criterion's comparison cannot yet be made; resolve-by is 2027-12-31.

statement: All of those trials wrap up in the next month, and there is a report on the results, as I understand it, that has yet to be published.
criterion: Ministry of Justice documentation of the Better Outcomes for Victims pilots; true if the Manukau and Whangārei pilots concluded on or before 31 May 2025, false if any of them was still running past that date or was extended.
reasoning: The criterion names Ministry of Justice documentation of the Better Outcomes for Victims pilots. The April 2023 Beehive announcement establishes three pilots in the Whangārei and Manukau courts running from mid-2023 'over the next year', with evaluation promised and scaling considered if successful. Beyond that I could find no MoJ publication giving the pilots' actual end dates, no evaluation report, and no status statement on the Ministry's victims work-programme pages — searches for the pilots' conclusion, extension, or evaluation returned only the 2023 launch material and unrelated overseas or sexual-violence-court pilots. So neither limb of the criterion (concluded on or before 31 May 2025 vs still running/extended) can be established from the named source. Absence of documentation is not evidence the trials failed to wrap up.

statement: There will be tens of thousands of new products available very soon.
criterion: MBIE announcements and Gazette notices recognising overseas standards/certification schemes under the Act, plus MBIE's own estimate of products covered; true if the schemes recognised within about a year cover products numbering in the tens of thousands, false if only a handful of standards are recognised or the count remains in the hundreds.
reasoning: The Act received assent 7 April 2025 and recognitions followed well inside a year. MBIE/the Minister recognised the Australian WaterMark scheme, covering over 90,000 products (614 certificates, 22 notices), usable in consent applications from 1 October 2025; a second tranche on 11 February 2026 added 54 recognition notices covering ~38,274 more products. The separate Building Product Specifications pathway (130 cited standards) took effect 28 July 2025. The criterion's false condition — a handful of standards, or a count remaining in the hundreds — is clearly not met; the counts are in the tens of thousands and beyond. Checked for the opposite case: the only 'small number' figure found is the 130 standards in the Building Product Specifications, but a standard covers many products, and the product-level counts in MBIE's own notices are the figure the criterion asks for.

statement: We often forget renters as part of this conversation, and as we see that more and more people in Aotearoa will be renting in the near future, this is something that is very much top of mind.
criterion: Stats NZ household tenure statistics (Census / Household Economic Survey): true if the share of households renting is higher in the most recent release than at April 2025, false if the renting share is flat or falling.
reasoning: No tenure measurement from the criterion's named source has been released since April 2025 that could settle this, and the resolve-by date (2028-06-30) has not passed. The most recent census measurement remains the 2023 Census, restated in Stats NZ's 'Housing in Aotearoa New Zealand: 2025' (June 2025), and it points the OTHER way: household home ownership rose from 64.5% (2018) to 66.0% (2023), so the renting share fell. The quarterly Dwelling and Household Estimates do show rented at 31.9% (March 2026 quarter), up from 30.7%, but that change is a revision correcting a 2023 Census base error (dwellings under construction wrongly included) applied back to 2018, not a new measurement — and in that series the rented proportion is increased by modelling assumption each quarter between censuses, so it cannot independently confirm the trend. Separately, the criterion may become unresolvable as written: the Government has cancelled the 2028 census, replacing it with administrative data and smaller annual surveys, so 2023 is the last census release.

statement: It’s shortly to become law.
criterion: New Zealand Legislation / Parliament bill record for the Building (Overseas Building Products, Standards, and Certification Schemes) Amendment Bill: true if it received royal assent within a few months of 2 April 2025, false if it lapsed, was defeated, or was still not enacted by the end of 2025.
reasoning: Foster spoke during the bill's third reading on 2 April 2025. The Building (Overseas Building Products, Standards, and Certification Schemes) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 19) received royal assent on 7 April 2025 and came into force 8 April 2025 — five days after the statement, comfortably inside the criterion's 'within a few months'. The criterion's false conditions (lapsed, defeated, or not enacted by end of 2025) do not apply.

statement: There’s just been a report on the news that after this bill is passed, it’s forecast that 12,000 new building products will enter New Zealand’s market. That is going to make it cheaper and easier to build in New Zealand.
criterion: MBIE reporting on products recognised under the overseas products/standards pathway, plus Stats NZ capital goods price index for residential building construction; true if on the order of 12,000 additional overseas products become usable in NZ and building input costs stop rising or fall, false if the count is a small fraction of 12,000 or construction costs continue rising at trend.
reasoning: The product-count limb is decisively met and then some: MBIE's first tranche of recognition notices under the Act (22 notices, 614 certificates, ~92,000 WaterMark-certified plumbing/drainage products) became usable in building consent applications from 1 October 2025, and a second tranche in February 2026 added 54 notices covering ~38,274 products — roughly 128,000 cumulative, about ten times the forecast 12,000. The separate Building Product Specifications document was announced as covering up to 250,000 products. The 'cheaper to build' limb has not happened. Building input costs kept rising: CGPI residential construction +1.4% in the June 2026 quarter (after +0.5% in March), PPI construction inputs +1.8% YoY at Q1 2026, Cordell CCCI +2.3% annual to December 2025, and Mitre 10 announced increases of 2-70% across timber, glass, aluminium and insulation between June and September 2026 (GIB +3.9%, Pink Batts +4%). The construction sector's assessment a year after passage was that the rules had made little difference to costs, and Penk himself moved to saying the reforms would 'dampen inflation' rather than reduce prices. Note the cost growth is below the CCCI long-run average of 4.1%, so the criterion's strict false condition ('continue rising at trend') is not squarely met either — hence partly_correct rather than wrong. The cost limb remains formally open until the 2027-04-02 resolve-by date, but 12 months of post-commencement data all point the same way.

statement: Simply, this bill provides for more competition, which means more choices, lower prices for building products, increased resilience to supply chain disruptions so we can get products from more countries, and a quicker building process with fewer barriers and faster consenting.
criterion: Stats NZ Capital Goods Price Index / Producer Price Index series for residential building materials, and MBIE/Commerce Commission monitoring of building product prices: true if building product prices fall in real terms after the regime takes effect; false if they continue to rise in real terms.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-12-31 and the regime has only been operative since July 2025 (Building Product Specifications) / 1 October 2025 (first recognition notices usable in consents), so barely 12 months of data exist. The criterion names MBIE/Commerce Commission monitoring of building product prices as the test; no such monitoring of this regime has been published — the Commission's 2026 State of Competition report is an economy-wide baseline, not building-product price monitoring. The price series give no clean read on the real-terms test. Nominally, building product and input prices are still rising: PPI construction inputs +1.8% YoY at Q1 2026, CGPI residential +1.2% YoY at Q1 2026 then +1.4% in the June 2026 quarter alone, GIB +3.9%, Pink Batts +4%, and Mitre 10 increases of 2-70% announced for June-September 2026. Those nominal rises sit below CPI inflation (3.1% annual to March 2026, 4.1% to June 2026), which would arithmetically make them a real-terms fall — but the CPI gap is almost entirely a petrol/diesel spike (petrol +27.5%, diesel +71%), not a building-products story, and the direction of travel in building materials is upward. On the non-price limbs, the choice/competition claim has partly materialised (~128,000 overseas-certified products recognised in two tranches), while the sector reported the regime had made little difference to costs. Interim evidence leans against the price limb, but the window is open.

statement: These adjustments are to help drive that growth, and I’m sure, even with these improvements, the National-led Government still won’t catch up to us.
criterion: Stats NZ real GDP series; compare average annual real GDP growth over the National-led term (2023/24–2026 fiscal years) with the average over the preceding Labour term (2017/18–2023). True if the National-led term average is lower, false if it equals or exceeds the Labour term average.
reasoning: The comparison the criterion asks for is already fully published and the gap is not close. Real GDP growth over Labour's term averaged about 2.5% a year (World Bank annual series: 2018 +3.32%, 2019 +2.32%, 2020 -0.24%, 2021 +4.30%, 2022 +3.35%, 2023 +1.81%; mean 2.48%). Over the National-led term the average is about 0.4%: 2024 -0.87%, 2025 +0.46%, with GDP up 1.7% in the year ended June 2026 and 0.8% in the year ended March 2026 (June 2026 quarter +0.2%, March 2026 quarter +0.9% revised). Trading Economics' full-year series gives the same picture on a different vintage (-0.30% in 2024, +0.20% in 2025). Even crediting the whole of a stronger 2026 (Treasury BEFU 2026 forecast 1.2% annual average for 2025/26, consensus ~2.1% calendar 2026), the three-year average stays near 0.7% against Labour's 2.5%. Nothing in the remaining window to the 2027-06-30 resolve-by date could close a two-percentage-point gap. I checked for the disconfirming case — a National-led term outgrowing Labour's — and the only years that come near are forecasts for 2027-28, which fall outside the fiscal years the criterion names. Note the criterion tests growth outcomes, not attribution: the Labour-term average is flattered by the 2021-22 post-Covid rebound off a lockdown base.

statement: Let the record show tonight—or tomorrow, when this bill ultimately passes—that political ideology has driven this repeal and that vulnerable Māori children will be the ones who pay the price.
criterion: Parliamentary record for the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading on 2 or 3 April 2025 (or shortly after) and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, withdrawn or still not passed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion tests only whether the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 2-3 April 2025 (or shortly after) and received Royal assent. It passed its third reading on 3 April 2025 — the 'tomorrow' Prime named, speaking on 2 April — and received Royal assent on 7 April 2025 as the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act 2025, Public Act No 20. Both prongs satisfied well inside the 2025-06-30 resolve-by date; it was not defeated, withdrawn or delayed. Checked for the opposite: Te Pāti Māori publicly urged the Governor-General to block assent, and assent followed anyway. The quote's further assertion that ideology drove the repeal and that Māori children will pay the price is not part of the criterion as written, so it is not scored here.

statement: Alongside these savings, the benefit of this decision is that Tīwai Point stays in New Zealand and provides jobs and economic growth to our regions.
criterion: Operating status of the NZAS Tīwai Point smelter; true if it is still smelting aluminium and employing staff at the resolve-by date, false if it has announced closure or ceased production.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the operating status of the NZAS Tīwai Point smelter at the resolve-by date of 2027-12-31, which is about 15 months after today (2026-09-28), so the prediction is not yet due. The criterion's falsifying condition — closure announced or production ceased — is already testable and is not met. As of H1 2026 Rio Tinto reports NZAS operated at full capacity, producing 165,000 t of aluminium in the six months to June; the parent Pacific Aluminium (NZ) posted a ~USD176m/NZ$180m profit for FY2025 and booked closure provisions on the assumption of operation to 2044; employment is around 1,000 FTE plus contractors, with a 2025 socio-economic assessment putting 917 direct jobs and $298m of Invercargill GDP behind it; long-term fixed-price power contracts with Meridian run to 2044; and in May 2026 Rio Tinto and Contact Energy signed a letter of intent to restart the idle Line 4 potline. Searching deliberately for the opposite (closure, curtailment, strategic review) turned up only the superseded 2020 wind-down announcement, nothing current. So the claim is on track but the window has not closed.

statement: I have consistently said that nothing about this repeal will stop Oranga Tamariki’s existing strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations or prevent them from entering into new ones.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki annual reports and strategic partnership register after the repeal commences: true if the set of strategic partnerships with iwi/Māori organisations is maintained and at least one new partnership is entered into post-repeal; false if partnerships lapse or are terminated citing the removal of s7AA, or if no new partnerships can be formed.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2026-12-31, three months after today, and the two sources the criterion names are not yet usable. Oranga Tamariki's strategic-partnership register still shows 2023 publication dates for its nine listed partnerships, and the section 7AA page states only that the repeal took effect 7 April 2025 and 'We will update this page in due course' — so the register cannot evidence post-repeal additions. The 2024/25 annual report covers only to 30 June 2025 (weeks after commencement); the 2025/26 report, the first covering a full post-repeal year, is not published. On the falsifying side the evidence is clear and negative: I found no partnership lapsed or terminated citing the removal of s7AA, and the amending Act deliberately retained the chief executive's duty to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations as a new section 7, so partnerships remain legally formable. Ten s7AA agreements plus nine post-settlement-governance-entity relationships were in place at repeal, and CE Amanda Malu (in post from February 2026) referred in June 2026 to 'working closely with our iwi and strategic partners'. What is missing is the criterion's positive prong — at least one new partnership actually entered into post-repeal — for which I could find no evidence either way. Absence of that evidence is not falsification, and the deadline has not passed.

statement: I believe it is well placed to effectively manage higher-value claims, and I expect that claims will slowly increase as people become aware and confident in taking higher claims to the tribunal, and this will also be closely monitored by the Ministry of Justice.
criterion: Ministry of Justice disputes tribunal caseload statistics for the two years following commencement of the expanded jurisdiction: true if total applications (and applications above $30,000) rise year on year after commencement; false if applications are flat or fall.
reasoning: The expanded jurisdiction ($30,000 -> $60,000) under the Disputes Tribunal Amendment Act 2025 commenced 24 January 2026, about eight months ago. The criterion requires Ministry of Justice caseload statistics for the TWO years following commencement (i.e. to January 2028), including applications above $30,000. No post-commencement application counts have been published by MoJ, and not even one full year has elapsed. Nothing found either way on whether volumes are rising, flat or falling. Note the resolve-by date (2027-12-31) falls slightly before the criterion's two-year window closes.

statement: So we are going to have to engage in purchasing offshore credits.
criterion: New Zealand government records and Article 6 / mitigation-purchase agreements covering the NDC1 period to 2030; true if the Crown contracts or pays for offshore mitigation outcomes counted toward NDC1, false if NDC1 is met by domestic action alone (or if no offshore purchases are ever made).
reasoning: The NDC1 period runs to 2030 and the criterion resolves 2031-12-31. As of September 2026 the Crown has NOT contracted or paid for offshore mitigation outcomes: it holds preparatory bilateral MOUs (Thailand, Philippines) and supported the Asian Development Bank carbon market at COP29, but Climate Change Minister Simon Watts stated in November 2025 only that 'we've got the mechanism should we need to deploy that', with no purchase decision made, and Budget 2026 committed no money to meeting the Paris pledge. Disconfirming check (could NDC1 be met domestically?): Treasury and MfE point the other way -- a projected shortfall of roughly 84 Mt over 2021-2030 and an estimated NZ$4.4-5.0b offshore mitigation cost, so domestic-only compliance is judged unlikely. That makes Swarbrick's prediction plausible but unresolved; the government has also publicly flirted with simply not buying ('won't send billions offshore'), which is the live path to a 'wrong' verdict.

statement: They were very, very clear that in the education sector, we are not supporting the investment that needs to be made in pilot training and that is going to leave us with a significant shortage of pilots. It’s already occurring and it’s going to get worse over the next two or three years.
criterion: Air New Zealand / CAA NZ and aviation training-sector reporting to April 2028: true if a pilot shortage is documented as worsening over 2025-2028 (e.g. Air NZ or regional operators publicly attributing cancelled or reduced services to pilot availability, or CAA/industry workforce reports recording a growing shortfall), false if pilot supply is reported as adequate or improving over that period.
reasoning: The criterion's window runs to April 2028 and we are roughly halfway through it, with the evidence currently mixed. Supporting the prediction: the Aviation Industry Association of NZ / Ringa Hora workforce development report finds NZ needs about 100 more pilots a year, with the supply-demand gap widening 2-3% annually and aircraft groundings/schedule cuts projected from 2028 for small operators, 2030 for turboprops, 2032 for jets; the $70k student loan cap against ~$120k course costs was still unchanged as of January 2026, and NZ Herald reports trainees dropping out on cost. Disconfirming evidence checked and found: Air New Zealand says it does not currently face a pilot shortage (ageing workforce noted) and its Mangopare cadetship drew ~2,000 applicants for 30 places, indicating supply of candidates rather than scarcity; and the actual regional service losses in the window (Originair's Taupo-Wellington in May 2025, Wellington-Westport in August 2026) are attributed to aircraft/route economics and funding, not pilot availability. So 'it's already occurring' is not documented, and no operator has publicly attributed cut services to pilot supply. Too early to call either way.

statement: But it’s not only in the West Coast; in Coromandel, the Wharekirauponga Underground Mine is likely to sustain over 1,000 jobs.
criterion: Employment figures for the Wharekirauponga Underground Mine (OceanaGold) once the project is consented and operating, from company reporting or regional employment statistics. True if the project sustains more than 1,000 jobs; false if it sustains materially fewer, or if it is not consented and operating by the resolve date.
reasoning: Resolve date is 2031-12-31 and today is 2026-09-28, so no operating employment figures can exist yet. The Waihi North Project (including Wharekirauponga Underground) was consented by the fast-track Expert Panel in December 2025 and tunnelling mobilised in H1 2026, but OceanaGold's own release targets first gold from WUG in 2032 with ore extraction from active mining areas in 2033 — i.e. on the criterion as written ('false if it is not consented and operating by the resolve date'), the company schedule puts production after the deadline, so this is on track to resolve false at the deadline unless the criterion's 'operating' clause is read loosely. On the magnitude: the government's approval release cites ~800 jobs 'in Hauraki District and beyond' over the 18-year life, and OceanaGold's commissioned Eaqub & Eaqub analysis cites 895 jobs annually. Both are multiplier-based totals including indirect and induced jobs (the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment objected to that method in submissions). Direct mine employment is in the low hundreds — 357 direct at Waihi in 2023, supporting 1,053 total jobs on the multiplier basis; current total workforce ~600. So 'over 1,000 jobs' is only reachable on a direct+indirect basis, not direct headcount.

statement: I expect and welcome an increase in tertiary enrolments this year.
criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission provider-based enrolment statistics for the 2025 academic year; true if total tertiary enrolments (equivalent full-time students or headcount) exceed the 2024 figure, false if they are flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion allows either EFTS or headcount, and the two measures disagree for 2025. Ministry of Education provider-based statistics (Education Counts, 12 months to end December 2025): total enrolments FELL 1.1% (-4,590), from 399,685 in 2024 to 395,095 in 2025, while total EFTS ROSE 3.7% — fewer students, each doing more study. The rise is concentrated in international students: international headcount +15% (52,145 to 59,890) and international EFTS +20%, while domestic headcount fell 3.5% (-12,335) and domestic EFTS rose only 0.9%. By subsector, university enrolments rose 3.7% but polytechnics fell 4.3% and PTEs fell 8.5%. Māori enrolments fell 1.3%. So an 'increase in tertiary enrolments' holds only on the study-load measure and only because of international growth — not on the headcount reading that the bare phrase signals, and not for domestic or Māori students.

statement: They have an opportunity to support the bill now but I don’t anticipate that they’re going to do so, given the things they’ve been saying, which, unfortunately, haven’t been based on fact.
criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill; true if the Opposition parties voted against, false if any/all of them voted in favour.
reasoning: The third reading party vote on 3 April 2025 was Ayes 68 (National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8) and Noes 54 (Labour 34, Green Party 14, Te Pāti Māori 6). All three Opposition parties voted against, exactly as the criterion requires for 'true'; the bill passed and received Royal Assent on 7 April 2025. Disconfirming check: no Opposition party or individual Opposition member is recorded voting in favour — the party vote totals match each Opposition party's full caucus strength, leaving no room for a split. Note the criterion scores only the vote prediction; Mooney's separate assertion that the Opposition's statements 'haven't been based on fact' is a different claim and is not covered here.

statement: If the member wants to campaign on slapping a tax on Aucklanders again, well, he’s welcome to do that; I suspect that he actually won’t.
criterion: Labour's published 2026 transport/revenue policy and campaign material; false if Labour campaigns on reinstating an Auckland regional fuel tax, true if it does not.
reasoning: Labour's published 2026 platform contains no Auckland regional fuel tax: its transport offer is a $20/week PT fare cap, its revenue policy a 28% investment-property CGT. Labour has instead campaigned on freezing fuel excise and RUCs for a full term and scrapping National's scheduled 12c/l increase. Searching for the disconfirming case (Labour restoring the regional fuel tax scrapped in 2024) found nothing in policy documents or campaign coverage. Residual uncertainty only because the election is 7 Nov 2026, ~6 weeks after this check.

statement: The City Rail Link (CRL) is the most obvious example, which spans the last two or three Governments, and quite a lot of focus is now going into getting the network ready for the onset of CRL when it eventually opens next year.
criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport opening records: true if CRL opens for passenger services at any point in calendar year 2026; false if the first passenger services run in 2027 or later.
reasoning: Said in April 2025, 'next year' = 2026. Auckland Transport's own release and independent rail press confirm City Rail Link opened to passenger services on Sunday 13 September 2026, with the first weekday timetable on 14 September — inside calendar 2026 as the criterion requires.

statement: It’s going to result in the Crown spending far less than the failed iReX project.
criterion: Treasury/Ministry of Transport published total Crown cost of the replacement ferry and landside programme once contracted and delivered, compared with the final iReX cost estimate (~$3b): true if the replacement total is clearly lower, false if it equals or exceeds the iReX estimate.
reasoning: The criterion requires the published total 'once contracted and delivered', with a resolve-by of 2030-06-30. The programme is contracted (fixed-price ~$596m shipbuilding contract; ~$1.86b total programme, Crown contribution under the $1.7b allocated) against iReX at ~$3b total / ~$2.2b Crown, so current figures point the predicted way, but the ferries do not enter service until 2029 and the delivered cost is not yet established. Interim evidence favours the prediction; it cannot be graded yet.

statement: The bill will come before the House tomorrow, and, as a result, it’s going to get voted down.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the Treaty Principles Bill's second reading: true if the bill was negatived/defeated on that vote, false if it passed or the vote did not occur.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill's second reading was taken on 10 April 2025 — the sitting day after Luxon spoke — and the bill was negatived 112 votes to 11, with ACT the only party voting in favour. The criterion (defeated on that vote) is satisfied exactly.

statement: Those students will be on campus at the start of next year and entering the workforce in 2027.
criterion: University/Health NZ enrolment records for the expanded clinical psychology internship and associate psychologist programmes; true if a cohort is enrolled and on campus by the start of the 2026 academic year and registered practitioners from that pathway are working in the workforce during 2027, false if enrolment or workforce entry slips beyond those dates.
reasoning: The pathway is the associate psychologist (renamed 'psychology assistant') one-year postgraduate diploma at University of Canterbury and AUT. A first cohort of ~20 did enrol in 2026, but began in early July 2026 — a mid-year start, not 'on campus at the start of next year'; UC's own July 2026 announcement dates the start to two weeks prior and puts the next intake at February 2028. So the enrolment half of the criterion slipped by about a semester. The workforce half is still on track but not yet observable: graduates are expected to enter the workforce during 2027 (UC says 2027; Health NZ materials say mid-2027), and 2027 has not begun. The parallel clinical-psychology internship expansion he was also speaking to has over-delivered (40 funded interns in 2023 to 74-76 against a 60 target, heading to 85 by 2027). Substance holds, timing materially overstated on the enrolment leg; the 2027 workforce leg remains pending until 2027-12-31.

statement: So we’ve seen that he’s flip-flopping on that and I can anticipate he’ll be flip-flopping on tax.
criterion: Labour Party tax policy announcements and Hipkins' public statements between April 2025 and the 2026 general election; true if Labour under Hipkins adopts or campaigns on a capital gains tax after his earlier ruling-out of one, false if he maintains that position through to the election.
reasoning: Hipkins ruled out a capital gains tax in July 2023 ('Under a government I lead there will be no wealth or capital gains tax after the election. End of story.'). On 28 October 2025 Labour announced it would campaign on a 28% capital gains tax on residential investment and commercial property (family home excluded, gains after 1 July 2027), and Hipkins has campaigned on it through 2026 into the 7 November 2026 general election. That is precisely the reversal the criterion names, and it occurred inside the April 2025 - October 2026 window, so the prediction resolves before the 2026-10-31 due date.

statement: While we congratulate the member—and I’m sure all the coalition parties will vote for it anyway, so it will go through anyway—regretfully, we cannot support this legislation.
criterion: The first reading division record for the Employment Relations (Termination of Employment by Agreement) Amendment Bill: true if National, ACT and New Zealand First all voted in favour and the bill passed its first reading to select committee; false if any coalition party voted against or the bill failed at first reading.
reasoning: The Employment Relations (Termination of Employment by Agreement) Amendment Bill passed its first reading on 9 April 2025 and was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee (submissions closed 22 May 2025; committee reported 29 Oct 2025 recommending passage; bill reached Committee of the whole House in 2026). On the party question, a contemporaneous employment-law firm note states it 'passed its first reading in Parliament with the support of ACT, National and New Zealand First', adding that 'National and New Zealand First have said they will support the bill to the select committee stage and then reconsider'. Caveat: the Hansard division table itself could not be retrieved — parliament.nz returns 404 to the fetcher, bills.parliament.nz is a JS-only SPA, and the Scoop Hansard reprint returned 403 — so the exact Ayes/Noes tally is unverified. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no source reports any coalition party voting against, and the select committee record shows government members supporting the bill's intent while Labour and Green members dissented. Note that passage alone would not prove NZ First's vote (National+ACT = 60 vs opposition 55), so the verdict rests on the explicit party-support statement, not on arithmetic.

statement: I’m pretty sure it’ll get through the House.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; false if it is voted down at any reading or lapses at the end of the parliamentary term without passing.
reasoning: The Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill (member's bill, Carl Bates) completed its passage: first reading and referral to the Justice Committee 9 April 2025, reported back 23 September 2025, second reading 22 October 2025, Committee of the whole House 12 November 2025, third reading 18 February 2026, Royal assent 20 February 2026. It is now the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Act 2026 (Public Act 2026/5), in force from 21 February 2026 — the Ministry of Justice page confirms 'Parliament has passed' the bill and that it 'will come into force on 21 February 2026'. It was neither voted down at any reading nor left to lapse, so the criterion's true condition is met.

statement: I’m sure there’ll be lots of good submissions from places like the legal fraternities that come together to put their heads together on what the impacts will be on the justice system.
criterion: The Justice Committee's published submissions list for the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill; true if one or more legal professional bodies (e.g. NZ Law Society, Criminal Bar Association, NZ Bar Association) lodged submissions, false if no such organisation submitted.
reasoning: A legal professional body did submit. I read the PDF directly: 'Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill — Submission of the New Zealand Law Society Te Kāhui Ture o Aotearoa', dated 21 May 2025, which says the Law Society 'welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill' and that the submission 'has been prepared with input from the Law Society's Criminal Law Committee'. It supports the Bill's intention while urging an assessment of effects on public trust and confidence. The Bill was before the Justice Committee (referred 9 April 2025, reported 23 September 2025). Age Concern NZ also submitted, though it is not a legal body. The exact Justice Committee submissions list page on parliament.nz could not be fetched (host blocks the fetcher), so I relied on the submitting organisation's own published copy; the Law Society's submission alone satisfies the criterion.

statement: Over time, it’s cheaper to own a little Nissan Leaf or a Hyundai IONIQ, or whatever it is people own, and that’s where the market’s going to go, because petrol prices are going to rise, and electricity is a great comparative advantage for New Zealand.
criterion: NZTA new light-vehicle registration statistics by fuel type: true if BEV/PHEV share of new light-vehicle registrations in calendar 2030 exceeds the 2025 share by a clear margin; false if the share is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on BEV/PHEV share of new light-vehicle registrations in calendar 2030 versus 2025; that year has not occurred and the resolve-by date is 2031-03-31. Interim direction favours the prediction rather than against it: EV share was roughly flat in 2025 (EVs about 8.0% of new registrations in the June 2025 quarter, share unchanged year-on-year after the rebate ended and road user charges began), while 2026 monthly figures are far higher — BEVs 11.1% plus PHEVs 11.9% in April 2026, BEVs 20.4% plus PHEVs 10.4% in June 2026, with combined BEV+PHEV share around 26-34% in March-June 2026. Nothing here resolves the 2030 comparison, and monthly data are volatile, so no verdict is available yet.

statement: More importantly, with the new management of the main kitchen preparing the meals, there is less and less and very soon no need for any kind of substitute meal, which completely eliminates the possibility of that happening.
criterion: Ministry of Education / School Lunch Collective reporting on substitute-meal (alternative meal) provision; true if substitute meals ceased to be served across the programme by the end of the 2025 school year, false if substitute meals continued to be supplied.
reasoning: The reporting the criterion names does not exist: the Auditor-General's June 2026 inquiry into the Healthy School Lunches Programme, which draws on the Ministry of Education's own monitoring, never uses the term 'substitute meals' and publishes no measure of substitute/alternative-meal provision ('alternative meals' appears once, at para 4.13, and only about Term 1 2025). The surrounding evidence supports the direction of Seymour's prediction but not its absolutes. Supporting it: the externally sourced stopgap meals were a Term 1 2025 response to Libelle's 11 March 2025 liquidation — para 4.11 records that 'other suppliers were engaged to help fulfil production requirements', including some from Australia, and footnotes a 1News item on pies and Pita Pit being served — and after Compass bought and took over Libelle's operations (the 'new management of the main kitchen') production stabilised: weekly average delivered-in-full-on-time was 98.77%, 99.67% and 99.5% in Terms 2, 3 and 4 of 2025, against production 'often falling below 50%' in Term 1. Cutting against it: the rate never reached 100%, so a residual of missed and late deliveries persisted to the end of the 2025 school year; schools were reimbursed roughly $100,000 to source and supply their own food, with further unquantified costs for additional suppliers engaged by the Collective and the Ministry; the draft business continuity plan with its 500,000-meal buffer stock 'does not appear to have been finalised until September 2025'; the Auditor-General specifically faulted weak back-up planning; and the claim that the change 'completely eliminates the possibility of that happening' is contradicted by continuing food-safety incidents — 21 food-safety investigations between 1 May 2024 and 14 November 2025, and the 1 December 2025 Haeata Community Campus mouldy-lunch incident inside the criterion's window. So: substantially right that reliance on substitute supply fell away after the kitchen changed hands, materially overstated in claiming no need for any substitute meal and the complete elimination of the risk, and not cleanly resolvable either way against the named source.

statement: So this bill will actually enable that increase in access to medicines for New Zealanders through that streamlined verification pathway for medicines.
criterion: Medsafe's medicines approval records and reporting on the verification pathway introduced by the Medicines Amendment Bill; true if medicines have been approved for New Zealand distribution via the new two-overseas-jurisdiction verification pathway within two years of enactment, false if the pathway is not in operation or no medicines have been approved through it by then.
reasoning: The criterion's two-year window has not closed (resolve-by 2027-06-30). The Medicines Amendment Act 2025 was enacted and came into force on 19 November 2025, introducing the verification pathway under which Medsafe can approve a medicine already granted full marketing authorisation by two recognised overseas regulators (Australia, US, Canada, UK, EU centralised procedure, Singapore, Switzerland), with a decision required within 30 working days. The pathway is now operational: the Medicines (Consent by Verification) Rules 2026 were made on 20 May 2026 and came into force on 3 July 2026, and the Ministry of Health announced the same day that medicines approved by two recognised overseas regulators could from then be assessed through the streamlined pathway. That disposes of the criterion's 'false if the pathway is not in operation' leg. On the second leg I searched for approvals granted through the pathway and found none reported — Medsafe's September 2026 recent-approvals list names Intuniv (guanfacine) and Beyfortus (nirsevimab) as new active ingredients but does not identify the pathway used, and I found no Medsafe or Ministry record of a consent by verification having been granted. With the pathway only three months old and the window open until mid-2027, the correct answer is that this is not yet resolvable, not that it has failed.

statement: Congratulations to Helen White, and I’d encourage Mark Patterson to maybe rethink New Zealand First’s position, because I think you’ve made the wrong call on this one, mate, and I know we can get you there tonight.
criterion: The first reading division record for Helen White's labour hire member's bill debated 9 April 2025; true if New Zealand First voted in favour, false if New Zealand First voted against and the bill was defeated.
reasoning: The official Hansard daily volume for 9 April 2025 records the first reading of the Employment Relations (Collective Agreements in Triangular Relationships) Amendment Bill (Helen White's labour hire member's bill) as a party vote: Ayes 55 (New Zealand Labour 34; Green Party 15; Te Pati Maori 6); Noes 68 (New Zealand National 49; ACT New Zealand 11; New Zealand First 8); 'Motion not agreed to.' New Zealand First voted against with all 8 votes and the bill was defeated, so it never reached the Education and Workforce Committee. In the debate itself Mark Patterson had already stated 'So New Zealand First will not be supporting this bill,' citing labour-market flexibility and an absence of evidence the bill would lift wages. Boyack's prediction that NZ First would rethink and that Labour could 'get you there tonight' did not come to pass. This matches the criterion's false branch exactly: NZ First voted against and the bill was defeated.

statement: It’ll be welcomed by the hospitality industry, which have had a very difficult few years. It won’t be opposed by workers because it actually allows them to work under the same conditions that they are trained to do every other day of the year.
criterion: Submissions to the Justice Committee on the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Sales on Anzac Day Morning, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and Christmas Day) Amendment Bill: true if hospitality industry bodies (e.g. Hospitality New Zealand) submit in support and no union or worker organisation submits in opposition; false if a union (e.g. E tū, FIRST Union) submits against it or the industry opposes it.
reasoning: Hospitality-industry support is clearly established. Retail NZ's 22 May 2025 submission to the Justice Committee backs the bill and argues it 'does not go far enough,' recommending the scope be widened. The Restaurant Association of NZ submitted in support (20 May 2025), arguing the restrictions burden hospitality workers. Hospitality New Zealand publicly urged MPs to pass the bill and welcomed its progress at every stage, as did the NZ Alcohol Beverages Council and Clubs New Zealand (the latter with RSA-specific caveats, not opposition to the premise). On the worker side, no union or worker organisation opposition is findable. The Justice Committee received 232 submissions and heard 25 oral submitters; its report characterises the opposing submissions exclusively in terms of alcohol-related harm ('Submitters who were opposed to clause 6 expressed concern that the amendments proposed by the bill would result in significant alcohol-related harm'), with no worker or employment objection recorded anywhere in the commentary or in the ACT and New Zealand First differing views. Searches of the NZCTU (union.org.nz), E tu, FIRST Union and Unite Union sites, and of news coverage across the bill's passage, surfaced no submission against this bill; the union objections that do exist in the record (FIRST Union on workers losing guaranteed days off) attach to Cameron Luxton's earlier shop-trading bill, which changed which businesses could open — McAnulty's bill deliberately did not touch trading or labour law. Limitation worth recording: the full list of 232 submitters could not be retrieved (bills.parliament.nz is a client-rendered SPA returning an empty shell, and the committee report carries no submitter appendix), so the 'no union submitted against' half rests on the committee's own summary of opposing views plus unsuccessful targeted searching, not on a direct reading of the submitter list.

statement: So anything that moves the choice vote forward a bit further I’m in support of, and I think I can say that a lot of my ACT colleagues will be in support of, because that’s what we want to do.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Sales on Anzac Day Morning, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and Christmas Day) Amendment Bill on 9 April 2025 (a personal/conscience vote): true if a clear majority of ACT MPs recorded votes in favour, false if most ACT MPs voted against or abstained.
reasoning: The Hansard daily volume for 9 April 2025 records that Assistant Speaker Greg O'Connor determined the vote a conscience issue and accepted a personal vote on the first reading of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Sales on Anzac Day Morning, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and Christmas Day) Amendment Bill. The named division is Ayes 67, Noes 54, motion agreed to, bill referred to the Justice Committee. All eleven ACT New Zealand MPs appear in the Ayes list — Cameron, Chhour, Court, Hoggard, Luxton C (Cameron Luxton), McClure, McKee, Parmar, Seymour, Stephenson and van Velden — and no ACT MP appears among the 54 Noes. That is a unanimous ACT caucus in favour, well beyond the 'clear majority of ACT MPs recorded votes in favour' the criterion requires, so Todd Stephenson's prediction that 'a lot of my ACT colleagues will be in support' holds. (NZ Herald reported the same 67-54 totals and confirmed the conscience-vote framing; the ACT caucus also voted as a bloc in support at the third reading on 1 April 2026.)

statement: But without doubt, he’s the next leader of the National Party—and probably the first Māori Prime Minister—when the coup takes place in National over the next few months.
criterion: The National Party leadership record between April 2025 and the end of 2025; true if James Meager became National Party leader in that period, false if the leadership did not change to him.
reasoning: No National Party leadership change occurred between April 2025 and the end of 2025. Christopher Luxon remained leader and Prime Minister throughout 2025 and into 2026 — he survived leadership votes in April 2026 and again in August 2026, and was still PM/leader as of August 2026 reporting. James Meager was promoted to Minister for Youth on 24 January 2025 and remains an MP for Rangitata; he has been described in commentary as a possible future leader but never became leader, so he also did not become New Zealand's first Māori Prime Minister. The predicted 'coup ... over the next few months' did not take place in the window the criterion specifies.

statement: But to put a bill into the House that we know is never going to be passed so that we can see some of the hateful rhetoric coming out, is simply divisive, wasteful, and wrong.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill; true if the bill is defeated or lapses without becoming an Act, false if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi (Treaty Principles) Bill was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with only ACT MPs supporting it. It never reached a third reading and never received Royal assent, which satisfies the criterion's 'true' condition (defeated or lapsed without becoming an Act). Worth noting on the predictive value: the statement was made during the second-reading debate itself, and National and NZ First had already publicly committed to voting it down, so the outcome was already effectively settled — but the claim as written is borne out by the parliamentary record.

statement: This bill will increase access to medicines for New Zealanders by introducing a streamlined verification pathway for medicines.
criterion: Medsafe records of applications approved under the new verification/recognition pathway after the Medicines Amendment Bill commences. True if medicines are approved via that pathway and reach the New Zealand market that would not otherwise have been approved, or are approved materially faster than the standard route; false if the pathway is used for no or negligible approvals, or approval times do not improve.
reasoning: The legislative machinery exists but the evidence the criterion asks for cannot exist yet. The Medicines Amendment Act 2025 came into force on 19 November 2025, inserting ss 22A–22F into the Medicines Act 1981 (consent by verification for medicines already approved by two recognised overseas regulators — Australia, US, Canada, UK, EU, Singapore, Switzerland). The pathway only became operable when the Medicines (Consent by Verification) Rules 2026, made 20 May 2026, came into force on 3 July 2026. As of today (2 October 2026) that is roughly three months of operation against a statutory 30-working-day verification target, and I found no Medsafe publication or news report of any application approved via the pathway, nor any comparative approval-time data. Absence of such records this early is not evidence the pathway is unused or ineffective. The criterion's resolve-by date of 30 June 2027 has not passed.

statement: Two new ferries for the next 30 years—both will move 1,500 people and 2.4 kilometres of lanes for cars, trucks, and rail wagons each movement.
criterion: Published specifications of the ferries contracted and delivered by Ferry Holdings/Rail Ferries NZ; true if each vessel's rated passenger capacity is ~1,500 and lane metres ~2,400, false if materially below either figure.
reasoning: Published specifications for the two contracted vessels (Kupe and Cook, built by Guangzhou Shipyard International for Ferry Holdings, delivery 2029) are 200 m long, 1,530 passengers, 2,400 lane metres of freight and 40 rail wagons each — matching both figures in the quote (~1,500 people, 2.4 km of lanes) against the criterion. Caveat: the ships are contracted but not yet delivered (2029), so this is confirmed against the published contracted specification, not against in-service vessels; the resolve-by date of 2030-06-30 allows for delivery slipping or specs changing. The '30 years' service-life element is not separately documented.

statement: This will allow banks to pass on meaningfully reduced interest rates to community housing providers, creating neutrality between Kāinga Ora (KO) and the community housing sector.
criterion: HUD/Treasury and Community Housing Aotearoa reporting on the CHP loan guarantee scheme: true if a guarantee scheme is operating and participating banks are documented lending to CHPs at materially lower rates than pre-scheme, false if no scheme is in place or CHP borrowing costs are unchanged.
reasoning: First half of the criterion is met: the Community Housing Provider Loan Guarantee Scheme is in place and operating (launched 1 October 2025; Crown guarantees 80% of eligible CHP lending, up to $900m including refinancing of 50% of existing lending, loans available until 30 June 2027), with ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Kiwibank and Westpac participating and BNZ committing $125m. Second half is not documented: no Treasury/HUD or bank reporting I could find quantifies CHP borrowing rates under the scheme versus pre-scheme — BNZ's own release says only that the guarantee enables 'more competitive interest rates and lending terms', with no margin or basis-point figure, and the Treasury scheme page states the pass-through as design intent ('will enable banks to pass on reduced interest rates'), not as measured outcome (that page returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; content reached via search summary). Disconfirming evidence on the 'neutrality' claim: in June 2026 Labour's Kieran McAnulty criticised the scheme for guaranteeing the banks rather than the Community Housing Funding Agency's bonds, and proposed a $950m CHFA guarantee expected to cut borrowing costs by about half a percentage point — i.e. a gap with Kainga Ora's Crown-balance-sheet borrowing is still asserted to exist 14 months on. So the mechanism Bishop predicted exists and banks are in it, but materially reduced realised rates and KO/CHP neutrality are not evidenced. Resolve-by (2026-12-31) has not yet passed, so quantified reporting may still appear.

statement: Even if we agreed, which we don’t, and even if it were to pass—and it won’t—a subsequent Parliament could change the definitions, and so the cycle would continue.
criterion: The division record for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill: true if the bill fails at second reading or otherwise does not become law; false if it passes its remaining stages and receives Royal assent.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was defeated at its second reading on 10 April 2025 by 112 votes to 11, with ACT the only party voting in favour (National, Labour, NZ First, Greens and Te Pati Maori all opposed). It did not proceed to further stages and received no Royal assent, so the criterion's true-condition ('fails at second reading or otherwise does not become law') is satisfied. Note the prediction was made on the day of the vote, so the horizon was hours rather than months — and National and NZ First had already publicly committed to opposing it at second reading, so the outcome was close to settled when Costello spoke.

statement: The Treasury forecast under the previous Government was for unemployment to reach 5.3 percent. That is the continued forecast despite there being more challenging economic times than were originally anticipated.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate series through the forecast horizon: true if the peak quarterly rate is 5.3% (±0.1pp), false if the rate peaks materially above or below that.
reasoning: Stats NZ HLFS: 5.3% Sep 2025 quarter, 5.4% Dec 2025 (then an 11-year high), 5.3-5.4% Mar 2026, and 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter — the highest since 2014/15 and above the 5.3-5.4% the RBNZ and bank economists expected. The actual rate passed the 5.3% forecast peak within the forecast horizon and was still rising at the last reading before the resolve-by date, so the peak is materially above the criterion's 5.3% ±0.1pp band.

statement: On the funding information that Willow-Jean was asking for, I understand that Oranga Tamariki is planning to publish the information on its spend on contractor services, broken down by service, in the coming months, once all the final contract adjustments have been completed for this financial year.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki website/published reporting: true if a breakdown of contractor or community services spend by service is published by the stated horizon; false if no such breakdown appears by then.
reasoning: Oranga Tamariki's Official Information Act responses page lists a release dated 19 September 2025, 'Budgeted spend on contracted services for 2024/25 broken down by category' — i.e. a by-category breakdown of contracted-services spend was published well inside the 2025-12-31 horizon. But it is budgeted spend disclosed via an OIA response, not the final actual spend by service after contract adjustments that Chhour described, and I found no separate proactive publication of actual contractor/community services spend broken down by service (the 2024/25 Annual Report reports contractor and consultant expenditure in aggregate: $12.28m, down $8.49m on 2023/24). Substance of the undertaking was broadly met, but in a weaker form than signalled.

statement: We know the Commissioner of Police has said it won’t happen this year; it’ll happen early next year, potentially, or in June next year.
criterion: New Zealand Police workforce reporting on the coalition commitment of 500 additional police; true if the 500th additional officer was recorded as delivered between 1 January and 30 June 2026, false if delivery fell outside that window.
reasoning: The coalition formally missed its 500-additional-police commitment when the 27 November 2025 deadline passed, and the target was pushed out again in November 2025. By September 2026 the Prime Minister put the count at 366 additional officers with more than 300 still in training, expecting 500 to be reached 'before the end of the year'; media in September 2026 described the government as more than 100 short. The 500th additional officer was therefore not delivered between 1 January and 30 June 2026 — delivery fell outside the predicted window.

statement: This agreement is also unlikely to have immediate commercial or economic benefit to exporters in Aotearoa, and there’s no evidence that the enforceable Investment Facilitation chapter and the enforceable bilateral investment agreement will increase investment from UAE to Aotearoa as well.
criterion: Stats NZ merchandise/services export statistics for NZ-UAE trade and Statistics NZ/Treasury foreign direct investment stock from the UAE, for the first 12 months after the CEPA enters into force: false if exports to the UAE or UAE investment stock rise materially above the pre-agreement trend in that period; true if neither does.
reasoning: The CEPA entered into force 28 August 2025, so the criterion's 12-month window has closed. EXPORT HALF — evidence runs against the speaker: NZ goods exports to the UAE were up 7% to NZ$1.4bn in the agreement's first year, dairy +15% (+NZ$128m, to ~NZ$1bn), wood +70%, sheepmeat +61% vs the previous year, with tariffs removed on 98.5% of NZ exports from day one and a six-hour perishables clearance commitment. Those are immediate commercial benefits to exporters, which is what 'unlikely to have immediate commercial or economic benefit to exporters' denied. Caveat that keeps this from being a clean 'wrong': the 7%/NZ$1.4bn figure comes from the governing party's own 28 Aug 2026 release, with an unstated reference period and no published series behind it. The Stats NZ pre-agreement annual series the criterion names was not retrievable — MFAT's key-facts page still carries only pre-CEPA year-to-March-2025 data (NZ$1.28bn, goods AND services combined, of which dairy $766m), and Trading Economics gives only calendar-2025 in USD (US$849m, UN COMTRADE), which is not comparable to an NZD CEPA-year window. So 'materially above the pre-agreement trend' is unverified; the large sector moves suggest it, but that step is not confirmed. INVESTMENT HALF — the claim stands: no Stats NZ/Treasury FDI-stock figure shows UAE investment in NZ rising after the Investment Facilitation chapter and the bilateral investment treaty took effect. Only projections (bilateral trade 'over US$5bn by 2032') and general UAE sovereign-wealth activity, neither of which is realised investment into NZ.

statement: The first withdrawal is forecast to be in the 2027-2028 fiscal year, a very modest withdrawal of $32 million.
criterion: Treasury/NZ Super Fund accounts for the year ended 30 June 2028; true if a net withdrawal of roughly $32 million (order of magnitude) occurs in that year, false if contributions rather than withdrawals occur or the amount differs materially.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against the Treasury/NZ Super Fund accounts for the year ended 30 June 2028. Those do not exist (today is 2 October 2026; resolve-by 31 October 2028), so no verdict is available yet. Willis accurately described the Budget 2025 forecast as it stood when she spoke in May 2025 — a first-ever net withdrawal of $32m in 2027/28. Disconfirming evidence, now confirmed from the PRIMARY document rather than search summaries: the Budget 2026 release of 28 May 2026 ('Government Super Fund contributions increase', Hon Nicola Willis) states in her own words that 'updated population projections, new inflation forecasts and other changes to formula inputs mean we are continuing to make contributions over the next few years, rather than drawing down from the Fund as expected in last year's Budget', and that 'withdrawals from the Super Fund are now expected from 2054 onwards'. Contributions are set by legislated formula and rise from $562m next financial year to just over $1bn in 2029/30, totalling $3.1bn over four years — $2.2bn more than the December Half Year Update. The Guardians also cut their long-run expected-return assumption from 7.8% to 7.2%. So her own Budget a year later moved the first withdrawal out by 26 years, and the criterion's 'contributions rather than withdrawals occur' branch (which it marks false) is the one on track. Remaining gap: the $32m Budget 2025 figure itself rests on secondary reporting — newstalkzb.co.nz and budget.govt.nz HTML pages both returned HTTP 403 — though nothing I found contradicts it.

statement: The system-wide boost in maths education is a game-changer and will raise achievement in schools across the country.
criterion: National maths achievement monitoring after the interventions begin — NMSSA / curriculum-benchmark or the new years 0–2 maths check national results; true if national maths achievement measures show a statistically meaningful improvement over pre-2026 baselines, false if they are flat or decline.
reasoning: None of the instruments the criterion names has produced a post-intervention national maths result. The Year 2 Maths Check was piloted in a small number of schools Oct-Nov 2025, ran Trial 1 in March 2026 (~100 schools and kura) and Trial 2 in July-August 2026, and only becomes available for general school use from Term 4 2026 — so no national baseline-vs-outcome comparison can exist from it before 2027. NMSSA ended with the 2022 cycle (maths report published July 2023, the last pre-intervention benchmark); its successor, the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study, was established in 2023 and I found no published national mathematics results from it — educationcounts.govt.nz returned HTTP 403, so CIPS is unconfirmed rather than confirmed absent. Disconfirming evidence checked: a 9 September 2026 RNZ/1News report headlined as a turnaround in international maths and science testing initially looked like it might resolve this, but it is PISA (not an instrument the criterion names), it reports maths up ONE point to 480, explicitly statistically insignificant, against a sample bias the Ministry of Education itself estimates at roughly 10-15 PISA points in NZ's favour, and it makes no causal link to the new maths curriculum or the 2025 package — no ministerial comment at all. NZ maths remains 43 points below its early-2000s high, with 29% low performers (nearly double 2003-09) and 11% top performers (about half). TIMSS 2023 (Year 5 maths 490 from 487; Year 9 485 from 482) was sat before the intervention; next cycle 2027. Resolve-by 31 December 2028.

statement: We have changed the law, and under a new law, we expect pay equity claims to come forward, sadly.
criterion: Public Service Commission / MBIE records of pay equity claims raised under the Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025: true if one or more new claims are formally raised and accepted as arguable after the amendment; false if no new claim is raised in that period.
reasoning: The first limb of the criterion is met: new claims have been formally raised under the amended Act. NZNO filed the first two on 8 September 2025 (Hospice ~750 members, Whānau Āwhina Plunket ~800) — reported as "the first claims filed under the Government's new regime" — and raised a third for more than 380 Bupa aged residential care RNs by 22 May 2026; the NZ Herald (22 Jun 2026) refers to "the three pay equity claims in the works" and to the Government's unbudgeted exposure if they succeed. Van Velden has said claims "are already progressing under the new system." The second limb is not confirmable: no public source reports any of the three being accepted by the employer as meeting the new "merit" test (the amended Act replaced "arguability" with "merit", decided by the employer within 60 working days), nor declined. Health NZ's claims/settlements page (updated 22 Jul 2026) lists only pre-amendment claims. So Luxon's prediction as spoken — claims would come forward — holds; the criterion's acceptance requirement remains undocumented. Note also that the criterion's own falsifier (no new claim raised) is clearly not satisfied, and the largest union, the PSA, has stated it "will be not be pursuing any claims under the current legislation", so volume is far below the 33 cancelled claims.

statement: We expect that there will be additional pay equity settlements for further workforces under the Government’s improved pay equity regime.
criterion: Public Service Commission / MBIE records of pay equity settlements: true if at least one new pay equity settlement covering a workforce is concluded under the amended (2025) pay equity regime by the resolve-by date; false if no such settlement is concluded.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-12-31 and the date has not passed. As at 2 October 2026 no pay equity settlement has been concluded under the amended (2025) regime: Health NZ's claims-and-settlements page (last updated 22 Jul 2026) lists only pre-amendment settlements (nursing 2021, administration/clerical 2022, allied/scientific/technical 2023, librarians and interpreters 2023, midwifery 2023), and the National Party's own "Pay Equity – the facts" page says claims "are still able to be raised under the new system and further pay equity settlements are expected" — expected, not achieved, naming none. The three live claims under the new Act (Hospice, Plunket, Bupa) have no reported outcome. So Collins' prediction is neither borne out nor refuted yet; there is still over a year to run, and at least three claims in train that could produce a settlement.

statement: Four, and a very clear claim: those who do pursue new claims will almost certainly get less under the new formula that the Government has come up with.
criterion: Pay equity settlements concluded under the Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025 regime, compared with settlements reached for comparable workforces under the pre-2025 regime; true if the later settlements are materially lower in value or narrower in coverage, false if they are comparable or larger.
reasoning: The criterion requires comparing settlements concluded under the 2025 regime against settlements for comparable workforces under the pre-2025 regime. No settlement has been concluded under the amended regime as at 2 October 2026, so the comparison the criterion specifies cannot yet be made; resolve-by is 2027-12-31, which has not passed. Directional evidence exists but does not satisfy the criterion: settlements concluded before 15 May 2025 can no longer be used as comparators (so NZNO cannot benchmark other health-sector nurses against the 2023 Te Whatu Ora settlement, where it had estimated a gap of at least 18%), the ERA can no longer award backpay, settlements may be phased over up to three years, the mandatory post-settlement review was removed, and employers may opt out of multi-employer claims without reason — all of which point toward lower value and narrower coverage. Coverage has narrowed on the claims side already: the three new-regime claims cover roughly 1,900 workers versus 33 cancelled claims covering more than 150,000. But "will get less" is a claim about settlement outcomes, and no outcome exists to measure.

statement: We saw huge turnouts across the country, at very short notice, to protest against this, and we will see more over the coming weeks.
criterion: News reporting of organised public protests against the Equal Pay Amendment Act between 14 May and 30 June 2025; true if further multi-centre protests occur in that window, false if no further organised protests are reported.
reasoning: Criterion: news reporting of organised public protests against the Equal Pay Amendment Act between 14 May and 30 June 2025; true if further multi-centre protests occur in that window, false if no further organised protests are reported. The large nationwide wave (22+ towns, Auckland to Invercargill, 8-10 May 2025) falls BEFORE Tinetti spoke on 14 May and cannot count toward her forecast. In-window events found, with their evidentiary strength stated honestly rather than smoothed over: (a) 15 MAY 2025, Parliament, Wellington - STRONGEST, confirmed verbatim by Kaitiaki (NZNO's publication, by-lined 15 May and using 'today'): an intergenerational pay-equity protest hosted by Labour and the Greens, nurses bringing mothers, children and wider whanau to Parliament; Tinetti herself spoke at it, the day after the quote. No crowd figure given. (b) 22 MAY 2025, outside Parliament, Budget day - PROBABLE but weakly sourced: the Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor page returns HTTP 403, and the Wikipedia 2025 Budget detail came from a model summary of a truncated page, not verbatim text. (c) 30 MAY 2025, Christchurch, about 50 protesters confronting Finance Minister Nicola Willis outside Addington Raceway - rests on search-result summaries plus a Scoop URL path dated 2025/05/31, because both the RNZ original and its Scoop syndication return HTTP 403 to automated fetching. (d) 16 May 2025, Johnsonville, Wellington, outside Willis's electorate office, with Green MP Tamatha Paul present - the Te Ao Maori News page gives no explicit event date and no crowd figure, and its phrasing sits awkwardly with the posted date. Wellington is therefore well attested; the MULTI-CENTRE element leans on the Christchurch report, which I could not read directly. Disconfirming check, run deliberately: I looked for evidence the campaign went quiet after 14 May. The NZCTU's pay-equity events page has been deleted, union.org.nz's surviving hub shows nothing between 20 May and 11 June 2025, and Wikipedia's article on the Act records no street protests at all; the next comparable mass mobilisation was the nationwide Women's Day of Action on 20 September 2025 (22 active locations), outside the window. Organised protest plainly continued past 14 May, satisfying the criterion as written, but it was markedly smaller and more scattered than the 'huge turnouts' Tinetti was extrapolating from; a reading that required continued huge turnouts would make this partly_correct.

statement: I think, in this case, what we are looking at here is that we have received reassurance from the Office of the Controller and Auditor-General that they are on track to ensure that they go back into that fiscally neutral environment, with no additional capital injection required other than a transfer of funding from the 2023-24 appropriation into the 2024-25 Budget.
criterion: Vote Audit appropriations and the OAG annual report for the following financial year; true if no new capital injection to the Office of the Controller and Auditor-General is appropriated beyond the described transfer, false if a further capital injection is sought or granted.
reasoning: The criterion names two sources - Vote Audit appropriations and the OAG annual report for the following financial year - and asks whether any new capital injection beyond the described transfer was sought or granted. Both were checked directly, and both are decisive. The Estimates of Appropriations 2026/27, Vote Audit (B.5 Vol.4), page 4, 'Capital Injection Authorisations', carries one line - 'Controller and Auditor-General - Capital Injection (M78) (A1)' - shown as nil ('-') in all three columns: 2025/26 Final Budgeted, 2025/26 Estimated Actual, and 2026/27 Budget. The Audit Office's 2024/25 annual report (B.28) states the Office 'did not receive any capital injections without, or in excess of, appropriation or other authority' in the year ended 30 June 2025 (2024: Nil). Its statement of changes in equity does show a $7.000m memorandum-account capital contribution in 2024/25, but Note 15 identifies that as a drawdown of a non-repayable capital injection approved back in Budget 2023 - the same $7.000m appears in the 2023/24 column - and the 2025/26 Main Estimates forecast a $7.000m WITHDRAWAL from that account with the taxpayers'-funds capital contribution at nil. So no further injection was sought or granted. Disconfirming check: the Office did get more money in the period, but through mechanisms the criterion does not cover - a Supplementary Estimates uplift (total operating 157,769 to 172,564 $000, driven by audit fee revenue) and a $1.000m In-Principle Expense Transfer approved by the Officers of Parliament Committee in March 2025.
