Two caveats worth recording against the quote rather than the criterion: that IPET runs 2024/25 into 2025/26, not 2023/24 into 2024/25 as Xu-Nan described, so the specific transfer he named is not the one I could document; and the 'fiscally neutral environment' limb is weakly supported at best, since the 2025/26 Main Estimates forecast a $(7,790)k deficit on the combined Audit and Assurance appropriations plus a $(3,940)k memorandum-account deficit, the 2026/27 Estimates describe 'a buffer of just over $7 million in 2025/26 to address potential deficits', and the phrases 'fiscally neutral' and 'break-even' appear nowhere in the annual report. The criterion tests only the capital injection, and on that test the prediction held.

statement: With these policies, we are on track to meet New Zealand’s first and second emissions budget and could reach net zero as early as 2044.
criterion: Ministry for the Environment emissions budget reporting and the NZ Greenhouse Gas Inventory; true if reported net emissions for 2022-2025 are within EB1 and for 2026-2030 within EB2, false if either budget is exceeded.
reasoning: The criterion requires reported net emissions for 2022-2025 to fall within EB1 and for 2026-2030 to fall within EB2, resolving by 30 June 2032. As at October 2026 neither budget is settled. EB1's period closed on 31 December 2025 and its final assessment depends on the Greenhouse Gas Inventory covering calendar 2025, not yet published; EB2 does not close until 2030. Interim indications, which are not the test the criterion sets: the Climate Change Commission's monitoring reports say EB1 is likely to be met, projecting 282.3 MtCO2e against a 290 MtCO2e budget - though the Commission notes methodological improvements to the Inventory mean EB1 effectively requires about 7 MtCO2e less abatement than originally intended, so most of that 7.7 MtCO2e of headroom is accounting rather than abatement. Disconfirming check, aimed squarely at the EB2 half where the claim is most exposed: the Commission's 2026 monitoring report finds EB2 is at significant risk and that the risk has INCREASED over the past year - it projects EB2 could be met by only 3.6 MtCO2e while more than half the planned reductions, 12.4 MtCO2e, are at significant risk; it says recent government actions to cut emissions are likely to be outweighed by other actions that may increase them; and it notes it is now too late to plant additional forest to cover a shortfall in that budget. It also finds the rate of decarbonisation must more than double for net zero by 2050, which bears on the separate 'net zero as early as 2044' limb the criterion does not test. The claim is live but trending against the speaker on the second budget. Not resolvable yet - and under the rules that is a correct answer, not a failure to find evidence.

statement: When it comes to the removal of NELP, which I have mentioned before, the removal of NELP also meant that we are fundamentally going to remove some of the action plans for certain communities that are much needed, including the action plan for Pacific students and Pacific education.
criterion: Ministry of Education publications and ministerial statements after the bill's passage; true if the Action Plan for Pacific Education is discontinued, revoked or ceases to be maintained following the removal of the NELP, false if it remains in force or is replaced by an equivalent Pacific education action plan.
reasoning: The NELP was in fact removed: the Education and Training Amendment Act 2025 repealed the Minister's power to issue a statement of National Education and Learning Priorities (the existing NELP expired November 2025). But the predicted consequence did not follow. The Action Plan for Pacific Education 2020-2030 remains in force and actively maintained: the Ministry of Education published the APPE biennial progress report for 2023-2024 on 9 April 2026 (last updated 20 April 2026), and the Action Plan pages carry no discontinued/archived/superseded marking, still describe the plan as mapping 'the Government's commitment to transforming outcomes for Pacific learners', and still commit to biennial progress reporting across the plan's 10-year lifespan. Looking for the disconfirming case: nothing in the NELP consultation or bill material proposes removing any community action plan. The consultation page is silent on the Pacific and Maori action plans; the consequences it spells out are confined to board and service obligations (boards no longer having to have regard to the NELP, private schools and early learning services likewise) and to barring a future NELP. The one adjacent change is to ECE network-approval strategic priorities, which did affect Pacific bilingual/immersion services, but that is not the Action Plan. Note the plan was never a creature of the NELP, which is why its removal did not take the plan with it. Against the criterion as written -- false if the Action Plan remains in force -- the prediction is wrong, and with ~3 months to the resolve-by date and a 2026 reporting cycle under way, that is effectively settled.

statement: I also think that she may want to take up the opportunity to describe this bill as simply taking measures to reduce people receiving income support by 50,000, because this is ultimately what it will do.
criterion: MSD benefit recipient statistics; true if the number of people receiving main benefits (or Jobseeker Support, per the Government's 50,000 target) falls by about 50,000 from the 2023/24 baseline by the target date, false if the fall is materially smaller or numbers rise.
reasoning: The criterion ties resolution to the Government's own 50,000 target, which MSD states as reducing Jobseeker Support from about 190,000 (when the government took office; 196,434 at end-June 2024) to 140,000 by 2030. That date has not passed, so the prediction is not yet resolvable. Interim evidence runs strongly against it. MSD's BEFU 2026 publication (Treasury update released 28 May 2026, MSD forecasts finalised 10 April 2026) records 216,300 on Jobseeker Support in March 2026 -- about 26,000 ABOVE the baseline, not 50,000 below -- and 409,700 on a working-age benefit, both 'expected to remain around this level throughout 2026'. Its end-of-forecast point is ~194,000 Jobseeker and ~387,300 working-age by June 2030, i.e. roughly flat against the 2023/24 baseline and about 54,000 short of the 140,000 target; RNZ reported the Government projected 44 percent over target. Checking the disconfirming side: exits to work did rise (about 86,500, up ~6,000 year on year), which is the mechanism the target relies on, but it has not reduced the caseload. One caveat on comparability: the MSD forecast page defines working-age benefits as Jobseeker Support (ex Student Hardship) plus Sole Parent Support and Supported Living Payment at all ages on a month-average basis, which differs from the official 18-64 month-end 'main benefit' series, so baseline and forecast should be compared within one series. On current official forecasts the prediction would fail at 2030, but that is a forecast, not an outcome.

statement: And while we recognise the financial role that the TAB plays for sport and racing, it’s crucial to acknowledge what’s not being adequately addressed: the global virtual betting market is forecast to quadruple in the next seven years, from US$118 billion to US$448 billion.
criterion: Published global virtual/virtual-sports betting market size estimates (e.g. Grand View Research, Research and Markets) for 2032; true if the market is at or near US$448 billion, false if materially below (e.g. under US$300 billion).
reasoning: The criterion points at published global virtual/virtual-sports betting market estimates for 2032 and fails the claim below about US$300 billion. No published estimate comes close to US$448 billion, and none puts the current market near US$118 billion. The one report with a 2032 horizon, Credence Research, gives USD 12,615 million in 2024 rising to USD 48,389 million by 2032 -- i.e. US$12.6bn to US$48.4bn. That is a 3.84x multiple against the quoted 3.80x, so the quoted pair looks like Credence's figures with a tenfold units error (millions read as billions). Peers agree on the order of magnitude: SkyQuest US$12.67bn (2024) to US$53.27bn (2033); market.us US$14.4bn (2024) to US$110.5bn (2034); Business Research Insights US$21.64bn (2026) to US$127.5bn (2035). I checked the generous readings too, in case 'virtual betting' meant online betting broadly: global online gambling 2032-2034 forecasts run about US$149bn to US$280bn (Data Bridge US$149bn by 2032, SNS US$218bn by 2032, IMARC US$168bn by 2032, Polaris US$279bn by 2034), still under the criterion's US$300bn threshold, and 2024-25 base values of about US$78-122bn only loosely bracket US$118bn. Repeated searches on the exact figures returned nothing. The substance of the growth claim -- roughly quadrupling over seven years at a high-teens-to-low-20s CAGR -- is well supported; it is the absolute magnitudes, which is what the criterion tests, that are off by about an order of magnitude. Because the claim as spoken reports an existing forecast rather than her own projection, it is checkable now and does not need to wait for 2032.

statement: Today, Parliament will pass the Treaty settlement bill for Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Ranginui, and of course it is my great honour to stand on behalf of the Greens to express our support for its passage.
criterion: The Hansard record and the bill's progress page for the Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Ranginui Claims Settlement Bill; true if the third reading is agreed on 14 May 2025, false if the reading is adjourned, defeated or not completed that day.
reasoning: The Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Ranginui Claims Settlement Bill completed its second AND third readings in one sitting and received Royal Assent as the Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Ranginui Claims Settlement Act 2025 (2025 No 24). The reading was not adjourned, defeated or left incomplete — Goldsmith's Beehive release announcing the third reading and the settlement of the 17-year negotiation is dated 15 May 2025, and the NZ Herald report says the third reading happened 'today' on a page stamped 15 May. Date caveat: the criterion names 14 May 2025, but every independent source puts the readings on Thursday 15 May 2025 (the iwi's own pre-event notice: 'Second and Third Readings … live from Parliament at 10am, Thursday 15 May'). Doyle said 'today', so the 14 May date comes from our corpus's Hansard day label, not from the speaker; NZ Hansard publishes straddling volumes ('Wednesday … continued on Thursday'), the likely source of the one-day offset. The predicted event — Parliament passing the bill that sitting day, with Green support — occurred exactly as stated, so this is correct rather than a failure on a labelling artefact. I could not retrieve the Hansard transcript itself (parliament.nz Hansard URLs 404'd, legislation.govt.nz returned 403), so the sitting date rests on four converging secondary sources rather than the primary record.

statement: And shortly, the hard-working Justice Committee will report back on legislation to make stalking an illegal and jailable offence for up to five years—much work to be done there.
criterion: Justice Committee report-back record on the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Bill: true if the committee reported back within a few months of 15 May 2025 on a bill creating a stalking offence punishable by up to five years' imprisonment; false if no report-back occurred in that period or the penalty in the reported-back bill differs.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are met. The Justice Committee reported back on the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Bill on 10 June 2025 — under four weeks after the 15 May statement, comfortably 'shortly' and within 'a few months'. The bill creates a new stalking and harassment offence in the Crimes Act 1961 with a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, and that penalty was unchanged by the select committee: the committee's recommendations altered the pattern-of-behaviour threshold (from three acts in 12 months to two acts in 24 months) and added doxing, firearms prohibition orders and related powers, but not the five-year maximum. The Act as finally passed (Royal Assent 26 November 2025, in force 26 May 2026) still carries the five-year maximum, confirming the penalty never differed. Checked for disconfirmation — no evidence of a deferred report-back, an extended deadline, or a changed penalty in the reported-back version.

statement: The major banks will have until December to get ready for open banking, and that means that there will be certainty that open banking will be live by this Christmas.
criterion: MBIE/Commerce Commission and Customer and Product Data Act regulations: true if the designated major banks are subject to live open-banking (customer data sharing) obligations by 25 December 2025; false if the go-live date for the major banks slipped past December 2025.
reasoning: The Customer and Product Data (Banking and Other Deposit Taking) Standards 2025, made under the Customer and Product Data Act 2025, came into force on 1 December 2025, and the four designated major banks — ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac — were obliged from that date to support secure customer data sharing with MBIE-accredited requestors (designated data covers names, contact details, account numbers and types, balances, up to two years of transaction history and statements). Simpson's own release on the day — 'Open banking goes live today' — confirms it actually went live rather than merely being scheduled, so the December go-live for the major banks did not slip past 25 December 2025. Looked for the disconfirming case (a deferral or phase-in grace period for the majors) and found only the opposite pattern: the deferrals apply to institutions outside the four majors, with Kiwibank required from June 2026 (payments) and December 2026 (other data sharing) and other deposit-takers able to opt in voluntarily. Simpson's 'until December to get ready' and 'live by this Christmas' both hold.

statement: Thank you to your representatives, who have come here today; I’m sure we will see many more of your iwi coming to this House as this bill progresses through the House.
criterion: Hansard records and gallery/acknowledgement remarks for the second and third readings of the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Bill; true if members of Ngāti Hāua are recorded as present in the gallery in greater numbers at subsequent readings, false if the bill's later stages proceed without recorded iwi attendance.
reasoning: First reading (15 May 2025) was attended by "a small delegation of tribal members" per Local Democracy Reporting. By the third reading on 29 January 2026, nearly 200 Ngāti Hāua members travelled from Taumarunui and Whanganui, stayed at Pipitea Marae, were welcomed onto Parliament and went to the public gallery for the 3pm reading; the NZ Herald reports after the fact that "nearly 200 iwi members were in the House", and Te Ao News confirms "Ngāti Hāua trustees, whānau and supporters were present in the House for the final reading". Gallery numbers for the second reading (4 Nov 2025) are not recorded in any source I could reach, so the "second and third readings" element of the criterion is only half-documented — but the criterion's false branch (later stages proceeding without recorded iwi attendance) is clearly contradicted, and attendance plainly grew.

statement: I am absolutely certain that he will manage the process of getting this bill through the committee—every part of it—in a way that, hopefully, we see the second reading before the end of the year.
criterion: The Parliament NZ bill record for the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Bill: true if the second reading was held on or before 31 December 2025; false if the second reading had not occurred by that date.
reasoning: The Parliament bill record for the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Bill (2025, Whanganui/Taumarunui iwi — not the 2013-14 Waikato "Ngāti Hauā" bill) shows: first reading and referral to the Māori Affairs Committee 14/15 May 2025, reported back 24 October 2025, second reading 4 November 2025, committee of the whole House 28 January 2026, third reading 29 January 2026, Royal assent February 2026. That puts the second reading well inside the criterion's 31 December 2025 deadline. Corroboration: RNZ's The House reports Parliament sitting under extended hours on three settlement bills with the Ngāti Hāua bill back from select committee for its second reading (quoting NZ First's Jenny Marcroft on the statutory pardons), in the same sitting block in which the Ngāti Pāoa bill passed (5 November 2025). Caveat: bills.parliament.nz and legislation.govt.nz are JavaScript shells / 403 to direct fetching, so the stage dates come via search indexing of those official pages rather than a page I rendered myself; the surrounding news record (report-back in Oct 2025, third reading 29 Jan 2026) is consistent with them.

statement: I will never apologise for what I do in this House, but I feel an apology to my people—that you will be silenced for 21 days, when one of the most ruthless legislations will hit this House next week and a Budget that will ignore you.
criterion: The House's resolution on the Privileges Committee report concerning the November 2024 haka; true if the House agrees to suspend Rawiri Waititi for 21 sitting days, false if a shorter suspension, a lesser penalty, or no penalty is imposed.
reasoning: The House adopted the Privileges Committee's recommendation unchanged on 5 June 2025: Rawiri Waititi suspended for 21 days (68 votes to 53), Debbie Ngarewa-Packer 21 days (68-54), Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke 7 days (68-55), taking effect immediately. Opposition amendments for lighter treatment — the Greens moved to drop the suspensions in favour of censure, Labour pushed for a weaker penalty — failed for want of numbers; government MPs rejected every lighter proposal, and no reduction was agreed. Two qualifications that do not change the verdict under the criterion as written: (1) none of the news sources I reached uses the phrase "21 sitting days" — they all say "21 days", and "sitting days" appears only in describing the previous three-sitting-day record, so the sitting-day characterisation rests on the Privileges Committee report rather than on anything I verified; (2) the timing Waititi signalled did not hold — the debate was adjourned on 20 May 2025 expressly so the MPs could take part in the Budget, so his suspension began on 5 June and he was not silenced during Budget week or the week after 14 May. The criterion tests only the penalty the House imposed, and on that he was exactly right.

statement: No matter how much the Government members on the other side may try to spin this as a positive thing to help people get into unemployment, the facts speak for themselves: this bill will increase inequality, poverty, homelessness, and will not support people into employment.
criterion: Stats NZ household income inequality (Gini/P80:P20) and child poverty material hardship series, and the MSD/HUD housing register and severe housing deprivation estimates, for the two years after the bill's commencement, plus MSD exits-to-work from Jobseeker Support; true if hardship, inequality and housing-register measures rise outside sampling error while work exits do not improve, false if hardship and the housing register fall or work exits improve.
reasoning: The criterion requires Stats NZ inequality/child-poverty and MSD/HUD housing-register and work-exit series for the two years after commencement. The Social Security Amendment Act 2025 commenced 26 May 2025 (parts on 1 July and 20 October 2025), so the two-year window closes in 2027 and the relevant HES/child-poverty releases are not published yet. Interim MSD data is directionally consistent with the prediction (218,481 on Jobseeker Support at June 2026, among the highest in five years, with the share of the working-age population rising in most regions between June 2025 and June 2026), but Jobseeker caseload is not the inequality/hardship/housing-register measure the criterion names, and a weak labour market is a confound. Disconfirming check: no published hardship, Gini or housing-register series yet covers the post-commencement window in either direction.

statement: My Philadelphia Eagles won the Super Bowl recently and I expect them to repeat next year.
criterion: The result of Super Bowl LX (February 2026). True if the Philadelphia Eagles win it; false if any other team does.
reasoning: Super Bowl LX was played 8 February 2026 at Levi's Stadium, Santa Clara; the Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 29-13 (Kenneth Walker III MVP). The Philadelphia Eagles did not win it, so under the criterion ('false if any other team does') the prediction fails. Confirmed on ESPN, NFL.com and Wikipedia rather than from the SEO-farm pages that dominated the first search.

statement: This amendment will extend TAB New Zealand’s exclusive right for sports and racing betting to include online platforms, but it will be a boost for Kiwi sports and racing. It’s expected that that revenue will mean more will be fed back into sporting bodies.
criterion: TAB NZ / Entain NZ annual distributions to national sporting organisations and the racing codes for the first full financial year after the online monopoly takes effect; true if distributions rise materially against the pre-amendment baseline, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires actual TAB NZ/Entain NZ distributions to NSOs and the racing codes for the first full financial year after the online monopoly takes effect. The Racing Industry Amendment Act 2025 received assent 27 June 2025 with most provisions in force 28 June 2025 (ss 17, 19, 23 deferred, commencing 30 June 2026 by Order in Council). TAB NZ's financial year ends 31 July, so the first full year under the monopoly is Aug 2025-Jul 2026, and its latest published Annual Report plus Distribution Notice covers Aug 2024-Jul 2025 (released 23 January 2026) - the FY26 actuals are not out as at 2 October 2026. Only forecasts and contractual minimums exist: racing-code minimum distributions projected at ~NZ$180m for 2025/26 and NZ$185m for 2026/27 versus NZ$125m in 2022/23, and a NZ$100m Entain payment triggered by the legislation with ~NZ$20m earmarked for Sport NZ. Directionally supportive but not realised figures. Disconfirming checks worth noting for the eventual verdict: the NSO-side uplift is largely the pre-existing 2023 Entain deal's one-off NZ$15m over three years rather than an effect of this amendment, and TAB NZ has previously cut racing distributions when revenue and profit missed budget, so a rise is not automatic.

statement: I’m confident that this bill will promote more harmonious industrial relations across New Zealand.
criterion: MBIE work stoppages statistics for the two full years after the Act's commencement: true if the annual number of work stoppages (and days lost) is lower than the two years preceding commencement, false if it is the same or higher.
reasoning: The bill is the Employment Relations (Pay Deductions for Partial Strikes) Amendment Bill (second reading 20 May 2025), assented 30 June 2025 and in force 1 July 2025. The criterion requires MBIE work-stoppages counts and days lost for the two FULL years after commencement (i.e. ~2026 and 2027); calendar 2026 is not finished and MBIE's annual series for it is unpublished, so the comparison the criterion specifies cannot be made. Note for later resolution: pre-commencement baseline is 36 stoppages (2023) and 47 (2024), and post-commencement industrial action has been heavy so far (the Oct 2025 'mega strike' of 100,000+ workers, continued health/fire action into 2026), which points against the prediction — but 2025 is the commencement year, not one of the two post-commencement years, and absence of final data is not evidence of falsity.

statement: More than 22 million commuter journeys use the train in Auckland and Wellington, and that figure will rise once the City Rail Link opens—widely supported across the House—and when new trains arrive in Wellington.
criterion: Auckland Transport and Metlink annual patronage statistics for the first full year after City Rail Link opening: true if combined annual rail boardings exceed 22 million, false if they remain at or below that level.
reasoning: City Rail Link opened 13 September 2026, three weeks before today's date. The criterion requires AT and Metlink annual patronage for the first FULL year after opening (ending ~September 2027, published later), which does not yet exist. Current evidence suggests the prediction is on track rather than failing: AT rail was ~13.89M annual boardings in the year to 30 April 2026 and Metlink rail ~10.33M in 2024/25 (combined ~24M, already above 22M), and CRL's first week set a network record of 528,007 boardings against 325,203 the week before (+62%), with the first full weekday ~90,000 boardings (+55%). Still, the measurement window named in the criterion has not elapsed.

statement: As part of Budget 2025, Kiwis needing care will benefit from our $164 million funding boost for urgent and after-hours services across the country. Once implemented, our investment will mean that 98 percent of New Zealanders will be able to receive in-person urgent care within one hour’s drive of their homes.
criterion: Health New Zealand urgent care coverage reporting or a ministerial update on drive-time access once the five new 24/7 services and extended hours are operating: true if measured coverage reaches ~98% within one hour's drive, false if it remains materially below that.
reasoning: The criterion conditions resolution on the five new 24/7 urgent care services and extended hours being operational. The published rollout schedule stages them: Counties Manukau and Dunedin by late 2025, Tauranga by mid-2026, and Whangarei and Palmerston North by mid-2027. As of October 2026 the last two are not due, so full coverage cannot be in place, and I found no Health New Zealand drive-time coverage measurement or ministerial update reporting an achieved figure to test against ~98%. The $164M over four years and the 98%-within-one-hour claim are confirmed as what was announced, but the outcome measurement the criterion names is not yet available.

statement: I would say that, to that comment that there hasn’t been enough consultation on this bill, this bill is going to the select committee, as the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs has said, the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That will be the opportunity for people to submit and have their say during the select committee process.
criterion: Parliament's bills record for the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Bill; true if it was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee and public submissions were called for, false if it was not referred to that committee or no submissions process opened.
reasoning: The Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee on 20 May 2025 — the same day Parmar spoke — with an instruction to report back by 20 October 2025. FEC opened the call for submissions on 21 May 2025, closing 23 June 2025, and received 1,635 submissions from groups and individuals plus oral evidence from 35 submitters at hearings in Wellington and by videoconference. The committee reported the bill back (version 137-2) and recommended by majority that it be passed. Both limbs of the criterion — referral to that specific committee, and a public submissions process actually opening — are satisfied. Disconfirming check: no evidence of referral to any other committee, and no sign the submissions process was skipped or curtailed; the large submission count (1,543 of them opposing the retrospective provisions) is itself proof the public could and did have their say. Caveat on sourcing: parliament.nz refused direct fetching, so the bill record is confirmed via legislation.govt.nz, Parliament's republished call-for-submissions release, and law-firm bill trackers rather than the parliament.nz page the criterion names.

statement: It will go to the Finance and Expenditure Committee for scrutinisation over the next five or so months before it gets reported back, so the work has only just begun.
criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill: true if the Finance and Expenditure Committee reports the bill back approximately five months after 20 May 2025 (report presented between about September and November 2025); false if it is reported back materially earlier or later, or not at all.
reasoning: The referral limb is right: the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill (introduced 31 March 2025 by Commerce Minister Scott Simpson) passed first reading on 20 May 2025 and went to the Finance and Expenditure Committee. The timing limb is right about the deadline as set and wrong about what happened. The House's original report-back date was 20 October 2025 — exactly the 'five or so months' Brewer described, so he was accurately reporting the instruction on the order paper. But that date was extended to 30 January 2026 so the committee could consider an Amendment Paper (covering climate-related disclosures and director liability relief), and 30 January 2026 is when FEC actually reported the bill back — roughly eight months after 20 May 2025, about three months outside the criterion's September–November 2025 window. Disconfirming check: I looked for an earlier or on-time report back and for a second, earlier FEC report; there is none — commentary from two independent law firms both date the report back to 30 January and both state the extension from 20 October 2025. So on a strict reading of the criterion ('false if reported back materially later') this fails; partly_correct reflects that the substance of his claim — FEC scrutiny on a roughly five-month clock — was accurate at the time and only the actual delivery slipped. Caveat on sourcing: parliament.nz blocked direct fetching, so dates come from law-firm bill trackers and a parliament.nz call-for-submissions page captured as PDF.

statement: But every single announcement will be paid for from women workers’ future pay and depriving people in genuine need of the homes that they need.
criterion: Budget 2025 documents (Fiscal Strategy Report and Budget at a Glance, 22 May 2025); true if savings booked from the pay equity amendment and from emergency housing form the principal funding source for new Budget spending, false if the bulk of new spending is funded from other savings or revenue.
reasoning: The criterion's substance holds; the quote's absolutism does not. Budget 2025 (22 May 2025) booked about $21b in savings over four years, and the pay equity amendment was by far the largest single component at $12.8b of 'fiscal headroom' per the Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update — Willis contrasted this with the $3.7b four-year cost Treasury estimated in 2020. Emergency housing contributed a further $1.026b in operating savings over four years (reported as >$1b over five years), realised by beating the emergency-housing reduction target early, and explicitly earmarked for reinvestment in the Budget. Together those two account for roughly two thirds of booked savings, so they do form the principal funding source — the criterion's true branch. Disconfirming check, which is why this is not a clean 'correct': McAnulty said 'every single announcement', and the Budget's $6.7b a year in new funding was offset by $5.3b a year in savings, reprioritisation AND new revenue, drawing on sources he did not name — almost $2.5b in KiwiSaver contribution savings plus more than $500m in expected KiwiSaver revenue, Best Start means-testing, Jobseeker changes for 18–19 year olds, and 116 stopped or cancelled initiatives. Pay equity alone funds something closer to 40–45% of the new operating spend, not all of it, and large items such as the $6.6b Investment Boost were not covered by these two savings lines alone. Caveat on sourcing: treasury.govt.nz returned 403 to direct fetching, so the Fiscal Strategy Report figures come via contemporaneous reporting quoting the Budget documents rather than the primary PDF the criterion names.

statement: The first stage of the Northland corridor project kicks off in late 2025.
criterion: NZTA project records and ministerial announcements; true if stage one of the Northland corridor formally commenced (construction or contract award) before 31 December 2025, false if commencement slipped into 2026 or later.
reasoning: Stage one of the Northland Corridor is Warkworth to Te Hana (26km, Dome Valley twin-bore tunnel). Neither leg of the criterion was met before 31 December 2025: three consortia were shortlisted in June 2025, the preferred bidder was named in early 2026, and NZTA awarded the PPP to the Northway consortium (Acciona, Downer, AECOM) with the Project Agreement signed and financial close reached on 30 July 2026; detailed design, site mobilisation and early construction works were expected from late 2026. Checking for disconfirming evidence: the only late-2025 Northland corridor event was Chris Bishop's 20 October 2025 announcement of $187m for design, consenting and route protection on the LATER sections (Te Hana to Port Marsden, Port Marsden to Whangarei, Brynderwyns alternative) — pre-construction planning money on different stages, not commencement of stage one. Commencement slipped roughly a year past the predicted 'late 2025'. Evidence caveat: direct page fetches of the NZTA project page and the Beehive releases returned empty bodies and RNZ returned 403, so these dates come from search-result extracts of those same pages rather than full page reads; the convergence of five independent sources on a July 2026 signing is nonetheless unambiguous.

statement: The Reserve Bank told us just two weeks ago that 60 percent of mortgage lending will reprice to lower rates in the next six months and around 80 percent within a year.
criterion: RBNZ mortgage repricing / fixed-rate maturity data; true if roughly 60% of mortgage lending had repriced by November 2025 and about 80% by May 2026, false if the realised share falls materially short.
reasoning: The attribution checks out: the RBNZ's May 2025 Financial Stability Report, published roughly two weeks before the 21 May 2025 speech, projected around 60% of mortgage lending to reprice to lower rates within six months and around 80% within a year, so Brewer quoted the central bank correctly. On realisation the two legs diverge. The one-year leg landed: BNZ reports 81% of fixed-rate mortgage borrowings repriced over calendar 2025, a 13-year high, and the average rate actually paid (RBNZ yield on residential mortgage loans) fell from a 6.39% peak in October 2024 to 5.17% by November 2025, with a forecast trough near 4.85% around mid-2026 — about 83% of the total decline done by November 2025. The six-month leg looks overstated: BNZ puts six-month expiry volumes at roughly 27% of total borrowings on long-run average and 34% in the unusually concentrated first half of 2026, well short of 60%, and relief was further slowed by borrowers taking floating exposure (a record 49% of new lending went floating in November 2025). Note also that BNZ's separate 'roughly 80% complete' refers to the share of the total fall in the average paid rate, not the share of the loan book rolled over, so it should not be read as confirming the RBNZ's 80%.

statement: Lower mortgage costs mean a boost to disposable income, which in turn will mean household spending gradually lifting.
criterion: Stats NZ household consumption expenditure / retail trade volumes; true if real household spending rises across the four quarters following May 2025, false if it is flat or falls over that period.
reasoning: Real household final consumption expenditure over the four quarters after May 2025 did not rise continuously: it fell 0.1% in the December 2025 quarter, rose 0.5% in the March 2026 quarter (audio-visual equipment, used motor vehicles, grocery food), and was essentially flat at +0.1% in the June 2026 quarter, where Stats NZ noted higher fuel prices crowding out hospitality and travel spending. The net direction is a small rise, consistent with 'gradually lifting', and BNZ independently describes a 'slow reflation of retail spending appetites over the second half of 2025' driven partly by the refixing cash-flow windfall — though it notes much of that windfall went to additional principal repayment rather than spending. But the criterion asked for a rise across the four quarters, and one quarter fell while another was flat. Evidence caveat: stats.govt.nz renders article bodies client-side and could not be fetched directly, so these quarter-on-quarter figures come from search-result extracts of the Stats NZ releases rather than the release tables, and I have no household consumption figure for the September 2025 quarter.

statement: We fully expect, sadly, that there will be pay equity claims.
criterion: MBIE / Ministry for Women records of pay equity claims raised under the Equal Pay Act as amended in May 2025; true if one or more claims were raised and accepted as meeting the new threshold, false if none had been raised by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: New pay equity claims were in fact raised under the Equal Pay Act as amended in May 2025, well before the 2026-06-30 resolve-by date. NZNO filed the first two claims under the new regime on 8 September 2025 — Whānau Āwhina Plunket nurses (~800 members) and hospice nurses (~750) — described in NZNO's own release and in RNZ/Kaitiaki coverage as the first claims lodged under the new system. A third was raised in May 2026 for ~380 registered nurses at Bupa's 40 aged residential care homes. The criterion's false condition (no claims raised by the resolve-by date) is therefore clearly not met. Partial caveat on the criterion's second leg: I could find no public record of an employer formally deciding that any of these claims is eligible and 'has merit' under the new 70%-female / 10-consecutive-years / merit test. Under the amended Act the employer is the gatekeeper at the raising stage (60 working days to decide), and no source — union, employer, MBIE or press — reports a decision either way; as of the most recent coverage (2 October 2026) the status is still 'raised'. So acceptance is unverified rather than refuted. Disconfirming evidence I checked for and found: in July 2025 Health NZ said it was 'not aware of any new pay equity claims' and the Ministry of Education said 'no new pay equity claims have been raised since the amendments', and the PSA said it had 'no intention to file any claims' under the amended Act — i.e. claim volume is tiny, which is consistent with Luxon's hedged 'sadly, that there will be pay equity claims' but does mean the regime has produced only a handful of single-employer claims, none yet accepted on the record.

statement: It is deeply concerning because what will happen in New Zealand as a result of this is that we will see more strikes.
criterion: MBIE/Stats NZ work stoppages series (number of stoppages and person-days lost); true if stoppages in the 12–24 months after the Act commences exceed the equivalent period before it, false if they are flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion measures stoppages in the 12–24 months after the Act commences against the equivalent period before. The Equal Pay Amendment Act received royal assent on 13 May 2025 (passed under urgency 6 May), so the comparison window runs to roughly May 2027, and the stated resolve-by date is 2027-06-30 — eight months after today (2026-10-02). The window has not closed. Separately, the data the criterion names does not yet exist for that window: Employment New Zealand's 'Annual work stoppages' table (sourced from Stats NZ and MBIE) still ends at the part-year '2025 to 26 Sep' (22 stoppages, 18,035 employees involved, 16,942 person-days lost, $4.6m), with no 2026 row at all, even though other tables on the same page run to 30 June 2026. For reference the pre-Act years are 2024: 47 stoppages / 11,827 person-days; 2023: 36 / 69,837; 2022: 57 / 302,948 — note how volatile person-days lost is year to year, which means a single large public-sector dispute can swing the series either way. Suggestive but non-decisive signals in the right direction: ~2,700 MBIE staff held stop-work meetings in July 2026 and about 10,000 public servants took a half-day strike on 9 September 2026 amid bargaining for 10,000+ collective-agreement workers. Those are consistent with Andersen's prediction but (a) fall partly outside the criterion's window, (b) include stop-work meetings, which Employment NZ explicitly excludes from the stoppages count, and (c) are driven by public-sector pay bargaining rather than demonstrably by the pay equity law. No verdict is possible until the series is published.

statement: The bill is intended to be passed and enacted towards the end of this year, with the redesigned vocational education and training system commencing on 1 January 2026.
criterion: The legislative record for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: true if it received royal assent during 2025 and the redesigned system (regional polytechnics and industry skills boards) commenced on 1 January 2026; false if assent came later than 31 December 2025 or commencement was deferred beyond 1 January 2026.
reasoning: Both legs of the criterion hold. (1) Royal assent during 2025: the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill passed its third reading and received royal assent on 20 October 2025, becoming the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Act 2025 (Public Act 2025 No 56); a Commencement Order followed on 1 December 2025. That is comfortably inside the 'towards the end of this year' framing and before the 31 December 2025 cut-off. (2) Commencement on 1 January 2026: the redesigned system started operating on 1 January 2026 — Te Pūkenga was disestablished as the centralised model, 10 regionally governed polytechnics began operating as independent institutions, and 8 Industry Skills Boards replaced the Workforce Development Councils from that date, taking over standard-setting, qualification development and (for a two-year transitional period) work-based training. Checked for disconfirming evidence of deferral: the one wrinkle is that four polytechnics (NorthTec, WITT, WelTec/Whitireia, Tai Poutini) remained inside the renamed transitional entity (New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology) pending viability decisions in the first half of 2026, and the former work-based learning divisions operate temporarily as divisions of the Industry Skills Boards. That is a transitional tail within the redesigned system, not a deferral of its commencement, so it does not trigger the criterion's false condition.

statement: Yes, and particularly around Budget 2025, which is all about growing the economy to create jobs and help Kiwis get ahead. The Government’s economic plan is working. By stopping wasteful spending, inflation is down, interest rates are falling, our economy is expected to grow, on average, 2.7 percent—that means 240,000 new jobs being created in the next four years—and, most importantly, wages are growing faster than inflation. This is a Government that’s proud of what it’s doing to get New Zealand back on track.
criterion: Stats NZ GDP series average annual growth over the four years from mid-2025 to mid-2029, and HLFS employment level change over the same period; true if average growth is near 2.7% and employment rises by roughly 240,000, false if materially below either.
reasoning: The criterion measures average GDP growth and HLFS employment change over mid-2025 to mid-2029, resolve-by 2029-09-30; only one year of data exists. Tracking so far is below the claim: GDP +1.7% over the year ended June 2026 (June 2026 quarter +0.2%), HLFS employment 2,905,000 in June 2026 with unemployment at 5.6%, i.e. roughly flat rather than ~60k jobs a year. Not enough of the window has elapsed to grade a four-year average.

statement: So in answer to the question: Investment Boost will lift capital investment and it will increase productivity.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts (gross fixed capital formation by businesses, plant/machinery/equipment) and the Stats NZ productivity statistics series; true if business capital investment and labour productivity both rise over the two full years following the policy's introduction in May 2025, false if either is flat or falls over that period.
reasoning: The criterion requires both business capital investment and labour productivity over the two full years after May 2025 (i.e. through mid-2027). The investment leg is tracking up: gross fixed capital formation +2.0% in the March 2026 quarter with plant/machinery/equipment +5.5% (capital goods imports +9.4%), and +1.5% in the June 2026 quarter. The productivity leg cannot be evaluated at all yet: Stats NZ's latest productivity release (23 April 2026) covers the year ended March 2025, which predates the policy, so no published productivity year overlaps Investment Boost.

statement: At the heart of the issue—which is why this particular Minister is producing great outcomes in relation to natural resources—we must stop relying on other sources of coal and critical minerals in terms of self-sufficiency, which is why titanium and vanadium, soon to be discovered in vast quantities off the coast of Taranaki, is on its way.
criterion: Public reporting from NZ Petroleum and Minerals / the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, or company announcements (e.g. Trans-Tasman Resources / Manuka Resources South Taranaki Bight project), on offshore Taranaki titanium and vanadium resources: true if a new resource of titanium and/or vanadium of commercially significant scale is publicly reported as discovered offshore Taranaki after 3 June 2025; false if no such discovery is reported by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: No new offshore Taranaki titanium/vanadium discovery has been publicly reported since 3 June 2025, but the resolve-by date (2027-12-31) has not passed, so the criterion's 'false' condition is not yet met. Two pieces of disconfirming context: (1) the deposit was already defined before the quote — Manuka Resources/Trans-Tasman Resources released the 3.2 Bt Taranaki VTM (vanadium titanomagnetite) resource, including a maiden vanadium resource, to the ASX on 1 March 2023, so nothing was 'soon to be discovered'; (2) the only development pathway went backwards — the Fast-track Expert Panel declined consent in a draft decision and TTR withdrew the application on 19 February 2026. Post-2025 offshore Taranaki permitting activity has been petroleum (Sunda Energy application, EnZed Energy permit), not minerals exploration, so a fresh mineral discovery in the remaining window is unlikely.

statement: It’s not possible to model every single interaction that workers and businesses have on a shop floor. But what we can say with confidence is that our intention is that we will see a decrease in deaths and a decrease in serious injury because we are asking business owners, workers, and WorkSafe to focus on reductions of critical risks.
criterion: WorkSafe NZ / Stats NZ work-related fatality and serious non-fatal injury statistics; true if both the fatality count and the serious injury rate are lower in the 2027/28 year than the 2024/25 baseline, false if either is flat or higher.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on 2027/28 WorkSafe/Stats NZ figures against a 2024/25 baseline; today is 2026-10-02, so the comparison year has not started and only the baseline exists. Baseline is established and the source series are live: WorkSafe's 2024/25 annual report and fatality data show 70 work-related fatalities in calendar 2024 at a provisional 1.9 per 100,000 (2.2 in 2023). Disconfirming check for later resolution: the criterion requires BOTH measures to fall, and the serious non-fatal injury rate has risen about 18% over the past decade even as the fatality rate fell ~35%, so the serious-injury leg is the one most likely to fail. Nothing resolvable now.

statement: There will be 22,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit as a result of this Government’s decisions.
criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / Treasury BEFU 2025 forecasts for jobseeker support recipients: true if the number of jobseeker support recipients rises by approximately 22,000 (or the official forecast track shows that increase) by mid-2026; false if the increase is materially smaller or numbers fall.
reasoning: Due date (2026-06-30) has passed and the data exist. MSD Benefit Fact Sheets: 196,434 on Jobseeker Support at June 2024; 216,009 at June 2025 (+19,575, i.e. the year BEFORE the claim); ~218,500 at June 2026, up only about 2,500 year-on-year. So measured from the claim date (3 June 2025) to mid-2026 — the criterion's baseline — the rise is ~2,500, roughly a ninth of the 22,000 claimed. The second limb of the criterion also fails: the official forecast track available when she spoke (MSD/Treasury BEFU 2025, released 22 May 2025, finalised 11 April 2025) had Jobseeker at 210,800 in March 2025, peaking at ~217,900 in December 2025 and then declining to ~181,800 by June 2029 — it never showed a +22,000 forward increase. BEFU 2026 likewise has ~216,300 in March 2026, flat through 2026, falling to ~194,000 by June 2030. Searched for disconfirming evidence (i.e. a reading under which 22,000 holds) and found one: counted cumulatively rather than forward, the stock is up ~22,100 from June 2024 and ~28,000 from the ~190,000 at the change of government, so the magnitude is defensible on a since-the-term-began baseline. Her future tense did not signal that baseline. Direction correct, magnitude correct only under an unsignalled reading, materially overstated as a forward prediction — hence partly_correct rather than correct or wrong.

statement: This comes in an environment where we know that our superannuation costs are blowing out. They will be $71 billion in 25 years, by 2050.
criterion: Crown accounts / Treasury reporting of gross New Zealand Superannuation expenditure for the year ending June 2050: true if annual spend is approximately $71 billion (nominal), false if materially below or above that figure.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on Crown accounts / Treasury reporting of gross NZ Superannuation expenditure for the year ending June 2050 — 24 years away. No outturn can exist. I also searched for an official nominal 2050 figure that would let the $71b be checked against the projection it presumably came from, and did not find one: Treasury's long-term fiscal work (He Tirohanga Mokopuna 2025) reports NZ Super as a share of GDP (5.1% now rising to about 8% by 2065 with no policy change) and as spend per person ($2,980 in 2024/25 to $6,412 in 2064/65), not as a nominal annual dollar total for a single out-year. So the figure is neither confirmed nor contradicted by a published Treasury number I could locate, and the claim stays open.

statement: Fieldays is the largest event in the Southern Hemisphere, and over 100,000 visitors are going to be there.
criterion: Official NZ National Fieldays Society attendance figure for Fieldays 2025: true if reported attendance exceeds 100,000, false if below.
reasoning: The criterion asks only about official NZ National Fieldays Society attendance for Fieldays 2025 exceeding 100,000. Fieldays' own post-event reporting and the Mystery Creek case study both state the 57th Fieldays (June 2025) drew 110,000+ visitors and ~1,100 exhibitors, so the threshold was cleared. (Checked for disconfirming figures: no official or media report puts 2025 below 100,000; the 2026 event was reported at 132,000+, consistent with the scale.) Note outside the criterion: the 'largest event in the Southern Hemisphere' framing is Fieldays' own marketing claim in its narrower form — largest agricultural event in the Southern Hemisphere — and was not assessed here.

statement: Here is my prediction: it will be delayed. They’ll build this $500 million hospital, it’ll probably end up costing a lot more and it will be delayed, and we will be back in 10 years’ time to have another conversation, because guess what!
criterion: Health NZ project reporting on the Nelson Hospital rebuild: true if the completion date announced in 2025 is missed and/or the final approved cost exceeds $500m; false if the building is delivered by the announced date at or under $500m.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on whether the completion date announced in 2025 is missed and/or the final approved cost exceeds $500m; its own resolve-by is 2032-12-31. The 26 May 2025 announcement committed 'over half a billion dollars' across four years for stage 2, with a 128-bed inpatient building expected by 2029 (stated as two years earlier than previously planned). As of October 2026 that date has not arrived: enabling works are underway, main construction was still expected to start around late 2026, and a February 2026 Cabinet paper concerns the delegated approval process for the redevelopment — i.e. the final approved cost is not yet fixed. The widely cited $1.1b figure is the full multi-phase programme/earlier scoped plan, not a final approved cost for the announced build, so it does not settle the cost limb either. No completion-date miss and no final cost are yet on the record.

statement: It is disciplined, it is growth oriented, and it sets out a clear path to return the Government books back to surplus by 2028-29.
criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30 June 2029 (and intervening HYEFU/BEFU updates); true if OBEGALx records a surplus for 2028-29, false if a deficit is recorded.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30 June 2029, which cannot exist before late 2029 (criterion resolve-by 2029-12-31). The intervening updates the criterion also names point the claim's way rather than against it: BEFU 2026 (May 2026) forecast an OBEGALx surplus of about $2.6b in 2028/29 — a year earlier than HYEFU 2025 had it — and Treasury's September 2026 pre-election update lifted that to roughly $4b, driven by higher tax revenue. I looked for the disconfirming case (a forecast pushing surplus out past 2028/29) and the most recent updates do the opposite. These remain forecasts, not an outturn, so the prediction is still pending.

statement: Some later speakers in this debate may criticise the fact that a majority of the Regulations Review Committee made this decision, rather than it being a unanimous decision.
criterion: The Hansard transcript of the remainder of this disallowance debate (21 May 2025): true if at least one later speaker criticises the committee's decision for being a majority rather than a unanimous one, false if no later speaker raises that point.
reasoning: The Hansard transcript named in the criterion could not be retrieved (parliament.nz Hansard 404s to fetchers, www3.parliament.nz is behind a Radware bot wall, hansard.parliament.nz is a JS SPA serving only 'Loading...', web.archive.org is blocked and the Wayback availability API reports no snapshot for these URLs). Working from contemporaneous reporting of that same debate instead: Newsroom's account records Green justice spokesperson Lawrence Xu-Nan — a speaker in the debate, after Mooney — making precisely the predicted criticism, that partially reversing the regulations 'by a simple majority went against the traditional approach of consensus for such changes'. Newsroom also reports Mooney in the debate 'defending the decision to change the regulations by majority', which independently corroborates that the majority/unanimity point was live in the chamber and that he pre-empted it. The NZ Herald confirms the committee split (unanimous against disallowing the stand-alone-subject aspect, majority only on the compulsory-component aspect), and LawNews (Gary Judd KC) sets out the same split. Victoria University law professor Dean Knight made the identical argument to Newsroom — 'the lack of unanimity was also striking', against a long-standing convention of consensus — though as an academic he is not a 'speaker in this debate'. Disconfirming check: Labour committee chair Arena Williams, the most-quoted opposition MP, criticised the mechanism (disallowance rather than a bill) and not the split, so the criticism was not universal among later speakers. The criterion needs only one. Residual uncertainty: Xu-Nan's remark reaches me as a journalist's paraphrase, and I cannot fully exclude that he made it to the reporter rather than in the chamber. Mooney's prediction was hedged ('may criticise'), a low bar, and the evidence shows the criticism did surface from a later speaker in that debate.

statement: So I’m sure he will give a much more detailed committee stage speech during this debate.
criterion: Hansard record of the committee stage of the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Amendment Bill; true if Shanan Halbert delivers a committee-stage speech on the bill longer and more detailed than Sepuloni's, false if he does not speak in that committee stage.
reasoning: The criterion points squarely at the Hansard record of the bill's committee stage, and that record is not retrievable. parliament.nz Hansard paths return HTTP 404 to every fetcher tried (both /en/ and /mi/, both HansDeb_20250521_20250521_28 and the whole-day HansD_20250521_20250521 index); www3.parliament.nz returns 200 but only a 125-character Radware 'Verifying your browser' interstitial; hansard.parliament.nz is a client-side SPA returning 'Loading...' and 'An unhandled error has occurred'; web.archive.org is blocked to this environment and the archive.org availability API reports no snapshot ever captured for these URLs; legislation.govt.nz returns HTTP 403 so the Act's legislative-history notes are also unavailable. What I did establish: the committee stage of the Auckland Harbour Board and Takapuna Borough Council Empowering Act Amendment Bill was indeed scheduled for 21 May 2025, third on that Members' Day order paper after two debates and before the first readings of Halbert's own Enabling Crown Entities to Adopt Maori Names Bill and Andy Foster's bill — so Sepuloni's 21 May remark 'during this debate' is consistent with her speaking in that committee stage. Simon Watts (National, North Shore) was the member in charge; the bill received royal assent on 5 August 2025. Shanan Halbert is independently recorded as having spoken at the bill's second reading on 12 March 2025, which makes it plausible he also spoke in committee — but plausible is not verified. Whether he spoke in that committee stage, and whether his contribution was longer and more detailed than Sepuloni's, exists only in the Hansard transcript. A minor local bill's committee stage attracted no press coverage, so there is no substitute source. Absence of a retrievable transcript is not evidence the prediction failed.

statement: Is there any chance that any RMA replacement legislation will do anything like that? No, there is not.
criterion: The text of the Government's RMA replacement Bills as introduced/enacted: false (prediction wrong) if they contain mandatory mana whenua consultation or decision-making participation provisions broadly comparable to those in the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023; true if they contain no such comparable provisions.
reasoning: The RMA replacement legislation is now enacted and can be assessed: the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill were introduced 9 December 2025, reported back by the Environment Committee 20 July 2026, passed third reading 22 September 2026 and received royal assent 30 September 2026 as the Planning Act 2026 and Natural Environment Act 2026. BROOKING IS RIGHT ON THE DECISION-MAKING LIMB. No source describes any analogue to the NBA 2023's National Maori Entity (the independent monitor of whether te Tiriti principles were given effect) or to te Oranga o te Taiao. There is no mandatory mana whenua seat on any planning or spatial-plan committee: the NBA 2023 required regional planning committees of at least six members with at least two appointed by iwi authorities and hapu groups via a regional iwi-and-hapu committee, whereas under the new regime spatial plan committees have their terms of reference set by local authorities with no iwi/hapu appointment right described, and Te Ao News reports 'no guaranteed decision-making role for iwi in spatial planning, no co-governance mechanisms'. The RMA's general Treaty obligation (s 8) is replaced by a descriptive clause that merely 'recognises the Crown's responsibilities'. Mana Whakahono a Rohe references were removed in July 2026 and replaced with narrower 'iwi participation agreements', with the voluntary iwi-initiated pathway closed off — new agreements cannot be established unless required by a Treaty settlement. Kahukuraariki's select committee submission calls the Bills 'a material regression in the recognisation and protection of iwi and hapu authority' and 'a deliberate dilution of the constitutional status of iwi and hapu as Te Tiriti partners'; Labour's own minority view (Brooking and Radhakrishnan) used 'regressive'. BUT THE FLAT 'No, there is not' IS OVERSTATED. The Acts do contain mandatory mana whenua consultation provisions: DLA Piper's clause-level account lists 'consultation with iwi authorities before notification of a proposed national instrument' and 'specific consultation duties when preparing regional spatial plans' in both Bills; Russell McVeagh emphasises consultation is 'required before any national instrument is notified'; Te Ao News reports the legislation 'requires the Crown and councils to consult iwi authorities' at national-instrument, regional-spatial-plan and local-land-use-plan stages, that decision-makers must 'have regard to' iwi management plans and statutory acknowledgements, and that councils 'must notify iwi when consents meet certain thresholds'. Treaty settlement obligations carry over (Schedule 3 Part 4 of the Planning Bill is the settlement-redress schedule), and the NBA 2023's own consultation limb — Crown engagement with iwi authorities when preparing the national planning framework — has a direct counterpart in the national-instrument consultation duty. So mandatory consultation exists and is not 'nothing like' the NBA; what is absent is the participation and co-governance architecture. Disconfirming evidence checked: Minister Chris Bishop rejects the weakening characterisation ('I don't think it weakens it; in a way, it makes it clearer for everybody'), and Waatea frames the outcome as still contingent on how early mana whenua are engaged, with the issues before the Waitangi Tribunal in Wai 3450. Caveat on method: legislation.govt.nz returned HTTP 403 to every request, so I could not read the enacted text or the membership Schedules directly; this rests on secondary legal analysis (DLA Piper, Russell McVeagh), a primary select committee submission, Te Ao News and Wikipedia. The absence of a National Maori Entity analogue and of mandatory committee seats is therefore an absence across all accessible sources rather than a confirmed reading of the statute.

statement: With all of this, Budget 2025 is forecasting a real GDP growth of 2.9 percent in the 2025-26 year, an additional 240,000 people in jobs over the next four years, and wage growth that is consistently outpacing inflation.
criterion: Stats NZ real GDP series for the year ended June 2026; true if annual real GDP growth is approximately 2.9%, false if materially below or above. Employment leg checked against Stats NZ HLFS employment level in 2029 versus 2025.
reasoning: The quote faithfully restates BEFU 2025 (real GDP growth 2.9% in 2025/26, 240,000 more jobs over four years, wages outpacing inflation), so this is a genuine prediction. The dated leg has now resolved and missed: Stats NZ reported real GDP up 1.7% in the year ended June 2026 vs the year ended June 2025 (released 17 Sep 2026), against the 2.9% forecast — a 1.2pp shortfall, materially below the criterion's threshold. The wage leg also failed in its first year: Labour Cost Index all salary and wage rates +2.0% and QES average ordinary-time hourly earnings +2.8% in the year to June 2026, against CPI inflation of 4.1% — real wages fell, so wage growth was not 'consistently outpacing inflation'. The 240,000-jobs leg is not yet due (criterion checks HLFS employment in 2029 vs 2025) and I am not grading it, but the first year ran well short of the ~60k/yr implied pace: HLFS employment ~2,905,000 in June 2026, about +35,000 (1.2%) year-on-year, with unemployment rising to 5.6% and the employment rate flat at 66.7%. Verdict is 'wrong' rather than 'partly_correct' because the one leg whose date has passed is materially below the forecast and the wage leg is directionally reversed, not merely overstated.

statement: Well, this country is on track to have a national debt of over $200 billion by the end of the decade if we don’t make some savings and turn things around.
criterion: Treasury Crown accounts / Budget Economic and Fiscal Update debt series to 2030: true if gross or net core Crown debt is reported above $200 billion by the end of the decade, false if it remains below $200 billion.
reasoning: The criterion allows either gross or net core Crown debt from the Treasury Crown accounts / BEFU debt series to 2030. Gross debt has already passed the threshold: the interim Financial Statements of the Government for the 11 months ended 31 May 2026 report gross debt of $222.5b (49.3% of GDP), with net core Crown debt at $186.0b (41.3% of GDP). On the net measure, Treasury's forecast series also crosses $200b well before the end of the decade — Budget 2026 and PREFU 2026 (29 Sep 2026) both have net core Crown debt rising through the low $200b range from 2026/27-2027/28 and reaching roughly $230b+ by 2029/30 (PREFU is the lower path, about $13.4b below the Budget Update by June 2030). I checked for the disconfirming case — a forecast that holds net debt under $200b through 2030 — and no Treasury vintage since Budget 2025 does so. Two caveats on the substance rather than the arithmetic: the out-years are still forecast, not outturn; and the conditional framing ('if we don't make some savings and turn things around') is undercut, because debt exceeds $200b in Treasury's own forecasts that already incorporate the government's savings, so the threshold is not contingent on failing to save.

statement: As Simon Court from ACT said, our debt is going to balloon to $200 billion by 2029.
criterion: Treasury core Crown debt figures for the 2028/29 fiscal year: true if Crown debt reaches or exceeds $200 billion by 2029; false if it remains materially below $200 billion.
reasoning: The criterion points at Treasury core Crown debt figures for 2028/29 and asks only whether debt reaches or exceeds $200b by 2029. Treasury's current forecast series clears that comfortably: net core Crown debt is projected in the $230b-$241b range around 2028/29-2029/30 (PREFU 2026, 29 Sep 2026, is the lower path; Budget 2026 in May had a higher one peaking near $246b by 2030), and gross debt is already $222.5b as at 31 May 2026 per the interim Crown financial statements. So the $200b threshold is met, and Bidois's figure understates the forecast rather than overstating it — net debt crosses $200b around 2026/27-2027/28, two years earlier than 2029. Two limits worth recording: the 2028/29 year ends June 2029, so this rests on the forecast series (which is what the criterion names) and not on outturn; and the forecast gap between vintages is large enough that the dollar level, as opposed to the threshold crossing, should not be treated as settled. Checked the disconfirming direction: no post-Budget-2025 Treasury vintage keeps core Crown debt below $200b through 2028/29 on either the gross or net measure.

statement: By 2040, two out of every five people will be over the age of 60.
criterion: Stats NZ national population projections/estimates for 2040: true if 40% or more of the New Zealand population is aged over 60 in 2040; false if the share is materially below 40%.
reasoning: Stats NZ national population projections (2024-base, released 3-4 June 2025, the day after the statement) project the 65+ share at 1 in 6 currently, 1 in 5 (~20%) from the mid-2030s, and only about 1 in 4 by 2060, against a total population passing 6 million shortly before 2040 (6,284,400 by 2043 on the median projection). The 60-64 band is about 6% of the population (5.82% at mid-2021 on the UNSD/Stats NZ age table). Combining these, the share aged over 60 in 2040 is roughly 26-28%, not 40% - materially below the criterion's threshold, so false on the criterion as written. Disconfirming check performed: the only official NZ figure resembling 'two out of every five' is the old-age dependency ratio, projected at 33-41 people aged 65+ per 100 aged 15-64 in 2040. That is a ratio to the working-age population, not a share of the total, and is the likeliest origin of the error. No Stats NZ or other official source states a ~40% 60+ share for 2040. (A 50+ threshold would land near 40% in 2040, so this may be a misstated age cut, but it is wrong as spoken.)

statement: Lines company expenditure on growth and renewals is set to increase from $717 million in 2022 to $1.4 billion a year in 2031.
criterion: Commerce Commission electricity distribution business expenditure disclosures for the 2031 regulatory year; true if combined growth-and-renewal capex is approximately $1.4 billion, false if materially below or above.
reasoning: The criterion requires Commerce Commission electricity distribution business expenditure disclosures for the 2031 regulatory year. Those cannot exist before 2032, and the resolve-by date is 2031-12-31, so the claim is not resolvable in October 2026. I also could not locate the source of the specific $717m (2022) -> $1.4bn (2031) growth-and-renewals pair: it is not on the Commerce Commission's electricity distributor performance and data pages (including the asset management plan review pages, which carry no dollar figures), and not on Electricity Networks Aotearoa's site, whose only capex headline is backward-looking ($6.8bn invested over five years). The BCG 'The Future is Electric' report (Oct 2022) is the likeliest origin but exceeded the fetch size limit, and its NZ-sector appendix had no extractable text layer. Nothing found contradicts the forecast's direction: the Commission's DPP4 decision (Nov 2024) allowed $5.7bn of capex across 2025-2030 (~$1.14bn/yr), and MBIE's August 2026 discussion document reports EDBs forecasting over $32bn across the coming decade - so a roughly doubling trajectory is consistent with the regulatory record; it simply cannot be graded yet.

statement: It will no longer be rolled out around the country, and our judiciary will do their best but won’t have the financial resources to do it effectively.
criterion: Ministry of Justice / District Court annual reports and Te Ao Mārama implementation updates; false if the programme is operating in more than eight District Court locations by the resolve-by date, true if it remains at eight or fewer.
reasoning: Te Ao Marama remains at its original eight District Court locations - Kaitaia, Kaikohe, Whangarei, Hamilton, Tauranga, Gisborne, Napier and Hastings - per both the District Courts' 'About Te Ao Marama' page and the Ministry of Justice initiative page (last updated 21 January 2026), which defers decisions on funding expansion 'beyond the 8 existing sites' to future Budget processes pending an evaluation due in 2026. Budget 2025 returned the $32.1m of tagged contingency set aside for the rollout (expansion had already been paused at Budget 2024), and the NZ Law Society's Budget 2026 summary does not mention Te Ao Marama at all - no expansion funding, no reinstatement. The District Courts page further states that 'Extra funding has been allocated for the active locations only at this stage', with all other courts free to adopt best-practice approaches voluntarily and unfunded. So the criterion's 'true' branch - eight or fewer locations - holds, and both halves of Webb's statement are supported: the funded rollout stopped, and courts outside the eight carry it without money. Two caveats: (1) the resolve-by date of 2027-06-30 has not passed, but the determining action has already occurred and no additional site could be stood up unfunded within the remaining window, so I am grading rather than deferring; (2) recency - the newest Te Ao Marama-specific source is January 2026, so a change later in 2026 would not be captured here.

statement: It is likely the Government will not meet any of their 2028 child poverty reduction targets.
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics for the year ending June 2028, measured against the three primary measures in the Government's 2028 targets; true if none of the targets is met, false if at least one is met.
reasoning: The criterion requires Stats NZ child poverty statistics for the year ending June 2028, measured against the three primary 2028 targets (6% material hardship, 5% before-housing-costs, 10% after-housing-costs). That release is due around February 2029; the criterion's own resolve-by is 2029-06-30. No measurement against it is possible yet. Context only, not a verdict: the most recent release (year ended June 2025, published 26 Feb 2026) shows 14.3% of children in material hardship, the Children's Commissioner described progress as stalled, and Treasury forecasts have the income measures well above target into 2029 — so the trajectory is unfavourable, but the targets resolve on 2028 data.

statement: So unemployment is actually relatively high—it’s at about 5.1 percent—but if we actually realise what this Budget’s going to deliver, that will actually help us in driving the unemployment rate in the right direction down itself.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate in the quarters following Budget 2025; true if the rate falls below 5.1% within 18 months of the statement, false if it remains at or above 5.1% throughout that period.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the HLFS seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell below 5.1% within 18 months of 3 June 2025 (i.e. by 3 December 2026). The published series went the other way throughout: Mar 2025 5.1%, Jun 2025 5.2%, Sep 2025 5.3%, Dec 2025 5.4%, Mar 2026 5.3%, Jun 2026 5.6% — the latest is the highest in the series. Every quarter inside the window that has been published is at or above 5.1%. Disconfirming check: the one quarter inside the window still unreleased is Sep 2026 (due early Nov 2026); a fall from 5.6% to below 5.1% in a single quarter is far outside the observed variation of this series, so the criterion's false-branch is effectively satisfied. Flagging that residual quarter as the only open element.

statement: As a result, this Budget will put some universities in a financial position that is no longer viable, particularly those who have less STEM subjects available.
criterion: Published annual reports of the eight NZ universities and TEC financial monitoring: true if at least one university reports an operating deficit or formally signals financial unviability/restructuring attributed to the Budget 2025 funding settings; false if all universities report viable positions over the period.
reasoning: The criterion's true-branch is met: Otago forecast an $11.8m deficit for 2025 and budgeted a $9m deficit for 2026, and Lincoln confirmed 40 FTE job cuts in March 2026 citing TEC signals of reduced 2026 funding plus enrolment shortfalls. Budget 2025 did not extend the 4% emergency teaching-subsidy top-up (expiring end-2025), lifting grants only in health, education and STEM; Universities NZ put the net effect at a 0.8% revenue increase, behind inflation. But the quote is materially overstated on both of its specifics. (1) No university has reached or formally signalled unviability: Otago expects a small surplus in 2027, Massey has a TEC-agreed runway to surplus, Lincoln is debt-free and heading for a modest surplus. Deficits of this size are continuous with the sector's pre-Budget-2025 pattern rather than a new viability cliff. (2) The 'less STEM' asymmetry is not borne out — the institution that actually cut staff in 2026 is Lincoln, a land-based science university, not a humanities-weighted one. Caveat on sourcing: several prominent search hits on NZ university finances (ODT 'Most universities forecasting deficits again', THE 'universities flounder as lifeline pulled back') are 2023 articles with current-reading headlines, and were excluded; so were academicjobs.com pages that appear machine-generated. The ODT Otago article is paywalled, so its figures come from the search-indexed excerpt, not the full text.

statement: There’ll be fewer jobs; we won’t see wage growth.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey (total employment) and the Labour Cost Index / Quarterly Employment Survey wage series: true if total employment is lower and wage growth is flat or negative over the year following the statement, false if employment grows or wages continue to rise.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion's 'false' condition were met. HLFS employment rose over the year following the statement: 2,905,000 in the June 2026 quarter (+0.5% on the quarter, ~+1.2% on the year) against ~2,882,000 in June 2025. Wages continued to rise: LCI all salary and wage rates +2.0% for the year to June 2026 (private 2.0%, public 1.7%), QES average ordinary-time hourly earnings $44.62 (+2.8%) and average weekly earnings $1,730 (+3.0%). Mitigating context she could claim: the labour market did weaken — unemployment 5.2% -> 5.6% (highest since Sept 2015), underutilisation 13.8%, employment -0.2% y/y in the Sept 2025 quarter and filled jobs -0.1% y/y in Dec 2025, and with CPI at 4.1% real wages fell and LCI growth was the slowest since March 2021. But the series the criterion names show employment higher and nominal wage growth positive, so the prediction fails as written.

statement: They have shown resilience, and, for the first time ever, the apple industry is going to surpass $1 billion.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for the Primary Industries (or NZ Apples & Pears) apple/pipfruit export revenue for the year ending June 2025 or June 2026: true if reported revenue exceeds $1 billion and no earlier year did; false if it remains below $1 billion.
reasoning: MPI SOPI (June 2026 dataset, figures current as at 20 May 2026) records apples & pears export revenue of $1,246 million actual for the year ended June 2025 — the first year above $1 billion in the series back to 2004. The prior peak was $932m (YE June 2024), with $892m in 2023 and $865m in 2022, so no earlier year met or approached the threshold; the YE June 2026 forecast is $1,320m. The criterion's 'true' condition (revenue exceeds $1b and no earlier year did) is satisfied on the named source. Caveat checked and discarded: the February 2025 Fruitnet/NZAPI '$1bn for the first time' story concerns orchard-gate revenue for 2024, a different measure, and does not itself support the export claim — but the SOPI export series does independently. The series is nominal NZD and starts in 2004, so 'first ever' strictly means first since 2004.
