statement: Violence will grow under this Budget and that blood will be on the hands of this Government.
criterion: NZ Police recorded family harm investigations and Stats NZ/NZ Crime and Victims Survey measures of family and sexual violence for the years following Budget 2025; true if these show a sustained increase over the 2025 baseline, false if they are flat or falling.
reasoning: The criterion requires a sustained increase over a 2025 baseline across the years following Budget 2025 (22 May 2025), resolvable by 30 June 2027; only about 16 months have elapsed and neither named source has post-Budget data. No annual NZ Police family harm investigation totals for 2025/26 are published in any reachable source — Vine's government-data page points to policedata.nz rolling data and an old 2016-2018 table rather than a current annual series. The latest NZCVS is Cycle 8 (2025), published March 2026, covering roughly the 12 months to mid-2025, i.e. almost entirely before Budget 2025, so no post-Budget cycle exists. Checked for disconfirming and confirming evidence: a prominent NZ Herald 'family harm investigations drop' article is dated 29 July 2024 and predates the statement, so it is not evidence either way; fragmentary 2025 indicators point both ways (Police Safety Orders 27,077 in 2025 vs 24,676 in 2024, +9.7%, while NZCVS family-violence victim counts fell). One partial year of mixed signals cannot establish or refute a sustained multi-year increase, and the causal attribution to the Budget is not testable from these series.

statement: We all know what’s going to happen over there, don’t we? He’s going to get smashed in the Oxford debate.
criterion: The result of the Oxford Union debate David Seymour participates in: true if the floor vote goes against the side he spoke for, or contemporaneous reporting records him as clearly losing the exchange; false if his side wins the vote or reporting records him as holding his own.
reasoning: The Oxford Union debate was held 5 June 2025 on the motion 'This House believes that no one can be illegal on stolen land'. Seymour spoke in opposition; the motion passed 98-82, so the floor vote went against the side he spoke for, which is the criterion's stated true-condition. NZ Herald reported it as his side losing. The margin was narrow (16 votes) and he was not reported as being personally demolished, so 'smashed' overstates the manner, but the criterion tests the vote outcome and that went against him.

statement: I think that there is going to be one error in the Budget: there’s going to be underestimation of the impact of the Investment Boost programme.
criterion: Treasury/IRD reporting on Investment Boost uptake and fiscal cost in subsequent Budget Economic and Fiscal Updates against the Budget 2025 forecast; true if realised uptake/fiscal cost or measured business investment response materially exceeds the Budget 2025 estimate, false if it comes in at or below that estimate.
reasoning: The prediction was that Budget 2025 would UNDERestimate Investment Boost's impact. The evidence since points the other way. An Inland Revenue survey (fielded December 2025, published March 2026) found roughly a third of businesses had limited or no awareness of the scheme, only about 58% of aware firms that had invested had claimed or intended to claim the deduction, and just 11% of aware investing firms reported a significant increase in spending directly attributable to the policy; Kiwibank's August 2025 soundings found most spending was catching up on deferred purchases. BEFU 2026 maintained Treasury's prior assumptions (Investment Boost lifting real GDP by up to 0.4% over the forecast period) rather than revising the impact upward, and I found no Treasury or IRD statement revising uptake or fiscal cost above the Budget 2025 estimate. Checked specifically for the opposite (a cost overrun or an upside investment surprise attributed to the scheme) and found none. Caveat: the resolve-by date of 2027-05-31 has not passed and the 2025/26 tax-return outturn is not final, so this is the direction of the evidence available through PREFU 2026 rather than a closed book.

statement: I’m telling you now that it will keep kids out of court, it will keep them out of police cells, it will get them into jobs that would not otherwise have been realised.
criterion: Ministry of Education evaluation of the Budget 2025 learning support expansion together with Ministry of Justice youth court and Police youth apprehension statistics: true if published evaluation or official statistics show reduced youth justice involvement and improved employment outcomes for the cohorts receiving the expanded early intervention; false if evaluation finds no such effect or the relevant youth justice measures do not improve for those cohorts.
reasoning: The criterion requires a Ministry of Education evaluation of the Budget 2025 learning support expansion plus Ministry of Justice youth court and Police youth apprehension statistics for the cohorts receiving the early intervention. The package (NZ$746m, including extending the Early Intervention Service from ECE through to end of Year 1 and Learning Support Coordinators for Year 1-8 schools) only began rolling out from 2025; no evaluation has been published, and the children receiving extended early intervention are years away from appearing in youth justice or employment statistics. Resolve-by is 2035-12-31.

statement: I know that they’ll roll over; it’ll be part of the coalition agreement to actually push this through. Maybe they’ve had a road to Damascus experience and are now happy to sell out New Zealand.
criterion: The committee-stage and third-reading voting record for the Invest New Zealand Bill; true if New Zealand First voted against the Labour amendments to clauses 10 and 11 and for the bill, false if it supported either amendment.
reasoning: The prediction's substance held: the Invest New Zealand Bill was pushed through, passing on 25 June 2025 (Act 2025 No 33, Royal assent 27 June 2025, agency operating 1 July 2025), taken under urgency without a select committee process. NZ First necessarily voted for it — National (49) + ACT (11) = 60 of 123 seats is short of a majority, so the bill could not have passed without NZ First, which satisfies the second limb of the criterion. CAVEAT on the first limb: the committee-stage division record on Labour amendments to clauses 10 and 11 could not be retrieved. legislation.govt.nz returns 403 to fetchers, bills.parliament.nz is a JavaScript-only shell, parliament.nz Hansard paths 404, web.archive.org is blocked in this environment, and the Scoop Hansard mirrors 403; voted.nz carries conscience votes only. I could not confirm that Labour tabled Amendment Papers on those clauses at all, and no source indicated NZ First supported any opposition amendment (an event that would have drawn coverage). So the 'voted against the Labour amendments' limb rests on inference from confirmed passage and absence of any disconfirming report, not on the division record itself. A strict reading of the criterion would make this uncheckable.

statement: Why not consider other forms of support for people over the age of 65 such as increasing the super, such as over-65s who are renting—we know that there’s going to be an increasing number of people who do not own their own home over the age of 65 over the next decade, so it just seems like there’s a missed opportunity there.
criterion: Stats NZ census/household economic survey home-ownership data for the 65+ age group; true if the number of over-65s not owning their own home in the mid-2030s exceeds the 2025 figure, false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Stats NZ home-ownership data for the 65+ group in the mid-2030s (resolve-by 2035-06-04), so no outcome data exists yet. Supporting context only, not a resolution: Te Ara Ahunga Ora Retirement Commission modelling projects around 600,000 New Zealanders aged 65+ needing to rent by 2048, roughly a 100% increase on 2022, with the renting share of the older population doubling to about 40%; overall home ownership fell from 75% (1991) to 60% (2023) and is projected at 48% by 2048. The direction of travel is consistent with the claim, but the named Stats NZ comparison cannot be made until the mid-2030s.

statement: There is a date here and it says that if it hasn’t been enacted by July, then it won’t come into effect. But it will be enacted by then, and therefore we are now contingent upon territorial authorities having the equipment and ability to be able to roll this out effectively and in a way that doesn’t make a difference so that somebody in one part of the country is receiving the full benefit and somebody else may not due to the territorial authority’s capacity to be able to deliver.
criterion: The New Zealand legislation register: true if the Rates Rebate Amendment Act 2025 received Royal assent on or before 1 July 2025; false if assent came later or the bill did not pass.
reasoning: The criterion is satisfied as written: the Rates Rebate Amendment Act 2025 (Public Act 2025 No 31) received Royal assent on 27 June 2025, on or before the 1 July 2025 deadline, and comes into force on 1 July 2025 immediately after the Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order 2025 comes into force. So Leary's 'it will be enacted by then' came true and the Act did not lapse. Note on evidence quality: legislation.govt.nz returns 403 to automated fetchers, so the assent date comes from the search index's reading of the official Act page rather than a page I rendered myself; three independent queries returned the same date (27 June 2025) and the same commencement wording. Her further contingent claim about uneven delivery due to territorial authority capacity is outside the scope of this criterion and was not assessed.

statement: This will now be used every time we consider something in the Privileges Committee as the bar, and I think that’s shameful.
criterion: Privileges Committee reports and House debates on questions of privilege between June 2025 and the end of 2028; true if subsequent committee reports treat the 2025 suspension length as the reference point or benchmark for penalties, false if later cases are decided on earlier, lesser precedents or without reference to it.
reasoning: The criterion's window runs from June 2025 to the end of 2028 and the resolve-by date (2028-12-31) has not passed, so the prediction cannot be closed. Interim evidence points against it rather than for it: only two privileges matters have arisen since June 2025, and neither treats the 21/21/7-day suspensions as a benchmark. In the MBIE case (contempt found 26 Aug 2026 for deliberately misleading the Education and Workforce Committee about the cancelled $35m Biometric Capability Update) the committee recommended NO further punishment — no reprimand at the bar, no fine — saying 'We intend that our findings will be of sufficient consequence on their own'; the explicit precedent comparison in the coverage was the 2023 Tinetti case, not 2025. The leaked Governance and Administration Committee draft FENZ report (referred Sep 2026) was unresolved with three sitting days left in the term. Neither case concerned MP conduct or a suspension, so neither is a clean test of the claim. Caveat: parliament.nz blocked all fetches (404s on committee/report pages), so the absence of a 2025 reference rests on media coverage of the reports, not the report texts.

statement: In the coming days and weeks it is expected that this Parliament is scheduled to debate the second reading of the Mental Health Bill, a bill that is critical for reform in this country, and we all agree that this is critical.
criterion: Hansard / the Parliament bills database for the Mental Health Bill: true if the second reading debate is held before 31 July 2025; false if the second reading had not been taken by that date.
reasoning: The second reading was not held before 31 July 2025 — it was still outstanding nearly a year later. The Health Select Committee reported the bill back on 17 April 2025 'ready for the Bill's second reading', but the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission's release of 20 April 2026 is headlined 'Mental Health Bill debate stalled' and states it is 'one year since the Mental Health Bill was returned to Parliament for its second reading' and that 'Since then, we have not seen movement in this critical area', warning the then-intended July 2027 commencement was at risk. A 20 May 2025 MHWC commentary also refers to the second reading in the future tense ('Following the next stage of the Bill's development - the second reading'). The bill's final (third) reading was on Saturday 4 July 2026, with commencement pushed to 1 July 2028. So the second reading fell somewhere between April and July 2026 — roughly a year past the criterion's deadline, not 'the coming days and weeks'.

statement: We have seen evidence of a knock to domestic business confidence and investment intention, and these global events mean it will be very challenging to sustain the previous level of growth into the June quarter.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP release for the June 2025 quarter: true if seasonally adjusted quarterly growth is below 0.8%, false if it equals or exceeds 0.8%.
reasoning: Stats NZ's June 2025 quarter national accounts show seasonally adjusted GDP FELL 0.9 percent, following a 0.9 percent rise in the March 2025 quarter (0.8 percent as first published, later revised up). That is well below the criterion's 0.8 percent threshold — not a slowdown but an outright contraction, described as broad-based with falls in 10 of 16 industries, manufacturing down 3.5 percent the largest contributor, GDP per capita down 1.1 percent. The previous level of growth was not sustained, which is exactly what Willis said would be very challenging. Checked for the disconfirming case — a June quarter at or above 0.8 percent — and no source supports it; the 0.9 percent fall is the official figure from the Stats NZ release of 18 September 2025 and is reported identically by RNZ and the NZ Herald.

statement: I know my colleagues on the other side won’t be taking a call on this, but I’m sure that if they would, they would say that that is fair enough because that might affect the business.
criterion: The Hansard record of the committee stage of the Employment Relations (Pay Deductions for Partial Strikes) Amendment Bill on and after 4 June 2025; true if no government backbencher takes a call on clause 5 during the remainder of that committee stage, false if one or more do.
reasoning: The criterion names the Hansard record of the committee stage, and that record could not be reached. hansard.parliament.nz and www.parliament.nz serve only a ~450-byte Angular shell ("Loading...") to every fetch, direct API-path guesses hit a Radware bot interstitial, a rendering proxy (r.jina.ai) got past the bot check but returned the same unrendered shell, the Wayback availability API reports zero snapshots for the transcript URL and web.archive.org is blocked, NZLII returns 403, and no plain-HTML mirror of the debate exists (WhereTheyStand carries the bill's stages but no committee-stage speaker list; Scoop republishes some NZ debates but not this one). So I have no speaker list for clause 5 and cannot say whether a government backbencher took a call. What is confirmed is only that the committee stage happened under urgency/extended sittings and the bill was read a third time 25 June 2025 and assented 29-30 June 2025 — the record exists, I just could not read it. Not findable from here is not evidence the prediction failed. Note for the project: this is resolvable offline against the repo's own scraped Hansard corpus (data/corpus/hansard_v2.json), which this session was not permitted to read.

statement: They have no licence, and they’ll find very shortly that they’re going to be out of this place.
criterion: Official Electoral Commission results for the next general election; true if Te Pāti Māori returns no MPs to the House, false if it holds one or more seats after that election.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on official Electoral Commission results for the next general election. That election is set for 7 November 2026 and has not been held as of today, 2 October 2026, so no results exist to judge against. Te Pati Maori remains in the House in the 54th Parliament (it won six seats in 2023 and currently sits with four to six members depending on the count after by-election/membership changes), so the claim that they would be "out of this place" has not been tested. The resolve-by date of 31 December 2026 is after the election, so this becomes checkable in about five weeks.

statement: The Privileges Committee of the future will have a new precedent, without a doubt—a new range of penalties against members who err in the future. You can guarantee that.
criterion: Privileges Committee reports and House suspension records after June 2025: true if a subsequent Privileges Committee recommends a suspension of a member exceeding the pre-2025 norm (i.e. longer than a few days) or expressly cites the 2025 Te Pāti Māori decision as precedent; false if no such recommendation or citation occurs.
reasoning: The criterion runs to 30 November 2029 and asks for a subsequent Privileges Committee recommendation either exceeding the pre-2025 suspension norm or expressly citing the 2025 Te Pati Maori decision. Fifteen months in, neither has occurred, but the window is wide open. I looked for the disconfirming case as well as the confirming one: the only Privileges Committee report since June 2025 is the 26 August 2026 finding that MBIE deliberately misled the Education and Workforce Committee over a cancelled biometric IT project. It concerned officials (MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley and former Immigration NZ head Alison McDonald), not members, so no suspension was available, and the committee expressly recommended no further sanction ("We intend that our findings will be of sufficient consequence on their own"); reporting on it makes no reference to the 2025 haka case, the 21-day/7-day suspensions, or any new penalty range. No member has been referred since 2025 either: after the unsanctioned haka following Oriini Kaipara's October 2025 maiden statement, Speaker Brownlee said he had received no requests to refer any MP and pursued a standards crackdown instead. So the one post-2025 data point runs against Rurawhe's "you can guarantee that", but the prediction cannot be scored until a Privileges Committee case involving a member arises.

statement: The Reserve Bank, for example, is forecasting positive but subdued growth in the June and September quarters before picking up again strongly at the end of the year.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP outturns for June, September and December 2025: true if June and September are positive but below roughly 0.5%, and December is materially stronger; false if any of those quarters is negative or the end-of-year pick-up does not appear.
reasoning: Criterion required June and September 2025 quarters positive but under ~0.5%, with a materially stronger December. Stats NZ outturns: June 2025 quarter GDP FELL 0.9% (negative — an explicit falsifier in the criterion); September 2025 rose 1.1%, later revised to 0.9% (positive, but far above the 'subdued' band); December 2025 rose only 0.2%, below the RBNZ's own 0.5% projection and much weaker than September, so the forecast end-of-year pick-up did not appear either. Both falsifying conditions are met, so no reading rescues the forecast: the June contraction was a large miss, and what strength there was arrived in September rather than at the end of the year.

statement: It will enter into force some time over the next one to two years.
criterion: Depositary/MFAT records of ACCTS entry into force: true if the agreement is in force on or before 30 June 2027, false if it is not.
reasoning: The criterion allows until 30 June 2027 and that date has not passed (today 2026-10-02). Checked the depositary-side records directly: the NZ Treaties Register records ACCTS with NZ Adherence Status 'In Progress', 'Requires Ratification: Yes', 'Ratified or Signed: No', notes that 'the four signatories are currently undertaking the necessary legal procedures', and quotes the trigger — entry into force on the first day of the third month after at least three signatories notify the depositary (New Zealand) in writing. MFAT still files ACCTS under 'free trade agreements concluded but NOT in force'. No per-party notification dates are published, and the register's own expectation of 'late 2025 or early 2026' has already slipped. The one apparent counter-source, a NZ Customs notice saying 'domestic ratification ... has been completed and it will come into effect 1 July 2025', refers to the Tariff (ACCTS) Amendment Order 2025 taking effect in NZ domestic law rather than to international entry into force; that page was last updated 13 June 2025 and still links to MFAT's 'not in force' index. McClay's 'one to two years' from June 2025 is therefore still open — on the slow edge of his own range, but not yet decidable.

statement: Queen City Law managing director, Marcus Beveridge, described the scheme as “A ray of sunshine” and said that he wouldn’t be surprised if we exceeded $10 billion a year coming in through this programme.
criterion: Immigration NZ / Treasury reporting of funds actually transferred and invested under the Active Investor Plus visa in any 12-month period to mid-2027; true if the total exceeds NZ$10 billion in a single year, false if it does not.
reasoning: The criterion runs to mid-2027 and 12-month periods ending between now and 30 June 2027 have not closed, so the window is open. Primary Immigration NZ data (page updated 25 September 2026, covering 1 April 2025 – 24 September 2026) gives, for the ~18 months since the category reopened: investment pipeline (in progress + approved in principle) NZD $2.26 billion; 'capital committed (approved applications and funding transferred to New Zealand)' NZD $2.88 billion; headline blend ~NZD $5.15 billion 'added to the investment pipeline or committed'. 949 applications / 3,092 people, 496 approved. So across a year and a half the cumulative committed total is under $3 billion — reaching $10 billion inside any single 12-month period would take a step change of several times the current run-rate. Recorded not_yet_due rather than wrong only because the criterion's own deadline has not arrived. One caveat for whoever re-resolves it: INZ publishes no standalone figure for funds ACTUALLY TRANSFERRED — its 'capital committed' line deliberately merges approved applications with transfers, and the by-investment-type table (NZD $2.12 billion as at 30 June 2026) is also 'committed'. The Beehive '$3 billion' release returned an empty body on two attempts and the Q4 FY25/26 quarterly PDF would not parse, so I could not confirm whether that $3bn is transferred or committed. On the criterion's exact wording this item may therefore resolve partly uncheckable even after mid-2027; 'committed' must not be silently substituted for 'transferred'.

statement: I was really pleased to see an item on the news the other day saying that they’re on track to have no emergency motels by the end of this year.
criterion: MSD / Rotorua Lakes Council emergency housing figures as at 31 December 2025: true if no contracted emergency housing motels remain in Rotorua; false if any remain in use.
reasoning: Criterion as written asks whether any CONTRACTED emergency housing motels remained in Rotorua at 31 December 2025. They did not: referrals into contracted EH motels ceased 15 June 2025, the final residents moved out in November 2025, and the Government announced the programme's conclusion on 15 December 2025 — from a peak of 240+ households across 13 motels down to zero, with the last motels returning to the visitor market. Disconfirming check: emergency motel use in Rotorua did not stop entirely. MSD continued funding non-contracted motel accommodation via Emergency Housing Special Needs Grants, and post-closure reporting named Victoria Lodge and Gibson Court as still used for emergency housing (the council finding two such motels lacked resource consent). So the contracted-motel test in the criterion is met, while the speaker's looser phrase 'no emergency motels' overstates what happened. Note: direct page fetches were blocked (1News 404, Beehive empty body, NZ Herald/Newstalk/Scoop 403), so this rests on search-result extracts of those articles rather than full page reads.

statement: The effect of this—of clarifying the purpose; of consolidating the test; and ensuring that the overwhelming majority, I suspect, of consents will be processed in just 15 business days—is that New Zealanders get more investment.
criterion: Stats NZ foreign direct investment inflow/stock series and Overseas Investment Office consent statistics for the two years after the Act's commencement; true if approved/actual inbound investment rises materially above the pre-enactment baseline, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion measures FDI inflows/stock and OIO consent statistics over the two years AFTER the Act's commencement. The Overseas Investment (National Interest Test and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2025 received assent in 2025 but came into force on 6 March 2026 (by commencement order, alongside the Overseas Investment Amendment Regulations 2026), so the two-year observation window runs to March 2028 — well past the item's own resolve-by date of 31 December 2027, and only ~7 months have elapsed as at today (2 October 2026). The 15-business-day pathway for low-risk significant-business-asset transactions is in the enacted regime as described, but no post-commencement investment series long enough to test 'rises materially above the pre-enactment baseline' exists yet. Not findable is not the same as false; this is simply early.

statement: We know that there are a large number of interest groups in our community—community groups, family groups—who are looking towards this particular bill and will, no doubt, make submissions on this bill, and we encourage those voices to come through in this process in order to make this bill robust and something that we can all look back on our time in this House as a progressive and smart move moving forward.
criterion: The Governance and Administration Committee's published submissions record for the Immigration (Fiscal Sustainability and System Integrity) Amendment Bill; true if a substantial number of submissions (dozens or more) are received, including from community/family/migrant organisations, false if submissions are negligible.
reasoning: The prediction was that a large number of interest groups — community, family, migrant — would make submissions on the bill. The committee record bears this out: the bill was referred on 26 June 2025, public submissions closed 11.59pm 28 July 2025, and the committee received and considered submissions from 78 interested groups and individuals, hearing oral evidence from 22 of them, before reporting back within the 13 November 2025 deadline (bill assented 27 November 2025). 78 submitters clears the criterion's 'dozens or more' threshold. Submitters span community and advocacy organisations (Citizens Advice Bureau, UNHCR, Mana Mokopuna / Children and Young People's Commission, Equal Justice Project), legal bodies (NZ Law Society, The Law Association) and employer/industry groups (BusinessNZ, EMA, WPMA, PrintNZ, Transporting NZ). One correction to the criterion rather than the claim: the committee was the Education and Workforce Committee, not Governance and Administration. Disconfirming check for 'submissions negligible' found no support — media coverage of the committee stage reports contested submissions on the deportation and levy provisions.
